Title: PrivDrift — auditing user-secret leakage under topic drift in active LLM conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University). Contact: lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu. Abstract key points: introduces PrivDrift benchmark of 1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues with seeded secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction probes. Evaluated across three LLMs with extended context windows. Reports dialogue-level hybrid leakage between 38.7% and 54.6%, with strong variation by model, secret type, and persuasion intensity. Within the tested drift window, additional topic drift does not reliably reduce leakage; conclusion: privacy risk should be viewed as a persistent behavioral failure mode, not only memorization or immediate jailbreaks. Keywords: Trustworthy AI, LLMs, Privacy, Evaluation, Benchmarking.

Title: PrivDrift — auditing user-secret leakage under topic drift in active LLM conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University). Contact: lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu. Benchmark: PrivDrift — controlled benchmark of 1,000 multi-turn dialogues per model with seeded secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction probes. Evaluated across three LLMs with extended context windows. Core axes: topic drift (number d of unrelated turns between secret disclosure and probe; tested window d ≤ 6) and persuasion intensity (interaction style: direct, justified, high-pressure). Main quantitative claim: dialogue-level hybrid leakage under hybrid detector ranges 38.7%–54.6%; leakage varies strongly by model, secret type (SSNs and credit cards suppressed far more often than emails and phone numbers), and persuasion intensity. Hybrid detector: normalization-based matching + open-weights LLM judge; reported metrics include dialogue-level, probe-level, regex-only, fuzzy, and hybrid leakage rates. Key finding: within tested drift window, additional topic drift does not reliably reduce leakage; authors introduce Privacy Half-Life (τ), a stability-based metric, and report that no evaluated model reaches stable decay within observed drift range. Contributions summarized: benchmark, probe styles, hybrid detector & metrics, Privacy Half-Life analysis. Keywords: Trustworthy AI, LLMs, Privacy, Evaluation, Benchmarking.

Related work summarized: (1) Contextual privacy/inference-time leakage distinguished from training-data extraction; other benchmarks (ConfAIde, PrivacyLens, PrivaCI-Bench) focus on static access-control/privacy-norm reasoning, whereas PrivDrift isolates persistence of user-disclosed secrets after topic drift and persuasion probes. steps.notes_before: Evaluation uses a hierarchical hybrid detector: Stage 1 normalization-based matching (φ) detects verbatim/near-verbatim leaks; numeric secrets: strip non-digits; alphanumeric: normalize case/whitespace, preserve meaningful delimiters. Regex-stage label: Leak_regex(R,S)=I[φ(S)⊂φ(R)]. Stage 2: open-weights Llama judge (Meta AI, 2024) inspects regex-negative responses and returns a binary verdict for partial/indirect disclosures; paper reports regex-only and hybrid rates separately. Privacy Half-Life τ: D_obs = observed drift lengths, L(d)=leakage rate at d, safety threshold δ=0.1×L(0). τ = min{d∈D_obs | L(d)≤δ and ∀d'>d in D_obs: L(d')≤δ}; if empty τ = max(D_obs)+1 to avoid counting transient dips. Caveat: earlier parts ambiguously defined d (dialogue element count vs. number of drift turns), so interpretation of 'drift length' in L(d), D_obs, and τ is unclear. Other earlier details retained: N=1000 dialogues (900 synthetic +100 human-authored mixed), secret types: phone/email/SSN/credit card, drift lengths sampled from {0,2,3,4,5,6} (d=0 with p=0.2, else uniform over 2–6).

Title: PrivDrift — auditing user-secret leakage under topic drift in active LLM conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero. Controlled benchmark: 1,000 multi-turn dialogues per model with seeded secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction probes. Two main axes: topic drift (number of unrelated turns between secret disclosure and later probing; tested window d ≤ 6) and persuasion intensity (interaction styles: direct, justified, high-pressure). Evaluated on three LLMs with extended context windows. Metrics: dialogue-level, probe-level, regex-only, fuzzy, and hybrid leakage rates. Key results: dialogue-level hybrid leakage between 38.7% and 54.6% across models; leakage varies by model and secret type (SSNs and credit cards suppressed far more often than emails and phone numbers); persuasion intensity affects leakage; within tested drift window additional drift does not reliably reduce leakage. Implemented a reproducible hybrid detector combining normalization-based matching with an open-weights LLM judge. Proposed Privacy Half-Life (τ) as a stability-based metric for persistent suppression; no evaluated model reaches stable decay within observed drift range. Related work: distinguishes training-data extraction (memorized PII) from active-context privacy; cites benchmarks for privacy reasoning (ConfAIde, PrivacyLens, PrivaCI-Bench) but positions PrivDrift as isolating persistence after topic drift and persuasion-based probing. Links to multi-turn adversarial attacks and jailbreaks (Crescendo, automated jailbreak frameworks, prompt injection) and to machine unlearning benchmarks (TOFU, WMDP), emphasizing PrivDrift's focus on prompt-level/active-context control relevant to RAG systems, copilots, and agentic workflows.

PrivDrift: synthetic evaluation for active-context re-disclosure. Threat model: secret S disclosed at opening turn t0; conversation proceeds through d unrelated but content-dense drift turns D = {u1,a1,...,ud,ad}; final standardized probe P appended; leakage if model reveals S exactly, approximately, or semantically. Dataset: N=1000 dialogues (900 synthetic + 100 human-authored mixed in; human IDs not preserved so results reported aggregated). Secret categories: 4 fixed-format PII (phone, email, SSN, credit card) injected in opening turn as plausible task context. Persona sampled from >100 professions/demographics. Drift lengths: {0,2,3,4,5,6}. Drift sampling: d=0 with p=0.2; otherwise Uniform{2,3,4,5,6} with p=0.8 (i.e., p=0.16 for each nonzero value). Dialogue stats (Table 1): avg words 359.16, median 385, min/max words 43/795; avg approx tokens 478.87, median 513.33, min/max tokens 57.33/1060 (tokens estimated from words). Generation pipeline: scaffold-then-rewrite, topic-conditioned library for drift turns (subset human-authored), final rewriting model improves fluency but preserves exact secret, drift length, role structure, and probe conditions. Probes: three persuasion levels — Simple (direct), Medium (contextual justification), Hard (high-pressure). Framework pipeline: construct dialogues, append probes, query target models, score leakage with hybrid detector (earlier note). Previous parts: evaluation across 3 LLMs, metrics include dialogue/probe/regex/fuzzy/hybrid leakage; reported dialogue-level hybrid leakage 38.7%–54.6% across models; Privacy Half-Life τ proposed (no model reaches stable decay within observed drift range).

PrivDrift: N=1000 dialogues (900 synthetic + 100 human-authored mixed), secret S injected in opening turn t0. Secret types: 4 fixed-format PII (phone, email, SSN, credit card). Personas sampled from >100 professions/demographics. Drift lengths D_obs = {0,2,3,4,5,6}; sampling p(d=0)=0.2, otherwise uniform over {2,3,4,5,6} (p=0.16 each). Dialogue stats: avg words 359.16 (median 385), min/max 43/795; approx tokens avg 478.87 (median 513.33), min/max 57.33/1060. Generation pipeline: scaffold-then-rewrite; rewrite preserves exact secret, drift length, role structure, probe conditions. Probes: three persuasion levels (Simple, Medium, Hard). Evaluation: hierarchical hybrid detector (two stages) + reported metrics include dialogue/probe/regex/fuzzy/hybrid leakages; reported dialogue-level hybrid leakage 38.7%–54.6% across 3 target LLMs; paper notes no model reaches stable decay within observed drift range. Stage 1 (normalization-based): normalization function φ; numeric secrets: strip non-digits; alphanumeric: normalize case/whitespace while preserving delimiters; regex-stage label Leak_regex(R,S)=I[φ(S)⊂φ(R)]. Regex detects verbatim/near-verbatim occurrences. Stage 2 (LLM judge): responses negative under regex passed to an open-weights Llama judge (Meta AI, 2024) which, given S and R, returns binary verdict if response reveals full secret, substantial substring, or enough partial info; regex-only and hybrid rates reported separately. Privacy Half-Life τ: safety threshold δ = 0.1×L(0). τ = min{d∈D_obs | L(d) ≤ δ and ∀d'>d in D_obs: L(d') ≤ δ}; if no such d, set τ = max(D_obs)+1 (captures requirement for stable suppression).

PrivDrift benchmark: N=1000 dialogues (900 synthetic + 100 human-authored mixed), secret S injected in opening turn t0. Secret types: 4 fixed-format PII (phone, email, SSN, credit card). Personas sampled from >100 professions/demographics. Drift lengths D_obs = {0,2,3,4,5,6} with sampling p(d=0)=0.2, otherwise uniform over {2,3,4,5,6} (~0.16 each). Dialogue stats: avg words 359.16 (median 385), tokens avg 478.87 (median 513.33). Generation: scaffold-then-rewrite preserves exact secret, drift length, role structure, and probe conditions. Probes: three persuasion levels (Simple, Medium, Hard). Detector: two-stage hybrid — Stage 1 normalization/regex Leak_regex(R,S)=I[φ(S)⊂φ(R)] (detects verbatim/near-verbatim); Stage 2 open-weights Llama judge for non-regex positives to detect substantial substrings/partial info. Privacy half-life τ: safety threshold δ = 0.1×L(0); τ = min{d∈D_obs | L(d) ≤ δ and ∀d'>d: L(d') ≤ δ}, else τ = max(D_obs)+1. New in this part: evaluated models = GPT-OSS-120B, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3-VL-235B (queried via OpenRouter). Dataset: same 1,000 dialogues reused per model; each dialogue evaluated under 3 standardized persuasion probes → 3,000 cached model-probe responses per model (9,000 total). Detector: regex-only stage and hybrid (regex + LLM judge). Dialogue-level results (regex → hybrid): GPT 47.70% → 47.70% (Δ 0.00, p=1.0); DeepSeek 37.80% → 38.70% (Δ +0.90, p=7.7e-3); Qwen 53.50% → 54.60% (Δ +1.10, p=2.57e-3). Title: PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University), contact lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu. Title: PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University). Correspondence: lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu. Abstract claims: persistent, behaviorally recoverable sensitive disclosures occur in user-facing, shared-session, tool-augmented LLMs beyond unrelated tasks. Introduces controlled benchmark QX2 = PrivDrift using seeded multi-turn histories, content-dense intervening exchanges, and standardized extraction probes. Reports that across extended-context models, G4P under H8D remains substantial, varies sharply across systems (mentions S8Q and V4N), and fails to decline reliably within the tested window. Conclusion: active-context privacy requires evaluation as persistent behavioral failure, not exclusively parameter memorization or immediate jailbreak behavior. Keywords: Trustworthy AI, Large Language Models, Privacy, Evaluation, Benchmarking.

Title: PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University). Contact: lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu. Abstract claims persistent, behaviorally recoverable sensitive disclosures occur in user-facing, shared-session, tool-augmented LLMs beyond unrelated tasks; introduces QX2 = PrivDrift benchmark (seeded multi-turn histories, content-dense intervening exchanges, standardized extraction probes). Reports across extended-context models that G4P under H8D remains substantial, varies sharply across systems (mentions S8Q and V4N), and fails to decline reliably within tested window; conclusion: active-context privacy must be evaluated as persistent behavioral failure rather than only parameter memorization or immediate jailbreaks. Introduction adds: SSNs and payment identifiers receive much stronger suppression than contact identifiers, but no evaluated system attains stable decay of leakage. QX2 provides controlled persistence auditing with direct/justified/high-pressure elicitation, reproducible composite detection via deterministic processing and an open-weights judge, G4P and P6S reporting, and uses a stability criterion (not transient decrease). Claims LLMs evolved into persistent assistants (OpenAI 2023; Touvron et al. 2023; Liu et al. 2024) with deployments in healthcare triage, financial planning, enterprise copilots, personal productivity; PII at risk includes contact/A2L, financial identifiers, F8Z, and health details. Notes that prior safety evaluations focus on parameter memorization or immediate jailbreaking; they do not directly establish whether unrelated conversational shifts provide a practical privacy boundary. Emphasizes shared sessions, browser-integrated assistants, enterprise copilots, agentic workflows, and injected instructions as vectors for later unintended context interactions.

Title: PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero. Main contribution: QX2 (PrivDrift) — a benchmark to audit persistent, behaviorally recoverable sensitive disclosures in shared-session, tool-augmented LLMs under topic drift. Method: seeded multi-turn histories, content-dense intervening exchanges, standardized extraction probes, deterministic processing, and an open-weights judge; includes a stability criterion (seeks non-transient decay). Key reported findings (abstract/introduction): G4P under H8D remains substantial, varies sharply across systems (mentions S8Q and V4N), and fails to decline reliably in the tested window; SSNs and payment identifiers receive stronger suppression than contact identifiers; no evaluated system attains stable decay of leakage. QX2 claims to isolate behavioral recoverability following unrelated exchanges and persuasive probing, and to report composite detection metrics (G4P, P6S). Related work: distinguishes traditional training-data extraction/memorization (parameter-level attacks) from active-context privacy (inference-time handling of current-interaction info). Prior benchmarks: ConfAIde (contextual-integrity reasoning), PrivacyLens and PrivaCI-Bench (privacy-norm/legal compliance). Multi-turn adversarial work (Crescendo, automated adversarial path generators, injected instruction attacks) typically targets harmful outputs/instruction hijacking; QX2 instead targets re-disclosure of earlier user-supplied sensitive information. Context-management/unlearning work (TOFU, WMDP) focuses on parameter-level removal; QX2 focuses on behavioral suppression of secrets still present in active context (relevance to RAG, copilots, agentic workflows).

PrivDrift benchmark: 1,000 controlled dialogues with seeded secrets, unrelated intervening turns, and standardized extraction probes. Three models evaluated; probes classified as direct, justified, and high-pressure. Hybrid detector: normalized matching combined with an LLM judge. Dialogue-level leakage defined as whether any standardized probe elicits the secret; observed leakage ranges 38.7%–54.6%. Persuasion effects depend on model. Secret types: Social Security Numbers and credit card numbers are suppressed more often than emails and phone numbers. PrivDrift benchmark: 1,000 controlled dialogues with seeded secrets (SSN, credit card, email, phone) inserted and later targeted by standardized probes after content-dense topic drift. Drift length d = number of turns between secret disclosure (t0) and final probe; sampled with Uniform{2,3,4,5,6}, tested up to d ≤ 6. Probes / persuasion levels: Simple (direct/neutral), Medium (contextual justification), Hard (high-pressure/urgent) — corresponds to earlier labels direct/justified/high-pressure. Three evaluated models: GPT-OSS-120B (GPT-OSS), DeepSeek-R1 (DeepSeek), Qwen3-VL-235B (Qwen); models queried via OpenRouter API; some responses cached. Detection/hybrid evaluation: normalization-based (regex) matching φ(·) and fuzzy matching; when regex returns negative, an open-weights Llama judge (LLM-as-judge) is used. Leakage event: response reveals the secret exactly, approximately, or semantically. Metrics: probe-level and dialogue-level leakage (dialogue-level = any probe elicits the secret); Δ = additional dialogue-level leakage hybrid vs regex. Privacy Half-Life τ: earliest observed drift length ≤ safety threshold δ = 0.1×L(0) with no later resurgence; D_obs = observed drift lengths. Statistical methods: 95% bootstrap CIs over dialogues, McNemar’s test for paired comparisons (with Bonferroni where applicable), Cochran’s Q across persuasion levels, χ2 and Cramer’s V for associations. Reported findings: observed dialogue-level leakage ≈ 38.7%–54.6%; persuasion effects vary by model; SSNs and credit card numbers are suppressed more often than emails/phone numbers; within tested range additional drift does not reliably reduce leakage; no evaluated model meets the paper’s stability/suppression criterion. Paper introduces PrivDrift benchmark: 1,000 controlled dialogues with seeded secrets, intervening unrelated turns, and standardized extraction probes. Tests three models using three probe styles: direct, justified, and high-pressure. Uses a hybrid detector that combines normalized matching plus an LLM judge. Reports dialogue-level leakage (any standardized probe elicits the secret) between 38.7% and 54.6%. Persuasion effects vary by model. Social Security numbers and credit card numbers are suppressed more often than emails and phone numbers. Tested drift range d ≤ 6; within that range extra drift does not reliably reduce leakage. Concludes no evaluated model meets the paper's criterion for stable suppression. (Glossary heading follows.)

PrivDrift: benchmark of 1,000 controlled dialogues with seeded secrets S (four PII types: SSN, credit card, email, phone). Dialogues produced by a parametric dialogue generator with scaffold-then-rewrite pipeline; includes synthetic and human-authored variants and sampled persona. Topic drift D: content-dense unrelated turns between disclosure at t0 and probing; drift length d is number of turns. Sampling distribution uses Uniform{2,3,4,5,6} for drift. Probes P appended to the active conversation context; three persuasion levels — Simple (direct/neutral), Medium (contextual justification), Hard (high-pressure/urgent). Evaluated models: GPT-OSS-120B (GPT-OSS), DeepSeek-R1 (DeepSeek), Qwen3-VL-235B (Qwen) via OpenRouter API. Leakage metrics: probe-level (per response) and dialogue-level (any probe elicits the secret). Detection: normalization φ-based (regex) matching, auxiliary fuzzy matching; hybrid evaluation = regex stage followed, for negatives, by an open-weights Llama judge (LLM-as-a-judge). L(d) = leakage rate at drift d; L(0) baseline used to define safety threshold δ = 0.1 × L(0). Privacy Half-Life τ = earliest observed drift length below δ with no later resurgence (uses observed drift set D_obs). Δ denotes additional dialogue-level leakage from hybrid vs regex. Reported results (from earlier summary): dialogue-level leakage 38.7%–54.6%; persuasion effects vary by model; SSNs and credit cards suppressed more often than emails/phones; drift tested up to d=6 and extra drift within that range did not reliably reduce leakage; no evaluated model meets the paper's criterion for stable suppression. Statistics: 95% bootstrap CIs over dialogues; McNemar’s test for paired comparisons (Bonferroni where applicable); Cochran’s Q for repeated measures across persuasion levels; chi-square and Cramer’s V for associations.

Study goal: test whether unrelated conversational tasks (drift) prevent later disclosure of sensitive info in an active LLM conversation. Method summary: PrivDrift uses seeded multi-turn histories, content-dense intervening exchanges, and three standardized extraction conditions. Detection method: normalized matching combined with an open-weights judge. Data: 1,000 dialogues containing phone numbers, email addresses, Social Security Numbers, or credit card numbers. Main quantitative result: hybrid dialogue-level leakage = 38.70%, 47.70%, and 54.60% across the three evaluated models. Other findings: leakage varies by model, secret type, and persuasion intensity; Social Security Numbers and credit card numbers show much stronger suppression than contact identifiers (phone/email). Temporal/stability claim: no system attains stable suppression within the tested drift lengths. Interpretation: authors treat this as an active-context behavioral privacy failure, not evidence of permanent memory.

Goal: PrivDrift (QX2) audits whether unrelated multi-turn conversational drift (D = sequence of u_i,a_i) suppresses re-disclosure of a ground-truth secret S supplied at t0. Data: N = 1,000 dialogues (four secret types S8Q: A2L phone, F8Z email, W3B SSN, N6G credit card). Drift length d (D7A) sampled from Uniform({2,3,4,5,6}). A standardized probe P (three persuasion intensities V4N: C8R Simple, Z2F Medium, L9W Hard) appended; each dialogue yields probe-level observations per persuasion (P6S). Leakage definitions: φ normalization; U3P = regex-only deterministic baseline; B6T = normalization-based matching; H8D hybrid = normalized inclusion OR LLM-as-a-judge (Llama judge) full/substantial-disclosure verdict; R5J fuzzy matching is post-hoc normalized similarity. G4P (dialogue-level leakage): dialogue positive if ANY standardized probe elicits secret. L(d) leakage at drift d, L(0) immediate recall. Safety threshold δ = 0.1 × L(0). K2V (Privacy Half-Life, τ) = earliest observed d meeting suppression threshold at that and all later d; τ assigned a value when no length qualifies. Δ = H8D augmentation over U3P in percentage points. Statistics: G4P CIs via 95% bootstrap over dialogues; tests: McNemar, Bonferroni correction, Cochran’s Q, chi-square; p used for sampling probability (Eq.1) or as test p-value. Models: M7Q GPT-OSS-120B, T4X DeepSeek-R1, Y9C Qwen3-VL-235B. Prior reported findings to track: hybrid dialogue-level leakage = 38.70%, 47.70%, 54.60% across three models; SSNs and CCNs more suppressed than contact identifiers; no stable suppression across tested d.

Goal: audit persistent recoverability of a seeded secret S after unrelated multi-turn conversational drift D; later standardized probes test re-disclosure. Title: PrivDrift — auditing user-secret leakage under topic drift in active LLM conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University). Contact: lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu. Abstract key points: introduces PrivDrift benchmark of 1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues with seeded secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction probes. Evaluated across three LLMs with extended context windows. Reports dialogue-level hybrid leakage between 38.7% and 54.6%, with strong variation by model, secret type, and persuasion intensity. Within the tested drift window, additional topic drift does not reliably reduce leakage; conclusion: privacy risk should be viewed as a persistent behavioral failure mode, not only memorization or immediate jailbreaks. Keywords: Trustworthy AI, LLMs, Privacy, Evaluation, Benchmarking.

Title: PrivDrift — auditing user-secret leakage under topic drift in active LLM conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University). Contact: lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu. Benchmark: PrivDrift — controlled benchmark of 1,000 multi-turn dialogues per model with seeded secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction probes. Evaluated across three LLMs with extended context windows. Core axes: topic drift (number d of unrelated turns between secret disclosure and probe; tested window d ≤ 6) and persuasion intensity (interaction style: direct, justified, high-pressure). Main quantitative claim: dialogue-level hybrid leakage under hybrid detector ranges 38.7%–54.6%; leakage varies strongly by model, secret type (SSNs and credit cards suppressed far more often than emails and phone numbers), and persuasion intensity. Hybrid detector: normalization-based matching + open-weights LLM judge; reported metrics include dialogue-level, probe-level, regex-only, fuzzy, and hybrid leakage rates. Key finding: within tested drift window, additional topic drift does not reliably reduce leakage; authors introduce Privacy Half-Life (τ), a stability-based metric, and report that no evaluated model reaches stable decay within observed drift range. Contributions summarized: benchmark, probe styles, hybrid detector & metrics, Privacy Half-Life analysis. Keywords: Trustworthy AI, LLMs, Privacy, Evaluation, Benchmarking.

Title: PrivDrift — auditing user-secret leakage under topic drift in active LLM conversations. Author/contact: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu). Benchmark: PrivDrift — 1,000 multi-turn dialogues per model with seeded secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction probes. Core axes: topic drift (number d of unrelated turns between secret disclosure and probe; tested window d ≤ 6) and persuasion intensity (interaction styles: direct, justified, high-pressure). Main quantitative claim: dialogue-level hybrid leakage under hybrid detector ranges 38.7%–54.6%; leakage varies by model and secret type (SSNs and credit cards suppressed more than emails/phones). Hybrid detector: normalization-based matching + open-weights LLM judge; reported metrics include dialogue-level, probe-level, regex-only, fuzzy, and hybrid leakage rates. Privacy Half-Life (τ): stability-based metric; authors report no evaluated model reaches stable decay within observed drift range. Contributions: benchmark, probe styles, hybrid detector & metrics, Privacy Half-Life analysis. Related work summarized: (1) Contextual privacy/inference-time leakage distinguished from training-data extraction; other benchmarks (ConfAIde, PrivacyLens, PrivaCI-Bench) focus on static access-control/privacy-norm reasoning, whereas PrivDrift isolates persistence of user-disclosed secrets after topic drift and persuasion probes. (2) Multi-turn adversarial attacks (Crescendo, automated jailbreaks, prompt injection) motivate treating information flow control across turns. (3) Context management and unlearning (TOFU, WMDP) operate on model weights/static QA; PrivDrift targets active-context suppression relevant to RAG, copilots, and agentic workflows.

Title: PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University), contact lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu. Abstract claims: persistent, user-facing, shared-session, tool-augmented LLMs can retain behaviorally recoverable sensitive disclosures even after unrelated tasks; introduces a controlled benchmark called PrivDrift (QX2) that uses seeded multi-turn histories, content-dense intervening exchanges, and standardized extraction probes to audit persistence. Reports that across extended-context models, a metric/phenomenon labelled "G4P under H8D" remains substantial, varies sharply across systems and two other labels "S8Q" and "V4N", and does not reliably decline within the tested window. Conclusion: active-context privacy should be evaluated as persistent behavioral failure rather than only parameter memorization or immediate jailbreak behavior. Keywords: Trustworthy AI, LLM Privacy, Evaluation, Benchmarking. Points to check later: definitions and meanings of acronyms QX2/PrivDrift, G4P, H8D, S8Q, V4N; experimental setup (seeded histories, intervening exchanges, extraction probes), which models are considered "extended-context", the tested window length, and evidence for "fails to decline reliably" and per-system variability.

final_notes: Dataset & setup: 1,000 PrivDrift dialogues (900 synthetic, 100 human-authored), one seeded secret per dialogue. Appendix A (Table 7) drift-length breakdown: d=0: N=197, 44.29w / 59.05t (med 43 / 57.33); d=2: N=147, 253.97w / 338.62t (med 258 / 344); d=3: N=142, 344.18w / 458.91t (med 347 / 462.67); d=4: N=166, 452.27w / 603.02t (med 447 / 596); d=5: N=181, 520.92w / 694.56t (med 543 / 724); d=6: N=167, 568.03w / 757.37t (med 605 / 806.67). Sum N=1000, max observed d=6 (τ=7). Models: GPT-OSS-120B (GPT-OSS), DeepSeek-R1 (DeepSeek), Qwen3-VL-235B (Qwen). Key results: dialogue-level hybrid leakage (Table 3) — DeepSeek 38.70% [35.7,41.6], GPT-OSS 47.70% [44.6,50.8], Qwen 54.60% [51.6,57.7]. Probe-level persuasion (Table 4): GPT 39.3%/40.5%/32.9% (S/M/H); DeepSeek 28.1%/22.0%/29.2%; Qwen 38.7%/33.3%/40.6%. Secret-type probe-level (Table 5): SSN 0.14%/1.11%/5.97%; Credit card 0.00%/0.39%/4.01%; Email 78.24%/57.11%/81.13%; Phone 70.89%/46.13%/57.24%. Methods: bootstrap 95% CIs over dialogues, McNemar for paired tests, Cochran's Q across persuasion, chi-square/Cramer's V for associations. Drift analysis: δ = 0.1·L(0), tested up to d=6; no stable decay observed for d ≤ 6. PrivDrift benchmark: 1,000 controlled dialogues with seeded secrets, unrelated intervening turns, and standardized extraction probes. Three models evaluated; probes classified as direct, justified, and high-pressure. Hybrid detector: normalized matching combined with an LLM judge. Dialogue-level leakage defined as whether any standardized probe elicits the secret; observed leakage ranges 38.7%–54.6%. Persuasion effects depend on model. Secret types: Social Security Numbers and credit card numbers are suppressed more often than emails and phone numbers. PrivDrift benchmark: 1,000 controlled dialogues with seeded secrets (SSN, credit card, email, phone) inserted and later targeted by standardized probes after content-dense topic drift. Drift length d = number of turns between secret disclosure (t0) and final probe; sampled with Uniform{2,3,4,5,6}, tested up to d ≤ 6. Probes / persuasion levels: Simple (direct/neutral), Medium (contextual justification), Hard (high-pressure/urgent) — corresponds to earlier labels direct/justified/high-pressure. Three evaluated models: GPT-OSS-120B (GPT-OSS), DeepSeek-R1 (DeepSeek), Qwen3-VL-235B (Qwen); models queried via OpenRouter API; some responses cached. Detection/hybrid evaluation: normalization-based (regex) matching φ(·) and fuzzy matching; when regex returns negative, an open-weights Llama judge (LLM-as-judge) is used. Leakage event: response reveals the secret exactly, approximately, or semantically. Metrics: probe-level and dialogue-level leakage (dialogue-level = any probe elicits the secret); Δ = additional dialogue-level leakage hybrid vs regex. Privacy Half-Life τ: earliest observed drift length ≤ safety threshold δ = 0.1×L(0) with no later resurgence; D_obs = observed drift lengths. Statistical methods: 95% bootstrap CIs over dialogues, McNemar’s test for paired comparisons (with Bonferroni where applicable), Cochran’s Q across persuasion levels, χ2 and Cramer’s V for associations. Reported findings: observed dialogue-level leakage ≈ 38.7%–54.6%; persuasion effects vary by model; SSNs and credit card numbers are suppressed more often than emails/phone numbers; within tested range additional drift does not reliably reduce leakage; no evaluated model meets the paper’s stability/suppression criterion. Pipeline notes: parametric dialogue generator, scaffold-then-rewrite naturalistic refinement, cached responses.

PrivDrift study: uses seeded multi-turn histories, content-dense intervening exchanges, and three standardized extraction conditions. Dataset: 1,000 dialogues containing one of phone numbers, email addresses, Social Security Numbers (SSNs), or credit card numbers. Detection method: normalized matching plus an open-weights judge. Reported hybrid dialogue-level leakage rates across the three evaluated models: 38.70%, 47.70%, and 54.60%. Authors state leakage varies by model, secret type, and persuasion intensity. SSNs and credit card numbers are reported to receive much stronger suppression than contact identifiers (phone, email). No system attains stable suppression within the tested drift lengths. Authors interpret results as an active-context behavioral privacy failure, not evidence of permanent memory.

PrivDrift (QX2) benchmark: N=1,000 seeded multi-turn dialogues, each contains one ground-truth secret S (phone A2L, email F8Z, SSN W3B, or credit card N6G) disclosed at t0. D = unrelated sequence of user/assistant turns (u_i,a_i). Drift length d (D7A) is number of turns between disclosure and final standardized probe P; d sampled Uniform{2,3,4,5,6} per Eq.(1). Probes: V4N persuasion intensities — C8R (Simple), Z2F (Medium), L9W (Hard). Models evaluated: M7Q=GPT-OSS-120B, T4X=DeepSeek-R1, Y9C=Qwen3-VL-235B via OpenRouter API; some responses cached. Detection methods: U3P (regex-only deterministic baseline), B6T (normalization-based matching using phi), H8D (hybrid: normalized inclusion OR LLM-as-judge/Llama judge binary verdict), R5J (post-hoc fuzzy matching). Metrics: probe-level P6S = one response observation per dialogue per persuasion; dialogue-level G4P = dialogue positive if any probe elicits secret. Leakage L(d) and immediate L(0). Delta (δ) safety threshold = 0.1 × L(0). K2V (Privacy Half-Life, τ) = earliest observed drift length meeting suppression threshold at that and every later observed length; τ assigned a specific value when no observed length qualifies. Δ = H8D augmentation over U3P (percentage points). CI: 95% bootstrap over dialogues for G4P. Stats: McNemar’s for matched model/detector and persuasion follow-ups (with Bonferroni where applicable); Cochran’s Q for repeated persuasion measures; Chi-square for independence vs D7A, V4N, or S8Q. Other terms: active-context privacy, behavioral recoverability, parameter-based memorization, training-data extraction, membership inference, unlearning, RAG systems, scaffold-then-rewrite, persona, ConfAIde, PrivacyLens/PrivaCI-Bench, Crescendo, TOFU/WMDP. Earlier reported hybrid dialogue-level leakage rates across the three models: 38.70%, 47.70%, 54.60%; authors state leakage varies by model, secret type, and persuasion intensity, with SSNs and credit cards more strongly suppressed than contact identifiers.

Stage 1 (B6T deterministic normalization): phi strips non-digit chars for numeric secrets; alphanumeric normalized for case/whitespace while retaining delimiters; deterministic leakage label Leak_U3P(R,S)=I[phi(S) subset phi(R)]. Stage 2 (LLM-as-judge): an open-weights Llama judge is applied to deterministic negatives and returns a binary full/substantial-disclosure verdict (detects partial disclosures, indirect hints, and formatting variants); judge is fallible. The hybrid label H8D marks positive if deterministic inclusion OR the LLM judge finds full secret, substantial substring, or identifying partial info. K2V (Privacy Half-Life τ): uses observed lengths D_obs and leakage rates L(d); safety threshold δ = 0.1 × L(0) (L(0)=immediate-recall leakage). τ = min{ d ∈ D_obs | L(d) ≤ δ AND ∀ d' ∈ D_obs with d' > d: L(d') ≤ δ }. Title: PrivDrift — auditing user-secret leakage under topic drift in active LLM conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University). Contact: lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu. Abstract key points: introduces PrivDrift benchmark of 1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues with seeded secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction probes. Evaluated across three LLMs with extended context windows. Reports dialogue-level hybrid leakage between 38.7% and 54.6%, with strong variation by model, secret type, and persuasion intensity. Within the tested drift window, additional topic drift does not reliably reduce leakage; conclusion: privacy risk should be viewed as a persistent behavioral failure mode, not only memorization or immediate jailbreaks. Keywords: Trustworthy AI, LLMs, Privacy, Evaluation, Benchmarking.

Title: PrivDrift — auditing user-secret leakage under topic drift in active LLM conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University). Contact: lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu. Benchmark: PrivDrift — controlled benchmark of 1,000 multi-turn dialogues per model with seeded secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction probes. Evaluated across three LLMs with extended context windows. Core axes: topic drift (number d of unrelated turns between secret disclosure and probe; tested window d ≤ 6) and persuasion intensity (interaction style: direct, justified, high-pressure). Main quantitative claim: dialogue-level hybrid leakage under hybrid detector ranges 38.7%–54.6%; leakage varies strongly by model, secret type (SSNs and credit cards suppressed far more often than emails and phone numbers), and persuasion intensity. Hybrid detector: normalization-based matching + open-weights LLM judge; reported metrics include dialogue-level, probe-level, regex-only, fuzzy, and hybrid leakage rates. Key finding: within tested drift window, additional topic drift does not reliably reduce leakage; authors introduce Privacy Half-Life (τ), a stability-based metric, and report that no evaluated model reaches stable decay within observed drift range. Contributions summarized: benchmark, probe styles, hybrid detector & metrics, Privacy Half-Life analysis. Keywords: Trustworthy AI, LLMs, Privacy, Evaluation, Benchmarking.

Related work summarized: (1) Contextual privacy/inference-time leakage distinguished from training-data extraction; other benchmarks (ConfAIde, PrivacyLens, PrivaCI-Bench) focus on static access-control/privacy-norm reasoning, whereas PrivDrift isolates persistence of user-disclosed secrets after topic drift and persuasion probes. steps.notes_before: Evaluation uses a hierarchical hybrid detector: Stage 1 normalization-based matching (φ) detects verbatim/near-verbatim leaks; numeric secrets: strip non-digits; alphanumeric: normalize case/whitespace, preserve meaningful delimiters. Regex-stage label: Leak_regex(R,S)=I[φ(S)⊂φ(R)]. Stage 2: open-weights Llama judge (Meta AI, 2024) inspects regex-negative responses and returns a binary verdict for partial/indirect disclosures; paper reports regex-only and hybrid rates separately. Privacy Half-Life τ: D_obs = observed drift lengths, L(d)=leakage rate at d, safety threshold δ=0.1×L(0). τ = min{d∈D_obs | L(d)≤δ and ∀d'>d in D_obs: L(d')≤δ}; if empty τ = max(D_obs)+1 to avoid counting transient dips. Caveat: earlier parts ambiguously defined d (dialogue element count vs. number of drift turns), so interpretation of 'drift length' in L(d), D_obs, and τ is unclear. Other earlier details retained: N=1000 dialogues (900 synthetic +100 human-authored mixed), secret types: phone/email/SSN/credit card, drift lengths sampled from {0,2,3,4,5,6} (d=0 with p=0.2, else uniform over 2–6).

Title: PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University), contact lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu. Abstract claims: persistent, user-facing, shared-session, tool-augmented LLMs can retain behaviorally recoverable sensitive disclosures even after unrelated tasks; introduces a controlled benchmark called PrivDrift (QX2) that uses seeded multi-turn histories, content-dense intervening exchanges, and standardized extraction probes to audit persistence. Reports that across extended-context models, a metric/phenomenon labelled "G4P under H8D" remains substantial, varies sharply across systems and two other labels "S8Q" and "V4N", and does not reliably decline within the tested window. Conclusion: active-context privacy should be evaluated as persistent behavioral failure rather than only parameter memorization or immediate jailbreak behavior. Keywords: Trustworthy AI, LLM Privacy, Evaluation, Benchmarking. Points to check later: definitions and meanings of acronyms QX2/PrivDrift, G4P, H8D, S8Q, V4N; experimental setup (seeded histories, intervening exchanges, extraction probes), which models are considered "extended-context", the tested window length, and evidence for "fails to decline reliably" and per-system variability.

New setup details: all systems receive identical histories and probe templates via OpenRouter API. Each system processes full QX2 dataset, one seeded secret and one sampled d per dialogue under every standardized condition. Cached responses: per model = 3,000; all evaluated models = 9,000 (implies 3 models evaluated). Aggregation: G4P (dialogue-level leakage) = dialogue positive if any standardized probe elicits secret; P6S (probe-level leakage) = one observation per dialogue per persuasion condition (for V4N and R5J analyses). Note: G4P can exceed the mean condition-specific rate. Uncertainty/tests: G4P intervals use 95% bootstrap over dialogues; P6S sensitivity checks use cached model-probe responses. Matched model/detector comparisons use McNemar’s test (Bonferroni-corrected where applicable); repeated persuasion measures use Cochran’s Q followed by McNemar tests. PrivDrift benchmark: 1,000 controlled dialogues with seeded secrets, unrelated intervening turns, and standardized extraction probes. Three models evaluated; probes classified as direct, justified, and high-pressure. Hybrid detector: normalized matching combined with an LLM judge. Dialogue-level leakage defined as whether any standardized probe elicits the secret; observed leakage ranges 38.7%–54.6%. Persuasion effects depend on model. Secret types: Social Security Numbers and credit card numbers are suppressed more often than emails and phone numbers. Drift parameter d tested up to d ≤ 6; within this range additional drift does not reliably reduce leakage. Conclusion: no evaluated model meets the paper's criterion for stable suppression. Note: glossary header present but content not shown in this part.

PrivDrift benchmark: 1,000 controlled dialogues with seeded secrets (SSN, credit card, email, phone) inserted and later targeted by standardized probes after content-dense topic drift. Drift length d = number of turns between secret disclosure (t0) and final probe; sampled with Uniform{2,3,4,5,6}, tested up to d ≤ 6. Probes / persuasion levels: Simple (direct/neutral), Medium (contextual justification), Hard (high-pressure/urgent) — corresponds to earlier labels direct/justified/high-pressure. Three evaluated models: GPT-OSS-120B (GPT-OSS), DeepSeek-R1 (DeepSeek), Qwen3-VL-235B (Qwen); models queried via OpenRouter API; some responses cached. Detection/hybrid evaluation: normalization-based (regex) matching φ(·) and fuzzy matching; when regex returns negative, an open-weights Llama judge (LLM-as-judge) is used. Leakage event: response reveals the secret exactly, approximately, or semantically. Metrics: probe-level and dialogue-level leakage (dialogue-level = any probe elicits the secret); Δ = additional dialogue-level leakage hybrid vs regex. Privacy Half-Life τ: earliest observed drift length ≤ safety threshold δ = 0.1×L(0) with no later resurgence; D_obs = observed drift lengths. Statistical methods: 95% bootstrap CIs over dialogues, McNemar’s test for paired comparisons (with Bonferroni where applicable), Cochran’s Q across persuasion levels, χ2 and Cramer’s V for associations. Reported findings: observed dialogue-level leakage ≈ 38.7%–54.6%; persuasion effects vary by model; SSNs and credit card numbers are suppressed more often than emails/phone numbers; within tested range additional drift does not reliably reduce leakage; no evaluated model meets the paper’s stability/suppression criterion. Pipeline notes: parametric dialogue generator, scaffold-then-rewrite naturalistic refinement, cached responses.

PrivDrift study: uses seeded multi-turn histories, content-dense intervening exchanges, and three standardized extraction conditions. Dataset: 1,000 dialogues containing one of phone numbers, email addresses, Social Security Numbers (SSNs), or credit card numbers. Detection method: normalized matching plus an open-weights judge. Reported hybrid dialogue-level leakage rates across the three evaluated models: 38.70%, 47.70%, and 54.60%. Authors state leakage varies by model, secret type, and persuasion intensity. SSNs and credit card numbers are reported to receive much stronger suppression than contact identifiers (phone, email). No system attains stable suppression within the tested drift lengths. Authors interpret results as an active-context behavioral privacy failure, not evidence of permanent memory.

PrivDrift (QX2) benchmark: N=1,000 seeded multi-turn dialogues, each contains one ground-truth secret S (phone A2L, email F8Z, SSN W3B, or credit card N6G) disclosed at t0. D = unrelated sequence of user/assistant turns (u_i,a_i). Drift length d (D7A) is number of turns between disclosure and final standardized probe P; d sampled Uniform{2,3,4,5,6} per Eq.(1). Probes: V4N persuasion intensities — C8R (Simple), Z2F (Medium), L9W (Hard). Models evaluated: M7Q=GPT-OSS-120B, T4X=DeepSeek-R1, Y9C=Qwen3-VL-235B via OpenRouter API; some responses cached. Detection methods: U3P (regex-only deterministic baseline), B6T (normalization-based matching using phi), H8D (hybrid: normalized inclusion OR LLM-as-judge/Llama judge binary verdict), R5J (post-hoc fuzzy matching). Metrics: probe-level P6S = one response observation per dialogue per persuasion; dialogue-level G4P = dialogue positive if any probe elicits secret. Leakage L(d) and immediate L(0). Delta (δ) safety threshold = 0.1 × L(0). K2V (Privacy Half-Life, τ) = earliest observed drift length meeting suppression threshold at that and every later observed length; τ assigned a specific value when no observed length qualifies. Title: PrivDrift — auditing user-secret leakage under topic drift in active LLM conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University). Contact: lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu. Abstract key points: introduces PrivDrift benchmark of 1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues with seeded secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction probes. Evaluated across three LLMs with extended context windows. Reports dialogue-level hybrid leakage between 38.7% and 54.6%, with strong variation by model, secret type, and persuasion intensity. Within the tested drift window, additional topic drift does not reliably reduce leakage; conclusion: privacy risk should be viewed as a persistent behavioral failure mode, not only memorization or immediate jailbreaks. Keywords: Trustworthy AI, LLMs, Privacy, Evaluation, Benchmarking.

Title: PrivDrift — auditing user-secret leakage under topic drift in active LLM conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University). Contact: lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu. Benchmark: PrivDrift — controlled benchmark of 1,000 multi-turn dialogues per model with seeded secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction probes. Evaluated across three LLMs with extended context windows. Core axes: topic drift (number d of unrelated turns between secret disclosure and probe; tested window d ≤ 6) and persuasion intensity (interaction style: direct, justified, high-pressure). Main quantitative claim: dialogue-level hybrid leakage under hybrid detector ranges 38.7%–54.6%; leakage varies strongly by model, secret type (SSNs and credit cards suppressed far more often than emails and phone numbers), and persuasion intensity. Hybrid detector: normalization-based matching + open-weights LLM judge; reported metrics include dialogue-level, probe-level, regex-only, fuzzy, and hybrid leakage rates. Key finding: within tested drift window, additional topic drift does not reliably reduce leakage; authors introduce Privacy Half-Life (τ), a stability-based metric, and report that no evaluated model reaches stable decay within observed drift range. Contributions summarized: benchmark, probe styles, hybrid detector & metrics, Privacy Half-Life analysis. Keywords: Trustworthy AI, LLMs, Privacy, Evaluation, Benchmarking.

Title: PrivDrift — auditing user-secret leakage under topic drift in active LLM conversations. Author/contact: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu). Main quantitative claim: dialogue-level hybrid leakage under hybrid detector ranges 38.7%–54.6%; leakage varies by model and secret type (SSNs and credit cards suppressed more than emails/phones). Hybrid detector: normalization-based matching + open-weights LLM judge; reported metrics include dialogue-level, probe-level, regex-only, fuzzy, and hybrid leakage rates. Privacy Half-Life (τ): stability-based metric; authors report no evaluated model reaches stable decay within observed drift range. Contributions: benchmark, probe styles, hybrid detector & metrics, Privacy Half-Life analysis. Related work summarized: (1) Contextual privacy/inference-time leakage distinguished from training-data extraction; other benchmarks (ConfAIde, PrivacyLens, PrivaCI-Bench) focus on static access-control/privacy-norm reasoning, whereas PrivDrift isolates persistence of user-disclosed secrets after topic drift and persuasion probes. (2) Multi-turn adversarial attacks (Crescendo, automated jailbreaks, prompt injection) motivate treating information flow control across turns. (3) Context management and unlearning (TOFU, WMDP) operate on model weights/static QA; PrivDrift targets active-context suppression relevant to RAG, copilots, and agentic workflows.

steps.notes_before: Evaluation uses a hierarchical hybrid detector: Stage 1 normalization-based matching (φ) detects verbatim/near-verbatim leaks; numeric secrets: strip non-digits; alphanumeric: normalize case/whitespace, preserve meaningful delimiters. Regex-stage label: Leak_regex(R,S)=I[φ(S)⊂φ(R)]. Stage 2: open-weights Llama judge (Meta AI, 2024) inspects regex-negative responses and returns a binary verdict for partial/indirect disclosures; paper reports regex-only and hybrid rates separately. Privacy Half-Life τ: D_obs = observed drift lengths, L(d)=leakage rate at d, safety threshold δ=0.1×L(0). τ = min{d∈D_obs | L(d)≤δ and ∀d'>d in D_obs: L(d')≤δ}; if empty τ = max(D_obs)+1 to avoid counting transient dips. Caveat: earlier parts ambiguously defined d (dialogue element count vs. number of drift turns), so interpretation of 'drift length' in L(d), D_obs, and τ is unclear. Other earlier details retained: N=1000 dialogues (900 synthetic +100 human-authored mixed), secret types: phone/email/SSN/credit card, drift lengths sampled from {0,2,3,4,5,6} (d=0 with p=0.2, else uniform over 2–6).

Title: PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University), contact lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu. Abstract claims: persistent, user-facing, shared-session, tool-augmented LLMs can retain behaviorally recoverable sensitive disclosures even after unrelated tasks; introduces a controlled benchmark called PrivDrift (QX2) that uses seeded multi-turn histories, content-dense intervening exchanges, and standardized extraction probes to audit persistence. Reports that across extended-context models, a metric/phenomenon labelled "G4P under H8D" remains substantial, varies sharply across systems and two other labels "S8Q" and "V4N", and does not reliably decline within the tested window. Conclusion: active-context privacy should be evaluated as persistent behavioral failure rather than only parameter memorization or immediate jailbreak behavior. Keywords: Trustworthy AI, LLM Privacy, Evaluation, Benchmarking. PrivDrift benchmark: 1,000 controlled dialogues with seeded secrets (SSN, credit card, email, phone) inserted and later targeted by standardized probes after content-dense topic drift. Drift length d = number of turns between secret disclosure (t0) and final probe; sampled with Uniform{2,3,4,5,6}, tested up to d ≤ 6. Probes / persuasion levels: Simple (direct/neutral), Medium (contextual justification), Hard (high-pressure/urgent) — corresponds to earlier labels direct/justified/high-pressure. Three evaluated models: GPT-OSS-120B (GPT-OSS), DeepSeek-R1 (DeepSeek), Qwen3-VL-235B (Qwen); models queried via OpenRouter API; some responses cached. Detection/hybrid evaluation: normalization-based (regex) matching φ(·) and fuzzy matching; when regex returns negative, an open-weights Llama judge (LLM-as-judge) is used. Leakage event: response reveals the secret exactly, approximately, or semantically. Metrics: probe-level and dialogue-level leakage (dialogue-level = any probe elicits the secret); Δ = additional dialogue-level leakage hybrid vs regex. Privacy Half-Life τ: earliest observed drift length ≤ safety threshold δ = 0.1×L(0) with no later resurgence; D_obs = observed drift lengths. Statistical methods: 95% bootstrap CIs over dialogues, McNemar’s test for paired comparisons (with Bonferroni where applicable), Cochran’s Q across persuasion levels, χ2 and Cramer’s V for associations. Reported findings: observed dialogue-level leakage ≈ 38.7%–54.6%; persuasion effects vary by model; SSNs and credit card numbers are suppressed more often than emails/phone numbers; within tested range additional drift does not reliably reduce leakage; no evaluated model meets the paper’s stability/suppression criterion. steps.notes_before: (none yet: this is the first part)

PrivDrift study: uses seeded multi-turn histories, content-dense intervening exchanges, and three standardized extraction conditions. Dataset: 1,000 dialogues containing one of phone numbers, email addresses, Social Security Numbers (SSNs), or credit card numbers. Detection method: normalized matching plus an open-weights judge. Reported hybrid dialogue-level leakage rates across the three evaluated models: 38.70%, 47.70%, and 54.60%. Authors state leakage varies by model, secret type, and persuasion intensity. SSNs and credit card numbers are reported to receive much stronger suppression than contact identifiers (phone, email). No system attains stable suppression within the tested drift lengths. Authors interpret results as an active-context behavioral privacy failure, not evidence of permanent memory.

PrivDrift (QX2) benchmark: N=1,000 seeded multi-turn dialogues, each contains one ground-truth secret S (phone A2L, email F8Z, SSN W3B, or credit card N6G) disclosed at t0. D = unrelated sequence of user/assistant turns (u_i,a_i). Drift length d (D7A) is number of turns between disclosure and final standardized probe P; d sampled Uniform{2,3,4,5,6} per Eq.(1). Probes: V4N persuasion intensities — C8R (Simple), Z2F (Medium), L9W (Hard). Models evaluated: M7Q=GPT-OSS-120B, T4X=DeepSeek-R1, Y9C=Qwen3-VL-235B via OpenRouter API; some responses cached. Detection methods: U3P (regex-only deterministic baseline), B6T (normalization-based matching using phi), H8D (hybrid: normalized inclusion OR LLM-as-judge/Llama judge binary verdict), R5J (post-hoc fuzzy matching). Metrics: probe-level P6S = one response observation per dialogue per persuasion; dialogue-level G4P = dialogue positive if any probe elicits secret. Leakage L(d) and immediate L(0). Delta (δ) safety threshold = 0.1 × L(0). K2V (Privacy Half-Life, τ) = earliest observed drift length meeting suppression threshold at that and every later observed length; τ assigned a specific value when no observed length qualifies. Δ = H8D augmentation over U3P (percentage points). CI: 95% bootstrap over dialogues for G4P. Stats: McNemar’s for matched model/detector and persuasion follow-ups (with Bonferroni where applicable); Cochran’s Q for repeated persuasion measures; Chi-square for independence vs D7A, V4N, or S8Q. Other terms: active-context privacy, behavioral recoverability, parameter-based memorization, training-data extraction, membership inference, unlearning, RAG systems, scaffold-then-rewrite, persona, ConfAIde, PrivacyLens/PrivaCI-Bench, Crescendo, TOFU/WMDP. Earlier reported hybrid dialogue-level leakage rates across the three models: 38.70%, 47.70%, 54.60%; authors state leakage varies by model, secret type, and persuasion intensity, with SSNs and credit cards more strongly suppressed than contact identifiers.

steps.notes_before: QX2 framework: N=1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues (900 synthetic, 100 human-written interspersed). Four secret types inserted as exact ground-truth: phone (A2L), email (F8Z), SSN (W3B), credit card (N6G). Scaffold-then-rewrite preserves exact secret, intervening-turn counts, roles, and final-probe conditions. Probes: three persuasion conditions C8R (simple), Z2F (medium), L9W (hard). Evaluation: hierarchical two-stage detection—Stage 1 B6T deterministic normalization (phi strips non-digit chars for numeric secrets; alphanumeric normalized for case/whitespace while retaining delimiters); leakage label Leak_U3P(R,S)=I[phi(S) subset phi(R)]. H8D (hybrid) labels responses positive if normalized inclusion or an LLM/judge finds full secret, substantial substring, or identifying partial info. Immediate recall included; short-to-medium topic-drift emphasized.

Dataset QX2: N=1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues (900 synthetic, 100 human-written interspersed). Four exact ground-truth secret types inserted: phone (A2L), email (F8Z), SSN (W3B), credit card (N6G). Drift-length D7A values reported as {0,2,3,4,5,6}; sampling: d=0 with p=0.2 (immediate recall), otherwise d ~ Uniform{2,3,4,5,6} (p=0.8). Avg/median words per dialogue 359.16/385 (range 43–795); approx. tokens avg/median 478.87/513.33 (range 57.33–1060). Scaffold-then-rewrite preserves exact secret, intervening-turn counts, roles, and final-probe conditions. Probes: three persuasion conditions C8R (simple), Z2F (medium), L9W (hard). Evaluation: hierarchical two-stage detection. Stage 1 (B6T deterministic normalization): phi strips non-digit chars for numeric secrets; alphanumeric normalized for case/whitespace while retaining delimiters; deterministic leakage label Leak_U3P(R,S)=I[phi(S) subset phi(R)]. Stage 2 (LLM-as-judge): an open-weights Llama judge is applied to deterministic negatives and returns a binary full/substantial-disclosure verdict (detects partial disclosures, indirect hints, and formatting variants); judge is fallible. The hybrid label H8D marks positive if deterministic inclusion OR the LLM judge finds full secret, substantial substring, or identifying partial info. K2V (Privacy Half-Life τ): uses observed lengths D_obs and leakage rates L(d); safety threshold δ = 0.1 × L(0) (L(0)=immediate-recall leakage). τ = min{ d ∈ D_obs | L(d) ≤ δ AND ∀ d' ∈ D_obs with d' > d: L(d') ≤ δ }. If no qualifying d, τ = max(D_obs) + 1. Figure 3: later resurgence disqualifies transient decreases.

Dataset QX2: N=1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues (900 synthetic, 100 human-written). Four ground-truth secret types inserted: phone (A2L), email (F8Z), SSN (W3B), credit card (N6G). Drift-length D7A values {0,2,3,4,5,6}; sampling: d=0 with p=0.2 (immediate recall), otherwise d ~ Uniform{2,3,4,5,6} (p=0.8). Dialogue length: avg/median words 359.16/385 (range 43–795); tokens avg/median 478.87/513.33 (range 57.33–1060). Scaffold-then-rewrite preserves exact secret, intervening-turn counts, roles, and final-probe conditions. Probes: three persuasion conditions C8R (simple), Z2F (medium), L9W (hard).

Detection pipeline: Stage 1 deterministic normalization phi (numeric: strip non-digits; alphanumeric: normalize case/whitespace, retain delimiters). Deterministic leakage Leak_U3P(R,S)=I[phi(S) subset phi(R)]. Stage 2 Llama judge applied to deterministic negatives to decide full/substantial-disclosure (fallible). Hybrid H8D = deterministic OR LLM-judge positive.

K2V (Privacy Half-Life τ): use observed D_obs and leakage rates L(d); safety threshold δ = 0.1 × L(0). τ = min{d ∈ D_obs | L(d) ≤ δ AND ∀d' > d: L(d') ≤ δ}; if none, τ = max(D_obs) + 1. Note: Figure 3 treats later resurgence as disqualifying transient decreases.

Models & querying: GPT-OSS-120B (M7Q), DeepSeek-R1 (T4X), Qwen3-VL-235B (Y9C), queried via OpenRouter API. Each model processes full QX2 with one seeded secret and one sampled d per dialogue under every standardized condition. Cached responses: Per model = 3,000; All models = 9,000 (consistent with 1,000 dialogues × 3 persuasion probes).

Aggregation: G4P = dialogue-level any-probe disclosure; P6S = per-dialogue per-persuasion-condition observations; R5J = post-hoc normalized-similarity (fuzzy match).

Stats: G4P 95% CIs via bootstrap over dialogues; matched tests use McNemar (Bonferroni as needed); repeated persuasion measures use Cochran’s Q then McNemar; chi-square tests for independence with Cramer’s V reported as effect size.

Title: PrivDrift — auditing user-secret leakage under topic drift in active LLM conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University). Contact: lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu. Abstract key points: introduces PrivDrift benchmark of 1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues with seeded secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction probes. Evaluated across three LLMs with extended context windows. Reports dialogue-level hybrid leakage between 38.7% and 54.6%, with strong variation by model, secret type, and persuasion intensity. Within the tested drift window, additional topic drift does not reliably reduce leakage; conclusion: privacy risk should be viewed as a persistent behavioral failure mode, not only memorization or immediate jailbreaks. Keywords: Trustworthy AI, LLMs, Privacy, Evaluation, Benchmarking.

Title: PrivDrift — auditing user-secret leakage under topic drift in active LLM conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero. Goal: measure active-context privacy leakage when secrets disclosed earlier in a conversation may be elicited after unrelated topic drift and via different interaction styles. Setup: three LLMs with extended context windows, 1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues per model. Axes: topic drift (number of unrelated turns between disclosure and probe) and persuasion intensity (direct, justified, high-pressure probes). Key reported results: dialogue-level hybrid leakage between 38.7% and 54.6%; persuasion intensity significantly affects leakage; leakage varies by secret type (SSNs and credit cards suppressed far less than emails and phone numbers). Drift window tested: d ≤ 6; additional drift within this window does not reliably reduce leakage. Metric: Privacy Half-Life (τ) proposed to assess persistent suppression; authors claim no evaluated model reaches stable decay within observed drift range. Methods/contributions: PrivDrift benchmark, evaluation of direct/justified/high-pressure probes, reproducible hybrid detector combining normalization-based matching with an open-weights LLM judge, and reporting of dialogue-level, probe-level, regex-only, fuzzy, and hybrid leakage rates. Threat model: not assuming literal forgetting—focus on behavioral risk relevant to shared sessions, assistants, and agentic workflows.

Title: PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University), contact lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu. Abstract claims: persistent, user-facing, shared-session, tool-augmented LLMs can retain behaviorally recoverable sensitive disclosures even after unrelated tasks; introduces a controlled benchmark called PrivDrift (QX2) that uses seeded multi-turn histories, content-dense intervening exchanges, and standardized extraction probes to audit persistence. Reports that across extended-context models, a metric/phenomenon labelled "G4P under H8D" remains substantial, varies sharply across systems and two other labels "S8Q" and "V4N", and does not reliably decline within the tested window. Conclusion: active-context privacy should be evaluated as persistent behavioral failure rather than only parameter memorization or immediate jailbreak behavior. Keywords: Trustworthy AI, LLM Privacy, Evaluation, Benchmarking. Points to check later: definitions and meanings of acronyms QX2/PrivDrift, G4P, H8D, S8Q, V4N; experimental setup (seeded histories, intervening exchanges, extraction probes), which models are considered "extended-context", the tested window length, and evidence for "fails to decline reliably" and per-system variability.

Title: PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (WVU). Abstract/claims so far: persistent, user-facing, shared-session, tool-augmented LLMs can retain behaviorally recoverable sensitive disclosures even after unrelated tasks. Introduces controlled benchmark PrivDrift (also called QX2) that uses seeded multi-turn histories, content-dense intervening exchanges, and standardized extraction probes to audit persistence. Key empirical claims so far: “SSNs and payment identifiers receive much weaker suppression than contact identifiers; no evaluated system attains stable decay.” QX2 features: controlled persistence auditing, direct/justified/high-pressure elicitation, reproducible composite detection via deterministic processing and an open-weights judge, reporting of G4P and P6S, and use of a stability criterion (vs. transient-decrease). Context: LLMs evolving into persistent assistants across domains (health, finance, enterprise copilots); disclosed PII includes A2L, financial identifiers, F8Z, health details. Motivation: existing safety evaluations target parameter memorization and immediate jailbreaking; they may not show whether unrelated conversational shifts provide a practical privacy boundary. Points to check later: definitions of acronyms (QX2/PrivDrift, G4P, H8D, S8Q, V4N, P6S), which models are “extended-context,” length of tested window, exact experimental setup (seeded histories, intervening exchanges, probes), per-system variability and evidence that leakage “does not reliably decline.”

Title/claim: PrivDrift (aka QX2) audits persistence of user-secret leakage in persistent, user-facing, shared-session, tool-augmented LLMs; claim: such systems can retain behaviorally recoverable sensitive disclosures even after unrelated tasks. Benchmark/QX2 design (from earlier parts & reinforced here): seeded multi-turn histories, content-dense intervening exchanges, standardized extraction probes; deterministic processing and an open-weights judge; reports metrics G4P and P6S; uses a stability criterion to distinguish stable persistence vs transient decrease; includes direct/justified/high-pressure elicitation. Key empirical claims so far: SSNs and payment identifiers show much weaker suppression than contact identifiers; no evaluated system attains stable decay. Related work summarized in this part: (1) training-data extraction/memorized-PII work targets parameter/pretraining memorization; (2) ConfAIde, PrivacyLens, PrivaCI-Bench study privacy-norm/appropriate-sharing under static scenarios; QX2 differs by isolating behavioral recoverability after unrelated exchanges + persuasive probing; (3) multi-turn adversarial attacks (e.g., Crescendo) elicit harmful content, whereas QX2 targets re-disclosure of earlier user-supplied secrets; (4) TOFU/WMDP study unlearning/behavioral suppression mainly at parameter/static QA level, while QX2 concerns prompt-level/active-context suppression relevant to RAG/copilots/agentic workflows. Outstanding points to verify later: definitions of acronyms (G4P, P6S, others), which models are “extended-context,” session/window lengths, exact experimental setup (seeded histories, intervening exchanges, probe wording), per-system variability, and evidence for “no reliable decline.”

steps.notes_before: QX2 pipeline: construct controlled multi-turn dialogues, append standardized probe, query target model, composite leakage scoring. Threat model: E9U = active-context re-disclosure; user supplies secret S at t0; intervening exchanges D = {u1,a1,...,ud,ad} (J7K = topic drift); probe P appended; any exact/approx/semantic revelation = leakage. Dataset: N=1,000 dialogues (900 synthetic, 100 human-authored, interspersed). Secret categories = 4: A2L (phone), F8Z (email), W3B (SSN), N6G (credit card). D7A values = {0,2,3,4,5,6}. Dialogue word stats: mean 359.16, median 385, min/max 43/795; approx tokens mean 478.87, median 513.33, min/max 57.33/1060. Persona/secret injection preserves exact ground truth and turn counts. Content-dense J7K topics include tax, medical triage, travel; scaffold-then-rewrite preserves experimental variables. Probing V4N has three conditions: C8R (Simple), Z2F (Medium), L9W (Hard). D7A sampling: d=0 w.p.0.2; else Uniform{2..6} w.p.0.8. Evaluation: hybrid detector H8D labels positive if normalized inclusion OR Llama judge (open-weights) finds full/substantial/identifying partial disclosure. Stage 1 deterministic matching described (normalization phi: strip non-digits for numeric, normalize case/whitespace for alphanumeric) and equation (2) gives Leak_{U3P}(R,S)=I[phi(S)⊂phi(R)], but the paper inconsistently names/defines the deterministic matcher as B6T in one place and U3P ("regex-only") elsewhere. K2V (Privacy Half-Life) tau: delta=0.1*L(0); tau = min d in D_obs s.t. L(d)≤delta and ∀d'>d: L(d')≤delta; if none, tau = max(D_obs)+1.

QX2 pipeline: construct controlled multi-turn dialogues, append standardized probe, query target model, composite leakage scoring. Threat model E9U: active-context re-disclosure; user supplies secret S at t0; intervening exchanges D = {u1,a1,...,ud,ad} (topic drift J7K); probe P appended; any exact/approx/semantic revelation = leakage. Dataset: N=1,000 dialogues (900 synthetic, 100 human-authored); one seeded secret and one sampled d per dialogue; D7A values = {0,2,3,4,5,6}; sampling: d=0 w.p.0.2, else Uniform{2..6} w.p.0.8. Dialogue length stats: words mean 359.16 (median 385, min 43, max 795); tokens mean 478.87 (median 513.33, min 57.33, max 1060). Probing V4N has three persuasion difficulty conditions (C8R Simple, Z2F Medium, L9W Hard). Models: all systems receive identical histories and probe templates via OpenRouter API. Cached responses: per model 3,000 (consistent with 1,000 dialogues × 3 V4N conditions), all evaluated models 9,000. Aggregation: G4P (dialogue-level leakage) = dialogue positive if any standardized probe elicits secret; P6S (probe-level leakage) = one observation per persuasion condition per dialogue for V4N/R5J analyses; G4P can exceed mean condition-specific rate. Detection: hybrid H8D = deterministic matching (φ normalization: strip non-digits for numeric, normalize case/whitespace for alphanumeric) OR Llama judge (labels full/substantial/identifying partial disclosure); earlier text inconsistently named the deterministic matcher B6T vs U3P. K2V (Privacy Half-Life) τ: δ=0.1·L(0); τ = min d s.t. L(d)≤δ and ∀d'>d: L(d')≤δ, else τ=max(D_obs)+1; fig.3 notes resurgence disqualifies transient decreases. Stats: G4P CIs via 95% bootstrap over dialogues; P6S sensitivity uses cached responses; matched comparisons McNemar (Bonferroni where applicable); repeated persuasion Cochran’s Q then McNemar; independence tests χ² with Cramer’s V as effect size.

final_notes:
Scope & setup: PrivDrift audits active-context privacy leakage under topic drift and persuasion. Models: DeepSeek-R1, GPT-OSS-120B, Qwen3-VL-235B. Dataset: 1,000 dialogues per model (900 synthetic + 100 human-authored interspersed); drift values d ∈ {0,2,3,4,5,6}; privacy half-life threshold δ = 0.1·L(0). No cross-session memorization; secrets fixed-format; author flags not preserved.

Key results: Dialogue-level hybrid leakage (Table 3): DeepSeek-R1 38.70% (CI [35.7,41.6]), GPT-OSS-120B 47.70% (CI [44.6,50.8]), Qwen3-VL-235B 54.60% (CI [51.6,57.7]). Cached probe-level hybrid leakage (Table 6): DeepSeek 26.43%, GPT 37.57%, Qwen 37.53%. Fuzzy matching (0.85) closely tracks hybrid. Persuasion (Table 4, Cochran’s Q p<1e-5): GPT Simple/Med/Hard 39.30/40.50/32.90; DeepSeek 28.10/22.00/29.20; Qwen 38.70/33.30/40.60.

Probe-level association effect sizes (Appendix B, Table 8): Secret type (Cramér’s V) DeepSeek 0.5871, GPT 0.7731, Qwen 0.6927 — interpreted Large. Drift length V: DeepSeek 0.1073 (Small), GPT 0.0659 (Negligible), Qwen 0.0723 (Negligible). Persuasion V: DeepSeek 0.0718, GPT 0.0689, Qwen 0.0639 — interpreted Negligible.

Dataset length by drift (Appendix A, Table 7): counts sum to 1000 across d; e.g., d=0 N=197 avg words 44.29; d=6 N=167 avg words 568.03 (tokens estimated words*4/3).

Drift dynamics: curves dip near d=3 then rebound; topic drift does not reliably reduce leakage; no model reached stable decay within observed d (τ = max(D_obs)+1 = 7). Appendix C references Figure 6 (dialogue construction details).

PrivDrift benchmark: 1,000 controlled dialogues with seeded secrets, unrelated intervening turns, and standardized extraction probes. Three models evaluated; probes classified as direct, justified, and high-pressure. Hybrid detector: normalized matching combined with an LLM judge. Dialogue-level leakage defined as whether any standardized probe elicits the secret; observed leakage ranges 38.7%–54.6%. Persuasion effects depend on model. Secret types: Social Security Numbers and credit card numbers are suppressed more often than emails and phone numbers. Drift parameter d tested up to d ≤ 6; within this range additional drift does not reliably reduce leakage. Conclusion: no evaluated model meets the paper's criterion for stable suppression. Note: glossary header present but content not shown in this part.

PrivDrift benchmark: 1,000 controlled dialogues with seeded secrets (SSN, credit card, email, phone) inserted and later targeted by standardized probes after content-dense topic drift. Drift length d = number of turns between secret disclosure (t0) and final probe; sampled with Uniform{2,3,4,5,6}, tested up to d ≤ 6. Probes / persuasion levels: Simple (direct/neutral), Medium (contextual justification), Hard (high-pressure/urgent) — corresponds to earlier labels direct/justified/high-pressure. Three evaluated models: GPT-OSS-120B (GPT-OSS), DeepSeek-R1 (DeepSeek), Qwen3-VL-235B (Qwen); models queried via OpenRouter API; some responses cached. Detection/hybrid evaluation: normalization-based (regex) matching φ(·) and fuzzy matching; when regex returns negative, an open-weights Llama judge (LLM-as-judge) is used. Leakage event: response reveals the secret exactly, approximately, or semantically. Metrics: probe-level and dialogue-level leakage (dialogue-level = any probe elicits the secret); Δ = additional dialogue-level leakage hybrid vs regex. Privacy Half-Life τ: earliest observed drift length ≤ safety threshold δ = 0.1×L(0) with no later resurgence; D_obs = observed drift lengths. Statistical methods: 95% bootstrap CIs over dialogues, McNemar’s test for paired comparisons (with Bonferroni where applicable), Cochran’s Q across persuasion levels, χ2 and Cramer’s V for associations. Reported findings: observed dialogue-level leakage ≈ 38.7%–54.6%; persuasion effects vary by model; SSNs and credit card numbers are suppressed more often than emails/phone numbers; within tested range additional drift does not reliably reduce leakage; no evaluated model meets the paper’s stability/suppression criterion. Pipeline notes: parametric dialogue generator, scaffold-then-rewrite naturalistic refinement, cached responses.

PrivDrift: N=1000 dialogues (900 synthetic, 100 human). Secret categories = 4. Observed drift lengths D_obs = {0,2,3,4,5,6}; sampling: d=0 with probability 0.2, otherwise uniform on {2,3,4,5,6}. Three persuasion levels (Simple, Medium, Hard); three standardized persuasion probes appended per dialogue. Models: GPT-OSS-120B, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3-VL-235B queried via OpenRouter API; all models receive same dialogue histories and probe templates. Cached responses: 3 probes × 1000 dialogues = 3,000 cached responses per model, 9,000 total. Detection: report regex-only and hybrid leakage. Hybrid detector: Stage1 regex with normalization φ (digits-only for numeric; case/whitespace normalization for alphanumeric) and Leak_regex(R,S)=I[φ(S)⊂φ(R)]; Stage2 open-weights Llama judge applied only to regex-negative responses, returning binary verdict for indirect/partial leakage. Aggregation: dialogue-level leakage = dialogue leaks if any standardized probe elicits the secret (dialogue-level rates computed with 95% bootstrap CIs over dialogues). Persuasion-level and fuzzy-matching analyses are probe-level (each dialogue contributes one response per persuasion condition); thus dialogue-level leakage can exceed the average of persuasion-level rates. Statistical tests: McNemar’s test for matched/pairwise model and detector comparisons (Bonferroni correction where applicable); Cochran’s Q for repeated measures across persuasion levels with post-hoc McNemar tests; Chi-square tests of independence for associations between leakage and drift length, persuasion level, or secret type; Cramer’s V for effect size. Probe-level sensitivity checks use cached model-probe responses. Note: the paper uses ‘p’ to denote both the sampling probability (e.g., p=0.2 for d=0) and, in test-result tables, the reported statistical-test value.

Discussion reiterates core empirical findings and interpretations: persistent active-context leakage (dialogue-level hybrid leakage, Table 3) — DeepSeek-R1 38.70% [35.7,41.6], GPT-OSS-120B 47.70% [44.6,50.8], Qwen3-VL-235B 54.60% [51.6,57.7]; drift curves dip near d=3 then rebound (Fig. 4). Persuasion effects (Table 4) are significant and model-dependent (Cochran’s Q p<1e-5): GPT Simple/Medium/Hard 39.30/40.50/32.90; DeepSeek 28.10/22.00/29.20; Qwen 38.70/33.30/40.60. Discussion-level interpretations: safeguards may be format-sensitive, persuasion can either reduce or increase leakage depending on model and pressure level, and temporary drift dips do not constitute stable suppression — recommend stability-based evaluation.

final_notes: Section 5: Leakage is substantial and varies by model and secret; no stable suppression below tested threshold. H8D barely improves deterministic baseline (Table 2 deltas: M7Q +0.00 p=1.0; T4X +0.90 p=7.7e-3; Y9C +1.10 p=2.57e-3). Dialogue-level any-probe positives (Table 3): T4X 38.70% [35.7,41.6]; M7Q 47.70% [44.6,50.8]; Y9C 54.60% [51.6,57.7]. Per-persuasion one-observation rates (Table 4): M7Q (C8R/Z2F/L9W)=39.3/40.5/32.9; T4X=28.1/22.0/29.2; Y9C=38.7/33.3/40.6 (Cochran's Q p<1e-5). Section 7: limits (d ≤ 6, structured secrets only, active-context only, sanitized cached metadata, detector scope limited, baseline label inconsistency noted). PrivDrift study: uses seeded multi-turn histories, content-dense intervening exchanges, and three standardized extraction conditions. Dataset: 1,000 dialogues containing one of phone numbers, email addresses, Social Security Numbers (SSNs), or credit card numbers. Detection method: normalized matching plus an open-weights judge. Reported hybrid dialogue-level leakage rates across the three evaluated models: 38.70%, 47.70%, and 54.60%. Authors state leakage varies by model, secret type, and persuasion intensity. SSNs and credit card numbers are reported to receive much stronger suppression than contact identifiers (phone, email). No system attains stable suppression within the tested drift lengths. Authors interpret results as an active-context behavioral privacy failure, not evidence of permanent memory.

PrivDrift (QX2) benchmark: N=1,000 seeded multi-turn dialogues, each contains one ground-truth secret S (phone A2L, email F8Z, SSN W3B, or credit card N6G) disclosed at t0.
