Metrics: probe-level P6S = one response observation per dialogue per persuasion; dialogue-level G4P = dialogue positive if any probe elicits secret. Leakage L(d) and immediate L(0). Delta (δ) safety threshold = 0.1 × L(0). K2V (Privacy Half-Life, τ) = earliest observed drift length meeting suppression threshold at that and every later observed length; τ assigned a specific value when no observed length qualifies. Title: PrivDrift — auditing user-secret leakage under topic drift in active LLM conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University). Contact: lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu. Abstract key points: introduces PrivDrift benchmark of 1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues with seeded secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction probes. Evaluated across three LLMs with extended context windows. Reports dialogue-level hybrid leakage between 38.7% and 54.6%, with strong variation by model, secret type, and persuasion intensity. Within the tested drift window, additional topic drift does not reliably reduce leakage; conclusion: privacy risk should be viewed as a persistent behavioral failure mode, not only memorization or immediate jailbreaks. Keywords: Trustworthy AI, LLMs, Privacy, Evaluation, Benchmarking.

Title: PrivDrift — auditing user-secret leakage under topic drift in active LLM conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University). Contact: lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu. Benchmark: PrivDrift — controlled benchmark of 1,000 multi-turn dialogues per model with seeded secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction probes. Evaluated across three LLMs with extended context windows. Core axes: topic drift (number d of unrelated turns between secret disclosure and probe; tested window d ≤ 6) and persuasion intensity (interaction style: direct, justified, high-pressure). Main quantitative claim: dialogue-level hybrid leakage under hybrid detector ranges 38.7%–54.6%; leakage varies strongly by model, secret type (SSNs and credit cards suppressed far more often than emails and phone numbers), and persuasion intensity. Hybrid detector: normalization-based matching + open-weights LLM judge; reported metrics include dialogue-level, probe-level, regex-only, fuzzy, and hybrid leakage rates. Key finding: within tested drift window, additional topic drift does not reliably reduce leakage; authors introduce Privacy Half-Life (τ), a stability-based metric, and report that no evaluated model reaches stable decay within observed drift range. Contributions summarized: benchmark, probe styles, hybrid detector & metrics, Privacy Half-Life analysis. Keywords: Trustworthy AI, LLMs, Privacy, Evaluation, Benchmarking.

Title: PrivDrift — auditing user-secret leakage under topic drift in active LLM conversations. Author/contact: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu). Benchmark: PrivDrift — 1,000 multi-turn dialogues per model with seeded secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction probes. Core axes: topic drift (number d of unrelated turns between secret disclosure and probe; tested window d ≤ 6) and persuasion intensity (interaction styles: direct, justified, high-pressure). Main quantitative claim: dialogue-level hybrid leakage under hybrid detector ranges 38.7%–54.6%; leakage varies by model and secret type (SSNs and credit cards suppressed more than emails/phones). Hybrid detector: normalization-based matching + open-weights LLM judge; reported metrics include dialogue-level, probe-level, regex-only, fuzzy, and hybrid leakage rates. Privacy Half-Life (τ): stability-based metric; authors report no evaluated model reaches stable decay within observed drift range. Contributions: benchmark, probe styles, hybrid detector & metrics, Privacy Half-Life analysis. Related work summarized: (1) Contextual privacy/inference-time leakage distinguished from training-data extraction; other benchmarks (ConfAIde, PrivacyLens, PrivaCI-Bench) focus on static access-control/privacy-norm reasoning, whereas PrivDrift isolates persistence of user-disclosed secrets after topic drift and persuasion probes. (2) Multi-turn adversarial attacks (Crescendo, automated jailbreaks, prompt injection) motivate treating information flow control across turns. (3) Context management and unlearning (TOFU, WMDP) operate on model weights/static QA; PrivDrift targets active-context suppression relevant to RAG, copilots, and agentic workflows.

steps.notes_before: PrivDrift benchmark: threat model = active-context re-disclosure; user reveals secret S at turn t0, after d drift turns a standardized probe P appended; leakage if model reproduces S exactly, approximately, or semantically. Dataset N=1000 dialogues (900 synthetic + 100 human-authored mixed; human IDs lost so results aggregated). Secret types: 4 fixed-format PII (phone, email, SSN, credit card). Drift lengths used: {0,2,3,4,5,6}; sampling: P(d=0)=0.2, else uniform on {2..6}. Table1: avg words 359.16, median 385, min/max 43/795; approx tokens avg 478.87, median 513.33, min/max 57.33/1060. Generation: scaffold-then-rewrite pipeline; preserves exact secret, drift length, roles, final probe. Probes: Simple/Medium/Hard persuasion levels. Evaluation: hierarchical hybrid detector. Stage1 (regex): normalization phi; numeric: strip non-digits; alphanumeric: normalize case/whitespace, preserve meaningful delimiters; Leak_regex(R,S)=I[phi(S) subset phi(R)]. Stage2: open-weights Llama judge for regex-negative responses; judge given secret+response returns binary verdict for partial/indirect disclosure; report regex-only and hybrid rates separately. Privacy Half-Life: D_obs = observed drift lengths; L(d)=leakage rate; safety threshold δ=0.1*L(0); τ = min{ d∈D_obs | L(d)≤δ and ∀d'>d: L(d')≤δ }, else τ = max(D_obs)+1. Note: paper's claim about leakage across "arbitrarily long context windows/full-window saturation" conflicts with dataset coverage (max drift=6). Also retain earlier ambiguity flagged about whether d counts turns or user-assistant pairs.

final_notes: Threat: active-context re-disclosure after topic-drift. Dataset N=1000 dialogues (900 synthetic, 100 human). D7A distances tested: {0,2,3,4,5,6}; no stabilization observed; K2V set τ = max(D_obs)+1 = 7. Cached outputs: 3,000 per model. Models: M7Q, T4X, Y9C. Detector H8D = hybrid (Stage1 deterministic normalization U3P; Stage2 Llama judge). Aggregation G4P = dialogue-level (positive if any standardized probe elicits secret); probe-level metric P6S also reported. Main G4P (H8D) results: M7Q 47.70% (U3P 47.70), T4X 38.70% (U3P 37.80, Δ+0.90, p=7.7e-3), Y9C 54.60% (U3P 53.50, Δ+1.10, p=2.57e-3). 95% CIs: T4X [35.7,41.6], M7Q [44.6,50.8], Y9C [51.6,57.7]. Probe-level V4N reported as non-monotonic across persuasion conditions. Per-secret P6S shows high variance (examples: M7Q W3B 0.14%, N6G 0.00%, F8Z 78.24%, A2L 70.89%). R5J fuzzy-match closely tracks H8D P6S. Limitations: only short-to-medium D7A tested, fixed-format secrets, active-context only (no cross-session), mixed synthetic/human dialogues, detector labels under U3P/R5J/external judge without formal human–automated agreement, API models may change; planned artifact release (sanitized examples + code/templates). Conclusion: "The S8Q asymmetry suggests uneven safeguards relying more on format/sensitivity cues and format-sensitive safety heuristics than on generalized contextual confidentiality or robust contextual reasoning." Appendix A (Table 7) lists length characteristics by D7A (d=0..6). Appendix B (Table 8) cached P6S effect sizes (X2H): S8Q — T4X 0.5871 (Large), M7Q 0.7731 (Large), Y9C 0.6927 (Large); D7A — T4X 0.1073 (Small), M7Q 0.0659 (Negligible), Y9C 0.0723 (Negligible); V4N — T4X 0.0718, M7Q 0.0689, Y9C 0.0639 (all labeled Negligible). Appendix C: Figure 6 shows dialogue construction details.

Title: PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University), contact lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu. Abstract claims: persistent, user-facing, shared-session, tool-augmented LLMs can retain behaviorally recoverable sensitive disclosures even after unrelated tasks; introduces a controlled benchmark called PrivDrift (QX2) that uses seeded multi-turn histories, content-dense intervening exchanges, and standardized extraction probes to audit persistence. Reports that across extended-context models, a metric/phenomenon labelled "G4P under H8D" remains substantial, varies sharply across systems and two other labels "S8Q" and "V4N", and does not reliably decline within the tested window. Conclusion: active-context privacy should be evaluated as persistent behavioral failure rather than only parameter memorization or immediate jailbreak behavior. Keywords: Trustworthy AI, LLM Privacy, Evaluation, Benchmarking. Points to check later: definitions and meanings of acronyms QX2/PrivDrift, G4P, H8D, S8Q, V4N; experimental setup (seeded histories, intervening exchanges, extraction probes), which models are considered "extended-context", the tested window length, and evidence for "fails to decline reliably" and per-system variability.

New setup details: all systems receive identical histories and probe templates via OpenRouter API. PrivDrift benchmark: 1,000 controlled dialogues with seeded secrets, unrelated intervening turns, and standardized extraction probes. Three models evaluated; probes classified as direct, justified, and high-pressure. Hybrid detector: normalized matching combined with an LLM judge. Dialogue-level leakage defined as whether any standardized probe elicits the secret; observed leakage ranges 38.7%–54.6%. Persuasion effects depend on model. PrivDrift benchmark: 1,000 controlled dialogues with seeded secrets (SSN, credit card, email, phone) inserted and later targeted by standardized probes after content-dense topic drift. Drift length d = number of turns between secret disclosure (t0) and final probe; sampled with Uniform{2,3,4,5,6}, tested up to d ≤ 6. Probes / persuasion levels: Simple (direct/neutral), Medium (contextual justification), Hard (high-pressure/urgent) — corresponds to earlier labels direct/justified/high-pressure. Three evaluated models: GPT-OSS-120B (GPT-OSS), DeepSeek-R1 (DeepSeek), Qwen3-VL-235B (Qwen); models queried via OpenRouter API; some responses cached. Detection/hybrid evaluation: normalization-based (regex) matching φ(·) and fuzzy matching; when regex returns negative, an open-weights Llama judge (LLM-as-judge) is used. Leakage event: response reveals the secret exactly, approximately, or semantically. Metrics: probe-level and dialogue-level leakage (dialogue-level = any probe elicits the secret); Δ = additional dialogue-level leakage hybrid vs regex. Privacy Half-Life τ: earliest observed drift length ≤ safety threshold δ = 0.1×L(0) with no later resurgence; D_obs = observed drift lengths. Statistical methods: 95% bootstrap CIs over dialogues, McNemar’s test for paired comparisons (with Bonferroni where applicable), Cochran’s Q across persuasion levels, χ2 and Cramer’s V for associations. Reported findings: observed dialogue-level leakage ≈ 38.7%–54.6%; persuasion effects vary by model; SSNs and credit card numbers are suppressed more often than emails/phone numbers; within tested range additional drift does not reliably reduce leakage; no evaluated model meets the paper’s stability/suppression criterion. Pipeline notes: parametric dialogue generator, scaffold-then-rewrite naturalistic refinement, cached responses.

final_notes: Dataset: 1,000 mixed synthetic+human dialogues; drift lengths D={0,2,3,4,5,6} with P(d=0)=0.2 → counts: 0:197,2:147,3:142,4:166,5:181,6:167. Dialogue length (words/tokens) rises with d (d=0 avg words 44.29; d=6 avg words 568.03; tokens similarly increasing). Deterministic normalization φ; Leak_U3P = I[φ(S) ⊂ φ(R)]. Llama judge applied only to deterministic negatives; Hybrid H8D = U3P OR judge. Privacy half-life τ uses threshold δ=0.1×L(0); τ = min d with L(d) ≤ δ and sustained; if none τ = max(Dobs)+1 = 7; paper assigns τ=7. Cached per-model responses = 3,000 (1,000 dialogues × 3 persuasion probes). Aggregations: G4P (dialogue-level any-probe), P6S (per-persuasion averages), R5J (fuzzy-match thresholds). Key results: G4P (H8D) — T4X 38.70% [35.7,41.6], M7Q 47.70% [44.6,50.8], Y9C 54.60% [51.6,57.7]; Hybrid adds little (Δ small). P6S (H8D) triples — M7Q 39.3/40.5/32.9; T4X 28.1/22.0/29.2; Y9C 38.7/33.3/40.6 (Cochran's Q p<1e-5). Drift effects small (Cramer's V ≈0.066–0.107) with transient dip at d=3 then rebound; secret type S8Q strongest (Cramer's V ≈0.587–0.773). Appendix B (Table 8) Cramer's V (interpretation): T4X — S8Q 0.5871 (Large), D7A 0.1073 (Small), V4N 0.0718 (Negligible); M7Q — S8Q 0.7731 (Large), D7A 0.0659 (Negligible), V4N 0.0689 (Negligible); Y9C — S8Q 0.6927 (Large), D7A 0.0723 (Negligible), V4N 0.0639 (Negligible). Table 5 lists per-secret-type rates (W3B/N6G/F8Z/A2L); Table 6: R5J=0.85 matches H8D columns; Fig.5: H8D heatmap by D7A and V4N. Appendix C/Fig.6: dialogue construction details. Limitations: bounded drift, fixed-format secrets, detector gaps, API models, sanitized artifacts; notes internal contradiction about generalizing to arbitrarily long/full-window contexts.

PrivDrift study: uses seeded multi-turn histories, content-dense intervening exchanges, and three standardized extraction conditions. Dataset: 1,000 dialogues containing one of phone numbers, email addresses, Social Security Numbers (SSNs), or credit card numbers. Detection method: normalized matching plus an open-weights judge. Reported hybrid dialogue-level leakage rates across the three evaluated models: 38.70%, 47.70%, and 54.60%. Authors state leakage varies by model, secret type, and persuasion intensity. SSNs and credit card numbers are reported to receive much stronger suppression than contact identifiers (phone, email). No system attains stable suppression within the tested drift lengths. Authors interpret results as an active-context behavioral privacy failure, not evidence of permanent memory.

PrivDrift (QX2) benchmark: N=1,000 seeded multi-turn dialogues, each contains one ground-truth secret S (phone A2L, email F8Z, SSN W3B, or credit card N6G) disclosed at t0. D = unrelated sequence of user/assistant turns (u_i,a_i). Drift length d (D7A) is number of turns between disclosure and final standardized probe P; d sampled Uniform{2,3,4,5,6} per Eq.(1). Probes: V4N persuasion intensities — C8R (Simple), Z2F (Medium), L9W (Hard). Models evaluated: M7Q=GPT-OSS-120B, T4X=DeepSeek-R1, Y9C=Qwen3-VL-235B via OpenRouter API; some responses cached. Detection methods: U3P (regex-only deterministic baseline), B6T (normalization-based matching using phi), H8D (hybrid: normalized inclusion OR LLM-as-judge/Llama judge binary verdict), R5J (post-hoc fuzzy matching). Metrics: probe-level P6S = one response observation per dialogue per persuasion; dialogue-level G4P = dialogue positive if any probe elicits secret. Leakage L(d) and immediate L(0). Delta (δ) safety threshold = 0.1 × L(0). K2V (Privacy Half-Life, τ) = earliest observed drift length meeting suppression threshold at that and every later observed length; τ assigned a specific value when no observed length qualifies. Δ = H8D augmentation over U3P (percentage points). CI: 95% bootstrap over dialogues for G4P. Stats: McNemar’s for matched model/detector and persuasion follow-ups (with Bonferroni where applicable); Cochran’s Q for repeated persuasion measures; Chi-square for independence vs D7A, V4N, or S8Q. Other terms: active-context privacy, behavioral recoverability, parameter-based memorization, training-data extraction, membership inference, unlearning, RAG systems, scaffold-then-rewrite, persona, ConfAIde, PrivacyLens/PrivaCI-Bench, Crescendo, TOFU/WMDP. Earlier reported hybrid dialogue-level leakage rates across the three models: 38.70%, 47.70%, 54.60%; authors state leakage varies by model, secret type, and persuasion intensity, with SSNs and credit cards more strongly suppressed than contact identifiers.

steps.notes_before: QX2 framework: N=1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues (900 synthetic, 100 human-written interspersed). Four secret types inserted as exact ground-truth: phone (A2L), email (F8Z), SSN (W3B), credit card (N6G). Drift-length D7A values reported as {0,2,3,4,5,6}; sampling: d=0 with p=0.2 (immediate recall), otherwise d ~ Uniform{2,3,4,5,6} (p=0.8). Avg/median words per dialogue 359.16/385 (range 43–795); approx. tokens avg/median 478.87/513.33 (range 57.33–1060). Scaffold-then-rewrite preserves exact secret, intervening-turn counts, roles, and final-probe conditions. Probes: three persuasion conditions C8R (simple), Z2F (medium), L9W (hard). Evaluation: hierarchical two-stage detection—Stage 1 B6T deterministic normalization (phi strips non-digit chars for numeric secrets; alphanumeric normalized for case/whitespace while retaining delimiters); leakage label Leak_U3P(R,S)=I[phi(S) subset phi(R)]. H8D (hybrid) labels responses positive if normalized inclusion or an LLM/judge finds full secret, substantial substring, or identifying partial info. Immediate recall included; short-to-medium topic-drift emphasized.

Dataset QX2: N=1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues (900 synthetic, 100 human-written interspersed). Four exact ground-truth secret types inserted: phone (A2L), email (F8Z), SSN (W3B), credit card (N6G). Drift-length D7A values reported as {0,2,3,4,5,6}; sampling: d=0 with p=0.2 (immediate recall), otherwise d ~ Uniform{2,3,4,5,6} (p=0.8). Avg/median words per dialogue 359.16/385 (range 43–795); approx. tokens avg/median 478.87/513.33 (range 57.33–1060). Scaffold-then-rewrite preserves exact secret, intervening-turn counts, roles, and final-probe conditions. Probes: three persuasion conditions C8R (simple), Z2F (medium), L9W (hard). Evaluation: hierarchical two-stage detection. Stage 1 (B6T deterministic normalization): phi strips non-digit chars for numeric secrets; alphanumeric normalized for case/whitespace while retaining delimiters; deterministic leakage label Leak_U3P(R,S)=I[phi(S) subset phi(R)]. Stage 2 (LLM-as-judge): an open-weights Llama judge is applied to deterministic negatives and returns a binary full/substantial-disclosure verdict (detects partial disclosures, indirect hints, and formatting variants); judge is fallible. The hybrid label H8D marks positive if deterministic inclusion OR the LLM judge finds full secret, substantial substring, or identifying partial info. K2V (Privacy Half-Life τ): uses observed lengths D_obs and leakage rates L(d); safety threshold δ = 0.1 × L(0) (L(0)=immediate-recall leakage). τ = min{ d ∈ D_obs | L(d) ≤ δ AND ∀ d' ∈ D_obs with d' > d: L(d') ≤ δ }. If no qualifying d, τ = max(D_obs) + 1. Figure 3: later resurgence disqualifies transient decreases.

Dataset QX2: N=1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues (900 synthetic, 100 human-written). Four ground-truth secret types inserted: phone (A2L), email (F8Z), SSN (W3B), credit card (N6G). Drift-length D7A values {0,2,3,4,5,6}; sampling: d=0 with p=0.2 (immediate recall), otherwise d ~ Uniform{2,3,4,5,6} (p=0.8). Dialogue length: avg/median words 359.16/385 (range 43–795); tokens avg/median 478.87/513.33 (range 57.33–1060). Scaffold-then-rewrite preserves exact secret, intervening-turn counts, roles, and final-probe conditions. Probes: three persuasion conditions C8R (simple), Z2F (medium), L9W (hard).

Detection pipeline: Stage 1 deterministic normalization phi (numeric: strip non-digits; alphanumeric: normalize case/whitespace, retain delimiters). Deterministic leakage Leak_U3P(R,S)=I[phi(S) subset phi(R)]. Stage 2 Llama judge applied to deterministic negatives to decide full/substantial-disclosure (fallible). Hybrid H8D = deterministic OR LLM-judge positive.

K2V (Privacy Half-Life τ): use observed D_obs and leakage rates L(d); safety threshold δ = 0.1 × L(0). τ = min{d ∈ D_obs | L(d) ≤ δ AND ∀d' > d: L(d') ≤ δ}; if none, τ = max(D_obs) + 1. Note: Figure 3 treats later resurgence as disqualifying transient decreases.

Models & querying: GPT-OSS-120B (M7Q), DeepSeek-R1 (T4X), Qwen3-VL-235B (Y9C), queried via OpenRouter API. Each model processes full QX2 with one seeded secret and one sampled d per dialogue under every standardized condition. Cached responses: Per model = 3,000; All models = 9,000 (consistent with 1,000 dialogues × 3 persuasion probes).

Aggregation: G4P = dialogue-level any-probe disclosure; P6S = per-dialogue per-persuasion-condition observations; R5J = post-hoc normalized-similarity (fuzzy match).

Stats: G4P 95% CIs via bootstrap over dialogues; matched tests use McNemar (Bonferroni as needed); repeated persuasion measures use Cochran’s Q then McNemar; chi-square tests for independence with Cramer’s V reported as effect size.

final_notes: PrivDrift benchmark: audits active-context privacy leakage under topic drift and persuasion intensity. Models: GPT-OSS-120B, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3-VL-235B. Dataset: 1,000 dialogues per model seeded with one secret; manuscript inconsistent about origin (some parts say all 1,000 pipeline-generated; Part 9 says 900 synthetic + 100 human-authored) and cached metadata reportedly does not preserve mapping to human-authored rows. Probes: 3 standardized persuasion probes → 3,000 model-probe responses per model. Detector: hierarchical hybrid — Stage1 regex normalization (Leak_regex), Stage2 Llama judge applied to regex-negative outputs; fuzzy-matching thresholds (~0.85/0.80) track hybrid closely. Aggregation at probe- and response-level; dialogue-level leak = any probe elicits secret. Key results: dialogue-level hybrid leakage — DeepSeek 38.70% [35.7,41.6], GPT-OSS 47.70% [44.6,50.8], Qwen 54.60% [51.6,57.7]; regex-only slightly lower. Probe-level hybrid averages: DeepSeek 26.43, GPT-OSS 37.57, Qwen 37.53. Persuasion: Cochran's Q p<1e-5; per-model non-monotonic patterns. Topic drift: small-to-negligible effect sizes (Cramer’s V range ≈0.065–0.107), with dip at d=3 and no reliable decay within tested d ∈ {0,2,3,4,5,6}; privacy half-life τ ≈ 7 (extrapolated beyond observed window). Secret type is the strongest predictor of leakage (probe-level Cramer’s V ≈0.59–0.77); SSN/CC leak less than emails/phones. Appendix A (Table 7) dataset counts by drift sum to 1000 (d=0:197, d=2:147, d=3:142, d=4:166, d=5:181, d=6:167) and include avg/median words and token estimates. Appendix B (Table 8) probe-level Cramer’s V for hybrid leakage associations: DeepSeek — secret type 0.5871 (Large), drift length 0.1073 (Small), persuasion 0.0718 (Negligible); GPT-OSS — secret type 0.7731 (Large), drift 0.0659 (Negligible), persuasion 0.0689 (Negligible); Qwen — secret type 0.6927 (Large), drift 0.0723 (Negligible), persuasion 0.0639 (Negligible). Appendix C: Figure 6 dialogue construction details. Limitations: bounded drift only, fixed-format secrets, active-context only, cached metadata loss, detector-equivalence claim overreaches. Authors plan to release generation code, probe templates, evaluation scripts, aggregate results and a sanitized subset.

Title: PrivDrift — auditing user-secret leakage under topic drift in active LLM conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University). Contact: lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu. Abstract key points: introduces PrivDrift benchmark of 1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues with seeded secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction probes. Evaluated across three LLMs with extended context windows. Reports dialogue-level hybrid leakage between 38.7% and 54.6%, with strong variation by model, secret type, and persuasion intensity. Within the tested drift window, additional topic drift does not reliably reduce leakage; conclusion: privacy risk should be viewed as a persistent behavioral failure mode, not only memorization or immediate jailbreaks. Keywords: Trustworthy AI, LLMs, Privacy, Evaluation, Benchmarking.

Title: PrivDrift — auditing user-secret leakage under topic drift in active LLM conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University). Contact: lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu. Benchmark: PrivDrift — controlled benchmark of 1,000 multi-turn dialogues per model with seeded secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction probes. Evaluated across three LLMs with extended context windows. Core axes: topic drift (number d of unrelated turns between secret disclosure and probe; tested window d ≤ 6) and persuasion intensity (interaction style: direct, justified, high-pressure). Main quantitative claim: dialogue-level hybrid leakage under hybrid detector ranges 38.7%–54.6%; leakage varies strongly by model, secret type (SSNs and credit cards suppressed far more often than emails and phone numbers), and persuasion intensity. Hybrid detector: normalization-based matching + open-weights LLM judge; reported metrics include dialogue-level, probe-level, regex-only, fuzzy, and hybrid leakage rates. Key finding: within tested drift window, additional topic drift does not reliably reduce leakage; authors introduce Privacy Half-Life (τ), a stability-based metric, and report that no evaluated model reaches stable decay within observed drift range. Contributions summarized: benchmark, probe styles, hybrid detector & metrics, Privacy Half-Life analysis. Keywords: Trustworthy AI, LLMs, Privacy, Evaluation, Benchmarking.

Related work summarized: (1) Contextual privacy/inference-time leakage distinguished from training-data extraction; other benchmarks (ConfAIde, PrivacyLens, PrivaCI-Bench) focus on static access-control/privacy-norm reasoning, whereas PrivDrift isolates persistence of user-disclosed secrets after topic drift and persuasion probes. steps.notes_before: Evaluation uses a hierarchical hybrid detector: Stage 1 normalization-based matching (φ) detects verbatim/near-verbatim leaks; numeric secrets: strip non-digits; alphanumeric: normalize case/whitespace, preserve meaningful delimiters. Regex-stage label: Leak_regex(R,S)=I[φ(S)⊂φ(R)]. Stage 2: open-weights Llama judge (Meta AI, 2024) inspects regex-negative responses and returns a binary verdict for partial/indirect disclosures; paper reports regex-only and hybrid rates separately. Privacy Half-Life τ: D_obs = observed drift lengths, L(d)=leakage rate at d, safety threshold δ=0.1×L(0). τ = min{d∈D_obs | L(d)≤δ and ∀d'>d in D_obs: L(d')≤δ}; if empty τ = max(D_obs)+1 to avoid counting transient dips. Caveat: earlier parts ambiguously defined d (dialogue element count vs. number of drift turns), so interpretation of 'drift length' in L(d), D_obs, and τ is unclear. Other earlier details retained: N=1000 dialogues (900 synthetic +100 human-authored mixed), secret types: phone/email/SSN/credit card, drift lengths sampled from {0,2,3,4,5,6} (d=0 with p=0.2, else uniform over 2–6).

Title: PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University), contact lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu. Abstract claims: persistent, user-facing, shared-session, tool-augmented LLMs can retain behaviorally recoverable sensitive disclosures even after unrelated tasks; introduces a controlled benchmark called PrivDrift (QX2) that uses seeded multi-turn histories, content-dense intervening exchanges, and standardized extraction probes to audit persistence. Keywords: Trustworthy AI, LLM Privacy, Evaluation, Benchmarking. PrivDrift benchmark: 1,000 controlled dialogues with seeded secrets, unrelated intervening turns, and standardized extraction probes. Three models evaluated; probes classified as direct, justified, and high-pressure. Hybrid detector: normalized matching combined with an LLM judge. Dialogue-level leakage defined as whether any standardized probe elicits the secret; observed leakage ranges 38.7%–54.6%. Persuasion effects depend on model. Secret types: Social Security Numbers and credit card numbers are suppressed more often than emails and phone numbers. Drift parameter d tested up to d ≤ 6; within this range additional drift does not reliably reduce leakage. Conclusion: no evaluated model meets the paper's criterion for stable suppression. Note: glossary header present but content not shown in this part.

PrivDrift benchmark: 1,000 controlled dialogues with seeded secrets (SSN, credit card, email, phone) inserted and later targeted by standardized probes after content-dense topic drift. Drift length d = number of turns between secret disclosure (t0) and final probe; sampled with Uniform{2,3,4,5,6}, tested up to d ≤ 6. Probes / persuasion levels: Simple (direct/neutral), Medium (contextual justification), Hard (high-pressure/urgent) — corresponds to earlier labels direct/justified/high-pressure. Three evaluated models: GPT-OSS-120B (GPT-OSS), DeepSeek-R1 (DeepSeek), Qwen3-VL-235B (Qwen); models queried via OpenRouter API; some responses cached. Detection/hybrid evaluation: normalization-based (regex) matching φ(·) and fuzzy matching; when regex returns negative, an open-weights Llama judge (LLM-as-judge) is used. Leakage event: response reveals the secret exactly, approximately, or semantically. Metrics: probe-level and dialogue-level leakage (dialogue-level = any probe elicits the secret); Δ = additional dialogue-level leakage hybrid vs regex. Privacy Half-Life τ: earliest observed drift length ≤ safety threshold δ = 0.1×L(0) with no later resurgence; D_obs = observed drift lengths. Statistical methods: 95% bootstrap CIs over dialogues, McNemar’s test for paired comparisons (with Bonferroni where applicable), Cochran’s Q across persuasion levels, χ2 and Cramer’s V for associations. Reported findings: observed dialogue-level leakage ≈ 38.7%–54.6%; persuasion effects vary by model; SSNs and credit card numbers are suppressed more often than emails/phone numbers; within tested range additional drift does not reliably reduce leakage; no evaluated model meets the paper’s stability/suppression criterion. Pipeline notes: parametric dialogue generator, scaffold-then-rewrite naturalistic refinement, cached responses.

PrivDrift study: uses seeded multi-turn histories, content-dense intervening exchanges, and three standardized extraction conditions. Dataset: 1,000 dialogues containing one of phone numbers, email addresses, Social Security Numbers (SSNs), or credit card numbers. Detection method: normalized matching plus an open-weights judge. Reported hybrid dialogue-level leakage rates across the three evaluated models: 38.70%, 47.70%, and 54.60%. Authors state leakage varies by model, secret type, and persuasion intensity. Authors interpret results as an active-context behavioral privacy failure, not evidence of permanent memory.

PrivDrift (QX2) benchmark: N=1,000 seeded multi-turn dialogues, each contains one ground-truth secret S (phone A2L, email F8Z, SSN W3B, or credit card N6G) disclosed at t0. Title: PrivDrift — auditing user-secret leakage under topic drift in active LLM conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University). Contact: lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu. Abstract key points: introduces PrivDrift benchmark of 1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues with seeded secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction probes. Evaluated across three LLMs with extended context windows. Reports dialogue-level hybrid leakage between 38.7% and 54.6%, with strong variation by model, secret type, and persuasion intensity. Within the tested drift window, additional topic drift does not reliably reduce leakage; conclusion: privacy risk should be viewed as a persistent behavioral failure mode, not only memorization or immediate jailbreaks. Keywords: Trustworthy AI, LLMs, Privacy, Evaluation, Benchmarking.

Title: PrivDrift — auditing user-secret leakage under topic drift in active LLM conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University). Contact: lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu. Benchmark: PrivDrift — controlled benchmark of 1,000 multi-turn dialogues per model with seeded secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction probes. Evaluated across three LLMs with extended context windows. Core axes: topic drift (number d of unrelated turns between secret disclosure and probe; tested window d ≤ 6) and persuasion intensity (interaction style: direct, justified, high-pressure). Main quantitative claim: dialogue-level hybrid leakage under hybrid detector ranges 38.7%–54.6%; leakage varies strongly by model, secret type (SSNs and credit cards suppressed far more often than emails and phone numbers), and persuasion intensity. Hybrid detector: normalization-based matching + open-weights LLM judge; reported metrics include dialogue-level, probe-level, regex-only, fuzzy, and hybrid leakage rates. Key finding: within tested drift window, additional topic drift does not reliably reduce leakage; authors introduce Privacy Half-Life (τ), a stability-based metric, and report that no evaluated model reaches stable decay within observed drift range. Contributions summarized: benchmark, probe styles, hybrid detector & metrics, Privacy Half-Life analysis. Keywords: Trustworthy AI, LLMs, Privacy, Evaluation, Benchmarking.

Contributions: benchmark, probe styles, hybrid detector & metrics, Privacy Half-Life analysis. Related work summarized: (1) Contextual privacy/inference-time leakage distinguished from training-data extraction; other benchmarks (ConfAIde, PrivacyLens, PrivaCI-Bench) focus on static access-control/privacy-norm reasoning, whereas PrivDrift isolates persistence of user-disclosed secrets after topic drift and persuasion probes. (2) Multi-turn adversarial attacks (Crescendo, automated jailbreaks, prompt injection) motivate treating information flow control across turns. (3) Context management and unlearning (TOFU, WMDP) operate on model weights/static QA; PrivDrift targets active-context suppression relevant to RAG, copilots, and agentic workflows.

steps.notes_before: Evaluation uses a hierarchical hybrid detector: Stage 1 normalization-based matching (φ) detects verbatim/near-verbatim leaks; numeric secrets: strip non-digits; alphanumeric: normalize case/whitespace, preserve meaningful delimiters. Regex-stage label: Leak_regex(R,S)=I[φ(S)⊂φ(R)]. Stage 2: open-weights Llama judge (Meta AI, 2024) inspects regex-negative responses and returns a binary verdict for partial/indirect disclosures; paper reports regex-only and hybrid rates separately. Privacy Half-Life τ: D_obs = observed drift lengths, L(d)=leakage rate at d, safety threshold δ=0.1×L(0). τ = min{d∈D_obs | L(d)≤δ and ∀d'>d in D_obs: L(d')≤δ}; if empty τ = max(D_obs)+1 to avoid counting transient dips. Caveat: earlier parts ambiguously defined d (dialogue element count vs. number of drift turns), so interpretation of 'drift length' in L(d), D_obs, and τ is unclear. Title: PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University), contact lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu. Abstract claims: persistent, user-facing, shared-session, tool-augmented LLMs can retain behaviorally recoverable sensitive disclosures even after unrelated tasks; introduces a controlled benchmark called PrivDrift (QX2) that uses seeded multi-turn histories, content-dense intervening exchanges, and standardized extraction probes to audit persistence. Reports that across extended-context models, a metric/phenomenon labelled "G4P under H8D" remains substantial, varies sharply across systems and two other labels "S8Q" and "V4N", and does not reliably decline within the tested window. Conclusion: active-context privacy should be evaluated as persistent behavioral failure rather than only parameter memorization or immediate jailbreak behavior. Keywords: Trustworthy AI, LLM Privacy, Evaluation, Benchmarking. Points to check later: definitions and meanings of acronyms QX2/PrivDrift, G4P, H8D, S8Q, V4N; experimental setup (seeded histories, intervening exchanges, extraction probes), which models are considered "extended-context", the tested window length, and evidence for "fails to decline reliably" and per-system variability.

Note: G4P can exceed the mean condition-specific rate. Uncertainty/tests: G4P intervals use 95% bootstrap over dialogues; P6S sensitivity checks use cached model-probe responses. Matched model/detector comparisons use McNemar’s test (Bonferroni-corrected where applicable); repeated persuasion measures use Cochran’s Q followed by McNemar tests. PrivDrift benchmark: 1,000 controlled dialogues with seeded secrets, unrelated intervening turns, and standardized extraction probes. Three models evaluated; probes classified as direct, justified, and high-pressure. Hybrid detector: normalized matching combined with an LLM judge. Dialogue-level leakage defined as whether any standardized probe elicits the secret; observed leakage ranges 38.7%–54.6%. Persuasion effects depend on model. Secret types: Social Security Numbers and credit card numbers are suppressed more often than emails and phone numbers. Drift parameter d tested up to d ≤ 6; within this range additional drift does not reliably reduce leakage. Conclusion: no evaluated model meets the paper's criterion for stable suppression. Note: glossary header present but content not shown in this part.

PrivDrift benchmark: 1,000 controlled dialogues with seeded secrets (SSN, credit card, email, phone) inserted and later targeted by standardized probes after content-dense topic drift. Drift length d = number of turns between secret disclosure (t0) and final probe; sampled with Uniform{2,3,4,5,6}, tested up to d ≤ 6. Probes / persuasion levels: Simple (direct/neutral), Medium (contextual justification), Hard (high-pressure/urgent) — corresponds to earlier labels direct/justified/high-pressure. Three evaluated models: GPT-OSS-120B (GPT-OSS), DeepSeek-R1 (DeepSeek), Qwen3-VL-235B (Qwen); models queried via OpenRouter API; some responses cached. Detection/hybrid evaluation: normalization-based (regex) matching φ(·) and fuzzy matching; when regex returns negative, an open-weights Llama judge (LLM-as-judge) is used. Leakage event: response reveals the secret exactly, approximately, or semantically. Metrics: probe-level and dialogue-level leakage (dialogue-level = any probe elicits the secret); Δ = additional dialogue-level leakage hybrid vs regex. Privacy Half-Life τ: earliest observed drift length ≤ safety threshold δ = 0.1×L(0) with no later resurgence; D_obs = observed drift lengths. Statistical methods: 95% bootstrap CIs over dialogues, McNemar’s test for paired comparisons (with Bonferroni where applicable), Cochran’s Q across persuasion levels, χ2 and Cramer’s V for associations. Reported findings: observed dialogue-level leakage ≈ 38.7%–54.6%; persuasion effects vary by model; SSNs and credit card numbers are suppressed more often than emails/phone numbers; within tested range additional drift does not reliably reduce leakage; no evaluated model meets the paper’s stability/suppression criterion. Pipeline notes: parametric dialogue generator, scaffold-then-rewrite naturalistic refinement, cached responses.

PrivDrift study: uses seeded multi-turn histories, content-dense intervening exchanges, and three standardized extraction conditions. Dataset: 1,000 dialogues containing one of phone numbers, email addresses, Social Security Numbers (SSNs), or credit card numbers. Detection method: normalized matching plus an open-weights judge. Reported hybrid dialogue-level leakage rates across the three evaluated models: 38.70%, 47.70%, and 54.60%. Authors state leakage varies by model, secret type, and persuasion intensity. SSNs and credit card numbers are reported to receive much stronger suppression than contact identifiers (phone, email). No system attains stable suppression within the tested drift lengths. Authors interpret results as an active-context behavioral privacy failure, not evidence of permanent memory.

PrivDrift (QX2) benchmark: N=1,000 seeded multi-turn dialogues, each contains one ground-truth secret S (phone A2L, email F8Z, SSN W3B, or credit card N6G) disclosed at t0. D = unrelated sequence of user/assistant turns (u_i,a_i). Drift length d (D7A) is number of turns between disclosure and final standardized probe P; d sampled Uniform{2,3,4,5,6} per Eq.(1). Probes: V4N persuasion intensities — C8R (Simple), Z2F (Medium), L9W (Hard). Models evaluated: M7Q=GPT-OSS-120B, T4X=DeepSeek-R1, Y9C=Qwen3-VL-235B via OpenRouter API; some responses cached. Detection methods: U3P (regex-only deterministic baseline), B6T (normalization-based matching using phi), H8D (hybrid: normalized inclusion OR LLM-as-judge/Llama judge binary verdict), R5J (post-hoc fuzzy matching). Metrics: probe-level P6S = one response observation per dialogue per persuasion; dialogue-level G4P = dialogue positive if any probe elicits secret. Leakage L(d) and immediate L(0). Delta (δ) safety threshold = 0.1 × L(0). K2V (Privacy Half-Life, τ) = earliest observed drift length meeting suppression threshold at that and every later observed length; τ assigned a specific value when no observed length qualifies. Δ = H8D augmentation over U3P (percentage points). CI: 95% bootstrap over dialogues for G4P. Stats: McNemar’s for matched model/detector and persuasion follow-ups (with Bonferroni where applicable); Cochran’s Q for repeated persuasion measures; Chi-square for independence vs D7A, V4N, or S8Q. Other terms: active-context privacy, behavioral recoverability, parameter-based memorization, training-data extraction, membership inference, unlearning, RAG systems, scaffold-then-rewrite, persona, ConfAIde, PrivacyLens/PrivaCI-Bench, Crescendo, TOFU/WMDP. Earlier reported hybrid dialogue-level leakage rates across the three models: 38.70%, 47.70%, 54.60%; authors state leakage varies by model, secret type, and persuasion intensity, with SSNs and credit cards more strongly suppressed than contact identifiers.

steps.notes_before: QX2 framework: N=1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues (900 synthetic, 100 human-written interspersed). Four secret types inserted as exact ground-truth: phone (A2L), email (F8Z), SSN (W3B), credit card (N6G). Drift-length D7A values reported as {0,2,3,4,5,6}; sampling: d=0 with p=0.2 (immediate recall), otherwise d ~ Uniform{2,3,4,5,6} (p=0.8). Avg/median words per dialogue 359.16/385 (range 43–795); approx. tokens avg/median 478.87/513.33 (range 57.33–1060). Scaffold-then-rewrite preserves exact secret, intervening-turn counts, roles, and final-probe conditions. Probes: three persuasion conditions C8R (simple), Z2F (medium), L9W (hard). Evaluation: hierarchical two-stage detection—Stage 1 B6T deterministic normalization (phi strips non-digit chars for numeric secrets; alphanumeric normalized for case/whitespace while retaining delimiters); leakage label Leak_U3P(R,S)=I[phi(S) subset phi(R)]. H8D (hybrid) labels responses positive if normalized inclusion or an LLM/judge finds full secret, substantial substring, or identifying partial info. Immediate recall included; short-to-medium topic-drift emphasized.

Dataset QX2: N=1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues (900 synthetic, 100 human-written interspersed). Four exact ground-truth secret types inserted: phone (A2L), email (F8Z), SSN (W3B), credit card (N6G). Drift-length D7A values reported as {0,2,3,4,5,6}; sampling: d=0 with p=0.2 (immediate recall), otherwise d ~ Uniform{2,3,4,5,6} (p=0.8). Avg/median words per dialogue 359.16/385 (range 43–795); approx. tokens avg/median 478.87/513.33 (range 57.33–1060). Scaffold-then-rewrite preserves exact secret, intervening-turn counts, roles, and final-probe conditions. Probes: three persuasion conditions C8R (simple), Z2F (medium), L9W (hard). Evaluation: hierarchical two-stage detection. Stage 1 (B6T deterministic normalization): phi strips non-digit chars for numeric secrets; alphanumeric normalized for case/whitespace while retaining delimiters; deterministic leakage label Leak_U3P(R,S)=I[phi(S) subset phi(R)]. Stage 2 (LLM-as-judge): an open-weights Llama judge is applied to deterministic negatives and returns a binary full/substantial-disclosure verdict (detects partial disclosures, indirect hints, and formatting variants); judge is fallible. The hybrid label H8D marks positive if deterministic inclusion OR the LLM judge finds full secret, substantial substring, or identifying partial info. K2V (Privacy Half-Life τ): uses observed lengths D_obs and leakage rates L(d); safety threshold δ = 0.1 × L(0) (L(0)=immediate-recall leakage). τ = min{ d ∈ D_obs | L(d) ≤ δ AND ∀ d' ∈ D_obs with d' > d: L(d') ≤ δ }. If no qualifying d, τ = max(D_obs) + 1. Figure 3: later resurgence disqualifies transient decreases.

Dataset QX2: N=1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues (900 synthetic, 100 human-written). Four ground-truth secret types inserted: phone (A2L), email (F8Z), SSN (W3B), credit card (N6G). Drift-length D7A values {0,2,3,4,5,6}; sampling: d=0 with p=0.2 (immediate recall), otherwise d ~ Uniform{2,3,4,5,6} (p=0.8). Dialogue length: avg/median words 359.16/385 (range 43–795); tokens avg/median 478.87/513.33 (range 57.33–1060). Scaffold-then-rewrite preserves exact secret, intervening-turn counts, roles, and final-probe conditions. Probes: three persuasion conditions C8R (simple), Z2F (medium), L9W (hard).

Detection pipeline: Stage 1 deterministic normalization phi (numeric: strip non-digits; alphanumeric: normalize case/whitespace, retain delimiters). Deterministic leakage Leak_U3P(R,S)=I[phi(S) subset phi(R)]. Stage 2 Llama judge applied to deterministic negatives to decide full/substantial-disclosure (fallible). Hybrid H8D = deterministic OR LLM-judge positive.

K2V (Privacy Half-Life τ): use observed D_obs and leakage rates L(d); safety threshold δ = 0.1 × L(0). τ = min{d ∈ D_obs | L(d) ≤ δ AND ∀d' > d: L(d') ≤ δ}; if none, τ = max(D_obs) + 1. Note: Figure 3 treats later resurgence as disqualifying transient decreases.

Models & querying: GPT-OSS-120B (M7Q), DeepSeek-R1 (T4X), Qwen3-VL-235B (Y9C), queried via OpenRouter API. Each model processes full QX2 with one seeded secret and one sampled d per dialogue under every standardized condition. Cached responses: Per model = 3,000; All models = 9,000 (consistent with 1,000 dialogues × 3 persuasion probes).

Aggregation: G4P = dialogue-level any-probe disclosure; P6S = per-dialogue per-persuasion-condition observations; R5J = post-hoc normalized-similarity (fuzzy match).

Stats: G4P 95% CIs via bootstrap over dialogues; matched tests use McNemar (Bonferroni as needed); repeated persuasion measures use Cochran’s Q then McNemar; chi-square tests for independence with Cramer’s V reported as effect size.

Title: PrivDrift — auditing user-secret leakage under topic drift in active LLM conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University). Contact: lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu. Abstract key points: introduces PrivDrift benchmark of 1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues with seeded secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction probes. Evaluated across three LLMs with extended context windows. Reports dialogue-level hybrid leakage between 38.7% and 54.6%, with strong variation by model, secret type, and persuasion intensity. Within the tested drift window, additional topic drift does not reliably reduce leakage; conclusion: privacy risk should be viewed as a persistent behavioral failure mode, not only memorization or immediate jailbreaks. Keywords: Trustworthy AI, LLMs, Privacy, Evaluation, Benchmarking.

Title: PrivDrift — auditing user-secret leakage under topic drift in active LLM conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University). Contact: lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu. Benchmark: PrivDrift — controlled benchmark of 1,000 multi-turn dialogues per model with seeded secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction probes. Evaluated across three LLMs with extended context windows. Core axes: topic drift (number d of unrelated turns between secret disclosure and probe; tested window d ≤ 6) and persuasion intensity (interaction style: direct, justified, high-pressure). Main quantitative claim: dialogue-level hybrid leakage under hybrid detector ranges 38.7%–54.6%; leakage varies strongly by model, secret type (SSNs and credit cards suppressed far more often than emails and phone numbers), and persuasion intensity. Hybrid detector: normalization-based matching + open-weights LLM judge; reported metrics include dialogue-level, probe-level, regex-only, fuzzy, and hybrid leakage rates. Key finding: within tested drift window, additional topic drift does not reliably reduce leakage; authors introduce Privacy Half-Life (τ), a stability-based metric, and report that no evaluated model reaches stable decay within observed drift range. Contributions summarized: benchmark, probe styles, hybrid detector & metrics, Privacy Half-Life analysis. Keywords: Trustworthy AI, LLMs, Privacy, Evaluation, Benchmarking.

Related work summarized: (1) Contextual privacy/inference-time leakage distinguished from training-data extraction; other benchmarks (ConfAIde, PrivacyLens, PrivaCI-Bench) focus on static access-control/privacy-norm reasoning, whereas PrivDrift isolates persistence of user-disclosed secrets after topic drift and persuasion probes. (2) Multi-turn adversarial attacks (Crescendo, automated jailbreaks, prompt injection) motivate treating information flow control across turns. (3) Context management and unlearning (TOFU, WMDP) operate on model weights/static QA; PrivDrift targets active-context suppression relevant to RAG, copilots, and agentic workflows.

steps.notes_before: Evaluation uses a hierarchical hybrid detector: Stage 1 normalization-based matching (φ) detects verbatim/near-verbatim leaks; numeric secrets: strip non-digits; alphanumeric: normalize case/whitespace, preserve meaningful delimiters. Regex-stage label: Leak_regex(R,S)=I[φ(S)⊂φ(R)]. Stage 2: open-weights Llama judge (Meta AI, 2024) inspects regex-negative responses and returns a binary verdict for partial/indirect disclosures; paper reports regex-only and hybrid rates separately. Privacy Half-Life τ: D_obs = observed drift lengths, L(d)=leakage rate at d, safety threshold δ=0.1×L(0). τ = min{d∈D_obs | L(d)≤δ and ∀d'>d in D_obs: L(d')≤δ}; if empty τ = max(D_obs)+1 to avoid counting transient dips. Caveat: earlier parts ambiguously defined d (dialogue element count vs. number of drift turns), so interpretation of 'drift length' in L(d), D_obs, and τ is unclear. Other earlier details retained: N=1000 dialogues (900 synthetic +100 human-authored mixed), secret types: phone/email/SSN/credit card, drift lengths sampled from {0,2,3,4,5,6} (d=0 with p=0.2, else uniform over 2–6).

Title: PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University), contact lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu. Abstract claims: persistent, user-facing, shared-session, tool-augmented LLMs can retain behaviorally recoverable sensitive disclosures even after unrelated tasks; introduces a controlled benchmark called PrivDrift (QX2) that uses seeded multi-turn histories, content-dense intervening exchanges, and standardized extraction probes to audit persistence. Reports that across extended-context models, a metric/phenomenon labelled "G4P under H8D" remains substantial, varies sharply across systems and two other labels "S8Q" and "V4N", and does not reliably decline within the tested window. Conclusion: active-context privacy should be evaluated as persistent behavioral failure rather than only parameter memorization or immediate jailbreak behavior. Keywords: Trustworthy AI, LLM Privacy, Evaluation, Benchmarking. Points to check later: definitions and meanings of acronyms QX2/PrivDrift, G4P, H8D, S8Q, V4N; experimental setup (seeded histories, intervening exchanges, extraction probes), which models are considered "extended-context", the tested window length, and evidence for "fails to decline reliably" and per-system variability.

PrivDrift benchmark: 1,000 controlled dialogues with seeded secrets (SSN, credit card, email, phone) inserted and later targeted by standardized probes after content-dense topic drift. Drift length d = number of turns between secret disclosure (t0) and final probe; sampled with Uniform{2,3,4,5,6}, tested up to d ≤ 6. Probes / persuasion levels: Simple (direct/neutral), Medium (contextual justification), Hard (high-pressure/urgent) — corresponds to earlier labels direct/justified/high-pressure. Three evaluated models: GPT-OSS-120B (GPT-OSS), DeepSeek-R1 (DeepSeek), Qwen3-VL-235B (Qwen); models queried via OpenRouter API; some responses cached. Detection/hybrid evaluation: normalization-based (regex) matching φ(·) and fuzzy matching; when regex returns negative, an open-weights Llama judge (LLM-as-judge) is used. Leakage event: response reveals the secret exactly, approximately, or semantically. Metrics: probe-level and dialogue-level leakage (dialogue-level = any probe elicits the secret); Δ = additional dialogue-level leakage hybrid vs regex. Privacy Half-Life τ: earliest observed drift length ≤ safety threshold δ = 0.1×L(0) with no later resurgence; D_obs = observed drift lengths. Statistical methods: 95% bootstrap CIs over dialogues, McNemar’s test for paired comparisons (with Bonferroni where applicable), Cochran’s Q across persuasion levels, χ2 and Cramer’s V for associations. Reported findings: observed dialogue-level leakage ≈ 38.7%–54.6%; persuasion effects vary by model; SSNs and credit card numbers are suppressed more often than emails/phone numbers; within tested range additional drift does not reliably reduce leakage; no evaluated model meets the paper’s stability/suppression criterion. Pipeline notes: parametric dialogue generator, scaffold-then-rewrite naturalistic refinement, cached responses.

Paper asks whether unrelated conversational tasks (drift) prevent later disclosure of sensitive info in an active LLM conversation. Method (PrivDrift): seeded multi-turn histories, content-dense intervening exchanges, three standardized extraction conditions. Dataset: 1,000 dialogues containing phone numbers, email addresses, Social Security Numbers (SSNs), or credit card numbers. Detection: normalized matching combined with an open-weights judge. Reported hybrid dialogue-level leakage across three evaluated models: 38.70%, 47.70%, and 54.60%. Leakage varies by model, secret type, and persuasion intensity. SSNs and credit card numbers show much stronger suppression than contact identifiers (phone/email). No system attains stable suppression within the tested drift lengths. Authors interpret results as an active-context behavioral privacy failure, not evidence of permanent memory.

PrivDrift (QX2) audits re-disclosure of user-supplied secrets S (phone A2L, email F8Z, SSN W3B, credit card N6G) inserted at time t0. Dataset: N = 1,000 dialogues. Each dialogue includes a drift sequence D of user/assistant exchanges (u_i, a_i) of length d (D7A). Drift lengths sampled Uniform({2,3,4,5,6}) per Eq.(1); immediate-recall leakage L(0) also defined. Final standardized probe P appended; three persuasion intensities V4N: C8R (Simple), Z2F (Medium), L9W (Hard). Models evaluated: M7Q (GPT-OSS-120B), T4X (DeepSeek-R1), Y9C (Qwen3-VL-235B) via OpenRouter API; some cached responses used. Detection: deterministic regex-only baseline U3P; normalization phi applied for inclusion checking (indicator I, B6T); H8D hybrid = normalized inclusion OR Llama judge (open-weights binary disclosure verdict). R5J fuzzy matching used post-hoc. Metrics: probe-level P6S (one response observation per persuasion condition per dialogue) and dialogue-level G4P (dialogue positive if any probe elicits the secret). Delta (safety threshold) = 0.1 * L(0). K2V (Privacy Half-Life, tau) = earliest observed d meeting suppression threshold at that and every later observed length (tau includes assigned value when none qualifies). Reported tests: McNemar, Cochran’s Q, Chi-square; effect size X2H = Cramer’s V. Reported hybrid dialogue-level leakage across three models: 38.70%, 47.70%, 54.60%. Authors report SSNs and credit cards show stronger suppression than contact identifiers and that no system attains stable suppression within tested drift lengths.

PrivDrift (QX2) audits persistent re-disclosure of user-seeded secrets S (phone, email, SSN, credit card) inserted at t0 in N=1,000 dialogues. Table 5 (as quoted) gives for models M7Q/T4X/Y9C: W3B and N6G rows 0.14%/1.11%/5.97% and 0.00%/0.39%/4.01% (low rates), and F8Z and A2L rows 78.24%/57.11%/81.13% and 70.89%/46.13%/57.24% (high rates). No evaluated system attains stable decay: Section 5.6 reports for every model-and-condition with observed d ≤ 6 an assigned tau = 7 (i.e., no qualifying stabilization within window).

PrivDrift (QX2) audits persistent re-disclosure of user-seeded secrets S (phone, email, SSN, credit card) inserted at t0 across N=1,000 dialogues. Each dialogue has a drift sequence D with length d ~ Uniform{2,3,4,5,6}; immediate-recall leakage L(0) defined. A standardized probe P is appended under three persuasion intensities V4N: C8R (Simple), Z2F (Medium), L9W (Hard). Models: M7Q (GPT-OSS-120B), T4X (DeepSeek-R1), Y9C (Qwen3-VL-235B). Detection: regex baseline U3P; normalization φ and indicator I/B6T; hybrid H8D = normalized inclusion OR Llama judge; R5J fuzzy matching used post-hoc. Metrics: probe-level P6S (one response observation per dialogue & persuasion condition), dialogue-level G4P (dialogue positive if any probe elicits secret). Safety delta = 0.1 * L(0). Privacy half-life K2V (τ) = earliest d meeting suppression threshold at that and every later observed length; set τ = d_max+1 when none qualifies (reported τ=7 for all evaluated model/condition windows d ≤ 6). Stats: McNemar, Cochran’s Q, Chi-square; Cramer’s V. Reported hybrid dialogue-level leakage (G4P, H8D): T4X 38.70%, M7Q 47.70%, Y9C 54.60% (Table 3). Contact identifiers leak far more than government/payment: Table 5 shows W3B/N6G rows (low) 0.14%/1.11%/5.97% and 0.00%/0.39%/4.01%; F8Z/A2L rows (high) 78.24%/57.11%/81.13% and 70.89%/46.13%/57.24%. Related work: QX2 distinguishes active-context recoverability (re-disclosure after unrelated exchanges and persuasive probing) from parameter-held training-data extraction, static privacy-norm tests (ConfAIde, PrivacyLens, PrivaCI-Bench), multi-turn adversarial harms (Crescendo, etc.), and parameter unlearning (TOFU, WMDP); emphasizes prompt/context management in deployed systems (RAG, copilots).

Title: PrivDrift — auditing user-secret leakage under topic drift in active LLM conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University). Contact: lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu. Abstract key points: introduces PrivDrift benchmark of 1,000 controlled multi-turn dialogues with seeded secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction probes. Evaluated across three LLMs with extended context windows. Reports dialogue-level hybrid leakage between 38.7% and 54.6%, with strong variation by model, secret type, and persuasion intensity. Within the tested drift window, additional topic drift does not reliably reduce leakage; conclusion: privacy risk should be viewed as a persistent behavioral failure mode, not only memorization or immediate jailbreaks. Keywords: Trustworthy AI, LLMs, Privacy, Evaluation, Benchmarking.

Title: PrivDrift — auditing user-secret leakage under topic drift in active LLM conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University). Contact: lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu. Benchmark: PrivDrift — controlled benchmark of 1,000 multi-turn dialogues per model with seeded secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction probes. Evaluated across three LLMs with extended context windows. Core axes: topic drift (number d of unrelated turns between secret disclosure and probe; tested window d ≤ 6) and persuasion intensity (interaction style: direct, justified, high-pressure). Main quantitative claim: dialogue-level hybrid leakage under hybrid detector ranges 38.7%–54.6%; leakage varies strongly by model, secret type (SSNs and credit cards suppressed far more often than emails and phone numbers), and persuasion intensity. Hybrid detector: normalization-based matching + open-weights LLM judge; reported metrics include dialogue-level, probe-level, regex-only, fuzzy, and hybrid leakage rates. Key finding: within tested drift window, additional topic drift does not reliably reduce leakage; authors introduce Privacy Half-Life (τ), a stability-based metric, and report that no evaluated model reaches stable decay within observed drift range. Contributions summarized: benchmark, probe styles, hybrid detector & metrics, Privacy Half-Life analysis. Keywords: Trustworthy AI, LLMs, Privacy, Evaluation, Benchmarking.

Title: PrivDrift — auditing user-secret leakage under topic drift in active LLM conversations. Author/contact: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu). Benchmark: PrivDrift — 1,000 multi-turn dialogues per model with seeded secrets, content-dense drift turns, and standardized extraction probes. Core axes: topic drift (number d of unrelated turns between secret disclosure and probe; tested window d ≤ 6) and persuasion intensity (interaction styles: direct, justified, high-pressure). Main quantitative claim: dialogue-level hybrid leakage under hybrid detector ranges 38.7%–54.6%; leakage varies by model and secret type (SSNs and credit cards suppressed more than emails/phones). Hybrid detector: normalization-based matching + open-weights LLM judge; reported metrics include dialogue-level, probe-level, regex-only, fuzzy, and hybrid leakage rates. Privacy Half-Life (τ): stability-based metric; authors report no evaluated model reaches stable decay within observed drift range. Contributions: benchmark, probe styles, hybrid detector & metrics, Privacy Half-Life analysis. Related work summarized: (1) Contextual privacy/inference-time leakage distinguished from training-data extraction; other benchmarks (ConfAIde, PrivacyLens, PrivaCI-Bench) focus on static access-control/privacy-norm reasoning, whereas PrivDrift isolates persistence of user-disclosed secrets after topic drift and persuasion probes. (2) Multi-turn adversarial attacks (Crescendo, automated jailbreaks, prompt injection) motivate treating information flow control across turns. (3) Context management and unlearning (TOFU, WMDP) operate on model weights/static QA; PrivDrift targets active-context suppression relevant to RAG, copilots, and agentic workflows.

steps.notes_before: Evaluation uses a hierarchical hybrid detector: Stage 1 normalization-based matching (φ) detects verbatim/near-verbatim leaks; numeric secrets: strip non-digits; alphanumeric: normalize case/whitespace, preserve meaningful delimiters. Regex-stage label: Leak_regex(R,S)=I[φ(S)⊂φ(R)]. Stage 2: open-weights Llama judge (Meta AI, 2024) inspects regex-negative responses and returns a binary verdict for partial/indirect disclosures; paper reports regex-only and hybrid rates separately. Privacy Half-Life τ: D_obs = observed drift lengths, L(d)=leakage rate at d, safety threshold δ=0.1×L(0). τ = min{d∈D_obs | L(d)≤δ and ∀d'>d in D_obs: L(d')≤δ}; if empty τ = max(D_obs)+1 to avoid counting transient dips. Caveat: earlier parts ambiguously defined d (dialogue element count vs. number of drift turns), so interpretation of 'drift length' in L(d), D_obs, and τ is unclear. Other earlier details retained: N=1000 dialogues (900 synthetic +100 human-authored mixed), secret types: phone/email/SSN/credit card, drift lengths sampled from {0,2,3,4,5,6} (d=0 with p=0.2, else uniform over 2–6).

Aggregation: dialogue-level leak = any probe elicits secret; persuasion-level and fuzzy-matching computed at probe level (each dialogue contributes one response per persuasion condition). Statistics: dialogue-level 95% bootstrap CIs over dialogues; probe-level rates over cached responses; paired comparisons use McNemar with Bonferroni; repeated measures use Cochran's Q with post-hoc McNemar; associations tested with chi-square and Cramer's V. final_notes: Threat model: active-context re-disclosure after topic-drift. Dataset N=1000 (900 synthetic, 100 human). D7A distances {0,2,3,4,5,6}; sampling: d=0 ≈197 (19.7%), others roughly uniform. Cached outputs 3,000 per model. Privacy half-life K2V not reached (τ = max(D_obs)+1 = 7). D7A pattern: dip near d=3 then rebound; no stable suppression within tested window. Appendix A (D7A length stats by d): d=0 N=197 Avg words 44.29 Avg tokens ~59.05; d=2 N=147 Avg words 253.97 Avg tokens ~338.62; d=3 N=142 Avg words 344.18 Avg tokens ~458.91; d=4 N=166 Avg words 452.27 Avg tokens ~603.02; d=5 N=181 Avg words 520.92 Avg tokens ~694.56; d=6 N=167 Avg words 568.03 Avg tokens ~757.37. Models: M7Q (GPT-OSS-120B), T4X (DeepSeek-R1), Y9C (Qwen3-VL-235B). Detectors: H8D hybrid (U3P normalization + Llama judge), U3P, R5J fuzzy-match. Key H8D results: T4X 38.70% [35.7,41.6]; M7Q 47.70% [44.6,50.8]; Y9C 54.60% [51.6,57.7]. U3P→H8D deltas: M7Q Δ0.00 (p=1.0); T4X Δ+0.90 (p=7.7e-3); Y9C Δ+1.10 (p=2.57e-3). Title: PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations. Author: Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero (West Virginia University), contact lrm00020@mix.wvu.edu. Abstract claims: persistent, user-facing, shared-session, tool-augmented LLMs can retain behaviorally recoverable sensitive disclosures even after unrelated tasks; introduces a controlled benchmark called PrivDrift (QX2) that uses seeded multi-turn histories, content-dense intervening exchanges, and standardized extraction probes to audit persistence. Reports that across extended-context models, a metric/phenomenon labelled "G4P under H8D" remains substantial, varies sharply across systems and two other labels "S8Q" and "V4N", and does not reliably decline within the tested window. Conclusion: active-context privacy should be evaluated as persistent behavioral failure rather than only parameter memorization or immediate jailbreak behavior. Keywords: Trustworthy AI, LLM Privacy, Evaluation, Benchmarking. Points to check later: definitions and meanings of acronyms QX2/PrivDrift, G4P, H8D, S8Q, V4N; experimental setup (seeded histories, intervening exchanges, extraction probes), which models are considered "extended-context", the tested window length, and evidence for "fails to decline reliably" and per-system variability.

final_notes: Scope: circuit-level interpretability; main claim that circuit-derived regulatory evidence can fail the Y3W protocol. Model/task: single canonical model Q7V (GPT-2 small). Grid: 7,561 claim-producing specifications → 3,218 distinct circuits. Pairwise D quantiles: 1% 0.196, 25% 0.788, median 0.960, 75% 0.998. Median circuit size 200 edges; median shared-edge fraction 4%; analytic random Jaccard at median size 0.0031; expected random overlap for 500-edge circuits 0.008. Pooled discovered F = 0.7316 (95% CI 0.7247–0.7380). Axis-standardised residuals: metric F 0.5939 (removes 0.1377); seed 0.7307 (removes 0.0009). REML: ablation–corruption interaction explains 78.8% of structural variance; metric-standardised percentage disagreement 59.4%. Fixed-size pooled F = 0.2706 (95% CI 0.2550–0.2859; reported 27.1%). Pooled vs A6N: 0.7316 vs 0.6774. Fixed-size rows: K8Z discovered 0.2746 vs A6N 0.4230; E7R discovered 0.2706 vs A6N 0.3822. A6N degeneracy above 1,000 edges; discovery collapses at 5,000 and 10,000 edges (Table 7), leaving 2,692 specs with no flips. Functional diagnostics: pooled per-example agreement 0.6028; pooled functional instability 0.3972; smallest-circuit instability 0.4777. Cohen’s kappa 0.0146 (per-size range elsewhere 0.016–0.047). Band carrying pooled gap: 500–2,000 edges; sizes failing gap threshold 6/10; sizes with negative gap 5/10. Y3W protocol: declare S and φ, compute π* = max_c n_c/N over S and F; evidence passes at tolerance α iff π* ≥ 1−α; report π*, F, discard rates and within-group decompositions. Limitations: one model/task; planned second model M9B (Pythia-160m) 924-cell grid unrun; instrument library excludes C4Y so measured F is a lower bound; discard rate high/uneven; bootstrap invalid for some small groups (2–5 specs); unusable intervals replaced by point estimates. Reproducibility: public commit tag `prereg-p1-confirmatory`; archive verification finds one environment across all 1,320 confirmatory cells and 22/22 files identical; analysis needs no GPU. One script recomputes headline quantities (36 checks, 0 failures; F recomputed by three routes including brute-force pairs); another checks every manuscript numeric token; tables emitted directly; test suite contains 343 tests.

Title: Explanation Multiplicity: Circuit-Level Interpretability. Author: Ajay Pravin Mahale. Date: 12 Aug 2026. Domain: circuit-level interpretability. Main claim (from preface): circuit-derived regulatory evidence fails Y3W across plausibly acceptable tolerances: competent analysts using the same system and tool can produce incompatible statements under different defensible settings. Introduction notes: auditing framed as requiring two auditors to reach the same conclusion (a commissioning requirement, not an ML definition). Regulatory motivation: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (consolidated text amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, CELEX 02024R1689-20260727; read 11 Aug 2026) asks for “general logic” (Annex IV 2(b)) and measures to facilitate interpretation (2(e)); Article 86(1) asks for clear explanations of the AI system’s role. Mechanistic interpretability (circuit discovery) returns a subgraph said to explain behavior; filing such accounts presumes compatibility between analysts. H3: size confounds — holding size fixed reverses ordering and drops pooled F to ≈0.2746 (size has a very large effect; decomposition suggests ~0.457 effect). Many specs collapse at high edge thresholds (2,692 specs produce no flips). H4 pooled agreement ≈0.6028 (instability ≈0.3972); gap to claim flip ≈0.3344 (95% CI [0.3297,0.3394]). Filability protocol described (π*, F, discard rates). Limitations: one model/one task; some pre-registered replication unrun; instrument omits optimal ablation; discards high and metric-imbalanced; bootstrap invalid for tiny conditioning groups. Noted internal inconsistency from earlier: Discussion's claim that "metric is the biggest lever (removes 0.1377)" conflicts with H3 (size produces a larger effect ~0.457) and the reported leftover CI after subtracting metric is inconsistent with the component CIs (should be ≈[0.5829,0.6003]). Reproducibility (this part): prereg commit tagged "prereg-p1-confirmatory" made before confirmatory sweep; archive verifies a single environment across 1,320 cells; content-addressed comparison recovered the code commit: 22 of 22 files identical; analysis layer runs without a GPU; verification script recomputes every headline quantity (36 checks, 0 failures) and derives F by three routes including brute-force pairwise; numeric tokens and tables checked/emitted from stored results; test suite contains 343 tests.

Formalism (this part): specification s = (o,a,d,m,τ,P,r,g). Discovery returns C(s) ⊂ E with |E| = 32,491 edges. Closed-form edge breakdown: attention in block b receives from 1+13b sources at 3 input slots for each of 12 heads; MLP_b receives from those sources plus its own block’s heads; output receives from all 157 non-terminal sources. Components counted: 144 attention heads + 12 MLPs = 156 components. Circuit instability D(s_i,s_j) = 1 − |C_i ∩ C_j|/|C_i ∪ C_j| (mean Jaccard ̄J). Claim instability F = 1 − (Σ_c n_c(n_c − 1))/(N(N − 1)) (Gini–Simpson); modal share π* = max_c n_c / N. Within-group flip F_within(G) given by Eq.3 reduces to Eq.2 when G empty. Stated ceiling F ≤ 1 − 1/k; with k=9 observed classes ceiling = 0.8889 and observed F is ~82.3% of that. Unit tests compared Eq.2 to brute-force. final_notes: Dataset/grid: GPT-2 small, indirect-object ID. Discovery grid: 6 axes → 1,320 discovery cells → 15,840 specs (12 specs/cell). Original multiverse produced 15,840 specs; metric-relative discard left ~7,561 surviving specs (~52.3% discard), 3,218 distinct circuits. Pooled flip-rate F = 0.7316 (95% CI 0.7247–0.7380). Standardising the metric reduces F by 0.1377 to 0.5939 (CI 0.5803–0.6063). Holding size fixed collapses/reverses the effect (e.g., medium discovered F=0.2746 vs null 0.4230; coarse discovered F=0.2706 vs null 0.3822); size distribution drives pooled effect (fixing size drops pooled F from 0.7316 to 0.2746). Functional H4: per-example agreement 0.6028 (instability 0.3972); flip-rate gap 0.3344 (95% CI 0.3297–0.3394) > preregistered 0.10 but fails at 6/10 sizes; pooled effect driven by 500–2,000-edge band. Cohen's kappa: overall 0.0146 vs per-size kappas 0.016–0.047 (potential inconsistency). Filability protocol: declare spec space S and deterministic claim map φ, compute π* and F, filable if π* ≥ 1−α (note earlier inconsistent phrasing about π*). Limitations: one-model/one-task; replication preregistered but unrun; circuit size treated as outcome not axis (threshold selects size); multiverse omits optimal ablation so F is a lower bound; bootstrap invalid for small conditioning groups (2–5 specs) so point estimates used. Instrument issue noted: paper gives conflicting descriptions of a failed objective (claims both "one of seven" and "all 220 cells in that arm fail" — arithmetic inconsistent since 1,320/7 ≠ 220). Replication cell-count mismatch flagged: reported 924 vs expected 792 if only seed levels changed 5→3. Reproducibility section: preregistration commit 'prereg-p1-confirmatory' made before confirmatory sweep; claims every reported number traces to a config/seed/environment fingerprint; results archive verifies a single environment across all 1,320 cells; content-addressed comparison found 22 of 22 files identical; analysis layer runs without a GPU; verification script recomputes every headline quantity (36 checks, 0 failures) and derives F by three routes including brute-force pairwise; second script checks every numeric token against stored results and tables are emitted from results; test suite contains 343 tests.
