Paper title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Setup: use linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations to detect deception behaviors; evaluate generalization across 3 held-out deception detection datasets (only two named here: Insider Trading Report and Sandbagging). Key claim: projecting inputs onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) from the training activation distribution enables cross-domain transfer that nearly matches probes trained on the target/test distribution. Method extension: interpret PCs and use an LLM judge to score each PC by whether its most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; then probe using top-scoring PCs. Results: this PC-selection method closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and by 25% on Sandbagging. Interpretation claim: source-probe-weighted directions encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and in ways capturable by natural language descriptions. Broad claim: OOD robustness of probes largely determined by subspace selection. Venue noted: Machine Learning, ICML.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Setup: train linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations (source dataset: Roleplaying deception scenarios); evaluate OOD on three held-out target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Core idea: work in the source-domain PCA basis and select a small subset of source PCs to train probes that avoid spurious surface correlations and transfer to targets. Key empirical claims: (1) A small transferable subspace exists (Sec. 4.2): a target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds ~8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe. (2) Source-side and target-side weight-based rankings fail to recover this subspace (Sec. 4.3): ranking PCs by source or target probe weights does not outperform the full-representation baseline. (3) An LLM judge can partially recover the subspace without target labels (Sec. 4.5): it interprets PCs via their extreme examples and selects transferable PCs. Prior-note results: PC-selection method closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Interpretation claim: transferable directions encode more abstract contrasts describable in language; probe OOD robustness largely determined by subspace selection. Figure 1 outlines pipeline: project activations into source PCA basis, filter candidate PCs, train probes on selected low-dim subspace.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Setup: train linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations using a source dataset of roleplaying deception scenarios; evaluate OOD on three held-out target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Method: compute PCA on source activations, work in source PCA basis, filter candidate PCs, and select a small subset of source PCs to train linear probes on the low-dimensional subspace. Key empirical claims: (1) A small transferable subspace exists: target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds ~8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe (Sec. 4.2). (2) Weight-based rankings on source or target probes fail to recover this subspace and do not outperform full-representation baseline (Sec. 4.3). (3) An LLM judge can partially recover the subspace without target labels by interpreting PCs via extreme examples and selecting transferable PCs (Sec. 4.5). Reported quantitative impact: PC-selection method closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Context from related work: literature reports linear/low-dim directions for high-level properties and behaviors, examples of single-direction control (refusal/assistant axis), skepticism about probes (probe may learn task/exploit surface correlates; OOD probe generalization can be uneven), and use of LLMs to generate natural-language explanations of features and to inform interventions.

Datasets: Roleplaying is the source; targets are Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Each response labeled by GPT-4o as honest (0), ambiguous (-1), or deceptive (1); ambiguous examples removed. Language model activations: layer-15 residual stream of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; token activations averaged over the assistant response. Preprocessing: standardize source activations (zero mean, unit variance) and apply the same source statistics to standardize target activations. PCA: run PCA on the scaled source activations and retain the top 100 PCs. Probes: logistic regression (regularization λ=10). For experiments using a subset S of PCs, project activations onto S before training/evaluation; baseline probes train on the full standardized activations. Motivation for 100 PCs: lower-index PCs align more with SAE decoder features (Appendix C) and are easier to interpret, but authors do not claim low-index PCs inherently generalize better; Section 4.1 reportedly shows the 100-PC subspace suffices to separate deceptive vs. honest on every target.

Datasets: source = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Confirm, Insider Trading Report, Sandbagging. Responses labeled honest (0), ambiguous (-1), deceptive (1); ambiguous examples removed. Model activations: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer-15 residual stream; token activations averaged over assistant response. Preprocessing: standardize source activations (zero mean, unit variance) and apply same source statistics to standardize target activations. PCA: run PCA on scaled source activations and retain top 100 PCs. Probes: logistic regression (λ=10). Key results (Section 4.1): source-trained probe (full rep) AUROC on targets: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Probe trained on target data within top-100 source PCs (5-fold CV) achieves AUROC ≈ 0.936 (Confirm) / 0.950 (Report) / 0.869 (Sandbagging) — so 100-PC subspace suffices to separate classes on every target.

Greedy PC-selection (Section 4.2): start empty, iteratively add from top-100 PCs the PC that most improves AUROC on target; to evaluate a candidate, project source activations onto current subset and train probe on source projections; PC choice guided by target labeled folds (5-fold CV) while probe weights always fit on source; stop when AUROC improvement ≤0.001. Avg subset sizes: Report 15 PCs, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14. Greedy improves over baseline (full-rep baseline) by ~+0.22 (Report) and +0.23 (Sandbagging) and approaches target-trained performance; top-k-by-variance matched greedy only for Confirm.

Section 4.3 tests two hypotheses for transferable PCs (separate target classes alone vs PCs source probe leans on). Compare rankings by standardized coefficient = |coef| * std(PC) from probes trained on activations projected to source-PCA basis (source-probe vs target-probe vs greedy oracle).

Datasets: source = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Confirm, Insider Trading Report, Sandbagging. Labels: honest(0), ambiguous(-1) (removed), deceptive(1). Representations: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer-15 residual stream; token activations averaged over assistant response; standardize using source mean/var and apply same stats to targets. PCA: run on scaled source activations, keep top 100 PCs. Probes: logistic regression (λ=10). Baselines: probes on full standardized representations; PC-subset experiments project activations onto chosen subset before training/eval. Key baseline numbers: source-trained probe (full rep) AUROC on targets: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probe on top-100 source PCs (5-fold CV) AUROC ≈ Confirm 0.936, Report 0.950, Sandbagging 0.869 (so 100-PC subspace suffices for target separation). Greedy PC-selection (target labels guide PC choice, probe weights fit on source; stop when AUROC improvement ≤0.001): CV average subset sizes Report 15, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14; greedy boosted AUROC over full-rep by ~+0.22 (Report) and +0.23 (Sandbagging); top-k-by-variance only matched greedy for Confirm. Cross-target ranking experiment (Sec 4.3): define source-PCA and target-PCA rankings (both use source-PCA basis); to pick k, run greedy on full target dataset (single k): Report k=13, Confirm k=7, Sandbagging k=14 (differs slightly from CV sizes). Results: both hypotheses fail — source-PCA probe transfers ~as well as full-rep baseline (i.e., doesn't generalize); target-PCA probe does well on Report, worse than greedy on Confirm, and below-random on Sandbagging. Interpretability (Sec 4.4): for each top-100 PC, collect 8 most/least activating examples and have an LLM judge describe poles and give 1–10 OOD scores; max observed score=6; keep PCs that scored 6 in both runs → 19 interp-selected PCs. Of 5 PCs that appeared in greedy selections for multiple targets, 3 had max OOD; only 1 of top-5 source-PCA PCs got max OOD. Sec 4.5 evaluates probe AUROC for interp-selected 19 PCs vs controls (full-rep, top-19 by variance, remaining 81). Figures and appendices provide full results.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Setup: study generalization of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct linear probes on 3 held-out deception-detection datasets. Main empirical claim: projecting inputs onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) computed from the training distribution of activations enables cross-domain transfer that nearly matches probes trained on the target/test distribution. Interpretation claim: PC interpretations can identify a subset of transferable PCs. Method: use an LLM judge to score each PC by whether its most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; then train probes using the highest-scoring PCs. Reported results: this procedure closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on the Insider Trading Report dataset and by 25% on Sandbagging. Qualitative claim: source-probe-weighted directions encode source-specific surface features, whereas truly transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and are capturable by natural-language descriptions. Conclusion: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection. Venue: Machine Learning, ICML.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Goal: study cross-domain generalization of linear probes for deception detection. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Setup: train probes on a single source dataset (Roleplaying deception scenarios) and evaluate on 3 held-out target datasets (Insider Trading Report; Insider Trading Confirm; Sandbagging). Method: compute PCA on source-domain activations, project activations into source-domain PC basis, select a subset of PCs, and train linear probes on that low-dimensional subspace (Fig.1). Key empirical claims: (1) A small transferable subspace exists — a target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds ~8–15 components where a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained (oracle) probe (Section 4.2). (2) Simple rankings by source- or target-probe weights fail to recover this subspace and do not transfer better than the full-representation baseline (Section 4.3). (3) An LLM judge can partially recover the transferable subspace without target data by interpreting/selecting PCs (Section 4.5); earlier notes record that this procedure closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Interpretation/qualitative claim: source-probe-weighted directions tend to encode surface/source-specific features, whereas truly transferable directions encode more abstract contrasts capturable by natural-language descriptions. Conclusion: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Goal: study cross-domain generalization of linear probes for deception detection. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Datasets: source = Roleplaying deception scenarios; targets = Insider Trading Report (ITR), Insider Trading Confirm (ITC), Sandbagging. Method: compute PCA on source-domain activations, project activations into source PCA basis, select subset of PCs, train linear probes on that low-dimensional subspace. Key empirical claims: (1) A small transferable subspace exists — a target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds ~8–15 components where a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained (oracle) probe. (2) Simple rankings by source- or target-probe weights fail to recover this subspace and do not transfer better than the full-representation baseline. (3) An LLM judge can partially recover the transferable subspace without target data by interpreting/selecting PCs; reported that this procedure closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by ~78% on ITR and ~25% on Sandbagging. Interpretation: source-probe-weighted directions tend to encode surface/source-specific features, whereas transferable directions encode more abstract contrasts capturable by natural-language descriptions. Conclusion: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection. Related work summarized: evidence for linear concept directions and single-direction behavior (Marks & Tegmark; Park et al.; Zou et al.; Arditi et al.; Lu et al.), longstanding probe-skepticism about probes learning tasks or exploiting artifacts (Hewitt & Liang; Ravichander et al.), recent findings of uneven OOD probe generalization, and prior uses of LLMs/natural-language for neuron/feature explanation and intervention (Bills et al.; Paulo et al.; Bricken et al.; Casademunt et al.).

Datasets: Source = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Report (ITR), Insider Trading Confirm (ITC), Sandbagging. Responses labeled honest (0), ambiguous (-1), deceptive (1) by GPT-4o; ambiguous responses removed for experiments. Model & activations: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; use layer-15 residual stream activations (chosen for highest cross-domain AUROC per Ying et al.); token activations averaged over the assistant’s response. Preprocessing & PCA: Standardize source activations to zero mean and unit variance; apply same source statistics to standardize target activations. Run PCA on scaled source activations and retain top 100 PCs (chosen because alignment with SAE decoder features decreases with PC index — lower-index PCs more amenable to natural-language interpretation; not a claim that low-index PCs generalize better). Probes: Logistic regression classifiers (regularization λ=10). For experiments using subset S of PCs, project activations onto S before training/evaluation; baseline probes train on full standardized activations (original activation dimensionality). Section 4.1 is said to confirm the 100-PC subspace retains enough information to separate deceptive vs. honest on every target. Earlier high-level claims (from prior parts): a small transferable subspace (~8–15 PCs) can let a source-trained probe nearly match a target-trained oracle; simple rankings by source/target probe weights do not recover this subspace; LLM-based natural-language selection can partly recover transferable PCs.

Datasets: Source = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Report (ITR), Insider Trading Confirm (ITC), Sandbagging. Labels: honest (0) vs deceptive (1); ambiguous (-1) removed. Model/activations: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; layer-15 residual stream; token activations averaged over assistant response. Preprocessing/PCA: Standardize source activations (zero mean, unit variance); apply same stats to targets; run PCA on scaled source activations; retain top 100 PCs. Probes: logistic regression (regularization λ=10). For subset experiments, project activations onto that subset before training; baseline probes train on full standardized activations. 4.1 baseline: source-trained probe on full representations transfers with AUROC: ITC 0.874, ITR 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probes on top-100 source PCs (5-fold CV) achieve 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869 AUROC across the three targets (paper reports triplet but does not explicitly map each number in-line; overall conclusion: 100-PC subspace contains sufficient signal). 4.2 greedy-PC selection: iterative greedy search over top-100 PCs; for each candidate, project source activations to current subset, train LR on source, evaluate AUROC on target (selection guided by non-held-out target folds in 5-fold CV); stop when no PC improves AUROC > 0.001. Average selected PC counts: ITR 15, ITC 8, Sandbagging 14. Greedy nearly matches target-trained probes for ITR and Sandbagging, improving on the full-representation baseline by ~0.22 and ~0.23 AUROC respectively. Top-k-by-variance (k matched to greedy) only matches greedy for ITC and falls behind for ITR and Sandbagging. 4.3 hypotheses: transferable PCs might be (1) PCs that individually separate target classes, or (2) PCs with large standardized source-probe coefficients. They compare rankings by standardized coefficient (|coef| * PC stddev) from probes trained on activations projected to the source-PCA basis (source-probe vs target-probe rankings).

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Abstract claim: directions weighted by a source probe encode source-specific surface features; transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly (capturable in natural language). Main claim: probe OOD robustness largely determined by subspace selection. Background: linear probes expose semantic info but can fail OOD despite strong in-distribution performance. Assertion that behavioral concepts have linear representations but probes often learn spurious correlations; such unreliability is problematic for harmful-interaction monitoring. Method/approach keywords: work in source Q7 coordinates to avoid privileging model latent dims; these coordinates provide data-driven representation structure. Prior findings cited: removing leading components can improve downstream embedding performance (Mu et al., 2018); leading-component projections used as a probing baseline (Kantamneni et al., 2025). Problem framed as selecting dimensions that permit generalization vs. spurious source-trained classification. Pipeline (Fig.1): projection into source N4D basis, filtering candidate Q7 directions, probe training in selected low-dimensional subspace.

Goal: probe OOD robustness largely determined by subspace selection; pipeline projects activations into a source data-driven basis (source N4D / Q7 coordinates), filters candidate directions, and trains probes in the selected low-dim subspace. Prior findings: removing leading components can improve downstream embedding performance; leading-component projections used as a baseline. Related work summarized here: (1) Linear concept directions: studies report cross-dataset linear structure for true/false and other behaviors (Marks & Tegmark 2024; Park et al. 2024 formalize the linear representation hypothesis). Single directions reported for refusal and an “assistant” axis (Arditi et al. 2024; Lu et al. 2026); other work finds population-level directions for honesty/emotion (Zou et al. 2025). (2) Linear probes limits: probes can learn task/surface correlates rather than reveal intrinsic representation; encoded vs. recoverable information distinction; strong in-distribution probes often generalize unevenly—safety evaluation must separate robust internal signals from dataset artifacts. (3) Interpreting features with natural-language explanations: LLM-generated neuron explanations from high-activation examples (Bills et al. 2023), automated sparse-autoencoder feature labeling (Paulo et al. 2025; Bricken et al. 2023), and concept identification + ablation during fine-tuning (Casademunt et al. 2025).

Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6). Use layer-15 residual-stream activations (per Ying et al. 2026); activations averaged over assistant-response tokens. Data: four Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025) datasets — one source (Roleplaying: V8) and three held-out targets: Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), Sandbagging (J9). Only Roleplaying used as source. Labels: annotated by GPT-4o (K8, OpenAI 2024) with mapping honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous responses removed (binary honest vs deceptive). Preprocessing: source activations standardized to zero mean, unit variance; same source statistics used to standardize targets. Dimensionality reduction: PCA on source (N4D), retain leading 100 principal components (PCs Q7); probes trained on projections to subset S of these PCs. Classifiers: logistic regression (regularization λ=10) for all classifiers; comparator (full-representation baseline B8Q) trains on all standardized activations (no PCA). Choice of 100 PCs driven by interpretability comparability (alignment with U9/Bricken et al. 2023 decreases with PC index, so lower-index PCs are easier to interpret), not because low-index PCs generalize best. Error bars denote 95% confidence intervals.

Datasets: source Roleplaying (V8); targets Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), Sandbagging (J9). Key experimental results/methods (Part 4): W6 transfer reasonably good, C2R moderate, J9 poor. Target-trained classifiers within the 100-PC source subspace separate classes on every target; the single source-trained direction fails to generalize. Greedy oracle search (H2) uses target labels to pick PCs: start empty, consider each of 100 PCs, fit source logistic weights on candidate subset, add PC that most improves target F3 (CV selection on non-held-out folds; stop if no candidate >0.001). Variance-ranked baseline (Y4) matches H2 only on easy W6; explained variance poorly predicts transfer utility. Ranking probes: source-PCA (T6) and target-PCA (M9) order PCs by standardized coefficient X4 = |coef| * PC std (on source-projected activations); evaluated probes are then trained on source projections to top-k. T6 ≈ B8Q; M9: good on C2R, worse than H2 on W6, below random on J9. Interpretation (C7): for each leading PC, LLM judge sees top-8 and bottom-8 source examples, writes pole/whole descriptions and assigns OOD score (R5). Interp-selected intersection (L2) = PCs reaching observed max in both scoring runs; A7 = its complement; Y4 also used as equal-dim control. L2 (language-only) improves over B8Q and A7, especially on C2R and J9.

Key results: target-trained classifiers within 100-PC source subspace separate classes on every target; a single source-trained direction fails to generalize. Transfer performance: W6 transfer reasonably good/easy (high baselines), C2R moderate, J9 poor and most OOD. Greedy oracle search (H2): uses target labels to pick PCs greedily, stop if best candidate improvement ≤0.001. Limitations (Part 5): single-model/single-source limits generality; W6’s high baseline reduces informativeness; J9 likely suffers distribution shift; pipeline is fully linear (N4D projection + logistic regression)—nonlinear probes and other readout locations not explored; interpretive claims are descriptive/correlational (no causal ablations of high-rated directions).

steps.notes_before: Paper title and authors: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection — Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Abstract claim: directions heavily weighted by a source probe encode source-specific surface features; transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly; probe OOD robustness is largely determined by subspace selection. Main approach (Introduction): work in source Q7 coordinates to avoid privileging model latent dimensions; these coordinates provide data-driven representation structure. Cited observations: removing leading components can improve downstream embedding performance (Mu et al., 2018); leading-component projections used as a probing baseline (Kantamneni et al., 2025). Problem framed as selecting dimensions that permit generalization rather than spurious source-trained classification. Figure 1 caption mentions projection into a source N4D basis and filtering candidate Q7 directions (inconsistent naming of coordinate/basis). References to several recent works and to OOD failures of probes.

Paper: "Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection" — Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Abstract/main claims: probe directions heavily weighted by a source probe encode source-specific surface features; transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly; probe OOD robustness is largely determined by subspace selection. Approach: operate in source 'Q7' coordinates (data-driven basis) to avoid privileging model latent dims; Figure 1 caption earlier noted inconsistent naming (source N4D vs Q7). Related work (this part):
- Linear concept directions: cross-dataset linear structure (Marks & Tegmark 2024); Park et al. (2024) formalize linear representation hypothesis; population-level activation directions for honesty/emotion (Zou et al. 2025); single-direction refusal (Arditi et al. 2024); assistant axis (Lu et al. 2026). Issue: whether concepts are stable vs context-dependent correlations remains unresolved.
- Linear probes & limitations: long history (Alain & Bengio 2018; Hewitt & Liang 2019); probes can learn task or exploit surface correlates, so high in-distribution accuracy doesn't guarantee representation; encoded vs recoverable information distinction (Ravichander et al. 2021); strong in-distribution probes generalize unevenly (kramár2026...); safety evaluation must separate robust internal signals from dataset artifacts.
- Natural-language feature interpretation: LLM-generated neuron explanations (Bills et al. 2023); sparse-autoencoder labeling (Paulo et al. 2025; Bricken et al. 2023); automated concept identification and ablation during fine-tuning reduces misaligned behavior (Casademunt et al. 2025).

Paper: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection” — Yoo & Skapars. Main claims: probe directions weighted by a source probe encode source-specific surface features; transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly; probe OOD robustness is largely determined by subspace selection. Implementation/setup (Part 3): model Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6); use layer-15 residual-stream activations; activations averaged over assistant-response tokens. Data: four Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025) datasets — source: Roleplaying (V8); held-out targets: Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), Sandbagging (J9). Labels by GPT-4o (K8): honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous responses are removed. Preprocessing: source activations standardized to zero-mean/unit-variance; those source statistics also used to standardize targets. Dimensionality reduction: PCA (N4D) fit on source, retain leading 100 principal components (PCs labeled Q7); projection to subset S of these PCs precedes training/evaluation. Classifiers: logistic regression (regularization λ=10) for all classifiers; full-representation baseline (B8Q) trains on all standardized activations (i.e., no PCA-subspace selection). Choice of 100 PCs driven by interpretability comparability (alignment with U9 decreases with PC index), not claimed superior low-index generalization. Error bars in reported results denote 95% CIs. Note: earlier parts flagged an inconsistent naming in Figure 1 caption (N4D vs Q7); current part uses N4D=PCA and Q7=PCs.

Paper: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection” (Yoo & Skapars). Setup (from Part 3): model Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; layer-15 residual-stream activations averaged over assistant-response tokens. Data: source = Roleplaying (V8); targets = Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), Sandbagging (J9). Labels by GPT-4o: honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous responses removed. Preproc: standardize source activations (zero-mean, unit-variance) and apply same stats to targets. Dimensionality reduction: PCA on source (N4D), keep top 100 PCs (Q7). Projection to subsets S of these PCs precedes training/evaluation. Classifiers: logistic regression (λ=10) everywhere; full-representation baseline = B8Q (no PCA). 5-fold CV used; error bars = 95% CIs.

Part 4 experiments summary:
- 4.1 baseline: W6 transfers best, C2R moderate, J9 worst. Target-trained classifiers in the 100-PC source subspace separate classes on all targets; the single source-trained probe does not generalize.
- 4.2 transferable subspace: greedy search (H2) uses target labels (CV or full-target variant) to add PCs that improve target F3 (>0.001 stop); small source-trained subspaces (H2) nearly match target-trained probes, esp. C2R/J9. Variance-ranked top-k (Y4) matches H2 only on easy W6; explained variance is a poor predictor.
- 4.3 hypotheses: source-side (T6) and target-side (M9) rankings use X4 = |coeff| * PC_std (PC std from source N4D projections). Neither ranking recovers H2; T6 ~ B8Q; M9: good on C2R, worse than H2 on W6, below random on J9.
- 4.4 interpretation: LLM judge (C7) gets top/ bottom 8 examples per PC, produces pole/whole descriptions and OOD rating (R5); selection keeps PCs that hit observed maxima in both scoring runs (intersection).
- 4.5 language-only selection (L2 = interp-selected PCs) improves over B8Q and variance control (Y4), exceeds A7 (interp-ablated) — substantially closes baseline–H2 gap on C2R, partially on J9; W6 has little headroom.

final_notes: Model & setup: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer 15. Pipeline: standardize source activations → PCA on scaled source activations (top-100 PCs) → logistic probes (λ=10). Key AUROCs: source-trained (Roleplay deception → targets) transfer: Report 0.706, Confirm 0.874, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained on the 100-PC subspace: Report 0.936, Confirm 0.950, Sandbagging 0.869. Greedy selection sizes: within-CV mean k = Report 15, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14; earlier in-paper full-data greedy ks reported as 13/7/14 (R/C/S) — noted inconsistency. Appendix D Table 2: lists source-probe top-15 PCs, greedy selections (Report:13, Confirm:7, Sandbagging:15) and target separability rankings; my computed Jaccard (greedy vs target) ≈ 0.167/0.10/0.154 (R/C/S) which disagrees with the paper’s reported 0.182/0.077/0.167. Also Table 2’s Sandbagging greedy list length (15) contradicts earlier-stated final k=14. Greedy transfer performance is near target-trained (e.g., Report ≈0.929; Sandbagging ≈0.832). Appendix E (PC interpretability): Table 3 (repeatedly greedy-selected PCs) lists PC62, PC57, PC9, PC81, PC86 with OOD scores 6/6/3/3/6 respectively (PC62/57/9 labeled Report+Sandbagging; PC81/86 labeled Confirm+Sandbagging). Table 4 (leading source-probe PCs) lists PC7/PC8/PC11/PC12/PC4 with OOD scores 3/4/3/3/6. All high-score PCs include caveats about lexical dependence/brittleness/false positives. Limitations noted: single model/layer/source; linear pipeline; no causal ablation.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars.
Goal: Can selecting principal components (PCs), i.e., directions in a source activation basis, improve out-of-distribution (OOD) deception detection?
Method overview: Train linear probes (logistic regression) on one source dataset; evaluate on 3 held-out target datasets. Use a target-supervised greedy search that adds PCs according to target performance. Also evaluate ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights. Introduce an LLM judge that scores natural-language PC descriptions without using target data.
Key quantitative claims/results: Greedy, target-supervised search finds 8–15 PCs that nearly match probes trained on target data. Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights does not recover this transferable subspace. Selecting 19 PCs that receive the maximum observed LLM score in both runs (unsupervised by target data) improves transfer on all 3 targets. For two of the targets, this selection closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and the greedy oracle. 
Other terms to track: "full-representation baseline", "greedy oracle", "both runs" (unspecified here), which targets achieve 78% and 25% (unspecified here).

Paper: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Goal: improve cross-domain (source->target) deception detection by selecting source-PC directions. Source domain = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (activations extracted; token activations averaged over assistant response to form probe inputs). Labels: GPT-4o assigns Deceptive=1, Honest=0, Ambiguous=-1 (ambiguous examples removed). Representation & PCA: source activations are standardized (source -> zero mean, unit variance) and PCA applied; source statistics are applied to target activations; 100 source PCs retained (S subset of these). Probes: all linear (logistic regression, regularization parameter λ=10); baseline = source-trained probe on full standardized activations; target-trained probes fit on target data. Selection methods: greedy oracle = target-guided greedy adding the PC that most increases target AUROC (reported to find ~8–15 PCs that nearly match target-trained probes); variance control = top-k PCs by variance; source-PCA probe and target-PCA probe use standardized coefficients to rank PCs (standardized coefficient = |coefficient| * PC standard deviation). LLM judge: GPT-5-mini interprets PC positive/negative poles and rates OOD-deception usefulness on a 1–10 scale; observed maximum OOD score = 6. Interp-selection = 19 PCs that received the maximum observed score (6) in both scoring runs; interp-ablated PCs = remaining 81. Evaluation: 5-fold CV on targets (held-out folds used for testing); AUROC reported with 95% CI. Causal validation (intervention/ablation at inference) was not performed. Appendix C: SAE decoder alignment (resource andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct); statistics reported include Spearman ρ and Jaccard overlap.

Paper: "Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection..." Targets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Model/representations: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; layer-15 residual-stream activations averaged over assistant response. Preprocessing/PCA: standardize source activations (zero mean/unit var), apply same stats to targets, run PCA on scaled source activations and retain top 100 PCs (PCA-based probes project onto subsets of these 100 PCs). Probes: logistic regression (λ=10). Baseline: probe trained on full standardized activations. Metric: AUROC (cross-domain), 5-fold CV for target-trained probes; error bars = 95% CIs.

Key results in this part:
- Full-representation source-trained AUROC (target eval): Insider Trading Confirm 0.874, Insider Trading Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606.
- Target-trained probes on the 100-PC subspace achieve AUROCs 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869 (reported across the three targets).
- Conclusion: 100-PC subspace contains enough target-class information; limited transfer is due to source-learned direction, not missing info.
- Greedy (oracle) PC-selection: searches top-100 PCs, at each step adds PC that most improves target AUROC (probe weights always fit on source; selection uses labeled non-held-out target folds in 5-fold CV); stop when improvement <0.001.
- Greedy average subset sizes: Report 15 PCs, Confirm 8 PCs, Sandbagging 14 PCs.
- Greedy improves baseline AUROC by +0.22 (Report) and +0.23 (Sandbagging), coming close to target-trained performance; variance-ranked k control matches greedy only on Confirm and falls far behind on Report and Sandbagging.
- Section 4.3 initial claim: neither source- nor target-probe coefficient rankings recover greedy transfer performance.

Paper studies probe transfer from a source task to three targets (Insider Trading Report, Confirm, Sandbagging). Preprocessing: standardize source activations, apply same stats to targets, run PCA on scaled source activations and retain top 100 PCs. Probes: logistic regression (λ=10). Metrics: AUROC transfer; target-trained probes use 5-fold CV.
Key reported numbers (earlier): source-trained (full-representation) AUROC on targets = Report 0.706, Confirm 0.874, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probes on the 100-PC subspace AUROC = Report 0.936, Confirm 0.950, Sandbagging 0.869. Greedy (oracle) PC-selection (search top 100 PCs, add PC improving target AUROC most until improvement <0.001) gave average subset sizes (within-CV) = Report 15, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14.
This part: defines standardized coefficient = |probe coeff| * PC std; two rankings: source-PCA (weights from source) and target-PCA (weights from target), both over activations in the source-PCA basis. To pick k for transfer comparisons they run greedy on the full target dataset (not per-fold), yielding k = 13 (Report), 7 (Confirm), 14 (Sandbagging) — noted as differing slightly from Section 4.2 numbers. Results: both source- and target-weight rankings fail to recover greedy transfer. Source-PCA ranking transfers about like the full-representation baseline; target-PCA ranking does well on Report, worse than greedy on Confirm, and below random on Sandbagging. Jaccard overlaps between greedy and target-ranked sets = 0.182 / 0.077 / 0.167.
Interpretability: for each of the top 100 PCs, collect 8 most/least activating examples; LLM describes poles; a judge assigns OOD score 1–10 (max observed = 6). Repeated scoring retains PCs scoring 6 in both runs, producing 19 interp-selected PCs. Five PCs are selected by greedy for >1 target; 3 of those 5 have score 6. Comparison claims reference PCs such as PC62, PC57, PC86, etc. Section 4.5 compares probes trained on the 19 interp-selected PCs vs controls (full, top-19 by variance, remaining 81).

Weight-ranking methods (standardized coefficient = |coef| * PC std) evaluated: source-PCA and target-PCA rankings fail to recover greedy; source-PCA ranking ≈ full-representation baseline; target-PCA ranking: does well on Report, worse on Confirm, below random on Sandbagging. Paper studies probe transfer from a source task (Roleplaying) to three Insider Trading targets: Report, Confirm, Sandbagging. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer 15. Preprocessing: standardize source activations, apply same stats to targets, PCA on scaled source activations retaining top 100 PCs. Probes: logistic regression (λ=10). Metric: AUROC transfer; target-trained probes use 5-fold CV. Key numbers: source-trained (full-representation) AUROC on targets = Report 0.706, Confirm 0.874, Sandbagging 0.606. Weight-ranking methods (standardized coefficient) performed poorly relative to greedy; Jaccard overlap greedy vs target-ranked sets low. Interpretability: for each top-100 PC collect extreme examples; LLM describes poles; human judge scores PCs OOD 1–10 (max observed 6); PCs scoring 6 in both runs → 19 interp-selected PCs. Limitations acknowledged: single model/layer/source, linear PCA+logistic pipeline, modest Sandbagging gains, and no causal (inference-time ablation) validation of PCs.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Setup: Train linear probes (logistic regression) on one source dataset; evaluate on 3 held-out target datasets. Key methods/results: A target-supervised greedy search that adds PCs based on target performance finds a transferable subspace of ~8–15 principal components that nearly match probes trained on target data. Simple rankings of PCs by source- or target-probe weights do not recover this transferable subspace. An LLM judge scores natural-language descriptions of PCs without using target data. Selecting 19 PCs that received the maximum observed LLM score in both runs improves transfer on all 3 targets; for two targets this selection closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and the greedy oracle. Terms mentioned: full-representation baseline, greedy oracle, transferable subspace (selected PCs), LLM judge, source vs target probe weight rankings.

Representation & pipeline: Layer-15 residual-stream token activations (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) averaged across assistant response form probe inputs. Source activations are standardized (source mean/var → zero mean/unit var) and the same source statistics are applied to target activations. PCA is fit to scaled source activations; 100 source PCs are retained (S ⊆ 100). Probes: logistic regression (λ = 10) throughout; baseline = source-trained probe on full standardized activations. Metrics & eval: AUROC reported; 5-fold cross-validation on targets; 95% CIs shown as error bars. Labels & data: GPT-4o labeled responses as Ambiguous (−1, removed), Honest (0), Deceptive (1). Source dataset = Roleplaying; three held-out target datasets include Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Selection methods: greedy oracle = target-supervised greedy addition of PCs maximizing target-AUROC; variance control = top-k PCs by source variance; source-/target-PCA probes = ranking PCs by standardized coefficients (|coef| × PC std). Main prior claims (to check later): a transferable subspace of ≈8–15 PCs nearly matches target-trained probes; simple rankings by source/target probe weights fail to recover this subspace. LLM judge: GPT-5-mini interprets PC poles (positive/negative/shared) from example tokens (format token<TAB>activation in range −10..+10) and rates OOD deception usefulness 1–10 (max observed = 6). Interp-selection = 19 PCs that received the maximum observed OOD score in both runs; interp-ablated PCs = the other 81. Appendix C: SAE decoder-alignment analysis uses andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct; Spearman ρ and Jaccard overlap reported.

Paper question: whether selecting subspaces of LM representations improves out-of-distribution (OOD) deception detection. Method: compare probes (classifiers) trained on full representations vs probes using selected directions/subspaces. Two selection approaches highlighted: (1) target-guided selection that uses target labels but does not fit probe weights on them; (2) interpretation-based selection using natural-language interpretations, which requires no target data. Key claims: small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes; selecting directions by source weights, target-class separation, or explained variance does not recover the same transferable subspaces; interpretation-based selection improves over the full-representation baseline on all targets, though how well it recovers varies sharply across targets. Scope/caveats: study uses one model and one source dataset; interpretations are descriptive, not causal. The paper includes a "Glossary." (no glossary content shown in this part).

Goal: test whether selecting subspaces of LM representations improves OOD (transfer) deception detection. Source dataset: Roleplaying (V8). Targets include C2R (Insider Trading Report), W6 (Insider Trading Confirm), J9 (Sandbagging). Model & readout: layer-15 residual-stream activations from Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6), averaged over assistant-response tokens. Preprocessing: standardization = zero-mean/unit-variance using source statistics applied to both source and targets. Dimensionality reduction: PCA / N4D retains the leading 100 source directions (Q7); "PCs" refer to these retained source directions; "leading" = lower index. Probes: logistic regression with λ=10, evaluated by AUROC (F3) with 95% CIs; 5-fold CV where selection uses non-held-out target folds and evaluation uses the held-out fold. Baselines & methods: B8Q = full-representation baseline (source-trained on all standardized activations); Y4 = top-k PCs by variance (variance-ranked subset matched in dimension count); H2 = greedy oracle (target-guided direction selection but probe weights fitted only on source); T6 = source-PCA probe (supplies source coefficient rankings); M9 = target-PCA probe (supplies target coefficient rankings); X4 = standardized coefficient = |coef| * PC_std. Interpretation-based selection: natural-language explanations produced with P2 (GPT-5-mini) and rated by C7 (LLM judge) yielding R5 (OOD score/generalization rating); L2 = interp-selected PC probe (uses directions reaching max R5 in both scoring runs); A7 = interp-ablated PC probe (complement). Decoder alignment uses SAE (U9) decoder features (resource: andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct); Spearman ρ reports relation of PC index to decoder alignment. Scope: one model, one source dataset; interpretations are descriptive, not causal.

Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6); use layer-15 residual-stream activations, averaged over assistant-response tokens. Datasets: Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025) collection — one source Roleplaying (V8) and three held-out targets: Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), Sandbagging (J9). Labeling: GPT-4o (K8) maps honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous responses removed. Preprocessing: source activations standardized to zero-mean/unit-variance; same source statistics applied to targets. Dimensionality reduction: PCA (N4D) on source; retain leading 100 PCs (Q7). Activations may be projected to a subset S of these directions before training/eval. Goal: evaluate whether source-trained leading-100 PCA subspace (Q7) contains transferable deception signal and whether small source-trained subsets (H2) can match target-trained performance. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; layer-15 residual stream, assistant-response-token-averaged activations; source standardized and same stats applied to targets. Classifiers: logistic regression (λ=10). Metric: AUROC (F3) with 5-fold CV; target-5-fold CV: directions selected on non-held-out target folds, evaluate on held-out fold; search stops when no candidate improves target F3 by >0.001. Retained 100 PCs used for comparisons.

Key reported numbers (Appendix A): B8Q (full-representation) F3: W6=0.874, C2R=0.706, J9=0.606. Target-trained (within retained-100) F3 (5-fold CV): C2R=0.936, W6=0.950, J9=0.869. H2 (target-guided greedy source-trained subset) mean sizes (target CV): C2R=15, W6=8, J9=14; full-target H2 k: C2R=13, W6=7, J9=14. H2 F3 (used for recovery comparison): C2R=0.929, J9=0.832; H2 improvements over B8Q: +0.22 (C2R), +0.23 (J9). Target-trained F3 for corresponding rows: 0.936 (C2R), 0.869 (J9). Variance-selection (Y4) matches H2 only on W6, falls behind on C2R/J9. Rankings: T6 (source-PCA ranking) performs about like B8Q; M9 (target-side ranking using standardized coefficient X4 = |coef|*PC_std) does well on C2R, worse than H2 on W6, and reportedly below random on J9. Interpretability: H2-selected directions have higher-level contrasts that partially transfer; L2 and A7 probes used in interpretation pipeline. Figures: Fig2 (source-trained full, source-trained leading100, target-trained leading100), Fig3 (B8Q, Y4, H2), Fig4 (T6, M9, H2).

Selection & interpretation: For each leading source PC, an LLM judge (C7) is shown the 8 most- and 8 least-activating source examples and writes positive-pole, negative-pole, and whole-direction descriptions and assigns an OOD/generalization rating R5. Two noisy scoring runs; selection retains directions that reach the observed maximum R5 in both runs. Appendix E reports maximum R5 = 6, 2 scoring runs, and 19 directions reaching R5=6 in both runs. Paper title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Setup: use linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations to detect deception behaviors; evaluate generalization across 3 held-out deception detection datasets (only two named here: Insider Trading Report and Sandbagging). Key claim: projecting inputs onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) from the training activation distribution enables cross-domain transfer that nearly matches probes trained on the target/test distribution. Method extension: interpret PCs and use an LLM judge to score each PC by whether its most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; then probe using top-scoring PCs. Results: this PC-selection method closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and by 25% on Sandbagging. Interpretation claim: source-probe-weighted directions encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and in ways capturable by natural language descriptions. Broad claim: OOD robustness of probes largely determined by subspace selection. Venue noted: Machine Learning, ICML.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Setup: train linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations (source dataset: Roleplaying deception scenarios); evaluate OOD on three held-out target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Core idea: work in the source-domain PCA basis and select a small subset of source PCs to train probes that avoid spurious surface correlations and transfer to targets. Key empirical claims: (1) A small transferable subspace exists (Sec. 4.2): a target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds ~8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe. (2) Source-side and target-side weight-based rankings fail to recover this subspace (Sec. 4.3): ranking PCs by source or target probe weights does not outperform the full-representation baseline. (3) An LLM judge can partially recover the subspace without target labels (Sec. 4.5): it interprets PCs via their extreme examples and selects transferable PCs. Prior-note results: PC-selection method closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Interpretation claim: transferable directions encode more abstract contrasts describable in language; probe OOD robustness largely determined by subspace selection. Figure 1 outlines pipeline: project activations into source PCA basis, filter candidate PCs, train probes on selected low-dim subspace.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Setup: train linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations using a source dataset of roleplaying deception scenarios; evaluate OOD on three held-out target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Method: compute PCA on source activations, work in source PCA basis, filter candidate PCs, and select a small subset of source PCs to train linear probes on the low-dimensional subspace. Key empirical claims: (1) A small transferable subspace exists: target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds ~8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe (Sec. 4.2). (2) Weight-based rankings on source or target probes fail to recover this subspace and do not outperform full-representation baseline (Sec. 4.3). (3) An LLM judge can partially recover the subspace without target labels by interpreting PCs via extreme examples and selecting transferable PCs (Sec. 4.5). Reported quantitative impact: PC-selection method closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Context from related work: literature reports linear/low-dim directions for high-level properties and behaviors, examples of single-direction control (refusal/assistant axis), skepticism about probes (probe may learn task/exploit surface correlates; OOD probe generalization can be uneven), and use of LLMs to generate natural-language explanations of features and to inform interventions.

Datasets: Roleplaying is the source; targets are Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Each response labeled by GPT-4o as honest (0), ambiguous (-1), or deceptive (1); ambiguous examples removed. Language model activations: layer-15 residual stream of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; token activations averaged over the assistant response. Preprocessing: standardize source activations (zero mean, unit variance) and apply the same source statistics to standardize target activations. PCA: run PCA on the scaled source activations and retain the top 100 PCs. Probes: logistic regression (regularization λ=10). For experiments using a subset S of PCs, project activations onto S before training/evaluation; baseline probes train on the full standardized activations. Motivation for 100 PCs: lower-index PCs align more with SAE decoder features (Appendix C) and are easier to interpret, but authors do not claim low-index PCs inherently generalize better; Section 4.1 reportedly shows the 100-PC subspace suffices to separate deceptive vs. honest on every target.

Datasets: source = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Confirm, Insider Trading Report, Sandbagging. Responses labeled honest (0), ambiguous (-1), deceptive (1); ambiguous examples removed. Model activations: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer-15 residual stream; token activations averaged over assistant response. Preprocessing: standardize source activations (zero mean, unit variance) and apply same source statistics to standardize target activations. PCA: run PCA on scaled source activations and retain top 100 PCs. Probes: logistic regression (λ=10). Baselines: probes trained on full standardized representations; for PC-subset experiments project activations onto subset before training/evaluation.

Key results (Section 4.1): source-trained probe (full rep) AUROC on targets: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Probe trained on target data within top-100 source PCs (5-fold CV) achieves AUROC ≈ 0.936 (Confirm) / 0.950 (Report) / 0.869 (Sandbagging) — so 100-PC subspace suffices to separate classes on every target.

Greedy PC-selection (Section 4.2): start empty, iteratively add from top-100 PCs the PC that most improves AUROC on target; to evaluate a candidate, project source activations onto current subset and train probe on source projections; PC choice guided by target labeled folds (5-fold CV) while probe weights always fit on source; stop when AUROC improvement ≤0.001. Avg subset sizes: Report 15 PCs, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14. Greedy improves over baseline (full-rep baseline) by ~+0.22 (Report) and +0.23 (Sandbagging) and approaches target-trained performance; top-k-by-variance matched greedy only for Confirm.

Section 4.3 tests two hypotheses for transferable PCs (separate target classes alone vs PCs source probe leans on). Compare rankings by standardized coefficient = |coef| * std(PC) from probes trained on activations projected to source-PCA basis (source-probe vs target-probe vs greedy oracle).

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Abstract claim: directions weighted by a source probe encode source-specific surface features; transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly (capturable in natural language). Main claim: probe OOD robustness largely determined by subspace selection. Background: linear probes expose semantic info but can fail OOD despite strong in-distribution performance. Assertion that behavioral concepts have linear representations but probes often learn spurious correlations; such unreliability is problematic for harmful-interaction monitoring. Method/approach keywords: work in source Q7 coordinates to avoid privileging model latent dims; these coordinates provide data-driven representation structure. Prior findings cited: removing leading components can improve downstream embedding performance (Mu et al., 2018); leading-component projections used as a probing baseline (Kantamneni et al., 2025). Problem framed as selecting dimensions that permit generalization vs. spurious source-trained classification. Pipeline (Fig.1): projection into source N4D basis, filtering candidate Q7 directions, probe training in selected low-dimensional subspace.

Goal: probe OOD robustness largely determined by subspace selection; pipeline projects activations into a source data-driven basis (source N4D / Q7 coordinates), filters candidate directions, and trains probes in the selected low-dim subspace. Prior findings: removing leading components can improve downstream embedding performance; leading-component projections used as a baseline. Related work summarized here: (1) Linear concept directions: studies report cross-dataset linear structure for true/false and other behaviors (Marks & Tegmark 2024; Park et al. 2024 formalize the linear representation hypothesis). Single directions reported for refusal and an “assistant” axis (Arditi et al. 2024; Lu et al. 2026); other work finds population-level directions for honesty/emotion (Zou et al. 2025). (2) Linear probes limits: probes can learn task/surface correlates rather than reveal intrinsic representation; encoded vs. recoverable information distinction; strong in-distribution probes often generalize unevenly—safety evaluation must separate robust internal signals from dataset artifacts. (3) Interpreting features with natural-language explanations: LLM-generated neuron explanations from high-activation examples (Bills et al. 2023), automated sparse-autoencoder feature labeling (Paulo et al. 2025; Bricken et al. 2023), and concept identification + ablation during fine-tuning (Casademunt et al. 2025).

Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6). Use layer-15 residual-stream activations (per Ying et al. 2026); activations averaged over assistant-response tokens. Data: four Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025) datasets — one source (Roleplaying: V8) and three held-out targets: Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), Sandbagging (J9). Only Roleplaying used as source. Labels: annotated by GPT-4o (K8, OpenAI 2024) with mapping honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous responses removed (binary honest vs deceptive). Preprocessing: source activations standardized to zero mean, unit variance; same source statistics used to standardize targets. Dimensionality reduction: PCA on source (N4D), retain leading 100 principal components (PCs Q7); probes trained on projections to subset S of these PCs. Classifiers: logistic regression (regularization λ=10) for all classifiers; comparator (full-representation baseline B8Q) trains on all standardized activations (no PCA). Choice of 100 PCs driven by interpretability comparability (alignment with U9/Bricken et al. 2023 decreases with PC index, so lower-index PCs are easier to interpret), not because low-index PCs generalize best. Error bars denote 95% confidence intervals.

Interpretability: LLM judges used; authors retained 19 interp-selected PCs (overall). Interp-selected probe AUROCs reported: Report 0.881 (≈78% gap recovery), Sandbagging 0.662 (≈25% gap recovery).

Table 4 (leading source-probe PCs) — PC7=3; PC8=4 (QA/roleplay note); PC11=3; PC12=3; PC4=6. High OOD scores still accompanied by caveats (noise, lexical dependence, brittleness, false positives).

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars.
Goal: Can selecting principal components (PCs), i.e., directions in a source activation basis, improve out-of-distribution (OOD) deception detection?
Method overview: Train linear probes (logistic regression) on one source dataset; evaluate on 3 held-out target datasets. Use a target-supervised greedy search that adds PCs according to target performance. Also evaluate ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights. Introduce an LLM judge that scores natural-language PC descriptions without using target data.
Key quantitative claims/results: Greedy, target-supervised search finds 8–15 PCs that nearly match probes trained on target data. Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights does not recover this transferable subspace. Selecting 19 PCs that receive the maximum observed LLM score in both runs (unsupervised by target data) improves transfer on all 3 targets. For two of the targets, this selection closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and the greedy oracle. 
Other terms to track: "full-representation baseline", "greedy oracle", "both runs" (unspecified here), which targets achieve 78% and 25% (unspecified here).

Paper: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Goal: improve cross-domain (source->target) deception detection by selecting source-PC directions. Source domain = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (activations extracted; token activations averaged over assistant response to form probe inputs). Labels: GPT-4o assigns Deceptive=1, Honest=0, Ambiguous=-1 (ambiguous examples removed). Representation & PCA: source activations are standardized (source -> zero mean, unit variance) and PCA applied; source statistics are applied to target activations; 100 source PCs retained (S subset of these). Probes: all linear (logistic regression, regularization parameter λ=10); baseline = source-trained probe on full standardized activations; target-trained probes fit on target data. Selection methods: greedy oracle = target-guided greedy adding the PC that most increases target AUROC (reported to find ~8–15 PCs that nearly match target-trained probes); variance control = top-k PCs by variance; source-PCA probe and target-PCA probe use standardized coefficients to rank PCs (standardized coefficient = |coefficient| * PC standard deviation). LLM judge: GPT-5-mini interprets PC positive/negative poles and rates OOD-deception usefulness on a 1–10 scale; observed maximum OOD score = 6. Interp-selection = 19 PCs that received the maximum observed score (6) in both scoring runs; interp-ablated PCs = remaining 81. Evaluation: 5-fold CV on targets (held-out folds used for testing); AUROC reported with 95% CI. Causal validation (intervention/ablation at inference) was not performed. Appendix C: SAE decoder alignment (resource andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct); statistics reported include Spearman ρ and Jaccard overlap.

Paper question: whether selecting subspaces of LM representations improves out-of-distribution (OOD) deception detection. Method: compare probes (classifiers) trained on full representations vs probes using selected directions/subspaces. Two selection approaches highlighted: (1) target-guided selection that uses target labels but does not fit probe weights on them; (2) interpretation-based selection using natural-language interpretations, which requires no target data. Key claims: small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes; selecting directions by source weights, target-class separation, or explained variance does not recover the same transferable subspaces; interpretation-based selection improves over the full-representation baseline on all targets, though how well it recovers varies sharply across targets. Scope/caveats: study uses one model and one source dataset; interpretations are descriptive, not causal. The paper includes a "Glossary." (no glossary content shown in this part).

Goal: test whether selecting subspaces of LM representations improves OOD (transfer) deception detection. Source dataset: Roleplaying (V8). Targets include C2R (Insider Trading Report), W6 (Insider Trading Confirm), J9 (Sandbagging). Model & readout: layer-15 residual-stream activations from Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6), averaged over assistant-response tokens. Preprocessing: standardization = zero-mean/unit-variance using source statistics applied to both source and targets. Dimensionality reduction: PCA / N4D retains the leading 100 source directions (Q7); "PCs" refer to these retained source directions; "leading" = lower index. Paper title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Setup: use linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations to detect deception behaviors; evaluate generalization across 3 held-out deception detection datasets (only two named here: Insider Trading Report and Sandbagging). Key claim: projecting inputs onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) from the training activation distribution enables cross-domain transfer that nearly matches probes trained on the target/test distribution. Method extension: interpret PCs and use an LLM judge to score each PC by whether its most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; then probe using top-scoring PCs. Results: this PC-selection method closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and by 25% on Sandbagging. Interpretation claim: source-probe-weighted directions encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and in ways capturable by natural language descriptions. Broad claim: OOD robustness of probes largely determined by subspace selection. Venue noted: Machine Learning, ICML.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Setup: train linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations (source dataset: Roleplaying deception scenarios); evaluate OOD on three held-out target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Core idea: work in the source-domain PCA basis and select a small subset of source PCs to train probes that avoid spurious surface correlations and transfer to targets. Key empirical claims: (1) A small transferable subspace exists (Sec. 4.2): a target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds ~8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe. (2) Source-side and target-side weight-based rankings fail to recover this subspace (Sec. 4.3): ranking PCs by source or target probe weights does not outperform the full-representation baseline. (3) An LLM judge can partially recover the subspace without target labels (Sec. 4.5): it interprets PCs via their extreme examples and selects transferable PCs. Prior-note results: PC-selection method closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Interpretation claim: transferable directions encode more abstract contrasts describable in language; probe OOD robustness largely determined by subspace selection. Figure 1 outlines pipeline: project activations into source PCA basis, filter candidate PCs, train probes on selected low-dim subspace.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Setup: train linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations using a source dataset of roleplaying deception scenarios; evaluate OOD on three held-out target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Method: compute PCA on source activations, work in source PCA basis, filter candidate PCs, and select a small subset of source PCs to train linear probes on the low-dimensional subspace. Key empirical claims: (1) A small transferable subspace exists: target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds ~8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe (Sec. 4.2). (2) Weight-based rankings on source or target probes fail to recover this subspace and do not outperform full-representation baseline (Sec. 4.3). (3) An LLM judge can partially recover the subspace without target labels by interpreting PCs via extreme examples and selecting transferable PCs (Sec. 4.5). Reported quantitative impact: PC-selection method closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Context from related work: literature reports linear/low-dim directions for high-level properties and behaviors, examples of single-direction control (refusal/assistant axis), skepticism about probes (probe may learn task/exploit surface correlates; OOD probe generalization can be uneven), and use of LLMs to generate natural-language explanations of features and to inform interventions.

Datasets: Roleplaying is the source; targets are Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Each response labeled by GPT-4o as honest (0), ambiguous (-1), or deceptive (1); ambiguous examples removed. Language model activations: layer-15 residual stream of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; token activations averaged over the assistant response. Preprocessing: standardize source activations (zero mean, unit variance) and apply the same source statistics to standardize target activations. PCA: run PCA on the scaled source activations and retain the top 100 PCs. Probes: logistic regression (regularization λ=10). For experiments using a subset S of PCs, project activations onto S before training/evaluation; baseline probes train on the full standardized activations. Motivation for 100 PCs: lower-index PCs align more with SAE decoder features (Appendix C) and are easier to interpret, but authors do not claim low-index PCs inherently generalize better; Section 4.1 reportedly shows the 100-PC subspace suffices to separate deceptive vs. honest on every target.

Datasets: source = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Confirm, Insider Trading Report, Sandbagging. Responses labeled honest (0), ambiguous (-1), deceptive (1); ambiguous examples removed. Model activations: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer-15 residual stream; token activations averaged over assistant response. Preprocessing: standardize source activations (zero mean, unit variance) and apply same source statistics to standardize target activations. PCA: run PCA on scaled source activations and retain top 100 PCs. Probes: logistic regression (λ=10). Baselines: probes trained on full standardized representations; for PC-subset experiments project activations onto subset before training/evaluation.

Key results (Section 4.1): source-trained probe (full rep) AUROC on targets: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Probe trained on target data within top-100 source PCs (5-fold CV) achieves AUROC ≈ 0.936 (Confirm) / 0.950 (Report) / 0.869 (Sandbagging) — so 100-PC subspace suffices to separate classes on every target.

Greedy PC-selection (Section 4.2): start empty, iteratively add from top-100 PCs the PC that most improves AUROC on target; to evaluate a candidate, project source activations onto current subset and train probe on source projections; PC choice guided by target labeled folds (5-fold CV) while probe weights always fit on source; stop when AUROC improvement ≤0.001. Avg subset sizes: Report 15 PCs, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14. Greedy improves over baseline (full-rep baseline) by ~+0.22 (Report) and +0.23 (Sandbagging) and approaches target-trained performance; top-k-by-variance matched greedy only for Confirm.

Section 4.3 tests two hypotheses for transferable PCs (separate target classes alone vs PCs source probe leans on). Compare rankings by standardized coefficient = |coef| * std(PC) from probes trained on activations projected to source-PCA basis (source-probe vs target-probe vs greedy oracle).

Datasets: source = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Confirm, Insider Trading Report, Sandbagging. Labels: honest(0), ambiguous(-1) (removed), deceptive(1). Representations: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer-15 residual stream; token activations averaged over assistant response; standardize using source mean/var and apply same stats to targets. PCA: run on scaled source activations, keep top 100 PCs. Probes: logistic regression (λ=10). Baselines: probes on full standardized representations; PC-subset experiments project activations onto chosen subset before training/eval. Key baseline numbers: source-trained probe (full rep) AUROC on targets: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probe on top-100 source PCs (5-fold CV) AUROC ≈ Confirm 0.936, Report 0.950, Sandbagging 0.869 (so 100-PC subspace suffices for target separation). Greedy PC-selection (target labels guide PC choice, probe weights fit on source; stop when AUROC improvement ≤0.001): CV average subset sizes Report 15, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14; greedy boosted AUROC over full-rep by ~+0.22 (Report) and +0.23 (Sandbagging); top-k-by-variance only matched greedy for Confirm. Cross-target ranking experiment (Sec 4.3): define source-PCA and target-PCA rankings (both use source-PCA basis); to pick k, run greedy on full target dataset (single k): Report k=13, Confirm k=7, Sandbagging k=14 (differs slightly from CV sizes). Results: both hypotheses fail — source-PCA probe transfers ~as well as full-rep baseline (i.e., doesn't generalize); target-PCA probe does well on Report, worse than greedy on Confirm, and below-random on Sandbagging. Interpretability (Sec 4.4): for each top-100 PC, collect 8 most/least activating examples and have an LLM judge describe poles and give 1–10 OOD scores; max observed score=6; keep PCs that scored 6 in both runs → 19 interp-selected PCs. Of 5 PCs that appeared in greedy selections for multiple targets, 3 had max OOD; only 1 of top-5 source-PCA PCs got max OOD. Sec 4.5 evaluates probe AUROC for interp-selected 19 PCs vs controls (full-rep, top-19 by variance, remaining 81). Figures and appendices provide full results.
