Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Abstract claim: directions weighted by a source probe encode source-specific surface features; transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly (capturable in natural language). Main claim: probe OOD robustness largely determined by subspace selection. Background: linear probes expose semantic info but can fail OOD despite strong in-distribution performance. Assertion that behavioral concepts have linear representations but probes often learn spurious correlations; such unreliability is problematic for harmful-interaction monitoring. Method/approach keywords: work in source Q7 coordinates to avoid privileging model latent dims; these coordinates provide data-driven representation structure. Prior findings cited: removing leading components can improve downstream embedding performance (Mu et al., 2018); leading-component projections used as a probing baseline (Kantamneni et al., 2025). Problem framed as selecting dimensions that permit generalization vs. spurious source-trained classification. Pipeline (Fig.1): projection into source N4D basis, filtering candidate Q7 directions, probe training in selected low-dimensional subspace.

Goal: probe OOD robustness largely determined by subspace selection; pipeline projects activations into a source data-driven basis (source N4D / Q7 coordinates), filters candidate directions, and trains probes in the selected low-dim subspace. Prior findings: removing leading components can improve downstream embedding performance; leading-component projections used as a baseline. Related work summarized here: (1) Linear concept directions: studies report cross-dataset linear structure for true/false and other behaviors (Marks & Tegmark 2024; Park et al. 2024 formalize the linear representation hypothesis). Single directions reported for refusal and an “assistant” axis (Arditi et al. 2024; Lu et al. 2026); other work finds population-level directions for honesty/emotion (Zou et al. 2025). (2) Linear probes limits: probes can learn task/surface correlates rather than reveal intrinsic representation; encoded vs. recoverable information distinction; strong in-distribution probes often generalize unevenly—safety evaluation must separate robust internal signals from dataset artifacts. (3) Interpreting features with natural-language explanations: LLM-generated neuron explanations from high-activation examples (Bills et al. 2023), automated sparse-autoencoder feature labeling (Paulo et al. 2025; Bricken et al. 2023), and concept identification + ablation during fine-tuning (Casademunt et al. 2025).

Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6). Use layer-15 residual-stream activations (per Ying et al. 2026); activations averaged over assistant-response tokens. Data: four Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025) datasets — one source (Roleplaying: V8) and three held-out targets: Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), Sandbagging (J9). Only Roleplaying used as source. Labels: annotated by GPT-4o (K8, OpenAI 2024) with mapping honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous responses removed (binary honest vs deceptive). Preprocessing: source activations standardized to zero mean, unit variance; same source statistics used to standardize targets. Dimensionality reduction: PCA on source (N4D), retain leading 100 principal components (PCs Q7); probes trained on projections to subset S of these PCs. Classifiers: logistic regression (regularization λ=10) for all classifiers; comparator (full-representation baseline B8Q) trains on all standardized activations (no PCA). Choice of 100 PCs driven by interpretability comparability (alignment with U9/Bricken et al. 2023 decreases with PC index, so lower-index PCs are easier to interpret), not because low-index PCs generalize best. Error bars denote 95% confidence intervals.

Model/data: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6); layer-15 residual-stream activations averaged over assistant-response tokens. Datasets: source Roleplaying (V8); targets Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), Sandbagging (J9). Labels: GPT-4o annotations mapped honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous removed → binary. Preprocessing: source activations standardized (zero mean, unit variance); same source stats used to standardize targets. PCA on standardized source (N4D); retain leading 100 PCs (Q7). Probes: logistic regression (λ=10) on projections to subsets S of the 100 PCs; comparator B8Q trains on full standardized activations (no PCA). Metrics/CI: target F3 reported; 5-fold CV used for many evaluations; error bars = 95% CI.

Key experimental results/methods (Part 4): W6 transfer reasonably good, C2R moderate, J9 poor. Target-trained classifiers within the 100-PC source subspace separate classes on every target; the single source-trained direction fails to generalize. Greedy oracle search (H2) uses target labels to pick PCs: start empty, consider each of 100 PCs, fit source logistic weights on candidate subset, add PC that most improves target F3 (CV selection on non-held-out folds; stop if no candidate >0.001). Variance-ranked baseline (Y4) matches H2 only on easy W6; explained variance poorly predicts transfer utility. Ranking probes: source-PCA (T6) and target-PCA (M9) order PCs by standardized coefficient X4 = |coef| * PC std (on source-projected activations); evaluated probes are then trained on source projections to top-k. T6 ≈ B8Q; M9: good on C2R, worse than H2 on W6, below random on J9. Interpretation (C7): for each leading PC, LLM judge sees top-8 and bottom-8 source examples, writes pole/whole descriptions and assigns OOD score (R5). Interp-selected intersection (L2) = PCs reaching observed max in both scoring runs; A7 = its complement; Y4 also used as equal-dim control. L2 (language-only) improves over B8Q and A7, especially on C2R and J9.

Model/data: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6); layer-15 residual-stream activations averaged over assistant-response tokens. Source dataset: Roleplaying (V8). Targets: Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), Sandbagging (J9). Labels: GPT-4o annotations mapped honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous removed → binary. Preprocessing: source activations standardized (zero mean, unit variance); same source stats used to standardize targets. PCA on standardized source (N4D); retain leading 100 PCs. Probes: logistic regression (λ=10) on projections to subsets S of the 100 PCs; comparator B8Q: logistic regression on full standardized activations (no PCA). Metric: target F3; 5-fold CV; 95% CIs. Key results: target-trained classifiers within 100-PC source subspace separate classes on every target; a single source-trained direction fails to generalize. Transfer performance: W6 transfer reasonably good/easy (high baselines), C2R moderate, J9 poor and most OOD. Greedy oracle search (H2): uses target labels to pick PCs greedily, stop if best candidate improvement ≤0.001. Baselines: variance-ranked (Y4) matches H2 only on easy W6; explained variance poorly predicts transfer utility. Ranking probes: source-PCA (T6) ≈ B8Q; target-PCA (M9) orders by |coef|*PC std and is good on C2R, worse than H2 on W6, below random on J9. Interpretation (C7): for each leading PC, human judge sees top-8 and bottom-8 source examples, writes pole/whole descriptions and assigns OOD score. Interp-selected intersection (L2) = PCs reaching observed max in both scoring runs; A7 = complement; L2 (language-only) improves over B8Q and A7, especially on C2R and J9. Limitations (Part 5): single-model/single-source limits generality; W6’s high baseline reduces informativeness; J9 likely suffers distribution shift; pipeline is fully linear (N4D projection + logistic regression)—nonlinear probes and other readout locations not explored; interpretive claims are descriptive/correlational (no causal ablations of high-rated directions).

Targets: Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), Sandbagging (J9). Labels: GPT-4o annotations mapped honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous removed → binary. Preprocessing: source activations standardized (zero mean, unit variance); same source stats used to standardize targets. PCA on standardized source (N4D); retain leading 100 PCs. Probes: logistic regression (λ=10) on projections to subsets S of the 100 PCs; comparator B8Q: logistic regression on full standardized activations (no PCA). Metric: target F3; 5-fold CV; 95% CIs. Key results: target-trained classifiers within 100-PC source subspace separate classes on every target; a single source-trained direction fails to generalize. Transfer performance: W6 transfers well/high baseline, C2R moderate, J9 poor/most OOD. Greedy oracle search (H2) picks PCs using target labels greedily. Baselines: variance-ranked (Y4) matches H2 only on easy W6; explained variance poorly predicts transfer utility. Ranking probes: source-PCA (T6) ≈ B8Q; target-PCA (M9) (rank by |coef|*PC std) good on C2R, worse than H2 on W6, below random on J9. Interpretation: human judge inspects top/bottom source examples per PC, writes pole/whole descriptions and assigns OOD score. Interp-selected intersection (L2) = PCs reaching observed max in both scoring runs; A7 = complement; L2 (language-only) improves over B8Q and A7, especially on C2R and J9. Limitations: single-model/source, W6 high baseline, J9 distribution shift, pipeline fully linear, interpretations descriptive/correlational. Conclusion: OOD probing requires representation selection (not just classifier fitting); full-representation probes can mix spurious surface cues with general behavior and harm transfer; sparse directional subspaces can better isolate general behavioral structure.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars.
Goal: Can selecting principal components (PCs), i.e., directions in a source activation basis, improve out-of-distribution (OOD) deception detection?
Method overview: Train linear probes (logistic regression) on one source dataset; evaluate on 3 held-out target datasets. Use a target-supervised greedy search that adds PCs according to target performance. Also evaluate ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights. Introduce an LLM judge that scores natural-language PC descriptions without using target data.
Key quantitative claims/results: Greedy, target-supervised search finds 8–15 PCs that nearly match probes trained on target data. Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights does not recover this transferable subspace. Selecting 19 PCs that receive the maximum observed LLM score in both runs (unsupervised by target data) improves transfer on all 3 targets. For two of the targets, this selection closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and the greedy oracle. 
Other terms to track: "full-representation baseline", "greedy oracle", "both runs" (unspecified here), which targets achieve 78% and 25% (unspecified here).

Paper: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Goal: improve cross-domain (source->target) deception detection by selecting source-PC directions. Source domain = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (activations extracted; token activations averaged over assistant response to form probe inputs). Labels: GPT-4o assigns Deceptive=1, Honest=0, Ambiguous=-1 (ambiguous examples removed). Representation & PCA: source activations are standardized (source -> zero mean, unit variance) and PCA applied; source statistics are applied to target activations; 100 source PCs retained (S subset of these). Probes: all linear (logistic regression, regularization parameter λ=10); baseline = source-trained probe on full standardized activations; target-trained probes fit on target data. Selection methods: greedy oracle = target-guided greedy adding the PC that most increases target AUROC (reported to find ~8–15 PCs that nearly match target-trained probes); variance control = top-k PCs by variance; source-PCA probe and target-PCA probe use standardized coefficients to rank PCs (standardized coefficient = |coefficient| * PC standard deviation). LLM judge: GPT-5-mini interprets PC positive/negative poles and rates OOD-deception usefulness on a 1–10 scale; observed maximum OOD score = 6. Interp-selection = 19 PCs that received the maximum observed score (6) in both scoring runs; interp-ablated PCs = remaining 81. Evaluation: 5-fold CV on targets (held-out folds used for testing); AUROC reported with 95% CI. Causal validation (intervention/ablation at inference) was not performed. Appendix C: SAE decoder alignment (resource andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct); statistics reported include Spearman ρ and Jaccard overlap.

Key results in this part:
- Full-representation source-trained AUROC (target eval): Insider Trading Confirm 0.874, Insider Trading Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606.
- Target-trained probes on the 100-PC subspace achieve AUROCs 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869 (reported across the three targets).
- Conclusion: 100-PC subspace contains enough target-class information; limited transfer is due to source-learned direction, not missing info.
- Greedy (oracle) PC-selection: searches top-100 PCs, at each step adds PC that most improves target AUROC (probe weights always fit on source; selection uses labeled non-held-out target folds in 5-fold CV); stop when improvement <0.001.
- Greedy average subset sizes: Report 15 PCs, Confirm 8 PCs, Sandbagging 14 PCs.
- Greedy improves baseline AUROC by +0.22 (Report) and +0.23 (Sandbagging), coming close to target-trained performance; variance-ranked k control matches greedy only on Confirm and falls far behind on Report and Sandbagging.

This part: defines standardized coefficient = |probe coeff| * PC std; two rankings: source-PCA (weights from source) and target-PCA (weights from target), both over activations in the source-PCA basis. Paper question: whether selecting subspaces of LM representations improves out-of-distribution (OOD) deception detection. Method: compare probes (classifiers) trained on full representations vs probes using selected directions/subspaces. Two selection approaches highlighted: (1) target-guided selection that uses target labels but does not fit probe weights on them; (2) interpretation-based selection using natural-language interpretations, which requires no target data. Key claims: small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes; selecting directions by source weights, target-class separation, or explained variance does not recover the same transferable subspaces; interpretation-based selection improves over the full-representation baseline on all targets, though how well it recovers varies sharply across targets. Scope/caveats: study uses one model and one source dataset; interpretations are descriptive, not causal. The paper includes a "Glossary." (no glossary content shown in this part).

Goal: test whether selecting subspaces of LM representations improves OOD (transfer) deception detection. Source dataset: Roleplaying (V8). Targets include C2R (Insider Trading Report), W6 (Insider Trading Confirm), J9 (Sandbagging). Model & readout: layer-15 residual-stream activations from Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6), averaged over assistant-response tokens. Preprocessing: standardization = zero-mean/unit-variance using source statistics applied to both source and targets. Dimensionality reduction: PCA / N4D retains the leading 100 source directions (Q7); "PCs" refer to these retained source directions; "leading" = lower index. Probes: logistic regression with λ=10, evaluated by AUROC (F3) with 95% CIs; 5-fold CV where selection uses non-held-out target folds and evaluation uses the held-out fold. Baselines & methods: B8Q = full-representation baseline (source-trained on all standardized activations); Y4 = top-k PCs by variance (variance-ranked subset matched in dimension count); H2 = greedy oracle (target-guided direction selection but probe weights fitted only on source); T6 = source-PCA probe (supplies source coefficient rankings); M9 = target-PCA probe (supplies target coefficient rankings); X4 = standardized coefficient = |coef| * PC_std. Interpretation-based selection: natural-language explanations produced with P2 (GPT-5-mini) and rated by C7 (LLM judge) yielding R5 (OOD score/generalization rating); L2 = interp-selected PC probe (uses directions reaching max R5 in both scoring runs); A7 = interp-ablated PC probe (complement). Decoder alignment uses SAE (U9) decoder features (resource: andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct); Spearman ρ reports relation of PC index to decoder alignment. Scope: one model, one source dataset; interpretations are descriptive, not causal.

Paper title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Setup: use linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations to detect deception behaviors; evaluate generalization across 3 held-out deception detection datasets (only two named here: Insider Trading Report and Sandbagging). Key claim: projecting inputs onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) from the training activation distribution enables cross-domain transfer that nearly matches probes trained on the target/test distribution. Method extension: interpret PCs and use an LLM judge to score each PC by whether its most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; then probe using top-scoring PCs. Results: this PC-selection method closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and by 25% on Sandbagging. Interpretation claim: source-probe-weighted directions encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and in ways capturable by natural language descriptions. Broad claim: OOD robustness of probes largely determined by subspace selection. Venue noted: Machine Learning, ICML.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Setup: train linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations (source dataset: Roleplaying deception scenarios); evaluate OOD on three held-out target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Core idea: work in the source-domain PCA basis and select a small subset of source PCs to train probes that avoid spurious surface correlations and transfer to targets. Key empirical claims: (1) A small transferable subspace exists (Sec. 4.2): a target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds ~8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe. (2) Source-side and target-side weight-based rankings fail to recover this subspace (Sec. 4.3): ranking PCs by source or target probe weights does not outperform the full-representation baseline. (3) An LLM judge can partially recover the subspace without target labels (Sec. 4.5): it interprets PCs via their extreme examples and selects transferable PCs. Prior-note results: PC-selection method closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Interpretation claim: transferable directions encode more abstract contrasts describable in language; probe OOD robustness largely determined by subspace selection. Figure 1 outlines pipeline: project activations into source PCA basis, filter candidate PCs, train probes on selected low-dim subspace.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Setup: train linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations using a source dataset of roleplaying deception scenarios; evaluate OOD on three held-out target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Method: compute PCA on source activations, work in source PCA basis, filter candidate PCs, and select a small subset of source PCs to train linear probes on the low-dimensional subspace. Key empirical claims: (1) A small transferable subspace exists: target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds ~8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe (Sec. 4.2). (2) Weight-based rankings on source or target probes fail to recover this subspace and do not outperform full-representation baseline (Sec. 4.3). (3) An LLM judge can partially recover the subspace without target labels by interpreting PCs via extreme examples and selecting transferable PCs (Sec. 4.5). Reported quantitative impact: PC-selection method closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Context from related work: literature reports linear/low-dim directions for high-level properties and behaviors, examples of single-direction control (refusal/assistant axis), skepticism about probes (probe may learn task/exploit surface correlates; OOD probe generalization can be uneven), and use of LLMs to generate natural-language explanations of features and to inform interventions.

Datasets: Roleplaying is the source; targets are Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Each response labeled by GPT-4o as honest (0), ambiguous (-1), or deceptive (1); ambiguous examples removed. Language model activations: layer-15 residual stream of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; token activations averaged over the assistant response. Preprocessing: standardize source activations (zero mean, unit variance) and apply the same source statistics to standardize target activations. PCA: run PCA on the scaled source activations and retain the top 100 PCs. Probes: logistic regression (regularization λ=10). For experiments using a subset S of PCs, project activations onto S before training/evaluation; baseline probes train on the full standardized activations. Motivation for 100 PCs: lower-index PCs align more with SAE decoder features (Appendix C) and are easier to interpret, but authors do not claim low-index PCs inherently generalize better; Section 4.1 reportedly shows the 100-PC subspace suffices to separate deceptive vs. honest on every target.

Model activations: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer-15 residual stream; token activations averaged over assistant response. Key results (Section 4.1): source-trained probe (full rep) AUROC on targets: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Probe trained on target data within top-100 source PCs (5-fold CV) achieves AUROC ≈ 0.936 (Confirm) / 0.950 (Report) / 0.869 (Sandbagging) — so 100-PC subspace suffices to separate classes on every target.

Greedy PC-selection (Section 4.2): start empty, iteratively add from top-100 PCs the PC that most improves AUROC on target; to evaluate a candidate, project source activations onto current subset and train probe on source projections; PC choice guided by target labeled folds (5-fold CV) while probe weights always fit on source; stop when AUROC improvement ≤0.001. Avg subset sizes: Report 15 PCs, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14. Greedy improves over baseline (full-rep baseline) by ~+0.22 (Report) and +0.23 (Sandbagging) and approaches target-trained performance; top-k-by-variance matched greedy only for Confirm.

Section 4.3 tests two hypotheses for transferable PCs (separate target classes alone vs PCs source probe leans on). Compare rankings by standardized coefficient = |coef| * std(PC) from probes trained on activations projected to source-PCA basis (source-probe vs target-probe vs greedy oracle).

Datasets: source = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Confirm, Insider Trading Report, Sandbagging. Labels: honest(0), ambiguous(-1) (removed), deceptive(1). Representations: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer-15 residual stream; token activations averaged over assistant response; standardize using source mean/var and apply same stats to targets. PCA: run on scaled source activations, keep top 100 PCs. Probes: logistic regression (λ=10). Baselines: probes on full standardized representations; PC-subset experiments project activations onto chosen subset before training/eval. Key baseline numbers: source-trained probe (full rep) AUROC on targets: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probe on top-100 source PCs (5-fold CV) AUROC ≈ Confirm 0.936, Report 0.950, Sandbagging 0.869 (so 100-PC subspace suffices for target separation). Greedy PC-selection (target labels guide PC choice, probe weights fit on source; stop when AUROC improvement ≤0.001): CV average subset sizes Report 15, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14; greedy boosted AUROC over full-rep by ~+0.22 (Report) and +0.23 (Sandbagging); top-k-by-variance only matched greedy for Confirm. Cross-target ranking experiment (Sec 4.3): define source-PCA and target-PCA rankings (both use source-PCA basis); to pick k, run greedy on full target dataset (single k): Report k=13, Confirm k=7, Sandbagging k=14 (differs slightly from CV sizes). Results: both hypotheses fail — source-PCA probe transfers ~as well as full-rep baseline (i.e., doesn't generalize); target-PCA probe does well on Report, worse than greedy on Confirm, and below-random on Sandbagging. Interpretability (Sec 4.4): for each top-100 PC, collect 8 most/least activating examples and have an LLM judge describe poles and give 1–10 OOD scores; max observed score=6; keep PCs that scored 6 in both runs → 19 interp-selected PCs. Of 5 PCs that appeared in greedy selections for multiple targets, 3 had max OOD; only 1 of top-5 source-PCA PCs got max OOD. Sec 4.5 evaluates probe AUROC for interp-selected 19 PCs vs controls (full-rep, top-19 by variance, remaining 81). Figures and appendices provide full results.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Abstract claim: directions weighted by a source probe encode source-specific surface features; transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly (capturable in natural language). Main claim: probe OOD robustness largely determined by subspace selection. Background: linear probes expose semantic info but can fail OOD despite strong in-distribution performance. Assertion that behavioral concepts have linear representations but probes often learn spurious correlations; such unreliability is problematic for harmful-interaction monitoring. Method/approach keywords: work in source Q7 coordinates to avoid privileging model latent dims; these coordinates provide data-driven representation structure. Prior findings cited: removing leading components can improve downstream embedding performance (Mu et al., 2018); leading-component projections used as a probing baseline (Kantamneni et al., 2025). Problem framed as selecting dimensions that permit generalization vs. spurious source-trained classification. Pipeline (Fig.1): projection into source N4D basis, filtering candidate Q7 directions, probe training in selected low-dimensional subspace.

Goal: probe OOD robustness largely determined by subspace selection; pipeline projects activations into a source data-driven basis (source N4D / Q7 coordinates), filters candidate directions, and trains probes in the selected low-dim subspace. Prior findings: removing leading components can improve downstream embedding performance; leading-component projections used as a baseline. Related work summarized here: (1) Linear concept directions: studies report cross-dataset linear structure for true/false and other behaviors (Marks & Tegmark 2024; Park et al. 2024 formalize the linear representation hypothesis). Single directions reported for refusal and an “assistant” axis (Arditi et al. 2024; Lu et al. 2026); other work finds population-level directions for honesty/emotion (Zou et al. 2025). (2) Linear probes limits: probes can learn task/surface correlates rather than reveal intrinsic representation; encoded vs. recoverable information distinction; strong in-distribution probes often generalize unevenly—safety evaluation must separate robust internal signals from dataset artifacts. (3) Interpreting features with natural-language explanations: LLM-generated neuron explanations from high-activation examples (Bills et al. 2023), automated sparse-autoencoder feature labeling (Paulo et al. 2025; Bricken et al. 2023), and concept identification + ablation during fine-tuning (Casademunt et al. 2025).

Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6). Use layer-15 residual-stream activations (per Ying et al. 2026); activations averaged over assistant-response tokens. Data: four Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025) datasets — one source (Roleplaying: V8) and three held-out targets: Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), Sandbagging (J9). Only Roleplaying used as source. Labels: annotated by GPT-4o (K8, OpenAI 2024) with mapping honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous responses removed (binary honest vs deceptive). Preprocessing: source activations standardized to zero mean, unit variance; same source statistics used to standardize targets. Dimensionality reduction: PCA on source (N4D), retain leading 100 principal components (PCs Q7); probes trained on projections to subset S of these PCs. Classifiers: logistic regression (regularization λ=10) for all classifiers; comparator (full-representation baseline B8Q) trains on all standardized activations (no PCA). Choice of 100 PCs driven by interpretability comparability (alignment with U9/Bricken et al. 2023 decreases with PC index, so lower-index PCs are easier to interpret), not because low-index PCs generalize best. Error bars denote 95% confidence intervals.

Datasets: source Roleplaying (V8); targets Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), Sandbagging (J9). Labels: GPT-4o annotations mapped honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous removed → binary. Preprocessing: source activations standardized (zero mean, unit variance); same source stats used to standardize targets. PCA on standardized source (N4D); retain leading 100 PCs (Q7). Probes: logistic regression (λ=10) on projections to subsets S of the 100 PCs; comparator B8Q trains on full standardized activations (no PCA). Metrics/CI: target F3 reported; 5-fold CV used for many evaluations; error bars = 95% CI.

Key experimental results/methods (Part 4): W6 transfer reasonably good, C2R moderate, J9 poor. Target-trained classifiers within the 100-PC source subspace separate classes on every target; the single source-trained direction fails to generalize. Greedy oracle search (H2) uses target labels to pick PCs: start empty, consider each of 100 PCs, fit source logistic weights on candidate subset, add PC that most improves target F3 (CV selection on non-held-out folds; stop if no candidate >0.001). Variance-ranked baseline (Y4) matches H2 only on easy W6; explained variance poorly predicts transfer utility. Ranking probes: source-PCA (T6) and target-PCA (M9) order PCs by standardized coefficient X4 = |coef| * PC std (on source-projected activations); evaluated probes are then trained on source projections to top-k. T6 ≈ B8Q; M9: good on C2R, worse than H2 on W6, below random on J9. Interpretation (C7): for each leading PC, LLM judge sees top-8 and bottom-8 source examples, writes pole/whole descriptions and assigns OOD score (R5). Interp-selected intersection (L2) = PCs reaching observed max in both scoring runs; A7 = its complement; Y4 also used as equal-dim control. L2 (language-only) improves over B8Q and A7, especially on C2R and J9.

Key results: target-trained classifiers within 100-PC source subspace separate classes on every target; a single source-trained direction fails to generalize. Transfer performance: W6 transfer reasonably good/easy (high baselines), C2R moderate, J9 poor and most OOD. Greedy oracle search (H2): uses target labels to pick PCs greedily, stop if best candidate improvement ≤0.001. Limitations (Part 5): single-model/single-source limits generality; W6’s high baseline reduces informativeness; J9 likely suffers distribution shift; pipeline is fully linear (N4D projection + logistic regression)—nonlinear probes and other readout locations not explored; interpretive claims are descriptive/correlational (no causal ablations of high-rated directions).

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars.
Goal: Can selecting principal components (PCs), i.e., directions in a source activation basis, improve out-of-distribution (OOD) deception detection?
Method overview: Train linear probes (logistic regression) on one source dataset; evaluate on 3 held-out target datasets. Use a target-supervised greedy search that adds PCs according to target performance. Also evaluate ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights. Introduce an LLM judge that scores natural-language PC descriptions without using target data.
Key quantitative claims/results: Greedy, target-supervised search finds 8–15 PCs that nearly match probes trained on target data. Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights does not recover this transferable subspace. Selecting 19 PCs that receive the maximum observed LLM score in both runs (unsupervised by target data) improves transfer on all 3 targets. For two of the targets, this selection closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and the greedy oracle. 
Other terms to track: "full-representation baseline", "greedy oracle", "both runs" (unspecified here), which targets achieve 78% and 25% (unspecified here).

Paper: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Goal: improve cross-domain (source->target) deception detection by selecting source-PC directions. Source domain = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (activations extracted; token activations averaged over assistant response to form probe inputs). Labels: GPT-4o assigns Deceptive=1, Honest=0, Ambiguous=-1 (ambiguous examples removed). Representation & PCA: source activations are standardized (source -> zero mean, unit variance) and PCA applied; source statistics are applied to target activations; 100 source PCs retained (S subset of these). Probes: all linear (logistic regression, regularization parameter λ=10); baseline = source-trained probe on full standardized activations; target-trained probes fit on target data. Selection methods: greedy oracle = target-guided greedy adding the PC that most increases target AUROC (reported to find ~8–15 PCs that nearly match target-trained probes); variance control = top-k PCs by variance; source-PCA probe and target-PCA probe use standardized coefficients to rank PCs (standardized coefficient = |coefficient| * PC standard deviation). LLM judge: GPT-5-mini interprets PC positive/negative poles and rates OOD-deception usefulness on a 1–10 scale; observed maximum OOD score = 6. Interp-selection = 19 PCs that received the maximum observed score (6) in both scoring runs; interp-ablated PCs = remaining 81. Evaluation: 5-fold CV on targets (held-out folds used for testing); AUROC reported with 95% CI. Causal validation (intervention/ablation at inference) was not performed. Appendix C: SAE decoder alignment (resource andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct); statistics reported include Spearman ρ and Jaccard overlap.

Study: transfer-of-probes from single-source task (Roleplaying) on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer 15. Preprocessing: standardize source activations (apply same stats to targets), run PCA on scaled source activations, keep top 100 PCs. Probe: logistic regression (L2 λ=10). Greedy (oracle) PC-selection: within-CV mean subset sizes 15 / 8 / 14 (Report / Confirm / Sandbagging); greedy-on-full-target pick k = 13 / 7 / 14. Paper question: whether selecting subspaces of LM representations improves out-of-distribution (OOD) deception detection. Method: compare probes (classifiers) trained on full representations vs probes using selected directions/subspaces. Two selection approaches highlighted: (1) target-guided selection that uses target labels but does not fit probe weights on them; (2) interpretation-based selection using natural-language interpretations, which requires no target data. Key claims: small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes; selecting directions by source weights, target-class separation, or explained variance does not recover the same transferable subspaces; interpretation-based selection improves over the full-representation baseline on all targets, though how well it recovers varies sharply across targets. Scope/caveats: study uses one model and one source dataset; interpretations are descriptive, not causal. The paper includes a "Glossary." (no glossary content shown in this part).

Goal: test whether selecting subspaces of LM representations improves OOD (transfer) deception detection. Source dataset: Roleplaying (V8). Targets include C2R (Insider Trading Report), W6 (Insider Trading Confirm), J9 (Sandbagging). Model & readout: layer-15 residual-stream activations from Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6), averaged over assistant-response tokens. Preprocessing: standardization = zero-mean/unit-variance using source statistics applied to both source and targets. Dimensionality reduction: PCA / N4D retains the leading 100 source directions (Q7); "PCs" refer to these retained source directions; "leading" = lower index. Probes: logistic regression with λ=10, evaluated by AUROC (F3) with 95% CIs; 5-fold CV where selection uses non-held-out target folds and evaluation uses the held-out fold. Baselines & methods: B8Q = full-representation baseline (source-trained on all standardized activations); Y4 = top-k PCs by variance (variance-ranked subset matched in dimension count); H2 = greedy oracle (target-guided direction selection but probe weights fitted only on source); T6 = source-PCA probe (supplies source coefficient rankings); M9 = target-PCA probe (supplies target coefficient rankings); X4 = standardized coefficient = |coef| * PC_std. Interpretation-based selection: natural-language explanations produced with P2 (GPT-5-mini) and rated by C7 (LLM judge) yielding R5 (OOD score/generalization rating); L2 = interp-selected PC probe (uses directions reaching max R5 in both scoring runs); A7 = interp-ablated PC probe (complement). Decoder alignment uses SAE (U9) decoder features (resource: andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct); Spearman ρ reports relation of PC index to decoder alignment. Appendix E (PC interpretability): Table 3 lists PCs judged transferable: PC62 (Report+Sandbagging, OOD 6), PC57 (Report+Sandbagging, OOD 6), PC9 (Report+Sandbagging, OOD 3) — note PC9's text mentions "medical/leave vs project/status" (domain mismatch), PC81 (Confirm+Sandbagging, OOD 3), PC86 (Confirm+Sandbagging, OOD 6). Paper title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Setup: use linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations to detect deception behaviors; evaluate generalization across 3 held-out deception detection datasets (only two named here: Insider Trading Report and Sandbagging). Key claim: projecting inputs onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) from the training activation distribution enables cross-domain transfer that nearly matches probes trained on the target/test distribution. Method extension: interpret PCs and use an LLM judge to score each PC by whether its most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; then probe using top-scoring PCs. Results: this PC-selection method closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and by 25% on Sandbagging. Interpretation claim: source-probe-weighted directions encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and in ways capturable by natural language descriptions. Broad claim: OOD robustness of probes largely determined by subspace selection. Venue noted: Machine Learning, ICML.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Setup: train linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations (source dataset: Roleplaying deception scenarios); evaluate OOD on three held-out target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Core idea: work in the source-domain PCA basis and select a small subset of source PCs to train probes that avoid spurious surface correlations and transfer to targets. Key empirical claims: (1) A small transferable subspace exists (Sec. 4.2): a target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds ~8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe. (2) Source-side and target-side weight-based rankings fail to recover this subspace (Sec. 4.3): ranking PCs by source or target probe weights does not outperform the full-representation baseline. (3) An LLM judge can partially recover the subspace without target labels (Sec. 4.5): it interprets PCs via their extreme examples and selects transferable PCs. Prior-note results: PC-selection method closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Interpretation claim: transferable directions encode more abstract contrasts describable in language; probe OOD robustness largely determined by subspace selection. Figure 1 outlines pipeline: project activations into source PCA basis, filter candidate PCs, train probes on selected low-dim subspace.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Setup: train linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations using a source dataset of roleplaying deception scenarios; evaluate OOD on three held-out target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Method: compute PCA on source activations, work in source PCA basis, filter candidate PCs, and select a small subset of source PCs to train linear probes on the low-dimensional subspace. Key empirical claims: (1) A small transferable subspace exists: target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds ~8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe (Sec. 4.2). (2) Weight-based rankings on source or target probes fail to recover this subspace and do not outperform full-representation baseline (Sec. 4.3). (3) An LLM judge can partially recover the subspace without target labels by interpreting PCs via extreme examples and selecting transferable PCs (Sec. 4.5). Reported quantitative impact: PC-selection method closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Context from related work: literature reports linear/low-dim directions for high-level properties and behaviors, examples of single-direction control (refusal/assistant axis), skepticism about probes (probe may learn task/exploit surface correlates; OOD probe generalization can be uneven), and use of LLMs to generate natural-language explanations of features and to inform interventions.

Datasets: Roleplaying is the source; targets are Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Each response labeled by GPT-4o as honest (0), ambiguous (-1), or deceptive (1); ambiguous examples removed. Language model activations: layer-15 residual stream of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; token activations averaged over the assistant response. Preprocessing: standardize source activations (zero mean, unit variance) and apply the same source statistics to standardize target activations. PCA: run PCA on the scaled source activations and retain the top 100 PCs. Probes: logistic regression (regularization λ=10). For experiments using a subset S of PCs, project activations onto S before training/evaluation; baseline probes train on the full standardized activations. Motivation for 100 PCs: lower-index PCs align more with SAE decoder features (Appendix C) and are easier to interpret, but authors do not claim low-index PCs inherently generalize better; Section 4.1 reportedly shows the 100-PC subspace suffices to separate deceptive vs. honest on every target.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Abstract claim: directions weighted by a source probe encode source-specific surface features; transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly (capturable in natural language). Main claim: probe OOD robustness largely determined by subspace selection. Background: linear probes expose semantic info but can fail OOD despite strong in-distribution performance. Assertion that behavioral concepts have linear representations but probes often learn spurious correlations; such unreliability is problematic for harmful-interaction monitoring. Method/approach keywords: work in source Q7 coordinates to avoid privileging model latent dims; these coordinates provide data-driven representation structure. Prior findings cited: removing leading components can improve downstream embedding performance (Mu et al., 2018); leading-component projections used as a probing baseline (Kantamneni et al., 2025). Problem framed as selecting dimensions that permit generalization vs. spurious source-trained classification. Pipeline (Fig.1): projection into source N4D basis, filtering candidate Q7 directions, probe training in selected low-dimensional subspace.

Goal: probe OOD robustness largely determined by subspace selection; pipeline projects activations into a source data-driven basis (source N4D / Q7 coordinates), filters candidate directions, and trains probes in the selected low-dim subspace. Prior findings: removing leading components can improve downstream embedding performance; leading-component projections used as a baseline. Related work summarized here: (1) Linear concept directions: studies report cross-dataset linear structure for true/false and other behaviors (Marks & Tegmark 2024; Park et al. 2024 formalize the linear representation hypothesis). Single directions reported for refusal and an “assistant” axis (Arditi et al. 2024; Lu et al. 2026); other work finds population-level directions for honesty/emotion (Zou et al. 2025). (2) Linear probes limits: probes can learn task/surface correlates rather than reveal intrinsic representation; encoded vs. recoverable information distinction; strong in-distribution probes often generalize unevenly—safety evaluation must separate robust internal signals from dataset artifacts. (3) Interpreting features with natural-language explanations: LLM-generated neuron explanations from high-activation examples (Bills et al. 2023), automated sparse-autoencoder feature labeling (Paulo et al. 2025; Bricken et al. 2023), and concept identification + ablation during fine-tuning (Casademunt et al. 2025).

Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6). Use layer-15 residual-stream activations (per Ying et al. 2026); activations averaged over assistant-response tokens. Data: four Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025) datasets — one source (Roleplaying: V8) and three held-out targets: Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), Sandbagging (J9). Only Roleplaying used as source. Labels: annotated by GPT-4o (K8, OpenAI 2024) with mapping honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous responses removed (binary honest vs deceptive). Preprocessing: source activations standardized to zero mean, unit variance; same source statistics used to standardize targets. Dimensionality reduction: PCA on source (N4D), retain leading 100 principal components (PCs Q7); probes trained on projections to subset S of these PCs. Classifiers: logistic regression (regularization λ=10) for all classifiers; comparator (full-representation baseline B8Q) trains on all standardized activations (no PCA). Choice of 100 PCs driven by interpretability comparability (alignment with U9/Bricken et al. 2023 decreases with PC index, so lower-index PCs are easier to interpret), not because low-index PCs generalize best. Error bars denote 95% confidence intervals.

Key experimental results/methods (Part 4): W6 transfer reasonably good, C2R moderate, J9 poor. Target-trained classifiers within the 100-PC source subspace separate classes on every target; the single source-trained direction fails to generalize. Greedy oracle search (H2) uses target labels to pick PCs: start empty, consider each of 100 PCs, fit source logistic weights on candidate subset, add PC that most improves target F3 (CV selection on non-held-out folds; stop if no candidate >0.001). Variance-ranked baseline (Y4) matches H2 only on easy W6; explained variance poorly predicts transfer utility. Ranking probes: source-PCA (T6) and target-PCA (M9) order PCs by standardized coefficient X4 = |coef| * PC std (on source-projected activations); evaluated probes are then trained on source projections to top-k. T6 ≈ B8Q; M9: good on C2R, worse than H2 on W6, below random on J9. Interpretation (C7): for each leading PC, LLM judge sees top-8 and bottom-8 source examples, writes pole/whole descriptions and assigns OOD score (R5). Interp-selected intersection (L2) = PCs reaching observed max in both scoring runs; A7 = its complement; Y4 also used as equal-dim control. L2 (language-only) improves over B8Q and A7, especially on C2R and J9.

Key results: target-trained classifiers within 100-PC source subspace separate classes on every target; a single source-trained direction fails to generalize. Transfer performance: W6 transfer reasonably good/easy (high baselines), C2R moderate, J9 poor and most OOD. Greedy oracle search (H2): uses target labels to pick PCs greedily, stop if best candidate improvement ≤0.001. Baselines: variance-ranked (Y4) matches H2 only on easy W6; explained variance poorly predicts transfer utility. Ranking probes: source-PCA (T6) ≈ B8Q; target-PCA (M9) orders by |coef|*PC std and is good on C2R, worse than H2 on W6, below random on J9. Key results: target-trained classifiers within 100-PC source subspace separate classes on every target; a single source-trained direction fails to generalize. Transfer performance: W6 transfers well/high baseline, C2R moderate, J9 poor/most OOD. Greedy oracle search (H2) picks PCs using target labels greedily. Baselines: variance-ranked (Y4) matches H2 only on easy W6; explained variance poorly predicts transfer utility. Ranking probes: source-PCA (T6) ≈ B8Q; target-PCA (M9) (rank by |coef|*PC std) good on C2R, worse than H2 on W6, below random on J9. Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars.
Goal: Can selecting principal components (PCs), i.e., directions in a source activation basis, improve out-of-distribution (OOD) deception detection?
Method overview: Train linear probes (logistic regression) on one source dataset; evaluate on 3 held-out target datasets. Use a target-supervised greedy search that adds PCs according to target performance. Also evaluate ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights. Introduce an LLM judge that scores natural-language PC descriptions without using target data.
Key quantitative claims/results: Greedy, target-supervised search finds 8–15 PCs that nearly match probes trained on target data. Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights does not recover this transferable subspace. Selecting 19 PCs that receive the maximum observed LLM score in both runs (unsupervised by target data) improves transfer on all 3 targets. For two of the targets, this selection closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and the greedy oracle. 
Other terms to track: "full-representation baseline", "greedy oracle", "both runs" (unspecified here), which targets achieve 78% and 25% (unspecified here).

Paper: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Goal: improve cross-domain (source->target) deception detection by selecting source-PC directions. Source domain = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (activations extracted; token activations averaged over assistant response to form probe inputs). Labels: GPT-4o assigns Deceptive=1, Honest=0, Ambiguous=-1 (ambiguous examples removed). Representation & PCA: source activations are standardized (source -> zero mean, unit variance) and PCA applied; source statistics are applied to target activations; 100 source PCs retained (S subset of these). Probes: all linear (logistic regression, regularization parameter λ=10); baseline = source-trained probe on full standardized activations; target-trained probes fit on target data. Selection methods: greedy oracle = target-guided greedy adding the PC that most increases target AUROC (reported to find ~8–15 PCs that nearly match target-trained probes); variance control = top-k PCs by variance; source-PCA probe and target-PCA probe use standardized coefficients to rank PCs (standardized coefficient = |coefficient| * PC standard deviation). LLM judge: GPT-5-mini interprets PC positive/negative poles and rates OOD-deception usefulness on a 1–10 scale; observed maximum OOD score = 6. Interp-selection = 19 PCs that received the maximum observed score (6) in both scoring runs; interp-ablated PCs = remaining 81. Evaluation: 5-fold CV on targets (held-out folds used for testing); AUROC reported with 95% CI. Causal validation (intervention/ablation at inference) was not performed. Appendix C: SAE decoder alignment (resource andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct); statistics reported include Spearman ρ and Jaccard overlap.

Paper: "Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD deception detection." Model/data: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; source dataset = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Representations: token activations averaged across assistant response, standardized; PCA fitted on source activations (earlier claim: retain 100 source PCs — flagged potential later inconsistency with a PC-code table that lists only 58 entries). Probes: linear logistic regression (λ=10). Baselines: source-trained on full standardized activations. Main empirical claims: (1) A small transferable subspace exists — greedy target-supervised search (add PCs by target AUROC gain) finds ~8–15 PCs where a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe (Section 4.2; abstract reports greedy averages 15/8/14 across targets). (2) Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights fails to recover this subspace (Section 4.3). (3) An LLM judge can partially recover transferable PCs without target data: judge-selected set = 19 PCs; reported gap recovery = 78% (Insider Trading Report) and 25% (Sandbagging) (Section 4.5). Greedy/oracle details: greedy adds PCs by marginal AUROC gain; judge rates 1–10 examples (observed max score = 6); interp-selection noted as 19 PCs with score 6 in both runs and interp-ablated = remaining 81 (implies 100 PCs). Related work (this part): prior work supports linear concept directions and low-dimensional subspaces (Marks & Tegmark 2024; Park et al. 2024; Zou et al. 2025); probes are useful but can pick up surface correlates or learn the task (Hewitt & Liang 2019; Ravichander et al. 2021); natural-language feature explanations and interventions exist (Bills et al. 2023; Paulo et al. 2025; Bricken et al. 2023; Casademunt et al. 2025). No contradictions found between this Related Work section and earlier notes, but the earlier flagged inconsistency about "100 PCs" vs a later PC-code table with 58 entries remains to check.

Two PC-ranking hypotheses tested in 4.3: source-PCA probe (ranks PCs by standardized coefficient computed from source-trained probe) and target-PCA probe (ranks by standardized coefficient from target-trained probe). Standardized coefficient = |probe coefficient| × PC standard deviation. Both operate on activations projected into the source-PCA basis; probes for transfer are trained on source data projected onto the top k PCs per ranking.

Greedy k set by running greedy on the full target dataset (not CV): k = 13 (Report), 7 (Confirm), 14 (Sandbagging). These differ slightly from Section 4.2/CV means (earlier notes: 15/8/14).

Main result: neither ranking recovers greedy. Source-PCA ranking transfers about as well as the full-representation baseline (i.e., fails to recover greedy). Target-PCA ranking: does well on Report, worse than greedy on Confirm, and below random on Sandbagging. Jaccard overlaps (greedy vs target-ranked): 0.182 / 0.077 / 0.167. Figure 4 and Appendix D/Table 2 referenced.

4.4 interpretation: For each of top 100 source PCs, collect 8 most-/least-activating examples; LLM judge gives 1–10 OOD score (Appendix B). Paper question: whether selecting subspaces of LM representations improves out-of-distribution (OOD) deception detection. Method: compare probes (classifiers) trained on full representations vs probes using selected directions/subspaces. Two selection approaches highlighted: (1) target-guided selection that uses target labels but does not fit probe weights on them; (2) interpretation-based selection using natural-language interpretations, which requires no target data. Key claims: small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes; selecting directions by source weights, target-class separation, or explained variance does not recover the same transferable subspaces; interpretation-based selection improves over the full-representation baseline on all targets, though how well it recovers varies sharply across targets. Scope/caveats: study uses one model and one source dataset; interpretations are descriptive, not causal. The paper includes a "Glossary." (no glossary content shown in this part).

Goal: test whether selecting subspaces of LM representations improves OOD (transfer) deception detection. Source dataset: Roleplaying (V8). Targets include C2R (Insider Trading Report), W6 (Insider Trading Confirm), J9 (Sandbagging). Model & readout: layer-15 residual-stream activations from Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6), averaged over assistant-response tokens. Preprocessing: standardization = zero-mean/unit-variance using source statistics applied to both source and targets. Dimensionality reduction: PCA / N4D retains the leading 100 source directions (Q7); "PCs" refer to these retained source directions; "leading" = lower index. Probes: logistic regression with λ=10, evaluated by AUROC (F3) with 95% CIs; 5-fold CV where selection uses non-held-out target folds and evaluation uses the held-out fold. Baselines & methods: B8Q = full-representation baseline (source-trained on all standardized activations); Y4 = top-k PCs by variance (variance-ranked subset matched in dimension count); H2 = greedy oracle (target-guided direction selection but probe weights fitted only on source); T6 = source-PCA probe (supplies source coefficient rankings); M9 = target-PCA probe (supplies target coefficient rankings); X4 = standardized coefficient = |coef| * PC_std. Interpretation-based selection: natural-language explanations produced with P2 (GPT-5-mini) and rated by C7 (LLM judge) yielding R5 (OOD score/generalization rating); L2 = interp-selected PC probe (uses directions reaching max R5 in both scoring runs); A7 = interp-ablated PC probe (complement). Decoder alignment uses SAE (U9) decoder features (resource: andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct); Spearman ρ reports relation of PC index to decoder alignment. Scope: one model, one source dataset; interpretations are descriptive, not causal.

Goal: test whether selecting subspaces of LM representations (leading PCA directions) improves OOD (transfer) deception detection. (2025) collection — one source Roleplaying (V8) and three held-out targets: Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), Sandbagging (J9). Paper title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Task: deception detection using linear probes on LM activations. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Data: 3 held-out deception detection datasets totaling 1,216 non-ambiguous responses. Main claim: projecting inputs onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) from the training activation distribution enables cross-domain transfer that nearly matches probes trained on target/test distribution. PC interpretations can identify transferable PCs. Method: use an LLM judge to score each PC by whether its most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; then probe using highest-scoring PCs. Reported results: this closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Interpretation claim: source-probe-weighted directions encode source-specific surface features; transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and are capturable by natural language descriptions. Broader claim: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection.

Paper: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection (Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars). Task: deception detection via linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations. Setup: train on a single source dataset (Roleplaying deception scenarios) and evaluate on 3 held-out target datasets (Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging). Total held-out examples noted elsewhere: 1,216 non-ambiguous responses. Approach: work in the source-domain PCA basis (project activations onto source PCs) and select a small subset of PCs for probe training to avoid spurious surface correlations. Key contributions/results claimed: (1) A small transferable subspace exists — a target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds ~8–15 components where a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe (Sec 4.2). (2) Simple rankings fail — ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights does not recover the transferable subspace or outperform the full-representation baseline (Sec 4.3). (3) An LLM judge can partially recover the subspace without target labels by interpreting top/low activating examples per PC and selecting PCs likely to encode transferable behavioral contrast (Sec 4.5). Framing: hypothesis that OOD robustness of probes is determined by subspace selection; transferable PCs encode abstract contrast capturable by natural-language descriptions, while source-weighted directions capture surface features. Figure 1: pipeline overview (project -> filter PCs -> train probes). Relevant sections: 4.2 (transferable subspace), 4.3 (ranking failures), 4.5 (LLM judge selection).

Paper: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection (Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars). Task: deception detection via linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations. Train on a single source dataset (roleplaying deception scenarios) and evaluate on three held-out target datasets (Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging). Held-out evaluation: earlier note records 1,216 non-ambiguous responses. Approach: compute PCA on source-domain activations, project activations onto source PCs, and select a small subset of PCs for probe training to avoid spurious surface correlations. Key claimed contributions/results: (1) A small transferable subspace exists — a target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds ~8–15 components where a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe (Sec 4.2). (2) Simple rankings fail — ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights does not recover the transferable subspace or outperform the full-representation baseline (Sec 4.3). (3) An LLM judge can partially recover the subspace without target labels by interpreting top/low activating examples per PC and selecting PCs likely to encode transferable behavioral contrast (Sec 4.5). Related work summary from this part: prior work documents linear directions/subspaces for high-level behaviors and truthfulness (Marks & Tegmark 2024; Park et al. 2024; Zou et al. 2025), single directions mediating refusal/assistant behavior (Arditi et al. 2024; Lu et al. 2026), known limitations of probes and OOD generalization concerns (Hewitt & Liang 2019; Ravichander et al. 2021; recent work on OOD probe generalization), and use of LLMs to generate natural-language explanations for high-activation examples and label features (Bills et al. 2023; Paulo et al. 2025; Bricken et al. 2023), plus interventions via interpreted concepts (Casademunt et al. 2025). Sections to verify later: 4.2, 4.3, 4.5.

Datasets: Roleplaying = source; targets = Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Responses labeled by GPT-4o as honest(0), ambiguous(-1), deceptive(1); ambiguous responses removed (earlier note: 1,216 non‑ambiguous responses used for held-out evaluation). Model & activations: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer 15 residual stream activations; token activations averaged over the assistant's response. Preprocessing: standardize source activations to zero mean and unit variance; apply same source statistics to standardize target activations. Dimensionality reduction: run PCA on scaled source activations and retain top 100 PCs. Probes: logistic regression (regularization λ=10). For experiments using subsets S, project activations onto S before training/evaluation; baseline probes train on full standardized activations. Motivation: top 100 PCs chosen because alignment with SAE decoder features decreases with PC index (Appendix C) — lower-index PCs are more interpretable, though paper does NOT claim low-index PCs generalize better; Section 4.1 reportedly shows 100‑PC subspace suffices to separate deceptive vs honest on every target. Key claims to verify in later sections: (1) a small transferable subspace exists (~8–15 PCs) where source-trained probes nearly match target-trained probes (Sec 4.2), (2) simple rankings of PCs fail to recover the transferable subspace (Sec 4.3), (3) an LLM judge can partially recover subspace without target labels (Sec 4.5).

Datasets: Roleplaying = source; targets = Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Labels by GPT-4o: honest(0), ambiguous(-1), deceptive(1); ambiguous removed (1,216 non-ambiguous responses used for held-out eval). For subset experiments, project activations onto S before training/eval; baseline probes train on full standardized activations. Section 4.1 baseline (source-trained on full reps) AUROC on targets: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probes on top-100 source PCs (5-fold CV) achieve 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869 (Confirm / Report / Sandbagging), so 100-PC subspace contains sufficient signal. Section 4.2: Greedy PC selection (search among top 100 PCs, iteratively add PC that most improves AUROC on target; candidate evaluation: train probe on source projections and measure AUROC on non-held-out target folds; probe weights always fit on source; selection guided by target labels). 5-fold CV, stop when gain <0.001. Average greedy subset sizes: Report 15, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14. Greedy closes much of gap, improving baseline by +0.22 (Report) and +0.23 (Sandbagging); variance-based top-k matches greedy only for Confirm. Section 4.3: Hypotheses for transferable PCs: (1) PCs that individually separate target classes; (2) PCs the source probe leans on. Compare two PC rankings based on standardized coefficient = |coef| * PC std from probe trained on source-projected activations. Key claims to verify later: small transferable subspace (~8–15 PCs) exists, simple rankings fail to recover it, and an LLM judge can partially recover subspace without target labels.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Abstract claim: directions weighted by a source probe encode source-specific surface features; transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly (capturable in natural language). Main claim: probe OOD robustness largely determined by subspace selection. Background: linear probes expose semantic info but can fail OOD despite strong in-distribution performance. Assertion that behavioral concepts have linear representations but probes often learn spurious correlations; such unreliability is problematic for harmful-interaction monitoring. Method/approach keywords: work in source Q7 coordinates to avoid privileging model latent dims; these coordinates provide data-driven representation structure. Prior findings cited: removing leading components can improve downstream embedding performance (Mu et al., 2018); leading-component projections used as a probing baseline (Kantamneni et al., 2025). Problem framed as selecting dimensions that permit generalization vs. spurious source-trained classification. Pipeline (Fig.1): projection into source N4D basis, filtering candidate Q7 directions, probe training in selected low-dimensional subspace.

Goal: probe OOD robustness largely determined by subspace selection; pipeline projects activations into a source data-driven basis (source N4D / Q7 coordinates), filters candidate directions, and trains probes in the selected low-dim subspace. Prior findings: removing leading components can improve downstream embedding performance; leading-component projections used as a baseline. Related work summarized here: (1) Linear concept directions: studies report cross-dataset linear structure for true/false and other behaviors (Marks & Tegmark 2024; Park et al. 2024 formalize the linear representation hypothesis). Single directions reported for refusal and an “assistant” axis (Arditi et al. 2024; Lu et al. 2026); other work finds population-level directions for honesty/emotion (Zou et al. 2025). (2) Linear probes limits: probes can learn task/surface correlates rather than reveal intrinsic representation; encoded vs. recoverable information distinction; strong in-distribution probes often generalize unevenly—safety evaluation must separate robust internal signals from dataset artifacts. (3) Interpreting features with natural-language explanations: LLM-generated neuron explanations from high-activation examples (Bills et al. 2023), automated sparse-autoencoder feature labeling (Paulo et al. 2025; Bricken et al. 2023), and concept identification + ablation during fine-tuning (Casademunt et al. 2025).

Model & activations: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6). Use layer 15 residual-stream activations (per Ying et al. 2026); activations averaged over assistant-response tokens only. Datasets: four Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025) splits — one source (Roleplaying: V8) and three held-out targets (Insider Trading Report: C2R; Insider Trading Confirm: W6; Sandbagging: J9). After removing ambiguous labels, targets total 1,216 non-ambiguous responses. Labels: GPT-4o annotator maps honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous responses removed. Preprocessing: source activations standardized to zero mean/unit variance; same source statistics used to standardize target activations. Dimensionality reduction: PCA on source (N4D), keep leading 100 PCs (Q7); downstream uses projections into subsets S of these PCs. Classifiers: logistic regression with regularization λ=10 for all probes; comparator (full-representation baseline B8Q) trains on all standardized activations (no PCA). Choice of 100 PCs driven by interpretability: alignment with U9 (Bricken et al., 2023) decreases with PC index, so low-index PCs are more amenable to NL interpretation. Error bars reported as 95% CIs.

Experiments (Sect.4): three held-out targets W6 (Insider Trading Confirm), C2R (Insider Trading Report), J9 (Sandbagging). Overall: W6 transfer reasonably good, C2R moderate, J9 poor. Baseline: B8Q = source-trained probe on full standardized activations; also compare source-trained on leading-100 PCs (Q7) and target-trained on those PCs (5-fold CV). Dimensionality: PCA on source, keep leading 100 PCs. Search/oracle (H2): greedy, starts empty, considers each of 100 source PCs, projects source activations onto current subset, fits source logistic regression, adds direction that most improves target F3 (selection guided by target labels; probe weights always fit on source). Target 5-fold CV used for evaluation; stopping when no candidate improves F3 by >0.001. H2 is a transfer upper bound (not unbiased OOD). Variance control (Y4) = top-k PCs by source variance (k matched to H2). Ranking probes: T6 = source-PCA probe (source-trained ranking using X4), M9 = target-PCA probe (target-trained ranking using X4). X4 = standardized coefficient magnitude (abs coef * PC std). Results summary: small source-trained subspaces (H2) can nearly match target-trained probes, esp. on C2R and J9; variance selection (Y4) only matches H2 on easy W6 and fails on C2R/J9 (explained variance not predictive). Neither T6 nor M9 recovers transferable subspace or beats B8Q; T6 ≈ B8Q; M9 does well on C2R, worse than H2 on W6, below random on J9. Interpretation: For each leading source PC an interpreter LLM (C7) sees 8 highest/8 lowest-activating source examples and writes positive/negative/whole-direction descriptions and assigns OOD/generalization rating R5; selection retains directions hitting observed max in both scoring runs (scores noisy). Language-only interpreter selection (L2 = interp-selected PC probe) improves over B8Q, Y4, and A7 (interp-ablated complement), notably on C2R and J9; W6 has little headroom. All probes use logistic regression (λ=10) trained on source projections; error bars are 95% CIs.

Experiments: three held-out targets — W6 (Insider Trading Confirm), C2R (Insider Trading Report), J9 (Sandbagging). Overall transfer: W6 good/high baseline/low headroom, C2R moderate/robust improvements, J9 poor/most out-of-distribution (weakest) and improvements may reflect distribution shift. Probing pipeline: PCA on source activations (leading 100 PCs), project source activations (N4D), then logistic regression probes (λ=10) trained on source projections; evaluation on target via 5-fold CV. Baselines: B8Q = source-trained probe on full standardized activations; also source-trained on leading-100 PCs (Q7) and target-trained on those PCs (5-fold CV). H2 (search/oracle): greedy forward selection over 100 source PCs, fits source logistic regression at each step but uses target labels to choose additions; stops when no candidate improves target F3 by >0.001. H2 is a transfer upper bound (not unbiased). Variance control Y4 = top-k PCs by source variance (k matched to H2). Ranking probes: T6 = source-PCA probe (source-trained ranking using X4), M9 = target-PCA probe (target-trained ranking using X4). X4 = standardized coefficient magnitude (abs coef * PC std). Results summary: small source-trained subspaces (H2) can nearly match target-trained probes (esp. C2R and J9); variance selection Y4 only matches H2 on easy W6 and fails on C2R/J9 (explained variance not predictive). T6 ≈ B8Q; M9 does well on C2R, worse than H2 on W6, below random on J9. Interpreter LLM (C7) reviewed top/bottom 8 activating source examples per leading PC, wrote direction descriptions and OOD/generalization rating R5; selection retained directions that hit observed max in both scoring runs (scores noisy). Language-only interpreter selection (L2) improves over B8Q, Y4, and A7 (interp-ablated complement), notably on C2R and J9; W6 has little headroom. Limitations: single-model/single-source scope; W6 baseline high/uninformative; J9 OOD and weakest; pipeline fully linear (PCA projection + logistic regression) so transferable-subspace existence may be unsurprising; no causal verification — high-rated directions were not ablated during inference to test causal effect. Error bars are 95% CIs.

Experiments: three held-out targets — W6 (Insider Trading Confirm; easy, high baseline, low headroom), C2R (Insider Trading Report; moderate, robust improvements), J9 (Sandbagging; poor, most OOD, weakest; improvements may reflect distribution shift). Probing pipeline: PCA on source activations (leading 100 PCs), project source activations, standardize, train logistic regression probes (λ=10) on source projections; evaluate on targets via 5-fold CV. Baselines: B8Q = source-trained probe on full standardized activations; Q7 = source-trained on leading-100 PCs; target-trained on those PCs (5-fold CV). H2 (search/oracle): greedy forward selection over 100 source PCs; fits source logistic regression but uses target labels to pick PCs; stops when no candidate improves target F3 by >0.001; acts as an (unbiased) transfer upper bound (oracle). Variance control Y4 = top-k PCs by source variance (k matched to H2). Ranking probes: T6 = source-PCA probe (source-trained ranking using X4), M9 = target-PCA probe (target-trained ranking using X4). X4 = standardized coefficient magnitude (abs coef * PC std). Key empirical findings: small source-trained subspaces (H2) can nearly match target-trained probes (esp. C2R and J9); variance selection Y4 only matches H2 on easy W6 and fails on C2R/J9 (explained variance not predictive). T6 ≈ B8Q; M9 does well on C2R, worse than H2 on W6, below random on J9. Interpreter LLM (C7) described directions and rated OOD; language-only interpreter selection (L2) improves over B8Q, Y4, and A7 (interp-ablated complement), notably on C2R and J9. Conclusion: OOD/robust behavioral probing requires representation selection (finding where a linearly accessible signal is represented most robustly) as well as classifier fitting — sparse directional subspaces can filter dataset-specific surface cues and isolate general behavioral structure. Limitations: single-model/source scope; pipeline fully linear (so transferable-subspace existence may be unsurprising); no causal verification (no ablation to test directional causality); W6 baseline high/uninformative; error bars are 95% CIs.
