Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars.
Goal: Can selecting principal components (PCs), i.e., directions in a source activation basis, improve out-of-distribution (OOD) deception detection?
Method overview: Train linear probes (logistic regression) on one source dataset; evaluate on 3 held-out target datasets. Use a target-supervised greedy search that adds PCs according to target performance. Also evaluate ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights. Introduce an LLM judge that scores natural-language PC descriptions without using target data.
Key quantitative claims/results: Greedy, target-supervised search finds 8–15 PCs that nearly match probes trained on target data. Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights does not recover this transferable subspace. Selecting 19 PCs that receive the maximum observed LLM score in both runs (unsupervised by target data) improves transfer on all 3 targets. For two of the targets, this selection closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and the greedy oracle. 
Other terms to track: "full-representation baseline", "greedy oracle", "both runs" (unspecified here), which targets achieve 78% and 25% (unspecified here).

Paper: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Goal: improve cross-domain (source->target) deception detection by selecting source-PC directions. Source domain = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (activations extracted; token activations averaged over assistant response to form probe inputs). Labels: GPT-4o assigns Deceptive=1, Honest=0, Ambiguous=-1 (ambiguous examples removed). Representation & PCA: source activations are standardized (source -> zero mean, unit variance) and PCA applied; source statistics are applied to target activations; 100 source PCs retained (S subset of these). Probes: all linear (logistic regression, regularization parameter λ=10); baseline = source-trained probe on full standardized activations; target-trained probes fit on target data. Selection methods: greedy oracle = target-guided greedy adding the PC that most increases target AUROC (reported to find ~8–15 PCs that nearly match target-trained probes); variance control = top-k PCs by variance; source-PCA probe and target-PCA probe use standardized coefficients to rank PCs (standardized coefficient = |coefficient| * PC standard deviation). LLM judge: GPT-5-mini interprets PC positive/negative poles and rates OOD-deception usefulness on a 1–10 scale; observed maximum OOD score = 6. Interp-selection = 19 PCs that received the maximum observed score (6) in both scoring runs; interp-ablated PCs = remaining 81. Evaluation: 5-fold CV on targets (held-out folds used for testing); AUROC reported with 95% CI. Causal validation (intervention/ablation at inference) was not performed. Appendix C: SAE decoder alignment (resource andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct); statistics reported include Spearman ρ and Jaccard overlap.

Scope & data: Transfer of linear deception probes (logistic regression, L2 λ=10) trained on Roleplaying (source) to three held-out targets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Ambiguous responses removed; non-ambiguous N=1,216 (from earlier). Model & features: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; layer-15 residual-stream activations averaged over assistant-response tokens. Conclusion: 100-PC subspace contains sufficient target-class information; failure to transfer is due to source-trained direction mismatch. Greedy oracle (Section 4.2): iterative greedy adds PCs (from top 100) that most improve target AUROC (probe weights always fit on source; selection uses non-held-out target folds in 5-fold CV); stop when no PC improves AUROC >0.001. Greedy improves baseline AUROC by +0.22 (Report) and +0.23 (Sandbagging) and nearly matches target-trained probes on those tasks; variance-based k-match control only matches greedy on Confirm. Paper question: whether selecting subspaces of LM representations improves out-of-distribution (OOD) deception detection. Method: compare probes (classifiers) trained on full representations vs probes using selected directions/subspaces. Two selection approaches highlighted: (1) target-guided selection that uses target labels but does not fit probe weights on them; (2) interpretation-based selection using natural-language interpretations, which requires no target data. Key claims: small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes; selecting directions by source weights, target-class separation, or explained variance does not recover the same transferable subspaces; interpretation-based selection improves over the full-representation baseline on all targets, though how well it recovers varies sharply across targets. Scope/caveats: study uses one model and one source dataset; interpretations are descriptive, not causal. The paper includes a "Glossary." (no glossary content shown in this part).

Goal: test whether selecting subspaces of LM representations improves OOD (transfer) deception detection. Source dataset: Roleplaying (V8). Targets include C2R (Insider Trading Report), W6 (Insider Trading Confirm), J9 (Sandbagging). Model & readout: layer-15 residual-stream activations from Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6), averaged over assistant-response tokens. Preprocessing: standardization = zero-mean/unit-variance using source statistics applied to both source and targets. Dimensionality reduction: PCA / N4D retains the leading 100 source directions (Q7); "PCs" refer to these retained source directions; "leading" = lower index. Probes: logistic regression with λ=10, evaluated by AUROC (F3) with 95% CIs; 5-fold CV where selection uses non-held-out target folds and evaluation uses the held-out fold. Baselines & methods: B8Q = full-representation baseline (source-trained on all standardized activations); Y4 = top-k PCs by variance (variance-ranked subset matched in dimension count); H2 = greedy oracle (target-guided direction selection but probe weights fitted only on source); T6 = source-PCA probe (supplies source coefficient rankings); M9 = target-PCA probe (supplies target coefficient rankings); X4 = standardized coefficient = |coef| * PC_std. Interpretation-based selection: natural-language explanations produced with P2 (GPT-5-mini) and rated by C7 (LLM judge) yielding R5 (OOD score/generalization rating); L2 = interp-selected PC probe (uses directions reaching max R5 in both scoring runs); A7 = interp-ablated PC probe (complement). Decoder alignment uses SAE (U9) decoder features (resource: andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct); Spearman ρ reports relation of PC index to decoder alignment. Scope: one model, one source dataset; interpretations are descriptive, not causal.

Goal: test whether selecting subspaces of LM representations improves OOD (transfer) deception detection. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6) providing layer-15 residual-stream activations averaged over assistant-response tokens. Choice of layer follows Ying et al. (2026) as highest cross-domain discrimination. Data: four Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025) datasets — one source Roleplaying (V8) and three held-out targets (Insider Trading Report C2R; Insider Trading Confirm W6; Sandbagging J9); targets total 1,216 non-ambiguous responses after GPT-4o (K8) labeling (honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1); ambiguous responses removed. Preprocessing: standardize source activations to zero-mean/unit-variance; apply same source statistics to targets. Dimensionality reduction: PCA (N4D) on source, retain leading 100 PCs (Q7). Activations projected onto a chosen direction subset S (subspace) before training/eval. Classifiers: logistic regression (λ=10); full-representation baseline (B8Q) trains on all standardized activations. Error bars are 95% CIs. Interpretability: lower PCA indices align better with sparse-autoencoder decoder vectors U9 (Bricken et al., 2023), so lower indices considered more amenable to natural-language interpretation. Interpretation pipeline and labels (P2, R5, L2, A7) described earlier (appendices contain example R5s and AUROCs).

Experiments (Sec.4) compare full representations (B8Q), target-guided greedy subspaces (H2), variance-based top-k (Y4), and coefficient-ranking probes (T6 source-side, M9 target-side). Model/data/methods: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct layer-15 residual-stream activations averaged over assistant-response tokens; source activations standardized (zero-mean, unit-variance) and PCA on source retaining leading 100 PCs; logistic regression probes (λ=10); AUROC (F3) reported; 5-fold target CV used for target-trained evaluations. Baseline (Appendix A B8Q F3): W6 0.874, C2R 0.706, J9 0.606 (W6 best, J9 worst). Target-trained probes on the retained 100-PC source subspace (5-fold CV) separate classes on every target: W6 0.950, C2R 0.936, J9 0.869. H2 greedy search: start empty, consider each of 100 PCs, fit source LR on that subset, add the PC that most improves target F3 (target labels used only for selection), stop when improvement <0.001. Target CV selects directions on non-held-out folds (this is an upper bound). Mean H2 subset sizes (target CV): C2R 15, W6 8, J9 14; full-target H2 k: C2R 13, W6 7, J9 14. H2 substantially improves over B8Q on C2R/J9 (improvements ≈0.22/0.23; H2 F3s used for recovery: C2R 0.929, J9 0.832; target-trained F3s 0.936/0.869). Variance-selection Y4 matches H2 only on W6, failing on C2R/J9. Rankings use standardized coefficient X4 (|coefficient| × PC stddev on source); T6 ≈ B8Q, M9 does well on C2R, worse than H2 on W6, below random on J9. Interpretations: H2 directions indicate domain-stable contrasts but recovery is partial and scores are noisy.

Methods: layer-15 residual-stream activations (assistant-response tokens averaged); source activations standardized; PCA on source keep 100 PCs; logistic-reg probes (λ=10); AUROC (F3) reported. Baselines/targets: B8Q F3s — W6 0.874, C2R 0.706, J9 0.606. Target‑trained on 100-PC source subspace (5-fold CV): W6 0.950, C2R 0.936, J9 0.869. New from Part 8 (interpretation-based selection): An LLM judge (C7) sees top-8/bottom-8 examples per leading source PC, writes pos/neg/whole descriptions, and assigns an OOD/generalization rating R5. Selection rule: retain directions that reach the (observed) maximum R5 in both scoring runs. Appendix E reports max R5=6, 2 scoring runs, and 19 directions reached that max in both runs -> L2 (intersection) size = 19. A7 is the 81-direction complement; Y4 is an equal-dim variance-ranked control. Appendix E examples: Q7-62/57/86 each R5=6; Q7-9/81 each R5=3. "Max-rated directions among shared H2 selections" = 3/5; among top T6 = 1/5.

L2 (interpretation-only, no target data) improves over B8Q: C2R L2 0.881 vs B8Q 0.706; J9 L2 0.662 vs 0.606. L2 recovers baseline–H2 gap: C2R 78%, J9 25%. L2 > B8Q, Y4, A7 on all targets; W6 shows little headroom and methods (except A7) roughly tied. All L2/A7/Y4 probes are trained as source probes.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; method: linear probes on activations. Key claim: projecting inputs onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) from the training activation distribution enables cross-domain transfer that nearly matches probes trained directly on each test distribution. Experiments: evaluated on 3 held-out deception detection datasets (two named: Insider Trading Report, Sandbagging). PC interpretation method: use an LLM judge to score each PC by whether its most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; then probe using highest-scoring PCs. Quantitative claims: this closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and by 25% on Sandbagging. Observations: source-probe-weighted directions encode source-specific surface features; transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and are capturable by natural language descriptions. Conclusion: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection. Venue note: Machine Learning, ICML.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Task: train linear deception probes on activations from a single source dataset (Roleplaying deception scenarios) and evaluate on 3 held-out target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Method: project activations onto source-domain PCA basis and select a low-dimensional subset of source PCs to train probes on. PC selection methods studied: (1) target-supervised greedy search over source PCs (finds a small transferable subspace of ~8–15 components where a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe; Section 4.2), (2) ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights (fails to recover the transferable subspace; Section 4.3), (3) an LLM judge that interprets PCs via their most/least activating examples and can partially recover the subspace without target data (Section 4.5). Key empirical claims from earlier parts: projecting onto a small subset of PCs enables cross-domain transfer nearly matching target-trained probes; closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Observations: source-probe-weighted directions tend to capture source-specific surface features; transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and can be captured/described in natural language. Main conclusion: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection. Venue: Machine Learning / ICML.

PC selection methods studied: (1) target-supervised greedy search over source PCs — finds a small transferable subspace (~8–15 components) where a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe (Section 4.2); (2) ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights — fails to recover the transferable subspace (Section 4.3); (3) an LLM judge that interprets PCs via most/least activating examples and can partially recover the subspace without target data (Section 4.5). Main conclusion: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection. Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Datasets: 4 deception datasets (Roleplaying = source; Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging = targets). Labels assigned by GPT-4o: honest (0), ambiguous (-1), deceptive (1); ambiguous responses removed. LM & activations: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer 15 residual stream activations (highest cross-domain AUROC per Ying et al. 2026); token activations averaged over assistant response. Preprocessing & PCA: standardize source activations to zero mean/unit variance and apply same source stats to targets; run PCA on scaled source activations and retain top 100 PCs. Probes: logistic regression (λ=10). For subset S experiments, project onto S before training/evaluation; baseline probes train on full standardized activations (full-dimensional). Rationale for 100 PCs: alignment with SAE decoder features declines with PC index (Appendix C), so lower-index PCs are more interpretable; authors do not claim low-index PCs generalize better—Section 4.1 reportedly shows 100-PC subspace retains enough info to separate deceptive vs. honest on every target. Methods compared: (1) target-supervised greedy search finds small transferable subspace (~8–15 PCs) where a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe (Sec. 4.2); (2) ranking PCs by source-/target-probe weights fails (Sec. 4.3); (3) an LLM judge interpreting PCs via high/low-activation examples can partially recover transferable PCs without target labels (Sec. 4.5). Key claimed results: small PC subsets enable near-target transfer; closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Main conclusion: OOD robustness of probes largely determined by subspace selection.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Abstract claim: directions weighted by a source probe encode source-specific surface features; transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly (capturable in natural language). Main claim: probe OOD robustness largely determined by subspace selection. Background: linear probes expose semantic info but can fail OOD despite strong in-distribution performance. Assertion that behavioral concepts have linear representations but probes often learn spurious correlations; such unreliability is problematic for harmful-interaction monitoring. Method/approach keywords: work in source Q7 coordinates to avoid privileging model latent dims; these coordinates provide data-driven representation structure. Prior findings cited: removing leading components can improve downstream embedding performance (Mu et al., 2018); leading-component projections used as a probing baseline (Kantamneni et al., 2025). Problem framed as selecting dimensions that permit generalization vs. spurious source-trained classification. Pipeline (Fig.1): projection into source N4D basis, filtering candidate Q7 directions, probe training in selected low-dimensional subspace.

Goal: probe OOD robustness largely determined by subspace selection; pipeline projects activations into a source data-driven basis (source N4D / Q7 coordinates), filters candidate directions, and trains probes in the selected low-dim subspace. Prior findings: removing leading components can improve downstream embedding performance; leading-component projections used as a baseline. Related work summarized here: (1) Linear concept directions: studies report cross-dataset linear structure for true/false and other behaviors (Marks & Tegmark 2024; Park et al. 2024 formalize the linear representation hypothesis). Single directions reported for refusal and an “assistant” axis (Arditi et al. 2024; Lu et al. 2026); other work finds population-level directions for honesty/emotion (Zou et al. 2025). (2) Linear probes limits: probes can learn task/surface correlates rather than reveal intrinsic representation; encoded vs. recoverable information distinction; strong in-distribution probes often generalize unevenly—safety evaluation must separate robust internal signals from dataset artifacts. (3) Interpreting features with natural-language explanations: LLM-generated neuron explanations from high-activation examples (Bills et al. 2023), automated sparse-autoencoder feature labeling (Paulo et al. 2025; Bricken et al. 2023), and concept identification + ablation during fine-tuning (Casademunt et al. 2025).

Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6). Use layer-15 residual-stream activations (per Ying et al. 2026); activations averaged over assistant-response tokens. Data: four Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025) datasets — one source (Roleplaying: V8) and three held-out targets: Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), Sandbagging (J9). Only Roleplaying used as source. Labels: annotated by GPT-4o (K8, OpenAI 2024) with mapping honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous responses removed (binary honest vs deceptive). Preprocessing: source activations standardized to zero mean, unit variance; same source statistics used to standardize targets. Dimensionality reduction: PCA on source (N4D), retain leading 100 principal components (PCs Q7); probes trained on projections to subset S of these PCs. Classifiers: logistic regression (regularization λ=10) for all classifiers; comparator (full-representation baseline B8Q) trains on all standardized activations (no PCA). Choice of 100 PCs driven by interpretability comparability (alignment with U9/Bricken et al. 2023 decreases with PC index, so lower-index PCs are easier to interpret), not because low-index PCs generalize best. Error bars denote 95% confidence intervals.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars.
Goal: Can selecting principal components (PCs), i.e., directions in a source activation basis, improve out-of-distribution (OOD) deception detection?
Method overview: Train linear probes (logistic regression) on one source dataset; evaluate on 3 held-out target datasets. Use a target-supervised greedy search that adds PCs according to target performance. Also evaluate ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights. Introduce an LLM judge that scores natural-language PC descriptions without using target data.
Key quantitative claims/results: Greedy, target-supervised search finds 8–15 PCs that nearly match probes trained on target data. Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights does not recover this transferable subspace. Selecting 19 PCs that receive the maximum observed LLM score in both runs (unsupervised by target data) improves transfer on all 3 targets. For two of the targets, this selection closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and the greedy oracle. 
Other terms to track: "full-representation baseline", "greedy oracle", "both runs" (unspecified here), which targets achieve 78% and 25% (unspecified here).

Paper: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Goal: improve cross-domain (source->target) deception detection by selecting source-PC directions. Source domain = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (activations extracted; token activations averaged over assistant response to form probe inputs). Labels: GPT-4o assigns Deceptive=1, Honest=0, Ambiguous=-1 (ambiguous examples removed). Representation & PCA: source activations are standardized (source -> zero mean, unit variance) and PCA applied; source statistics are applied to target activations; 100 source PCs retained (S subset of these). Probes: all linear (logistic regression, regularization parameter λ=10); baseline = source-trained probe on full standardized activations; target-trained probes fit on target data. Selection methods: greedy oracle = target-guided greedy adding the PC that most increases target AUROC (reported to find ~8–15 PCs that nearly match target-trained probes); variance control = top-k PCs by variance; source-PCA probe and target-PCA probe use standardized coefficients to rank PCs (standardized coefficient = |coefficient| * PC standard deviation). LLM judge: GPT-5-mini interprets PC positive/negative poles and rates OOD-deception usefulness on a 1–10 scale; observed maximum OOD score = 6. Interp-selection = 19 PCs that received the maximum observed score (6) in both scoring runs; interp-ablated PCs = remaining 81. Evaluation: 5-fold CV on targets (held-out folds used for testing); AUROC reported with 95% CI. Causal validation (intervention/ablation at inference) was not performed. Appendix C: SAE decoder alignment (resource andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct); statistics reported include Spearman ρ and Jaccard overlap.

Paper: "Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection..." Targets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Model/representations: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; layer-15 residual-stream activations averaged over assistant response. Preprocessing/PCA: standardize source activations (zero mean/unit var), apply same stats to targets, run PCA on scaled source activations and retain top 100 PCs (PCA-based probes project onto subsets of these 100 PCs). Probes: logistic regression (λ=10). Baseline: probe trained on full standardized activations. Metric: AUROC (cross-domain), 5-fold CV for target-trained probes; error bars = 95% CIs.

Key results in this part:
- Full-representation source-trained AUROC (target eval): Insider Trading Confirm 0.874, Insider Trading Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606.
- Target-trained probes on the 100-PC subspace achieve AUROCs 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869 (reported across the three targets).
- Conclusion: 100-PC subspace contains enough target-class information; limited transfer is due to source-learned direction, not missing info.
- Greedy (oracle) PC-selection: searches top-100 PCs, at each step adds PC that most improves target AUROC (probe weights always fit on source; selection uses labeled non-held-out target folds in 5-fold CV); stop when improvement <0.001.
- Greedy average subset sizes: Report 15 PCs, Confirm 8 PCs, Sandbagging 14 PCs.
- Greedy improves baseline AUROC by +0.22 (Report) and +0.23 (Sandbagging), coming close to target-trained performance; variance-ranked k control matches greedy only on Confirm and falls far behind on Report and Sandbagging.
- Section 4.3 initial claim: neither source- nor target-probe coefficient rankings recover greedy transfer performance.

Flagged potential issue to watch: paper repeatedly says it retains 100 PCs, but a later PC list/table (not seen yet) may list only 58 entries.

Paper question: whether selecting subspaces of LM representations improves out-of-distribution (OOD) deception detection. Method: compare probes (classifiers) trained on full representations vs probes using selected directions/subspaces. Two selection approaches highlighted: (1) target-guided selection that uses target labels but does not fit probe weights on them; (2) interpretation-based selection using natural-language interpretations, which requires no target data. Key claims: small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes; selecting directions by source weights, target-class separation, or explained variance does not recover the same transferable subspaces; interpretation-based selection improves over the full-representation baseline on all targets, though how well it recovers varies sharply across targets. Scope/caveats: study uses one model and one source dataset; interpretations are descriptive, not causal. The paper includes a "Glossary." (no glossary content shown in this part).

Goal: test whether selecting subspaces of LM representations improves OOD (transfer) deception detection. Source dataset: Roleplaying (V8). Targets include C2R (Insider Trading Report), W6 (Insider Trading Confirm), J9 (Sandbagging). Model & readout: layer-15 residual-stream activations from Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6), averaged over assistant-response tokens. Preprocessing: standardization = zero-mean/unit-variance using source statistics applied to both source and targets. Dimensionality reduction: PCA / N4D retains the leading 100 source directions (Q7); "PCs" refer to these retained source directions; "leading" = lower index. Probes: logistic regression with λ=10, evaluated by AUROC (F3) with 95% CIs; 5-fold CV where selection uses non-held-out target folds and evaluation uses the held-out fold. Baselines & methods: B8Q = full-representation baseline (source-trained on all standardized activations); Y4 = top-k PCs by variance (variance-ranked subset matched in dimension count); H2 = greedy oracle (target-guided direction selection but probe weights fitted only on source); T6 = source-PCA probe (supplies source coefficient rankings); M9 = target-PCA probe (supplies target coefficient rankings); X4 = standardized coefficient = |coef| * PC_std. Paper title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Setup: use linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations to detect deception behaviors; evaluate generalization across 3 held-out deception detection datasets (only two named here: Insider Trading Report and Sandbagging). Key claim: projecting inputs onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) from the training activation distribution enables cross-domain transfer that nearly matches probes trained on the target/test distribution. Method extension: interpret PCs and use an LLM judge to score each PC by whether its most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; then probe using top-scoring PCs. Results: this PC-selection method closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and by 25% on Sandbagging. Interpretation claim: source-probe-weighted directions encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and in ways capturable by natural language descriptions. Broad claim: OOD robustness of probes largely determined by subspace selection. Venue noted: Machine Learning, ICML.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Setup: train linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations (source dataset: Roleplaying deception scenarios); evaluate OOD on three held-out target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Core idea: work in the source-domain PCA basis and select a small subset of source PCs to train probes that avoid spurious surface correlations and transfer to targets. Key empirical claims: (1) A small transferable subspace exists (Sec. 4.2): a target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds ~8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe. (2) Source-side and target-side weight-based rankings fail to recover this subspace (Sec. 4.3): ranking PCs by source or target probe weights does not outperform the full-representation baseline. (3) An LLM judge can partially recover the subspace without target labels (Sec. 4.5): it interprets PCs via their extreme examples and selects transferable PCs. Prior-note results: PC-selection method closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Interpretation claim: transferable directions encode more abstract contrasts describable in language; probe OOD robustness largely determined by subspace selection. Figure 1 outlines pipeline: project activations into source PCA basis, filter candidate PCs, train probes on selected low-dim subspace.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Setup: train linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations using a source dataset of roleplaying deception scenarios; evaluate OOD on three held-out target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Method: compute PCA on source activations, work in source PCA basis, filter candidate PCs, and select a small subset of source PCs to train linear probes on the low-dimensional subspace. Key empirical claims: (1) A small transferable subspace exists: target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds ~8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe (Sec. 4.2). (2) Weight-based rankings on source or target probes fail to recover this subspace and do not outperform full-representation baseline (Sec. 4.3). (3) An LLM judge can partially recover the subspace without target labels by interpreting PCs via extreme examples and selecting transferable PCs (Sec. 4.5). Reported quantitative impact: PC-selection method closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Context from related work: literature reports linear/low-dim directions for high-level properties and behaviors, examples of single-direction control (refusal/assistant axis), skepticism about probes (probe may learn task/exploit surface correlates; OOD probe generalization can be uneven), and use of LLMs to generate natural-language explanations of features and to inform interventions.

Datasets: Roleplaying is the source; targets are Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Each response labeled by GPT-4o as honest (0), ambiguous (-1), or deceptive (1); ambiguous examples removed. Language model activations: layer-15 residual stream of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; token activations averaged over the assistant response. Preprocessing: standardize source activations (zero mean, unit variance) and apply the same source statistics to standardize target activations. PCA: run PCA on the scaled source activations and retain the top 100 PCs. Probes: logistic regression (regularization λ=10). For experiments using a subset S of PCs, project activations onto S before training/evaluation; baseline probes train on the full standardized activations. Motivation for 100 PCs: lower-index PCs align more with SAE decoder features (Appendix C) and are easier to interpret, but authors do not claim low-index PCs inherently generalize better; Section 4.1 reportedly shows the 100-PC subspace suffices to separate deceptive vs. honest on every target.

Datasets: source = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Confirm, Insider Trading Report, Sandbagging. Responses labeled honest (0), ambiguous (-1), deceptive (1); ambiguous examples removed. Model activations: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer-15 residual stream; token activations averaged over assistant response. Preprocessing: standardize source activations (zero mean, unit variance) and apply same source statistics to standardize target activations. PCA: run PCA on scaled source activations and retain top 100 PCs. Probes: logistic regression (λ=10). Key results (Section 4.1): source-trained probe (full rep) AUROC on targets: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Probe trained on target data within top-100 source PCs (5-fold CV) achieves AUROC ≈ 0.936 (Confirm) / 0.950 (Report) / 0.869 (Sandbagging) — so 100-PC subspace suffices to separate classes on every target.

Greedy PC-selection (Section 4.2): start empty, iteratively add from top-100 PCs the PC that most improves AUROC on target; to evaluate a candidate, project source activations onto current subset and train probe on source projections; PC choice guided by target labeled folds (5-fold CV) while probe weights always fit on source; stop when AUROC improvement ≤0.001. Avg subset sizes: Report 15 PCs, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14. Greedy improves over baseline (full-rep baseline) by ~+0.22 (Report) and +0.23 (Sandbagging) and approaches target-trained performance; top-k-by-variance matched greedy only for Confirm.

Section 4.3 tests two hypotheses for transferable PCs (separate target classes alone vs PCs source probe leans on). Compare rankings by standardized coefficient = |coef| * std(PC) from probes trained on activations projected to source-PCA basis (source-probe vs target-probe vs greedy oracle).

Datasets: source = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Confirm, Insider Trading Report, Sandbagging. Labels: honest(0), ambiguous(-1) (removed), deceptive(1). Representations: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer-15 residual stream; token activations averaged over assistant response; standardize using source mean/var and apply same stats to targets. PCA: run on scaled source activations, keep top 100 PCs. Probes: logistic regression (λ=10). Baselines: probes on full standardized representations; PC-subset experiments project activations onto chosen subset before training/eval. Key baseline numbers: source-trained probe (full rep) AUROC on targets: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probe on top-100 source PCs (5-fold CV) AUROC ≈ Confirm 0.936, Report 0.950, Sandbagging 0.869 (so 100-PC subspace suffices for target separation). Greedy PC-selection (target labels guide PC choice, probe weights fit on source; stop when AUROC improvement ≤0.001): CV average subset sizes Report 15, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14; greedy boosted AUROC over full-rep by ~+0.22 (Report) and +0.23 (Sandbagging); top-k-by-variance only matched greedy for Confirm. Cross-target ranking experiment (Sec 4.3): define source-PCA and target-PCA rankings (both use source-PCA basis); to pick k, run greedy on full target dataset (single k): Report k=13, Confirm k=7, Sandbagging k=14 (differs slightly from CV sizes). Results: both hypotheses fail — source-PCA probe transfers ~as well as full-rep baseline (i.e., doesn't generalize); target-PCA probe does well on Report, worse than greedy on Confirm, and below-random on Sandbagging. Interpretability (Sec 4.4): for each top-100 PC, collect 8 most/least activating examples and have an LLM judge describe poles and give 1–10 OOD scores; max observed score=6; keep PCs that scored 6 in both runs → 19 interp-selected PCs. Of 5 PCs that appeared in greedy selections for multiple targets, 3 had max OOD; only 1 of top-5 source-PCA PCs got max OOD. Sec 4.5 evaluates probe AUROC for interp-selected 19 PCs vs controls (full-rep, top-19 by variance, remaining 81). Figures and appendices provide full results.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Abstract claim: directions weighted by a source probe encode source-specific surface features; transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly (capturable in natural language). Main claim: probe OOD robustness largely determined by subspace selection. Background: linear probes expose semantic info but can fail OOD despite strong in-distribution performance. Assertion that behavioral concepts have linear representations but probes often learn spurious correlations; such unreliability is problematic for harmful-interaction monitoring. Method/approach keywords: work in source Q7 coordinates to avoid privileging model latent dims; these coordinates provide data-driven representation structure. Prior findings cited: removing leading components can improve downstream embedding performance (Mu et al., 2018); leading-component projections used as a probing baseline (Kantamneni et al., 2025). Problem framed as selecting dimensions that permit generalization vs. spurious source-trained classification. Pipeline (Fig.1): projection into source N4D basis, filtering candidate Q7 directions, probe training in selected low-dimensional subspace.

Goal: probe OOD robustness largely determined by subspace selection; pipeline projects activations into a source data-driven basis (source N4D / Q7 coordinates), filters candidate directions, and trains probes in the selected low-dim subspace. Prior findings: removing leading components can improve downstream embedding performance; leading-component projections used as a baseline. Related work summarized here: (1) Linear concept directions: studies report cross-dataset linear structure for true/false and other behaviors (Marks & Tegmark 2024; Park et al. 2024 formalize the linear representation hypothesis). Single directions reported for refusal and an “assistant” axis (Arditi et al. 2024; Lu et al. 2026); other work finds population-level directions for honesty/emotion (Zou et al. 2025). (2) Linear probes limits: probes can learn task/surface correlates rather than reveal intrinsic representation; encoded vs. recoverable information distinction; strong in-distribution probes often generalize unevenly—safety evaluation must separate robust internal signals from dataset artifacts. (3) Interpreting features with natural-language explanations: LLM-generated neuron explanations from high-activation examples (Bills et al. 2023), automated sparse-autoencoder feature labeling (Paulo et al. 2025; Bricken et al. 2023), and concept identification + ablation during fine-tuning (Casademunt et al. 2025).

Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6). Use layer-15 residual-stream activations (per Ying et al. 2026); activations averaged over assistant-response tokens. Data: four Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025) datasets — one source (Roleplaying: V8) and three held-out targets: Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), Sandbagging (J9). Only Roleplaying used as source. Labels: annotated by GPT-4o (K8, OpenAI 2024) with mapping honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous responses removed (binary honest vs deceptive). Preprocessing: source activations standardized to zero mean, unit variance; same source statistics used to standardize targets. Dimensionality reduction: PCA on source (N4D), retain leading 100 principal components (PCs Q7); probes trained on projections to subset S of these PCs. Classifiers: logistic regression (regularization λ=10) for all classifiers; comparator (full-representation baseline B8Q) trains on all standardized activations (no PCA). Choice of 100 PCs driven by interpretability comparability (alignment with U9/Bricken et al. 2023 decreases with PC index, so lower-index PCs are easier to interpret), not because low-index PCs generalize best. Error bars denote 95% confidence intervals.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars.
Goal: Can selecting principal components (PCs), i.e., directions in a source activation basis, improve out-of-distribution (OOD) deception detection?
Method overview: Train linear probes (logistic regression) on one source dataset; evaluate on 3 held-out target datasets. Use a target-supervised greedy search that adds PCs according to target performance. Also evaluate ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights. Introduce an LLM judge that scores natural-language PC descriptions without using target data.
Key quantitative claims/results: Greedy, target-supervised search finds 8–15 PCs that nearly match probes trained on target data. Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights does not recover this transferable subspace. Selecting 19 PCs that receive the maximum observed LLM score in both runs (unsupervised by target data) improves transfer on all 3 targets. For two of the targets, this selection closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and the greedy oracle. 
Other terms to track: "full-representation baseline", "greedy oracle", "both runs" (unspecified here), which targets achieve 78% and 25% (unspecified here).

Paper: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Goal: improve cross-domain (source->target) deception detection by selecting source-PC directions. Source domain = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (activations extracted; token activations averaged over assistant response to form probe inputs). Labels: GPT-4o assigns Deceptive=1, Honest=0, Ambiguous=-1 (ambiguous examples removed). Representation & PCA: source activations are standardized (source -> zero mean, unit variance) and PCA applied; source statistics are applied to target activations; 100 source PCs retained (S subset of these). Probes: all linear (logistic regression, regularization parameter λ=10); baseline = source-trained probe on full standardized activations; target-trained probes fit on target data. Selection methods: greedy oracle = target-guided greedy adding the PC that most increases target AUROC (reported to find ~8–15 PCs that nearly match target-trained probes); variance control = top-k PCs by variance; source-PCA probe and target-PCA probe use standardized coefficients to rank PCs (standardized coefficient = |coefficient| * PC standard deviation). LLM judge: GPT-5-mini interprets PC positive/negative poles and rates OOD-deception usefulness on a 1–10 scale; observed maximum OOD score = 6. Interp-selection = 19 PCs that received the maximum observed score (6) in both scoring runs; interp-ablated PCs = remaining 81. Evaluation: 5-fold CV on targets (held-out folds used for testing); AUROC reported with 95% CI. Causal validation (intervention/ablation at inference) was not performed. Appendix C: SAE decoder alignment (resource andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct); statistics reported include Spearman ρ and Jaccard overlap.

Key results in this part:
- Full-representation source-trained AUROC (target eval): Insider Trading Confirm 0.874, Insider Trading Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606.
- Target-trained probes on the 100-PC subspace achieve AUROCs 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869 (reported across the three targets).
- Conclusion: 100-PC subspace contains enough target-class information; limited transfer is due to source-learned direction, not missing info.
- Greedy (oracle) PC-selection: searches top-100 PCs, at each step adds PC that most improves target AUROC (probe weights always fit on source; selection uses labeled non-held-out target folds in 5-fold CV); stop when improvement <0.001.
- Greedy average subset sizes: Report 15 PCs, Confirm 8 PCs, Sandbagging 14 PCs.
- Greedy improves baseline AUROC by +0.22 (Report) and +0.23 (Sandbagging), coming close to target-trained performance; variance-ranked k control matches greedy only on Confirm and falls far behind on Report and Sandbagging.
- Section 4.3 initial claim: neither source- nor target-probe coefficient rankings recover greedy transfer performance.

Paper studies probe transfer from a source task to three targets (Insider Trading Report, Confirm, Sandbagging). Preprocessing: standardize source activations, apply same stats to targets, run PCA on scaled source activations and retain top 100 PCs. Probes: logistic regression (λ=10). Metrics: AUROC transfer; target-trained probes use 5-fold CV.

Target-trained probes on the 100-PC subspace AUROC = Report 0.936, Confirm 0.950, Sandbagging 0.869. Greedy (oracle) PC-selection (search top 100 PCs, add PC improving target AUROC most until improvement <0.001) gave average subset sizes (within-CV) = Report 15, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14.
This part: defines standardized coefficient = |probe coeff| * PC std; two rankings: source-PCA (weights from source) and target-PCA (weights from target), both over activations in the source-PCA basis. To pick k for transfer comparisons they run greedy on the full target dataset (not per-fold), yielding k = 13 (Report), 7 (Confirm), 14 (Sandbagging) — noted as differing slightly from Section 4.2 numbers. Results: both source- and target-weight rankings fail to recover greedy transfer. Source-PCA ranking transfers about like the full-representation baseline; target-PCA ranking does well on Report, worse than greedy on Confirm, and below random on Sandbagging. Jaccard overlaps between greedy and target-ranked sets = 0.182 / 0.077 / 0.167.
Interpretability: for each of the top 100 PCs, collect 8 most/least activating examples; LLM describes poles; a judge assigns OOD score 1–10 (max observed = 6). Repeated scoring retains PCs scoring 6 in both runs, producing 19 interp-selected PCs. Five PCs are selected by greedy for >1 target; 3 of those 5 have score 6. Comparison claims reference PCs such as PC62, PC57, PC86, etc. Section 4.5 compares probes trained on the 19 interp-selected PCs vs controls (full, top-19 by variance, remaining 81).

Paper question: whether selecting subspaces of LM representations improves out-of-distribution (OOD) deception detection. Method: compare probes (classifiers) trained on full representations vs probes using selected directions/subspaces. Two selection approaches highlighted: (1) target-guided selection that uses target labels but does not fit probe weights on them; (2) interpretation-based selection using natural-language interpretations, which requires no target data. Key claims: small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes; selecting directions by source weights, target-class separation, or explained variance does not recover the same transferable subspaces; interpretation-based selection improves over the full-representation baseline on all targets, though how well it recovers varies sharply across targets. Scope/caveats: study uses one model and one source dataset; interpretations are descriptive, not causal. The paper includes a "Glossary." (no glossary content shown in this part).

Goal: test whether selecting subspaces of LM representations improves OOD (transfer) deception detection. Source dataset: Roleplaying (V8). Targets include C2R (Insider Trading Report), W6 (Insider Trading Confirm), J9 (Sandbagging). Model & readout: layer-15 residual-stream activations from Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6), averaged over assistant-response tokens. Preprocessing: standardization = zero-mean/unit-variance using source statistics applied to both source and targets. Dimensionality reduction: PCA / N4D retains the leading 100 source directions (Q7); "PCs" refer to these retained source directions; "leading" = lower index. Probes: logistic regression with λ=10, evaluated by AUROC (F3) with 95% CIs; 5-fold CV where selection uses non-held-out target folds and evaluation uses the held-out fold. Baselines & methods: B8Q = full-representation baseline (source-trained on all standardized activations); Y4 = top-k PCs by variance (variance-ranked subset matched in dimension count); H2 = greedy oracle (target-guided direction selection but probe weights fitted only on source); T6 = source-PCA probe (supplies source coefficient rankings); M9 = target-PCA probe (supplies target coefficient rankings); X4 = standardized coefficient = |coef| * PC_std. Interpretation-based selection: natural-language explanations produced with P2 (GPT-5-mini) and rated by C7 (LLM judge) yielding R5 (OOD score/generalization rating); L2 = interp-selected PC probe (uses directions reaching max R5 in both scoring runs); A7 = interp-ablated PC probe (complement). Decoder alignment uses SAE (U9) decoder features (resource: andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct); Spearman ρ reports relation of PC index to decoder alignment. Scope: one model, one source dataset; interpretations are descriptive, not causal.

Goal: test whether selecting subspaces of LM representations (leading PCA directions) improves OOD (transfer) deception detection. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6); use layer-15 residual-stream activations, averaged over assistant-response tokens. Datasets: Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025) collection — one source Roleplaying (V8) and three held-out targets: Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), Sandbagging (J9). Labeling: GPT-4o (K8) maps honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous responses removed. Preprocessing: source activations standardized to zero-mean/unit-variance; same source statistics applied to targets. Dimensionality reduction: PCA (N4D) on source; retain leading 100 PCs (Q7). Activations may be projected to a subset S of these directions before training/eval. All classifiers are logistic regression (λ=10); full-representation baseline (B8Q) trains on all standardized activations (no PCA truncation). Evaluation: AUROC with 95% CIs; earlier notes indicate 5-fold CV where direction selection uses non-held-out target folds and evaluation uses held-out fold. Interpretability: retained-100 chosen for comparability (not because low-index PCs generalize better); alignment with sparse-autoencoder decoder vectors U9 decreases with index, so lower indices are more interpretable. Interpretation pipeline: explanations generated by P2 (GPT-5-mini), rated by C7 producing R5; L2 = interp-selected PC probe (max R5), A7 = interp-ablated PC probe (complement). Example reported numbers (appendix): C2R — B8Q 0.706, H2 0.929, L2 0.881; J9 — B8Q 0.606, H2 0.832, L2 0.662. Error bars denote 95% CIs.

Goal: evaluate whether source-trained leading-100 PCA subspace (Q7) contains transferable deception signal and whether small source-trained subsets (H2) can match target-trained performance. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; layer-15 residual stream, assistant-response-token-averaged activations; source standardized and same stats applied to targets. Classifiers: logistic regression (λ=10). Metric: AUROC (F3) with 5-fold CV; target-5-fold CV: directions selected on non-held-out target folds, evaluate on held-out fold; search stops when no candidate improves target F3 by >0.001. Retained 100 PCs used for comparisons.

Key reported numbers (Appendix A): B8Q (full-representation) F3: W6=0.874, C2R=0.706, J9=0.606. Target-trained (within retained-100) F3 (5-fold CV): C2R=0.936, W6=0.950, J9=0.869. H2 (target-guided greedy source-trained subset) mean sizes (target CV): C2R=15, W6=8, J9=14; full-target H2 k: C2R=13, W6=7, J9=14. H2 F3 (used for recovery comparison): C2R=0.929, J9=0.832; H2 improvements over B8Q: +0.22 (C2R), +0.23 (J9). Target-trained F3 for corresponding rows: 0.936 (C2R), 0.869 (J9). Variance-selection (Y4) matches H2 only on W6, falls behind on C2R/J9. Rankings: T6 (source-PCA ranking) performs about like B8Q; M9 (target-side ranking using standardized coefficient X4 = |coef|*PC_std) does well on C2R, worse than H2 on W6, and reportedly below random on J9. Interpretability: H2-selected directions have higher-level contrasts that partially transfer; L2 and A7 probes used in interpretation pipeline. Figures: Fig2 (source-trained full, source-trained leading100, target-trained leading100), Fig3 (B8Q, Y4, H2), Fig4 (T6, M9, H2).

Interpretation procedure: For each leading source PC, LLM judge C7 sees top-8 and bottom-8 activating source examples, writes positive/negative/whole-direction descriptions, and assigns an OOD/generalization rating R5. Two noisy scoring runs; selection retains directions reaching the observed maximum R5 in both runs. Appendix E reports max R5=6, 2 runs, and 19 directions reaching that max in both runs.
L2 = interp-selected PC probe = intersection of retained directions across both scoring runs (19 dims). Controls: A7 = complement of L2 (81 dims); Y4 = variance-ranked control of equal dimension to L2 (so Y4 dims=19). All three are trained as source probes.
Key numeric results (from Appendix A / earlier notes): B8Q (full-representation) F3: W6=0.874, C2R=0.706, J9=0.606. L2 F3: C2R=0.881, J9=0.662 (W6 L2/Y4/A7 exact values not supplied here). Target-trained (within retained-100) F3: C2R=0.936, W6=0.950, J9=0.869. H2 (target-guided source subset) F3 used for recovery: C2R=0.929, J9=0.832; H2 mean sizes (target CV): C2R=15, W6=8, J9=14 (full-target H2 k: 13,7,14).
Recovery: "Baseline–H2 gap recovered by L2" reported as C2R 78%, J9 25% (consistent with numbers above). Recovery is partial: Appendix E reports 3/5 top-rated directions among shared H2 selections and 1/5 among top T6 selections. Specific H2 Q7 examples: Q7 62, 57, 86 have R5=6; Q7 9 and 81 have R5=3.
Claims: Language-only (interpretation-only) selection L2 improves over B8Q (notably on C2R and J9) and reportedly exceeds B8Q, Y4, and A7 on all targets; W6 methods except A7 are roughly tied. Figure references: Fig5 shows L2 (red), B8Q (blue), Y4 at L2 dimension count (teal), A7 (brown).

Interpretation/selection: For each leading source PC, an LLM judge (C7) saw top-8 & bottom-8 activating source examples, wrote pos/neg/whole-direction descriptions, and assigned an OOD/generalization rating R5. Two noisy scoring runs; directions retained if they reached the observed max R5 in both runs. Appendix E: max R5=6, 2 runs, 19 directions reached that max in both runs. All three trained as source probes. Probing pipeline is linear: N4D projection followed by logistic regression readout. No inference-time ablation/causal test reported; interpretation claims are descriptive (based on examples + C7 verbalizations). Scope limited to one model and one source dataset (Section 3). Section 4.4 describes example-based verbal interpretation.

errors.claim: "The ‘source-PCA probe’ ranks PCs by the weights learned by a probe trained on source data, while the ‘target-PCA probe’ ranks PCs by the weights learned by a probe trained on target data." vs. "In both cases, the probes are trained on source data that has been projected onto the top $k$ PCs, selected based to their respective rankings."

Paper title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Setup: use linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations to detect deception behaviors; evaluate generalization across 3 held-out deception detection datasets (only two named here: Insider Trading Report and Sandbagging). Key claim: projecting inputs onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) from the training activation distribution enables cross-domain transfer that nearly matches probes trained on the target/test distribution. Method extension: interpret PCs and use an LLM judge to score each PC by whether its most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; then probe using top-scoring PCs. Results: this PC-selection method closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and by 25% on Sandbagging. Interpretation claim: source-probe-weighted directions encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and in ways capturable by natural language descriptions. Broad claim: OOD robustness of probes largely determined by subspace selection. Venue noted: Machine Learning, ICML.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Setup: train linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations (source: Roleplaying deception scenarios) and evaluate cross-domain on 3 held-out deception datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Approach: operate in the source-domain PCA basis (project activations onto source PCs) and search for a small subset of source PCs that support generalizable probe training. Motivation: avoid assuming model latent dims are privileged; choice of PC subset matters (cite Mu et al. 2018, Kantamneni et al. 2025). Key empirical claims (by section refs): (1) A small transferable subspace exists (Sec 4.2): a target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds ~8–15 components where a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe. (2) Source-side and target-side rankings both fail (Sec 4.3): ranking PCs by source or target probe weights does not beat the full-representation baseline. (3) An LLM judge can partially recover the subspace without target data (Sec 4.5): it can interpret/select PCs likely to encode transferable behavioral contrast. Prior/note: earlier summary records that the PC-selection method reportedly closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Interpretation claim (from earlier): source-probe-weighted directions encode source-specific surface features; transferable directions encode the contrast more abstractly and are capturable by natural-language descriptions.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Setup: train linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations (source: roleplaying deception scenarios); evaluate cross-domain on three held-out deception datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Method: compute PCA on source activations, project activations onto source PCs, and search for a small subset of source PCs supporting generalizable probe training (greedy target-supervised search). Key empirical claims to check later: (Sec 4.2) a small transferable subspace exists — greedy search finds ~8–15 components where a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe; (Sec 4.3) source- and target-side rankings of PCs both fail to beat full-representation baseline; (Sec 4.5) an LLM judge can partially recover the subspace without target data. Reported baseline-to-oracle gap closure: 78% on Insider Trading Report, 25% on Sandbagging. Interpretation claim: source-probe-weighted directions encode source-specific surface features; transferable directions encode the contrast more abstractly and can be captured by natural-language descriptions. Related work (this part): evidence that high-level behaviors can be linear/subspace-like (Marks & Tegmark 2024; Park et al. 2024; Zou et al. 2025; Arditi et al. 2024; Lu et al. 2026). Probing limitations: probes can learn task/surface correlates and fail OOD (Alain & Bengio 2018; Hewitt & Liang 2019; Ravichander et al. 2021; Burns et al. 2024; Goldowsky-Dill et al. 2025; kramár2026...). Natural-language interpretation of features: LLM-based labeling and automated descriptions (Bills et al. 2023; Paulo et al. 2025; Bricken et al. 2023; Casademunt et al. 2025).

Datasets: Roleplaying = source; targets = Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Labels assigned by GPT-4o as honest (0), ambiguous (-1), deceptive (1); ambiguous responses removed. LM & activations: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; use layer-15 residual stream activations (Ying et al. 2026 / Grattafiori et al. 2024); extract token activations and average over assistant's response. Preprocessing: standardize source activations to zero mean/unit variance; apply same source mean/std to targets. Run PCA on scaled source activations and retain top 100 PCs (chosen because alignment with SAE decoder features decreases with PC index; Appendix C); note authors explicitly say this is NOT a claim that low-index PCs generalize better. Probes: logistic regression (regularization λ=10). For subset S of PCs, project activations onto S before training/evaluation; baseline trains on full standardized activations. Key empirical claims to verify in later sections: (Sec 4.2) greedy target-supervised search finds a small transferable subspace (~8–15 PCs) where a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe; (Sec 4.3) source- and target-side PC rankings both fail to beat full-representation baseline; (Sec 4.5) an LLM judge can partially recover the subspace without target data. Reported gap-closure numbers: 78% (Insider Trading Report), 25% (Sandbagging). Interpretation claim: source-probe-weighted directions encode source-specific surface features; transferable directions encode more abstract contrasts and can be captured by natural-language descriptions.

Model & data: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; extract layer-15 residual-stream token activations, average across assistant response. Standardize source activations (zero mean, unit variance); apply same source mean/std to targets. Run PCA on standardized source activations; keep top 100 PCs. Probes: logistic regression (λ=10). Datasets: source=Roleplaying; targets={Insider Trading Confirm, Insider Trading Report, Sandbagging}. Labels: honest=0, ambiguous=-1 removed, deceptive=1.

Baseline (Sec 4.1): source-trained probe on full representations transfers with AUROC: Confirm=0.874, Report=0.706, Sandbagging=0.606. Target-trained probe on top-100 source PCs (5-fold CV) achieves: Confirm=0.936, Report=0.950, Sandbagging=0.869. Conclusion: the 100-PC subspace contains discriminative signal; poor transfer stems from source-trained probe learning non-generalizing directions.

Greedy PC selection (Sec 4.2): iteratively add PCs (search over top 100) that most improve AUROC on target; probe weights always fit on source data; subset choice guided by target folds via 5-fold CV; stop when AUROC gain <0.001. Converged average subset sizes: Report=15, Confirm=8, Sandbagging=14. Greedy improves baseline by +0.22 (Report) and +0.23 (Sandbagging), approaching target-trained performance. Top-k-by-variance (k matched to greedy) matches greedy only for Confirm; fails for Report & Sandbagging. Greedy is an upper bound (uses target data).

Sec 4.3 setup: test two hypotheses about transferable PCs (those that alone separate target classes vs. those the source probe leans on). Compare PC rankings by standardized coefficients from source-probe and from target-probe; plot greedy oracle as reference.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars.
Abstract claims: directions heavily weighted by a source probe encode source-specific surface features; transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and are capturable in natural language. Main hypothesis: probe OOD robustness is largely determined by subspace selection.
Intro points: linear probes reveal semantic info but can fail OOD despite strong in-distribution performance. The paper works in "source Q7 coordinates" to avoid privileging model latent dimensions; these coordinates are data-driven. Observed structure: higher-index Q7 coordinates show stronger "U9 alignment." Removing leading components reportedly improves downstream embedding performance (Mu et al., 2018). Leading-component projections are used as a probing baseline (Kantamneni et al., 2025). The core selection problem: choose dimensions that permit generalization rather than capture spurious source-trained classification.
Figure 1 pipeline (caption): projection into the source N4D basis, filtering candidate Q7 directions, probe training in the selected low-dimensional subspace.
Key terms to track for consistency in later parts: "source probe", "transferable directions", "subspace selection", "Q7 coordinates", "N4D basis", "U9 alignment", "leading components" and claims about removing leading components improving performance.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Core hypothesis: probe OOD robustness is largely determined by subspace selection; directions heavily weighted by a source probe encode source-specific surface features while transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and can be captured in natural language. Work in data-driven "source Q7 coordinates" (to avoid privileging model latent dims); use N4D basis for projection; observed structure: higher-index Q7 coordinates show stronger "U9 alignment." Removing leading components reportedly improves downstream embedding performance (Mu et al., 2018); leading-component projections used as baseline (Kantamneni et al., 2025). Pipeline: project into source N4D basis, filter candidate Q7 directions, train probe in selected low-dimensional subspace. Key terms to track: "source probe", "transferable directions", "subspace selection", "Q7 coordinates", "N4D basis", "U9 alignment", "leading components" and claims about removing leading components improving performance.

Part 2 (Related Work) summary: 1) Linear concept directions in activation space — cross-dataset linear structure (Marks & Tegmark 2024); formalization of linear representation hypothesis (Park et al. 2024); examples of single directions for refusal/assistant axes; debate remains about stable concepts vs context-dependent correlations. 2) Linear probes & limitations — long history (Alain & Bengio 2018; Hewitt & Liang 2019); probes can learn tasks or exploit surface correlates, so high in-distribution accuracy doesn't imply model encodes property; encoded vs recoverable information distinction; strong in-distribution probes generalize unevenly, necessitating safety-probe evaluation to separate robust internal signals from dataset artifacts. 3) Interpreting features with natural-language explanations — LLM-generated neuron explanations (Bills et al. 2023); automatic sparse-autoencoder feature labeling for large feature sets (Paulo et al. 2025; Bricken et al. 2023); natural-language descriptions can support intervention (Casademunt et al. 2025) by identifying concepts and ablating them to reduce misaligned behavior.

steps.notes_before:
Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6). Use layer-15 residual-stream activations averaged over assistant-response tokens. Datasets: source Roleplaying (V8); held-out targets: Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), Sandbagging (J9). Labels by GPT-4o: honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous removed. Preprocessing: source activations standardized (zero-mean, unit-variance); same source stats applied to targets. PCA on source, retain leading 100 PCs (Q7); subsets of these used for projection. Classifier: logistic regression (lambda=10). Comparator B8Q trains on all standardized activations. Error bars: 95% CIs.

Main results: baseline transfer — W6 good, C2R moderate, J9 poor. Target-trained probes within the retained source subspace separate classes on every target (relevant info present); the single source-trained direction does not generalize. H2 (greedy oracle): iteratively adds leading-100 source PC directions that most improve target F3 (weights fit on source; target labels used only for selection); CV and full-target variants yield similar numbers. Small source-trained subspaces (H2) nearly match target-trained probes, especially C2R and J9. Variance-ranked selection (Y4) matches H2 only on easy W6; explained variance poorly predicts transfer usefulness.

Ranking probes: T6 = source-side ranking (source-PCA probe), M9 = target-side ranking (target-PCA probe). Neither recovers H2; T6 ≈ B8Q; M9: does well on C2R, worse than H2 on W6, below random on J9. Interpretability: LLM judge C7 inspects top/bottom 8 examples per PC and assigns OOD/generalization ratings (R5). L2 (interp-selected PC probe, language-only selection) improves generalization vs B8Q and Y4 (and vs A7 interp-ablated complement), especially on C2R and J9; recovery varies by target.

Model & data: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6). Use layer-15 residual-stream activations averaged over assistant-response tokens. Source dataset: Roleplaying (V8). Held-out targets: Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), Sandbagging (J9). Labels by GPT-4o: honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous examples removed. Classifier: logistic regression (lambda=10). Comparator B8Q trains on all standardized activations. Error bars: 95% CIs.

Main findings: Baseline transfer — W6 strong/good, C2R moderate, J9 poor. Target-trained probes within retained source subspace can separate classes on every target (relevant info present); a single source-trained direction does not generalize. H2 (greedy oracle) iteratively adds source-PC directions (up to leading-100) that most improve target F3; weights fit on source, target labels used only for selection; CV and full-target variants give similar selection sizes. Small H2 subspaces nearly match target-trained probes, especially C2R and J9. Variance-ranked selection (Y4) matches H2 only on easy W6; explained variance is a poor predictor of transfer usefulness. Ranking probes: T6 = source-PCA probe, M9 = target-PCA probe; neither recovers H2 (T6 ≈ B8Q; M9 good on C2R, worse on W6, below random on J9). Interpretability: LLM judge C7 inspects top/bottom examples per PC and rates OOD/generalization (R5). L2 (language-only interp-selected PC probe) improves generalization vs B8Q and Y4 (and vs A7 interp-ablated complement), especially on C2R and J9.

Limitations: single-model/single-source scope; W6’s high baseline limits informativeness; J9 is most OOD and weakest (modest gains may reflect distribution shift); pipeline fully linear (PCA projection + logistic regression); interpretive claims descriptive, not causal; no inference-time ablations performed.

Model & data: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6). Use layer-15 residual-stream activations averaged over assistant-response tokens. Source dataset: Roleplaying (V8). Held-out targets: Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), Sandbagging (J9). Labels by GPT-4o: honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous removed. Preprocessing: source activations standardized (zero-mean, unit-variance); same source stats applied to targets. PCA on source; retain leading 100 PCs; subsets of these used for projection. Classifier: logistic regression (lambda=10). Error bars: 95% CIs.

Main empirical findings: Baseline transfer (full-representation probe trained on source activations) — W6 strong/good, C2R moderate, J9 poor. Target-trained probes within retained source subspace can separate classes on every target (relevant info present in source subspace); a single source-trained direction does not generalize. H2 (greedy oracle) iteratively adds source-PC directions (up to leading-100) that most improve target F3; weights fit on source; target labels used only for selection; CV and full-target variants give similar selection sizes. Small H2 subspaces nearly match target-trained probes, especially C2R and J9. Variance-ranked selection (Y4) matches H2 only on easy W6; explained variance is a poor predictor of transfer usefulness. Ranking probes: T6 = source-PCA probe, M9 = target-PCA probe; neither recovers H2 (T6 ≈ full-representation baseline; M9 good on C2R, worse on W6, below random on J9). Interpretability: LLM judge C7 inspects top/bottom examples per PC and rates OOD/generalization (R5). L2 (language-only interp-selected PC probe) improves generalization vs baseline and Y4 (and vs A7 interp-ablated complement), especially on C2R and J9.

Conclusion / takeaway: Robust OOD behavioral probing requires representation selection (sparse directional subspaces isolating generalizable structure) as well as classifier fitting; full-representation probes can capture dataset-specific surface cues that harm transfer. Limitations: single-model/single-source, fully linear pipeline, interpretive claims descriptive not causal, no inference-time ablations.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars.
Goal: Can selecting principal components (PCs), i.e., directions in a source activation basis, improve out-of-distribution (OOD) deception detection?
Method overview: Train linear probes (logistic regression) on one source dataset; evaluate on 3 held-out target datasets. Use a target-supervised greedy search that adds PCs according to target performance. Also evaluate ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights. Introduce an LLM judge that scores natural-language PC descriptions without using target data.
Key quantitative claims/results: Greedy, target-supervised search finds 8–15 PCs that nearly match probes trained on target data. Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights does not recover this transferable subspace. Selecting 19 PCs that receive the maximum observed LLM score in both runs (unsupervised by target data) improves transfer on all 3 targets. For two of the targets, this selection closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and the greedy oracle. 
Other terms to track: "full-representation baseline", "greedy oracle", "both runs" (unspecified here), which targets achieve 78% and 25% (unspecified here).

Paper: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Goal: improve cross-domain (source->target) deception detection by selecting source-PC directions. Source domain = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (activations extracted; token activations averaged over assistant response to form probe inputs). Labels: GPT-4o assigns Deceptive=1, Honest=0, Ambiguous=-1 (ambiguous examples removed). Representation & PCA: source activations are standardized (source -> zero mean, unit variance) and PCA applied; source statistics are applied to target activations; 100 source PCs retained (S subset of these). Probes: all linear (logistic regression, regularization parameter λ=10); baseline = source-trained probe on full standardized activations; target-trained probes fit on target data. Selection methods: greedy oracle = target-guided greedy adding the PC that most increases target AUROC (reported to find ~8–15 PCs that nearly match target-trained probes); variance control = top-k PCs by variance; source-PCA probe and target-PCA probe use standardized coefficients to rank PCs (standardized coefficient = |coefficient| * PC standard deviation). LLM judge: GPT-5-mini interprets PC positive/negative poles and rates OOD-deception usefulness on a 1–10 scale; observed maximum OOD score = 6. Interp-selection = 19 PCs that received the maximum observed score (6) in both scoring runs; interp-ablated PCs = remaining 81. Evaluation: 5-fold CV on targets (held-out folds used for testing); AUROC reported with 95% CI. Causal validation (intervention/ablation at inference) was not performed. Appendix C: SAE decoder alignment (resource andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct); statistics reported include Spearman ρ and Jaccard overlap.

Paper question: whether selecting subspaces of LM representations improves out-of-distribution (OOD) deception detection. Method: compare probes (classifiers) trained on full representations vs probes using selected directions/subspaces. Two selection approaches highlighted: (1) target-guided selection that uses target labels but does not fit probe weights on them; (2) interpretation-based selection using natural-language interpretations, which requires no target data. Key claims: small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes; selecting directions by source weights, target-class separation, or explained variance does not recover the same transferable subspaces; interpretation-based selection improves over the full-representation baseline on all targets, though how well it recovers varies sharply across targets. Scope/caveats: study uses one model and one source dataset; interpretations are descriptive, not causal. The paper includes a "Glossary." (no glossary content shown in this part).

Goal: test whether selecting subspaces of LM representations improves OOD (transfer) deception detection. Source dataset: Roleplaying (V8). Targets include C2R (Insider Trading Report), W6 (Insider Trading Confirm), J9 (Sandbagging). Model & readout: layer-15 residual-stream activations from Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6), averaged over assistant-response tokens. Preprocessing: standardization = zero-mean/unit-variance using source statistics applied to both source and targets. Dimensionality reduction: PCA / N4D retains the leading 100 source directions (Q7); "PCs" refer to these retained source directions; "leading" = lower index. Probes: logistic regression with λ=10, evaluated by AUROC (F3) with 95% CIs; 5-fold CV where selection uses non-held-out target folds and evaluation uses the held-out fold. Baselines & methods: B8Q = full-representation baseline (source-trained on all standardized activations); Y4 = top-k PCs by variance (variance-ranked subset matched in dimension count); H2 = greedy oracle (target-guided direction selection but probe weights fitted only on source); T6 = source-PCA probe (supplies source coefficient rankings); M9 = target-PCA probe (supplies target coefficient rankings); X4 = standardized coefficient = |coef| * PC_std. Interpretation-based selection: natural-language explanations produced with P2 (GPT-5-mini) and rated by C7 (LLM judge) yielding R5 (OOD score/generalization rating); L2 = interp-selected PC probe (uses directions reaching max R5 in both scoring runs); A7 = interp-ablated PC probe (complement). Decoder alignment uses SAE (U9) decoder features (resource: andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct); Spearman ρ reports relation of PC index to decoder alignment. Scope: one model, one source dataset; interpretations are descriptive, not causal.
