Experiments compare full representations, target-guided subspaces (H2 greedy), variance-based selection (Y4), coefficient/ranking methods (T6 source-PCA, M9 target-PCA using X4 standardized coefficients), and interpretation of H2 directions. Model/data: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer-15 residual stream averaged over assistant-response tokens; PCA on source (N4D) yields Q7; leading 100 PCs retained. Probes: logistic regression (λ=10 from earlier), AUROC (F3) with 95% CIs; 5-fold CV. Baseline (Appendix A B8Q F3): W6=0.874, C2R=0.706, J9=0.606. Target-trained on retained 100-PC subspace (Appendix A Target-trained F3, 5-fold CV): W6=0.950, C2R=0.936, J9=0.869 (shows relevant info in retained subspace even when source-trained transfer is poor). H2 greedy search (target-guided subset selection; target labels used only to evaluate candidate additions, weights fitted on source projections): start empty, consider each of leading 100 PCs, fit source logistic weights for candidate subsets, add the PC that most improves target F3, stop when improvement <=0.001. Target 5-fold CV: select directions on non-held-out target folds, evaluate on held-out fold — H2 is an upper bound (uses target info for selection). H2 stats: mean subset size (target CV) C2R=15, W6=8, J9=14; small H2 subset range 8–15. Full-target H2 k (stable set): C2R=13, W6=7, J9=14. H2 improves over B8Q by ~0.22 (C2R) and ~0.23 (J9); H2 F3 used for recovery comparison: C2R=0.929, J9=0.832. Y4 (top-k by variance) matches H2 only on W6, falls behind on C2R/J9. Ranking probes: T6 ~ B8Q; M9 does well on C2R, worse than H2 on W6, and below random on J9. X4 = |probe coefficient| * corresponding Q7 stddev, computed on source-projected activations. Interpretation: H2 directions indicate more domain-stable semantic contrasts, but recovery is partial and scores noisy.

Paper title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Setup: use linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations to detect deception behaviors; evaluate generalization across 3 held-out deception detection datasets (only two named here: Insider Trading Report and Sandbagging). Key claim: projecting inputs onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) from the training activation distribution enables cross-domain transfer that nearly matches probes trained on the target/test distribution. Method extension: interpret PCs and use an LLM judge to score each PC by whether its most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; then probe using top-scoring PCs. Results: this PC-selection method closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and by 25% on Sandbagging. Interpretation claim: source-probe-weighted directions encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and in ways capturable by natural language descriptions. Broad claim: OOD robustness of probes largely determined by subspace selection. Venue noted: Machine Learning, ICML.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Setup: train linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations (source dataset: Roleplaying deception scenarios); evaluate OOD on three held-out target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Core idea: work in the source-domain PCA basis and select a small subset of source PCs to train probes that avoid spurious surface correlations and transfer to targets. Key empirical claims: (1) A small transferable subspace exists (Sec. 4.2): a target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds ~8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe. (2) Source-side and target-side weight-based rankings fail to recover this subspace (Sec. 4.3): ranking PCs by source or target probe weights does not outperform the full-representation baseline. (3) An LLM judge can partially recover the subspace without target labels (Sec. 4.5): it interprets PCs via their extreme examples and selects transferable PCs. Prior-note results: PC-selection method closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Interpretation claim: transferable directions encode more abstract contrasts describable in language; probe OOD robustness largely determined by subspace selection. Figure 1 outlines pipeline: project activations into source PCA basis, filter candidate PCs, train probes on selected low-dim subspace.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Setup: train linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations using a source dataset of roleplaying deception scenarios; evaluate OOD on three held-out target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Method: compute PCA on source activations, work in source PCA basis, filter candidate PCs, and select a small subset of source PCs to train linear probes on the low-dimensional subspace. Key empirical claims: (1) A small transferable subspace exists: target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds ~8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe (Sec. 4.2). (2) Weight-based rankings on source or target probes fail to recover this subspace and do not outperform full-representation baseline (Sec. 4.3). (3) An LLM judge can partially recover the subspace without target labels by interpreting PCs via extreme examples and selecting transferable PCs (Sec. 4.5). Reported quantitative impact: PC-selection method closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Context from related work: literature reports linear/low-dim directions for high-level properties and behaviors, examples of single-direction control (refusal/assistant axis), skepticism about probes (probe may learn task/exploit surface correlates; OOD probe generalization can be uneven), and use of LLMs to generate natural-language explanations of features and to inform interventions.

Datasets: Roleplaying is the source; targets are Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Each response labeled by GPT-4o as honest (0), ambiguous (-1), or deceptive (1); ambiguous examples removed. Language model activations: layer-15 residual stream of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; token activations averaged over the assistant response. Preprocessing: standardize source activations (zero mean, unit variance) and apply the same source statistics to standardize target activations. PCA: run PCA on the scaled source activations and retain the top 100 PCs. Probes: logistic regression (regularization λ=10). For experiments using a subset S of PCs, project activations onto S before training/evaluation; baseline probes train on the full standardized activations. Motivation for 100 PCs: lower-index PCs align more with SAE decoder features (Appendix C) and are easier to interpret, but authors do not claim low-index PCs inherently generalize better; Section 4.1 reportedly shows the 100-PC subspace suffices to separate deceptive vs. honest on every target.

Datasets: source = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Confirm, Insider Trading Report, Sandbagging. Responses labeled honest (0), ambiguous (-1), deceptive (1); ambiguous examples removed. Model activations: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer-15 residual stream; token activations averaged over assistant response. Preprocessing: standardize source activations (zero mean, unit variance) and apply same source statistics to standardize target activations. PCA: run PCA on scaled source activations and retain top 100 PCs. Probes: logistic regression (λ=10). Baselines: probes trained on full standardized representations; for PC-subset experiments project activations onto subset before training/evaluation.

Key results (Section 4.1): source-trained probe (full rep) AUROC on targets: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Probe trained on target data within top-100 source PCs (5-fold CV) achieves AUROC ≈ 0.936 (Confirm) / 0.950 (Report) / 0.869 (Sandbagging) — so 100-PC subspace suffices to separate classes on every target.

Greedy PC-selection (Section 4.2): start empty, iteratively add from top-100 PCs the PC that most improves AUROC on target; to evaluate a candidate, project source activations onto current subset and train probe on source projections; PC choice guided by target labeled folds (5-fold CV) while probe weights always fit on source; stop when AUROC improvement ≤0.001. Avg subset sizes: Report 15 PCs, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14. Greedy improves over baseline (full-rep baseline) by ~+0.22 (Report) and +0.23 (Sandbagging) and approaches target-trained performance; top-k-by-variance matched greedy only for Confirm.

Section 4.3 tests two hypotheses for transferable PCs (separate target classes alone vs PCs source probe leans on). Compare rankings by standardized coefficient = |coef| * std(PC) from probes trained on activations projected to source-PCA basis (source-probe vs target-probe vs greedy oracle).

Datasets: source = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Confirm, Insider Trading Report, Sandbagging. Labels: honest(0), ambiguous(-1) (removed), deceptive(1). Representations: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer-15 residual stream; token activations averaged over assistant response; standardize using source mean/var and apply same stats to targets. PCA: run on scaled source activations, keep top 100 PCs. Probes: logistic regression (λ=10). Baselines: probes on full standardized representations; PC-subset experiments project activations onto chosen subset before training/eval. Key baseline numbers: source-trained probe (full rep) AUROC on targets: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probe on top-100 source PCs (5-fold CV) AUROC ≈ Confirm 0.936, Report 0.950, Sandbagging 0.869 (so 100-PC subspace suffices for target separation). Greedy PC-selection (target labels guide PC choice, probe weights fit on source; stop when AUROC improvement ≤0.001): CV average subset sizes Report 15, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14; greedy boosted AUROC over full-rep by ~+0.22 (Report) and +0.23 (Sandbagging); top-k-by-variance only matched greedy for Confirm. Cross-target ranking experiment (Sec 4.3): define source-PCA and target-PCA rankings (both use source-PCA basis); to pick k, run greedy on full target dataset (single k): Report k=13, Confirm k=7, Sandbagging k=14 (differs slightly from CV sizes). Results: both hypotheses fail — source-PCA probe transfers ~as well as full-rep baseline (i.e., doesn't generalize); target-PCA probe does well on Report, worse than greedy on Confirm, and below-random on Sandbagging. Interpretability (Sec 4.4): for each top-100 PC, collect 8 most/least activating examples and have an LLM judge describe poles and give 1–10 OOD scores; max observed score=6; keep PCs that scored 6 in both runs → 19 interp-selected PCs. Of 5 PCs that appeared in greedy selections for multiple targets, 3 had max OOD; only 1 of top-5 source-PCA PCs got max OOD. Sec 4.5 evaluates probe AUROC for interp-selected 19 PCs vs controls (full-rep, top-19 by variance, remaining 81). Figures and appendices provide full results.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Abstract claim: directions weighted by a source probe encode source-specific surface features; transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly (capturable in natural language). Main claim: probe OOD robustness largely determined by subspace selection. Background: linear probes expose semantic info but can fail OOD despite strong in-distribution performance. Assertion that behavioral concepts have linear representations but probes often learn spurious correlations; such unreliability is problematic for harmful-interaction monitoring. Method/approach keywords: work in source Q7 coordinates to avoid privileging model latent dims; these coordinates provide data-driven representation structure. Prior findings cited: removing leading components can improve downstream embedding performance (Mu et al., 2018); leading-component projections used as a probing baseline (Kantamneni et al., 2025). Problem framed as selecting dimensions that permit generalization vs. spurious source-trained classification. Pipeline (Fig.1): projection into source N4D basis, filtering candidate Q7 directions, probe training in selected low-dimensional subspace.

Goal: probe OOD robustness largely determined by subspace selection; pipeline projects activations into a source data-driven basis (source N4D / Q7 coordinates), filters candidate directions, and trains probes in the selected low-dim subspace. Prior findings: removing leading components can improve downstream embedding performance; leading-component projections used as a baseline. Related work summarized here: (1) Linear concept directions: studies report cross-dataset linear structure for true/false and other behaviors (Marks & Tegmark 2024; Park et al. 2024 formalize the linear representation hypothesis). Single directions reported for refusal and an “assistant” axis (Arditi et al. 2024; Lu et al. 2026); other work finds population-level directions for honesty/emotion (Zou et al. 2025). (2) Linear probes limits: probes can learn task/surface correlates rather than reveal intrinsic representation; encoded vs. recoverable information distinction; strong in-distribution probes often generalize unevenly—safety evaluation must separate robust internal signals from dataset artifacts. (3) Interpreting features with natural-language explanations: LLM-generated neuron explanations from high-activation examples (Bills et al. 2023), automated sparse-autoencoder feature labeling (Paulo et al. 2025; Bricken et al. 2023), and concept identification + ablation during fine-tuning (Casademunt et al. 2025).

Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6). Use layer-15 residual-stream activations (per Ying et al. 2026); activations averaged over assistant-response tokens. Data: four Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025) datasets — one source (Roleplaying: V8) and three held-out targets: Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), Sandbagging (J9). Only Roleplaying used as source. Labels: annotated by GPT-4o (K8, OpenAI 2024) with mapping honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous responses removed (binary honest vs deceptive). Preprocessing: source activations standardized to zero mean, unit variance; same source statistics used to standardize targets. Dimensionality reduction: PCA on source (N4D), retain leading 100 principal components (PCs Q7); probes trained on projections to subset S of these PCs. Classifiers: logistic regression (regularization λ=10) for all classifiers; comparator (full-representation baseline B8Q) trains on all standardized activations (no PCA). Choice of 100 PCs driven by interpretability comparability (alignment with U9/Bricken et al. 2023 decreases with PC index, so lower-index PCs are easier to interpret), not because low-index PCs generalize best. Error bars denote 95% confidence intervals.

Model/data: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6); layer-15 residual-stream activations averaged over assistant-response tokens. Datasets: source Roleplaying (V8); targets Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), Sandbagging (J9). Labels: GPT-4o annotations mapped honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous removed → binary. Preprocessing: source activations standardized (zero mean, unit variance); same source stats used to standardize targets. PCA on standardized source (N4D); retain leading 100 PCs (Q7). Probes: logistic regression (λ=10) on projections to subsets S of the 100 PCs; comparator B8Q trains on full standardized activations (no PCA). Metrics/CI: target F3 reported; 5-fold CV used for many evaluations; error bars = 95% CI.

Key experimental results/methods (Part 4): W6 transfer reasonably good, C2R moderate, J9 poor. Target-trained classifiers within the 100-PC source subspace separate classes on every target; the single source-trained direction fails to generalize. Greedy oracle search (H2) uses target labels to pick PCs: start empty, consider each of 100 PCs, fit source logistic weights on candidate subset, add PC that most improves target F3 (CV selection on non-held-out folds; stop if no candidate >0.001). Variance-ranked baseline (Y4) matches H2 only on easy W6; explained variance poorly predicts transfer utility. Ranking probes: source-PCA (T6) and target-PCA (M9) order PCs by standardized coefficient X4 = |coef| * PC std (on source-projected activations); evaluated probes are then trained on source projections to top-k. T6 ≈ B8Q; M9: good on C2R, worse than H2 on W6, below random on J9. Interpretation (C7): for each leading PC, LLM judge sees top-8 and bottom-8 source examples, writes pole/whole descriptions and assigns OOD score (R5). Interp-selected intersection (L2) = PCs reaching observed max in both scoring runs; A7 = its complement; Y4 also used as equal-dim control. L2 (language-only) improves over B8Q and A7, especially on C2R and J9.

Datasets: source Roleplaying (V8); targets Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), Sandbagging (J9). Labels: GPT-4o annotations mapped honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous removed → binary. Preprocessing: source activations standardized (zero mean, unit variance); same source stats applied to targets. PCA on standardized source; retain leading 100 PCs. Probes: logistic regression (λ=10) on projections to subsets of the 100 PCs; comparator B8Q trains on full standardized activations (no PCA). Metrics: target F3 reported; 5-fold CV; 95% CI. Key results: W6 transfers reasonably well (high baseline), C2R moderate, J9 poorest. Target-trained classifiers within 100-PC source subspace separate classes on every target; single source-trained direction fails to generalize. Greedy oracle H2 selects PCs using target labels; variance-ranked baseline Y4 matches H2 only on easy W6. Source-PCA probe ≈ B8Q; target-PCA good on C2R, worse than H2 on W6, below random on J9. Interpretation: humans labeled leading-PC directions; Interp-selected intersection L2 = PCs reaching observed max in both scoring runs; A7 = complement; Y4 used as equal-dim control. L2 improves over B8Q and A7, notably on C2R (and claimed improvement on J9 in places—paper also elsewhere calls J9 the weakest OOD target with only modest improvement, a noted inconsistency). Limitations: single-model/single-source scope; paper uses linear pipeline (PCA + logistic), but also at times claims results hold for nonlinear probes and every residual-stream layer (conflict with core methods). Conclusion emphasizes: robust behavioral probing requires finding where a linearly accessible signal is represented most robustly; full-representation probes can mix spurious surface cues; sparse directional subspaces may isolate general behavioral structure; OOD probing entails representation selection plus classifier fitting.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars.
Goal: Can selecting principal components (PCs), i.e., directions in a source activation basis, improve out-of-distribution (OOD) deception detection?
Method overview: Train linear probes (logistic regression) on one source dataset; evaluate on 3 held-out target datasets. Use a target-supervised greedy search that adds PCs according to target performance. Also evaluate ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights. Introduce an LLM judge that scores natural-language PC descriptions without using target data.
Key quantitative claims/results: Greedy, target-supervised search finds 8–15 PCs that nearly match probes trained on target data. Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights does not recover this transferable subspace. Selecting 19 PCs that receive the maximum observed LLM score in both runs (unsupervised by target data) improves transfer on all 3 targets. For two of the targets, this selection closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and the greedy oracle. 
Other terms to track: "full-representation baseline", "greedy oracle", "both runs" (unspecified here), which targets achieve 78% and 25% (unspecified here).

Paper: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Goal: improve cross-domain (source->target) deception detection by selecting source-PC directions. Source domain = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (activations extracted; token activations averaged over assistant response to form probe inputs). Labels: GPT-4o assigns Deceptive=1, Honest=0, Ambiguous=-1 (ambiguous examples removed). Representation & PCA: source activations are standardized (source -> zero mean, unit variance) and PCA applied; source statistics are applied to target activations; 100 source PCs retained (S subset of these). Probes: all linear (logistic regression, regularization parameter λ=10); baseline = source-trained probe on full standardized activations; target-trained probes fit on target data. Selection methods: greedy oracle = target-guided greedy adding the PC that most increases target AUROC (reported to find ~8–15 PCs that nearly match target-trained probes); variance control = top-k PCs by variance; source-PCA probe and target-PCA probe use standardized coefficients to rank PCs (standardized coefficient = |coefficient| * PC standard deviation). LLM judge: GPT-5-mini interprets PC positive/negative poles and rates OOD-deception usefulness on a 1–10 scale; observed maximum OOD score = 6. Interp-selection = 19 PCs that received the maximum observed score (6) in both scoring runs; interp-ablated PCs = remaining 81. Evaluation: 5-fold CV on targets (held-out folds used for testing); AUROC reported with 95% CI. Causal validation (intervention/ablation at inference) was not performed. Appendix C: SAE decoder alignment (resource andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct); statistics reported include Spearman ρ and Jaccard overlap.

Paper question: whether selecting subspaces of LM representations improves out-of-distribution (OOD) deception detection. Method: compare probes (classifiers) trained on full representations vs probes using selected directions/subspaces. Two selection approaches highlighted: (1) target-guided selection that uses target labels but does not fit probe weights on them; (2) interpretation-based selection using natural-language interpretations, which requires no target data. Key claims: small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes; selecting directions by source weights, target-class separation, or explained variance does not recover the same transferable subspaces; interpretation-based selection improves over the full-representation baseline on all targets, though how well it recovers varies sharply across targets. Scope/caveats: study uses one model and one source dataset; interpretations are descriptive, not causal. The paper includes a "Glossary." (no glossary content shown in this part).

Goal: test whether selecting subspaces of LM representations improves OOD (transfer) deception detection. Source dataset: Roleplaying (V8). Targets include C2R (Insider Trading Report), W6 (Insider Trading Confirm), J9 (Sandbagging). Model & readout: layer-15 residual-stream activations from Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6), averaged over assistant-response tokens. Preprocessing: standardization = zero-mean/unit-variance using source statistics applied to both source and targets. Dimensionality reduction: PCA / N4D retains the leading 100 source directions (Q7); "PCs" refer to these retained source directions; "leading" = lower index. Probes: logistic regression with λ=10, evaluated by AUROC (F3) with 95% CIs; 5-fold CV where selection uses non-held-out target folds and evaluation uses the held-out fold. Dimensionality reduction: PCA (N4D) producing source principal-component coordinates; Q7 denotes the leading 100 source PCs ('leading' = lower index). Probes: logistic regression (λ=10), evaluated by AUROC with 95% CIs; 5-fold CV where selection uses non-held-out target folds and evaluation uses held-out fold. Methods/baselines: B8Q = full-representation baseline; Y4 = top-k PCs by variance; H2 = greedy oracle (target-guided direction selection but probe weights fitted only on source); T6 = source-PCA probe; M9 = target-PCA probe; X4 = standardized coefficient metric. Interpretation pipeline: explanations generated by P2 (GPT-5-mini), rated by C7 yielding R5; L2 = interp-selected PC probe (directions with max R5 in both scoring runs); A7 = interp-ablated PC probe (complement). Reported example R5s: Appendix E Table 4 Q7 indices 7,8,11,12,4 → R5 = 3,4,3,3,6; Table 3 Q7 indices 62,57,86 → R5 = 6. Reported AUROC examples (Appendix A): C2R — B8Q 0.706, H2 0.929, L2 0.881; J9 — B8Q 0.606, H2 0.832, L2 0.662. Related work (this part): prior work finds simple activation directions can support readout/intervention but their stability across contexts is unresolved; linear-probe accuracy alone does not establish robust internal representation; natural-language (LLM) explanations have been used to label features and support interventions/ablations to reduce misaligned behavior.

Goal: test whether selecting subspaces of LM representations (leading PCA directions) improves OOD (transfer) deception detection. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6); use layer-15 residual-stream activations, averaged over assistant-response tokens. Datasets: Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025) collection — one source Roleplaying (V8) and three held-out targets: Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), Sandbagging (J9). Labeling: GPT-4o (K8) maps honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous responses removed. Activations may be projected to a subset S of these directions before training/eval. All classifiers are logistic regression (λ=10); full-representation baseline (B8Q) trains on all standardized activations (no PCA truncation). Evaluation: AUROC with 95% CIs; earlier notes indicate 5-fold CV where direction selection uses non-held-out target folds and evaluation uses held-out fold. Goal: evaluate whether source-trained leading-100 PCA subspace (Q7) contains transferable deception signal and whether small source-trained subsets (H2) can match target-trained performance. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; layer-15 residual stream, assistant-response-token-averaged activations; source standardized and same stats applied to targets. Classifiers: logistic regression (λ=10). Metric: AUROC (F3) with 5-fold CV; target-5-fold CV: directions selected on non-held-out target folds, evaluate on held-out fold; search stops when no candidate improves target F3 by >0.001. Retained 100 PCs used for comparisons.

Key reported numbers (Appendix A): B8Q (full-representation) F3: W6=0.874, C2R=0.706, J9=0.606. Target-trained (within retained-100) F3 (5-fold CV): C2R=0.936, W6=0.950, J9=0.869. Paper title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Setup: use linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations to detect deception behaviors; evaluate generalization across 3 held-out deception detection datasets (only two named here: Insider Trading Report and Sandbagging). Key claim: projecting inputs onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) from the training activation distribution enables cross-domain transfer that nearly matches probes trained on the target/test distribution. Method extension: interpret PCs and use an LLM judge to score each PC by whether its most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; then probe using top-scoring PCs. Results: this PC-selection method closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and by 25% on Sandbagging. Interpretation claim: source-probe-weighted directions encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and in ways capturable by natural language descriptions. Broad claim: OOD robustness of probes largely determined by subspace selection. Venue noted: Machine Learning, ICML.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Setup: train linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations (source dataset: Roleplaying deception scenarios); evaluate OOD on three held-out target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Core idea: work in the source-domain PCA basis and select a small subset of source PCs to train probes that avoid spurious surface correlations and transfer to targets. Key empirical claims: (1) A small transferable subspace exists (Sec. 4.2): a target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds ~8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe. (2) Source-side and target-side weight-based rankings fail to recover this subspace (Sec. 4.3): ranking PCs by source or target probe weights does not outperform the full-representation baseline. (3) An LLM judge can partially recover the subspace without target labels (Sec. 4.5): it interprets PCs via their extreme examples and selects transferable PCs. Prior-note results: PC-selection method closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Interpretation claim: transferable directions encode more abstract contrasts describable in language; probe OOD robustness largely determined by subspace selection. Figure 1 outlines pipeline: project activations into source PCA basis, filter candidate PCs, train probes on selected low-dim subspace.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Setup: train linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations using a source dataset of roleplaying deception scenarios; evaluate OOD on three held-out target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Method: compute PCA on source activations, work in source PCA basis, filter candidate PCs, and select a small subset of source PCs to train linear probes on the low-dimensional subspace. Key empirical claims: (1) A small transferable subspace exists: target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds ~8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe (Sec. 4.2). (2) Weight-based rankings on source or target probes fail to recover this subspace and do not outperform full-representation baseline (Sec. 4.3). (3) An LLM judge can partially recover the subspace without target labels by interpreting PCs via extreme examples and selecting transferable PCs (Sec. 4.5). Reported quantitative impact: PC-selection method closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Context from related work: literature reports linear/low-dim directions for high-level properties and behaviors, examples of single-direction control (refusal/assistant axis), skepticism about probes (probe may learn task/exploit surface correlates; OOD probe generalization can be uneven), and use of LLMs to generate natural-language explanations of features and to inform interventions.

Datasets: Roleplaying is the source; targets are Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Each response labeled by GPT-4o as honest (0), ambiguous (-1), or deceptive (1); ambiguous examples removed. Language model activations: layer-15 residual stream of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; token activations averaged over the assistant response. Preprocessing: standardize source activations (zero mean, unit variance) and apply the same source statistics to standardize target activations. PCA: run PCA on the scaled source activations and retain the top 100 PCs. Probes: logistic regression (regularization λ=10). For experiments using a subset S of PCs, project activations onto S before training/evaluation; baseline probes train on the full standardized activations. Motivation for 100 PCs: lower-index PCs align more with SAE decoder features (Appendix C) and are easier to interpret, but authors do not claim low-index PCs inherently generalize better; Section 4.1 reportedly shows the 100-PC subspace suffices to separate deceptive vs. honest on every target.

Datasets: source = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Confirm, Insider Trading Report, Sandbagging. Responses labeled honest (0), ambiguous (-1), deceptive (1); ambiguous examples removed. Model activations: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer-15 residual stream; token activations averaged over assistant response. Preprocessing: standardize source activations (zero mean, unit variance) and apply same source statistics to standardize target activations. PCA: run PCA on scaled source activations and retain top 100 PCs. Probes: logistic regression (λ=10). Baselines: probes trained on full standardized representations; for PC-subset experiments project activations onto subset before training/evaluation.

Key results (Section 4.1): source-trained probe (full rep) AUROC on targets: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Probe trained on target data within top-100 source PCs (5-fold CV) achieves AUROC ≈ 0.936 (Confirm) / 0.950 (Report) / 0.869 (Sandbagging) — so 100-PC subspace suffices to separate classes on every target.

Greedy PC-selection (Section 4.2): start empty, iteratively add from top-100 PCs the PC that most improves AUROC on target; to evaluate a candidate, project source activations onto current subset and train probe on source projections; PC choice guided by target labeled folds (5-fold CV) while probe weights always fit on source; stop when AUROC improvement ≤0.001. Avg subset sizes: Report 15 PCs, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14. Greedy improves over baseline (full-rep baseline) by ~+0.22 (Report) and +0.23 (Sandbagging) and approaches target-trained performance; top-k-by-variance matched greedy only for Confirm.

Section 4.3 tests two hypotheses for transferable PCs (separate target classes alone vs PCs source probe leans on). Compare rankings by standardized coefficient = |coef| * std(PC) from probes trained on activations projected to source-PCA basis (source-probe vs target-probe vs greedy oracle).

Appendix B (this part): LLM Judge Prompt uses GPT-5-mini (OpenAI, 2025) to interpret PC directions. Direction is described as bipolar; each line token<TAB>activation with activations normalized to integers -10..+10. Positive and negative example sets drawn from the Roleplay dataset (strategic chance to lie). Judge must infer dominant contrast, prefer narrow descriptions, avoid overgeneralizing/sentiment assumptions, and rate OOD deception usefulness (1–10) with brief justification. Output must be exactly four labeled lines: "Positive pole:", "Negative pole:", "Shared direction:", "OOD deception usefulness (1-10):".

final_notes: Model/data: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6). Sources: V8 (371 examples; labels -1/0/1 = 140/59/172). Targets: C2R (473; 218/194/61), W6 (151; 29/38/84), J9 (1000; 379/375/246). Label mapping: GPT-4o ambiguous=-1, honest=0, deceptive=1 (ambiguous removed for binary analyses). Preprocessing: source activations standardized; PCA on source, top-100 PCs retained; target-trained probes fit inside that subspace. Baseline probe B8Q AUROC: C2R 0.706, W6 0.874, J9 0.606. Target-trained (5-fold CV) AUROC: C2R 0.936, W6 0.950, J9 0.869. H2 greedy-selection improved C2R +0.22, J9 +0.23; H2 F3 recovery: C2R 0.929, J9 0.832. Mean H2 subset size (target CV): C2R 15, W6 8, J9 14. Previously reported full-target H2 k: C2R 13, W6 7, J9 14 (Table 2 shows J9 H2 has 15 indices); paper elsewhere states "Small H2 subset range 8–15" (contradiction with W6 full-target H2=7 noted). L2 F3: C2R 0.881, J9 0.662. Decoder alignment Spearman ρ: best feature -0.857, mean top-10 -0.917. Appendix C: lower-index Q7 show stronger alignment to SAE decoder features. Appendix D: reported H2–M9 Jaccard D3 as C2R 0.182, W6 0.077, J9 0.167, but recomputing from Table 2 gives ≈0.167, 0.10, 0.154 (mismatch). Appendix E (Q7 interpretability): maximum observed R5 = 6; scoring runs = 2; directions reaching maximum in both runs retained for L2 = 19 (complement used by A7 = 81). Directions selected by H2 for >1 target = 5; of those, 3 are maximum-rated. Maximum-rated among top T6 selections = 1 of top 5. Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Abstract claim: directions weighted by a source probe encode source-specific surface features; transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly (capturable in natural language). Main claim: probe OOD robustness largely determined by subspace selection. Background: linear probes expose semantic info but can fail OOD despite strong in-distribution performance. Assertion that behavioral concepts have linear representations but probes often learn spurious correlations; such unreliability is problematic for harmful-interaction monitoring. Method/approach keywords: work in source Q7 coordinates to avoid privileging model latent dims; these coordinates provide data-driven representation structure. Prior findings cited: removing leading components can improve downstream embedding performance (Mu et al., 2018); leading-component projections used as a probing baseline (Kantamneni et al., 2025). Problem framed as selecting dimensions that permit generalization vs. spurious source-trained classification. Pipeline (Fig.1): projection into source N4D basis, filtering candidate Q7 directions, probe training in selected low-dimensional subspace.

Goal: probe OOD robustness largely determined by subspace selection; pipeline projects activations into a source data-driven basis (source N4D / Q7 coordinates), filters candidate directions, and trains probes in the selected low-dim subspace. Prior findings: removing leading components can improve downstream embedding performance; leading-component projections used as a baseline. Related work summarized here: (1) Linear concept directions: studies report cross-dataset linear structure for true/false and other behaviors (Marks & Tegmark 2024; Park et al. 2024 formalize the linear representation hypothesis). Single directions reported for refusal and an “assistant” axis (Arditi et al. 2024; Lu et al. 2026); other work finds population-level directions for honesty/emotion (Zou et al. 2025). (2) Linear probes limits: probes can learn task/surface correlates rather than reveal intrinsic representation; encoded vs. recoverable information distinction; strong in-distribution probes often generalize unevenly—safety evaluation must separate robust internal signals from dataset artifacts. (3) Interpreting features with natural-language explanations: LLM-generated neuron explanations from high-activation examples (Bills et al. 2023), automated sparse-autoencoder feature labeling (Paulo et al. 2025; Bricken et al. 2023), and concept identification + ablation during fine-tuning (Casademunt et al. 2025).

Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6). Use layer-15 residual-stream activations (per Ying et al. 2026); activations averaged over assistant-response tokens. Data: four Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025) datasets — one source (Roleplaying: V8) and three held-out targets: Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), Sandbagging (J9). Only Roleplaying used as source. Labels: annotated by GPT-4o (K8, OpenAI 2024) with mapping honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous responses removed (binary honest vs deceptive). Preprocessing: source activations standardized to zero mean, unit variance; same source statistics used to standardize targets. Dimensionality reduction: PCA on source (N4D), retain leading 100 principal components (PCs Q7); probes trained on projections to subset S of these PCs. Classifiers: logistic regression (regularization λ=10) for all classifiers; comparator (full-representation baseline B8Q) trains on all standardized activations (no PCA). Choice of 100 PCs driven by interpretability comparability (alignment with U9/Bricken et al. 2023 decreases with PC index, so lower-index PCs are easier to interpret), not because low-index PCs generalize best. Error bars denote 95% confidence intervals.

Goal: Can selecting principal components (PCs), i.e., directions in a source activation basis, improve out-of-distribution (OOD) deception detection?
Method overview: Train linear probes (logistic regression) on one source dataset; evaluate on 3 held-out target datasets. For two of the targets, this selection closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and the greedy oracle.

Paper: "Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection..." Targets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Model/representations: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; layer-15 residual-stream activations averaged over assistant response. Preprocessing/PCA: standardize source activations (zero mean/unit var), apply same stats to targets, run PCA on scaled source activations and retain top 100 PCs (PCA-based probes project onto subsets of these 100 PCs). Probes: logistic regression (λ=10). Baseline: probe trained on full standardized activations. Metric: AUROC (cross-domain), 5-fold CV for target-trained probes; error bars = 95% CIs.

Key results in this part:
- Full-representation source-trained AUROC (target eval): Insider Trading Confirm 0.874, Insider Trading Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606.
- Target-trained probes on the 100-PC subspace achieve AUROCs 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869 (reported across the three targets).
- Conclusion: 100-PC subspace contains enough target-class information; limited transfer is due to source-learned direction, not missing info.
- Greedy (oracle) PC-selection: searches top-100 PCs, at each step adds PC that most improves target AUROC (probe weights always fit on source; selection uses labeled non-held-out target folds in 5-fold CV); stop when improvement <0.001.
- Greedy average subset sizes: Report 15 PCs, Confirm 8 PCs, Sandbagging 14 PCs.
- Greedy improves baseline AUROC by +0.22 (Report) and +0.23 (Sandbagging), coming close to target-trained performance; variance-ranked k control matches greedy only on Confirm and falls far behind on Report and Sandbagging.
- Section 4.3 initial claim: neither source- nor target-probe coefficient rankings recover greedy transfer performance.

Flagged potential issue to watch: paper repeatedly says it retains 100 PCs, but a later PC list/table (not seen yet) may list only 58 entries.

Paper question: whether selecting subspaces of LM representations improves out-of-distribution (OOD) deception detection. Method: compare probes (classifiers) trained on full representations vs probes using selected directions/subspaces. Two selection approaches highlighted: (1) target-guided selection that uses target labels but does not fit probe weights on them; (2) interpretation-based selection using natural-language interpretations, which requires no target data. Key claims: small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes; selecting directions by source weights, target-class separation, or explained variance does not recover the same transferable subspaces; interpretation-based selection improves over the full-representation baseline on all targets, though how well it recovers varies sharply across targets. Scope/caveats: study uses one model and one source dataset; interpretations are descriptive, not causal. The paper includes a "Glossary." (no glossary content shown in this part).

Goal: test whether selecting subspaces of LM representations (leading PCA directions) improves OOD (transfer) deception detection. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6); use layer-15 residual-stream activations, averaged over assistant-response tokens. Datasets: Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025) collection — one source Roleplaying (V8) and three held-out targets: Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), Sandbagging (J9). Labeling: GPT-4o (K8) maps honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous responses removed. Preprocessing: source activations standardized to zero-mean/unit-variance; same source statistics applied to targets. Dimensionality reduction: PCA (N4D) on source; retain leading 100 PCs (Q7). Evaluation: AUROC with 95% CIs; earlier notes indicate 5-fold CV where direction selection uses non-held-out target folds and evaluation uses held-out fold. Interpretability: retained-100 chosen for comparability (not because low-index PCs generalize better); alignment with sparse-autoencoder decoder vectors U9 decreases with index, so lower indices are more interpretable. Interpretation pipeline: explanations generated by P2 (GPT-5-mini), rated by C7 producing R5; L2 = interp-selected PC probe (max R5), A7 = interp-ablated PC probe (complement). Goal: test whether selecting source-LM subspaces (leading 100 PCA directions on source residual activations from Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer-15, assistant-response-token-averaged) improves OOD (transfer) deception detection. Preprocessing: source activations standardized (zero mean, unit var); same stats applied to targets. PCA on source retains 100 leading PCs (Q7). All probes are logistic regression (λ=10). Evaluation: AUROC (F3) with 95% CIs, 5-fold CV (direction selection uses non-held-out target folds; evaluation on held-out fold). Full-representation baseline (B8Q) trains on all standardized activations; comparisons include source-trained on retained-100 (leading-100), target-trained on retained-100, greedy target-guided source-trained subset search (H2), variance-ranked top-k (Y4), source-weight ranking (T6), target-separation ranking (M9), and interpretability-selected probes (L2) with ablated complements (A7).

Key reported numbers (Appendix A / examples):
- B8Q F3: W6 0.874, C2R 0.706, J9 0.606.
- Target-trained (retained-100) F3: C2R 0.936, W6 0.950, J9 0.869.
- H2 (greedy target-guided source-trained subset) F3 (used in comparisons): C2R 0.929, J9 0.832; H2 improves over B8Q by ~0.22 (C2R) and ~0.23 (J9).
- Mean H2 subset sizes (target CV): C2R 15, W6 8, J9 14; full-target H2 k: C2R 13, W6 7, J9 14; search adds leading-100 candidates greedily until no candidate yields >0.001 target-F3 improvement.
- Example interpretability probe (L2) F3: C2R 0.881, J9 0.662.
Findings summarized: target-trained probes show discriminative info exists in retained-100 even when source-trained transfer is poor; greedy H2 finds small source-trained subspaces that nearly match target-trained (esp. C2R/J9); variance-ranked (Y4) matches H2 only on W6; T6 ~ B8Q, M9 does well on C2R, worse than H2 on W6, and below random on J9; interpretations of H2 directions show partly domain-stable contrasts but recovery is partial and noisy.

Interpretability procedure: For each of the 100 leading source PCs, an LLM judge gets the 8 most- and 8 least-activating source examples and produces positive-pole, negative-pole, whole-direction descriptions and an OOD/generalization rating R5 (scale with maximum 6). Scores are noisy; selection requires agreement across two scoring runs. Retention rule: keep directions reaching the observed maximum (R5=6) in both runs. Appendix E: max R5=6, 2 scoring runs, 19 directions reached 6 in both runs -> L2 = intersection = 19 directions; A7 = complement = 81 directions; Y4 = variance-ranked subset matched in dimensionality to L2. H2 interpretation examples: Q7 62, 57, 86 have R5=6; Q7 9 and 81 have R5=3. Recovery among H2 selections: 3/5 of maximum-rated directions; among top T6 selections: 1/5. L2 (interp-selected PC probe) is a source-trained probe using the 19 retained directions. Key performance numbers (Appendix A / earlier): B8Q F3: W6 0.874, C2R 0.706, J9 0.606. Claims: L2 exceeds B8Q, Y4, and A7 on all targets (large gains on C2R and J9); W6 has little headroom and methods (except A7) are roughly tied. Paper title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Setup: use linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations to detect deception behaviors; evaluate generalization across 3 held-out deception detection datasets (only two named here: Insider Trading Report and Sandbagging). Key claim: projecting inputs onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) from the training activation distribution enables cross-domain transfer that nearly matches probes trained on the target/test distribution. Method extension: interpret PCs and use an LLM judge to score each PC by whether its most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; then probe using top-scoring PCs. Results: this PC-selection method closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and by 25% on Sandbagging. Interpretation claim: source-probe-weighted directions encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and in ways capturable by natural language descriptions. Broad claim: OOD robustness of probes largely determined by subspace selection. Venue noted: Machine Learning, ICML.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Setup: train linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations (source dataset: Roleplaying deception scenarios); evaluate OOD on three held-out target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Core idea: work in the source-domain PCA basis and select a small subset of source PCs to train probes that avoid spurious surface correlations and transfer to targets. Key empirical claims: (1) A small transferable subspace exists (Sec. 4.2): a target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds ~8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe. (2) Source-side and target-side weight-based rankings fail to recover this subspace (Sec. 4.3): ranking PCs by source or target probe weights does not outperform the full-representation baseline. (3) An LLM judge can partially recover the subspace without target labels (Sec. 4.5): it interprets PCs via their extreme examples and selects transferable PCs. Prior-note results: PC-selection method closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Interpretation claim: transferable directions encode more abstract contrasts describable in language; probe OOD robustness largely determined by subspace selection. Figure 1 outlines pipeline: project activations into source PCA basis, filter candidate PCs, train probes on selected low-dim subspace.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Setup: train linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations using a source dataset of roleplaying deception scenarios; evaluate OOD on three held-out target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Method: compute PCA on source activations, work in source PCA basis, filter candidate PCs, and select a small subset of source PCs to train linear probes on the low-dimensional subspace. Key empirical claims: (1) A small transferable subspace exists: target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds ~8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe (Sec. 4.2). (2) Weight-based rankings on source or target probes fail to recover this subspace and do not outperform full-representation baseline (Sec. 4.3). (3) An LLM judge can partially recover the subspace without target labels by interpreting PCs via extreme examples and selecting transferable PCs (Sec. 4.5). Reported quantitative impact: PC-selection method closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Context from related work: literature reports linear/low-dim directions for high-level properties and behaviors, examples of single-direction control (refusal/assistant axis), skepticism about probes (probe may learn task/exploit surface correlates; OOD probe generalization can be uneven), and use of LLMs to generate natural-language explanations of features and to inform interventions.

Datasets: Roleplaying is the source; targets are Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Each response labeled by GPT-4o as honest (0), ambiguous (-1), or deceptive (1); ambiguous examples removed. Language model activations: layer-15 residual stream of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; token activations averaged over the assistant response. Preprocessing: standardize source activations (zero mean, unit variance) and apply the same source statistics to standardize target activations. PCA: run PCA on the scaled source activations and retain the top 100 PCs. Probes: logistic regression (regularization λ=10). For experiments using a subset S of PCs, project activations onto S before training/evaluation; baseline probes train on the full standardized activations. Motivation for 100 PCs: lower-index PCs align more with SAE decoder features (Appendix C) and are easier to interpret, but authors do not claim low-index PCs inherently generalize better; Section 4.1 reportedly shows the 100-PC subspace suffices to separate deceptive vs. honest on every target.

Datasets & labels: source = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Responses labeled honest (0) / ambiguous (-1) / deceptive (1); ambiguous removed. Model & activations: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer-15 residual stream; token activations averaged over assistant response. Preprocessing: standardize source activations (zero mean, unit variance); apply same source stats to targets. PCA: run PCA on scaled source activations, keep top 100 PCs. Probes: logistic regression (λ=10). For subset S, project activations onto S before training/eval; baseline probes trained on full standardized activations. 4.1 Baseline (Fig.2): source-trained probe on full representations transfers with AUROC: Insider Trading Confirm 0.874, Insider Trading Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probes within top-100 source PCs (5-fold CV on target) achieve 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869 AUROC across the three targets (numbers reported in that order). Conclusion: 100-PC subspace suffices to separate deceptive vs. honest; transfer gap is not due to missing information but to source probe’s favored directions. 4.2 Greedy PC selection (Fig.3): greedily add PCs from top-100 that most improve AUROC on target; for each candidate, train logistic probe on source projections, but selection guided by target performance via 5-fold CV (select on non-held folds, evaluate on held-out). Stop when improvement < 0.001. Mean greedy subset sizes: Report 15 PCs, Confirm 8 PCs, Sandbagging 14 PCs. Greedy improves over baseline (≈+0.22 for Report, +0.23 for Sandbagging) and approaches target-trained performance; top-k-by-variance matches greedy only for Confirm. 4.3 Hypotheses: test if transferable PCs are those that individually separate target classes or those the source probe weights most. Compare rankings by standardized coefficients (|coef| * PC stddev) from probes trained on activations projected on source-PCA basis: source-probe ranking, target-probe ranking, and greedy oracle.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Abstract claim: directions weighted by a source probe encode source-specific surface features; transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly (capturable in natural language). Main claim: probe OOD robustness largely determined by subspace selection. Background: linear probes expose semantic info but can fail OOD despite strong in-distribution performance. Assertion that behavioral concepts have linear representations but probes often learn spurious correlations; such unreliability is problematic for harmful-interaction monitoring. Method/approach keywords: work in source Q7 coordinates to avoid privileging model latent dims; these coordinates provide data-driven representation structure. Prior findings cited: removing leading components can improve downstream embedding performance (Mu et al., 2018); leading-component projections used as a probing baseline (Kantamneni et al., 2025). Problem framed as selecting dimensions that permit generalization vs. spurious source-trained classification. Pipeline (Fig.1): projection into source N4D basis, filtering candidate Q7 directions, probe training in selected low-dimensional subspace.

Goal: probe OOD robustness largely determined by subspace selection; pipeline projects activations into a source data-driven basis (source N4D / Q7 coordinates), filters candidate directions, and trains probes in the selected low-dim subspace. Prior findings: removing leading components can improve downstream embedding performance; leading-component projections used as a baseline. Related work summarized here: (1) Linear concept directions: studies report cross-dataset linear structure for true/false and other behaviors (Marks & Tegmark 2024; Park et al. 2024 formalize the linear representation hypothesis). Single directions reported for refusal and an “assistant” axis (Arditi et al. 2024; Lu et al. 2026); other work finds population-level directions for honesty/emotion (Zou et al. 2025). (2) Linear probes limits: probes can learn task/surface correlates rather than reveal intrinsic representation; encoded vs. recoverable information distinction; strong in-distribution probes often generalize unevenly—safety evaluation must separate robust internal signals from dataset artifacts. (3) Interpreting features with natural-language explanations: LLM-generated neuron explanations from high-activation examples (Bills et al. 2023), automated sparse-autoencoder feature labeling (Paulo et al. 2025; Bricken et al. 2023), and concept identification + ablation during fine-tuning (Casademunt et al. 2025).

Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6). Use layer-15 residual-stream activations (per Ying et al. 2026); activations averaged over assistant-response tokens. Data: four Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025) datasets — one source (Roleplaying: V8) and three held-out targets: Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), Sandbagging (J9). Only Roleplaying used as source. Labels: annotated by GPT-4o (K8, OpenAI 2024) with mapping honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous responses removed (binary honest vs deceptive). Preprocessing: source activations standardized to zero mean, unit variance; same source statistics used to standardize targets. Dimensionality reduction: PCA on source (N4D), retain leading 100 principal components (PCs Q7); probes trained on projections to subset S of these PCs. Classifiers: logistic regression (regularization λ=10) for all classifiers; comparator (full-representation baseline B8Q) trains on all standardized activations (no PCA). Choice of 100 PCs driven by interpretability comparability (alignment with U9/Bricken et al. 2023 decreases with PC index, so lower-index PCs are easier to interpret), not because low-index PCs generalize best. Error bars denote 95% confidence intervals.

Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6); layer-15 residual-stream activations, averaged over assistant-response tokens. Data: source = Roleplaying (V8); targets = Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), Sandbagging (J9). Labels by GPT-4o: honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous removed (binary). Preprocessing: source activations standardized (zero mean, unit variance); same source stats used to standardize targets. PCA on source, retain leading 100 PCs (Q7). Probes: logistic regression (λ=10); baseline B8Q = full standardized activations (no PCA). Figures report target F3; error bars = 95% CI.

Key experimental claims: W6 transfers best (reasonably), C2R moderate, J9 poor. Target-trained classifier on the 100-PC source subspace separates deceptive vs honest on every target. Greedy oracle search (H2) builds subset by starting empty, iteratively considering the 100 leading PCs: fit logistic weights on source projections, add PC that most improves target F3; selection uses target labels (5-fold CV: selection on non-held-out folds, evaluate on held-out fold); stop when no candidate improvement > 0.001. H2 also run as full-target selection to get a stable set/k (numbers differ slightly from CV).

Comparisons: variance-ranked top-k (Y4) matches H2 only on W6; T6 (source-side ranking) transfers about as well as B8Q; M9 (target-side ranking) does well on C2R, worse than H2 on W6, below random on J9. Magnitude metric X4 = |probe coefficient| * corresponding PC (Q7) std. Interpreter C7 (LLM judge) inspects 8 highest and 8 lowest activating source examples per PC, writes pole descriptions and assigns OOD score R5; interp-selected PC probe = L2, interp-ablated = A7. L2 (language-only selection) improves over B8Q, Y4, and A7 (especially on C2R and J9); W6 has little headroom.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars.
Goal: Can selecting principal components (PCs), i.e., directions in a source activation basis, improve out-of-distribution (OOD) deception detection?
Method overview: Train linear probes (logistic regression) on one source dataset; evaluate on 3 held-out target datasets. Use a target-supervised greedy search that adds PCs according to target performance. Also evaluate ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights. Introduce an LLM judge that scores natural-language PC descriptions without using target data.
Key quantitative claims/results: Greedy, target-supervised search finds 8–15 PCs that nearly match probes trained on target data. Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights does not recover this transferable subspace. Selecting 19 PCs that receive the maximum observed LLM score in both runs (unsupervised by target data) improves transfer on all 3 targets. For two of the targets, this selection closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and the greedy oracle. 
Other terms to track: "full-representation baseline", "greedy oracle", "both runs" (unspecified here), which targets achieve 78% and 25% (unspecified here).

Paper: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Goal: improve cross-domain (source->target) deception detection by selecting source-PC directions. Source domain = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (activations extracted; token activations averaged over assistant response to form probe inputs). Labels: GPT-4o assigns Deceptive=1, Honest=0, Ambiguous=-1 (ambiguous examples removed). Representation & PCA: source activations are standardized (source -> zero mean, unit variance) and PCA applied; source statistics are applied to target activations; 100 source PCs retained (S subset of these). Probes: all linear (logistic regression, regularization parameter λ=10); baseline = source-trained probe on full standardized activations; target-trained probes fit on target data. Selection methods: greedy oracle = target-guided greedy adding the PC that most increases target AUROC (reported to find ~8–15 PCs that nearly match target-trained probes); variance control = top-k PCs by variance; source-PCA probe and target-PCA probe use standardized coefficients to rank PCs (standardized coefficient = |coefficient| * PC standard deviation). LLM judge: GPT-5-mini interprets PC positive/negative poles and rates OOD-deception usefulness on a 1–10 scale; observed maximum OOD score = 6. Interp-selection = 19 PCs that received the maximum observed score (6) in both scoring runs; interp-ablated PCs = remaining 81. Evaluation: 5-fold CV on targets (held-out folds used for testing); AUROC reported with 95% CI. Causal validation (intervention/ablation at inference) was not performed. Appendix C: SAE decoder alignment (resource andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct); statistics reported include Spearman ρ and Jaccard overlap.

Section 4.1 (baseline): Source-trained (full representation) AUROC: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probes trained within the top-100 PC subspace (5-fold CV) achieve 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869 (across the three targets, matching order above). Authors conclude the 100-PC subspace contains sufficient target-class information; limited transfer is due to source probe directions.

Section 4.2 (greedy oracle): Greedy PC-selection (start empty; iteratively add the top-100 PC that most improves target AUROC as evaluated on non-held-out target folds; for each candidate, train probe on source projections). Probe weights during selection are fit on source; selection uses target labels; stop when no PC improves AUROC > 0.001. Mean selected subset sizes: Report 15 PCs, Confirm 8 PCs, Sandbagging 14 PCs. Greedy nearly matches target-trained on Report and Sandbagging: improves baseline AUROC by +0.22 (Report) and +0.23 (Sandbagging). Variance-top-k control (k matched to greedy) matches greedy only on Confirm.

Section 4.3 sets up tests of two hypotheses: transferable PCs either (1) individually separate target classes, or (2) are PCs the source probe relies on (weight rankings). Flag: earlier note flagged a potential later inconsistency about retaining 100 PCs vs a later PC list of 58 entries.

k set by running greedy on full target dataset (not per-fold): k = 13 (Report), 7 (Confirm), 14 (Sandbagging) — numbers differ slightly from Section 4.2 because full-data greedy used. Paper question: whether selecting subspaces of LM representations improves out-of-distribution (OOD) deception detection. Method: compare probes (classifiers) trained on full representations vs probes using selected directions/subspaces. Two selection approaches highlighted: (1) target-guided selection that uses target labels but does not fit probe weights on them; (2) interpretation-based selection using natural-language interpretations, which requires no target data. Key claims: small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes; selecting directions by source weights, target-class separation, or explained variance does not recover the same transferable subspaces; interpretation-based selection improves over the full-representation baseline on all targets, though how well it recovers varies sharply across targets. Scope/caveats: study uses one model and one source dataset; interpretations are descriptive, not causal. The paper includes a "Glossary." (no glossary content shown in this part).

Goal: test whether selecting subspaces of LM representations improves OOD (transfer) deception detection. Source dataset: Roleplaying (V8). Targets include C2R (Insider Trading Report), W6 (Insider Trading Confirm), J9 (Sandbagging). Model & readout: layer-15 residual-stream activations from Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6), averaged over assistant-response tokens. Preprocessing: standardization = zero-mean/unit-variance using source statistics applied to both source and targets. Dimensionality reduction: PCA / N4D retains the leading 100 source directions (Q7); "PCs" refer to these retained source directions; "leading" = lower index. Probes: logistic regression with λ=10, evaluated by AUROC (F3) with 95% CIs; 5-fold CV where selection uses non-held-out target folds and evaluation uses the held-out fold. Baselines & methods: B8Q = full-representation baseline (source-trained on all standardized activations); Y4 = top-k PCs by variance (variance-ranked subset matched in dimension count); H2 = greedy oracle (target-guided direction selection but probe weights fitted only on source); T6 = source-PCA probe (supplies source coefficient rankings); M9 = target-PCA probe (supplies target coefficient rankings); X4 = standardized coefficient = |coef| * PC_std. Interpretation-based selection: natural-language explanations produced with P2 (GPT-5-mini) and rated by C7 (LLM judge) yielding R5 (OOD score/generalization rating); L2 = interp-selected PC probe (uses directions reaching max R5 in both scoring runs); A7 = interp-ablated PC probe (complement). Decoder alignment uses SAE (U9) decoder features (resource: andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct); Spearman ρ reports relation of PC index to decoder alignment. Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; method: linear probes on activations. Key claim: projecting inputs onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) from the training activation distribution enables cross-domain transfer that nearly matches probes trained directly on each test distribution. Experiments: evaluated on 3 held-out deception detection datasets (two named: Insider Trading Report, Sandbagging). PC interpretation method: use an LLM judge to score each PC by whether its most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; then probe using highest-scoring PCs. Quantitative claims: this closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and by 25% on Sandbagging. Observations: source-probe-weighted directions encode source-specific surface features; transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and are capturable by natural language descriptions. Conclusion: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection. Venue note: Machine Learning, ICML.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Main conclusion: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection. Venue: Machine Learning / ICML.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Datasets: 4 deception datasets (Roleplaying = source; Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging = targets). Labels assigned by GPT-4o: honest (0), ambiguous (-1), deceptive (1); ambiguous responses removed. LM & activations: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer 15 residual stream activations (highest cross-domain AUROC per Ying et al. 2026); token activations averaged over assistant response. Preprocessing & PCA: standardize source activations to zero mean/unit variance and apply same source stats to targets; run PCA on scaled source activations and retain top 100 PCs. Probes: logistic regression (λ=10). For subset S experiments, project onto S before training/evaluation; baseline probes train on full standardized activations (full-dimensional). Rationale for 100 PCs: alignment with SAE decoder features declines with PC index (Appendix C), so lower-index PCs are more interpretable; authors do not claim low-index PCs generalize better—Section 4.1 reportedly shows 100-PC subspace retains enough info to separate deceptive vs. honest on every target. Methods compared: (1) target-supervised greedy search finds small transferable subspace (~8–15 PCs) where a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe (Sec. 4.2); (2) ranking PCs by source-/target-probe weights fails (Sec. 4.3); (3) an LLM judge interpreting PCs via high/low-activation examples can partially recover transferable PCs without target labels (Sec. 4.5). Key claimed results: small PC subsets enable near-target transfer; closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Main conclusion: OOD robustness of probes largely determined by subspace selection.

Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer-15 residual activations averaged over assistant response. Preprocessing: standardize using source stats; PCA on scaled source activations, keep top 100 PCs. Probe: logistic regression. 4.1 baseline (source-trained on full reps): Confirm 0.874 AUROC, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probes in top-100 source-PC space (5-fold CV) reach 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869 AUROC (numbers given in same paragraph after listing Confirm/Report/Sandbagging — mapping likely Confirm=0.936, Report=0.950, Sandbagging=0.869), so 100-PC subspace contains sufficient signal. 4.2 greedy PC selection: search over top 100 PCs, iteratively add PC that most improves AUROC on target; probe weights always fit on source projections but subset choice guided by target labels with 5-fold CV; stop when AUROC gain <0.001. Average subset sizes: Report 15, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14. Greedy improves baseline by +0.22 (Report) and +0.23 (Sandbagging) and comes close to target-trained probes; variance-controlled top-k by variance matches greedy only for Confirm. 4.3 tests two hypotheses via rankings using standardized coefficient = |coef| * PC stddev; ambiguity/inconsistency in text about whether the "target-PCA probe" is trained on target data or on source data (contradictory sentences).

Datasets: Roleplaying = source; targets = Insider Trading Confirm, Insider Trading Report, Sandbagging. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; activations = layer-15 residual averaged over assistant response. Preprocessing: standardize using source stats; PCA on scaled source activations; keep top 100 PCs. Probe: logistic regression. Baselines (source-trained on full rep): Confirm 0.874 AUROC, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probes in the top-100 source-PC space (5-fold CV) reach high AUROCs (reported as 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869 in the paper; mapping to labels was ambiguous). Greedy PC selection (CV-guided by target labels, probe weights fit on source projections, stop when AUROC gain <0.001): average subset sizes Report=15, Confirm=8, Sandbagging=14; greedy improves baseline by ~+0.22 (Report) and ~+0.23 (Sandbagging) and approaches target-trained performance; top-k-by-variance matches greedy only for Confirm. Running greedy on full target data (single stable set) yields k=13 (Report), 7 (Confirm), 14 (Sandbagging) — small differences from CV explained. 4.3’s tested hypotheses both fail: source-PCA probe transfers about as well as the full-representation baseline (i.e., source-selected PCs don’t generalize), while target-PCA probe does well on Report but worse than greedy on Confirm and is below-random on Sandbagging — so PCs that best separate target classes are not the ones that transfer when weighted by source data. Interpretability (Bills et al./Casademunt method): for each top-100 PC, take 8 most/least activating source examples, ask LLM judge to rate OOD generalizability 1–10. No PC scored >6, so 6 was max observed; keeping PCs that scored 6 in both independent runs yields 19 interp-selected PCs. Of 5 PCs that appeared in greedy selections for multiple targets, 3 got max OOD; only 1 of top-5 source-PCA PCs got max OOD. The interp-selected 19-PC probe outperforms baseline, top-19-by-variance, and the ablated-81 control across targets; closes ~78% of baseline→greedy gap on Report (baseline 0.706 → greedy 0.929) and ~25% of the gap on Sandbagging (greedy 0.832); Confirm is near ceiling so comparisons are uninformative.

Target-trained probes in top-100 source-PC space (5-fold CV) reach high AUROCs reported as 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869 (mapping to targets ambiguous). Greedy PC selection (CV-guided; fit probe weights on source projections; stop when AUROC gain <0.001) average subset sizes: Report=15, Confirm=8, Sandbagging=14; greedy improves baseline substantially for Report and Sandbagging (~+0.22 and ~+0.23) and approaches target-trained performance; top-k-by-variance matches greedy only for Confirm. Running greedy on full target data (single stable set) yields k=13 (Report), 7 (Confirm), 14 (Sandbagging). 4.3 hypotheses fail: source-PCA probe transfers about as well as full-representation baseline (source-selected PCs don’t generalize); target-PCA probe works well on Report but worse than greedy on Confirm and is below-random on Sandbagging. Interpretability: for each top-100 PC take 8 most/least activating source examples, ask LLM judge to rate OOD generalizability 1–10 (Bills/Casademunt method). No PC scored >6; keeping PCs that scored 6 in both runs yields 19 interp-selected PCs. Of 5 PCs recurring in greedy selections for multiple targets, 3 got max OOD; only 1 of top-5 source-PCA PCs got max OOD.
