Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Abstract claim: directions weighted by a source probe encode source-specific surface features; transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly (capturable in natural language). Main claim: probe OOD robustness largely determined by subspace selection. Background: linear probes expose semantic info but can fail OOD despite strong in-distribution performance. Assertion that behavioral concepts have linear representations but probes often learn spurious correlations; such unreliability is problematic for harmful-interaction monitoring. Method/approach keywords: work in source Q7 coordinates to avoid privileging model latent dims; these coordinates provide data-driven representation structure. Prior findings cited: removing leading components can improve downstream embedding performance (Mu et al., 2018); leading-component projections used as a probing baseline (Kantamneni et al., 2025). Problem framed as selecting dimensions that permit generalization vs. spurious source-trained classification. Pipeline (Fig.1): projection into source N4D basis, filtering candidate Q7 directions, probe training in selected low-dimensional subspace.

Goal: probe OOD robustness largely determined by subspace selection; pipeline projects activations into a source data-driven basis (source N4D / Q7 coordinates), filters candidate directions, and trains probes in the selected low-dim subspace. Prior findings: removing leading components can improve downstream embedding performance; leading-component projections used as a baseline. Related work summarized here: (1) Linear concept directions: studies report cross-dataset linear structure for true/false and other behaviors (Marks & Tegmark 2024; Park et al. 2024 formalize the linear representation hypothesis). Single directions reported for refusal and an “assistant” axis (Arditi et al. 2024; Lu et al. 2026); other work finds population-level directions for honesty/emotion (Zou et al. 2025). (2) Linear probes limits: probes can learn task/surface correlates rather than reveal intrinsic representation; encoded vs. recoverable information distinction; strong in-distribution probes often generalize unevenly—safety evaluation must separate robust internal signals from dataset artifacts. (3) Interpreting features with natural-language explanations: LLM-generated neuron explanations from high-activation examples (Bills et al. 2023), automated sparse-autoencoder feature labeling (Paulo et al. 2025; Bricken et al. 2023), and concept identification + ablation during fine-tuning (Casademunt et al. 2025).

Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6). Use layer-15 residual-stream activations (per Ying et al. 2026); activations averaged over assistant-response tokens. Data: four Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025) datasets — one source (Roleplaying: V8) and three held-out targets: Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), Sandbagging (J9). Only Roleplaying used as source. Labels: annotated by GPT-4o (K8, OpenAI 2024) with mapping honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous responses removed (binary honest vs deceptive). Preprocessing: source activations standardized to zero mean, unit variance; same source statistics used to standardize targets. Dimensionality reduction: PCA on source (N4D), retain leading 100 principal components (PCs Q7); probes trained on projections to subset S of these PCs. Classifiers: logistic regression (regularization λ=10) for all classifiers; comparator (full-representation baseline B8Q) trains on all standardized activations (no PCA). Choice of 100 PCs driven by interpretability comparability (alignment with U9/Bricken et al. 2023 decreases with PC index, so lower-index PCs are easier to interpret), not because low-index PCs generalize best. Error bars denote 95% confidence intervals.

Labels: GPT-4o annotations, honest=0 / deceptive=1 (ambiguous removed). Preprocessing: source activations standardized (0 mean, unit variance); same source stats used on targets. PCA on source (N4D); retain leading 100 PCs (Q7). Probes: logistic regression (λ=10) on projected activations; comparator B8Q = probe on full standardized activations (no PCA). Error bars = 95% CIs.

High-level results (Section 4): transfer performance: W6 best (reasonably good), C2R moderate, J9 poor. Target-trained classification within the retained 100-PC source subspace separates deceptive vs honest on every target (i.e., relevant info present); a single source-trained direction often fails to generalize.

Search/selection methods: greedy oracle (H2) — starts empty, greedily adds one of the 100 leading PCs that most improves target F3; selection uses target labels (target 5-fold CV described; stopping threshold 0.001); probe weights always fitted on source projections (selection guided by target labels is an upper bound). H2 also run in full-target mode to yield a stable set/k (numbers differ slightly from CV).

Ranking hypotheses: T6 = source-PCA ranking; M9 = target-PCA ranking. Both use X4 = |coefficient| * PC std (standardized coefficient) computed on source-projected activations. T6 transfers ~B8Q; M9 mixed (good on C2R, worse on W6, below random on J9). Rankings do not recover H2 transferable subspace.

Interpretability: For each leading source PC, LLM judge (C7) receives top-8 and bottom-8 activating source examples to produce pole/whole descriptions and an OOD generalization rating (R5). Selection retains directions reaching observed maxima in both scoring runs (scores noisy).

Language-only selection (L2): interp-selected PC probe (intersection of interpreter picks) — without target data — outperforms B8Q and variance control (Y4) widely on C2R/J9 and beats A7 (interp-ablated) everywhere; W6 shows little headroom.

PCA on source (N4D); retain leading 100 PCs (Q7). Probes: logistic regression (λ=10) on projected activations; comparator B8Q = probe on full standardized activations (no PCA). Error bars = 95% CIs. Main results: transfer performance — W6 best (high baseline, little headroom), C2R moderate/robust improvement, J9 poor/weakest and most OOD (modest gains likely reflect distribution shift). Target-trained classification within retained 100-PC source subspace separates deceptive vs honest on every target; single source-trained direction often fails to generalize. Pipeline: residual activations standardized; PCA on scaled source activations, retain top-100 PCs. Probe: logistic regression (L2 λ=10). Metric: AUROC (cross-domain). Model/layer/source: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer 15, source Roleplaying.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars.
Goal: Can selecting principal components (PCs), i.e., directions in a source activation basis, improve out-of-distribution (OOD) deception detection?
Method overview: Train linear probes (logistic regression) on one source dataset; evaluate on 3 held-out target datasets. Use a target-supervised greedy search that adds PCs according to target performance. Also evaluate ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights. Introduce an LLM judge that scores natural-language PC descriptions without using target data.
Key quantitative claims/results: Greedy, target-supervised search finds 8–15 PCs that nearly match probes trained on target data. Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights does not recover this transferable subspace. Selecting 19 PCs that receive the maximum observed LLM score in both runs (unsupervised by target data) improves transfer on all 3 targets. For two of the targets, this selection closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and the greedy oracle. 
Other terms to track: "full-representation baseline", "greedy oracle", "both runs" (unspecified here), which targets achieve 78% and 25% (unspecified here).

Paper: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Goal: improve cross-domain (source->target) deception detection by selecting source-PC directions. Source domain = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (activations extracted; token activations averaged over assistant response to form probe inputs). Labels: GPT-4o assigns Deceptive=1, Honest=0, Ambiguous=-1 (ambiguous examples removed). Representation & PCA: source activations are standardized (source -> zero mean, unit variance) and PCA applied; source statistics are applied to target activations; 100 source PCs retained (S subset of these). Probes: all linear (logistic regression, regularization parameter λ=10); baseline = source-trained probe on full standardized activations; target-trained probes fit on target data. Selection methods: greedy oracle = target-guided greedy adding the PC that most increases target AUROC (reported to find ~8–15 PCs that nearly match target-trained probes); variance control = top-k PCs by variance; source-PCA probe and target-PCA probe use standardized coefficients to rank PCs (standardized coefficient = |coefficient| * PC standard deviation). LLM judge: GPT-5-mini interprets PC positive/negative poles and rates OOD-deception usefulness on a 1–10 scale; observed maximum OOD score = 6. Interp-selection = 19 PCs that received the maximum observed score (6) in both scoring runs; interp-ablated PCs = remaining 81. Evaluation: 5-fold CV on targets (held-out folds used for testing); AUROC reported with 95% CI. Causal validation (intervention/ablation at inference) was not performed. Appendix C: SAE decoder alignment (resource andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct); statistics reported include Spearman ρ and Jaccard overlap.

Setup recap: standardize source residual-stream activations (zero mean/unit var), apply same source stats to targets, run PCA on scaled source activations and retain top 100 PCs. Probes: logistic regression (linear) with regularization λ=10. Metric: AUROC (cross-domain). Baseline: probe trained on full standardized activations.

Key results in this part (order of targets used: Insider Trading Confirm, Insider Trading Report, Sandbagging):
- Full-representation source-trained AUROC (target eval): Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606.
- Target-trained within top-100 source-PC subspace (5-fold CV) AUROC: 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869 (interpreted as Confirm / Report / Sandbagging). Conclusion: 100-PC subspace contains sufficient target information.

Greedy selection (oracle): start empty; at each step consider top-100 source PCs, add PC that maximally improves target AUROC (candidate probes trained on source data; selection evaluated on non-held-out target folds); stop when no candidate improves AUROC > 0.001; final eval on held-out fold.
- Mean greedy subset sizes: Report 15 PCs, Confirm 8 PCs, Sandbagging 14 PCs.
- Greedy improves baseline AUROC by ~0.22 (Report) and ~0.23 (Sandbagging), nearly matching target-trained for those tasks. Variance-top-k control (k matched to greedy) matches greedy only for Confirm; falls short for Report and Sandbagging.

Hypotheses to be tested next: transferable PCs are (a) individually separable on target vs (b) those the source probe relies on. Flag: earlier note flagged a potential later table listing only 58 PC entries despite repeated claim of retaining 100 PCs—watch for inconsistency.

final_notes: Goal: robust behavioral probing — OOD probing = representation selection + classifier fitting. Representation selection: PCA on source, keep top-100 PCs. LLM judge (R5 1–10) run twice; per-run retention = PCs rated maximum; L2 = intersection of max-PCs across runs = 19 PCs; A7 complement = 81 PCs. Probing: project into subspace, train logistic regression (L2, λ=10). Controls: B8Q (full-representation), Y4 (variance-matched), H2 (target-guided greedy/oracle). Datasets & sizes: V8 (371), C2R (473), W6 (151), J9 (1000). Key metrics: B8Q AUROC — C2R 0.706, W6 0.874, J9 0.606. Target-trained (5-fold CV in top-100): C2R 0.936, W6 0.950, J9 0.869. H2 (oracle) F3: C2R 0.929, J9 0.832. L2 F3: C2R 0.881, J9 0.662. L2 recovers Baseline→H2 gap: C2R 78%, J9 25%. H2 subset sizes (mean, target-CV): C2R 15, W6 8, J9 14 (note earlier one place reported 13,7,14). Table 2 selections (Q7 indices): T6 source top-15 [7,8,11,12,4,5,2,3,6,27,22,21,1,41,18]; H2 C2R [6,89,62,66,26,14,57,25,93,9,70,97,78]; H2 W6 [71,53,28,86,32,81,77]; H2 J9 [37,62,54,41,46,9,57,44,51,43,19,48,86,81,33]; M9 lists given too. Appendix E (Q7 Interpretability): scoring runs = 2; maximum observed R5 = 6; 19 directions reached max in both runs (kept for L2); A7 = 81. H2 selected the same direction for more than one target: 5 directions (62,57,9,81,86) with R5s [6,6,3,3,6]; max-rated among those = 3/5 (62,57,86). Top T6 top-5 [7,8,11,12,4] have R5s [3,4,3,3,6] so 1/5 max-rated. Interpretations emphasize lexical/surface cues (denial, hedging, PR-style defensive wording), likely brittle OOD. Note: earlier Appendix D/Table 2 produced a Jaccard computation mismatch versus reported D3 values and an H2-J9 list-length inconsistency (reported k=14 vs list of 15).

Paper question: whether selecting subspaces of LM representations improves out-of-distribution (OOD) deception detection. Method: compare probes (classifiers) trained on full representations vs probes using selected directions/subspaces. Two selection approaches highlighted: (1) target-guided selection that uses target labels but does not fit probe weights on them; (2) interpretation-based selection using natural-language interpretations, which requires no target data. Key claims: small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes; selecting directions by source weights, target-class separation, or explained variance does not recover the same transferable subspaces; interpretation-based selection improves over the full-representation baseline on all targets, though how well it recovers varies sharply across targets. Scope/caveats: study uses one model and one source dataset; interpretations are descriptive, not causal. The paper includes a "Glossary." (no glossary content shown in this part).

Goal: test whether selecting subspaces of LM representations improves OOD (transfer) deception detection. Source dataset: Roleplaying (V8). Targets include C2R (Insider Trading Report), W6 (Insider Trading Confirm), J9 (Sandbagging). Model & readout: layer-15 residual-stream activations from Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6), averaged over assistant-response tokens. Preprocessing: standardization = zero-mean/unit-variance using source statistics applied to both source and targets. Dimensionality reduction: PCA / N4D retains the leading 100 source directions (Q7); "PCs" refer to these retained source directions; "leading" = lower index. Probes: logistic regression with λ=10, evaluated by AUROC (F3) with 95% CIs; 5-fold CV where selection uses non-held-out target folds and evaluation uses the held-out fold. Baselines & methods: B8Q = full-representation baseline (source-trained on all standardized activations); Y4 = top-k PCs by variance (variance-ranked subset matched in dimension count); H2 = greedy oracle (target-guided direction selection but probe weights fitted only on source); T6 = source-PCA probe (supplies source coefficient rankings); M9 = target-PCA probe (supplies target coefficient rankings); X4 = standardized coefficient = |coef| * PC_std. Interpretation-based selection: natural-language explanations produced with P2 (GPT-5-mini) and rated by C7 (LLM judge) yielding R5 (OOD score/generalization rating); L2 = interp-selected PC probe (uses directions reaching max R5 in both scoring runs); A7 = interp-ablated PC probe (complement). Decoder alignment uses SAE (U9) decoder features (resource: andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct); Spearman ρ reports relation of PC index to decoder alignment. Scope: one model, one source dataset; interpretations are descriptive, not causal.

Related work (this part): prior work finds simple activation directions can support readout/intervention but their stability across contexts is unresolved; linear-probe accuracy alone does not establish robust internal representation; natural-language (LLM) explanations have been used to label features and support interventions/ablations to reduce misaligned behavior.

Goal: test whether selecting subspaces of LM representations (leading PCA directions) improves OOD (transfer) deception detection. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6); use layer-15 residual-stream activations, averaged over assistant-response tokens. Datasets: Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025) collection — one source Roleplaying (V8) and three held-out targets: Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), Sandbagging (J9). Labeling: GPT-4o (K8) maps honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous responses removed. Preprocessing: source activations standardized to zero-mean/unit-variance; same source statistics applied to targets. Dimensionality reduction: PCA (N4D) on source; retain leading 100 PCs (Q7). Activations may be projected to a subset S of these directions before training/eval. All classifiers are logistic regression (λ=10); full-representation baseline (B8Q) trains on all standardized activations (no PCA truncation). Evaluation: AUROC with 95% CIs; earlier notes indicate 5-fold CV where direction selection uses non-held-out target folds and evaluation uses held-out fold. Interpretability: retained-100 chosen for comparability (not because low-index PCs generalize better); alignment with sparse-autoencoder decoder vectors U9 decreases with index, so lower indices are more interpretable. Interpretation pipeline: explanations generated by P2 (GPT-5-mini), rated by C7 producing R5; L2 = interp-selected PC probe (max R5), A7 = interp-ablated PC probe (complement). Example reported numbers (appendix): C2R — B8Q 0.706, H2 0.929, L2 0.881; J9 — B8Q 0.606, H2 0.832, L2 0.662. Error bars denote 95% CIs.

Goal: test whether selecting subspaces of LM representations (leading PCA directions) improves OOD (transfer) deception detection. Datasets: source Roleplaying (V8) and held-out targets C2R (Insider Trading Report), W6 (Insider Trading Confirm), J9 (Sandbagging). Labels from GPT-4o; ambiguous removed. Baseline B8Q = probe on full standardized activations. Evaluation: AUROC (F3) with 95% CIs; 5-fold CV where direction selection uses non-held-out target folds and evaluation uses held-out fold.

Key reported results (Appendix A / text):
- B8Q F3 (baseline): W6 0.874, C2R 0.706, J9 0.606.
- Target-trained probes within retained-100: C2R 0.936, W6 0.950, J9 0.869 (separates classes even when source-trained transfer is poor).
- H2 (target-guided greedy search over top-100 PCs): mean subset sizes (CV) C2R 15, W6 8, J9 14; full-target H2 k: C2R 13, W6 7, J9 14.
- H2 F3 (used in some comparisons): C2R 0.929, J9 0.832; H2 improvements over B8Q ~0.22 (C2R) and 0.23 (J9).
- Variance selection (Y4, top-k by PC variance) matches H2 only on W6; falls far behind on C2R and J9.
- Hypothesis tests: T6 (source-PCA ranking) performs about like B8Q; M9 (target-PCA ranking) does well on C2R, worse than H2 on W6, and below random on J9. H2–M9 distances (D3): C2R 0.182, W6 0.077, J9 0.167.
Method details: H2 greedy search adds PC whose addition (source-trained weights) yields largest target F3 improvement; selection guided by target labels but probe weights always fit on source (transfer upper bound). Stop when improvement <= 0.001. Interpretability: explanations by P2, rated by C7 producing R5; L2 = interp-selected-PC probe, A7 = interp-ablated-PC probe. Interpretations indicate some domain-stable abstractions but partial recovery and noisy scores.

Interpretability selection: For each of the top-100 source PCs, an LLM judge (C7) sees the 8 most- and 8 least-activating source examples, writes positive/negative/whole-direction descriptions, and assigns an OOD/generalization rating R5. Per-run retention = PCs that attain the observed maximum R5; final L2 = intersection of PCs that hit max in both independent scoring runs. Appendix E: max R5 = 6, 2 scoring runs, 19 PCs reached max in both runs → L2 has 19 PCs, complement A7 has 81. Example ratings: Q7 62, 57, 86 each R5=6; Q7 9 and 81 each R5=3. Among H2 selections, 3/5 of shared H2 directions were max-rated; among top T6 selections 1/5 were max-rated. Scores are noisy. L2 is language-only (no target labels); all probes (L2, A7, Y4) are trained on source activations. Performance: Appendix A reports L2 F3 C2R=0.881 vs B8Q=0.706; J9 L2=0.662 vs B8Q=0.606. L2 recovers 78% of the baseline→H2 gap on C2R and 25% on J9. Paper states L2 exceeds B8Q, the variance-ranked control Y4 (matched dimension), and A7 on all targets; W6 values for L2/Y4/A7 are not given and methods (except A7) are described as roughly tied. (Retain earlier method/context: PCA on source 100 PCs; probes = logistic regression λ=10; B8Q baselines — W6 0.874, C2R 0.706, J9 0.606; H2 target-guided greedy H2 F3 C2R≈0.929, J9≈0.832.)

Two independent scoring runs; per-run retention = PCs that hit the observed max R5; final L2 = intersection of PCs that hit max in both runs → L2 has 19 PCs; complement A7 has 81. Paper title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Setup: use linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations to detect deception behaviors; evaluate generalization across 3 held-out deception detection datasets (only two named here: Insider Trading Report and Sandbagging). Key claim: projecting inputs onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) from the training activation distribution enables cross-domain transfer that nearly matches probes trained on the target/test distribution. Method extension: interpret PCs and use an LLM judge to score each PC by whether its most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; then probe using top-scoring PCs. Results: this PC-selection method closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and by 25% on Sandbagging. Interpretation claim: source-probe-weighted directions encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and in ways capturable by natural language descriptions. Broad claim: OOD robustness of probes largely determined by subspace selection. Venue noted: Machine Learning, ICML.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Setup: train linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations (source dataset: Roleplaying deception scenarios); evaluate OOD on three held-out target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Core idea: work in the source-domain PCA basis and select a small subset of source PCs to train probes that avoid spurious surface correlations and transfer to targets. Key empirical claims: (1) A small transferable subspace exists (Sec. 4.2): a target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds ~8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe. (2) Source-side and target-side weight-based rankings fail to recover this subspace (Sec. 4.3): ranking PCs by source or target probe weights does not outperform the full-representation baseline. (3) An LLM judge can partially recover the subspace without target labels (Sec. 4.5): it interprets PCs via their extreme examples and selects transferable PCs. Prior-note results: PC-selection method closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Interpretation claim: transferable directions encode more abstract contrasts describable in language; probe OOD robustness largely determined by subspace selection. Figure 1 outlines pipeline: project activations into source PCA basis, filter candidate PCs, train probes on selected low-dim subspace.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Setup: train linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations using a source dataset of roleplaying deception scenarios; evaluate OOD on three held-out target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Method: compute PCA on source activations, work in source PCA basis, filter candidate PCs, and select a small subset of source PCs to train linear probes on the low-dimensional subspace. Key empirical claims: (1) A small transferable subspace exists: target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds ~8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe (Sec. 4.2). (2) Weight-based rankings on source or target probes fail to recover this subspace and do not outperform full-representation baseline (Sec. 4.3). (3) An LLM judge can partially recover the subspace without target labels by interpreting PCs via extreme examples and selecting transferable PCs (Sec. 4.5). Reported quantitative impact: PC-selection method closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Context from related work: literature reports linear/low-dim directions for high-level properties and behaviors, examples of single-direction control (refusal/assistant axis), skepticism about probes (probe may learn task/exploit surface correlates; OOD probe generalization can be uneven), and use of LLMs to generate natural-language explanations of features and to inform interventions.

Datasets: Roleplaying is the source; targets are Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Each response labeled by GPT-4o as honest (0), ambiguous (-1), or deceptive (1); ambiguous examples removed. Language model activations: layer-15 residual stream of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; token activations averaged over the assistant response. Preprocessing: standardize source activations (zero mean, unit variance) and apply the same source statistics to standardize target activations. PCA: run PCA on the scaled source activations and retain the top 100 PCs. Probes: logistic regression (regularization λ=10). For experiments using a subset S of PCs, project activations onto S before training/evaluation; baseline probes train on the full standardized activations. Motivation for 100 PCs: lower-index PCs align more with SAE decoder features (Appendix C) and are easier to interpret, but authors do not claim low-index PCs inherently generalize better; Section 4.1 reportedly shows the 100-PC subspace suffices to separate deceptive vs. honest on every target.

Datasets: source = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Confirm, Insider Trading Report, Sandbagging. Responses labeled honest (0), ambiguous (-1), deceptive (1); ambiguous examples removed. Model activations: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer-15 residual stream; token activations averaged over assistant response. Preprocessing: standardize source activations (zero mean, unit variance) and apply same source statistics to standardize target activations. PCA: run PCA on scaled source activations and retain top 100 PCs. Probes: logistic regression (λ=10). Baselines: probes trained on full standardized representations; for PC-subset experiments project activations onto subset before training/evaluation.

Key results (Section 4.1): source-trained probe (full rep) AUROC on targets: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Probe trained on target data within top-100 source PCs (5-fold CV) achieves AUROC ≈ 0.936 (Confirm) / 0.950 (Report) / 0.869 (Sandbagging) — so 100-PC subspace suffices to separate classes on every target.

Greedy PC-selection (Section 4.2): start empty, iteratively add from top-100 PCs the PC that most improves AUROC on target; to evaluate a candidate, project source activations onto current subset and train probe on source projections; PC choice guided by target labeled folds (5-fold CV) while probe weights always fit on source; stop when AUROC improvement ≤0.001. Avg subset sizes: Report 15 PCs, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14. Greedy improves over baseline (full-rep baseline) by ~+0.22 (Report) and +0.23 (Sandbagging) and approaches target-trained performance; top-k-by-variance matched greedy only for Confirm.

Section 4.3 tests two hypotheses for transferable PCs (separate target classes alone vs PCs source probe leans on). Compare rankings by standardized coefficient = |coef| * std(PC) from probes trained on activations projected to source-PCA basis (source-probe vs target-probe vs greedy oracle).

Datasets: source = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Confirm, Insider Trading Report, Sandbagging. Labels: honest(0), ambiguous(-1) (removed), deceptive(1). Representations: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer-15 residual stream; token activations averaged over assistant response; standardize using source mean/var and apply same stats to targets. PCA: run on scaled source activations, keep top 100 PCs. Probes: logistic regression (λ=10). Baselines: probes on full standardized representations; PC-subset experiments project activations onto chosen subset before training/eval. Key baseline numbers: source-trained probe (full rep) AUROC on targets: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probe on top-100 source PCs (5-fold CV) AUROC ≈ Confirm 0.936, Report 0.950, Sandbagging 0.869 (so 100-PC subspace suffices for target separation). Greedy PC-selection (target labels guide PC choice, probe weights fit on source; stop when AUROC improvement ≤0.001): CV average subset sizes Report 15, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14; greedy boosted AUROC over full-rep by ~+0.22 (Report) and +0.23 (Sandbagging); top-k-by-variance only matched greedy for Confirm. Cross-target ranking experiment (Sec 4.3): define source-PCA and target-PCA rankings (both use source-PCA basis); to pick k, run greedy on full target dataset (single k): Report k=13, Confirm k=7, Sandbagging k=14 (differs slightly from CV sizes). Results: both hypotheses fail — source-PCA probe transfers ~as well as full-rep baseline (i.e., doesn't generalize); target-PCA probe does well on Report, worse than greedy on Confirm, and below-random on Sandbagging. Interpretability (Sec 4.4): for each top-100 PC, collect 8 most/least activating examples and have an LLM judge describe poles and give 1–10 OOD scores; max observed score=6; keep PCs that scored 6 in both runs → 19 interp-selected PCs. Of 5 PCs that appeared in greedy selections for multiple targets, 3 had max OOD; only 1 of top-5 source-PCA PCs got max OOD. Sec 4.5 evaluates probe AUROC for interp-selected 19 PCs vs controls (full-rep, top-19 by variance, remaining 81). Figures and appendices provide full results.

Methods: single-model / single-source. Probes: logistic regression (L2, λ=10) on source activations projected to top-100 source PCs; comparator B8Q trains on full standardized activations (no PCA). Greedy oracle H2: add PCs greedily to maximize target F3 (5-fold CV), stop when no candidate improves >0.001. Ranking methods T6/M9 use X4 = |probe coeff| * PC std. LLM judge C7 used (prompt contradiction flagged earlier).

H2 selected 5 directions for >1 target; 3 of those 5 are maximum-rated (R5=6). "Maximum-rated directions among the top T6 selections" = 1 of top 5. Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Abstract claim: directions weighted by a source probe encode source-specific surface features; transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly (capturable in natural language). Main claim: probe OOD robustness largely determined by subspace selection. Background: linear probes expose semantic info but can fail OOD despite strong in-distribution performance. Assertion that behavioral concepts have linear representations but probes often learn spurious correlations; such unreliability is problematic for harmful-interaction monitoring. Method/approach keywords: work in source Q7 coordinates to avoid privileging model latent dims; these coordinates provide data-driven representation structure. Prior findings cited: removing leading components can improve downstream embedding performance (Mu et al., 2018); leading-component projections used as a probing baseline (Kantamneni et al., 2025). Problem framed as selecting dimensions that permit generalization vs. spurious source-trained classification. Pipeline (Fig.1): projection into source N4D basis, filtering candidate Q7 directions, probe training in selected low-dimensional subspace.

Goal: probe OOD robustness largely determined by subspace selection; pipeline projects activations into a source data-driven basis (source N4D / Q7 coordinates), filters candidate directions, and trains probes in the selected low-dim subspace. Prior findings: removing leading components can improve downstream embedding performance; leading-component projections used as a baseline. Related work summarized here: (1) Linear concept directions: studies report cross-dataset linear structure for true/false and other behaviors (Marks & Tegmark 2024; Park et al. 2024 formalize the linear representation hypothesis). Single directions reported for refusal and an “assistant” axis (Arditi et al. 2024; Lu et al. 2026); other work finds population-level directions for honesty/emotion (Zou et al. 2025). (2) Linear probes limits: probes can learn task/surface correlates rather than reveal intrinsic representation; encoded vs. recoverable information distinction; strong in-distribution probes often generalize unevenly—safety evaluation must separate robust internal signals from dataset artifacts. (3) Interpreting features with natural-language explanations: LLM-generated neuron explanations from high-activation examples (Bills et al. 2023), automated sparse-autoencoder feature labeling (Paulo et al. 2025; Bricken et al. 2023), and concept identification + ablation during fine-tuning (Casademunt et al. 2025).

Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6). Use layer-15 residual-stream activations (per Ying et al. 2026); activations averaged over assistant-response tokens. Data: four Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025) datasets — one source (Roleplaying: V8) and three held-out targets: Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), Sandbagging (J9). Only Roleplaying used as source. Labels: annotated by GPT-4o (K8, OpenAI 2024) with mapping honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous responses removed (binary honest vs deceptive). Preprocessing: source activations standardized to zero mean, unit variance; same source statistics used to standardize targets. Dimensionality reduction: PCA on source (N4D), retain leading 100 principal components (PCs Q7); probes trained on projections to subset S of these PCs. Classifiers: logistic regression (regularization λ=10) for all classifiers; comparator (full-representation baseline B8Q) trains on all standardized activations (no PCA). Choice of 100 PCs driven by interpretability comparability (alignment with U9/Bricken et al. 2023 decreases with PC index, so lower-index PCs are easier to interpret), not because low-index PCs generalize best. Error bars denote 95% confidence intervals.

Experiments evaluate transfer of deception probes (metric: target F3, 5-fold CV). High-level: W6 transfer (source->target) reasonably good, C2R moderate, J9 poor. However, target-trained classifiers (trained on target labels) within the retained 100-source-PC subspace separate honest vs deceptive on every target, so relevant signal exists though the single source-trained direction often fails to generalize. Probes: logistic regression (λ=10) trained on source projections; comparator B8Q = source-trained on full standardized activations (no PCA). PCA: 100 leading source PCs (Q7). Selection/search (greedy oracle H2): start empty, consider each of 100 PCs, project source activations, fit source logistic weights, add the PC that most improves target F3 (target labels drive subset selection only; probe weights always fit on source). Stopping threshold: no candidate improvement >0.001. Note: CV selection vs full-target H2 (stable set & k) can give slightly different numbers. Ranking methods: T6 (source-PCA probe ranking) and M9 (target-PCA probe ranking) use magnitude measure X4 = |probe coeff| * PC standard deviation (on source-projected activations) to order PCs; neither ranking recovers the transferable subspace or beats B8Q; T6 ≈ B8Q, M9 does well on C2R, worse on W6, below random on J9. Variance-based selection (Y4) matches H2 only on easy W6, falls far behind on C2R and J9 (explained variance does not predict usefulness). Interpretation: LLM judge C7 gets top-8 and bottom-8 activating source examples per PC, writes pos/neg/whole descriptions and assigns OOD generalization score R5; directions reaching observed maxima in both scoring runs are retained. Language-only interp-selection (L2) — intersection of retained directions across runs — (trained as source probe) reduces deceptive behavior across targets, exceeds B8Q and Y4 (widely on C2R/J9) and outperforms A7 (interp-ablated complement); W6 has little headroom and is uninformative.

Experiments evaluate transfer of deception probes (metric: target F3, 5-fold CV) for a single model / single-source. Probes: logistic regression (λ=10) trained on source projections after PCA (100 leading source PCs). Comparator B8Q: source-trained on full standardized activations (no PCA). Greedy oracle selection H2: start empty, consider each of 100 PCs, project source activations, fit source logistic weights, add PC that most improves target F3 (selection uses target labels; probe weights always fit on source); stop when no candidate improvement >0.001. Ranking methods T6/M9 use X4 = |probe coeff| * PC std; neither recovers transferable subspace or beats B8Q: T6 ≈ B8Q; M9 helps C2R, hurts W6, below random on J9. Variance-based Y4 matches H2 only on easy W6, fails on C2R/J9. High-level results: W6 transfer reasonably good but has very high baseline (little headroom/uninformative); C2R shows moderate/robust improvement; J9 is weakest/most OOD with modest improvement likely due to distribution shift. However, target-trained classifiers within the retained 100-source-PC subspace separate honest vs deceptive on every target (signal exists), yet single source-trained directions often fail to generalize. Interpretation: LLM judge C7 labels top-8/bottom-8 activating source examples per PC and assigns OOD generalization scores; retained directions are those with maxima across runs. Language-only interp-selection L2 (intersection across runs) as a source probe reduces deceptive behavior across targets and outperforms B8Q, Y4 and A7 on C2R/J9; W6 remains uninformative. Limitations noted: single-model/single-source scope, fully linear pipeline (N4D projection + logistic regression), interpretive descriptions are descriptive not causal, and high-rated directions were not ablated during inference; nonlinear probes/readout locations untested.

Experiments probe transfer of deception classifiers using target F3 (5-fold CV) for a single model / single-source. Source probes are logistic regression (L2 λ=10) fit on source activations projected to the top 100 source PCs (PCA). Comparator B8Q trains on full standardized activations (no PCA). Greedy oracle H2: start empty, evaluate each of 100 PCs by projecting source activations, fit source logistic weights, add the PC that most improves target F3 (uses target labels); stop when no candidate gives improvement >0.001. Two ranking methods (T6/M9) use X4 = |probe coeff| * PC std; neither reliably recovers transferable subspace or beats B8Q (T6 ≈ B8Q; M9 helps C2R, hurts W6, below random on J9). Variance-based Y4 matches H2 only on easy W6, fails on C2R/J9. Across targets: W6 shows reasonable transfer but very high baseline/uninformative; C2R shows moderate, robust improvement; J9 is most OOD with weakest transfer. Target-trained classifiers within the retained 100-source-PC subspace separate honest vs deceptive on every target (signal exists), yet single source-trained directions often fail to generalize. LLM judge C7 labels top-8/bottom-8 activating source examples per PC to score OOD generalization; retained directions are maxima across runs. Language-only intersection selection L2 (across runs) as a source probe reduces deceptive behavior across targets and outperforms B8Q, Y4 and A7 on C2R/J9; W6 remains uninformative. Limitations: single-model/single-source scope, fully linear pipeline (PCA projection + logistic probe), interpretive descriptions not causal, and no ablation of high-rated directions or nonlinear probes/readout tests. Conclusion: OOD probing requires representation selection (find robust linear loci), since full-representation probes can mix spurious surface cues while sparse directional subspaces may isolate general behavioral structure.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars.
Goal: Can selecting principal components (PCs), i.e., directions in a source activation basis, improve out-of-distribution (OOD) deception detection?
Method overview: Train linear probes (logistic regression) on one source dataset; evaluate on 3 held-out target datasets. Use a target-supervised greedy search that adds PCs according to target performance. Also evaluate ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights. Introduce an LLM judge that scores natural-language PC descriptions without using target data.
Key quantitative claims/results: Greedy, target-supervised search finds 8–15 PCs that nearly match probes trained on target data. Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights does not recover this transferable subspace. Selecting 19 PCs that receive the maximum observed LLM score in both runs (unsupervised by target data) improves transfer on all 3 targets. For two of the targets, this selection closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and the greedy oracle. 
Other terms to track: "full-representation baseline", "greedy oracle", "both runs" (unspecified here), which targets achieve 78% and 25% (unspecified here).

Paper: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Goal: improve cross-domain (source->target) deception detection by selecting source-PC directions. Source domain = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (activations extracted; token activations averaged over assistant response to form probe inputs). Labels: GPT-4o assigns Deceptive=1, Honest=0, Ambiguous=-1 (ambiguous examples removed). Representation & PCA: source activations are standardized (source -> zero mean, unit variance) and PCA applied; source statistics are applied to target activations; 100 source PCs retained (S subset of these). Probes: all linear (logistic regression, regularization parameter λ=10); baseline = source-trained probe on full standardized activations; target-trained probes fit on target data. Selection methods: greedy oracle = target-guided greedy adding the PC that most increases target AUROC (reported to find ~8–15 PCs that nearly match target-trained probes); variance control = top-k PCs by variance; source-PCA probe and target-PCA probe use standardized coefficients to rank PCs (standardized coefficient = |coefficient| * PC standard deviation). LLM judge: GPT-5-mini interprets PC positive/negative poles and rates OOD-deception usefulness on a 1–10 scale; observed maximum OOD score = 6. Interp-selection = 19 PCs that received the maximum observed score (6) in both scoring runs; interp-ablated PCs = remaining 81. Evaluation: 5-fold CV on targets (held-out folds used for testing); AUROC reported with 95% CI. Causal validation (intervention/ablation at inference) was not performed. Appendix C: SAE decoder alignment (resource andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct); statistics reported include Spearman ρ and Jaccard overlap.

Main empirical claims to verify later: small transferable subspace exists (greedy finds ≈8–15 PCs where source-trained ≈ target-trained); ranking PCs by source/target probe weights fails; LLM judge can partly recover transferable PCs without target data (judge-selected=19 PCs; reported gap recovery 78% for Insider Trading Report and 25% for Sandbagging). Key results in this part:
- Full-representation source-trained AUROC (target eval): Insider Trading Confirm 0.874, Insider Trading Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606.
- Target-trained probes on the 100-PC subspace achieve AUROCs 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869 (reported across the three targets).
- Conclusion: 100-PC subspace contains enough target-class information; limited transfer is due to source-learned direction, not missing info.
- Greedy (oracle) PC-selection: searches top-100 PCs, at each step adds PC that most improves target AUROC (probe weights always fit on source; selection uses labeled non-held-out target folds in 5-fold CV); stop when improvement <0.001.
- Greedy average subset sizes: Report 15 PCs, Confirm 8 PCs, Sandbagging 14 PCs.
- Greedy improves baseline AUROC by +0.22 (Report) and +0.23 (Sandbagging), coming close to target-trained performance; variance-ranked k control matches greedy only on Confirm and falls far behind on Report and Sandbagging.
- Section 4.3 initial claim: neither source- nor target-probe coefficient rankings recover greedy transfer performance.

This part: defines standardized coefficient = |probe coeff| * PC std; two rankings: source-PCA (weights from source) and target-PCA (weights from target), both over activations in the source-PCA basis. To pick k for transfer comparisons they run greedy on the full target dataset (not per-fold), yielding k = 13 (Report), 7 (Confirm), 14 (Sandbagging) — noted as differing slightly from Section 4.2 numbers. Results: both source- and target-weight rankings fail to recover greedy transfer. Source-PCA ranking transfers about like the full-representation baseline; target-PCA ranking does well on Report, worse than greedy on Confirm, and below random on Sandbagging. Jaccard overlaps between greedy and target-ranked sets = 0.182 / 0.077 / 0.167.
Interpretability: for each of the top 100 PCs, collect 8 most/least activating examples; LLM describes poles; a judge assigns OOD score 1–10 (max observed = 6). Repeated scoring retains PCs scoring 6 in both runs, producing 19 interp-selected PCs. Five PCs are selected by greedy for >1 target; 3 of those 5 have score 6. Comparison claims reference PCs such as PC62, PC57, PC86, etc. Section 4.5 compares probes trained on the 19 interp-selected PCs vs controls (full, top-19 by variance, remaining 81).

Paper question: whether selecting subspaces of LM representations improves out-of-distribution (OOD) deception detection. Method: compare probes (classifiers) trained on full representations vs probes using selected directions/subspaces. Two selection approaches highlighted: (1) target-guided selection that uses target labels but does not fit probe weights on them; (2) interpretation-based selection using natural-language interpretations, which requires no target data. Key claims: small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes; selecting directions by source weights, target-class separation, or explained variance does not recover the same transferable subspaces; interpretation-based selection improves over the full-representation baseline on all targets, though how well it recovers varies sharply across targets. Scope/caveats: study uses one model and one source dataset; interpretations are descriptive, not causal. The paper includes a "Glossary." (no glossary content shown in this part).

Goal: test whether selecting subspaces of LM representations improves OOD (transfer) deception detection. Source dataset: Roleplaying (V8). Targets include C2R (Insider Trading Report), W6 (Insider Trading Confirm), J9 (Sandbagging). Model & readout: layer-15 residual-stream activations from Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6), averaged over assistant-response tokens. Preprocessing: standardization = zero-mean/unit-variance using source statistics applied to both source and targets. Dimensionality reduction: PCA / N4D retains the leading 100 source directions (Q7); "PCs" refer to these retained source directions; "leading" = lower index. Goal: test whether selecting subspaces of LM representations (leading PCA directions) improves OOD (transfer) deception detection. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6); use layer-15 residual-stream activations, averaged over assistant-response tokens. Datasets: Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025) collection — one source Roleplaying (V8) and three held-out targets: Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), Sandbagging (J9). Labeling: GPT-4o (K8) maps honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous responses removed. Preprocessing: source activations standardized to zero-mean/unit-variance; same source statistics applied to targets. Dimensionality reduction: PCA (N4D) on source; retain leading 100 PCs (Q7). Activations may be projected to a subset S of these directions before training/eval. All classifiers are logistic regression (λ=10); full-representation baseline (B8Q) trains on all standardized activations (no PCA truncation). Evaluation: AUROC with 95% CIs; earlier notes indicate 5-fold CV where direction selection uses non-held-out target folds and evaluation uses held-out fold. Interpretability: retained-100 chosen for comparability (not because low-index PCs generalize better); alignment with sparse-autoencoder decoder vectors U9 decreases with index, so lower indices are more interpretable. Interpretation pipeline: explanations generated by P2 (GPT-5-mini), rated by C7 producing R5; L2 = interp-selected PC probe (max R5), A7 = interp-ablated PC probe (complement). Goal: evaluate whether source-trained leading-100 PCA subspace (Q7) contains transferable deception signal and whether small source-trained subsets (H2) can match target-trained performance. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; layer-15 residual stream, assistant-response-token-averaged activations; source standardized and same stats applied to targets. Classifiers: logistic regression (λ=10). Metric: AUROC (F3) with 5-fold CV; target-5-fold CV: directions selected on non-held-out target folds, evaluate on held-out fold; search stops when no candidate improves target F3 by >0.001. Retained 100 PCs used for comparisons.

Key reported numbers (Appendix A): B8Q (full-representation) F3: W6=0.874, C2R=0.706, J9=0.606. Target-trained (within retained-100) F3 (5-fold CV): C2R=0.936, W6=0.950, J9=0.869. H2 (target-guided greedy source-trained subset) mean sizes (target CV): C2R=15, W6=8, J9=14; full-target H2 k: C2R=13, W6=7, J9=14. H2 F3 (used for recovery comparison): C2R=0.929, J9=0.832; H2 improvements over B8Q: +0.22 (C2R), +0.23 (J9). Target-trained F3 for corresponding rows: 0.936 (C2R), 0.869 (J9). Variance-selection (Y4) matches H2 only on W6, falls behind on C2R/J9. Rankings: T6 (source-PCA ranking) performs about like B8Q; M9 (target-side ranking using standardized coefficient X4 = |coef|*PC_std) does well on C2R, worse than H2 on W6, and reportedly below random on J9. Interpretability: H2-selected directions have higher-level contrasts that partially transfer; L2 and A7 probes used in interpretation pipeline. Figures: Fig2 (source-trained full, source-trained leading100, target-trained leading100), Fig3 (B8Q, Y4, H2), Fig4 (T6, M9, H2).

Interpretation pipeline: for each leading source PC an LLM judge (C7) sees the 8 most- and 8 least-activating source examples, produces positive/negative/whole-direction descriptions, and assigns an OOD/generalization rating R5. Two noisy scoring runs; selection retains directions that reach the observed maximum in both runs (max R5=6). Appendix E: 19 directions reached max in both runs; these 19 define L2 (interp-selected subset). Complement (A7) has 81 directions (19+81=100 retained PCs). Y4 is an equal-dimensional (19) variance-ranked control. All three (L2, A7, Y4) are trained as source probes (no target data). H2 interpretation notes: Q7 62, 57, 86 have R5=6; Q7 9 and 81 have R5=3. Among shared H2 selections, 3/5 are maximum-rated; among top T6 selections, 1/5 is maximum-rated. Main claims: L2 (19 PCs) improves over B8Q on C2R and J9 (Appendix A: L2 F3: C2R=0.881 vs B8Q=0.706; J9=0.662 vs B8Q=0.606). L2 recovers 78% of the baseline–H2 gap on C2R and 25% on J9. Authors claim L2 exceeds B8Q, Y4, and A7 on all targets; W6 has little headroom and methods (except A7) are roughly tied. Figure 5 plots target F3: L2 (red), B8Q (blue), Y4 at L2 dimension count (teal), A7 (brown). Scores noted as noisy; selection requires agreement across runs.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Study: generalization of linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations across 3 held-out deception detection datasets (only two named here: Insider Trading Report, Sandbagging). Main findings: projecting inputs onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) from the training activation distribution enables cross-domain transfer that nearly matches probes trained on the target/test distribution. PC interpretations can identify transferable PCs: an LLM judge scores each PC by whether its most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; probing on top-scoring PCs substantially improves transfer. Quantified results: this method closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and by 25% on Sandbagging. Interpretation claim: source probe-weighted directions reflect source-specific surface features causing deceptive responses, while transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and are capturable by natural language descriptions. Conclusion: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Task: deception detection using linear probes. Source dataset: Roleplaying deception scenarios. Held-out target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Method: project source activations into the source-domain PCA basis; select a small subset of PCs and train linear probes on that low-dimensional subspace (Figure 1). Key claims/findings: (1) A small transferable subspace exists (Section 4.2): a target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds ~8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe. (2) Source-side and target-side rankings fail to recover this subspace (Section 4.3): ranking PCs by source or target probe weights does not outperform the full-representation baseline. (3) An LLM judge can partially recover the subspace without target data (Section 4.5): it scores PCs by whether their most/least activating examples indicate transferable behavioral contrast rather than surface patterns. Earlier-summary quantitative results (from prior part): method closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Purpose: study which PC subsets avoid spurious correlations and transfer to target domains.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Task: deception detection via linear probes. Source data: roleplaying deception scenarios. Held-out target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Method: compute PCA on source activations, project source activations to source PCA basis, select a small subset of source PCs, and train linear probes on that low-dimensional subspace. Selection strategies include a target-supervised greedy search and a zero-target LLM-based judge that scores PCs by natural-language interpretation of high/low-activation examples. Key findings: (1) A small transferable subspace exists — greedy search finds ~8–15 PCs where a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe. (2) Source-side and target-side rankings (e.g., ranking PCs by probe weights) fail to recover this subspace and do not outperform the full-representation baseline. (3) An LLM judge can partially recover the subspace without target data by preferring PCs whose example sets reflect transferable behavioral contrasts rather than surface patterns. Quantitative: method closes baseline-to-oracle gap by ~78% on Insider Trading Report and ~25% on Sandbagging. Related work: literature on linear concept directions (Marks & Tegmark 2024; Park 2024; Zou 2025), single-direction behavior mediation (Arditi 2024; Lu 2026), limits of probing and OOD generalization concerns (Hewitt & Liang 2019; Ravichander 2021; recent work on probe OOD failure), and LLM-based natural-language interpretation of neurons/features (Bills 2023; Paulo 2025; Bricken 2023; Casademunt 2025).

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Task: deception detection via linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Datasets: 4 sets from Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025): Roleplaying (source), Insider Trading Report (target), Insider Trading Confirm (target), Sandbagging (target). Labels: GPT-4o labels {honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1}; ambiguous examples removed. Model/activations: layer 15 residual stream of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; token activations averaged over assistant response. Preprocessing: standardize source activations to zero mean/unit variance; apply same source statistics to standardize targets. PCA: run PCA on scaled source activations, retain top 100 PCs. Probes: logistic regression (lambda=10); for subset S of PCs, project activations onto S before training/eval; baseline probes train on full standardized activations. Motivation for 100 PCs: alignment with SAE decoder features declines with PC index (App. C), so lower-index PCs are more interpretable; not claiming low-index PCs generalize better—Section 4.1 reportedly confirms 100-PC subspace retains enough info to separate deceptive vs honest on each target. Methods (from earlier parts): source-side greedy search (target-supervised) and zero-target LLM judge for PC selection; key results: small transferable subspace (~8–15 PCs) found by greedy search; LLM judge partially recovers it; quantitative gap closures: ~78% (Insider Trading Report), ~25% (Sandbagging).

Dataset/order: Insider Trading Confirm, Insider Trading Report, Sandbagging. Baselines (source-trained on full representations → AUROC on target): Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probe (trained on target data within source top-100 PC subspace, 5-fold CV) achieves 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869 AUROC across the three targets (order implied same as above), indicating the top-100 source-PC subspace contains sufficient signal. Conclusion: poor transfer of source-trained probe is not due to missing information but to learned source direction not generalizing. Greedy PC-selection (oracle) procedure: start empty, iteratively consider adding one of top-100 source PCs that most increases AUROC on the target; for each candidate, project source activations onto current subset and fit logistic regression on source; selection is guided by target labeled folds via 5-fold CV (selection on non-held-out folds, evaluate on held-out fold). Stop when no candidate improves AUROC by >0.001. Average greedy subset sizes: Report 15 PCs, Confirm 8 PCs, Sandbagging 14 PCs. Greedy improves over baseline by +0.22 AUROC (Report) and +0.23 AUROC (Sandbagging), coming close to target-trained performance (greedy is an upper bound since it uses target labels for selection). Comparison: selecting top-k PCs by variance (k matched to greedy) matches greedy only for Confirm; for Report and Sandbagging variance-ranking underperforms, so variance explained is not predictive of transfer usefulness. Section 4.3 sets up two hypotheses for what makes PCs transferable: (1) PCs that individually separate target classes well, (2) PCs the source probe heavily weights. They evaluate rankings based on the standardized coefficient per PC = |probe coefficient| * stddev(PC), computed from probes trained on activations projected to the source-PCA basis (separately for source-trained and target-trained probes as appropriate).

final_notes:
Paper: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD deception detection. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; representation = layer-15 residual stream averaged over assistant-response tokens. Source dataset: Roleplaying (V8). Targets: C2R, W6, J9. Labels from GPT-4o (honest=0, ambiguous=-1; Appendix Table 1 shows some -1 counts). Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars.
Goal: Can selecting principal components (PCs), i.e., directions in a source activation basis, improve out-of-distribution (OOD) deception detection?
Method overview: Train linear probes (logistic regression) on one source dataset; evaluate on 3 held-out target datasets. Use a target-supervised greedy search that adds PCs according to target performance. Also evaluate ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights. Introduce an LLM judge that scores natural-language PC descriptions without using target data.
Key quantitative claims/results: Greedy, target-supervised search finds 8–15 PCs that nearly match probes trained on target data. Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights does not recover this transferable subspace. Selecting 19 PCs that receive the maximum observed LLM score in both runs (unsupervised by target data) improves transfer on all 3 targets. For two of the targets, this selection closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and the greedy oracle. 
Other terms to track: "full-representation baseline", "greedy oracle", "both runs" (unspecified here), which targets achieve 78% and 25% (unspecified here).

Paper: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Goal: improve cross-domain (source->target) deception detection by selecting source-PC directions. Source domain = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (activations extracted; token activations averaged over assistant response to form probe inputs). Labels: GPT-4o assigns Deceptive=1, Honest=0, Ambiguous=-1 (ambiguous examples removed). Representation & PCA: source activations are standardized (source -> zero mean, unit variance) and PCA applied; source statistics are applied to target activations; 100 source PCs retained (S subset of these). Probes: all linear (logistic regression, regularization parameter λ=10); baseline = source-trained probe on full standardized activations; target-trained probes fit on target data. Selection methods: greedy oracle = target-guided greedy adding the PC that most increases target AUROC (reported to find ~8–15 PCs that nearly match target-trained probes); variance control = top-k PCs by variance; source-PCA probe and target-PCA probe use standardized coefficients to rank PCs (standardized coefficient = |coefficient| * PC standard deviation). LLM judge: GPT-5-mini interprets PC positive/negative poles and rates OOD-deception usefulness on a 1–10 scale; observed maximum OOD score = 6. Interp-selection = 19 PCs that received the maximum observed score (6) in both scoring runs; interp-ablated PCs = remaining 81. Evaluation: 5-fold CV on targets (held-out folds used for testing); AUROC reported with 95% CI. Causal validation (intervention/ablation at inference) was not performed. Greedy (oracle) selection: target-guided greedy adding PCs to maximize target AUROC; reported to need ~8–15 PCs (paper states greedy selection numbers 15 / 8 / 14 across the three targets). Interpretation-based probing purportedly closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Abstract/claims reiterate that a small source-PC subspace enables transfer and that PC interpretations (via LLM judge) partly identify that subspace. This part also supplies a PC code table listing 58 PC indices (PC1,PC2,...PC97 — nonconsecutive), used to identify source-PCA directions discussed elsewhere. No contradictions found between this part and prior notes.

Study setup: source = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Responses labeled by GPT-4o as honest (0), ambiguous (-1), deceptive (1); ambiguous responses removed. Model & activations: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; use layer-15 residual-stream activations, averaged over tokens in the assistant's response. Preprocessing: standardize source activations to zero mean/unit variance; apply same source mean/scale to target activations. PCA: run on scaled source activations; retain top 100 source PCs. Probes: logistic-regression (linear) probes with regularization λ=10. PC-based probes train/evaluate on projections onto subsets S of the top-100 PCs. Baseline probes train on the full standardized activations (full representation). Motivation for 100 PCs: alignment with SAE decoder features decreases with PC index (Appendix C), so low-index PCs are easier to interpret; authors explicitly do not claim low-index PCs generalize better. Section 4.1 will test that the 100-PC subspace retains enough information to separate deceptive vs honest on each target. (From earlier parts: greedy/oracle search finds small transferable subspaces (counts reported 15 / 8 / 14); weight-based rankings fail; LLM judge rates PC poles up to score 6; interpretation-driven selection used 19 PCs scoring 6 in both runs and recovers substantial fraction of baseline→oracle gap for some targets.)

Setup recap: source=Roleplaying; targets={Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging}. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; use layer-15 residual-stream activations averaged over assistant response tokens. Preproc: standardize source activations (zero mean, unit var); apply same source mean/scale to target activations. PCA on scaled source activations; keep top 100 source PCs. Key results (Part 4): Full-representation source-trained probe AUROCs: Confirm=0.874, Report=0.706, Sandbagging=0.606. Target-trained probes trained within the top-100 source-PC subspace (5-fold CV) achieve high AUROCs: 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869 (per-target; mapping implied by context: Report≈0.936, Confirm≈0.950, Sandbagging≈0.869). Thus the 100-PC subspace contains enough target-class information; poor source→target transfer is due to the source-learned direction.

Greedy oracle selection: iteratively add PCs (from top 100) that most improve target AUROC (probe weights always fit on source; selection uses non-held-out target folds in 5-fold CV; evaluate on held-out fold). Stop if no PC improves AUROC >0.001. Mean subset sizes: Report=15, Confirm=8, Sandbagging=14. Greedy improves baseline AUROC by +0.22 (Report) and +0.23 (Sandbagging), coming close to target-trained probes; variance-based top-k control matches greedy only on Confirm.

Next (4.3): test whether transferable PCs are those that individually separate target classes or those heavily used by the source probe (weight-based rankings).

PC-ranking comparison: rank PCs by standardized coefficient = |probe_coef| * PC_std, computed in source-PCA basis. Two rankings: source-PCA (weights from source probe) and target-PCA (weights from target probe). For each ranking, evaluate transfer by training probes on source data projected onto the top-k PCs in that ranking.
Greedy-on-full-data k (stable sets): Report k=13, Confirm k=7, Sandbagging k=14 (differs slightly from fold-wise means earlier: Report=15, Confirm=8, Sandbagging=14). If a ranking matched the transferable subspace, selecting its top-k should recover greedy performance.
Results: Neither ranking recovers greedy. Source-PCA selection transfers about as well as the full-representation source baseline (i.e., source-weighted PCs do not generalize). Target-PCA selection: does well on Report, worse than greedy on Confirm, and below random on Sandbagging. Jaccard overlap between greedy and target-ranked sets: 0.182 / 0.077 / 0.167 (Report/Confirm/Sandbagging).
Interpretability: For each top-100 source PC, take 8 most- and 8 least-activating source examples; LLM describes poles and contrast; judge assigns OOD score 1–10. Max observed score = 6 (no PC >6). Score twice and keep PCs scoring 6 in both runs => 19 interp-selected PCs. 5 PCs were selected by greedy for >1 target; 3 of those 5 have score 6 (PC62, PC57, PC86). Only 1 of the top-5 source-probe PCs got score 6 (PC4; others PC7/PC8/PC11/PC12 scored 3/4/3/3).
Section 4.5: interp-selected 19-PC subspace compared (Fig 5) to controls: full-rep baseline, top-19 by variance, and interp-ablated (remaining 81). Error bars are 95% CIs. Previous baseline/target AUROCs: source baseline Confirm=0.874, Report=0.706, Sandbagging=0.606; target-trained (within 100 PCs) ≈0.936/0.950/0.869.

Paper question: whether selecting subspaces of LM representations improves out-of-distribution (OOD) deception detection. Method: compare probes (classifiers) trained on full representations vs probes using selected directions/subspaces. Two selection approaches highlighted: (1) target-guided selection that uses target labels but does not fit probe weights on them; (2) interpretation-based selection using natural-language interpretations, which requires no target data. Key claims: small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes; selecting directions by source weights, target-class separation, or explained variance does not recover the same transferable subspaces; interpretation-based selection improves over the full-representation baseline on all targets, though how well it recovers varies sharply across targets. Scope/caveats: study uses one model and one source dataset; interpretations are descriptive, not causal. The paper includes a "Glossary." (no glossary content shown in this part).

Goal: test whether selecting subspaces of LM representations improves OOD (transfer) deception detection. Source dataset: Roleplaying (V8). Targets include C2R (Insider Trading Report), W6 (Insider Trading Confirm), J9 (Sandbagging). Model & readout: layer-15 residual-stream activations from Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6), averaged over assistant-response tokens. Preprocessing: standardization = zero-mean/unit-variance using source statistics applied to both source and targets. Dimensionality reduction: PCA / N4D retains the leading 100 source directions (Q7); "PCs" refer to these retained source directions; "leading" = lower index. Probes: logistic regression with λ=10, evaluated by AUROC (F3) with 95% CIs; 5-fold CV where selection uses non-held-out target folds and evaluation uses the held-out fold. Baselines & methods: B8Q = full-representation baseline (source-trained on all standardized activations); Y4 = top-k PCs by variance (variance-ranked subset matched in dimension count); H2 = greedy oracle (target-guided direction selection but probe weights fitted only on source); T6 = source-PCA probe (supplies source coefficient rankings); M9 = target-PCA probe (supplies target coefficient rankings); X4 = standardized coefficient = |coef| * PC_std. Interpretation-based selection: natural-language explanations produced with P2 (GPT-5-mini) and rated by C7 (LLM judge) yielding R5 (OOD score/generalization rating); L2 = interp-selected PC probe (uses directions reaching max R5 in both scoring runs); A7 = interp-ablated PC probe (complement). Decoder alignment uses SAE (U9) decoder features (resource: andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct); Spearman ρ reports relation of PC index to decoder alignment. Scope: one model, one source dataset; interpretations are descriptive, not causal.

Goal: test whether selecting subspaces of LM representations improves OOD (transfer) deception detection. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6), layer-15 residual-stream activations averaged over assistant-response tokens (layer chosen per Ying et al. 2026). Datasets: Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025) — source: Roleplaying (V8); targets: Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), Sandbagging (J9).
