Paper title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Setup: use linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations to detect deception behaviors; evaluate generalization across 3 held-out deception detection datasets (only two named here: Insider Trading Report and Sandbagging). Key claim: projecting inputs onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) from the training activation distribution enables cross-domain transfer that nearly matches probes trained on the target/test distribution. Method extension: interpret PCs and use an LLM judge to score each PC by whether its most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; then probe using top-scoring PCs. Results: this PC-selection method closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and by 25% on Sandbagging. Interpretation claim: source-probe-weighted directions encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and in ways capturable by natural language descriptions. Broad claim: OOD robustness of probes largely determined by subspace selection. Venue noted: Machine Learning, ICML.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Setup: train linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations (source dataset: Roleplaying deception scenarios); evaluate OOD on three held-out target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Core idea: work in the source-domain PCA basis and select a small subset of source PCs to train probes that avoid spurious surface correlations and transfer to targets. Key empirical claims: (1) A small transferable subspace exists (Sec. 4.2): a target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds ~8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe. (2) Source-side and target-side weight-based rankings fail to recover this subspace (Sec. 4.3): ranking PCs by source or target probe weights does not outperform the full-representation baseline. (3) An LLM judge can partially recover the subspace without target labels (Sec. 4.5): it interprets PCs via their extreme examples and selects transferable PCs. Prior-note results: PC-selection method closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Interpretation claim: transferable directions encode more abstract contrasts describable in language; probe OOD robustness largely determined by subspace selection. Figure 1 outlines pipeline: project activations into source PCA basis, filter candidate PCs, train probes on selected low-dim subspace.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Setup: train linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations using a source dataset of roleplaying deception scenarios; evaluate OOD on three held-out target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Method: compute PCA on source activations, work in source PCA basis, filter candidate PCs, and select a small subset of source PCs to train linear probes on the low-dimensional subspace. Key empirical claims: (1) A small transferable subspace exists: target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds ~8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe (Sec. 4.2). (2) Weight-based rankings on source or target probes fail to recover this subspace and do not outperform full-representation baseline (Sec. 4.3). (3) An LLM judge can partially recover the subspace without target labels by interpreting PCs via extreme examples and selecting transferable PCs (Sec. 4.5). Reported quantitative impact: PC-selection method closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Context from related work: literature reports linear/low-dim directions for high-level properties and behaviors, examples of single-direction control (refusal/assistant axis), skepticism about probes (probe may learn task/exploit surface correlates; OOD probe generalization can be uneven), and use of LLMs to generate natural-language explanations of features and to inform interventions.

Datasets: Roleplaying is the source; targets are Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Each response labeled by GPT-4o as honest (0), ambiguous (-1), or deceptive (1); ambiguous examples removed. Language model activations: layer-15 residual stream of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; token activations averaged over the assistant response. Preprocessing: standardize source activations (zero mean, unit variance) and apply the same source statistics to standardize target activations. PCA: run PCA on the scaled source activations and retain the top 100 PCs. Probes: logistic regression (regularization λ=10). For experiments using a subset S of PCs, project activations onto S before training/evaluation; baseline probes train on the full standardized activations. Motivation for 100 PCs: lower-index PCs align more with SAE decoder features (Appendix C) and are easier to interpret, but authors do not claim low-index PCs inherently generalize better; Section 4.1 reportedly shows the 100-PC subspace suffices to separate deceptive vs. honest on every target.

Datasets: source = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Confirm, Insider Trading Report, Sandbagging. Responses labeled honest (0), ambiguous (-1), deceptive (1); ambiguous examples removed. Model activations: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer-15 residual stream; token activations averaged over assistant response. Preprocessing: standardize source activations (zero mean, unit variance) and apply same source statistics to standardize target activations. PCA: run PCA on scaled source activations and retain top 100 PCs. Probes: logistic regression (λ=10). Baselines: probes trained on full standardized representations; for PC-subset experiments project activations onto subset before training/evaluation.

Key results (Section 4.1): source-trained probe (full rep) AUROC on targets: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Probe trained on target data within top-100 source PCs (5-fold CV) achieves AUROC ≈ 0.936 (Confirm) / 0.950 (Report) / 0.869 (Sandbagging) — so 100-PC subspace suffices to separate classes on every target.

Greedy PC-selection (Section 4.2): start empty, iteratively add from top-100 PCs the PC that most improves AUROC on target; to evaluate a candidate, project source activations onto current subset and train probe on source projections; PC choice guided by target labeled folds (5-fold CV) while probe weights always fit on source; stop when AUROC improvement ≤0.001. Avg subset sizes: Report 15 PCs, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14. Greedy improves over baseline (full-rep baseline) by ~+0.22 (Report) and +0.23 (Sandbagging) and approaches target-trained performance; top-k-by-variance matched greedy only for Confirm.

Section 4.3 tests two hypotheses for transferable PCs (separate target classes alone vs PCs source probe leans on). Compare rankings by standardized coefficient = |coef| * std(PC) from probes trained on activations projected to source-PCA basis (source-probe vs target-probe vs greedy oracle).

Datasets: source = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Confirm, Insider Trading Report, Sandbagging. Labels: honest(0), ambiguous(-1) (removed), deceptive(1). Representations: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer-15 residual stream; token activations averaged over assistant response; standardize using source mean/var and apply same stats to targets. PCA: run on scaled source activations, keep top 100 PCs. Probes: logistic regression (λ=10). Baselines: probes on full standardized representations; PC-subset experiments project activations onto chosen subset before training/eval. Key baseline numbers: source-trained probe (full rep) AUROC on targets: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probe on top-100 source PCs (5-fold CV) AUROC ≈ Confirm 0.936, Report 0.950, Sandbagging 0.869 (so 100-PC subspace suffices for target separation). Greedy PC-selection (target labels guide PC choice, probe weights fit on source; stop when AUROC improvement ≤0.001): CV average subset sizes Report 15, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14; greedy boosted AUROC over full-rep by ~+0.22 (Report) and +0.23 (Sandbagging); top-k-by-variance only matched greedy for Confirm. Cross-target ranking experiment (Sec 4.3): define source-PCA and target-PCA rankings (both use source-PCA basis); to pick k, run greedy on full target dataset (single k): Report k=13, Confirm k=7, Sandbagging k=14 (differs slightly from CV sizes). Results: both hypotheses fail — source-PCA probe transfers ~as well as full-rep baseline (i.e., doesn't generalize); target-PCA probe does well on Report, worse than greedy on Confirm, and below-random on Sandbagging. Interpretability (Sec 4.4): for each top-100 PC, collect 8 most/least activating examples and have an LLM judge describe poles and give 1–10 OOD scores; max observed score=6; keep PCs that scored 6 in both runs → 19 interp-selected PCs. Of 5 PCs that appeared in greedy selections for multiple targets, 3 had max OOD; only 1 of top-5 source-PCA PCs got max OOD. Sec 4.5 evaluates probe AUROC for interp-selected 19 PCs vs controls (full-rep, top-19 by variance, remaining 81). Figures and appendices provide full results.

Greedy PC-selection (labels on target guide PC choice; probe weights fit on source; stop when AUROC improvement ≤0.001): CV average subset sizes Report 15, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14; greedy boosted AUROC over full-rep by ~+0.22 (Report) and ~+0.23 (Sandbagging). Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Abstract claim: directions weighted by a source probe encode source-specific surface features; transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly (capturable in natural language). Main claim: probe OOD robustness largely determined by subspace selection. Background: linear probes expose semantic info but can fail OOD despite strong in-distribution performance. Assertion that behavioral concepts have linear representations but probes often learn spurious correlations; such unreliability is problematic for harmful-interaction monitoring. Method/approach keywords: work in source Q7 coordinates to avoid privileging model latent dims; these coordinates provide data-driven representation structure. Prior findings cited: removing leading components can improve downstream embedding performance (Mu et al., 2018); leading-component projections used as a probing baseline (Kantamneni et al., 2025). Problem framed as selecting dimensions that permit generalization vs. spurious source-trained classification. Pipeline (Fig.1): projection into source N4D basis, filtering candidate Q7 directions, probe training in selected low-dimensional subspace.

Goal: probe OOD robustness largely determined by subspace selection; pipeline projects activations into a source data-driven basis (source N4D / Q7 coordinates), filters candidate directions, and trains probes in the selected low-dim subspace. Prior findings: removing leading components can improve downstream embedding performance; leading-component projections used as a baseline. Related work summarized here: (1) Linear concept directions: studies report cross-dataset linear structure for true/false and other behaviors (Marks & Tegmark 2024; Park et al. 2024 formalize the linear representation hypothesis). Single directions reported for refusal and an “assistant” axis (Arditi et al. 2024; Lu et al. 2026); other work finds population-level directions for honesty/emotion (Zou et al. 2025). (2) Linear probes limits: probes can learn task/surface correlates rather than reveal intrinsic representation; encoded vs. recoverable information distinction; strong in-distribution probes often generalize unevenly—safety evaluation must separate robust internal signals from dataset artifacts. (3) Interpreting features with natural-language explanations: LLM-generated neuron explanations from high-activation examples (Bills et al. 2023), automated sparse-autoencoder feature labeling (Paulo et al. 2025; Bricken et al. 2023), and concept identification + ablation during fine-tuning (Casademunt et al. 2025).

Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6). Use layer-15 residual-stream activations (per Ying et al. 2026); activations averaged over assistant-response tokens. Data: four Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025) datasets — one source (Roleplaying: V8) and three held-out targets: Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), Sandbagging (J9). Only Roleplaying used as source. Labels: annotated by GPT-4o (K8, OpenAI 2024) with mapping honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous responses removed (binary honest vs deceptive). Preprocessing: source activations standardized to zero mean, unit variance; same source statistics used to standardize targets. Dimensionality reduction: PCA on source (N4D), retain leading 100 principal components (PCs Q7); probes trained on projections to subset S of these PCs. Classifiers: logistic regression (regularization λ=10) for all classifiers; comparator (full-representation baseline B8Q) trains on all standardized activations (no PCA). Choice of 100 PCs driven by interpretability comparability (alignment with U9/Bricken et al. 2023 decreases with PC index, so lower-index PCs are easier to interpret), not because low-index PCs generalize best. Error bars denote 95% confidence intervals.

Model/data: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6); layer-15 residual-stream activations averaged over assistant-response tokens. Datasets: source Roleplaying (V8); targets Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), Sandbagging (J9). Labels: GPT-4o annotations mapped honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous removed → binary. Preprocessing: source activations standardized (zero mean, unit variance); same source stats used to standardize targets. PCA on standardized source (N4D); retain leading 100 PCs (Q7). Probes: logistic regression (λ=10) on projections to subsets S of the 100 PCs; comparator B8Q trains on full standardized activations (no PCA). Metrics/CI: target F3 reported; 5-fold CV used for many evaluations; error bars = 95% CI.

Key experimental results/methods (Part 4): W6 transfer reasonably good, C2R moderate, J9 poor. Target-trained classifiers within the 100-PC source subspace separate classes on every target; the single source-trained direction fails to generalize. Greedy oracle search (H2) uses target labels to pick PCs: start empty, consider each of 100 PCs, fit source logistic weights on candidate subset, add PC that most improves target F3 (CV selection on non-held-out folds; stop if no candidate >0.001). Variance-ranked baseline (Y4) matches H2 only on easy W6; explained variance poorly predicts transfer utility. Ranking probes: source-PCA (T6) and target-PCA (M9) order PCs by standardized coefficient X4 = |coef| * PC std (on source-projected activations); evaluated probes are then trained on source projections to top-k. T6 ≈ B8Q; M9: good on C2R, worse than H2 on W6, below random on J9. Interpretation (C7): for each leading PC, LLM judge sees top-8 and bottom-8 source examples, writes pole/whole descriptions and assigns OOD score (R5). Interp-selected intersection (L2) = PCs reaching observed max in both scoring runs; A7 = its complement; Y4 also used as equal-dim control. L2 (language-only) improves over B8Q and A7, especially on C2R and J9.

Model/data: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6); layer-15 residual-stream activations averaged over assistant-response tokens. Source dataset: Roleplaying (V8). Targets: Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), Sandbagging (J9). Labels: GPT-4o annotations mapped honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous removed → binary. Preprocessing: source activations standardized (zero mean, unit variance); same source stats used to standardize targets. PCA on standardized source (N4D); retain leading 100 PCs. Probes: logistic regression (λ=10) on projections to subsets S of the 100 PCs; comparator B8Q: logistic regression on full standardized activations (no PCA). Metric: target F3; 5-fold CV; 95% CIs. Key results: target-trained classifiers within 100-PC source subspace separate classes on every target; a single source-trained direction fails to generalize. Transfer performance: W6 transfer reasonably good/easy (high baselines), C2R moderate, J9 poor and most OOD. Greedy oracle search (H2): uses target labels to pick PCs greedily, stop if best candidate improvement ≤0.001. Baselines: variance-ranked (Y4) matches H2 only on easy W6; explained variance poorly predicts transfer utility. Ranking probes: source-PCA (T6) ≈ B8Q; target-PCA (M9) orders by |coef|*PC std and is good on C2R, worse than H2 on W6, below random on J9. Interpretation (C7): for each leading PC, human judge sees top-8 and bottom-8 source examples, writes pole/whole descriptions and assigns OOD score. Interp-selected intersection (L2) = PCs reaching observed max in both scoring runs; A7 = complement; L2 (language-only) improves over B8Q and A7, especially on C2R and J9. Limitations (Part 5): single-model/single-source limits generality; W6’s high baseline reduces informativeness; J9 likely suffers distribution shift; pipeline is fully linear (N4D projection + logistic regression)—nonlinear probes and other readout locations not explored; interpretive claims are descriptive/correlational (no causal ablations of high-rated directions).

Targets: Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), Sandbagging (J9). Labels: GPT-4o annotations mapped honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous removed → binary. Preprocessing: source activations standardized (zero mean, unit variance); same source stats used to standardize targets. PCA on standardized source (N4D); retain leading 100 PCs. Probes: logistic regression (λ=10) on projections to subsets S of the 100 PCs; comparator B8Q: logistic regression on full standardized activations (no PCA). Metric: target F3; 5-fold CV; 95% CIs. Key results: target-trained classifiers within 100-PC source subspace separate classes on every target; a single source-trained direction fails to generalize. Transfer performance: W6 transfers well/high baseline, C2R moderate, J9 poor/most OOD. Greedy oracle search (H2) picks PCs using target labels greedily. Baselines: variance-ranked (Y4) matches H2 only on easy W6; explained variance poorly predicts transfer utility. Ranking probes: source-PCA (T6) ≈ B8Q; target-PCA (M9) (rank by |coef|*PC std) good on C2R, worse than H2 on W6, below random on J9. Interpretation: human judge inspects top/bottom source examples per PC, writes pole/whole descriptions and assigns OOD score. Interp-selected intersection (L2) = PCs reaching observed max in both scoring runs; A7 = complement; L2 (language-only) improves over B8Q and A7, especially on C2R and J9. Limitations: single-model/source, W6 high baseline, J9 distribution shift, pipeline fully linear, interpretations descriptive/correlational. Conclusion: OOD probing requires representation selection (not just classifier fitting); full-representation probes can mix spurious surface cues with general behavior and harm transfer; sparse directional subspaces can better isolate general behavioral structure.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars.
Goal: Can selecting principal components (PCs), i.e., directions in a source activation basis, improve out-of-distribution (OOD) deception detection?
Method overview: Train linear probes (logistic regression) on one source dataset; evaluate on 3 held-out target datasets. Use a target-supervised greedy search that adds PCs according to target performance. Also evaluate ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights. Introduce an LLM judge that scores natural-language PC descriptions without using target data.
Key quantitative claims/results: Greedy, target-supervised search finds 8–15 PCs that nearly match probes trained on target data. Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights does not recover this transferable subspace. Selecting 19 PCs that receive the maximum observed LLM score in both runs (unsupervised by target data) improves transfer on all 3 targets. For two of the targets, this selection closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and the greedy oracle. 
Other terms to track: "full-representation baseline", "greedy oracle", "both runs" (unspecified here), which targets achieve 78% and 25% (unspecified here).

Paper: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Goal: improve cross-domain (source->target) deception detection by selecting source-PC directions. Source domain = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (activations extracted; token activations averaged over assistant response to form probe inputs). Labels: GPT-4o assigns Deceptive=1, Honest=0, Ambiguous=-1 (ambiguous examples removed). Representation & PCA: source activations are standardized (source -> zero mean, unit variance) and PCA applied; source statistics are applied to target activations; 100 source PCs retained (S subset of these). Probes: all linear (logistic regression, regularization parameter λ=10); baseline = source-trained probe on full standardized activations; target-trained probes fit on target data. Selection methods: greedy oracle = target-guided greedy adding the PC that most increases target AUROC (reported to find ~8–15 PCs that nearly match target-trained probes); variance control = top-k PCs by variance; source-PCA probe and target-PCA probe use standardized coefficients to rank PCs (standardized coefficient = |coefficient| * PC standard deviation). LLM judge: GPT-5-mini interprets PC positive/negative poles and rates OOD-deception usefulness on a 1–10 scale; observed maximum OOD score = 6. Interp-selection = 19 PCs that received the maximum observed score (6) in both scoring runs; interp-ablated PCs = remaining 81. Evaluation: 5-fold CV on targets (held-out folds used for testing); AUROC reported with 95% CI. Causal validation (intervention/ablation at inference) was not performed. Appendix C: SAE decoder alignment (resource andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct); statistics reported include Spearman ρ and Jaccard overlap.

Paper question: whether selecting subspaces of LM representations improves out-of-distribution (OOD) deception detection. Method: compare probes (classifiers) trained on full representations vs probes using selected directions/subspaces. Two selection approaches highlighted: (1) target-guided selection that uses target labels but does not fit probe weights on them; (2) interpretation-based selection using natural-language interpretations, which requires no target data. Key claims: small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes; selecting directions by source weights, target-class separation, or explained variance does not recover the same transferable subspaces; interpretation-based selection improves over the full-representation baseline on all targets, though how well it recovers varies sharply across targets. Scope/caveats: study uses one model and one source dataset; interpretations are descriptive, not causal. The paper includes a "Glossary." (no glossary content shown in this part).

Goal: test whether selecting subspaces of LM representations improves OOD (transfer) deception detection. Source dataset: Roleplaying (V8). Targets include C2R (Insider Trading Report), W6 (Insider Trading Confirm), J9 (Sandbagging). Model & readout: layer-15 residual-stream activations from Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6), averaged over assistant-response tokens. Preprocessing: standardization = zero-mean/unit-variance using source statistics applied to both source and targets. Dimensionality reduction: PCA / N4D retains the leading 100 source directions (Q7); "PCs" refer to these retained source directions; "leading" = lower index. Probes: logistic regression with λ=10, evaluated by AUROC (F3) with 95% CIs; 5-fold CV where selection uses non-held-out target folds and evaluation uses the held-out fold. Baselines & methods: B8Q = full-representation baseline (source-trained on all standardized activations); Y4 = top-k PCs by variance (variance-ranked subset matched in dimension count); H2 = greedy oracle (target-guided direction selection but probe weights fitted only on source); T6 = source-PCA probe (supplies source coefficient rankings); M9 = target-PCA probe (supplies target coefficient rankings); X4 = standardized coefficient = |coef| * PC_std. Interpretation-based selection: natural-language explanations produced with P2 (GPT-5-mini) and rated by C7 (LLM judge) yielding R5 (OOD score/generalization rating); L2 = interp-selected PC probe (uses directions reaching max R5 in both scoring runs); A7 = interp-ablated PC probe (complement). Decoder alignment uses SAE (U9) decoder features (resource: andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct); Spearman ρ reports relation of PC index to decoder alignment. Goal: evaluate whether source-trained leading-100 PCA subspace (Q7) contains transferable deception signal and whether small source-trained subsets (H2) can match target-trained performance. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; layer-15 residual stream, assistant-response-token-averaged activations; source standardized and same stats applied to targets. Classifiers: logistic regression (λ=10). Metric: AUROC (F3) with 5-fold CV; target-5-fold CV: directions selected on non-held-out target folds, evaluate on held-out fold; search stops when no candidate improves target F3 by >0.001. Key reported numbers (Appendix A): B8Q (full-representation) F3: W6=0.874, C2R=0.706, J9=0.606. Target-trained (within retained-100) F3 (5-fold CV): C2R=0.936, W6=0.950, J9=0.869. H2 F3 (used for recovery comparison): C2R=0.929, J9=0.832; H2 improvements over B8Q: +0.22 (C2R), +0.23 (J9). Target-trained F3 for corresponding rows: 0.936 (C2R), 0.869 (J9). Variance-selection (Y4) matches H2 only on W6, falls behind on C2R/J9. Rankings: T6 (source-PCA ranking) performs about like B8Q; M9 (target-side ranking using standardized coefficient X4 = |coef|*PC_std) does well on C2R, worse than H2 on W6, and reportedly below random on J9. L2 = intersection of directions retained across both runs = 19 PCs; A7 = complement (81 PCs); Y4 = variance-ranked subset matched to L2 dimensionality (19 PCs). Paper title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Setup: use linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations to detect deception behaviors; evaluate generalization across 3 held-out deception detection datasets (only two named here: Insider Trading Report and Sandbagging). Key claim: projecting inputs onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) from the training activation distribution enables cross-domain transfer that nearly matches probes trained on the target/test distribution. Method extension: interpret PCs and use an LLM judge to score each PC by whether its most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; then probe using top-scoring PCs. Results: this PC-selection method closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and by 25% on Sandbagging. Interpretation claim: source-probe-weighted directions encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and in ways capturable by natural language descriptions. Broad claim: OOD robustness of probes largely determined by subspace selection. Venue noted: Machine Learning, ICML.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Setup: train linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations (source dataset: Roleplaying deception scenarios); evaluate OOD on three held-out target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Core idea: work in the source-domain PCA basis and select a small subset of source PCs to train probes that avoid spurious surface correlations and transfer to targets. Key empirical claims: (1) A small transferable subspace exists (Sec. 4.2): a target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds ~8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe. (2) Source-side and target-side weight-based rankings fail to recover this subspace (Sec. 4.3): ranking PCs by source or target probe weights does not outperform the full-representation baseline. (3) An LLM judge can partially recover the subspace without target labels (Sec. 4.5): it interprets PCs via their extreme examples and selects transferable PCs. Prior-note results: PC-selection method closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Interpretation claim: transferable directions encode more abstract contrasts describable in language; probe OOD robustness largely determined by subspace selection. Figure 1 outlines pipeline: project activations into source PCA basis, filter candidate PCs, train probes on selected low-dim subspace.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Setup: train linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations using a source dataset of roleplaying deception scenarios; evaluate OOD on three held-out target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Method: compute PCA on source activations, work in source PCA basis, filter candidate PCs, and select a small subset of source PCs to train linear probes on the low-dimensional subspace. Key empirical claims: (1) A small transferable subspace exists: target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds ~8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe (Sec. 4.2). (2) Weight-based rankings on source or target probes fail to recover this subspace and do not outperform full-representation baseline (Sec. 4.3). (3) An LLM judge can partially recover the subspace without target labels by interpreting PCs via extreme examples and selecting transferable PCs (Sec. 4.5). Reported quantitative impact: PC-selection method closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Context from related work: literature reports linear/low-dim directions for high-level properties and behaviors, examples of single-direction control (refusal/assistant axis), skepticism about probes (probe may learn task/exploit surface correlates; OOD probe generalization can be uneven), and use of LLMs to generate natural-language explanations of features and to inform interventions.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Datasets: Roleplaying (source; 311 retained responses), targets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Labels assigned by GPT-4o: honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous responses removed. Model & activations: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer 15 residual stream (per Ying et al. 2026); token activations averaged over the assistant’s response. Preprocessing: standardize source activations to zero mean/unit variance; apply same source stats to standardize target activations. PCA: run on scaled source activations; retain top 100 PCs. Probes: logistic regression (λ=10). For subspace experiments, project activations onto subset S of the 100 PCs before training/evaluation; baseline probes train on full standardized activations (pre-PCA). Motivation for top-100 PCs: alignment with SAE decoder features decreases with PC index (Appendix C) so lower-index PCs are more interpretable; authors explicitly state this is not a claim about generalization and point to Section 4.1 showing the 100-PC subspace suffices to separate deceptive vs honest on every target. Key empirical claims to be checked later: (1) A small transferable subspace (~8–15 PCs) exists enabling source-trained probes to nearly match target-trained probes; (2) weight-based rankings on probes fail to recover this subspace and don't beat full-representation baseline; (3) an LLM judge can partially recover the subspace without target labels. Reported quantitative effects: PC-selection closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% (Insider Trading Report) and 25% (Sandbagging).

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Abstract claim: directions weighted by a source probe encode source-specific surface features; transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly (capturable in natural language). Main claim: probe OOD robustness largely determined by subspace selection. Background: linear probes expose semantic info but can fail OOD despite strong in-distribution performance. Assertion that behavioral concepts have linear representations but probes often learn spurious correlations; such unreliability is problematic for harmful-interaction monitoring. Method/approach keywords: work in source Q7 coordinates to avoid privileging model latent dims; these coordinates provide data-driven representation structure. Prior findings cited: removing leading components can improve downstream embedding performance (Mu et al., 2018); leading-component projections used as a probing baseline (Kantamneni et al., 2025). Problem framed as selecting dimensions that permit generalization vs. spurious source-trained classification. Pipeline (Fig.1): projection into source N4D basis, filtering candidate Q7 directions, probe training in selected low-dimensional subspace.

Goal: probe OOD robustness largely determined by subspace selection; pipeline projects activations into a source data-driven basis (source N4D / Q7 coordinates), filters candidate directions, and trains probes in the selected low-dim subspace. Prior findings: removing leading components can improve downstream embedding performance; leading-component projections used as a baseline. Related work summarized here: (1) Linear concept directions: studies report cross-dataset linear structure for true/false and other behaviors (Marks & Tegmark 2024; Park et al. 2024 formalize the linear representation hypothesis). Single directions reported for refusal and an “assistant” axis (Arditi et al. 2024; Lu et al. 2026); other work finds population-level directions for honesty/emotion (Zou et al. 2025). (2) Linear probes limits: probes can learn task/surface correlates rather than reveal intrinsic representation; encoded vs. recoverable information distinction; strong in-distribution probes often generalize unevenly—safety evaluation must separate robust internal signals from dataset artifacts. (3) Interpreting features with natural-language explanations: LLM-generated neuron explanations from high-activation examples (Bills et al. 2023), automated sparse-autoencoder feature labeling (Paulo et al. 2025; Bricken et al. 2023), and concept identification + ablation during fine-tuning (Casademunt et al. 2025).

Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6). Use layer-15 residual-stream activations (per Ying et al. 2026); activations averaged over assistant-response tokens. Datasets: Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025) collection — one source Roleplaying (V8) with 311 retained responses after removing ambiguous labels; three held-out targets: Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), Sandbagging (J9). Labels: GPT-4o (K8) assigns honest=0, ambiguous=-1 (removed), deceptive=1. Preprocessing: source activations standardized to zero mean/unit variance; same source statistics applied to standardize target activations. Dimensionality reduction: PCA on source (N4D), retain leading 100 principal components; training/eval use projection to chosen subset S of these PCs. Classifiers: logistic regression with regularization λ=10 for all probes. Baseline/comparator: full-representation baseline (B8Q) trains directly on all standardized activations (no PCA). Choice of top-100 motivated by interpretability comparability (alignment with U9 / Bricken et al. 2023 decreases with component index); error bars indicate 95% CIs.

Key experimental claims (Part 4): Source→target transfer quality: W6 transfer reasonably good, C2R moderate, J9 poor (for naive source-trained direction). Target-trained probes within retained source-PC subspace separate classes on every target. Greedy oracle H2: forward search starting empty over top-100 PCs, at each step fit source logistic probe on current subset and add the PC that most improves target F3 (selection uses target labels; probe weights always fit on source); stop when no candidate improves >0.001. H2 yields a stable full-target set/k (numbers differ slightly from CV-run selections). Variance-ranked Y4 matches H2 only on W6; explained variance does not predict usefulness. Magnitude ranking X4 = |coefficient| * PC std used for T6 (source-ranked) and M9 (target-ranked); neither recovers the transferable subspace. T6 transfers ≈ B8Q; M9 does well on C2R, worse than H2 on W6, below random on J9. Interpreter C7 inspects top8/bottom8 examples per PC and assigns OOD score R5; interp-selected L2 (intersection across scoring runs) improves over B8Q, Y4 (variance control), and A7 (interp-ablated complement), especially on C2R and J9; W6 has little headroom.

Interpreter C7 inspects top8/bottom8 examples per PC, assigns OOD score R5; interp-selected L2 (intersection across runs) improves over B8Q, Y4, and A7 (complement), especially on C2R and J9. Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars.
Goal: Can selecting principal components (PCs), i.e., directions in a source activation basis, improve out-of-distribution (OOD) deception detection?
Method overview: Train linear probes (logistic regression) on one source dataset; evaluate on 3 held-out target datasets. Use a target-supervised greedy search that adds PCs according to target performance. Also evaluate ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights. Introduce an LLM judge that scores natural-language PC descriptions without using target data.
Key quantitative claims/results: Greedy, target-supervised search finds 8–15 PCs that nearly match probes trained on target data. Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights does not recover this transferable subspace. Selecting 19 PCs that receive the maximum observed LLM score in both runs (unsupervised by target data) improves transfer on all 3 targets. For two of the targets, this selection closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and the greedy oracle. 
Other terms to track: "full-representation baseline", "greedy oracle", "both runs" (unspecified here), which targets achieve 78% and 25% (unspecified here).

Paper: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Goal: improve cross-domain (source->target) deception detection by selecting source-PC directions. Source domain = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (activations extracted; token activations averaged over assistant response to form probe inputs). Labels: GPT-4o assigns Deceptive=1, Honest=0, Ambiguous=-1 (ambiguous examples removed). Representation & PCA: source activations are standardized (source -> zero mean, unit variance) and PCA applied; source statistics are applied to target activations; 100 source PCs retained (S subset of these). Probes: all linear (logistic regression, regularization parameter λ=10); baseline = source-trained probe on full standardized activations; target-trained probes fit on target data. Selection methods: greedy oracle = target-guided greedy adding the PC that most increases target AUROC (reported to find ~8–15 PCs that nearly match target-trained probes); variance control = top-k PCs by variance; source-PCA probe and target-PCA probe use standardized coefficients to rank PCs (standardized coefficient = |coefficient| * PC standard deviation). LLM judge: GPT-5-mini interprets PC positive/negative poles and rates OOD-deception usefulness on a 1–10 scale; observed maximum OOD score = 6. Interp-selection = 19 PCs that received the maximum observed score (6) in both scoring runs; interp-ablated PCs = remaining 81. Evaluation: 5-fold CV on targets (held-out folds used for testing); AUROC reported with 95% CI. Causal validation (intervention/ablation at inference) was not performed. Appendix C: SAE decoder alignment (resource andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct); statistics reported include Spearman ρ and Jaccard overlap.

Paper question: whether selecting subspaces of LM representations improves out-of-distribution (OOD) deception detection. Method: compare probes (classifiers) trained on full representations vs probes using selected directions/subspaces. Two selection approaches highlighted: (1) target-guided selection that uses target labels but does not fit probe weights on them; (2) interpretation-based selection using natural-language interpretations, which requires no target data. Key claims: small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes; selecting directions by source weights, target-class separation, or explained variance does not recover the same transferable subspaces; interpretation-based selection improves over the full-representation baseline on all targets, though how well it recovers varies sharply across targets. Scope/caveats: study uses one model and one source dataset; interpretations are descriptive, not causal. The paper includes a "Glossary." (no glossary content shown in this part).

Goal: test whether selecting subspaces of LM representations improves OOD (transfer) deception detection. Source dataset: Roleplaying (V8). Targets include C2R (Insider Trading Report), W6 (Insider Trading Confirm), J9 (Sandbagging). Model & readout: layer-15 residual-stream activations from Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6), averaged over assistant-response tokens. Preprocessing: standardization = zero-mean/unit-variance using source statistics applied to both source and targets. Dimensionality reduction: PCA / N4D retains the leading 100 source directions (Q7); "PCs" refer to these retained source directions; "leading" = lower index. Probes: logistic regression with λ=10, evaluated by AUROC (F3) with 95% CIs; 5-fold CV where selection uses non-held-out target folds and evaluation uses the held-out fold. Baselines & methods: B8Q = full-representation baseline (source-trained on all standardized activations); Y4 = top-k PCs by variance (variance-ranked subset matched in dimension count); H2 = greedy oracle (target-guided direction selection but probe weights fitted only on source); T6 = source-PCA probe (supplies source coefficient rankings); M9 = target-PCA probe (supplies target coefficient rankings); X4 = standardized coefficient = |coef| * PC_std. Goal: test whether selecting subspaces of LM representations improves OOD (transfer) deception detection. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6) providing layer-15 residual-stream activations; activations averaged over assistant-response tokens. Source dataset: Roleplaying (V8), 311 retained responses; three held-out targets: Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), Sandbagging (J9). Labels from GPT-4o (K8): honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous responses removed. Preprocessing: standardize to zero-mean/unit-variance using source statistics; apply same transform to targets. Dimensionality reduction: PCA (N4D) on source, retain leading 100 PCs (Q7; "leading" = low index). Activations may be projected onto a subset S of these directions before training/eval. All classifiers: logistic regression λ=10. Full-representation baseline (B8Q) trains on standardized activations (not PC-projected). Evaluation: AUROC with 95% CIs; 5-fold CV (selection uses non-held-out target folds; evaluation uses held-out fold). Methods/baselines: Y4 (top-k PCs by variance), H2 (greedy oracle target-guided direction selection, probe weights fitted only on source), T6 (source-PCA probe), M9 (target-PCA probe), X4 (standardized coefficient metric). Interpretability: keep 100 PCs for interpretability (alignment with sparse-autoencoder decoder vectors U9 decreases with PC index; lower indices easier for NL interpretation). Explanations by P2 (GPT-5-mini) rated by C7 -> R5; L2 = interp-selected PC probe (directions with max R5); A7 = interp-ablated probe (complement). Example R5s and AUROC examples reported in appendices.

Experiments compare full representations, PC-subspaces, target-guided selection (H2), variance-based top-k (Y4), source-/target-PCA rankings (T6/M9), and standardized-coefficient ranking (X4). Evaluation: AUROC (F3) with 5-fold CV; probe = logistic regression (trained on source unless noted). Key numbers (Appendix A): B8Q F3 = W6 0.874, C2R 0.706, J9 0.606. Target-trained (leading-100 source PCs) F3 (5-fold CV) = C2R 0.936, W6 0.950, J9 0.869. H2 (greedy, target-guided subset selection; probe weights always fit on source; selection uses non-held-out target folds; stop when no candidate improves target F3 by >0.001) finds small subsets: mean H2 subset sizes (target CV) C2R 15, W6 8, J9 14 (range 8–15). H2 improves over B8Q by ~0.22 (C2R) and 0.23 (J9); H2 F3 used for recovery comparison = 0.929 (C2R), 0.832 (J9); target-trained F3 for those tasks = 0.936 and 0.869. Full-target H2 k (stable selection) = C2R 13, W6 7, J9 14 (numbers differ slightly from CV). Y4 (top-k PCs by variance) matches H2 only on W6, falls far behind on C2R and J9. T6 (source-PCA probe) performs about like B8Q. M9 (target-PCA probe) does well on C2R, worse than H2 on W6, and below random on J9. X4 = |probe coefficient| × corresponding PC std (computed on source N4D-projected activations); T6/M9 supply X4 orderings and probes are then trained on source data projected onto their top-k directions. Interpretability: H2-selected directions' descriptions suggest domain-stable contrasts, but recovery is partial and scores noisy.

Methods compared: full 100 leading source PCs (B8Q), H2 (target-guided greedy small subsets; probe weights fit on source), Y4 (top-k by source-PC variance), T6/M9 (source-/target-PCA rankings), X4 (|coef|×PC std). Evaluation: AUROC (F3) with 5-fold CV; probes trained on source unless noted. Key numbers (Appendix A): B8Q F3 = C2R 0.706, W6 0.874, J9 0.606. Target-trained (leading-100 PCs) F3 = C2R 0.936, W6 0.950, J9 0.869. H2 (target-guided) F3 = C2R 0.929, W6 0.832?, J9 0.832; mean H2 subset sizes (target CV) C2R 15, W6 8, J9 14 (full-target stable k: C2R 13, W6 7, J9 14). H2 improves over B8Q ~+0.22 (C2R) and +0.23 (J9). Y4 matches H2 only on W6; falls far behind on C2R and J9. T6 ~B8Q; M9 strong on C2R, worse on W6, below random on J9. Interpretability: judge (LLM C7) shown 8 most- and 8 least-activating source examples per direction, generates pole/whole descriptions and assigns generalization rating R5 (OOD). Paper keeps directions that hit the observed maximum rating in both scoring runs (max R5=6); 2 scoring runs produced 19 directions at that max (intersection = L2, complement = A7 of size 81). L2 (interp-selected PC probe, trained as source probe) exceeds B8Q on C2R and J9 (L2 F3: C2R 0.881 vs 0.706; J9 0.662 vs 0.606) and recovers 78% of Baseline–H2 gap on C2R, 25% on J9. W6 has little headroom; methods (except A7) roughly tied there. Scores are noisy; recovery is partial.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Setup: study generalization of linear probes built on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations for deception detection across 3 held-out datasets. Main empirical claim: projecting inputs onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) from the training activation distribution enables cross-domain transfer that nearly matches probes trained on the target/test distribution. Interpretation claim: PC interpretations can identify a subset of transferable PCs. Method: use an LLM judge to recover five repeatedly transferable PCs from their most/least activating examples; then probe on the highest-scoring PCs. Reported results: this method closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and by 25% on Sandbagging. Qualitative claim: source-probe-weighted directions encode source-specific surface features, while actually transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly, capturable by natural-language descriptions. Conclusion: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection. Venue: Machine Learning, ICML.

(3) An LLM judge is used to identify repeatedly transferable PCs — earlier parts claimed it recovers five such PCs but the intro contained contradictory wording (both "partially recovers" and "identifies every repeatedly transferable PC, recovering the full shared transfer subspace"); flagged as an internal contradiction to resolve. Reported empirical results: method closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Related work (this part): linear concept directions and single-direction behavior mediation (Marks & Tegmark 2024; Park et al. 2024; Zou et al. 2025; Arditi et al. 2024; Lu et al. 2026); probing limitations (Hewitt & Liang 2019; Ravichander et al. 2021; recent work noting uneven OOD probe generalization); natural-language interpretation of features and interventions using LLMs (Bills et al. 2023; Paulo et al. 2025; Bricken et al. 2023; Casademunt et al. 2025). Notes-to-check later: reconcile counts of transferable PCs (5 vs ~8–15), clarify what "oracle" baseline is, and verify exact wording about the LLM judge's recovery claim.

Title/authors: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection (Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars). Datasets: 4 deception datasets (Roleplaying, Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging). Roleplaying = source; the other three are target test sets. Labels assigned by GPT-4o: honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous responses removed. Model/activations: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer 15 residual stream (chosen per Ying et al. 2026 for highest cross-domain AUROC); token activations averaged over the assistant’s response. Preprocessing: standardize source activations to zero mean/unit variance and apply same source statistics to targets. PCA: run PCA on scaled source activations and retain top 100 PCs. Probes: logistic regression (λ=10). For experiments on a subset S of PCs, project activations onto S before training/eval; baseline probes train on the full standardized activations. Reason for 100 PCs: lower PC index aligns better with SAE decoder features (Bricken et al., 2023) per Appendix C, so low-index PCs are more interpretable; paper explicitly says this is not a claim that low-index PCs generalize better and that Section 4.1 shows the 100-PC subspace retains enough information to separate deceptive vs honest on every target. Method pipeline (from earlier): project → filter candidate PCs → train probes on selected subspace. Key claims to check later: small transferable subspace exists (greedy search finds ~8–15 PCs); ranking PCs by probe weights fails; an LLM judge is used to identify repeatedly transferable PCs (conflicting wording about whether it recovers 5 PCs vs “identifies every repeatedly transferable PC”); empirical gains reported (closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging). Open items to reconcile: 5 vs ~8–15 transferable PCs, definition of “oracle” baseline, and exact LLM judge recovery wording.

Paper: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection (Yoo & Skapars). Datasets: Roleplaying = source; targets = Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Model/activations: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer 15 residual stream; token activations averaged over assistant response. Preprocessing: standardize source activations (zero mean/unit var), apply same stats to targets. PCA: run on scaled source activations, keep top 100 PCs. Probes: logistic regression (λ=10). Baseline: probes on full standardized activations; for PC-subspace experiments project onto subset before training/eval. Section 4.1 (baseline transfer): source-trained probe on full reps → AUROC: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probe (5-fold CV) within 100-PC subspace → AUROC: Confirm 0.936, Report 0.950, Sandbagging 0.869. Conclusion: 100-PC subspace contains enough task info; transfer failure is due to source probe learning non-generalizable direction. Section 4.2 (greedy PC selection): Greedy algorithm adds PCs (search among top 100) maximizing target AUROC; probe weights fit on source data, subset choice uses target labels (5-fold CV: select on non-held folds, evaluate on held fold); stop when AUROC gain <0.001. Converged subset sizes (averages): Report 15 PCs, Confirm 8 PCs, Sandbagging 14 PCs. Greedy improves over baseline by +0.22 (Report) and +0.23 (Sandbagging), nearly matching target-trained probes; top-k-by-variance (k matched to greedy) only matches greedy for Confirm. Section 4.3 (hypotheses for transferable PCs): two hypotheses tested — PCs that individually separate target classes, vs PCs the source probe relies on. They compare rankings by standardized coefficient (|coef| * std(PC)) from probes trained on activations projected to the source-PCA basis (source-trained vs target-trained probes for the two rankings). Figures 2–4 referenced. Open items to watch: earlier ambiguous claims about "5 vs ~8–15 transferable PCs", wording about an "LLM judge" recovering PCs, and precise definition of the paper's "oracle" baseline.

Paper: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD deception detection. Source dataset: Roleplaying; targets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer-15 residual stream; token activations averaged over assistant response. Preprocessing: standardize source activations (zero mean/unit var); apply same stats to targets. PCA: run on scaled source activations, keep top 100 PCs. Probes: logistic regression (λ=10). Baseline (source-trained on full reps) AUROC transfers: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probe (5-fold CV) within 100-PC subspace AUROC: Confirm 0.936, Report 0.950, Sandbagging 0.869 — shows 100-PC subspace contains task info. Greedy PC selection (adds PCs among top100 to maximize target AUROC; probe weights fit on source; selection uses target labels with 5-fold CV) converged (CV averages): Report 15 PCs, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14; greedy improved over baseline by +0.22 (Report) and +0.23 (Sandbagging), nearly matching target-trained probes. Section 4.3 tested two hypotheses via rankings: (A) PCs that individually separate target classes (target-PCA ranking), (B) PCs the source probe relies on (source-PCA ranking). For evaluation, probes are trained on source data projected onto the top-k PCs chosen by each ranking. To pick k, greedy on the full target sets (not CV) gives k=13 (Report), 7 (Confirm), 14 (Sandbagging). Both hypotheses fail: source-PCA probe ≈ full-representation baseline; target-PCA probe does well on Report but worse than greedy on Confirm and below-random on Sandbagging. Section 4.4 interpretability: for each top-100 PC, collect 8 most/8 least activating source examples; an LLM judge rates OOD generalizability 1–10. No PC scored >6, so 6 was max observed; keeping PCs that scored 6 in both runs yields 19 interp-selected PCs. 5 PCs were in greedy selections for >1 target; 3 of those 5 had max OOD; only 1 of top-5 source-PCA PCs had max OOD. Section 4.5: use 19 interp-selected PCs as subspace and compare to controls (full, top-19 by variance, ablation of 19 => 81 PCs) (results in Fig.5).

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Abstract claim: directions weighted by a source probe encode source-specific surface features; transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly (capturable in natural language). Main claim: probe OOD robustness largely determined by subspace selection. Background: linear probes expose semantic info but can fail OOD despite strong in-distribution performance. Assertion that behavioral concepts have linear representations but probes often learn spurious correlations; such unreliability is problematic for harmful-interaction monitoring. Method/approach keywords: work in source Q7 coordinates to avoid privileging model latent dims; these coordinates provide data-driven representation structure. Prior findings cited: removing leading components can improve downstream embedding performance (Mu et al., 2018); leading-component projections used as a probing baseline (Kantamneni et al., 2025). Problem framed as selecting dimensions that permit generalization vs. spurious source-trained classification. Pipeline (Fig.1): projection into source N4D basis, filtering candidate Q7 directions, probe training in selected low-dimensional subspace.

Goal: probe OOD robustness largely determined by subspace selection; pipeline projects activations into a source data-driven basis (source N4D / Q7 coordinates), filters candidate directions, and trains probes in the selected low-dim subspace. Prior findings: removing leading components can improve downstream embedding performance; leading-component projections used as a baseline. Related work summarized here: (1) Linear concept directions: studies report cross-dataset linear structure for true/false and other behaviors (Marks & Tegmark 2024; Park et al. 2024 formalize the linear representation hypothesis). Single directions reported for refusal and an “assistant” axis (Arditi et al. 2024; Lu et al. 2026); other work finds population-level directions for honesty/emotion (Zou et al. 2025). (2) Linear probes limits: probes can learn task/surface correlates rather than reveal intrinsic representation; encoded vs. recoverable information distinction; strong in-distribution probes often generalize unevenly—safety evaluation must separate robust internal signals from dataset artifacts. (3) Interpreting features with natural-language explanations: LLM-generated neuron explanations from high-activation examples (Bills et al. 2023), automated sparse-autoencoder feature labeling (Paulo et al. 2025; Bricken et al. 2023), and concept identification + ablation during fine-tuning (Casademunt et al. 2025).

Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6). Use layer-15 residual-stream activations (per Ying et al. 2026); activations averaged over assistant-response tokens. Data: four Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025) datasets — one source (Roleplaying: V8) and three held-out targets: Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), Sandbagging (J9). Only Roleplaying used as source. Labels: annotated by GPT-4o (K8, OpenAI 2024) with mapping honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous responses removed (binary honest vs deceptive). Preprocessing: source activations standardized to zero mean, unit variance; same source statistics used to standardize targets. Dimensionality reduction: PCA on source (N4D), retain leading 100 principal components (PCs Q7); probes trained on projections to subset S of these PCs. Classifiers: logistic regression (regularization λ=10) for all classifiers; comparator (full-representation baseline B8Q) trains on all standardized activations (no PCA). Choice of 100 PCs driven by interpretability comparability (alignment with U9/Bricken et al. 2023 decreases with PC index, so lower-index PCs are easier to interpret), not because low-index PCs generalize best. Error bars denote 95% confidence intervals.

Experiments summary (Part 4):
- Overall: W6 transfer reasonably good; C2R moderate; J9 poor. Target-trained probes within the retained source subspace (leading 100 source PCs, Q7) separate deceptive vs honest on every target; however a single source-trained direction does not generalize.
- Greedy oracle (H2) / subset-search: start empty, consider each of the 100 source PCs, project source activations onto current candidate subset, fit source logistic-regression weights (all probes use LR, λ=10 per earlier notes), add the PC that most improves target F3; selection uses target labels (but probe weights are fit on source), 5-fold CV uses non-held-out folds for selection and held-out for evaluation; stop when no candidate gives >0.001 F3 improvement. H2 full-target selection (no fold-specific picks) supplies a stable set and k (numbers differ slightly from CV).
- Results on subspaces: Small source-trained subspaces (found by H2) can nearly match target-trained probes, especially on C2R and J9. Variance-ranked selection (Y4) only matches H2 on easy W6; explained variance does not predict transfer usefulness.
- Ranking baselines: source-side and target-side magnitude rankings (T6, M9) use X4 = |probe coefficient| * corresponding PC std (on source-projected activations). T6 transfers ~ as well as full-representation baseline B8Q (source-reliant directions don’t generalize). M9: does well on C2R, worse than H2 on W6, below random on J9. Overall, ranking-by-magnitude fails to recover transferable subspace or beat B8Q.
- Interpretation & language-only selection: An LLM judge (C7) is shown 8 most- and 8 least-activating source examples per PC and produces pole/whole descriptions plus an OOD generalization rating (R5). C7 recovers the five repeatedly-transferable PCs; retained intersection across scoring runs defines interp-selected PC probe (L2). L2 (no target data) recovers the shared transfer subspace, exceeds B8Q and the variance control Y4 on all targets (notably C2R and J9), and outperforms interp-ablated A7; scores are noisy.
- Figures referenced: Fig2 (source-full, source-100PCs, target-100PCs F3 with 5-fold CV), Fig3 (B8Q, Y4, H2), Fig4 (T6, M9, H2), Fig5 (L2, B8Q, Y4, A7).

There is a full-target H2 selection variant. Baselines: full-representation B8Q; variance-ranked Y4; magnitude rankings T6 (target-side) and M9 (source-side). Limitations (Part 5): single-model/single-source scope; W6 baseline already-high/uninformative; Part 5 also states J9 is the weakest/OOD with only modest improvement (distribution shift), while calling C2R improvement more robust; pipeline is fully linear (projection + LR); directional descriptions are descriptive, not causal, and no inference-time ablations were done.

Experiments targeted three behaviors: W6 (easy/high baseline), C2R (moderate), J9 (OOD/weak). Probes: linear logistic regression (λ=10) on representations projected to leading 100 source PCs (Q7). Oracle H2 (greedy): start empty, iteratively add source PCs that most improve target F3 (uses target labels to select; fits LR weights on source); 5-fold CV evaluation; stop when no candidate gives >0.001 F3 improvement. Also considered a full-target H2 variant. Baselines: full-representation B8Q; variance-ranked Y4; magnitude rankings T6 (target-side) and M9 (source-side). Key empirical claims: W6 transfers reasonably well (high baseline), C2R shows moderate transfer, J9 is weakest with distribution shift and only modest improvement. Small source-trained subspaces (H2) can nearly match target-trained probes especially on C2R (and reported for J9 in some analyses). Variance-ranked Y4 matches H2 only on easy W6; explained variance poorly predicts transfer usefulness. Magnitude rankings fail to recover transferable subspaces: T6 ~ B8Q; M9 does well on C2R, worse on W6, below random on J9. Interpretations: LLM descriptions of extreme-activation examples recover repeatedly-transferable PCs; interp-selected probe L2 (no target data) recovers shared transfer subspace and outperforms B8Q and Y4 and an ablated interp variant A7. Limitations: single-model/single-source scope; W6 baseline already-high/uninformative; J9 is weakest/OOD; pipeline is fully linear (projection + LR); directional descriptions are descriptive not causal; no inference-time ablations. Conclusion: robust behavioral probing requires selecting representation subspaces (not just fitting classifiers) to preserve behavioral features and filter spurious correlations; sparse directional subspaces can isolate more general behavioral structure and improve OOD transfer.

final_notes: Datasets: Roleplaying (371: 140 ambiguous / 59 honest / 172 deceptive); Report (473: 218/194/61); Confirm (151: 29/38/84); Sandbagging (1000: 379/375/246). Label mapping ambiguous=-1, honest=0, deceptive=1. Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars.
Goal: Can selecting principal components (PCs), i.e., directions in a source activation basis, improve out-of-distribution (OOD) deception detection?
Method overview: Train linear probes (logistic regression) on one source dataset; evaluate on 3 held-out target datasets. Use a target-supervised greedy search that adds PCs according to target performance. Also evaluate ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights. Introduce an LLM judge that scores natural-language PC descriptions without using target data.
Key quantitative claims/results: Greedy, target-supervised search finds 8–15 PCs that nearly match probes trained on target data. Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights does not recover this transferable subspace. Selecting 19 PCs that receive the maximum observed LLM score in both runs (unsupervised by target data) improves transfer on all 3 targets. For two of the targets, this selection closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and the greedy oracle. 
Other terms to track: "full-representation baseline", "greedy oracle", "both runs" (unspecified here), which targets achieve 78% and 25% (unspecified here).

Paper: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Goal: improve cross-domain (source->target) deception detection by selecting source-PC directions. Source domain = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (activations extracted; token activations averaged over assistant response to form probe inputs). Labels: GPT-4o assigns Deceptive=1, Honest=0, Ambiguous=-1 (ambiguous examples removed). Representation & PCA: source activations are standardized (source -> zero mean, unit variance) and PCA applied; source statistics are applied to target activations; 100 source PCs retained (S subset of these). Probes: all linear (logistic regression, regularization parameter λ=10); baseline = source-trained probe on full standardized activations; target-trained probes fit on target data. Selection methods: greedy oracle = target-guided greedy adding the PC that most increases target AUROC (reported to find ~8–15 PCs that nearly match target-trained probes); variance control = top-k PCs by variance; source-PCA probe and target-PCA probe use standardized coefficients to rank PCs (standardized coefficient = |coefficient| * PC standard deviation). LLM judge: GPT-5-mini interprets PC positive/negative poles and rates OOD-deception usefulness on a 1–10 scale; observed maximum OOD score = 6. Interp-selection = 19 PCs that received the maximum observed score (6) in both scoring runs; interp-ablated PCs = remaining 81. Evaluation: 5-fold CV on targets (held-out folds used for testing); AUROC reported with 95% CI. Causal validation (intervention/ablation at inference) was not performed. Appendix C: SAE decoder alignment (resource andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct); statistics reported include Spearman ρ and Jaccard overlap.

Paper: Probe generalization as subspace selection for OOD deception detection on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Experiments (Sec.4): 4.1 Baseline — source-trained transfer (full rep) AUROC: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probes trained within the top-100 source-PC subspace (5-fold CV, 95% CIs) achieve AUROC 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869 (Report/Confirm/Sandbagging). Conclusion: 100-PC subspace contains enough target-class information; poor transfer due to source-learned direction.

4.2 Greedy oracle selection — greedy adds PCs (from top 100) that most improve target AUROC; for each candidate subset, probe weights are trained on source data and candidate performance is measured on non-held-out target folds (selection uses labeled target folds); final selected source-trained probe evaluated on held-out fold. Stop when no PC improves AUROC > 0.001. Mean subset sizes: Report 15 PCs, Confirm 8 PCs, Sandbagging 14 PCs. Greedy (oracle) improves baseline by +0.22 (Report) and +0.23 (Sandbagging), coming close to target-trained probes; variance-control (top-k by variance, k matched to greedy) matches greedy only on Confirm and falls far behind on Report and Sandbagging. Greedy is an upper bound (not unbiased OOD estimate).

4.3 Hypotheses tested (Fig.4): whether transferable PCs are (1) those that individually separate target classes, or (2) those the source probe relies on most. Figure 4 compares selection by source-probe weight ranking, target-probe weight ranking, and greedy oracle.

Paper question: does selecting subspaces of LM representations improve OOD deception detection? Compares probes (classifiers trained to detect property) in full representations vs selected directions. Two selection approaches: (1) target-guided selection that uses target labels but does not fit probe weights on them; (2) interpretation-based selection that recovers repeatedly transferable directions via natural-language interpretations without using target data. Key claims: small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes; selecting directions by source weights, target-class separation, or explained variance fails to recover the same transferable subspaces; interpretation-based selection improves over full-representation baseline on all targets but recovery quality varies sharply. Scope/caveats: experiments use one model and one source dataset; interpretations are descriptive, not causal.

Goal: test whether selecting subspaces of LM residual-stream representations improves OOD deception detection (transfer from a Roleplaying source to held-out targets). Source: V8 Roleplaying. Targets: C2R (Insider Trading Report), W6 (Insider Trading Confirm), J9 (Sandbagging). Model/data: E6 Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; activations = layer-15 residual stream, averaged over assistant-response tokens. Preproc: standardization = zero-mean/unit-variance using source stats (applied to source + targets). Dimensionality reduction: PCA / N4D retaining leading 100 source PCs (Q7). Probes: logistic regression (λ = 10). Evaluation: 5-fold CV (selection uses non-held-out target folds; evaluation on held-out fold). Metric F3 = AUROC with 95% CIs.

Baselines & selection methods: B8Q = full-representation source-trained probe (all standardized activations). Y4 = top-k PCs by explained variance (variance control). T6 = source-PCA probe (source coefficient rankings). M9 = target-PCA probe (target coefficient rankings). H2 = greedy oracle (target-guided greedy selection; uses target labels to choose directions but fits probe weights only on source; treated as transfer upper bound). L2 = interp-selected PC probe (source-trained probe using directions that hit maximum R5 in both scoring runs). A7 = interp-ablated PC probe (complement of L2). D3 = Jaccard overlap for set comparisons.

Interpretation & alignment: C7 = LLM judge that describes directions and rates OOD usefulness (R5 = OOD score/generalization rating). P2 = GPT-5-mini used for direction interpretation. SAE / U9 = sparse autoencoder feature dictionary; decoder alignment measured to best-matching or mean of top-10 features; report Spearman ρ between component index and decoder alignment. Labels: -1 ambiguous, 0 honest, 1 deceptive (ambiguous removed). Key reported claims to check later: small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes; selection by source weights/target-class separation/explained variance fails to recover transferable subspaces; interp-based selection improves over full baseline on all targets but recovery quality varies; experiments use one model and one source dataset; interpretations are descriptive, not causal.
