Paper title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Setup: use linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations to detect deception behaviors; evaluate generalization across 3 held-out deception detection datasets (only two named here: Insider Trading Report and Sandbagging). Key claim: projecting inputs onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) from the training activation distribution enables cross-domain transfer that nearly matches probes trained on the target/test distribution. Method extension: interpret PCs and use an LLM judge to score each PC by whether its most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; then probe using top-scoring PCs. Results: this PC-selection method closes the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and by 25% on Sandbagging. Interpretation claim: source-probe-weighted directions encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and in ways capturable by natural language descriptions. Broad claim: OOD robustness of probes largely determined by subspace selection. Venue noted: Machine Learning, ICML.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Setup: train linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations (source dataset: Roleplaying deception scenarios); evaluate OOD on three held-out target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging. Core idea: work in the source-domain PCA basis and select a small subset of source PCs to train probes that avoid spurious surface correlations and transfer to targets. Key empirical claims: (1) A small transferable subspace exists (Sec. 4.2): a target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds ~8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe. (2) Source-side and target-side weight-based rankings fail to recover this subspace (Sec. 4.3): ranking PCs by source or target probe weights does not outperform the full-representation baseline. (3) An LLM judge can partially recover the subspace without target labels (Sec. 4.5): it interprets PCs via their extreme examples and selects transferable PCs. Prior-note results: PC-selection method closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Interpretation claim: transferable directions encode more abstract contrasts describable in language; probe OOD robustness largely determined by subspace selection. Figure 1 outlines pipeline: project activations into source PCA basis, filter candidate PCs, train probes on selected low-dim subspace.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Setup: train linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations using a source dataset of roleplaying deception scenarios; evaluate OOD on three held-out target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Method: compute PCA on source activations, work in source PCA basis, filter candidate PCs, and select a small subset of source PCs to train linear probes on the low-dimensional subspace. Key empirical claims: (1) A small transferable subspace exists: target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds ~8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained probe (Sec. 4.2). (2) Weight-based rankings on source or target probes fail to recover this subspace and do not outperform full-representation baseline (Sec. 4.3). (3) An LLM judge can partially recover the subspace without target labels by interpreting PCs via extreme examples and selecting transferable PCs (Sec. 4.5). Reported quantitative impact: PC-selection method closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Context from related work: literature reports linear/low-dim directions for high-level properties and behaviors, examples of single-direction control (refusal/assistant axis), skepticism about probes (probe may learn task/exploit surface correlates; OOD probe generalization can be uneven), and use of LLMs to generate natural-language explanations of features and to inform interventions.

Datasets: Roleplaying is the source; targets are Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Each response labeled by GPT-4o as honest (0), ambiguous (-1), or deceptive (1); ambiguous examples removed. Language model activations: layer-15 residual stream of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; token activations averaged over the assistant response. Preprocessing: standardize source activations (zero mean, unit variance) and apply the same source statistics to standardize target activations. PCA: run PCA on the scaled source activations and retain the top 100 PCs. Probes: logistic regression (regularization λ=10). For experiments using a subset S of PCs, project activations onto S before training/evaluation; baseline probes train on the full standardized activations. Motivation for 100 PCs: lower-index PCs align more with SAE decoder features (Appendix C) and are easier to interpret, but authors do not claim low-index PCs inherently generalize better; Section 4.1 reportedly shows the 100-PC subspace suffices to separate deceptive vs. honest on every target.

Datasets: source = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Confirm, Insider Trading Report, Sandbagging. Responses labeled honest (0), ambiguous (-1), deceptive (1); ambiguous examples removed. Model activations: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer-15 residual stream; token activations averaged over assistant response. Preprocessing: standardize source activations (zero mean, unit variance) and apply same source statistics to standardize target activations. PCA: run PCA on scaled source activations and retain top 100 PCs. Probes: logistic regression (λ=10). Baselines: probes trained on full standardized representations; for PC-subset experiments project activations onto subset before training/evaluation.

Key results (Section 4.1): source-trained probe (full rep) AUROC on targets: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Probe trained on target data within top-100 source PCs (5-fold CV) achieves AUROC ≈ 0.936 (Confirm) / 0.950 (Report) / 0.869 (Sandbagging) — so 100-PC subspace suffices to separate classes on every target.

Greedy PC-selection (Section 4.2): start empty, iteratively add from top-100 PCs the PC that most improves AUROC on target; to evaluate a candidate, project source activations onto current subset and train probe on source projections; PC choice guided by target labeled folds (5-fold CV) while probe weights always fit on source; stop when AUROC improvement ≤0.001. Avg subset sizes: Report 15 PCs, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14. Greedy improves over baseline (full-rep baseline) by ~+0.22 (Report) and +0.23 (Sandbagging) and approaches target-trained performance; top-k-by-variance matched greedy only for Confirm.

Section 4.3 tests two hypotheses for transferable PCs (separate target classes alone vs PCs source probe leans on). Compare rankings by standardized coefficient = |coef| * std(PC) from probes trained on activations projected to source-PCA basis (source-probe vs target-probe vs greedy oracle).

Datasets: source = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Confirm, Insider Trading Report, Sandbagging. Labels: honest(0), ambiguous(-1) (removed), deceptive(1). Representations: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer-15 residual stream; token activations averaged over assistant response; standardize using source mean/var and apply same stats to targets. PCA: run on scaled source activations, keep top 100 PCs. Probes: logistic regression (λ=10). Baselines: probes on full standardized representations; PC-subset experiments project activations onto chosen subset before training/eval. Key baseline numbers: source-trained probe (full rep) AUROC on targets: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probe on top-100 source PCs (5-fold CV) AUROC ≈ Confirm 0.936, Report 0.950, Sandbagging 0.869 (so 100-PC subspace suffices for target separation). Greedy PC-selection (target labels guide PC choice, probe weights fit on source; stop when AUROC improvement ≤0.001): CV average subset sizes Report 15, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14; greedy boosted AUROC over full-rep by ~+0.22 (Report) and +0.23 (Sandbagging); top-k-by-variance only matched greedy for Confirm. Cross-target ranking experiment (Sec 4.3): define source-PCA and target-PCA rankings (both use source-PCA basis); to pick k, run greedy on full target dataset (single k): Report k=13, Confirm k=7, Sandbagging k=14 (differs slightly from CV sizes). Results: both hypotheses fail — source-PCA probe transfers ~as well as full-rep baseline (i.e., doesn't generalize); target-PCA probe does well on Report, worse than greedy on Confirm, and below-random on Sandbagging. Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars. Abstract claim: directions weighted by a source probe encode source-specific surface features; transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly (capturable in natural language). Main claim: probe OOD robustness largely determined by subspace selection. Background: linear probes expose semantic info but can fail OOD despite strong in-distribution performance. Assertion that behavioral concepts have linear representations but probes often learn spurious correlations; such unreliability is problematic for harmful-interaction monitoring. Method/approach keywords: work in source Q7 coordinates to avoid privileging model latent dims; these coordinates provide data-driven representation structure. Prior findings cited: removing leading components can improve downstream embedding performance (Mu et al., 2018); leading-component projections used as a probing baseline (Kantamneni et al., 2025). Problem framed as selecting dimensions that permit generalization vs. spurious source-trained classification. Pipeline (Fig.1): projection into source N4D basis, filtering candidate Q7 directions, probe training in selected low-dimensional subspace.

Goal: probe OOD robustness largely determined by subspace selection; pipeline projects activations into a source data-driven basis (source N4D / Q7 coordinates), filters candidate directions, and trains probes in the selected low-dim subspace. Prior findings: removing leading components can improve downstream embedding performance; leading-component projections used as a baseline. Related work summarized here: (1) Linear concept directions: studies report cross-dataset linear structure for true/false and other behaviors (Marks & Tegmark 2024; Park et al. 2024 formalize the linear representation hypothesis). Single directions reported for refusal and an “assistant” axis (Arditi et al. 2024; Lu et al. 2026); other work finds population-level directions for honesty/emotion (Zou et al. 2025). (2) Linear probes limits: probes can learn task/surface correlates rather than reveal intrinsic representation; encoded vs. recoverable information distinction; strong in-distribution probes often generalize unevenly—safety evaluation must separate robust internal signals from dataset artifacts. (3) Interpreting features with natural-language explanations: LLM-generated neuron explanations from high-activation examples (Bills et al. 2023), automated sparse-autoencoder feature labeling (Paulo et al. 2025; Bricken et al. 2023), and concept identification + ablation during fine-tuning (Casademunt et al. 2025).

Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6). Use layer-15 residual-stream activations (per Ying et al. 2026); activations averaged over assistant-response tokens. Data: four Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025) datasets — one source (Roleplaying: V8) and three held-out targets: Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), Sandbagging (J9). Only Roleplaying used as source. Labels: annotated by GPT-4o (K8, OpenAI 2024) with mapping honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous responses removed (binary honest vs deceptive). Preprocessing: source activations standardized to zero mean, unit variance; same source statistics used to standardize targets. Dimensionality reduction: PCA on source (N4D), retain leading 100 principal components (PCs Q7); probes trained on projections to subset S of these PCs. Classifiers: logistic regression (regularization λ=10) for all classifiers; comparator (full-representation baseline B8Q) trains on all standardized activations (no PCA). Choice of 100 PCs driven by interpretability comparability (alignment with U9/Bricken et al. 2023 decreases with PC index, so lower-index PCs are easier to interpret), not because low-index PCs generalize best. Error bars denote 95% confidence intervals.

Title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Authors: Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars.
Goal: Can selecting principal components (PCs), i.e., directions in a source activation basis, improve out-of-distribution (OOD) deception detection?
Method overview: Train linear probes (logistic regression) on one source dataset; evaluate on 3 held-out target datasets. Use a target-supervised greedy search that adds PCs according to target performance. Also evaluate ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights. Introduce an LLM judge that scores natural-language PC descriptions without using target data.
Key quantitative claims/results: Greedy, target-supervised search finds 8–15 PCs that nearly match probes trained on target data. Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights does not recover this transferable subspace. Selecting 19 PCs that receive the maximum observed LLM score in both runs (unsupervised by target data) improves transfer on all 3 targets. For two of the targets, this selection closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and the greedy oracle. 
Other terms to track: "full-representation baseline", "greedy oracle", "both runs" (unspecified here), which targets achieve 78% and 25% (unspecified here).

Paper: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection. Goal: improve cross-domain (source->target) deception detection by selecting source-PC directions. Source domain = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (activations extracted; token activations averaged over assistant response to form probe inputs). Labels: GPT-4o assigns Deceptive=1, Honest=0, Ambiguous=-1 (ambiguous examples removed). Representation & PCA: source activations are standardized (source -> zero mean, unit variance) and PCA applied; source statistics are applied to target activations; 100 source PCs retained (S subset of these). Probes: all linear (logistic regression, regularization parameter λ=10); baseline = source-trained probe on full standardized activations; target-trained probes fit on target data. Selection methods: greedy oracle = target-guided greedy adding the PC that most increases target AUROC (reported to find ~8–15 PCs that nearly match target-trained probes); variance control = top-k PCs by variance; source-PCA probe and target-PCA probe use standardized coefficients to rank PCs (standardized coefficient = |coefficient| * PC standard deviation). LLM judge: GPT-5-mini interprets PC positive/negative poles and rates OOD-deception usefulness on a 1–10 scale; observed maximum OOD score = 6. Interp-selection = 19 PCs that received the maximum observed score (6) in both scoring runs; interp-ablated PCs = remaining 81. Evaluation: 5-fold CV on targets (held-out folds used for testing); AUROC reported with 95% CI. Causal validation (intervention/ablation at inference) was not performed. Paper: "Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection..." Targets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Model/representations: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; layer-15 residual-stream activations averaged over assistant response. Preprocessing/PCA: standardize source activations (zero mean/unit var), apply same stats to targets, run PCA on scaled source activations and retain top 100 PCs (PCA-based probes project onto subsets of these 100 PCs). Key results in this part:
- Full-representation source-trained AUROC (target eval): Insider Trading Confirm 0.874, Insider Trading Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606.
- Target-trained probes on the 100-PC subspace achieve AUROCs 0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869 (reported across the three targets).
- Conclusion: 100-PC subspace contains enough target-class information; limited transfer is due to source-learned direction, not missing info.
- Greedy (oracle) PC-selection: searches top-100 PCs, at each step adds PC that most improves target AUROC (probe weights always fit on source; selection uses labeled non-held-out target folds in 5-fold CV); stop when improvement <0.001.
- Greedy average subset sizes: Report 15 PCs, Confirm 8 PCs, Sandbagging 14 PCs.
- Greedy improves baseline AUROC by +0.22 (Report) and +0.23 (Sandbagging), coming close to target-trained performance; variance-ranked k control matches greedy only on Confirm and falls far behind on Report and Sandbagging.
- Section 4.3 initial claim: neither source- nor target-probe coefficient rankings recover greedy transfer performance.

This part: defines standardized coefficient = |probe coeff| * PC std; two rankings: source-PCA (weights from source) and target-PCA (weights from target), both over activations in the source-PCA basis. Source-PCA ranking transfers about like the full-representation baseline; target-PCA ranking does well on Report, worse than greedy on Confirm, and below random on Sandbagging. Paper question: whether selecting subspaces of LM representations improves out-of-distribution (OOD) deception detection. Method: compare probes (classifiers) trained on full representations vs probes using selected directions/subspaces. Two selection approaches highlighted: (1) target-guided selection that uses target labels but does not fit probe weights on them; (2) interpretation-based selection using natural-language interpretations, which requires no target data. Key claims: small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes; selecting directions by source weights, target-class separation, or explained variance does not recover the same transferable subspaces; interpretation-based selection improves over the full-representation baseline on all targets, though how well it recovers varies sharply across targets. Scope/caveats: study uses one model and one source dataset; interpretations are descriptive, not causal. The paper includes a "Glossary." (no glossary content shown in this part).

Goal: test whether selecting subspaces of LM representations improves OOD (transfer) deception detection. Source dataset: Roleplaying (V8). Targets include C2R (Insider Trading Report), W6 (Insider Trading Confirm), J9 (Sandbagging). Model & readout: layer-15 residual-stream activations from Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6), averaged over assistant-response tokens. Preprocessing: standardization = zero-mean/unit-variance using source statistics applied to both source and targets. Dimensionality reduction: PCA / N4D retains the leading 100 source directions (Q7); "PCs" refer to these retained source directions; "leading" = lower index. Probes: logistic regression with λ=10, evaluated by AUROC (F3) with 95% CIs; 5-fold CV where selection uses non-held-out target folds and evaluation uses the held-out fold. Baselines & methods: B8Q = full-representation baseline (source-trained on all standardized activations); Y4 = top-k PCs by variance (variance-ranked subset matched in dimension count); H2 = greedy oracle (target-guided direction selection but probe weights fitted only on source); T6 = source-PCA probe (supplies source coefficient rankings); M9 = target-PCA probe (supplies target coefficient rankings); X4 = standardized coefficient = |coef| * PC_std. Interpretation-based selection: natural-language explanations produced with P2 (GPT-5-mini) and rated by C7 (LLM judge) yielding R5 (OOD score/generalization rating); L2 = interp-selected PC probe (uses directions reaching max R5 in both scoring runs); A7 = interp-ablated PC probe (complement). Decoder alignment uses SAE (U9) decoder features (resource: andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct); Spearman ρ reports relation of PC index to decoder alignment. Scope: one model, one source dataset; interpretations are descriptive, not causal.

Goal: test whether selecting subspaces of LM representations (leading PCA directions) improves OOD (transfer) deception detection. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6); use layer-15 residual-stream activations, averaged over assistant-response tokens. Datasets: Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025) collection — one source Roleplaying (V8) and three held-out targets: Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), Sandbagging (J9). Labeling: GPT-4o (K8) maps honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous responses removed. Preprocessing: source activations standardized to zero-mean/unit-variance; same source statistics applied to targets. Dimensionality reduction: PCA (N4D) on source; retain leading 100 PCs (Q7). Activations may be projected to a subset S of these directions before training/eval. All classifiers are logistic regression (λ=10); full-representation baseline (B8Q) trains on all standardized activations (no PCA truncation). Evaluation: AUROC with 95% CIs; earlier notes indicate 5-fold CV where direction selection uses non-held-out target folds and evaluation uses held-out fold. Interpretability: retained-100 chosen for comparability (not because low-index PCs generalize better); alignment with sparse-autoencoder decoder vectors U9 decreases with index, so lower indices are more interpretable. Interpretation pipeline: explanations generated by P2 (GPT-5-mini), rated by C7 producing R5; L2 = interp-selected PC probe (max R5), A7 = interp-ablated PC probe (complement). Example reported numbers (appendix): C2R — B8Q 0.706, H2 0.929, L2 0.881; J9 — B8Q 0.606, H2 0.832, L2 0.662. Error bars denote 95% CIs.

Goal: evaluate whether source-trained leading-100 PCA subspace (Q7) contains transferable deception signal and whether small source-trained subsets (H2) can match target-trained performance. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; layer-15 residual stream, assistant-response-token-averaged activations; source standardized and same stats applied to targets. Classifiers: logistic regression (λ=10). Metric: AUROC (F3) with 5-fold CV; target-5-fold CV: directions selected on non-held-out target folds, evaluate on held-out fold; search stops when no candidate improves target F3 by >0.001. Retained 100 PCs used for comparisons.

Key reported numbers (Appendix A): B8Q (full-representation) F3: W6=0.874, C2R=0.706, J9=0.606. Target-trained (within retained-100) F3 (5-fold CV): C2R=0.936, W6=0.950, J9=0.869. H2 (target-guided greedy source-trained subset) mean sizes (target CV): C2R=15, W6=8, J9=14; full-target H2 k: C2R=13, W6=7, J9=14. H2 F3 (used for recovery comparison): C2R=0.929, J9=0.832; H2 improvements over B8Q: +0.22 (C2R), +0.23 (J9). Target-trained F3 for corresponding rows: 0.936 (C2R), 0.869 (J9). Variance-selection (Y4) matches H2 only on W6, falls behind on C2R/J9. Rankings: T6 (source-PCA ranking) performs about like B8Q; M9 (target-side ranking using standardized coefficient X4 = |coef|*PC_std) does well on C2R, worse than H2 on W6, and reportedly below random on J9. Interpretability: H2-selected directions have higher-level contrasts that partially transfer; L2 and A7 probes used in interpretation pipeline. Figures: Fig2 (source-trained full, source-trained leading100, target-trained leading100), Fig3 (B8Q, Y4, H2), Fig4 (T6, M9, H2).

Selection & interpretation: For each leading source PC, an LLM judge (C7) is shown the 8 most- and 8 least-activating source examples and writes positive-pole, negative-pole, and whole-direction descriptions and assigns an OOD/generalization rating R5. Two noisy scoring runs; selection retains directions that reach the observed maximum R5 in both runs. Appendix E reports maximum R5 = 6, 2 scoring runs, and 19 directions reaching R5=6 in both runs. L2 = intersection of directions retained across both runs = 19 PCs; A7 = complement (81 PCs); Y4 = variance-ranked subset matched to L2 dimensionality (19 PCs). Controls: A7 and Y4; all are trained as source probes.

Key numbers / performance: B8Q (full) F3: W6=0.874, C2R=0.706, J9=0.606 (from earlier notes). L2 F3 (Appendix A) vs B8Q: C2R 0.881 vs 0.706; J9 0.662 vs 0.606. H2 F3 (earlier) C2R=0.929, J9=0.832. Baseline–H2 gap recovered by L2: C2R 78%, J9 25%. Paper claims L2 exceeds B8Q, Y4, and A7 on all targets; W6 has little headroom and methods (except A7) are roughly tied. H2 interpretation examples: Q7 62, 57, 86 have R5=6; Q7 9 and 81 have R5=3. Appendix E: "Maximum-rated directions among those shared H2 selections" = 3/5; "Maximum-rated directions among the top T6 selections" = 1/5. Paper: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (JMLR 15, 2014). Authors: Nitish Srivastava, Geoffrey Hinton, Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, Ruslan Salakhutdinov. Abstract/main claim: Dropout randomly drops units and their connections during training to prevent co-adaptation; training effectively samples from an exponential number of "thinned" networks. At test time, the effect of averaging these thinned networks is approximated by using a single unthinned network with scaled (smaller) weights. Dropout reportedly reduces overfitting and outperforms other regularization methods, producing major improvements and state-of-the-art results on benchmarks in vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology. Intro notes: deep nets are expressive and prone to overfitting; common regularizers include early stopping, L1/L2 penalties, and soft weight sharing. The paper states that with unlimited computation the best regularizer is averaging predictions over all parameter settings (sentence is cut off in this part). Figure 1 caption: left—standard net with 2 hidden layers; right—example thinned net after dropout where some units are dropped.

steps.notes_before: Paper: Dropout (JMLR 2014). Dropout: randomly remove (drop) hidden and visible units during training to prevent co-adaptation; training samples from an exponential number of 'thinned' networks. Authors propose to approximate an equally weighted geometric mean of predictions of these many learned models (to approach Bayesian averaging) using shared parameters. Simple dropout: retain each unit with probability p (often p=0.5 for hidden units; input units usually have retention closer to 1); p can be chosen by validation. At test time use a single unthinned network with weights scaled by p (Figure 2 shows training: unit present with prob. p and weight w; test: unit always present and weight pw) and the caption asserts test output equals the expected training-time output. Key numbers/claims: exponential number of thinned models, p≈0.5 for hidden, input retention ≈1, test-time weight scaling by p.

steps.notes_before: Paper: Dropout (JMLR 2014). Dropout randomly removes hidden/visible units during training, sampling a 'thinned' network each presentation; weights are shared across thinned models. Paper states there are exponentially many thinned networks (2^n), though this part prints '2n' (likely a typo/inconsistency). Total number of parameters remains O(n^2) or less due to sharing. Training: each update samples a new thinned network; thus each specific thinned net is trained rarely. Test-time: use single unthinned network with outgoing weights scaled by retention probability p (if unit retained with prob p during training, multiply its outgoing weights by p at test time) so that test-time activations match expected training-time activations. Typical choices: p≈0.5 for hidden units; input-unit retention closer to 1; choose p by validation. Dropout not limited to feed-forward nets—paper introduces dropout RBM and compares to standard RBMs, claiming improvements in some respects. Paper structure: Secs 2–9 and Appendix A (practical guide, hyperparameter advice).

Paper: Dropout (JMLR 2014). Core idea: during training randomly remove (drop out) hidden/visible units, sampling a 'thinned' network each presentation; weights are shared across thinned models. There are exponentially many thinned networks (paper elsewhere prints 2^n; an earlier printed '2n' looked like a typo). Total number of parameters remains O(n^2) or less due to sharing. Training: each update samples a new thinned network so any specific thinned net is trained rarely. Test-time: use single unthinned network with outgoing weights scaled by the unit's retention probability p so test activations match expected training activations. Typical p ≈ 0.5 for hidden units; input retention closer to 1; choose p by validation. Dropout not limited to feed-forward nets (paper introduces dropout RBM). Structure: Secs 2–9 and Appendix A (practical guide). New from current part: Motivation analogies — sexual reproduction: dropout viewed as preventing large co-adaptations, forcing each hidden unit to learn useful features that work with random subsets of partners, improving robustness; copying units to resist dropout is a poor solution (analogy to replica codes for noisy channels). Conspiracy analogy: many small conspiracies (small co-adaptations) more robust than one large co-adaptation, hence better generalization under non-stationarity. Related work: Dropout can be seen as regularization via adding noise to hidden units; this idea relates to Denoising Autoencoders (Vincent et al. 2008, 2010) which add noise to unit states.

steps.notes_before: Paper: Dropout trains by randomly dropping units (thinning) and sharing weights across exponentially many sub-networks. Training samples a new thinned net each presentation; backpropagate gradients through that thinned net. At test time use a single unthinned net with weights scaled by retention probabilities (W_test = p W^(l) per layer). Typical choices: drop ~50% hidden units (p_hidden ≈ 0.5), ~20% inputs (p_input ≈ 0.8); DAEs typically use 5% input noise but test-time scaling allows higher noise. Dropout can be applied to hidden layers and other neuron-based architectures (e.g., Boltzmann Machines, RBMs). Interpretation: stochastic regularization / model averaging; related to denoising autoencoders and marginalizing noise. Definition details: network with L hidden layers; y(0)=x; feed-forward recurrence given as z^{(l+1)} = W^{(l+1)} y^{(l)} + b^{(l+1)}, y^{(l+1)} = f(z^{(l+1)}). With dropout: sample r^{(l)} ~ Bernoulli(p) elementwise, form y_e^{(l)} = r^{(l)} * y^{(l)} and use y_e^{(l)} as input to next layer. Loss is minimized stochastically (expected loss); prior adversarial-drop work fixes max number dropped (no hidden-layer models).

Training: dropout nets trained by SGD on ‘‘thinned’’ nets — for each training case in a mini‑batch sample dropout mask, do forward/backprop on that thinned net; gradients averaged over mini‑batch; any case that omits a parameter contributes zero gradient for that parameter. Standard SGD tricks (momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 weight decay) help. Max‑norm regularization: constrain incoming weight vector w at each hidden unit to ||w||2 ≤ c by projecting back into the ball of radius c whenever it exceeds c (c is a tunable hyperparameter). Max‑norm often improves SGD even without dropout; combining dropout + max‑norm + large decaying LR + high momentum gives further gains (intuition: ball constraint prevents blowup so large LR can be used for exploration). Unsupervised pretraining: stacks of RBMs/autoencoders/DBMs can be used; pretraining stays the same, but when finetuning with dropout scale pretrained weights by 1/p so expected output under dropout matches pretraining output. If finetune LR is too large pretrained information can be lost; use smaller LR to retain gains. Experiments: datasets include MNIST, TIMIT, CIFAR‑10/100, SVHN, ImageNet, Reuters‑RCV1, and an Alternative Splicing RNA dataset; more details in Appendix B.

Reported classification results (Table): MNIST (2-layer, 1024 units) Bernoulli 1.08 ±0.04, Gaussian 0.95 ±0.04; CIFAR-10 (3 conv + 2 FC) Bernoulli 12.6 ±0.1, Gaussian 12.5 ±0.1. Section 10 (Multiplicative Gaussian Noise): propose multiplying activations by r0 ∼ N(1,σ^2) (special case N(1,1)); expectation preserved so no test-time scaling required. Equivalence: interpreting dropout as multiplying hi by rb ∈ {0,1/p} (E[rb]=1, Var=(1−p)/p); match moments by choosing Gaussian variance σ^2 = (1−p)/p. Paper claims Gaussian (higher entropy) may work slightly better; Table 10 uses MNIST p_hidden=0.5, p_input=0.8; CIFAR p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5) from input to top; results averaged over 10 seeds. Note: the paper inconsistently states σ^2 = (1−p)/p in one place and appears to set σ = (1−p)/p elsewhere (formatting garble), so it is unclear whether σ or σ^2 was intended.

Paper: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (JMLR 15 (2014) 1929-1958). Submitted 11/13; Published 6/14. Authors: Nitish Srivastava, Geoffrey Hinton, Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, Ruslan Salakhutdinov (Univ. of Toronto). Editor: Yoshua Bengio. Abstract / key claims: Deep nets are powerful but prone to overfitting; dropout randomly drops units and their connections during training to prevent co-adaptation; training with dropout samples from an exponential number of "thinned" networks; at test time, the effect of averaging these thinned networks can be approximated by a single unthinned network with scaled (smaller) weights; dropout significantly reduces overfitting and gives major improvements over other regularization methods; reported state-of-the-art results on benchmarks in vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology. Introduction reiterates dropout as random removal of hidden units, motivation as preventing overfitting; Figure 1 illustrates a standard 2-hidden-layer net and an example thinned net after dropout. (Keep these claims to check consistency with later parts.)

Paper: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (JMLR 2014). Goal: approach Bayesian/model-averaging performance with much less computation by approximating an equally weighted geometric mean of predictions from an exponential number of learned models that share parameters. Motivation: model combination improves performance but averaging many separately trained large nets is computationally infeasible and requires lots of data/hyperparameter tuning. Dropout: randomly drop units (hidden and visible) and their connections during training to (1) prevent co-adaptation/overfitting and (2) efficiently approximate averaging over many thinned networks. Mechanism: in simplest form, each unit is retained independently with fixed probability p (can be chosen via validation or set to 0.5, often near-optimal for many networks/tasks). For input units, optimal retention p is usually closer to 1. At test time, units are always present and outgoing weights are multiplied by p (Figure 2), so the test-time network approximates the expected output of the stochastic training process. Key claims to check later: p=0.5 recommendation, input p near 1, exponential number of thinned nets, test-time weight scaling accurately approximates averaging, empirical improvements across tasks/benchmarks.

steps.notes_before: Dropout: randomly drop units to sample a thinned network each presentation. Paper treats a net with n units as having exponentially many thinned nets (intended 2^n), though this part repeatedly writes '2n' (inconsistent with 'exponentially many'). Thinned nets share weights, so total parameters remain O(n^2) (or less). Training samples a new thinned net per case; each particular thinned net is trained rarely. At test time, use the full network with outgoing weights scaled by retention probability p so that a hidden unit's actual output matches its expected output under training dropout; this approximates averaging over the thinned nets. Dropout applies beyond feed-forward nets (introduce dropout RBM). Paper outlines sections: motivation, prior work, formal model, training algorithm, experiments, analysis, Dropout RBM, marginalizing dropout, and practical guide in Appendix A. Key claims to check later: recommended p values (often p=0.5 for hidden units, input p nearer 1), test-time weight scaling approximates model averaging, and empirical gains across domains.

Dropout: randomly drop units each presentation to sample thinned networks. Paper intends exponentially many thinned nets (2^n) but earlier text sometimes wrote '2n' (inconsistent). Thinned nets share weights; total params remain O(n^2) or less. Training samples a new thinned net per case; any particular thinned net is trained rarely. Test time: use the full network with outgoing weights scaled by retention probability p to approximate averaging over thinned nets. Recommended p often 0.5 for hidden units; input p nearer 1. Paper outline: motivation, prior work, formal model, training algorithm, experiments, analysis, Dropout RBM, marginalizing dropout, Appendix A with practical guide. Current part (Motivation): analogies to sexual reproduction and to conspiracies — sexual reproduction breaks complex co-adaptations but favors 'mix-ability' and robustness; similarly dropout forces hidden units to work with random subsets of other units, reducing co-adaptations and encouraging useful standalone features; conspiracy analogy: many small conspiracies (small co-adaptations) are more robust than one large conspiracy (big co-adaptation). Related work (start): dropout can be seen as regularization by adding noise to hidden units, related to Denoising Autoencoders (Vincent et al.).

steps.notes_before: Dropout extends input noise/DAE ideas to hidden layers and supervised learning; can apply to other neuron-based models (e.g., Boltzmann Machines). Typical settings reported: DAEs best with 5% noise; with dropout + test-time weight scaling, authors use much higher noise — dropping 20% of inputs (p_input=0.8) and 50% of hidden units (p_hidden=0.5) often optimal. Consider deterministic counterparts by marginalizing noise; references: van der Maaten et al. (blankout), Wang & Manning (speeding up by marginalizing), Chen et al. (DAE marginalization). Also mentions adversarial-dropout style work (Globerson & Roweis; Dekel et al.) that fixes max drops. Model description: network with L hidden layers, y(0)=x. Feed-forward (standard): z_i^{(l+1)} = w_i^{(l+1)T} y^{(l)} + b_i^{(l+1)}, y_i^{(l+1)} = f(z_i^{(l+1)}). With dropout: r_j^{(l)} ~ Bernoulli(p); e^{(l)} = r^{(l)} * y^{(l)}; use e^{(l)} as input to next layer; backprop through sampled sub-network. At test time use scaled weights W_test^{(l)} = p W^{(l)} (no dropout). Note: the paper inconsistently states l ∈ {1..L} then uses l ∈ {0..L−1} in formulas (indexing mismatch).

Dropout: at train time sample thinned nets by dropping units (r_j^(l) ~ Bernoulli(p)); at test time scale weights by p (W_test = pW). Paper has an indexing mismatch earlier (uses l in {1..L} then {0..L-1}). Training: use SGD on sampled thinned networks per training case in minibatch; average gradients over cases; cases that don't use a parameter contribute zero gradient. Standard SGD improvements (momentum, annealed learning rates, L2) help with dropout. Max-norm regularization: constrain incoming weight vector for each hidden unit to ||w||_2 ≤ c; implemented by projecting w onto ball of radius c when it exceeds c; c tuned on validation; typically helps even without dropout and allows using large learning rates safely. Pretraining: use RBMs/autoencoders/DBMs to leverage unlabeled data. When finetuning pretrained nets with dropout, scale pretrained weights up by factor 1/p so expected output under dropout matches pretraining; dropout can destroy pretrained info if finetune learning rates are too large—use smaller learning rates to retain pretrained information. Experiments: report that dropout improved generalization on all datasets tested; datasets listed include MNIST, TIMIT, CIFAR-10/100, SVHN, ImageNet, Reuters-RCV1, Alternative Splicing (Xiong et al., 2011). Appendix B has detailed experiment descriptions. (From earlier parts: authors often use p_input=0.8 (drop 20%) and p_hidden=0.5; DAEs typically used ~5% input noise.)

Section 7 (effect of dropout): 7.1 Co-adaptation: autoencoders with one hidden layer of 256 ReLU units on MNIST — Figure 7a (no dropout) vs 7b (dropout p=0.5). Both had similar test reconstruction errors; without dropout units co-adapt and features are less interpretable; with dropout units detect edges/strokes. 7.2 Sparsity: dropout yields sparser activations even without sparsity regularizers. From test minibatch histograms (Figure 8): mean activation per unit ~2.0 without dropout, ~0.7 with dropout; activation distribution has large mass away from zero without dropout but a sharp peak at zero with dropout. 7.3: p is defined as probability of retaining a unit; next they study varying p in two setups: (1) fixed number of hidden units, (2) change number so expected retained units constant.

7.3 Varying retention probability p (p = probability of retaining a unit). Two experiment types:
- Fixed architecture: 784-2048-2048-2048-10, no input dropout. Vary p; small p → very few units active during training → underfitting (training error high). Test error decreases as p increases, is roughly flat for 0.4 ≤ p ≤ 0.8, then increases as p → 1 (Figure 9a).
- Constant pn: hold pn constant (n = number of hidden units per layer) so expected active units after dropout equal across architectures. Set pn = 256 for first two hidden layers, pn = 512 for the last. Small p implies larger n; test nets (at test time) have different sizes. Figure 9b: errors for small p are much reduced compared to fixed-n; e.g., p=0.1 fell from 2.7% (Fig 9a) to 1.7% (Fig 9b). Best p ~0.6 for these pn choices; default p=0.5 near-optimal.
7.4 Effect of dataset size: MNIST experiments with architecture 784-1024-1024-2048-10. Dropout p(hidden)=0.5, p(input)=0.8. Vary training set size ∈ {100, 500, 1K, 5K, 10K, 50K}. For extremely small sets (100, 500) dropout gives no improvement (still overfits). As dataset size increases, benefit of dropout grows then declines — a ‘‘sweet spot’’ exists (Figure 10).
7.5 Monte-Carlo model averaging vs weight scaling: weight-scaling proposed as efficient test-time approximate averaging; Monte-Carlo sampling of k dropout nets is more correct but expensive (plot shows small differences in test error ~1.20–1.35%).

errors.claim: “QX2 linear regression is, in expectation, ridge regression with a particular penalty matrix: a dimension’s standard deviation scales its weight cost, squeezing more strongly the weights of highly variable dimensions.”
errors.evidence:
The math given immediately after is

\[\n\underset{\mathbf w}{\operatorname{minimize}}\quad
\|\mathbf y-p\mathbf X\mathbf w\|^2+
p(1-p)\|\mathbf\Gamma\mathbf w\|^2,
\]

\[\n\mathbf\Gamma
=\left(\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X)\right)^{1/2}.
\]
errors.explanation: The formula shows Gamma = (diag(X^T X))^{1/2}, i.e. Gamma_jj = sqrt(sum_i X_{ij}^2). Title: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting". Authors: Nitish Srivastava, Geoffrey Hinton, Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, Ruslan Salakhutdinov; Dept. of Computer Science, University of Toronto. Journal: JMLR 15 (2014). Header lists pages 1929–1958 while page map lists pages 1930–1955 (internal inconsistency noted). Abstract summary: introduces dropout (called "QX2: dropout") — a training procedure that temporarily removes randomly selected units and their connections, inhibiting excessive co-adaptation and effectively sampling exponentially many parameter-sharing thinned networks. At test time a single unthinned network with reduced weights approximates the averaged predictions of these thinned networks. Claims dropout substantially reduces overfitting versus other regularizers and yields major improvements, achieving state-of-the-art performance on many benchmarks in supervised vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology.

steps.notes_before: Title: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al., UToronto). Header/page-number inconsistency noted earlier. Dropout (QX2) randomly removes units/connections during training, producing exponentially many (2^n for n units) thinned networks; parameters are shared so total distinct parameters retained are O(n^2) or fewer. With unlimited computation, posterior-weighted averaging over parameters is ideal; the paper claims its method approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of these thinned models' predictions (introduction) — earlier abstract wording said it "approximates the averaged predictions", a potential arithmetic vs geometric-mean wording mismatch. Every presentation samples/trains a new thinned member; individual members are rarely trained thoroughly. Practical inference: T6R (weight scaling) uses one unthinned network at test time; X9M refers to Monte-Carlo model averaging (more expensive). Claims T6R gives much lower generalization error than other regularizers across tasks. Method extends to graphical models, e.g., Dropout RBM (B8T) from RBMs (U2L). Paper map: §2 motivation; §3 prior work; §4 formal model; §5 training algorithm; §6 experiments; §7 network/hyperparameter interactions; §8 Dropout RBMs; §9 marginalization; Appendix A practical guidance.

Title: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al.). Earlier: header/page-number inconsistency noted. Method overview: dropout (QX2) randomly removes units/connections during training, producing exponentially many (2^n) thinned networks; parameters are shared so total distinct parameters are O(n^2) or fewer. Training samples/train different thinned networks; individual thinned members rarely trained thoroughly. Test-time inference: T6R = weight-scaling using one unthinned network; X9M = Monte-Carlo model averaging (more expensive). Paper claims T6R yields much lower generalization error than other regularizers across tasks. Extensions: Dropout RBM (B8T). Paper map: §2 motivation; §3 prior work; §4 formal model; §5 training algorithm; §6 experiments; §7 interactions; §8 Dropout RBMs; §9 marginalization; Appendix A guidance. New from §2 (Motivation): authors use biological analogy—sexual vs asexual reproduction—and cite Livnat et al. (2010) arguing selection can favor gene "mix-ability" rather than individual-fitness optimization. Dropout is analogous: hidden units face randomly selected partners, which favors independently useful, robust features and reduces complex co-adaptations. Replicating units many times is deemed a poor robustness fix (analogy to replica codes and noisy channels). Conspiracy analogy: many small cooperating subsets are more robust under non-stationarity than a single large co-adapted set; complex co-adaptations may overfit training data and fail on novel test data.

Title: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al.). Method: dropout (QX2) randomly removes units/connections during training producing ~2^n thinned networks; parameters shared so distinct params O(n^2). Training: each SGD update samples a thinned network; individual thinned members rarely trained thoroughly. Test-time inference: T6R = weight-scaling using one unthinned network; X9M = Monte-Carlo model averaging (more expensive). Paper claims T6R gives much lower generalization error than other regularizers across tasks. Motivation (§2): biological analogy (mix-ability), reduces co-adaptations. Related work (§3): dropout interpretable as noise in hidden-unit states, extends denoising autoencoders (Vincent et al. 2008/2010) — effective hidden-layer corruption, model-averaging view, supervised/unsupervised use, applicable to Boltzmann Machines. Table: S2H (DAE) typical best noise ~5%; QX2 often optimal input-unit removal ~20%; QX2 often optimal hidden-unit removal ~50%. Adversarial-removal alternatives (Globerson & Roweis 2006; Dekel et al. 2010) consider worst-case removals under a budget and have no hidden units. Analytic marginalization can give deterministic regularizers in simple cases; van der Maaten et al. (2013) studied exponential-family input-noise (blankout) limited to models without hidden layers; Chen et al. (2012) studied marginalization for DAEs; Wang & Manning (2013) proposed marginalization to speed up dropout. Section map: §2 motivation; §3 prior work; §4 formal model; §5 training algorithm; §6 experiments; §7 interactions; §8 Dropout RBMs; §9 marginalization; Appendix A guidance.

Paper: Dropout regularization. Key idea: during training randomly delete (zero) units (hidden and/or visible) to sample many thinned subnetworks; parameters shared across subnetworks. Retention choices are independent Bernoulli variables with common probability p (can be chosen by validation). Typical defaults: hidden-unit retention p≈0.5 (i.e. ~50% removal); input-unit removal often ~20% (retention p≈0.8) — input retention usually nearer full. Training: each SGD update samples r^{(l)} (vector of independent Bernoulli(p)) and forms \tilde y^{(l)} = r^{(l)} * y^{(l)}; forward: z_i^{(l+1)} = w_i^{(l+1)} \tilde y^{(l)} + b_i^{(l+1)}, y_i^{(l+1)} = f(z_i^{(l+1)}). Backprop passes gradients through the sampled subnetwork. Notation: y^{(0)}=x; L hidden layers (indexed 1..L); feed-forward written for l=0..L-1 producing layer l+1. Activation f can be any (e.g. logistic). Test-time inference: no dropout; use one unthinned network with outgoing weights scaled by p: W_test^{(l)} = p W^{(l)} (equivalently unit outputs' expected training contribution equals test-time contribution with scaled weights). Figures illustrate training (stochastic gates r) vs testing (weights scaled by p). Other parts: training samples many subnetworks per SGD update; Monte-Carlo averaging at test-time is an alternative to weight-scaling but more expensive.

Part 5: QX2 (dropout) gives significant gains; combining it with high momentum, large decaying learning rates, and an incoming-weight constraint (V9C = max-norm) gives further improvement. V9C enforces ||w||_2 <= c with projection to the ball surface when exceeded; c is tuned by validation. Proposed optimization account claims large learning rates are safe inside the fixed-radius ball; QX2 provides noise exploration; learning rates decay to smaller steps. SGD differs from standard training only by per-case sampled thinned networks: each mini-batch case uses its own sampled network; gradients averaged across cases; a case not using a parameter contributes zero. Momentum, annealed (decaying) learning rates and other heuristics remain useful. Unsupervised pretraining is unchanged, but before QX2 finetuning pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p so each unit’s expected random-removal output matches its pretraining output. Smaller finetuning learning rates help preserve pretrained information. Pretraining (with unlabeled data) can improve over random init; applicable to stacked U2L, autoencoders, DBMs for finetuning.

errors.claim: “QX2 linear regression is, in expectation, ridge regression with a particular penalty matrix: a dimension’s standard deviation scales its weight cost, squeezing more strongly the weights of highly variable dimensions.”
errors.evidence:
The math given immediately after is

\[\n\underset{\mathbf w}{\operatorname{minimize}}\quad
\|\mathbf y-p\mathbf X\mathbf w\|^2+
p(1-p)\|\mathbf\Gamma\mathbf w\|^2,
\]

\[\n\mathbf\Gamma
=\left(\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X)\right)^{1/2}.
\]
errors.explanation: The formula shows Gamma = (diag(X^T X))^{1/2}, i.e. Gamma_jj = sqrt(sum_i X_{ij}^2). That is not the sample standard deviation (which is sqrt((1/N) sum_i (X_{ij}-mean_j)^2)) unless the columns are mean-centered and scaled by 1/√N. The textual claim that a feature's standard deviation scales its penalty is therefore imprecise/inconsistent with the exact formula given (no centering or 1/N normalization is stated).

steps.notes_before:
Part 8 recap: B8T is a dropout-like mixture on an RBM-style U2L model with per-hidden retention r_j ~ Bernoulli(p); conditionals factorize; notation mismatch found earlier in biases a/b. Empirical: B8T (p≈0.5) gives coarser but sparse features and few dead units. QX2 denotes dropout-like corruption; earlier sections report improvements on SVHN/CIFAR/ImageNet/TIMIT and sparser autoencoder/FF representations.

Part 9 summary: Marginalized (deterministic) QX2 models avoid Monte-Carlo noise and admit gradients of the marginalized loss. Linear regression: E[||y-(R*X)w||^2] = ||y - p X w||^2 + p(1-p) ||Gamma w||^2 with Gamma = (diag(X^T X))^{1/2}; equivalently with \tilde w = p w: ||y - X \tilde w||^2 + ((1-p)/p) ||Gamma \tilde w||^2. Thus dropout on inputs yields a ridge-like penalty whose overall strength grows as p decreases, and per-feature strength is proportional to sqrt(sum of squares per feature) (paper text describes this as 'standard deviation' scaling, but the formula uses unnormalized sum-of-squares unless data are centered/scaled).

Part 9.2: For logistic regression and deep nets, closed-form marginalization is hard; approximate Gaussian assumptions on pre-activation distributions give tractable mean/variance computations, but assumptions weaken with added layers so results don't directly transfer to deep networks.

Part 14: Multiplicative Gaussian (D4K) vs Bernoulli dropout (P7V). Preliminary results slightly favor Gaussian: H4Z errors P7V 1.08±0.04 vs D4K 0.95±0.04; J3V P7V 12.6±0.1 vs D4K 12.5±0.1. Protocol: H4Z hidden p=0.5, H4Z input p=0.8; J3V p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5) (input→top). D4K per-layer std σ = sqrt((1-p)/p). Results averaged over 10 random seeds. Multiplicative Gaussian r'~N(1,σ^2) is equivalent to additive noise h_i + h_i r with r~N(0,σ^2); choosing σ^2=(1-p)/p matches first two moments of the rescaled Bernoulli multiplier r_b (r_b=1/p w.p. p, 0 otherwise) which has E[r_b]=1 and Var[r_b]=(1-p)/p. Note relationship to earlier parameterizations: the {0,1} Bernoulli has Var=p(1-p) while the rescaled {0,1/p} representation has Var=(1-p)/p; Part 9's linear-regression penalty used both forms via ~tilde w = p w, yielding an equivalent ((1-p)/p) factor in the penalty on ~tilde w. Unchanged expected activations (E=1) remove the need for test-time rescaling.

Part 14 summary: Multiplicative Gaussian (D4K) vs Bernoulli dropout (P7V). Preliminary results slightly favor Gaussian: H4Z errors P7V 1.08±0.04 vs D4K 0.95±0.04; J3V P7V 12.6±0.1 vs D4K 12.5±0.1. Protocol: H4Z hidden p=0.5, H4Z input p=0.8; J3V p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5) (input→top). D4K per-layer std σ = sqrt((1-p)/p). Results averaged over 10 random seeds. Multiplicative Gaussian r'~N(1,σ^2) ≡ additive noise h_i + h_i r with r~N(0,σ^2); choose σ^2=(1-p)/p to match first two moments of rescaled Bernoulli multiplier r_b (r_b=1/p w.p. p, 0 otherwise) which has E[r_b]=1 and Var[r_b]=(1-p)/p. Note: {0,1} Bernoulli Var=p(1-p) vs rescaled {0,1/p} Var=(1-p)/p. Part 9: linear-regression penalty used both forms via ~w = p w, yielding an equivalent ((1-p)/p) factor in the penalty on ~w. Unchanged expected activations (E=1) remove need for test-time rescaling. New (Part 15) conclusion notes: large-model construction repeatedly samples/trains smaller submodels from an easily overfitted model; U2L fits this construction and B8T shows desirable empirical properties. QX2 methods claim state-of-the-art on A2F, K9D, W6R, H4Z and considerable improvement over standard nets on other collections. Training typically takes 2–3× longer than standard networks of same architecture; noisy parameter updates are a major cause because each training case samples a different random architecture and computed gradients are not gradients of the final inference architecture. Stochasticity likely prevents overfitting, implying an overfitting–training-time trade-off: more training time permits stronger QX2 and less overfitting. Noise marginalization gives some benefits without stochasticity via an expectation-equivalent regularizer; linear regression yields a modified Y5F, while equivalent regularizers for more complex models are unclear. Accelerating QX2 is left to future work.

Earlier empirical comparisons: multiplicative Gaussian (D4K) vs rescaled Bernoulli dropout (P7V) slightly favor Gaussian: H4Z error P7V 1.08±0.04 vs D4K 0.95±0.04; J3V P7V 12.6±0.1 vs D4K 12.5±0.1. Protocols: H4Z hidden p=0.5, H4Z input p=0.8; J3V p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5) (input→top). D4K uses per-layer σ^2=(1-p)/p so multiplicative r'~N(1,σ^2) matches first two moments of rescaled Bernoulli r_b (1/p w.p. p, 0 otherwise), both have E=1 and Var=(1-p)/p. Linear-regression analysis: using ~w = p w yields an equivalent ((1-p)/p) penalty; unchanged expected activations remove need for test-time rescaling. Conclusions: large-model construction repeatedly samples/trains smaller submodels (U2L fits this), QX2 shows strong empirical performance / SOTA on several collections; training usually takes ~2–3× longer due to noisy parameter updates (each case samples different random architecture), stochasticity reduces overfitting (overfitting–training-time tradeoff). Appendix A heuristics: QX2 layer width ≳ n/p for a standard-net layer of size n (otherwise removing units reduces capacity: only p·n units remain in expectation). Learning: use much larger LR (typically 10–100× standard-net optimal) and higher momentum (common 0.9; QX2 ~0.95–0.99). V9C: bound each hidden unit's incoming-weight-vector norm; c typically 3–4. Retention p: hidden typical 0.5–0.8, inputs typically ~0.8; simple default p=0.5; input optimum generally closer to 1.

Repro code: http://www.cs.toronto.edu/~nitish/dropout; GPU libs cudamat and cuda-convnet. Key prior results: multiplicative Gaussian (D4K) slightly better than rescaled Bernoulli (P7V): H4Z P7V 1.08±0.04 vs D4K 0.95±0.04; J3V P7V 12.6±0.1 vs D4K 12.5±0.1. D4K uses per-layer variance σ^2=(1-p)/p so N(1,σ^2) matches first two moments of rescaled Bernoulli (E=1, Var=(1-p)/p). Linear-regression view: using ~ w = p w yields ((1-p)/p) penalty; no test-time rescaling needed. QX2/large-model heuristics: sample/train many thinned submodels; training ≈2–3× longer; layer width ≳ n/p; use much larger LR (10–100× standard) and higher momentum (0.95–0.99); V9C (incoming-weight norm) typically c=3–4; retention p: hidden 0.5–0.8, inputs ≈0.8 (default p=0.5).

Appendix B experiment settings:
- H4Z (digits): held-out validation 10,000; weight-update endpoint 1,000,000 (both tuning and final combined-data runs); architecture sweep depths 2–4, uniform widths 1024 or 2048 (6 combos); hidden p=0.5, input p=0.8; final momentum 0.95; V9C c=2 for all layers; extra experiments with 2/3 layers and 4096/8192 units; largest two-layer model >65M params. Regularizer-comparison arch 784-1024-1024-2048-10; fixed-width arch 784-2048-2048-2048-10; fixed-expected-width pn first two=256, last=512; data-size comparisons used training sets of 100, 500, 1K, 5K, 10K, 50K.

- A2F (large image set): validation 6000 (400/class from standard portion, 200/class from additional); 3 conv layers (96,128,256 filters, 5x5 RF, stride1), each followed by 3x3 pooling stride2; two FC layers of 2048 units; activations F3N; retention p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5); V9C c=4 (all weights); momentum 0.95. Validation tuned hyperparams; final training kept validation separate and the best-val model used for test.

- J3V & W6R: 50K train, 10K test; 10 and 100 classes respectively; 5K validation; then combined final training as H4Z. Preproc: per-channel global contrast norm then ZCA; architecture and retention match A2F; input-layer LR smaller.

- N8Q (speech): 680 speakers across 8 dialects, 10 sentences each; Kaldi log-filter banks; monophone forced alignment; predict central-frame from frame windows; mean-centered, unit-variance inputs; no speaker-dependent ops.

Title: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting". Journal of Machine Learning Research 15 (2014) 1929–1958. Submitted 11/13; Published 6/14. Authors: Nitish Srivastava, Geoffrey Hinton, Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, Ruslan Salakhutdinov. Editor: Yoshua Bengio. Copyright © 2014 (authors). Front-matter lists figures, sections §2–§11, Acknowledgments, Appendices A and B, many tables/figures. Abstract: introduces dropout (referred to as "(QX2: dropout)") — during training randomly remove selected units and their connections (thinned networks) to inhibit excessive co-adaptation; this samples exponentially many parameter-sharing thinned networks. At test time, a single unthinned network with reduced weights approximates the averaged predictions of the thinned networks. Claims that, relative to other regularizers, dropout substantially reduces overfitting and yields major improvements, achieving state-of-the-art performance on many benchmarks in supervised vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology. Keywords: neural networks, regularization, model combination, deep learning.

Title: 'Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting' (JMLR 2014). Authors: Srivastava, Hinton, Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Salakhutdinov. Dropout (QX2): during training randomly remove selected units (thinned networks); each presentation samples a thinned member. Paper claims dropout approximates averaging over exponentially many (2^n) thinned networks with parameter sharing (parameters retained O(n^2)). Inference: practical weight scaling uses one unthinned network; alternative is Monte-Carlo averaging. Intro/map inconsistencies noted: mapping lists §2–§9 + Appendix A, earlier front-matter listed §2–§11 + Appendices A & B. Current part (§2 Motivation): draws analogy to sexual vs asexual reproduction and cites Livnat et al. (2010) idea of selection for gene "mix-ability" (genes that work well with random partners). Claim: QX2-trained hidden units face randomly selected partners, so they learn independently useful, robust features and avoid complex co-adaptations; replicating units is a poor robustness fix. Conspiracy analogy: many small conspiracies more robust under non-stationarity than one large co-adapted set. No internal contradictions found between this part and prior notes.

Paper: 'Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting' (Srivastava et al.). QX2 = dropout: during training randomly remove units (sample a thinned network each presentation); dropout approximates averaging over 2^n thinned networks with parameter sharing. Test-time inference: practical weight-scaling uses one unthinned network; alternative is Monte-Carlo averaging. §2 motivation: sexual-reproduction / mixability analogy — dropout-trained units face random partners, avoid complex co-adaptations; copying units is a poor robustness fix. (Earlier minor inconsistencies flagged: wording about an "equally weighted geometric mean" vs arithmetic mean for the averaging approximation; front-matter listed differing section ranges.) §3 Related Work: Interprets dropout as noise in hidden-unit states giving regularization, extending denoising autoencoders (S2H = DAEs, Vincent et al.) by effecting hidden-layer corruption, offering a model-averaging view, usable supervised/unsupervised and applicable to other neuron-based models (e.g., Boltzmann machines). Test-time T6R permits much higher noise than usually best for DAEs. Reported noise levels: S2H typical best 5%; QX2 often optimal input-unit removal 20%; QX2 often optimal hidden-unit removal 50%. Adversarial alternative (Globerson & Roweis; Dekel et al.) selects removals up to a max number (models have no hidden units). Marginalizing dropout yields deterministic regularizers in simple cases; van der Maaten et al. (2013) studied blankout noise but limited to models without hidden layers; Chen et al. (2012) examined marginalization for DAEs; Wang & Manning (2013) proposed marginalization to speed up dropout.

errors.claim: For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.
errors.evidence: "y_i^{(l+1)} = f(z_i^{(l+1)})" (nonlinear activation) and "z_i^{(l+1)} = w_i^{(l+1)} (r^{(l)} * y^{(l)}) + b_i^{(l+1)}" and "At inference, no units are removed and W_test^{(l)} = p W^{(l)}."
errors.explanation: The paper allows arbitrary (possibly nonlinear) activations f, so in general E[f(z)] != f(E[z]). The equality with scaled test weights holds for the linear preactivation (E[z] = z_test with W_test = pW), not for the post-nonlinearity output as the claim unqualifiedly states.

steps.notes_before: Dropout: randomly remove units during training; sample thinned subnetworks each presentation. §4 model: retention variables r_j^{(l)} are independent Bernoulli(p); thinned outputs \tilde{y}^{(l)} = r^{(l)} * y^{(l)}; feedforward z_i^{(l+1)} = w_i^{(l+1)} \tilde{y}^{(l)} + b_i^{(l+1)}; y_i^{(l+1)} = f(z_i^{(l+1)}) with f arbitrary (e.g., sigmoid). Hidden and visible units can be dropped. At inference use no dropout and scale weights: W_test^{(l)} = p W^{(l)} (practical weight-scaling). Paper's opening sentence of §4 asserts expected training "output" equals test-time output under scaled weights — mathematically this holds for expected preactivation (linear input) but not generally for outputs after a nonlinear f (E[f(z)] != f(E[z])). Earlier notes: typical defaults often p≈0.5 for hidden units, input retention nearer complete (e.g., input-drop ~20% => p≈0.8); alternative to weight-scaling is Monte Carlo averaging.

Dropout/QX2: training samples thinned subnetworks each presentation; retention variables r_j^(l) ~ Bernoulli(p); thinned outputs \tilde{y}^{(l)} = r^{(l)} * y^{(l)}; preactivation z_i^{(l+1)} = w_i^{(l+1)} \tilde{y}^{(l)} + b; y_i^{(l+1)} = f(z_i^{(l+1)}). At test time use no dropout and practical weight-scaling W_test^(l) = p W^(l). (Paper earlier asserted expected training “output” equals test-time output under scaled weights—this is exact for preactivations but not generally for post-nonlinearity outputs.) Typical defaults: p≈0.5 for hidden, p≈0.8 for inputs; Monte Carlo averaging is an alternative. QX2 alone gives significant gains; combining with high momentum, large decaying learning rates, and incoming-weight constraint V9C (max-norm) gives further boost. V9C: enforce ||w||_2 ≤ c and project to surface when exceeded; c is validation-tuned. SGD with dropout: each mini-batch case is propagated through its own sampled thinned network; gradients are averaged across cases and a case not using a parameter contributes zero. Momentum, annealed learning rates and Y5F remain useful. Pretraining is unchanged; before QX2 finetuning multiply pretrained weights by 1/p to match each unit’s expected random-removal output to its pretraining output. For finetuning pretrained nets use smaller learning rates (larger rates used for random init can erase pretrained information). Unlabeled-data pretraining via stacked U2L, autoencoders or DBMs is supported.

QX2 = dropout: retention r_j^(l) ~ Bernoulli(p); thinned outputs \tilde{y}=r*y; preactivation z=w\tilde{y}+b; y=f(z). At test time use no dropout and weight-scaling W_test^(l)=p W^(l). Typical p≈0.5 hidden, p≈0.8 inputs. Pretraining unchanged; before QX2 finetuning multiply pretrained weights by 1/p. Combine QX2 with high momentum, annealed learning rates, and incoming-weight constraint V9C (max-norm) for further gains. Experiments: claim generalization improved over non-QX2 on every tested data set (vision, speech, text, genetics). Data sets (Table 1): H4Z (MNIST) 784 dim, 60K train/10K test; A2F (SVHN) 3072, 600K/26K; J3V/W6R (CIFAR-10/100) 3072, 60K/10K (table lumps them); K9D (ImageNet) 65536, 1.2M/150K; N8Q (TIMIT) 2520, 1.1M frames/58K frames; M5X (Reuters) 2000, 200K/200K; Z7P (splicing) 1014, 2932/733. Image results: state of the art on five vision collections uses QX2. H4Z (Table 2): Standard NN 1.60%; SVM RBF 1.40%; QX2 NN logistic 1.35%; QX2+ReLU 1.25%; QX2+V9C (ReLU) down to 1.06/1.04/1.01/0.95 as size increases; Goodfellow maxout 0.94%; pretrained G6W finetune 1.18, E5Q finetune 0.96; G6W+QX2 0.92; E5Q+QX2 0.79 (best reported permutation-invariant). Fig.4: test-error-vs-weight-updates (0..1e6); vertical ticks listed 1.0,1.5,2.0,2.5. A2F: conv nets benefit from QX2 in FC layers and more when applied to conv layers; L8J (maxout) adds further gains; argument: lower-layer corruption reduces overfitting in higher FC layers.

Part 9 (current): deterministic noise-marginalized models need no randomness and allow gradients (contrast to Monte-Carlo QX2). Linear regression: masking inputs R (Bernoulli(p) per element) gives marginalized objective E_R ||y - (R*X)w||^2 = ||y - p X w||^2 + p(1-p)||Γ w||^2 with Γ = (diag(X^T X))^{1/2}. With ṽ = p w, alternative form is ||y - X ṽ||^2 + ((1-p)/p)||Γ ṽ||^2. Logistic/deep nets: closed-form marginalization hard; approximate marginalization models assume Gaussian distributions for unit inputs/gradients with computable means/variances, but applicability to deep nets is limited (text contains a logical wording error about assumptions getting "weaker" with depth).

Paper summary: Introduces dropout — randomly removing units and their connections during training, which samples many smaller networks that share weights. At test time, a single full network with scaled weights approximates the ensemble of sampled networks. Reports improvements on image, speech, text, and alternative-splicing tasks. Compares dropout with other regularizers and Bayesian neural networks. Studies learned features, sparsity, dropout rates, network size, training-set size, and test-time averaging; finds Dropout Restricted Boltzmann Machines learn qualitatively different features and sparser representations. For linear regression, marginalizing dropout yields a modified ridge-regression objective. Preliminary experiments compare Bernoulli dropout to multiplicative Gaussian noise. Limitation noted: training time typically 2–3× longer than standard networks with the same architecture.

Paper introduces dropout: during training randomly remove units and their incoming/outgoing connections (Bernoulli dropout uses binary vars that equal 1 with probability p, the retention probability). At test time the ensemble is approximated by a single deterministic model via weight scaling (multiply a unit’s outgoing weights by p) or by marginalizing dropout noise (deterministic dropout model); Monte-Carlo dropout/model averaging samples thinned networks at test time. Gaussian (multiplicative) dropout multiplies activations by Gaussian noise; paper compares Bernoulli and Gaussian variants. For linear regression, marginalized dropout is equivalent in expectation to a modified ridge (Tikhonov) regression. Dropout-RBMs are RBMs augmented with binary retention variables; CD-1/Contrastive Divergence used for RBM training; partition function Z(θ) appears in RBM formulation. Code Quality (alternative-splicing task) is the negative KL-divergence metric (higher is better). Other key methods/terms: DBN/DBM pretraining, max-norm constraint (bound hidden-unit incoming weight norms), L1/L2 weight penalties, KL-sparsity regularizer, ReLU and maxout units, pooling (max, L2, L4) in image models, max-pooling after conv layers, permutation-invariant vs 2-D MNIST settings, Top-1/Top-5 ImageNet error definitions, PCA/ZCA whitening used in preprocessing, mix-ability measure for genes. Noted limitation: training time typically 2–3× longer than standard networks with same architecture.

Notation and key definitions: L (# hidden layers), l (layer index); i,j (unit/dim/data indices). x = network input (y^(0)). z^(l) = inputs to layer l; y^(l) = outputs; ~y^(l) = outputs after elementwise dropout mask. W^(l), w_i^(l), b^(l) = layer weights, unit incoming weights, biases.
