Paper metadata: Title Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting. Authors: Nitish Srivastava, Geoffrey Hinton, Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, Ruslan Salakhutdinov (Univ. of Toronto). Editor: Yoshua Bengio. Journal: JMLR 15 (2014) 1929–1958.
Main idea: During training randomly remove units+connections (Bernoulli retention p) sampling exponential number of thinned networks; at test time use one unthinned network with scaled weights (W_test = p W) to approximate average predictions. Dropout claimed to reduce overfitting and prevent co-adaptation.
Claims/evidence (reported): improves across domains — image results in Tables 2–6; TIMIT rows in Table 7; Reuters: 31.05% (no dropout) -> 29.62% (with dropout) in Sect. 6.3; alternative-splicing rows 440 and 567 bits in Table 8; Table 9: dropout improves over other regularizers in all rows; Dropout+Max-norm = 1.05% vs Max-norm = 1.35% and L2 = 1.62%.
Key notation/definitions (from earlier): L layers; l index; x=y^(0); z^(l)=inputs; y^(l)=outputs; ~y^(l)=after dropout mask; W^(l), w_i^(l), b^(l); W_test^(l)=pW^(l); f activation (e.g. sigmoid); p retention prob; r^(l) Bernoulli mask; n units; k MC samples for averaging; max-norm c; regression and RBM notation summarized (X,y,w,R with R_ij~Bernoulli(p); RBM θ={W,a,b}, Z partition, etc.); multiplicative-noise and rescaled Bernoulli equivalents noted; TIMIT lr schedule ε0(1+t/T)^{-1}.

Paper: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al., JMLR 2014). Main idea: during training randomly drop units (Bernoulli retain prob p) to sample many "thinned" networks; at test time use a single unthinned network with outgoing weights scaled by p (W_test = p W) to approximate averaging. Key definitions: L layers, r^(l) Bernoulli masks, ~y^(l) after dropout. A net with n units corresponds to 2^n thinned nets; they share weights so parameter count stays O(n^2). Typical choices: p≈0.5 for hidden units (often close to optimal), input-unit p usually closer to 1. Scaling outgoing weights by p at test time ensures expected training-time output equals test-time output. Motivation: approximate an equally weighted geometric mean / Bayesian-like averaging of exponentially many models with much less computation. Dropout applicable beyond feed-forward nets (Dropout RBM introduced). Paper claims dropout + weight-scaling reduces overfitting and improves generalization across domains; experiments reported in Sections 6–8 (image results Tables 2–6, TIMIT Table 7, Reuters improvement 31.05%→29.62% in Sect.6.3, alternative-splicing bits in Table 8, Table 9 comparisons: Dropout+Max-norm 1.05% vs Max-norm 1.35% vs L2 1.62%). TIMIT learning-rate schedule earlier noted: ε0 (1 + t/T)^(-1). Paper structure: Sec 2 motivation, 3 related work, 4 model, 5 training, 6 experiments, 7 hyperparams/properties, 8 Dropout RBMs, 9 marginalizing dropout, Appendix A guidance.

Paper: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al., JMLR 2014). Core idea: during training randomly drop units (Bernoulli masks r^(l), retain prob p) to sample many thinned networks; at test time use the full network with outgoing weights scaled by p (weight-scaling) to approximate averaging. Typical p≈0.5 for hidden units; input p usually closer to 1. Scaling by p makes test-time output equal to the expected training-time output (approximate model averaging). Dropout applies beyond feed-forward nets (Dropout RBMs): Figures 12–13 show qualitative feature and sparsity comparisons but no numeric performance comparison is reported there. Experiments (Secs.6–8) report improved generalization across domains (image Tables 2–6, TIMIT Table 7, Tables 2–7 and 9 cited for cross-domain error reductions). Reuters (Sec.6.3) error improved from 31.05% to 29.62%. Table 9: Dropout+Max-norm 1.05% vs Max-norm 1.35% vs L2 1.62% (alternative-splicing results also in Table 8). TIMIT uses learning rate schedule ε0(1 + t/T)^(-1). Section 2 motivation uses analogies (sexual reproduction / mix-ability; conspiracies) to argue dropout reduces complex co-adaptations, forcing units to be robust and individually useful.

Paper: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al., JMLR 2014). Core idea: during training randomly drop units via Bernoulli masks r^(l) with retain prob p, sampling many thinned networks; at test time use full network with outgoing weights scaled by p (weight-scaling) to approximate averaging. Typical p ≈ 0.5 for hidden units; input p usually closer to 1. Dropout interpretable as adding noise to hidden-unit states; relates to Denoising Autoencoders (DAEs) which typically use ~5% input noise, but with weight-scaling dropout often uses much higher noise (e.g., drop 20% of inputs, 50% of hidden units). Dropout extends beyond unsupervised learning to supervised nets and other architectures (e.g., Dropout RBMs / Boltzmann Machines; Figures 12–13 show qualitative differences). In simple cases dropout noise can be marginalized analytically (Section 9.1 gives linear-regression derivations); related work on deterministic marginalization and "blankout" noise (van der Maaten et al., Wang & Manning, Chen et al.). Different adversarial-removal formulations studied by Globerson & Roweis (2006) and Dekel et al. (2010). Experiments (Secs. 6–8) report improved generalization across domains: Reuters (Sec.6.3) error improved from 31.05% to 29.62%; Table 9 reports Dropout+Max-norm 1.05% vs Max-norm 1.35% vs L2 1.62%; TIMIT used learning-rate schedule ε0(1 + t/T)^(-1). Section 2 gives motivational analogies (sexual reproduction/mix-ability, conspiracies).

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (Srivastava et al., JMLR 2014). Core idea: during training randomly drop units with independent Bernoulli masks r^{(l)} (retain prob p), sampling many thinned sub-networks; at test time use full network with outgoing weights scaled by p (weight-scaling). Typical p ≈ 0.5 for hidden units; input p usually closer to 1. Notation: L hidden layers (1..L); z^{(l)} = inputs into layer l, y^{(l)} = outputs (y^{(0)}=x), W^{(l)}, b^{(l)}. Standard forward: z_i^{(l+1)} = w_i^{(l+1)} y^{(l)} + b_i^{(l+1)}; y_i^{(l+1)} = f(z_i^{(l+1)}) (e.g., logistic f(x)=1/(1+e^{-x})). Dropout forward: r_j^{(l)} ~ Bernoulli(p) (each mask component independent, 1 with prob p), \tilde y^{(l)} = r^{(l)} * y^{(l)} (elementwise), then z_i^{(l+1)} = w_i^{(l+1)} \tilde y^{(l)} + b_i^{(l+1)}, y_i^{(l+1)} = f(z_i^{(l+1)}). Backpropagate loss derivatives through the sampled sub-network. Test-time: use full network without dropout and scale weights: W_test^{(l)} = p W^{(l)}. Section references: Sec.9.1 gives analytic marginalization in simple linear cases; experiments (Secs.6–8) report improved generalization (e.g., Reuters 31.05% → 29.62%; Table 9: Dropout+Max-norm 1.05% vs Max-norm 1.35% vs L2 1.62%); TIMIT used learning-rate schedule ε0(1+t/T)^{-1}. Figures illustrate standard vs dropout panels (bias +1, three inputs, masks in dropout).

Paper: Dropout (Srivastava et al., JMLR 2014). Core idea: during training randomly drop units with independent Bernoulli masks r^{(l)} (retain prob p), sampling many thinned sub-networks; at test time use full network with outgoing weights scaled by p (weight-scaling W_test = p W). Typical p ≈ 0.5 for hidden units; input p usually closer to 1. Training: use SGD (mini-batches); for each case sample a thinned network; forward/backprop only on that network. Gradients averaged across mini-batch; a case not using a parameter contributes zero gradient. Use momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 weight decay. Max-norm: constrain each unit’s incoming weight vector norm ||w||_2 ≤ c; if violated, project onto ball of radius c; c chosen by validation. Combining dropout with max-norm, large decaying learning rates and high momentum yields further gains. Reported MNIST figures (Table 9): Dropout + Max-norm 1.05%; Dropout + L2 1.25%; Max-norm (no dropout) 1.35%; L2 (no dropout) 1.62%. Unsupervised pretraining: can use RBMs, autoencoders, DBMs; pretraining uses unlabeled data and can help versus random init. When finetuning with dropout, pretrained weights should be multiplied by 1/p so each unit’s expected output under dropout equals its pretraining output. Authors observed pretrained information could be lost with large finetuning rates but preserved with smaller rates. Reported pretrained MNIST (Table 2): DBN rows 1.18% versus 0.92%; DBM rows 0.96% versus 0.79% (presented as dropout finetuning improving pretrained networks). Other notes: Reuters improved (31.05% → 29.62%); TIMIT used learning-rate schedule ε0(1+t/T)^{-1}.

steps.notes_before: Paper: Dropout — train with random binary masks (retain prob p, typically p≈0.5 for hidden units, input p nearer 1). At test time use full network with outgoing weights scaled by p. Training: SGD on mini-batches, sample thinned network per case; use momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 weight decay. Max-norm: constrain incoming weight vector ||w||_2 ≤ c, project if violated; combine with dropout for gains. Datasets used: MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet, TIMIT, Reuters-RCV1, Alternative Splicing (Table 1 gives dims and train/test sizes; note: ImageNet entry lists 65536 (256×256 color) which is inconsistent — 256×256×3=196608). Key MNIST results (Table 2): Standard NN (Simard) 1.60%; SVM Gaussian kernel 1.40%; Dropout NN (logistic, 3×1024) 1.35%; Dropout ReLU 1.25%; Dropout+max-norm (ReLU, 3×1024) 1.06 (improves further with larger nets down to ~0.95); Goodfellow maxout + dropout 0.94. Pretrained: DBN finetune 1.18 → DBN + dropout finetune 0.92; DBM finetune 0.96 → DBM + dropout finetune 0.79. Paper claims dropout improves generalization across all listed domains (see Tables 2–7; Reuters noted 31.05% → 29.62%). Appendix B has experiment details.

Test reconstruction errors reported as similar (exact numbers not given). Section 7 (Salient Features) summary and key numbers: 7.1 One-layer autoencoders (256 ReLUs) on MNIST: dropout (p=0.5) yields more interpretable features (strokes/edges) vs. no dropout; test reconstruction errors similar. 7.2 Dropout induces sparser activations without explicit sparsity regularizer: mean activation per unit (on a test minibatch) drops ~2.0 -> ~0.7; activation histogram shows a sharp peak at zero with dropout. 7.3 Effect of retention p studied two ways: (A) keep n fixed using 784-2048-2048-2048-10 (no input dropout): small p underfits (high training error); classification error falls as p increases, is flat for 0.4<=p<=0.8, then rises as p->1. (B) keep expected retained units pn fixed by increasing n as p decreases: used pn=256 for first two hidden layers and pn=512 for last; Figure 9b shows much smaller errors at low p than Figure 9a (at p=0.1 error falls from 2.7% to 1.7%). For these retained sizes p≈0.6 is best; default p=0.5 is close. 7.4 Effect of dataset size: varied MNIST training sizes 100, 500, 1K, 5K, 10K, 50K using 784-1024-1024-2048-10, p=0.5 hidden, p=0.8 input. Figure 10: for very small sets (100, 500) dropout gives no improvement; as data increases dropout’s gain first grows then declines (a suggested “sweet spot”). 7.5 Monte-Carlo model averaging vs weight scaling (MNIST): sampling k networks and averaging approaches true average as k→∞; around k≈50 sampled networks matches weight-scaling; more samples slightly better but within one standard deviation, so weight scaling is a fairly good approximation. Also recall earlier results: Sec 6.5 MNIST regularizers (Table 9) — Dropout+Max-norm best at 1.05% test error; Sec 6.4 (Table 8) Bayesian NN > Dropout NN > other non-Bayesian methods on small splicing dataset.

Section 7 (Salient Features) key points: 7.1 One-layer autoencoders (256 ReLUs) on MNIST: dropout (p=0.5) yields more interpretable features (strokes/edges) vs. no dropout; test reconstruction errors similar. 7.2 Dropout induces sparser activations without explicit sparsity regularizer: mean activation per unit (test minibatch) drops ~2.0 -> ~0.7; activation histogram shows sharp peak at zero with dropout. 7.3 Retention p effects: (A) keep n fixed (784-2048-2048-2048-10, no input dropout): small p underfits; classification error falls as p increases, flat for 0.4<=p<=0.8, then rises as p->1. (B) keep expected retained units pn fixed by increasing n as p decreases: pn=256 (first two layers), pn=512 (last); low-p with larger n gives much smaller errors (e.g. at p=0.1 error drops from 2.7% to 1.7%); p~0.6 best, default p=0.5 close. 7.4 Dataset size: varied MNIST training set (100,500,1K,5K,10K,50K) with 784-1024-1024-2048-10, p=0.5 hidden, p=0.8 input: dropout gives no gain for tiny sets (100,500); gain grows then declines as data increases (a "sweet spot"). 7.5 Monte-Carlo model averaging: sampling k networks approaches true average; ~50 samples matches weight-scaling approximation reasonably. (Earlier: Sec 6.5 Table 9: Dropout+Max-norm best 1.05% test error; Sec 6.4 Table 8: Bayesian NN > Dropout NN > other non-Bayesian on small splicing dataset.) Section 8 (Dropout RBMs): defines binary RBM with dropout mask r in {0,1}^F (retain prob p). Joint P(r,h,v)=P(r;p)P(h,v|r;θ) with constraint g enforcing h_j=0 when r_j=0; conditional P(h_j=1|r_j,v)=1(r_j=1)·σ(b_j+Σ_i W_ij v_i). Learning: sample r each minibatch and train with standard RBM methods (CD-1 used). Experiments on MNIST, 256 hidden units, p=0.5: Figure 12 — dropout RBM features look coarser than stroke-like standard RBM and appear to have fewer dead units; Figure 13 — activation histograms show much sparser representations with dropout (no numeric sparsity measures reported).

Section 7 (Salient Features) key points: 7.1 One-layer autoencoders (256 ReLUs) on MNIST: dropout (p=0.5) yields more interpretable features (strokes/edges) vs. no dropout; test reconstruction errors similar. 7.2 Dropout induces sparser activations without explicit sparsity regularizer: mean activation per unit (test minibatch) drops ~2.0 -> ~0.7; activation histogram shows sharp peak at zero with dropout. 7.3 Retention p effects: (A) keep n fixed: small p underfits; classification error falls as p increases, flat for 0.4<=p<=0.8, then rises as p->1. (B) keep expected retained units pn fixed by increasing n as p decreases: low-p with larger n can give much smaller errors; p~0.6 best, default p=0.5 close. 7.4 Dataset size: dropout gives no gain for tiny sets (100,500); gain grows then declines as data increases (a "sweet spot"). 7.5 Monte-Carlo model averaging: sampling k networks approaches true average; ~50 samples matches weight-scaling approximation reasonably. (Earlier: Sec 6.5 Table 9: Dropout+Max-norm best 1.05% test error; Sec 6.4 Table 8: Bayesian NN > Dropout NN > other non-Bayesian on small splicing dataset.) Section 8 (Dropout RBMs): sample hidden-mask r per minibatch (p=0.5), train with CD-1; dropout RBM features coarser, sparser activations, fewer dead units. Section 9 (Marginalizing Dropout): marginalizing dropout yields deterministic objectives with computable gradients. 9.1 Linear regression: minimizing E_R ||y-(R*X)w||^2 reduces to ||y-pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Gamma w||^2 where Gamma = (diag(X^T X))^{1/2}; with tilde w = p w this is ||y-X tilde w||^2 + ((1-p)/p)||Gamma tilde w||^2, so regularization grows as p decreases. 9.2 Logistic/deep nets: closed-form marginalization hard; Wang & Manning (2013) give Gaussian-based approximations that speed training and can improve generalization for logistic regression, but assumptions weaken with added layers and don't directly extend to deep networks.

Section 7 (Salient Features): 7.1 One-layer autoencoders (256 ReLUs) on MNIST: dropout (p=0.5) yields more interpretable features (strokes/edges) vs. no dropout; test reconstruction errors similar. 7.2 Dropout induces sparser activations w/o explicit sparsity regularizer: mean activation per unit drops ~2.0 -> ~0.7; activation histogram shows sharp peak at zero with dropout. 7.3 Retention p effects: (A) keep n fixed: small p underfits; classification error falls as p increases, flat for 0.4<=p<=0.8, then rises as p->1. (B) keep expected retained units pn fixed by increasing n as p decreases: low-p with larger n can give much smaller errors; p~0.6 best, default p=0.5 close. 7.4 Dataset size: dropout gives no gain for tiny sets (100,500); gain grows then declines as data increases (a "sweet spot"). 7.5 Monte-Carlo model averaging: sampling k networks approaches true average; ~50 samples matches weight-scaling approximation reasonably. Section 8 (Dropout RBMs): sample hidden-mask r per minibatch (p=0.5), train CD-1; dropout RBM features coarser, sparser activations, fewer dead units. Section 9 (Marginalizing Dropout): marginalizing yields deterministic objectives; 9.1 Linear regression: marginalizing yields objective ||y-pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Gamma w||^2, equivalently ||y-X tilde w||^2 + ((1-p)/p)||Gamma tilde w||^2 so regularization grows as p decreases. 9.2 Logistic/deep nets: closed-form marginalization hard; Gaussian approximations exist but weaken with depth. Section 10 (Multiplicative Gaussian Noise): generalize dropout by multiplying activations by r'~N(1,σ^2); equivalently add zero-mean noise h_i r, r~N(0,1), with noise std equal to |h_i| when σ^2=1. Using training variant that scales retained activations by 1/p gives Bernoulli multiplier r_b with E[r_b]=1, Var[r_b]=(1-p)/p; match Gaussian by setting σ^2=(1-p)/p so E[r_g]=1, Var[r_g]=(1-p)/p. Expected activation unchanged for Gaussian so no test-time weight scaling needed. Authors claim Gaussian (higher entropy) may be slightly better than Bernoulli (lower entropy). Table 10 (10 seeds): MNIST (2×1024) Bernoulli 1.08±0.04 vs Gaussian 0.95±0.04 (hidden p=0.5, input p=0.8); CIFAR-10 (3 conv + 2 fc) Bernoulli 12.6±0.1 vs Gaussian 12.5±0.1 (p per layer = 0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5; σ set to sqrt((1-p)/p)). Results labeled preliminary.

Dropout summary: randomly omitting (dropping) hidden units during training reduces overfitting by breaking co-adaptations; improves many domains (object classification, digits, speech, docs, computational biology) and achieves state-of-the-art results on SVHN, ImageNet, CIFAR-100, MNIST per paper tables. Dropout extends to RBMs: Dropout RBMs trained with minibatch hidden-mask (p=0.5) produce coarser, sparser features and fewer dead units (Figures 12–13). Training cost: dropout typically requires ~2–3× more training time due to noisy parameter updates and effectively training many random sub-architectures; more training time allows using stronger dropout to reduce overfitting. Claims/evidence cited in conclusion: Tables 2–8 and Sec 6.3 (Reuters error example: 31.05% versus 29.62%); image results called out: DBM+dropout finetuning 0.79% (Table 2), maxout 2.47% (Table 3), CIFAR-100 all-layer dropout 37.20% (Table 4), ImageNet rows in Tables 5–6. Marginalization: linear regression gives closed-form expected objective -> equivalent modified L2 regularizer (Sec 9.1: ||y-pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Γw||^2, equivalently scaled form with ((1-p)/p) factor). For deeper/nonlinear models closed-form marginalization is hard; Gaussian approximations possible but weaken with depth. Multiplicative Gaussian noise generalizes Bernoulli dropout: set σ^2=(1-p)/p so E[r]=1, Var=(1-p)/p; Table 10 (10 seeds) shows MNIST: Bernoulli 1.08±0.04 vs Gaussian 0.95±0.04; CIFAR-10: Bernoulli 12.6±0.1 vs Gaussian 12.5±0.1. Other relevant results: (Sec 7) dropout induces sparser activations (mean/unit ~2.0→~0.7), retention p effects (keep n fixed: small p underfits; error flat for 0.4–0.8; with pn fixed lower p + larger n can help; p~0.6 near-optimal), dataset-size "sweet spot" for benefit, and Monte-Carlo averaging: ~50 samples approximates true average.

Dropout summary: randomly omitting (dropping) hidden units during training reduces overfitting by breaking co-adaptations; yields strong results across domains (object classification, digits, speech, docs, computational biology) and achieves state-of-the-art results reported in the paper (e.g. DBM+dropout finetuning 0.79% Table 2; maxout 2.47% Table 3; CIFAR-100 all-layer dropout 37.20% Table 4; Reuters example reported earlier). RBM/representation effects: dropout RBMs (minibatch hidden-mask p=0.5) produce coarser, sparser features and fewer dead units. Training cost/optimization: dropout injects gradient noise and typically needs more training, often ~2–3× more training time; Appendix heuristics recommend using much larger learning rates (≈10–100× the standard-network optimum) and higher momentum (≈0.95–0.99 vs usual 0.9) to accelerate learning, but large updates necessitate max-norm regularization (bound c typically 3–4). Network sizing: a dropout layer with n units and retention p has expected pn active units; if n units are optimal without dropout, use ≈n/p units with dropout. Dropout rate p: typical hidden-unit p in 0.5–0.8; input retention depends on input type (e.g. real-valued image patches or speech frames often use p≈0.8). The choice of p must be paired with hidden-unit count n (smaller p requires larger n). Marginalization: for linear models closed-form equivalence to modified L2; multiplicative Gaussian noise generalizes Bernoulli (σ^2=(1-p)/p); Monte-Carlo averaging: ~50 samples approximates the ensemble average.

Appendix B: experiment details and preprocessing; GPU code (cudamat, cuda-convnet); reproduction code URL.
MNIST: 60k train, 10k test; 10k held-out val. Hyperparams chosen so best val error occurred after 1M weight updates; then train+val reunited and trained 1M updates before testing. Figure 4: all combos of 2/3/4 hidden layers × {1024,2048} units = 6 architectures. For these and Table 2 architectures: hidden-layer p=0.5, input p=0.8; final momentum=0.95; max-norm c=2. Also tried 2-/3-layer nets with 4096 and 8192 units: 2-layer improved (Table 2 max-norm rows: 4096 -> 1.01%, 8192 -> 0.95%); 3-layer slightly worse; stronger dropout didn’t beat 2-layer.
SVHN: ~600k train, ~26k test. Validation set = 6000 (400/class from standard, 200/class from extra) => 2/3 standard, 1/3 extra. Inputs: RGB, zero-mean unit-variance; contrast-N/ZCA gave no improvement. Best arch: 3 conv layers (96,128,256 filters, 5x5, stride 1), 3x3 pooling stride 2 after each conv, then two 2048-unit fully connected layers, ReLU. Retention p across (input,conv1,conv2,conv3,fc1,fc2) = (0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5). max-norm c=4; momentum=0.95. Validation not added back; reported test error of model with smallest val error = 2.55% (Table 3).
CIFAR-10/100: 50k train, 10k test; 5k val. Preproc: per-channel global contrast normalization then ZCA whitening. Architecture and dropout rates matched SVHN; input-layer learning rates had to be smaller.
TIMIT: Kaldi log-filter banks, monophone forced alignment, 21-frame context predicting central frame, inputs mean-centered and unit-variance, no speaker-dependent processing.
(From earlier appendix: training often needs ~2–3× more updates; heuristics recommend much larger learning rates and higher momentum ≈0.95–0.99 and max-norm bounds typically 3–4.)

errors.claim: The energy / joint probability is defined as P(h,v;θ) = (1/Z) exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v) (so a pairs with h and b with v)
errors.evidence: Energy: "P(h,v;θ) = (1/Z(θ)) exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v)". Later conditionals: "P(h_j=1 | r_j,v) = 1(r_j=1) σ(b_j + sum_i W_{ij} v_i)" and "P(v_i=1 | h) = σ(a_i + sum_j W_{ij} h_j)".
errors.explanation: In the energy expression a is the hidden-unit bias (a^T h) and b is the visible-unit bias (b^T v). But the conditional formulas use b_j as the hidden bias in P(h_j=1|...) and a_i as the visible bias in P(v_i=1|...), i.e. the names a and b are swapped between the joint distribution and the conditional probabilities.

Dropout: randomly removes units (and their connections) during training, effectively sampling many smaller networks that share weights. At test time, predictions of the ensemble of thinned networks are approximated by a single full network with scaled weights. Reported empirical improvements on image, speech, text, and alternative-splicing tasks. Paper compares dropout to other regularizers and to Bayesian neural networks. Analyses include learned features, sparsity, effects of dropout rates, network size, training-set size, and test-time averaging. Dropout applied to RBMs yields qualitatively different features and sparser representations. For linear regression, marginalizing dropout yields a modified ridge-regression objective. Preliminary experiments compare Bernoulli dropout with multiplicative Gaussian noise. Noted limitation: training time — dropout networks typically take 2–3× longer to train than standard networks of the same architecture.

Dropout: randomly and temporarily removes units and their incoming/outgoing connections during training (Bernoulli dropout uses Bernoulli(p) retention). At test time the ensemble is approximated by a single full network using weight scaling: multiply a unit’s outgoing weights by its retention probability p. Gaussian (multiplicative) dropout is an alternative noise model; entropy used to compare Bernoulli vs Gaussian with matched means/variances. Deterministic dropout model = marginalizing dropout noise; Monte-Carlo dropout/model averaging = sampling thinned networks at test time and averaging predictions. Marginalizing dropout for linear regression is equivalent in expectation to a modified ridge (Tikhonov) regression. RBMs: Dropout RBM augments hidden units with binary retention variables; CD-1 (Contrastive Divergence) used to train RBMs. DBN/DBM pretraining used for some nets. Code Quality (alt-splicing metric) = negative KL divergence (higher is better). Preprocessing: PCA and ZCA whitening used in some comparisons. Regularizers compared: L1, L2 (weight decay), max-norm (bound incoming weight norm by c), KL-sparsity. Image experiments use conv nets with convolutional and fully connected layers, ReLU/softmax units, max-pooling, L2/L4 pooling, top-1 and top-5 ImageNet errors reported. Other notes: training with dropout typically takes ~2–3x longer than standard nets; hyperparameters chosen by validation. Appendix A.1 discusses capacity reduction by dropping units.

Gaussian (multiplicative) dropout alternative; entropy used to compare Bernoulli vs Gaussian with matched mean/variance. Deterministic dropout = marginalizing noise; Monte-Carlo dropout = sample thinned nets at test time and average. For linear regression, marginalizing dropout ≃ modified ridge (Tikhonov). RBMs: dropout RBM augments hidden units with binary retention vars; trained with CD-1. DBN/DBM pretraining used for some nets. Code Quality (alternative-splicing metric) = negative KL divergence (higher is better), reported in bits (Table 8). Preprocessing: PCA and ZCA whitening. Regularizers: L1, L2 (weight decay), max-norm (bound incoming weight norm by c), KL-sparsity. Image experiments: conv nets with convolutional and fully connected layers, ReLU/softmax units, max-pooling, L2/L4 pooling; report top-1 and top-5 ImageNet errors. Training with dropout typically 2–3× longer; hyperparams chosen by validation. Appendix A.1 on capacity reduction. Datasets/labels/software: MNIST, TIMIT (preprocessed to log-filter banks via Kaldi; monophone system used for forced alignment), CIFAR-10/100, SVHN (RGB pixels normalized; also Binary Features (WDCH), HOG, KMeans listed), ImageNet / ILSVRC (2010/2012 referenced; Section 6.1.4), Reuters-RCV1, Alternative Splicing dataset (inc/exc/nc softmax targets). ImageNet comparison features: SIFT, LBP, GIST, CSIFT, Color Statistics, Fisher Vectors. Implementation: GPU-based using CUDA libs (cudamat, cuda-convnet) (Appendix B); code: http://www.cs.toronto.edu/~nitish/dropout. Table codes: Avg=average, val/test, NA=SVM unit/arch entry in Table 2, -- = unreported, K/M=thousands/millions, dim used in Table 1. Funding: OGS/NSERC/Early Researcher Award.

Notation and key quantities: L = number of hidden layers, l = layer index. i,j = unit/dimension/data indices. x (y^(0)) = network input. z^(l) = inputs to layer l; y^(l) = outputs; \tilde y^(l) = outputs after elementwise multiplication by dropout mask. W^(l), w_i^(l), b^(l) = layer weights, unit incoming weights, biases. W_test^(l) = test-time weights = p W^(l). f = activation (e.g. logistic 1/(1+exp(-x))). exp = exponential. p = probability of retaining a unit/input. r^(l) = vector of independent Bernoulli dropout vars per layer. * = elementwise multiplication. n = number of units (or hidden units in a layer); 2^n = number of possible thinned nets. O(n^2) used as parameter-count order/upper bound. pn = expected retained units. w = weight vector; ||w||_2 and c = incoming weight norm and its max-norm bound. ||·||^2 = squared norm. k = number of sampled networks for Monte-Carlo averaging. RBM: v (D) visible vector/size, h (F) hidden vector/size, spaces {0,1}^D, {0,1}^F. RBM params θ={W,a,b}; Z(θ) partition function. r = binary retention vector in Dropout RBM (also used as Gaussian noise variable in Sec.10). Z'(θ,r) = Dropout RBM normalization conditional on r. g(h_j,r_j) forces h_j=0 when r_j=0. 1(·) indicator. P(·) = distribution. σ = RBM conditional activation function; in Sec.10 σ also denotes Gaussian noise std. Transpose: ^⊤. Γ = (diag(X^⊤X))^{1/2} (matrix in marginalized regression cost). X∈R^{N×D}, y∈R^N, w∈R^D. R∈{0,1}^{N×D} with R_ij ~ Bernoulli(p). \tilde w = p w (rescaled weight vector). Multiplicative-noise: r' ~ N(1,σ^2) with σ^2 matched to (1−p)/p; r_b = rescaled Bernoulli (1/p w.p. p, else 0); r_g = Gaussian multiplier mean 1 var (1−p)/p. Learning-rate schedule (TIMIT): ε_0(1 + t/T)^{-1}. p_{i,t}^s = target prob for state s, tissue t, input i; q_t^s(r_i) predicted prob; \bar p^s average over i,t. |data points| used in Code Quality log expression. ± denotes variation beside mean errors in Table 10. Journal JMLR 15 (2014) 1929–1958; submitted 11/13; published 6/14.

Paper: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava, Hinton, Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Salakhutdinov). Editor: Yoshua Bengio. (JMLR 15 (2014) noted earlier.)

Abstract / key idea: During training randomly drop units/connections (multiplicative Bernoulli masks) sampling an exponential number of “thinned” networks; at test time use one unthinned network with scaled-down weights (W_test^(l) = p W^(l)) to approximate the average prediction. Dropout reduces co-adaptation and overfitting.

Claims/evidence (to verify later): image results reported in Tables 2–6; TIMIT rows in Table 7; Reuters: 31.05% error without dropout vs 29.62% with dropout (Section 6.3); alternative-splicing results: rows of 440 and 567 bits in Table 8; Table 9 claims dropout improves over other regularizers (all rows); combined Dropout + Max-norm: 1.05% vs Max-norm 1.35% vs L2 1.62%.

other regression/RBM symbols retained from prior notes.

Paper: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al., JMLR 2014). Key idea: during training randomly drop units (retain each with probability p), sampling thinned networks; at test time use one unthinned network with outgoing weights scaled by p so test-time outputs equal expected training-time outputs. Typical choices: p can be selected by validation or set to 0.5 for hidden units; input-unit p is usually closer to 1. A network with n units represents 2^n thinned networks; weights are shared so parameter count remains O(n^2). For each presentation of a training case a new thinned net is sampled and trained. Exact averaging of 2^n networks at test time is infeasible; weight scaling (multiply outgoing weights by p) approximates the ensemble. Dropout applies to feed-forward nets and graphical models (Dropout RBM introduced later). Paper outline: Sec.2 motivation, Sec.3 related work, Sec.4 model, Sec.5 training, Sec.6 experiments, Sec.7 network properties/hyperparams, Sec.8 Dropout RBMs, Sec.9 marginalizing dropout, Appendix A hyperparameter guidance. Previous notes to check later: numeric results in Tables 2–9 (e.g., Reuters, TIMIT, alternative-splicing, Table 9 comparisons, combined Dropout+Max-norm figures) and notation W_test^(l)=pW^(l); r used later in RBM/Sec.10 as Gaussian noise variable.

Core idea: randomly drop units during training (retain prob p), train many thinned nets with shared weights; approximate ensemble at test time by scaling weights (W_test^(l) = p W^(l)). Typical p=0.5 for hidden units; input retain p closer to 1. Outline: Sec.2 motivation, Sec.3 related (current), Sec.4 model, Sec.5 training, Sec.6 experiments, Sec.7 hyperparams, Sec.8 Dropout RBMs, Sec.9 marginalizing dropout, Appendix A. Current (Sec.3) key points: dropout viewed as regularization via noise on hidden-unit states, analogous to denoising autoencoders (DAEs) which use input noise; DAEs typically use ~5% input noise. Dropout extends noise to hidden layers and to supervised learning and other architectures (e.g., Boltzmann Machines). Authors state test-time weight scaling lets one use much higher noise; they report dropping ~20% of inputs and ~50% of hidden units was often optimal. Dropout can sometimes be marginalized analytically (simple cases); Section 9.1 provides linear-regression objectives. Related work: van der Maaten et al. (2013) on deterministic regularizers/"blankout" noise (inputs, no hidden layers); Wang & Manning (2013) on marginalizing dropout for speed; Chen et al. (2012) on marginalization for DAEs; Globerson & Roweis (2006) and Dekel et al. (2010) studied adversarial unit removal (different setting).

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting”. Core idea: during training randomly drop units (mask r^{(l)} with independent Bernoulli(p) entries) to train an ensemble of thinned networks that share weights; at test time approximate ensemble by scaling weights: W_test^{(l)} = p W^{(l)}. Notation: L hidden layers; y^{(0)}=x; for standard net z_i^{(l+1)} = w_i^{(l+1)} y^{(l)} + b_i^{(l+1)}, y_i^{(l+1)} = f(z_i^{(l+1)}) (example f = logistic). With dropout: r_j^{(l)} ~ Bernoulli(p), \tilde y^{(l)} = r^{(l)} * y^{(l)}, propagate z and y using \tilde y, backpropagate loss derivatives through the sampled sub-network. Typical settings: p≈0.5 for hidden units; input retain p closer to 1 (authors mention ~20% input dropout and ~50% hidden dropout often optimal). Section 3 relates dropout to denoising autoencoders (DAEs use small input noise ~5%); dropout extends noise to hidden layers and supervised nets; some cases allow analytic marginalization (see Sec.9, Sec.9.1 gives linear-regression objective). Dropout RBMs discussed (Figs.12–13 show qualitative features, increased sparsity). Earlier note: possible inconsistency in reported Reuters numbers (paper claims dropout reduces error across domains yet gave Reuters numbers “31.05% versus 29.62%” that appear contradictory).

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting”. Core idea: during training randomly drop units (r^(l) ~ Bernoulli(p)), training an ensemble of thinned nets that share weights; at test time approximate ensemble by scaling weights by p. Typical retains: hidden p≈0.5; input dropout often ~20% (retain ≈0.8).

Training: use SGD with mini-batches; for each case sample a thinned network; forward/backprop only on that network. Gradients averaged across mini-batch; cases that don’t use a parameter contribute zero. Use momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 weight decay. Max-norm regularization: bound each hidden unit’s incoming weight vector ||w||_2 ≤ c and project to ball surface when exceeded. Max-norm is especially useful with dropout and also helps without dropout.

Reported MNIST comparisons (Table 9 cited): Dropout + L2 = 1.25% vs Dropout + Max-norm = 1.05%. Without dropout: Max-norm = 1.35% vs L2 = 1.62%.

Unsupervised pretraining (RBMs, autoencoders, DBMs) can initialize weights before finetuning. When finetuning with dropout, multiply pretrained weights by 1/p so each unit’s expected output under dropout matches pretraining. Cited MNIST pretrained results (Table 2): DBN rows 1.18% versus 0.92%; DBM rows 0.96% versus 0.79% (text implies second number is after dropout finetuning). Pretrained information can be lost with large finetuning rates but preserved with smaller rates.

Keep prior flagged inconsistency (Reuters numbers 31.05% vs 29.62%) for later checking.

(Earlier I flagged an inconsistency: prose gave 20.5% for 8-layer non-dropout but table gives 20.7% and uses 20.5% for mcRBM-DBN.) Reuters-RCV1: best NN 31.05% -> dropout 29.62%. Alternative-splicing data (Table 8, metric 'Code Quality' in bits — higher better): Neural Network (early stopping) 440; Regression, PCA 463; SVM, PCA 487; Neural Network with dropout 567; Bayesian Neural Network 623. Claims: Bayesian > dropout; dropout > other listed methods; dropout nets have 1000s hidden units vs Bayesian a few tens; training set small (Table 1: 2932 training cases, 1014 input dims). Section 6.5 (one fixed MNIST architecture ReLU 784-1024-1024-2048-10): compared L2, L1+L2, L2+KL-sparsity, max-norm, dropout+L2, dropout+max-norm. Table 9 test errors: L2 1.62%, L2+L1 1.60%, L2+KL-sparsity 1.55%, Max-norm 1.35%, Dropout+L2 1.25%, Dropout+Max-norm 1.05% (dropout+max-norm lowest).

Section 7 studies how dropout changes learned features, sparsity and dependence on retention p. 7.1: Compare two identical 256-unit ReLU single-hidden-layer MNIST autoencoders (no dropout vs dropout p=0.5). Test reconstruction errors reported as similar; features without dropout look co-adapted and uninterpretable, with dropout units detect edges/strokes. 7.2: Sparsity histograms (Figure 8) on a test minibatch: no-dropout mean activation ≈ 2.0 and many activations away from zero; dropout mean activation ≈ 0.7 and a sharp peak at zero. Conclusion: dropout induces sparser activations without explicit sparsity regularizer. 7.3: Vary retention p under two regimes: (1) keep hidden-unit count n fixed (architecture used: 784-2048-2048-2048-10, no input dropout); (2) keep expected retained pn fixed (so smaller p ⇒ larger networks). For regime (1): small p ⇒ few active units and high training error (underfitting); error decreases as p increases, is roughly flat for 0.4≤p≤0.8, then increases as p→1. Figures show Test/Train error vs p with classification error ticks up to ~3.5% (panel a) and ~3.0% (panel b).

Section 7 (continued). 7.1–7.2 recap: single-hidden-layer (256 ReLU) MNIST autoencoders: no-dropout vs dropout p=0.5 have similar reconstruction error; dropout yields interpretable, less co-adapted features and sparser activations (no-dropout mean activation ≈ 2.0; dropout mean ≈ 0.7 with a peak at zero). 7.3 (retention p experiments): two regimes — (A) fixed hidden-unit count (architecture used: 784-2048-2048-2048-10, no input dropout) — small p underfits (few active units, high training error); error decreases with p, roughly flat for 0.4≤p≤0.8, then rises as p→1. (B) keep expected retained pn fixed (so n scales with 1/p): experiments set pn=256,256,512 for the three hidden layers (Figure 9b). Figure 9b shows much smaller errors at low p than Figure 9a; at p=0.1 error falls from 2.7% (fixed-n) to 1.7% (fixed-pn). For these pn, p≈0.6 performs best; default p=0.5 is near-optimal. 7.4 (data size): architecture 784-1024-1024-2048-10, p=0.5 hidden, p=0.8 input; training set sizes 100,500,1k,5k,10k,50k. Figure 10: dropout gives no improvement at 100 and 500; as data size grows dropout’s benefit first increases then decreases (a suggested “sweet spot”). 7.5 (MC averaging vs weight scaling): Figure 11 shows test error vs number of samples k (up to 120); Monte-Carlo averaging ≈ weight scaling by k≈50; more samples slightly better but within one standard deviation, so weight scaling is a good approximation.

errors.claim: The energy / joint probability is defined as P(h,v;θ) = (1/Z) exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v) (so a pairs with h and b with v)
errors.evidence: Energy: "P(h,v;θ) = (1/Z(θ)) exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v)". Later conditionals: "P(h_j=1 | r_j,v) = 1(r_j=1) σ(b_j + sum_i W_{ij} v_i)" and "P(v_i=1 | h) = σ(a_i + sum_j W_{ij} h_j)".
errors.explanation: In the energy expression a is the hidden-unit bias (a^T h) and b is the visible-unit bias (b^T v). But the conditional formulas use b_j as the hidden bias in P(h_j=1|...) and a_i as the visible bias in P(v_i=1|...), i.e. the names a and b are swapped between the joint distribution and the conditional probabilities.

Dropout: randomly remove units and their connections during training, effectively training many smaller networks that share parameters. At test time, use one complete network with reduced weights to approximate averaging the smaller networks' predictions. Claimed benefits: improves generalization over networks without dropout on every tested dataset; reports state-of-the-art results on several benchmarks. Experimental domains: images, speech, documents, gene-splicing prediction. Also examines learned features, sparsity, retention rates, effects of training-set size, Restricted Boltzmann Machines, noise marginalization, and Gaussian corruption. Training cost: typically takes 2–3× longer than training a standard network of the same architecture.

Dropout (QX2): randomly remove units and their connections during training; at test time use one unthinned network with outgoing weights multiplied by the retention probability (T6R) to approximate averaging the thinned-model predictions. The paper states this approximation corresponds to the geometric mean (equally weighted combination) of thinned-network predictions. Two corruption types: Bernoulli dropout (P7V) — binary multiplicative noise (Bernoulli variable =1 with prob p, 0 otherwise) — and Gaussian dropout (D4K) — Gaussian multiplicative noise. Marginalization = expectation over dropout noise to yield a deterministic objective/regularizer; Monte‑Carlo dropout/model averaging = stochastic sampling and averaging predictions from sampled thinned networks. Dropout RBM (B8T): described as a mixture of shared-weight RBMs using different hidden-unit subsets; U2L = RBM; pretraining (DBM/E5Q, DBN/G6W) then finetuning with backprop; mcRBM-G6W is a named pretrained variant. Regularizers: L1 (O3U), L2 (Y5F, Tikhonov), max-norm (V9C), KL-sparsity. Activations mentioned: logistic units, ReLU (F3N), maxout (L8J). Other glossary items to track: geometric mean vs. posterior-weighted averaging, blankout noise, ridge-regression connection (dropout expectation → ridge-like penalty matrix), convolutional-net components (filters, pooling variants), data augmentation, SVM/PCA baselines, terms like dead unit, mix-ability, replica code, and non-stationarity. These definitions and labels will be used in later parts for numerical and conceptual consistency checks.

Abstract summary: method called "QX2, or dropout"; it randomly removes units and their connections during training, inhibiting co-adaptation, sampling exponentially many thinned networks that share parameters. A single unthinned network with reduced weights approximates the averaged predictions of the thinned nets. Claims substantial reduction in overfitting and major improvements; supervised experiments in vision, speech recognition, document classification and computational biology reportedly attain state-of-the-art on many benchmarks. Evidence claimed in Tables 2–8 and an unnumbered text-classification table in §6.3; domain-specific comparisons listed in §6.

Paper: "Dropout (QX2)". Core idea: randomly remove units during training to train many shared-parameter thinned subnetworks (2^n possible thinned nets for n units) and approximate their combined predictions with one unthinned test-time network. Key terminology: QX2 = dropout; T6R = test-time weight scaling (use one unthinned net with scaled weights); X9M = Monte-Carlo model averaging (average sampled thinned nets at test); U2L/B8T = dropout extension to RBMs. Notation (carry-forward): n = unit count; expected retained width = p n; practical width heuristic = n/p; shared-parameter count O(n^2); L hidden layers with W^(l), b^(l), activations f; p = retention probability; test-time weights scaled by p (W_test = p W). Claims in this part: QX2 approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many models; a new thinned member is sampled and trained (rarely) per presentation of each training case; T6R is a cheap practical inference rule that gives significantly lower generalization error than other regularizers across varied problems; X9M is more expensive and needs around k≈50 samples (per §7.5 and App B.1) before matching T6R. Evidence pointer: Table 9 referenced for comparisons (rows quoted: Y5F=1.62, V9C=1.35, QX2+Y5F=1.25, QX2+V9C=1.05). Paper outline: §2 motivation, §3 prior work, §4 model, §5 training algorithm, §6 experiments, §7 effects and hyperparameter interactions, §8 RBM extension, §9 marginalization, Appendix A (practical guidance).

Paper: "Dropout (QX2)". Core idea: randomly remove units during training to train many shared-parameter thinned subnetworks (2^n possible thinned nets for n units) and approximate their combined predictions with one unthinned test-time network. Notation: n = unit count; p = retention probability; expected retained width = p n; practical width heuristic = n/p; shared-parameter count O(n^2); L hidden layers with W^(l), b^(l), activations f; test-time weights scaled by p (W_test = p W). Claims: QX2 approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many models; a new thinned member is sampled and trained (rarely unique) on each presentation of a training case; T6R (test-time weight scaling) is a cheap practical inference rule that gives significantly lower generalization error than other regularizers across varied problems; X9M (Monte-Carlo averaging) is more expensive and needs around k ≈ 50 samples (per §7.5 and App B.1) to match T6R. Evidence pointer: Table 9 comparisons (rows: Y5F=1.62, V9C=1.35, QX2+Y5F=1.25, QX2+V9C=1.05). New in §2: motivation via sexual-reproduction and conspiracy analogies — Livnat et al. (2010) "mix-ability" notion: selection favors genes that work well with random partners (robust, independently useful components). Analogy: QX2 forces hidden units to operate with randomly selected partners, discouraging complex co-adaptations and favoring robust features; replicating units is a poor remedy. Smaller cooperating subsets are argued to be more robust under non-stationarity than large co-adaptations. Outline pointers: §3 prior work, §4 model, §5 training algorithm, §6 experiments, §7 hyperparams, §8 RBM extension, §9 marginalization, Appendix A guidance.

Paper: "Dropout (QX2)". Core idea: randomly remove units during training to train many shared-parameter thinned subnetworks (2^n possible thinned nets for n units) and approximate their combined predictions with one unthinned test-time network. Notation/impl: n = unit count; p = retention probability; expected retained width = p n; practical width heuristic = n/p; shared-parameter count O(n^2); L hidden layers with weights W^(l), biases b^(l), activations f; test-time weights scaled by p (W_test = p W). Key claims: QX2 approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many models; a new thinned member is sampled and trained on each presentation; T6R (test-time weight scaling) is a cheap practical inference rule that often gives much lower generalization error than other regularizers; X9M (Monte-Carlo averaging) is more expensive and reportedly needs k ≈ 50 samples to match T6R (per §7.5 and App B.1). Empirical pointer: Table 9 example rows (Y5F=1.62, V9C=1.35, QX2+Y5F=1.25, QX2+V9C=1.05). Section 3 notes: DAEs (denoising autoencoders) corrupt inputs and reconstruct; QX2 extends corruption to hidden units and gives a model-averaging view; applies to supervised/unsupervised and other neuron-based architectures including Boltzmann Machines. T6R permits much higher noise than typical DAEs: table lists S2H/DAE typical best 5%, QX2 input-unit removal often optimal 20%, QX2 hidden-unit removal often optimal 50%. Related methods: Globerson & Roweis (2006) and Dekel et al. (2010) use adversarial removals (fixed max number) and have no hidden units. Marginalizing QX2 yields deterministic regularizers in simple cases; van der Maaten et al. (2013) call QX2 input noise "blankout noise" but limited to models without hidden layers; Chen et al. (2012) on marginalization for DAEs; Wang & Manning (2013) propose marginalization to accelerate QX2.

steps.notes_before: Paper: Dropout (QX2) — gate unit outputs during training, independently per unit with r_j^{(l)} ~ Bernoulli(p); tilde y^{(l)} = r^{(l)} * y^{(l)}. At inference no units removed; test-time weights scaled by retention p: W_test^{(l)} = p W^{(l)}. Expected preactivation under training dropout equals test preactivation with scaled weights. Both hidden and input (visible) units can be dropped. Validation can pick p; default often near optimal; input retention generally near complete retention. Forward equations: y^{(0)} = x; nominally z_i^{(l+1)} = w_i^{(l+1)} y^{(l)} + b_i^{(l+1)}, y_i^{(l+1)} = f(z_i^{(l+1)}). Example activation: logistic f(x)=1/(1+exp(-x)). Note: this part contains an indexing inconsistency — it first states l∈{1..L} then uses l∈{0..L-1} for the feed-forward formulas (treating y^{(0)} as input). Keep this in mind when later parts refer to layer indices.

Paper: QX2 = dropout (per-unit gate r_j^(l) ~ Bernoulli(p); ̃y^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l)). At test time do not drop units; scale weights by retention p (W_test = p W) so expected preactivation under dropout equals test preactivation. Both hidden and input units can be dropped (input retention usually near 1). Forward eqns use y^(0)=x; paper has an indexing inconsistency (uses l∈{1..L} then l∈{0..L-1}).

Sec.5 (Learning QX2 Nets): training = backprop through sampled subnetworks (one mask per case/minibatch case), gradients averaged across cases; a dropped parameter gets zero contribution. QX2 alone gives significant gains; combining QX2 with high momentum, large decaying learning rates and V9C (max-norm) gives further boost. V9C constrains each hidden unit's incoming weight vector via projection to ||w||_2 <= c (validation tunes c); projection returns w to the radius-c surface if exceeded. Proposed optimization story: fixed-radius weight ball allows huge LRs without explosion; QX2 noise explores; annealing settles.

Empirical notes cited: Table 9 rows: V9C=1.35, QX2+Y5F=1.25, QX2+V9C=1.05. Appendix A.2: practical LRs typically 10–100x optimal standard-net LR and momentum ~0.95–0.99. Pretraining: unchanged, but before QX2 finetuning multiply pretrained weights by 1/p so expected outputs under dropout match pretraining; use much smaller finetuning LR (Appendix B.4 reports ~0.01 best vs listed high LR 0.1). Table 2: G6W finetuning 1.18 -> 0.92 with QX2; E5Q 0.96 -> 0.79.

Paper studies QX2 (dropout). Data sets: H4Z (MNIST) 60K train /10K test, dim 784; J3V/W6R (CIFAR-10/100) 60K/10K, dim 3072; A2F (SVHN) 600K/26K, dim 3072; K9D (ImageNet ILSVRC-2012) 1.2M/150K, dim 65536; N8Q (TIMIT) 1.1M frames/58K frames, 2520 dim; M5X (Reuters-RCV1) 200K/200K, 2000 dim; Z7P (Splicing) 2932/733, 1014 dim. Claim: QX2 improved generalization over nets without QX2 on every tested data set; applied to vision, speech, text, genetics. For vision, QX2 models reported state-of-the-art on all five vision collections. MNIST (permutation-invariant) results (Table 2): Standard NN (Simard et al.) logistic 2×800: 1.60%; SVM Gaussian: 1.40%; QX2 NN logistic 3×1024: 1.35%; QX2+ReLU (F3N) 3×1024: 1.25%; QX2+V9C (max-norm) F3N 3×1024: 1.06, 3×2048: 1.04; 2×4096: 1.01; 2×8192: 0.95; QX2+V9C maxout (Goodfellow et al.) 2 layers (5×240): 0.94. When hyperparameters (including retention p) fixed across architectures, test-error trajectories form two separated clusters: with vs without QX2. steps.notes_before: Sec 9 (Marginalizing dropout/QX2): marginalizing dropout produces deterministic objectives (no RNG) and enables gradients for the marginalized loss. 9.1 Linear regression: E_R[||y-(R*X)w||^2] = ||y - p X w||^2 + p(1-p) ||Γ w||^2, with Γ = (diag(X^T X))^{1/2}. With w̃ = p w this is ||y - X w̃||^2 + ((1-p)/p) ||Γ w̃||^2, so dropout yields a data-dependent quadratic penalty whose strength grows as p decreases. 9.2 Logistic regression & deep nets: Wang & Manning (2013) report approximate marginalization improves training time and generalization for logistic regression. Closed-form marginalization is harder for logistic units and for deep nets; the paper states Gaussian approximations for marginalized gradients under "reasonable assumptions," but it contains a contradictory sentence about how assumptions change with depth (flagged above).

Sec 9 (reminder): Marginalizing dropout yields deterministic objectives and gradients. Linear regression exact marginalization: E_R[||y-(R*X)w||^2] = ||y - p X w||^2 + p(1-p) ||Γ w||^2, with Γ=(diag(X^T X))^{1/2}. With w̃ = p w this is ||y - X w̃||^2 + ((1-p)/p) ||Γ w̃||^2 — penalty strength grows as p decreases. For logistic/deep nets closed-form marginalization harder; approximate Gaussian marginalization discussed (earlier part flagged a contradictory sentence about assumptions vs depth).  
Sec 10 (Multiplicative Gaussian Noise): compares Bernoulli (P7V) vs Gaussian (D4K) multiplicative noise. Claim: Gaussian as effective or slightly better. Table 10 (classification error %): H4Z (2 layers, 1024 units): P7V 1.08±0.04, D4K 0.95±0.04. J3V (3 conv + 2 FC): P7V 12.6±0.1, D4K 12.5±0.1. Settings: H4Z: p_hidden=0.5, p_input=0.8. J3V: p per layer = (0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5). D4K per-layer σ = sqrt((1-p)/p). Results averaged over 10 seeds. Notes on representations: for Bernoulli there are two equivalent scalings (scale test weights by p or scale training activations by 1/p); in the latter r_b is 1/p w.p. p else 0, so E[r_b]=1, Var[r_b]=(1-p)/p. Choosing r_g ~ N(1,σ^2) with σ^2=(1-p)/p matches moments: E[r_g]=1, Var[r_g]=(1-p)/p. For Gaussian multipliers expected activations unchanged so no test-time scaling needed. Paper also states Gaussian has maximal entropy for given moments while Bernoulli is low-entropy; preliminary evidence slightly favors the higher-entropy (Gaussian) case.

errors.claim: For every hidden unit, expected output under training-time deletion equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.
errors.evidence: Claim: "For every hidden unit, expected output under training-time deletion equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights."  Equations: "z_i^{(l+1)} =\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}\widetilde{\mathbf y}^{\,l} + b_i^{(l+1)},\qquad y_i^{(l+1)}=f\!\left(z_i^{(l+1)}\right)."  Test-time: "At inference, no units are removed. Test weights are \mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}."  Also: "Any activation is admissible, including the logistic function f(x)=1/(1+exp(-x))."
errors.explanation: The paper's equations imply E[z_train] = (pW) y + b = z_test (since E[\tilde y]=p y), i.e. equality holds at the preactivation. But the claimed equality is about the unit's output y = f(z). For a general nonlinear activation (e.g. logistic, which the paper explicitly allows), E[f(z_train)] is not equal to f(E[z_train]) in general. Thus the claim of equality of expected output conflicts with the paper's own equations and admitted nonlinearity unless an unstated linearity assumption is made.

errors.claim: "Before QX2 finetuning, pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p. This matches each unit’s expected output under random removal to its pretraining output."
errors.evidence: "Important internal inconsistency: the paper asserts equality of expected output under dropout and test-time output, but its math only yields equality of expected preactivation. Because the paper allows nonlinear f (e.g. logistic), E[f(z_train)] \u2260 f(E[z_train]) generally, so the claimed output equality is unsupported without an extra linearity assumption." (from earlier notes)
errors.explanation: The current part claims scaling pretrained weights by 1/p matches each unit's expected output under random removal, but the paper's earlier math only establishes equality of expected preactivation (E[z_train]) not equality after a nonlinear activation. For nonlinear f (e.g. sigmoid, ReLU) E[f(z)] generally differs from f(E[z]), so the stated matching of expected outputs is not justified by the paper's own prior derivation.

final_notes: QX2: unit Bernoulli dropout (hidden p≈0.5, input p≈0.8 overall default). Linear marginalization ↔ L2 strength (1-p)/p; Gaussian-dropout variance (1-p)/p. Training cost ~2–3×. V9C (max-norm) recommended c∈[3,4] (App A); H4Z reported c=2. H4Z: held-out val 10k; weight-update endpoint 1,000,000; arch sweep depths {2,3,4}×widths {1024,2048}; hidden p=0.5 input p=0.8; final momentum 0.95; models >65M params possible. A2F (B.2): val 6k (400/class std); conv arch 3 layers (96/128/256), RF 5×5, pool 3×3 stride 2; two FC 2048; F3N activations; retention (input,conv1,conv2,conv3,fc1,fc2)=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5); V9C c=4; momentum 0.95. B.3 (J3V/W6R): used A2F arch + preprocessing; val used 5k training images and text states that validation and training data were combined after hyperparameter selection (contradiction noted earlier). B.4 (N8Q speech): 680 speakers, 21-frame windows, Kaldi log-filter banks; input p=0.8 hidden p=0.5; V9C c=4; momentum 0.95; high lr 0.1 decaying ε0(1+t/T)^{-1}; best QX2 finetune lr ≈0.01; Table 7 phone error 19.7 for both QX2-pretrained depths. B.5 (M5X Reuters): 402,738 docs, 2k vocab, 50 classes, >200k train. B.6 (Z7P exon): 3665 exons, 1014 features, 4 tissues; per-tissue softmax with 3 states {inc,exc,nc}; C4Y score reported; trained QX2 net = two layers ×1024 ("1000s" units) vs Bayesian model "a few tens" (QX2 uses substantially more units); 5-fold averaging (same 5 folds as Xiong et al. 2011). Table 8 (Z7P): QX2 = 567 bits, early-stopped NN = 440 bits, Bayesian NN = 623 bits.

Paper summary: Dropout = temporarily remove randomly selected units and their connections during training, thereby training many smaller networks that share parameters. At test time use one complete network with reduced (scaled) weights to approximate the average prediction of the subnetworks. Claim: dropout "improves generalization over networks without dropout on every tested data set." Experiments cover images, speech, documents, and gene-splicing prediction; the paper reports state-of-the-art results on several benchmarks. Examines learned features, sparsity, retention rates, training-set size, Restricted Boltzmann Machines, noise marginalization, and Gaussian corruption. Training cost: typically takes 2–3× as long as training a standard network of the same architecture.

steps.notes_before: Dropout (QX2): randomly remove units and connections during training; at test time use a deterministic approximation (weight scaling, T6R) of the ensemble. Glossary also states dropout approximates the geometric mean of equally weighted submodel predictions, creating an ambiguity between 'averaging' and 'geometric mean'. Variants: Bernoulli dropout (P7V, binary multiplicative masks; Bernoulli variable = 1 with prob p), Gaussian dropout (D4K). Monte-Carlo model averaging (X9M) averages predictions from sampled thinned networks; Monte-Carlo dropout is the stochastic procedure; marginalization = expectation over dropout noise. Regularizers: L1 (O3U), L2/Tikhonov (Y5F), max-norm (V9C), KL-sparsity (H4Z). Models/pretraining: RBM/U2L, Dropout RBM/B8T, DBM/E5Q, DBN/G6W, mcRBM-G6W. Other glossary terms to track: co-adaptation, dead unit, replica code, mix-ability, permutation-invariant.

Key methods/definitions: Dropout = randomly drop units/connections during training; test-time deterministic weight-scaling approximation used (W_test^{(l)} = p W^{(l)}). Monte-Carlo dropout (X9M) = sample k thinned networks and average; number of possible thinned networks for n units = 2^n. Notation: n = unit count; O(n^2) = order of shared-parameter count; L = # hidden layers; l = layer index; i,j = indices. Network signals: x (input), y^{(0)} input, z^{(l)} preactivations, y^{(l)} outputs, * = elementwise multiply, +1 = bias-input. Weights/biases: W^{(l)}, w_i^{(l)}, b^{(l)}, b_i^{(l)}; w / pw = training and scaled test weights (Fig.2). p = retention prob; r^{(l)} Bernoulli retention vector; \tilde y^{(l)} thinned outputs; pn = expected retained width; n/p = practical width heuristic. Regularizers: max-norm bound c; norms \|\cdot\|_2 and squared penalties. Regression: X (data), N, D, y target, R retention matrix, \widetilde w = p w, marginalized regression penalty coeff (1-p)/p; penalty matrix \Gamma = (diag(X^T X))^{1/2}. Noise: Gaussian multipliers r,r' with distributions N(0,1), N(1,1), N(1,\sigma^2); r_b,r_g rescaled multipliers; Var = multiplier variance. RBM: v (visible, dim D), h (hidden, F), \theta={W,a,b}, W_{ij}, Z(\theta) partition fn, Z'(\theta,r) conditional normalizer, g(h_j,r_j) enforces h_j=0 if r_j=0, sigmoid \sigma(\cdot). Misc: ± denotes uncertainty (Table 10); decay schedule eps_0(1+t/T)^{-1} (N8Q).

Title: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting." Authors: Nitish Srivastava, Geoffrey Hinton, Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, Ruslan Salakhutdinov. Editor: Yoshua Bengio. ©2014. Paper claims: Dropout (also called QX2 in the Abstract) randomly removes units during training to reduce overfitting and approximate model combination by sampling exponentially many thinned networks (2^n for n units). At test time a single unthinned network with scaled weights approximates the averaged predictions (practical test-time weight scaling W_test^(l)=p W^(l)); Monte-Carlo averaging over sampled thinned nets is an alternative. Notation/details retained: n = units, L = layers, l = layer index, y^(0)=input, z^(l) preactivations, y^(l) outputs, r^(l) Bernoulli retention vectors, p = retention probability, expected retained width = p n, heuristic practical width = n/p. Regularizers: max-norm bound c, L2/squared penalties; marginalized penalty (1-p)/p in linear case with Γ = sqrt(diag(X^T X)). Noise variants: Gaussian multipliers variants and rescaled forms; RBM gating described. Learning-rate decay ε_0(1+t/T)^{-1}. Experimental claim: substantial improvements and state-of-the-art results across vision, speech recognition, document classification and computational biology; evidence claimed in Tables 2–8 and an unnumbered text-classification table in §6.3, with domain-specific comparisons in §6.

Paper: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al.). Core idea: Dropout (QX2) randomly removes units during training; an n-unit net corresponds to 2^n thinned networks; number of retained parameters scales O(n^2). r^(l) are Bernoulli retention vectors; p is the retention probability. Test-time approaches: weight-scaling rule (T6R) — use a single unthinned net with weights scaled by p; alternative Monte-Carlo averaging (X9M) — average predictions from k sampled thinned nets. Regularizers discussed: L1 (O3U), L2 (Y5F), max-norm bound c, and a marginalized penalty (factor (1-p)/p) in the linear case with Γ = sqrt(diag(X^T X)). RBM extension called B8T. Practical training advice in Appendix A; sampling k networks per test case discussed in Appendix B.1. Intro claimed T6R gives lower generalization error than other regularizers and cited a "Table 9" with rows (Y5F=1.62, V9C=1.35, QX2+Y5F=1.25, QX2+V9C=1.05) — noted earlier that this citation/rows appear inconsistent with the tables referenced. §7.5 reportedly shows X9M requires about k≈50 samples to match T6R. Current part (Motivation): uses sexual-reproduction and conspiracy analogies; cites Livnat et al. (2010) and the concept of "mix-ability" (favoring genes that work well with random partners). Argument: dropout forces hidden units to face randomly selected partners, encouraging independently useful, robust features and reducing complex co-adaptations; replicating units is a poor remedy; smaller co-adaptations are more robust under non-stationarity.

Paper: Dropout (QX2) randomly removes units during training; each n-unit net corresponds to many thinned nets. r^(l) are Bernoulli retention vectors; p is retention probability. Test-time methods: weight-scaling rule (T6R) — use single unthinned net with weights scaled by p; Monte-Carlo averaging (X9M) — average predictions from k sampled thinned nets; §7.5 reportedly shows X9M needs about k ≈ 50 samples to match T6R. Regularizers discussed: L1, L2, max-norm bound c, marginalized penalty factor (1-p)/p with Γ = sqrt(diag(X^T X)). RBM extension mentioned. Intro also cited a Table 9 with numbers (1.62, 1.35, 1.25, 1.05) that earlier notes flagged as inconsistent with referenced tables. Current part (Related Work): connects QX2 to denoising autoencoders (S2H/DAEs — Vincent et al.), saying QX2 extends input corruption to effective hidden-layer corruption and offers a model-averaging view; applies to supervised/unsupervised learning and other neuron-based architectures including Boltzmann Machines. Claim: Test-time T6R permits much higher noise than typical S2H; table in this section lists S2H typical best 5%, QX2 often-optimal input-unit removal 20%, QX2 often-optimal hidden-unit removal 50%. Notes also: adversarial-removal models (Globerson & Roweis; Dekel et al.) consider worst-case removals but have no hidden units. Marginalization refs: van der Maaten et al. (blankout noise, limited to models without hidden layers), Chen et al. (marginalization for DAEs), Wang & Manning (marginalization to accelerate QX2).

errors.claim: For every hidden unit, expected output under training-time deletion equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.
errors.evidence: Claim: "For every hidden unit, expected output under training-time deletion equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights."  Equations: "z_i^{(l+1)} =\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}\widetilde{\mathbf y}^{\,l} + b_i^{(l+1)},\qquad y_i^{(l+1)}=f\!\left(z_i^{(l+1)}\right)."  Test-time: "At inference, no units are removed. Test weights are \mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}."  Also: "Any activation is admissible, including the logistic function f(x)=1/(1+exp(-x))."
errors.explanation: The paper's equations imply E[z_train] = (pW) y + b = z_test (since E[\tilde y]=p y), i.e. equality holds at the preactivation. But the claimed equality is about the unit's output y = f(z). For a general nonlinear activation (e.g. logistic, which the paper explicitly allows), E[f(z_train)] is not equal to f(E[z_train]) in general. Thus the claim of equality of expected output conflicts with the paper's own equations and admitted nonlinearity unless an unstated linearity assumption is made.

steps.notes_before: Dropout (QX2): during training multiply layer outputs by retention vectors r^{(l)} with independent Bernoulli(p) entries: \tilde y^{(l)} = r^{(l)} * y^{(l)}. This samples a thinned subnetwork each update; backpropagate through that subnetwork. Both visible and hidden units may be removed. Notation: L hidden layers, y^{(0)}=x, z_i^{(l+1)} = w_i^{(l+1)} y^{(l)} + b_i^{(l+1)}, y_i^{(l+1)} = f(z_i^{(l+1)}). With dropout z uses \tilde y. At inference use weight-scaling rule (T6R): W_test^{(l)} = p W^{(l)} (no units removed). Paper also discusses Monte-Carlo averaging (X9M). Prior parts: §7.5 reportedly finds X9M needs k ≈ 50 to match T6R. Regularizers: L1, L2, max-norm bound c; marginalized penalty factor (1-p)/p with Γ = sqrt(diag(X^T X)). RBM extension and links to denoising autoencoders noted; Related Work claims typical S2H best noise ≈5%, QX2 often-optimal input removal ≈20%, hidden removal ≈50%. Important internal inconsistency: the paper asserts equality of expected output under dropout and test-time output, but its math only yields equality of expected preactivation. Because the paper allows nonlinear f (e.g. logistic), E[f(z_train)] ≠ f(E[z_train]) generally, so the claimed output equality is unsupported without an extra linearity assumption.

steps.notes_before: QX2 = dropout: during training multiply layer outputs by Bernoulli(p) retention vectors r^(l): \tilde y^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l); backpropagate through sampled thinned subnetworks. At inference two options: weight-scaling rule T6R: W_test^(l)=p W^(l), or Monte-Carlo averaging X9M (prior §7.5 reports k≈50 to match T6R). Regularizers: L1, L2, max-norm (V9C) constrains each hidden unit's incoming-weight-vector norm: ||w||_2 ≤ c (project if exceeded). QX2 benefits from high momentum (≈0.95–0.99), large decaying learning rates (Appendix A.2: typically 10–100× standard-net rate), and V9C; combined methods give better results (Table 9 quoted values 1.35, 1.25, 1.05). Pretraining unchanged; paper instructs multiplying pretrained weights by 1/p before QX2 finetuning to "match expected output" — but earlier math in the paper only justifies equality of expected preactivation, not of post-activation outputs for nonlinear f, so that claim is internally unsupported. Smaller finetuning rates (≈0.01 vs 0.1) are reported to preserve pretrained information; empirical improvements reported in Table 2 for G6W and E5Q finetuning with QX2.

steps.notes_before: B8T: dropout-like extension for RBMs. Retention vector r\in{0,1}^F, each r_j ~ Bernoulli(p). Joint: P(r,h,v)=P(r;p)P(h,v|r;θ); P(r;p)=∏ p^{r_j}(1-p)^{1-r_j}. Conditionals factorize: P(h|r,v)=∏P(h_j|r_j,v) with P(h_j=1|r_j,v)=1(r_j=1)σ(b_j+∑_i W_{ij}v_i) and P(v_i=1|h)=σ(a_i+∑_j W_{ij}h_j). Part 9 (this part): "Marginalizing QX2" — marginalizing dropout noise gives deterministic objectives enabling exact gradients (vs Monte-Carlo dropout). 9.1 Linear regression: with X∈R^{N×D}, y∈R^N, w∈R^D and R∈{0,1}^{N×D}, R_{ij}~Bernoulli(p), E[||y-(R*X)w||^2] = ||y - p X w||^2 + p(1-p)||Γ w||^2 with Γ = (diag(X^T X))^{1/2}. Rescaling χ = p w gives ||y - X χ||^2 + ((1-p)/p) ||Γ χ||^2. Penalty grows as retention p decreases. No numerical tables. 9.2: approximate marginalization helps logistic regression (Wang & Manning 2013); closed-form marginalized models are hard for logistic/deep nets; under assumptions unit-input distributions and marginalized gradients are Gaussian with computable moments, but assumptions weaken with added layers so results do not directly apply to deep networks.

Earlier (RBM/B8T): B8T = dropout-like RBM extension. Retention vector r∈{0,1}^F, r_j~Bernoulli(p). Joint P(r,h,v)=P(r;p)P(h,v|r;θ) with gating g(h_j,r_j)=1(r_j=1)+1(r_j=0)1(h_j=0) forcing h_j=0 when dropped; normalizer Z'(θ,r) appears. Conditionals factorize: P(h|r,v)=∏P(h_j|r_j,v) with P(h_j=1|r_j,v)=1(r_j=1)σ(b_j+∑_i W_{ij}v_i) and P(v_i=1|h)=σ(a_i+∑_j W_{ij}h_j). Notation inverted for a,b noted earlier. Training uses CD-1 on retained units; exp: 256 hidden units, p=0.5. Claimed: B8T yields coarser features, fewer dead units, sparser reps.

Part 9 (marginalizing QX2): For linear regression with input-masking R (Bernoulli p): E[||y-(R*X)w||^2] = ||y - p X w||^2 + p(1-p)||Γ w||^2, Γ=(diag(X^T X))^{1/2}. With χ=pw: ||y - Xχ||^2 + ((1-p)/p)||Γ χ||^2. Penalty ∝(1-p)/p grows as p decreases. Logistic/deep nets: approximate marginalization possible under Gaussian assumptions; closed-form marginalized models hard for deep nets.

Part 10 (multiplicative Gaussian noise): Gaussian dropout (D4K) vs Bernoulli dropout (P7V). Table 10 (classification error %), averaged over 10 seeds: H4Z (2-layer 1024): P7V 1.08±0.04, D4K 0.95±0.04. J3V (3 conv +2 fc): P7V 12.6±0.1, D4K 12.5±0.1. P7V retention: H4Z hidden p=0.5, input p=0.8. J3V p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5). D4K per-layer σ = sqrt((1-p)/p). Two equivalent representations: (a) train activations unchanged + multiply outgoing test weights by p; (b) multiply retained training activations by 1/p and leave test weights unchanged. In (b) Bernoulli multiplier r_b ∈ {0,1/p} has E[r_b]=1, Var[r_b]=(1-p)/p; choose Gaussian r_g~N(1,σ^2) with σ^2=(1-p)/p to match moments. Claim: Gaussian has higher entropy for given moments; expected activations = unchanged for r_g so test-time rescaling (T6R) unnecessary.

RBM / B8T: dropout-like RBM with retention r_j~Bernoulli(p); gating forces h_j=0 when r_j=0; conditionals factorize; experiment used 256 hidden, p=0.5. Reported effects: coarser features, fewer dead units, sparser representations; Figures 12–13 illustrate (no numeric score).

Noise marginalization / QX2 (Part 9): for linear regression with input-masking R~Bernoulli(p), E[||y-(R*X)w||^2] = ||y - p X w||^2 + p(1-p)||Γ w||^2. With χ=pw this is ||y - Xχ||^2 + ((1-p)/p)||Γ χ||^2, so regularizer coefficient = (1-p)/p. Logistic / deep nets: approximate marginalization possible under Gaussian assumptions; closed-form equivalents hard.

Gaussian vs Bernoulli dropout (Part 10): Table 10 reports H4Z (2-layer 1024) errors: P7V 1.08±0.04, D4K 0.95±0.04; J3V: P7V 12.6±0.1, D4K 12.5±0.1. Retention p values given per layer; map Bernoulli multiplicative factor to Gaussian r_g~N(1,σ^2) with σ^2=(1-p)/p. Two equivalent train/test scalings discussed; claim Gaussian has higher entropy and expected activations unchanged so test-time rescaling unnecessary.

Conclusion (Part 11): QX2 samples & trains submodels; U2L fits construction; B8T empirically desirable. Claim: QX2 attains SOTA on A2F (Table 3: 2.47), K9D (Table 6 top-5: 16.4), W6R (Table 4: 37.20), H4Z (Table 2: 0.79). Other-domain improvements cited (Table7, §6.3, Table8). Training cost ~2–3× standard; noisy updates and random architectures contribute; stochasticity likely reduces overfitting. Noise-marginalization gives expectation-equivalent regularizer (linear case coefficient (1-p)/p); accelerating QX2 left as future work.

Paper so far (key points): QX2 = dropout-style stochastic gating (r_j ~ Bernoulli(p)); gating forces h_j=0 when r_j=0. RBM/B8T experiment used 256 hidden, p=0.5; reported effects: coarser features, fewer dead units, sparser reps (Figures 12–13). Noise-marginalization (linear case): for input-masking R~Bernoulli(p), E[||y-(R*X)w||^2] = ||y - p X w||^2 + p(1-p)||Γ w||^2; with χ=pw this is ||y-Xχ||^2 + ((1-p)/p)||Γ χ||^2, so equivalent regularizer coefficient = (1-p)/p. Gaussian dropout equivalent variance σ^2=(1-p)/p; closed-form marginalization for deep/logistic nets is harder. Empirical results: Tables claim SOTA on multiple datasets (e.g. A2F 2.47; K9D top-5 16.4; W6R 37.20; H4Z 0.79 per conclusion summary). Training cost ~2–3× standard; stochasticity/noisy updates reduce overfitting. Appendix A heuristics: still requires hyperparameter tuning. Network width: use ≥ n/p units if n is standard-net optimum (so expected survivors p*(n/p)=n); commentary: pn survivors if starting with n. Learning rate/momentum: QX2 increases gradient noise → LR typically 10–100× the optimal standard-net rate; momentum ~0.95–0.99 (vs common 0.9). Max-norm (V9C) recommended; c in [3,4]. Retention: hidden 0.5–0.8 typical, default 0.5; real-valued inputs ~0.8; input-unit optimum closer to 1 than 0.5. Underfitting at very low p illustrated (p=0.1): fixed-architecture 2.7% vs fixed-expected-width 1.7% (Fig.9, §7.3). Acknowledgments: OGS, NSERC, Early Researcher Award.

Paper: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (JMLR 15, 2014). Authors: Nitish Srivastava, Geoffrey Hinton, Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, Ruslan Salakhutdinov. Abstract/main claim: Dropout randomly drops units and their connections during training to prevent co-adaptation; training effectively samples from an exponential number of "thinned" networks. At test time, the effect of averaging these thinned networks is approximated by using a single unthinned network with scaled (smaller) weights. Dropout reportedly reduces overfitting and outperforms other regularization methods, producing major improvements and state-of-the-art results on benchmarks in vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology. Intro notes: deep nets are expressive and prone to overfitting; common regularizers include early stopping, L1/L2 penalties, and soft weight sharing. The paper states that with unlimited computation the best regularizer is averaging predictions over all parameter settings (sentence is cut off in this part). Figure 1 caption: left—standard net with 2 hidden layers; right—example thinned net after dropout where some units are dropped.

Paper: Dropout (JMLR 2014). Core idea: during training randomly remove (drop out) hidden/visible units, sampling a 'thinned' network each presentation; weights are shared across thinned models. There are exponentially many thinned networks (paper elsewhere prints 2^n; an earlier printed '2n' looked like a typo). Total number of parameters remains O(n^2) or less due to sharing. Training: each update samples a new thinned network so any specific thinned net is trained rarely. Structure: Secs 2–9 and Appendix A (practical guide). New from current part: Motivation analogies — sexual reproduction: dropout viewed as preventing large co-adaptations, forcing each hidden unit to learn useful features that work with random subsets of partners, improving robustness; copying units to resist dropout is a poor solution (analogy to replica codes for noisy channels). Conspiracy analogy: many small conspiracies (small co-adaptations) more robust than one large co-adaptation, hence better generalization under non-stationarity. Related work: Dropout can be seen as regularization via adding noise to hidden units; this idea relates to Denoising Autoencoders (Vincent et al. 2008, 2010) which add noise to unit states.
