steps.notes_before: Paper: Dropout trains by randomly dropping units (thinning) and sharing weights across exponentially many sub-networks. Training samples a new thinned net each presentation; backpropagate gradients through that thinned net. At test time use a single unthinned net with weights scaled by retention probabilities (W_test = p W^(l) per layer). Typical choices: drop ~50% hidden units (p_hidden ≈ 0.5), ~20% inputs (p_input ≈ 0.8); DAEs typically use 5% input noise but test-time scaling allows higher noise. Dropout can be applied to hidden layers and other neuron-based architectures (e.g., Boltzmann Machines, RBMs). Interpretation: stochastic regularization / model averaging; related to denoising autoencoders and marginalizing noise. Definition details: network with L hidden layers; y(0)=x; feed-forward recurrence given as z^{(l+1)} = W^{(l+1)} y^{(l)} + b^{(l+1)}, y^{(l+1)} = f(z^{(l+1)}). With dropout: sample r^{(l)} ~ Bernoulli(p) elementwise, form y_e^{(l)} = r^{(l)} * y^{(l)} and use y_e^{(l)} as input to next layer. Loss is minimized stochastically (expected loss); prior adversarial-drop work fixes max number dropped (no hidden-layer models).

Training: dropout nets trained by SGD on ‘‘thinned’’ nets — for each training case in a mini‑batch sample dropout mask, do forward/backprop on that thinned net; gradients averaged over mini‑batch; any case that omits a parameter contributes zero gradient for that parameter. Standard SGD tricks (momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 weight decay) help. Max‑norm regularization: constrain incoming weight vector w at each hidden unit to ||w||2 ≤ c by projecting back into the ball of radius c whenever it exceeds c (c is a tunable hyperparameter). Max‑norm often improves SGD even without dropout; combining dropout + max‑norm + large decaying LR + high momentum gives further gains (intuition: ball constraint prevents blowup so large LR can be used for exploration). Unsupervised pretraining: stacks of RBMs/autoencoders/DBMs can be used; pretraining stays the same, but when finetuning with dropout scale pretrained weights by 1/p so expected output under dropout matches pretraining output. If finetune LR is too large pretrained information can be lost; use smaller LR to retain gains. Experiments: datasets include MNIST, TIMIT, CIFAR‑10/100, SVHN, ImageNet, Reuters‑RCV1, and an Alternative Splicing RNA dataset; more details in Appendix B.

final_notes:
Additions from this part:
- Audio / frame-based model: consecutive frames per window = 21; input retention p=0.8; hidden retention p=0.5; V9C (all layers) c=4; momentum = 0.95; high learning rate = 0.1 with decay ε0(1+t/T)^{-1}; G6W pretraining algorithm = U2L trained with CD-1; Gaussian-U2L input-unit variance fixed to 1; best QX2 G6W-finetuning LR ≈ 0.01. Adding V9C during G6W finetuning gave no improvement; the smaller LR was important.

- B.5 M5X: used subset = 402,738 articles; 2000-word vocabulary; 50 disjoint categories (each doc in exactly one); equal-sized train/test splits → >200,000 training examples.

- B.6 Z7P: 3,665 cassette exons; 1,014 RNA features; 4 tissue types (derived from 27 mouse tissues). Each input has 4 target softmaxes (one per tissue); each softmax has states {inc, exc, nc}. Objective C4Y = Σ_i Σ_t Σ_s p_{i,t}^s log( q_t^s(r_i) /  ar p^s ), where  ar p^s averages p_{i,t}^s over i,t. QX2 hidden-unit scale = "1000s"; trained QX2 network = 2 layers × 1024 units; hidden p=0.5; input p=0.7; regularization/rate schedule = V9C (high decaying LRs); results averaged over same 5 folds as Xiong et al. (2011).

Keep earlier key results and previously noted internal mismatches (e.g., Appendix A typical V9C c≈3–4 vs Appendix B H4Z reported c=2; M5X prose/table percent-reduction mismatch; TIMIT 8-layer 20.5 vs 20.7%).

Title: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting". Authors: Nitish Srivastava, Geoffrey Hinton, Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, Ruslan Salakhutdinov; Dept. of Computer Science, University of Toronto. Journal: JMLR 15 (2014). Header lists pages 1929–1958 while page map lists pages 1930–1955 (internal inconsistency noted). Abstract summary: introduces dropout (called "QX2: dropout") — a training procedure that temporarily removes randomly selected units and their connections, inhibiting excessive co-adaptation and effectively sampling exponentially many parameter-sharing thinned networks. At test time a single unthinned network with reduced weights approximates the averaged predictions of these thinned networks. Claims dropout substantially reduces overfitting versus other regularizers and yields major improvements, achieving state-of-the-art performance on many benchmarks in supervised vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology.

errors.claim: "the proposed less expensive construction approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many learned, parameter-sharing models’ predictions."
errors.evidence: "At test time a single unthinned network with reduced weights approximates the averaged predictions of these thinned networks." (from earlier notes)
errors.explanation: This part states the approximation is an "equally weighted geometric mean", whereas my earlier notes (from the paper's abstract) say the single unthinned network "approximates the averaged predictions" of the thinned networks. "Averaged" ordinarily implies an arithmetic mean, which is not the same as a geometric mean, so the paper's wording appears inconsistent between parts.

steps.notes_before: Title: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al., UToronto). Header/page-number inconsistency noted earlier. Dropout (QX2) randomly removes units/connections during training, producing exponentially many (2^n for n units) thinned networks; parameters are shared so total distinct parameters retained are O(n^2) or fewer. With unlimited computation, posterior-weighted averaging over parameters is ideal; the paper claims its method approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of these thinned models' predictions (introduction) — earlier abstract wording said it "approximates the averaged predictions", a potential arithmetic vs geometric-mean wording mismatch. Every presentation samples/trains a new thinned member; individual members are rarely trained thoroughly. Practical inference: T6R (weight scaling) uses one unthinned network at test time; X9M refers to Monte-Carlo model averaging (more expensive). Claims T6R gives much lower generalization error than other regularizers across tasks. Method extends to graphical models, e.g., Dropout RBM (B8T) from RBMs (U2L). Paper map: §2 motivation; §3 prior work; §4 formal model; §5 training algorithm; §6 experiments; §7 network/hyperparameter interactions; §8 Dropout RBMs; §9 marginalization; Appendix A practical guidance.

Title: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al.). Earlier: header/page-number inconsistency noted. Method overview: dropout (QX2) randomly removes units/connections during training, producing exponentially many (2^n) thinned networks; parameters are shared so total distinct parameters are O(n^2) or fewer. Training samples/train different thinned networks; individual thinned members rarely trained thoroughly. Test-time inference: T6R = weight-scaling using one unthinned network; X9M = Monte-Carlo model averaging (more expensive). Paper claims T6R yields much lower generalization error than other regularizers across tasks. Extensions: Dropout RBM (B8T). Paper map: §2 motivation; §3 prior work; §4 formal model; §5 training algorithm; §6 experiments; §7 interactions; §8 Dropout RBMs; §9 marginalization; Appendix A guidance. New from §2 (Motivation): authors use biological analogy—sexual vs asexual reproduction—and cite Livnat et al. (2010) arguing selection can favor gene "mix-ability" rather than individual-fitness optimization. Dropout is analogous: hidden units face randomly selected partners, which favors independently useful, robust features and reduces complex co-adaptations. Replicating units many times is deemed a poor robustness fix (analogy to replica codes and noisy channels). Conspiracy analogy: many small cooperating subsets are more robust under non-stationarity than a single large co-adapted set; complex co-adaptations may overfit training data and fail on novel test data.

Title: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al.). Method: dropout (QX2) randomly removes units/connections during training producing ~2^n thinned networks; parameters shared so distinct params O(n^2). Training: each SGD update samples a thinned network; individual thinned members rarely trained thoroughly. Test-time inference: T6R = weight-scaling using one unthinned network; X9M = Monte-Carlo model averaging (more expensive). Paper claims T6R gives much lower generalization error than other regularizers across tasks. Motivation (§2): biological analogy (mix-ability), reduces co-adaptations. Related work (§3): dropout interpretable as noise in hidden-unit states, extends denoising autoencoders (Vincent et al. 2008/2010) — effective hidden-layer corruption, model-averaging view, supervised/unsupervised use, applicable to Boltzmann Machines. Table: S2H (DAE) typical best noise ~5%; QX2 often optimal input-unit removal ~20%; QX2 often optimal hidden-unit removal ~50%. Adversarial-removal alternatives (Globerson & Roweis 2006; Dekel et al. 2010) consider worst-case removals under a budget and have no hidden units. Analytic marginalization can give deterministic regularizers in simple cases; van der Maaten et al. (2013) studied exponential-family input-noise (blankout) limited to models without hidden layers; Chen et al. (2012) studied marginalization for DAEs; Wang & Manning (2013) proposed marginalization to speed up dropout. Section map: §2 motivation; §3 prior work; §4 formal model; §5 training algorithm; §6 experiments; §7 interactions; §8 Dropout RBMs; §9 marginalization; Appendix A guidance.

Paper: Dropout regularization. Key idea: during training randomly delete (zero) units (hidden and/or visible) to sample many thinned subnetworks; parameters shared across subnetworks. Retention choices are independent Bernoulli variables with common probability p (can be chosen by validation). Typical defaults: hidden-unit retention p≈0.5 (i.e. ~50% removal); input-unit removal often ~20% (retention p≈0.8) — input retention usually nearer full. Training: each SGD update samples r^{(l)} (vector of independent Bernoulli(p)) and forms \tilde y^{(l)} = r^{(l)} * y^{(l)}; forward: z_i^{(l+1)} = w_i^{(l+1)} \tilde y^{(l)} + b_i^{(l+1)}, y_i^{(l+1)} = f(z_i^{(l+1)}). Backprop passes gradients through the sampled subnetwork. Notation: y^{(0)}=x; L hidden layers (indexed 1..L); feed-forward written for l=0..L-1 producing layer l+1. Activation f can be any (e.g. logistic). Test-time inference: no dropout; use one unthinned network with outgoing weights scaled by p: W_test^{(l)} = p W^{(l)} (equivalently unit outputs' expected training contribution equals test-time contribution with scaled weights). Figures illustrate training (stochastic gates r) vs testing (weights scaled by p). Other parts: training samples many subnetworks per SGD update; Monte-Carlo averaging at test-time is an alternative to weight-scaling but more expensive.

Part 5: QX2 (dropout) gives significant gains; combining it with high momentum, large decaying learning rates, and an incoming-weight constraint (V9C = max-norm) gives further improvement. V9C enforces ||w||_2 <= c with projection to the ball surface when exceeded; c is tuned by validation. Proposed optimization account claims large learning rates are safe inside the fixed-radius ball; QX2 provides noise exploration; learning rates decay to smaller steps. SGD differs from standard training only by per-case sampled thinned networks: each mini-batch case uses its own sampled network; gradients averaged across cases; a case not using a parameter contributes zero. Momentum, annealed (decaying) learning rates and other heuristics remain useful. Unsupervised pretraining is unchanged, but before QX2 finetuning pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p so each unit’s expected random-removal output matches its pretraining output. Smaller finetuning learning rates help preserve pretrained information. Pretraining (with unlabeled data) can improve over random init; applicable to stacked U2L, autoencoders, DBMs for finetuning.

steps.notes_before: QX2 (dropout) improves generalization across all reported datasets. Data sets (from Table 1): H4Z (MNIST) 784 dim, 60K train, 10K test; A2F (SVHN) 3072 dim, 600K train, 26K test; J3V/W6R (CIFAR) 3072 dim, 60K train, 10K test; K9D (ImageNet/ILSVRC-2012) reported as 65536 (256 × 256 color) with 1.2M train, 150K test — dimensionality statement is internally inconsistent; N8Q (TIMIT frames) 2520 dim, 1.1M train frames, 58K test frames; M5X (Reuters) 2000 dim, 200K train, 200K test; Z7P (Alternative Splicing) 1014 dim, 2932 train, 733 test. H4Z results (Table 2): baseline Simard 2003 logistic 2×800 = 1.60% error; SVM Gaussian 1.40%; QX2 logistic 3×1024 1.35%; QX2 + ReLU 1.25%; QX2 + V9C (max-norm) with ReLU improves to 1.06% (3×1024) and down to 0.95% (2 layers, 8192 units); maxout (Goodfellow et al. 2013) 0.94%; pretrained models + QX2 finetuning: G6W+QX2 0.92%, E5Q+QX2 0.79% (best permutation-invariant reported). Figure 4: training curves separate into two clusters (with vs without QX2). For A2F, conv nets benefit from QX2 in fully connected and conv layers; maxout gives further gains. Pretraining/finetuning protocol (weights scaled by 1/p before QX2 finetuning, smaller LR) remains as described earlier.

errors.claim: "For visible units ... an ordinary U2L defines P(\mathbf h,\mathbf v;\theta) = \frac{1}{Z(\theta)} \exp( \mathbf v^\top\mathbf W\mathbf h+ \mathbf a^\top\mathbf h+ \mathbf b^\top\mathbf v )." and later "P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v) = \mathbf1(r_j=1)\, \sigma\!\left(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i\right)." and "P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h) = \sigma\!\left(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j\right)."
errors.evidence: The U2L joint is written with the term a^T h + b^T v (so a_j are the hidden biases and b_i the visible biases). Later the hidden conditional uses b_j in P(h_j=1|...) and the visible conditional uses a_i in P(v_i=1|...), i.e. the names a and b are swapped in the conditional formulas.
errors.explanation: The energy / joint distribution indicates a_j are hidden biases and b_i visible biases, so P(h_j=1|v) should use a_j (not b_j) and P(v_i=1|h) should use b_i (not a_i). The paper's conditional equations are inconsistent with its earlier parameter naming.

Section 8: B8T = mixture of exponentially many shared-weight U2Ls via retention vector r∈{0,1}^F; U2L energy P(h,v;θ) ∝ exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v); conditionals force h_j=0 when r_j=0; learning via CD-1 with r sampled per case; B8T learned coarser/stroke-like features, fewer dead units, much sparser representations (no explicit sparsity regularizer); caveat: paper swaps a and b between energy and conditional equations. Section 9: deterministic noise-marginalized losses yield gradients; linear regression marginalizes to ||y - X w~||^2 + ((1-p)/p)||Γ w~||^2 (adaptive ridge); logistic/deep nets require Gaussian approximations that degrade with depth. Section 10: multiplicative Gaussian (D4K) vs Bernoulli dropout (P7V) — Gaussian slightly favored in some comparisons (Table 10: H4Z P7V 1.08±0.04 vs D4K 0.95±0.04; J3V 12.6±0.1 vs 12.5±0.1); retention p settings and σ = sqrt((1-p)/p) make E=1, Var=(1-p)/p; removes test-time rescaling. Part 11 (Conclusion): large-model construction samples smaller submodels; U2L fits this and B8T shows desirable properties; paper states QX2 SOTA on A2F,K9D,W6R,H4Z and "considerable improvement" elsewhere (but this overgeneralizes given the M5X/table mismatch); training typically 2–3× longer due to noisy parameter updates and differing per-case architectures; noise marginalization gives expectation-equivalent regularizers (exact for linear regression); accelerating QX2 left for future work.

errors.claim: "For a task whose optimal standard-net layer has \(n\) hidden units, a good QX2 layer should contain at least \(n/p\) units. Removing units reduces capacity: only \(pn\) units remain in expectation,"
errors.evidence: "...a good QX2 layer should contain at least \(n/p\) units. Removing units reduces capacity: only \(pn\) units remain in expectation..."
errors.explanation: These two statements are mathematically inconsistent: if the layer contains n/p units and each unit is retained with probability p, the expected number of units remaining is (n/p)*p = n, not pn. The sentence contradicts itself about the expected remaining unit count.

grade.reason: The reviewer’s seventh reported error flags the claimed 14.3% relative reduction for M5X/QX2 and shows the table’s numbers (31.05% → 29.62%) imply ≈4.6% relative reduction, contradicting the planted 14.3% claim.

errors.claim: "ImageNet (ILSVRC-2012) | Vision | 65536 (256 × 256 color) | 1.2M | 150K" (Table 1)
errors.evidence: Table 1 lists ImageNet dimensionality as "65536 (256 × 256 color)".
errors.explanation: The numeric dimensionality 65,536 equals 256×256 (a single channel). For color images the dimensionality should include 3 channels: 256×256×3 = 196,608. Thus the stated number contradicts the parenthetical '(256 × 256 color)'.

errors.claim: "All dropout networks use p=0.5 for hidden units and p=0.8 for input units."
errors.evidence: "Retention probabilities, from input through convolutional and fully connected layers, were: p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5)."
errors.explanation: The paper's blanket statement that all dropout networks use p=0.5 (hidden) and p=0.8 (input) is contradicted by the SVHN experiment, which specifies different per-layer retention probabilities.

errors.claim: "This is a 14.3% relative reduction"
errors.evidence: "Our best neural network without dropout gives 31.05% error. Dropout reduces it to 29.62%. This is a 14.3% relative reduction..."
errors.explanation: The quoted numbers imply an absolute drop of 31.05 - 29.62 = 1.43 percentage points, which is 1.43 / 31.05 = 0.0461 ≈ 4.6% relative reduction, not 14.3%. The paper's stated 14.3% is arithmetically inconsistent with its own reported error rates.

errors.claim: "Similarly, for an 8-layer network, error falls from 20.5% to 19.7%."
errors.evidence: Prose: "...for an 8-layer network, error falls from 20.5% to 19.7%." Table 7: "DBN-pretrained NN (8 layers) (Mohamed et al., 2010) | 20.7" and "DBN-pretrained NN (8 layers) + dropout | 19.7"; Table 7 also shows "mcRBM-DBN-pretrained NN (5 layers) (Dahl et al., 2010) | 20.5".
errors.explanation: The prose attributes 20.5% as the pre-dropout error for the 8-layer DBN-pretrained model, but Table 7 lists that 8-layer pre-dropout error as 20.7%. The 20.5% figure in the table belongs to a different model (the 5-layer mcRBM-DBN).

errors.claim: "P(h,v;\theta) = \frac{1}{Z(\theta)}\exp\!(v^\top Wh + a^\top h + b^\top v)" defines a as the hidden biases and b as the visible biases, but later the conditional formulas use b_j for the hidden-unit bias and a_i for the visible-unit bias.
errors.evidence: "P(h,v;\theta) = \frac{1}{Z(\theta)} \exp\!\left(v^\top Wh+a^\top h+b^\top v\right)." and "P(h_j=1\mid r_j,v) = \mathbf1(r_j=1) \sigma\!\left(b_j+\sum_i W_{ij}v_i\right)." and "P(v_i=1\mid h) = \sigma\!\left(a_i+\sum_j W_{ij}h_j\right)."
errors.explanation: From the joint distribution a is paired with h and b with v, so the hidden conditional should use a_j and the visible conditional should use b_i. The paper's conditionals swap a and b, which is internally inconsistent.

errors.claim: "This form essentially scales the cost on weight w_i by the standard deviation of data dimension i. Dimensions that vary more have their weights squeezed more."
errors.evidence: "\Gamma=\left(\operatorname{diag}(X^\top X)\right)^{1/2}."
errors.explanation: Gamma is defined as the square root of the diagonal of X^T X, i.e. Gamma_i = sqrt(sum_n x_{n,i}^2) (root-sum-of-squares / RMS up to a factor), not the sample standard deviation unless the columns of X have been mean-centered and normalized. Thus claiming Gamma equals the data standard deviation is incorrect without an additional assumption about X.

final_notes:
Appendix B: dataset-specific hyperparams and setups.
Global/dropout/optim: common retention often p_input=0.8, p_hidden=0.5; momentum up to 0.95; initial learning rate often high (0.1) with decay schedule epsilon(t)=epsilon_0*(1+t/T)^{-1}. Max-norm regularization used but magnitude varied by experiment (c=2 in some Table/figure experiments; c=4 for several dataset runs).
DBN / speech (Appendix B.4 / TIMIT): RBMs pretrained with CD-1; Gaussian-RBM input-unit variance fixed to 1. Standard dropout finetuning used high lr=0.1, but DBN finetuning required smaller lr ~0.01 for best results; adding max-norm to DBN finetuning gave no improvement. Reported speech results (Table 7 dropout rows) are 21.8%, 19.7%, 19.7%.
MNIST: 60k train / 10k test; 10k of train held out for validation; hyperparams chosen so best validation error at 1,000,000 updates, then train+val retrained 1,000,000 updates before test. Experiments in Fig.4 / Table2 used p_hidden=0.5, p_input=0.8, final momentum=0.95, max-norm c=2; larger nets (4096/8192) explored.
SVHN: ~600k train, 26k test, 6k validation; best conv architecture + two 2048 FCs; dropout p per layer = (0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5); max-norm c=4; momentum 0.95; selected model test error 2.55%.
CIFAR-10/100: 50k train/10k test, 5k val then combined back; preprocessing GCN + ZCA; architecture/dropout matched SVHN but input-layer rates reduced.
Reuters (B.5): subset of 402,738 articles (vocab 2000, 50 classes), split equally into train/test (~201k each). Dropout improved all tried architectures but less than for image/speech; best-network numbers cited: 31.05% (no dropout) vs 29.62% (with dropout).
Alternative splicing (B.6): 3665 exons, 1014 features, 4 tissue types -> 4 softmaxes each with 3 states (inc, exc, nc). Code-Quality objective: sum_i sum_t sum_s p_{i,t}^s log( q_t^s(r_i) / \bar p^s ). Two-layer dropout net (1024 units/layer), p_input=0.7, p_hidden=0.5, max-norm used, trained with high decaying lrs; results averaged over same 5 folds as Xiong et al. (2011).

Paper summary: Introduces dropout — randomly removing units and their connections during training, which samples many smaller networks that share weights. At test time, a single full network with scaled weights approximates the ensemble of sampled networks. Reports improvements on image, speech, text, and alternative-splicing tasks. Compares dropout with other regularizers and Bayesian neural networks. Studies learned features, sparsity, dropout rates, network size, training-set size, and test-time averaging; finds Dropout Restricted Boltzmann Machines learn qualitatively different features and sparser representations. For linear regression, marginalizing dropout yields a modified ridge-regression objective. Preliminary experiments compare Bernoulli dropout to multiplicative Gaussian noise. Limitation noted: training time typically 2–3× longer than standard networks with the same architecture.

Paper introduces dropout: during training randomly remove units and their incoming/outgoing connections (Bernoulli dropout uses binary vars that equal 1 with probability p, the retention probability). At test time the ensemble is approximated by a single deterministic model via weight scaling (multiply a unit’s outgoing weights by p) or by marginalizing dropout noise (deterministic dropout model); Monte-Carlo dropout/model averaging samples thinned networks at test time. Gaussian (multiplicative) dropout multiplies activations by Gaussian noise; paper compares Bernoulli and Gaussian variants. For linear regression, marginalized dropout is equivalent in expectation to a modified ridge (Tikhonov) regression. Dropout-RBMs are RBMs augmented with binary retention variables; CD-1/Contrastive Divergence used for RBM training; partition function Z(θ) appears in RBM formulation. Code Quality (alternative-splicing task) is the negative KL-divergence metric (higher is better). Other key methods/terms: DBN/DBM pretraining, max-norm constraint (bound hidden-unit incoming weight norms), L1/L2 weight penalties, KL-sparsity regularizer, ReLU and maxout units, pooling (max, L2, L4) in image models, max-pooling after conv layers, permutation-invariant vs 2-D MNIST settings, Top-1/Top-5 ImageNet error definitions, PCA/ZCA whitening used in preprocessing, mix-ability measure for genes. Noted limitation: training time typically 2–3× longer than standard networks with same architecture.

Key methods: dropout — Bernoulli dropout uses binary retention vars (retain with prob p); at test time approximate ensemble by weight-scaling (multiply outgoing weights by p) or by marginalizing dropout noise (deterministic model); Monte-Carlo dropout averages samples of thinned networks at test time; Gaussian (multiplicative) dropout multiplies activations by Gaussian noise. For linear regression, marginalized dropout = modified ridge (Tikhonov). Dropout-RBMs include binary retention variables; trained with CD-1. Code Quality metric = negative KL-divergence (higher is better). Regularization/architecture details: DBN/DBM pretraining; max-norm constraint (bound hidden-unit incoming weight norms); L1/L2 penalties; KL-sparsity regularizer; ReLU and maxout units; pooling: max, L2, L4; max-pooling after conv layers; permutation-invariant vs 2-D MNIST distinction. Image tasks: Top-1/Top-5 ImageNet error metrics; PCA/ZCA whitening used in preprocessing. Datasets and features: MNIST; TIMIT (preprocessed to log-filter banks via Kaldi; monophone system used for forced alignment/speech-frame labels); CIFAR-10/100; SVHN (RGB pixels normalized; comparisons list Binary Features (WDCH), HOG, KMeans); ImageNet / ILSVRC (ILSVRC-2010, ILSVRC-2012; ILSVRC discussed in Sec. 6.1.4); Reuters-RCV1; Alternative Splicing dataset (RNA features; softmax targets inc/exc/nc; mix-ability measure). Notation and key definitions: L (# hidden layers), l (layer index); i,j (unit/dim/data indices). x = network input (y^(0)). z^(l) = inputs to layer l; y^(l) = outputs; ~y^(l) = outputs after elementwise dropout mask. W^(l), w_i^(l), b^(l) = layer weights, unit incoming weights, biases. W_test^(l)=pW^(l) (test-time weight-scaling). f activation (example sigmoid 1/(1+exp(-x))); exp used in activations/probabilities. p = retention probability. r^(l) = Bernoulli mask vector for layer l; * = elementwise multiplication. n = # units (hidden units in a layer); 2^n possible thinned networks; O(n^2) shared parameter order; pn expected retained units. w general weight vector; ||w||_2 and max-norm bound c; squared norm notation ||·||^2. k = # MC samples for prediction averaging. RBM notation: v (visible), D (# visible), h (hidden), F (# hidden), binary spaces {0,1}^D/{0,1}^F, θ={W,a,b}, Z(θ) partition, r binary retention in Dropout RBM (and r as Gaussian noise in Sect.10), Z'(θ,r) conditional normalization, g(h_j,r_j) enforces h_j=0 if r_j=0, 1(·) indicator, P(·) probability, σ = RBM activation (and in Sect.10 Gaussian noise SD). Transpose, ∏, ∑ as usual. Regression: X∈R^{N×D}, y∈R^N, w∈R^D, R∈{0,1}^{N×D} with R_ij~Bernoulli(p). E, Var. Γ=(diag(X^T X))^{1/2} used in marginalized dropout penalty; ~w = p w. Multiplicative noise: h_i, r'~N(1,σ^2) with σ^2 matched to (1-p)/p; r_b rescaled Bernoulli =1/p w.p. p; r_g Gaussian mean 1 var (1-p)/p. Also listed N(1,1), N(0,1) as example Gaussians. TIMIT lr schedule ε0(1+t/T)^{-1}. p_{i,t}^s targets, q_t^s(r_i) predictions, ¯p^s average; |data points| used in Code Quality. Journal: JMLR 15 (2014) 1929-1958.

Main idea: During training randomly remove units+connections (Bernoulli retention p) sampling exponential number of thinned networks; at test time use one unthinned network with scaled weights (W_test = p W) to approximate average predictions. Dropout claimed to reduce overfitting and prevent co-adaptation.
Claims/evidence (reported): improves across domains — image results in Tables 2–6; TIMIT rows in Table 7; Reuters: 31.05% (no dropout) -> 29.62% (with dropout) in Sect. 6.3; alternative-splicing rows 440 and 567 bits in Table 8; Table 9: dropout improves over other regularizers in all rows; Dropout+Max-norm = 1.05% vs Max-norm = 1.35% and L2 = 1.62%.

Paper: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al., JMLR 2014). Main idea: during training randomly drop units (Bernoulli retain prob p) to sample many "thinned" networks; at test time use a single unthinned network with outgoing weights scaled by p (W_test = p W) to approximate averaging. Key definitions: L layers, r^(l) Bernoulli masks, ~y^(l) after dropout. A net with n units corresponds to 2^n thinned nets; they share weights so parameter count stays O(n^2). Typical choices: p≈0.5 for hidden units (often close to optimal), input-unit p usually closer to 1. Scaling outgoing weights by p at test time ensures expected training-time output equals test-time output. Motivation: approximate an equally weighted geometric mean / Bayesian-like averaging of exponentially many models with much less computation. Dropout applicable beyond feed-forward nets (Dropout RBM introduced). Paper claims dropout + weight-scaling reduces overfitting and improves generalization across domains; experiments reported in Sections 6–8 (image results Tables 2–6, TIMIT Table 7, Reuters improvement 31.05%→29.62% in Sect.6.3, alternative-splicing bits in Table 8, Table 9 comparisons: Dropout+Max-norm 1.05% vs Max-norm 1.35% vs L2 1.62%). TIMIT learning-rate schedule earlier noted: ε0 (1 + t/T)^(-1). Paper structure: Sec 2 motivation, 3 related work, 4 model, 5 training, 6 experiments, 7 hyperparams/properties, 8 Dropout RBMs, 9 marginalizing dropout, Appendix A guidance.

Paper: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al., JMLR 2014). Core idea: during training randomly drop units (Bernoulli masks r^(l), retain prob p) to sample many thinned networks; at test time use the full network with outgoing weights scaled by p (weight-scaling) to approximate averaging. Typical p≈0.5 for hidden units; input p usually closer to 1. Scaling by p makes test-time output equal to the expected training-time output (approximate model averaging). Dropout applies beyond feed-forward nets (Dropout RBMs): Figures 12–13 show qualitative feature and sparsity comparisons but no numeric performance comparison is reported there. Experiments (Secs.6–8) report improved generalization across domains (image Tables 2–6, TIMIT Table 7, Tables 2–7 and 9 cited for cross-domain error reductions). Reuters (Sec.6.3) error improved from 31.05% to 29.62%. Table 9: Dropout+Max-norm 1.05% vs Max-norm 1.35% vs L2 1.62% (alternative-splicing results also in Table 8). TIMIT uses learning rate schedule ε0(1 + t/T)^(-1). Section 2 motivation uses analogies (sexual reproduction / mix-ability; conspiracies) to argue dropout reduces complex co-adaptations, forcing units to be robust and individually useful.

Paper: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al., JMLR 2014). Core idea: during training randomly drop units via Bernoulli masks r^(l) with retain prob p, sampling many thinned networks; at test time use full network with outgoing weights scaled by p (weight-scaling) to approximate averaging. Typical p ≈ 0.5 for hidden units; input p usually closer to 1. Dropout interpretable as adding noise to hidden-unit states; relates to Denoising Autoencoders (DAEs) which typically use ~5% input noise, but with weight-scaling dropout often uses much higher noise (e.g., drop 20% of inputs, 50% of hidden units). Dropout extends beyond unsupervised learning to supervised nets and other architectures (e.g., Dropout RBMs / Boltzmann Machines; Figures 12–13 show qualitative differences). In simple cases dropout noise can be marginalized analytically (Section 9.1 gives linear-regression derivations); related work on deterministic marginalization and "blankout" noise (van der Maaten et al., Wang & Manning, Chen et al.). Different adversarial-removal formulations studied by Globerson & Roweis (2006) and Dekel et al. (2010). Experiments (Secs. 6–8) report improved generalization across domains: Reuters (Sec.6.3) error improved from 31.05% to 29.62%; Table 9 reports Dropout+Max-norm 1.05% vs Max-norm 1.35% vs L2 1.62%; TIMIT used learning-rate schedule ε0(1 + t/T)^(-1). Section 2 gives motivational analogies (sexual reproduction/mix-ability, conspiracies).

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (Srivastava et al., JMLR 2014). Core idea: during training randomly drop units with independent Bernoulli masks r^{(l)} (retain prob p), sampling many thinned sub-networks; at test time use full network with outgoing weights scaled by p (weight-scaling). Typical p ≈ 0.5 for hidden units; input p usually closer to 1. Notation: L hidden layers (1..L); z^{(l)} = inputs into layer l, y^{(l)} = outputs (y^{(0)}=x), W^{(l)}, b^{(l)}. Standard forward: z_i^{(l+1)} = w_i^{(l+1)} y^{(l)} + b_i^{(l+1)}; y_i^{(l+1)} = f(z_i^{(l+1)}) (e.g., logistic f(x)=1/(1+e^{-x})). Dropout forward: r_j^{(l)} ~ Bernoulli(p) (each mask component independent, 1 with prob p), \tilde y^{(l)} = r^{(l)} * y^{(l)} (elementwise), then z_i^{(l+1)} = w_i^{(l+1)} \tilde y^{(l)} + b_i^{(l+1)}, y_i^{(l+1)} = f(z_i^{(l+1)}). Backpropagate loss derivatives through the sampled sub-network. Test-time: use full network without dropout and scale weights: W_test^{(l)} = p W^{(l)}. Section references: Sec.9.1 gives analytic marginalization in simple linear cases; experiments (Secs.6–8) report improved generalization (e.g., Reuters 31.05% → 29.62%; Table 9: Dropout+Max-norm 1.05% vs Max-norm 1.35% vs L2 1.62%); TIMIT used learning-rate schedule ε0(1+t/T)^{-1}. Figures illustrate standard vs dropout panels (bias +1, three inputs, masks in dropout).

Paper: Dropout (Srivastava et al., JMLR 2014). Core idea: during training randomly drop units with independent Bernoulli masks r^{(l)} (retain prob p), sampling many thinned sub-networks; at test time use full network with outgoing weights scaled by p (weight-scaling W_test = p W). Typical p ≈ 0.5 for hidden units; input p usually closer to 1. Training: use SGD (mini-batches); for each case sample a thinned network; forward/backprop only on that network. Gradients averaged across mini-batch; a case not using a parameter contributes zero gradient. Use momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 weight decay. Max-norm: constrain each unit’s incoming weight vector norm ||w||_2 ≤ c; if violated, project onto ball of radius c; c chosen by validation. Combining dropout with max-norm, large decaying learning rates and high momentum yields further gains. Reported MNIST figures (Table 9): Dropout + Max-norm 1.05%; Dropout + L2 1.25%; Max-norm (no dropout) 1.35%; L2 (no dropout) 1.62%. Unsupervised pretraining: can use RBMs, autoencoders, DBMs; pretraining uses unlabeled data and can help versus random init. When finetuning with dropout, pretrained weights should be multiplied by 1/p so each unit’s expected output under dropout equals its pretraining output. Authors observed pretrained information could be lost with large finetuning rates but preserved with smaller rates. errors.explanation: Gamma is defined as the square root of the diagonal of X^T X, i.e. Gamma_i = sqrt(sum_n x_{n,i}^2) (root-sum-of-squares / RMS up to a factor), not the sample standard deviation unless the columns of X have been mean-centered and normalized. Section 9 (current): Marginalizing dropout yields deterministic objectives (no random bits) and obtainable gradients. 9.1 Linear regression: with X∈R^{N×D}, mask R_{ij}~Bernoulli(p), E_R[||y-(R*X)w||^2] = ||y-pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Γw||^2 with Γ = (diag(X^T X))^{1/2}; equivalently with \tilde w = p w: ||y - X\tilde w||^2 + ((1-p)/p)||Γ\tilde w||^2, so regularization scales as (1-p)/p. Note: paper states Γ acts like standard deviation per feature, but Γ as defined is root-sum-of-squares (RMS) unless X is centered/normalized. 9.2 Logistic / deep nets: closed-form marginalization is hard; Wang & Manning (2013) give a Gaussian-approximation approach that computes means/variances efficiently and reportedly improves training time/generalization vs Monte-Carlo dropout, but assumptions weaken for deeper networks so extension is not direct.

Logistic/deep nets: closed-form marginalization hard; Gaussian-approximation methods compute means/variances but weaken for deep nets.

Section 11 (Conclusion): Dropout improves many domains; drawback: training typically takes ~2–3× longer due to noisy updates; marginalizing noise can give deterministic regularizers. Appendix A (practical heuristics): A.1 sizing heuristic: layer with n units and retention p has expected pn active units; if n units optimal for a standard net, use ≈n/p units with dropout. A.2 learning: use 10–100× the learning rate of a standard net; momentum ~0.95–0.99 recommended; high LR/momentum accelerate learning. A.3 max-norm regularization: bound incoming weight norms by c (typical c=3–4). A.4 dropout rates: hidden p typically 0.5–0.8; input p≈0.8 for images/speech; smaller p requires larger n (slows training; risk of underfitting if not compensated).

Appendix B gives dataset-specific implementation details. MNIST: 60k train / 10k test; 10k of train held out for validation. Hyperparameters chosen so best validation error occurred after 1,000,000 weight updates; then train+validation reunited and trained 1,000,000 updates before testing. Figure 4 examines 6 architectures (2/3/4 hidden layers × 1024/2048 units). For those and Table 2 architectures: hidden p=0.5, input p=0.8, final momentum=0.95, max-norm c=2. Also tried 2-/3-layer nets with 4096 and 8192 units: 2-layer improved (Table 2 max-norm rows: 4096→1.01%, 8192→0.95%); 3-layer slightly worse. SVHN: ~600k train, 26k test; 6k validation (400/class from standard, 200/class from extra → 2/3 standard, 1/3 extra). Inputs RGB normalized (zero mean, unit variance); contrast norm / ZCA gave no noticeable benefit. Best model: 3 conv layers (96,128,256 filters, 5×5, stride 1) each followed by 3×3 pooling stride 2; two FC layers of 2048 units (ReLU). Dropout/retention from input through layers: p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5). Max-norm c=4, momentum 0.95. Did not add validation back; report test error of model with smallest validation error (selected model reaches 2.55%). CIFAR-10/100: 50k train / 10k test; 5k for validation, then hyperparam selection and combine back with training. Preprocessing: per-channel global contrast normalization then ZCA whitening. Architecture and dropout rates matched SVHN; input-layer learning rates had to be smaller. TIMIT: Kaldi log-filter banks, monophone forced alignment, 21-frame input window predicting central frame, inputs mean-centered and unit variance.

"The reported results include Table 2’s 0.79 H4Z error; Table 3’s 2.47 A2F error; Table 4’s 11.68 J3V and 37.20 W6R errors; and Table 6’s 16.4 K9D top-5 test error." (this part)

Earlier tables/reporting in the paper (from my notes):
"A2F (SVHN): Table 3 — ... +QX2 in all layers: 2.55; L8J (Goodfellow): 2.47." 
"J3V/W6R (CIFAR-10/100): Table 4 — ... +QX2 all layers: 12.61 / 37.20; L8J: 11.68 / 38.57."
errors.explanation: The part asserts QX2 is state-of-the-art on all five vision sets and attributes 2.47 (SVHN) and 11.68 (CIFAR-10) to QX2, but the paper's own tables show those lower numbers belong to L8J (Goodfellow). Thus QX2 is not the best on SVHN and CIFAR-10 per the paper's tables, so the blanket SOTA claim contradicts the paper's own results.

errors.claim: "Prose comparison | Pre-QX2 error | 8-layer net | 20.5%" (prose baseline for the deeper pretrained network).
errors.evidence:
"Prose comparison | Pre-QX2 error | 8-layer net | 20.5%" (this part)

Table 7 (this part) lists:
"G6W-pretrained NN (8 layers) (Mohamed et al., 2010) | 20.7"
"mcRBM-G6W-pretrained NN (5 layers) (Dahl et al., 2010) | 20.5"

errors.claim: "The gain is a 14.3% relative reduction, smaller than in vision and speech classification."
errors.evidence: "Without QX2" 31.05% and "With QX2" 29.62% (table in this part).
errors.explanation: The table shows an absolute drop of 1.43 points from 31.05 to 29.62, which is a relative reduction of (31.05-29.62)/31.05 ≈ 4.6%, not 14.3%; the stated 14.3% is therefore inconsistent with the reported numbers.

errors.claim: Section 6 asserts QX2 improves neural-net comparisons and cites 'Table 8, 440 versus 567' as evidence.
errors.evidence: This part: "Table 8, 440 versus 567."  Earlier notes: "Bayesian (Z7P, Table 8 C4Y bits): NN (early stopping) 440; Regression+PCA 463; SVM+PCA 487; NN with QX2 567; Bayesian NN 623."
errors.explanation: Table 8 in the paper (per earlier notes) shows NN with QX2 = 567 compared to baseline NN = 440 (higher codelength), so the table actually indicates QX2 worsens this result rather than improves it. Citing 440 vs 567 as evidence of improvement is therefore internally inconsistent.

errors.claim: The part lists "Table 4, 15.60/43.48 versus 12.61/37.20" as evidence that QX2 improves results.

errors.explanation: The numbers in this part do not match the earlier-reported baseline numbers: earlier notes show the baseline for CIFAR-10 is 11.68 (not 15.60) and QX2 is 12.61 (which is worse than 11.68) while QX2 is better on CIFAR-100 (37.20 < 38.57). Thus the stated Table 4 pair and the claim of general improvement are inconsistent with earlier reported values.

errors.claim: The part cites "Table 2, 1.60 versus 1.35" as evidence of improvement.
errors.evidence: This part: "Table 2, 1.60 versus 1.35;"  Earlier notes: "H4Z regularizer comparison (Table 9): Y5F 1.62; Y5F+O3U 1.60; Y5F+KL 1.55; V9C 1.35; QX2+Y5F 1.25; QX2+V9C 1.05 (QX2+V9C lowest in that reported regularizer comparison)."

errors.claim: "Figure 10" horizontal axis ticks are 10^2, 10^3, 10^4, 10^5

errors.claim: "Let \theta=\{\mathbf W,\mathbf a,\mathbf b\} ... An ordinary U2L defines P(h,v;\theta)=... exp( v^\top W h + a^\top h + b^\top v )." and later "P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=1(r_j=1)\,\sigma\!(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i)" and "P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma\!(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j)"
errors.evidence:
The paper first defines the U2L energy with a^\top h + b^\top v (so a_j are the hidden-unit biases and b_i the visible biases):
"An ordinary U2L defines
P(\mathbf h,\mathbf v;\theta)=...\exp(\mathbf v^\top\mathbf W\mathbf h+\mathbf a^\top\mathbf h+\mathbf b^\top\mathbf v )."
But the conditional probabilities later use b_j as the hidden bias and a_i as the visible bias:
"P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\,\sigma\!(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i)"
"P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma\!(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j)"
errors.explanation: The paper inconsistently labels bias parameters: the U2L formula implies a_j are hidden biases and b_i visible biases, yet the hidden conditional uses b_j and the visible conditional uses a_i — the names a and b are swapped.

errors.claim: Figure captions say "Without QX2" and "QX2 with p=0.5" while the section repeatedly names the method B8T.
errors.evidence:
Section heading and opening: "## 8. B8T" and "B8T extends dropout to shared-weight Restricted Boltzmann Machines."
Figure caption: "**Figure 13.** (a) Without QX2: many activations away from zero. (b) QX2 with p=0.5: many activations near zero and very few high activations."
errors.explanation: The part introduces the RBM-dropout method as B8T but the figures label the applied method as QX2, creating an internal naming inconsistency (unclear whether QX2 and B8T are intended to be the same).

errors.claim: "The assumptions become successively weaker as layers are added. The results therefore do not apply directly to deep networks."
errors.evidence: "The assumptions become successively weaker as layers are added. The results therefore do not apply directly to deep networks."
errors.explanation: These two sentences contradict: if assumptions become weaker (easier to satisfy) as layers are added, the results would be more, not less, applicable to deep networks. The intended meaning was likely that assumptions become stronger/more restrictive with added layers.

errors.claim: If a task’s optimal standard-net layer has n hidden units, a good QX2 layer should have at least n/p units. Removal reduces capacity: only pn units remain in expectation.
errors.evidence: "If a task’s optimal standard-net layer has n hidden units, a good QX2 layer should have at least n/p units." / "Removal reduces capacity: only pn units remain in expectation."
errors.explanation: These two sentences are arithmetically inconsistent: if you start with n/p units and retain each with probability p, the expected survivors are p*(n/p) = n, not p*n (pn). The text therefore contradicts itself about the expected number of surviving units.

errors.claim: "V9C bound, all layers | c=2"
errors.evidence: "V9C bound, all layers | c=2" (this part) vs "A.3 (V9C): use max-norm bounds on incoming weight vectors; c in [3,4]." (earlier notes)
errors.explanation: Appendix A recommended using V9C max-norm bounds with c in [3,4], but the H4Z experiment here sets c=2, which lies outside that recommended range, creating an internal inconsistency.

errors.claim: "The large training set remained separate from validation during final training. The model with the smallest validation error supplied the reported test error."
errors.evidence: "After selecting hyperparameters, validation and training data were combined for optimization, as in the H4Z procedure."
errors.explanation: The part asserts both that validation was kept separate during final training and elsewhere that, following hyperparameter selection, validation and training data were combined for final optimization (the H4Z procedure). These two procedures are mutually exclusive, so the paper contradicts itself about whether validation data were merged into training for final training.

Dropout: randomly remove units and their connections during training, effectively training many smaller networks that share parameters. At test time, use one complete network with reduced weights to approximate averaging the smaller networks' predictions. Claimed benefits: improves generalization over networks without dropout on every tested dataset; reports state-of-the-art results on several benchmarks. Experimental domains: images, speech, documents, gene-splicing prediction. Also examines learned features, sparsity, retention rates, effects of training-set size, Restricted Boltzmann Machines, noise marginalization, and Gaussian corruption. Training cost: typically takes 2–3× longer than training a standard network of the same architecture.

Dropout (QX2): randomly remove units and their connections during training; at test time use one unthinned network with outgoing weights multiplied by the retention probability (T6R) to approximate averaging the thinned-model predictions. The paper states this approximation corresponds to the geometric mean (equally weighted combination) of thinned-network predictions. Two corruption types: Bernoulli dropout (P7V) — binary multiplicative noise (Bernoulli variable =1 with prob p, 0 otherwise) — and Gaussian dropout (D4K) — Gaussian multiplicative noise. Marginalization = expectation over dropout noise to yield a deterministic objective/regularizer; Monte‑Carlo dropout/model averaging = stochastic sampling and averaging predictions from sampled thinned networks. Dropout RBM (B8T): described as a mixture of shared-weight RBMs using different hidden-unit subsets; U2L = RBM; pretraining (DBM/E5Q, DBN/G6W) then finetuning with backprop; mcRBM-G6W is a named pretrained variant. Regularizers: L1 (O3U), L2 (Y5F, Tikhonov), max-norm (V9C), KL-sparsity. Activations mentioned: logistic units, ReLU (F3N), maxout (L8J). Other glossary items to track: geometric mean vs. posterior-weighted averaging, blankout noise, ridge-regression connection (dropout expectation → ridge-like penalty matrix), convolutional-net components (filters, pooling variants), data augmentation, SVM/PCA baselines, terms like dead unit, mix-ability, replica code, and non-stationarity. These definitions and labels will be used in later parts for numerical and conceptual consistency checks.

Marginalization = expectation over dropout noise → deterministic objective/regularizer; Monte Carlo dropout/model averaging = sample thinned nets and average predictions. Abstract summary: method called "QX2, or dropout"; it randomly removes units and their connections during training, inhibiting co-adaptation, sampling exponentially many thinned networks that share parameters. A single unthinned network with reduced weights approximates the averaged predictions of the thinned nets. Claims substantial reduction in overfitting and major improvements; supervised experiments in vision, speech recognition, document classification and computational biology reportedly attain state-of-the-art on many benchmarks. Evidence claimed in Tables 2–8 and an unnumbered text-classification table in §6.3; domain-specific comparisons listed in §6.

Paper: "Dropout (QX2)". Core idea: randomly remove units during training to train many shared-parameter thinned subnetworks (2^n possible thinned nets for n units) and approximate their combined predictions with one unthinned test-time network. Key terminology: QX2 = dropout; T6R = test-time weight scaling (use one unthinned net with scaled weights); X9M = Monte-Carlo model averaging (average sampled thinned nets at test); U2L/B8T = dropout extension to RBMs. Notation (carry-forward): n = unit count; expected retained width = p n; practical width heuristic = n/p; shared-parameter count O(n^2); L hidden layers with W^(l), b^(l), activations f; p = retention probability; test-time weights scaled by p (W_test = p W). Claims in this part: QX2 approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many models; a new thinned member is sampled and trained (rarely) per presentation of each training case; T6R is a cheap practical inference rule that gives significantly lower generalization error than other regularizers across varied problems; X9M is more expensive and needs around k≈50 samples (per §7.5 and App B.1) before matching T6R. Evidence pointer: Table 9 referenced for comparisons (rows quoted: Y5F=1.62, V9C=1.35, QX2+Y5F=1.25, QX2+V9C=1.05). Paper outline: §2 motivation, §3 prior work, §4 model, §5 training algorithm, §6 experiments, §7 effects and hyperparameter interactions, §8 RBM extension, §9 marginalization, Appendix A (practical guidance).

Paper: "Dropout (QX2)". Core idea: randomly remove units during training to train many shared-parameter thinned subnetworks (2^n possible thinned nets for n units) and approximate their combined predictions with one unthinned test-time network. Notation: n = unit count; p = retention probability; expected retained width = p n; practical width heuristic = n/p; shared-parameter count O(n^2); L hidden layers with W^(l), b^(l), activations f; test-time weights scaled by p (W_test = p W). Claims: QX2 approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many models; a new thinned member is sampled and trained (rarely unique) on each presentation of a training case; T6R (test-time weight scaling) is a cheap practical inference rule that gives significantly lower generalization error than other regularizers across varied problems; X9M (Monte-Carlo averaging) is more expensive and needs around k ≈ 50 samples (per §7.5 and App B.1) to match T6R. Evidence pointer: Table 9 comparisons (rows: Y5F=1.62, V9C=1.35, QX2+Y5F=1.25, QX2+V9C=1.05). New in §2: motivation via sexual-reproduction and conspiracy analogies — Livnat et al. (2010) "mix-ability" notion: selection favors genes that work well with random partners (robust, independently useful components). Analogy: QX2 forces hidden units to operate with randomly selected partners, discouraging complex co-adaptations and favoring robust features; replicating units is a poor remedy. Smaller cooperating subsets are argued to be more robust under non-stationarity than large co-adaptations. Outline pointers: §3 prior work, §4 model, §5 training algorithm, §6 experiments, §7 hyperparams, §8 RBM extension, §9 marginalization, Appendix A guidance.

Paper: "Dropout (QX2)". Core idea: randomly remove units during training to train many shared-parameter thinned subnetworks (2^n possible thinned nets for n units) and approximate their combined predictions with one unthinned test-time network. Notation/impl: n = unit count; p = retention probability; expected retained width = p n; practical width heuristic = n/p; shared-parameter count O(n^2); L hidden layers with weights W^(l), biases b^(l), activations f; test-time weights scaled by p (W_test = p W). Key claims: QX2 approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many models; a new thinned member is sampled and trained on each presentation; T6R (test-time weight scaling) is a cheap practical inference rule that often gives much lower generalization error than other regularizers; X9M (Monte-Carlo averaging) is more expensive and reportedly needs k ≈ 50 samples to match T6R (per §7.5 and App B.1). Empirical pointer: Table 9 example rows (Y5F=1.62, V9C=1.35, QX2+Y5F=1.25, QX2+V9C=1.05). Section 3 notes: DAEs (denoising autoencoders) corrupt inputs and reconstruct; QX2 extends corruption to hidden units and gives a model-averaging view; applies to supervised/unsupervised and other neuron-based architectures including Boltzmann Machines. T6R permits much higher noise than typical DAEs: table lists S2H/DAE typical best 5%, QX2 input-unit removal often optimal 20%, QX2 hidden-unit removal often optimal 50%. Related methods: Globerson & Roweis (2006) and Dekel et al. (2010) use adversarial removals (fixed max number) and have no hidden units. Marginalizing QX2 yields deterministic regularizers in simple cases; van der Maaten et al. (2013) call QX2 input noise "blankout noise" but limited to models without hidden layers; Chen et al. (2012) on marginalization for DAEs; Wang & Manning (2013) propose marginalization to accelerate QX2.

steps.notes_before: Paper: Dropout (QX2) — gate unit outputs during training, independently per unit with r_j^{(l)} ~ Bernoulli(p); tilde y^{(l)} = r^{(l)} * y^{(l)}. At inference no units removed; test-time weights scaled by retention p: W_test^{(l)} = p W^{(l)}. Expected preactivation under training dropout equals test preactivation with scaled weights. Both hidden and input (visible) units can be dropped. Validation can pick p; default often near optimal; input retention generally near complete retention. Forward equations: y^{(0)} = x; nominally z_i^{(l+1)} = w_i^{(l+1)} y^{(l)} + b_i^{(l+1)}, y_i^{(l+1)} = f(z_i^{(l+1)}). Example activation: logistic f(x)=1/(1+exp(-x)). Note: this part contains an indexing inconsistency — it first states l∈{1..L} then uses l∈{0..L-1} for the feed-forward formulas (treating y^{(0)} as input). Keep this in mind when later parts refer to layer indices.

Paper: QX2 = dropout (per-unit gate r_j^(l) ~ Bernoulli(p); ̃y^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l)). At test time do not drop units; scale weights by retention p (W_test = p W) so expected preactivation under dropout equals test preactivation. Both hidden and input units can be dropped (input retention usually near 1). Forward eqns use y^(0)=x; paper has an indexing inconsistency (uses l∈{1..L} then l∈{0..L-1}).

Sec.5 (Learning QX2 Nets): training = backprop through sampled subnetworks (one mask per case/minibatch case), gradients averaged across cases; a dropped parameter gets zero contribution. QX2 alone gives significant gains; combining QX2 with high momentum, large decaying learning rates and V9C (max-norm) gives further boost. V9C constrains each hidden unit's incoming weight vector via projection to ||w||_2 <= c (validation tunes c); projection returns w to the radius-c surface if exceeded. Proposed optimization story: fixed-radius weight ball allows huge LRs without explosion; QX2 noise explores; annealing settles.

Empirical notes cited: Table 9 rows: V9C=1.35, QX2+Y5F=1.25, QX2+V9C=1.05. Appendix A.2: practical LRs typically 10–100x optimal standard-net LR and momentum ~0.95–0.99. Pretraining: unchanged, but before QX2 finetuning multiply pretrained weights by 1/p so expected outputs under dropout match pretraining; use much smaller finetuning LR (Appendix B.4 reports ~0.01 best vs listed high LR 0.1). Table 2: G6W finetuning 1.18 -> 0.92 with QX2; E5Q 0.96 -> 0.79.

Paper studies QX2 (dropout). Data sets: H4Z (MNIST) 60K train /10K test, dim 784; J3V/W6R (CIFAR-10/100) 60K/10K, dim 3072; A2F (SVHN) 600K/26K, dim 3072; K9D (ImageNet ILSVRC-2012) 1.2M/150K, dim 65536; N8Q (TIMIT) 1.1M frames/58K frames, 2520 dim; M5X (Reuters-RCV1) 200K/200K, 2000 dim; Z7P (Splicing) 2932/733, 1014 dim. Claim: QX2 improved generalization over nets without QX2 on every tested data set; applied to vision, speech, text, genetics. For vision, QX2 models reported state-of-the-art on all five vision collections. errors.claim: "Let \theta=\{\mathbf W,\mathbf a,\mathbf b\} ... An ordinary U2L defines P(h,v;\theta)=... exp( v^\top W h + a^\top h + b^\top v )." and later "P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=1(r_j=1)\,\sigma\!(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i)" and "P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma\!(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j)"
errors.evidence:
The paper first defines the U2L energy with a^\top h + b^\top v (so a_j are the hidden-unit biases and b_i the visible biases):
"An ordinary U2L defines
P(\mathbf h,\mathbf v;\theta)=...\exp(\mathbf v^\top\mathbf W\mathbf h+\mathbf a^\top\mathbf h+\mathbf b^\top\mathbf v )."
But the conditional probabilities later use b_j as the hidden bias and a_i as the visible bias:
"P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\,\sigma\!(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i)"
"P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma\!(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j)"
errors.explanation: The paper inconsistently labels bias parameters: the U2L formula implies a_j are hidden biases and b_i visible biases, yet the hidden conditional uses b_j and the visible conditional uses a_i — the names a and b are swapped.

errors.claim: Figure captions say "Without QX2" and "QX2 with p=0.5" while the section repeatedly names the method B8T.
errors.evidence:
Section heading and opening: "## 8. B8T" and "B8T extends dropout to shared-weight Restricted Boltzmann Machines."
Figure caption: "**Figure 13.** (a) Without QX2: many activations away from zero. (b) QX2 with p=0.5: many activations near zero and very few high activations."
errors.explanation: The part introduces the RBM-dropout method as B8T but the figures label the applied method as QX2, creating an internal naming inconsistency (unclear whether QX2 and B8T are intended to be the same).

steps.notes_before: Section 8 (B8T) extends dropout to RBMs: retention vector r in {0,1}^F sampled iid Bernoulli(p). U2L energy given as exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v) with θ={W,a,b} and partition Z. Conditional P(h|r,v) factorizes; paper gives P(h_j=1|r_j,v)=1(r_j=1) σ(b_j + Σ_i W_ij v_i) and P(v_i=1|h)=σ(a_i + Σ_j W_ij h_j). (Inconsistency: a and b are swapped between the energy and the conditionals.) Learning uses CD-1, sampling r per case and training only retained hidden units. Claims: B8T features are coarser and have fewer dead units (Figure 12, 256 hidden units, p=0.5); B8T yields much sparser representations without extra regularizer (Figure 13). Figures use the label "QX2" in captions while the section calls the method B8T (naming ambiguity). No numerical dead-unit counts or quantitative sparsity scores provided.

errors.claim: "The assumptions become successively weaker as layers are added. The results therefore do not apply directly to deep networks."
errors.evidence: "The assumptions become successively weaker as layers are added. The results therefore do not apply directly to deep networks."
errors.explanation: These two sentences contradict: if assumptions become weaker (easier to satisfy) as layers are added, the results would be more, not less, applicable to deep networks. The intended meaning was likely that assumptions become stronger/more restrictive with added layers.

steps.notes_before: Section 8 (B8T): extends dropout to RBMs with retention r∈{0,1}^F, r_j∼Bernoulli(p). Energy written as exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v) with θ={W,a,b}. Conditionals given as P(h_j=1|r_j,v)=1(r_j=1) σ(b_j+Σ_i W_ij v_i) and P(v_i=1|h)=σ(a_i+Σ_j W_ij h_j) — internal inconsistency: a and b appear swapped between energy and conditionals. Learning uses CD-1, sample r per case, train only retained hidden units. Claims B8T features are coarser, fewer dead units, and sparser without extra regularizer (figures use label QX2 while text calls B8T — naming ambiguity). No quantitative dead-unit/sparsity counts provided. Section 9 (Marginalizing QX2): deterministic marginalization removes randomness and yields differentiable objectives. 9.1 Linear regression: with R_ij∼Bernoulli(p), E[||y-(R*X)w||^2] = ||y-pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Γw||^2 where Γ = (diag(X^T X))^{1/2}; with ṽ = p w this is ||y-Xṽ||^2 + (1-p)/p ||Γṽ||^2. 9.2 Logistic/deep nets: Wang & Manning (2013) report approximate marginalization helps logistic regression (time & generalization). Paper states closed-form marginalization is difficult for logistic and deep nets and makes a contradictory claim that assumptions "become successively weaker as layers are added" yet "therefore do not apply directly to deep networks" (likely a wording error: should read stronger/more restrictive).

Section 8 (B8T): extends dropout to RBMs with r_j ~ Bernoulli(p). Paper gives energy and conditionals but internally inconsistent (a and b appear swapped between energy and conditionals). Naming ambiguity: B8T vs QX2. Claims coarser features, fewer dead units, sparser features but provides no quantitative dead-unit/sparsity counts. Learning uses CD-1 and samples r per case.

Section 9 (Marginalizing QX2): deterministic marginalization yields differentiable objectives. Linear regression closed form: E[||y-(R*X)w||^2] = ||y-pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Γw||^2; with ṽ=pw gives ||y-Xṽ||^2 + (1-p)/p ||Γṽ||^2. Logistic/deep: closed-form marginalization is difficult; paper contains a contradictory wording about assumptions across layers (claims both weaker and not applicable).

Section 10 (Multiplicative Gaussian Noise — P7V = Bernoulli dropout, D4K = Gaussian dropout): Gaussian multiplicative noise matches first/second moments of inverted Bernoulli multiplier (r_b=1/p w.p. p has E=1, Var=(1-p)/p). Choose r_g ~ N(1,σ^2) with σ^2=(1-p)/p to match moments. Two equivalent representations (standard vs inverted dropout) described; for Gaussian E[r]=1 so test-time scaling is unnecessary. Table 10 (classification error %) reports slight advantage for Gaussian: H4Z 1.08±0.04 (P7V) vs 0.95±0.04 (D4K); J3V 12.6±0.1 vs 12.5±0.1. Settings: per-layer p listed; D4K σ = sqrt((1-p)/p); averages over 10 seeds. Entropy claim: Gaussian has max entropy for given moments, Bernoulli lowest.

Section 8 (B8T): extends dropout to RBMs with r_j ~ Bernoulli(p). Paper gives energy and conditional equations but they appear internally inconsistent (parameters a and b swapped between energy and conditionals). Naming ambiguity between B8T and the general QX2 label. Claims coarser features, fewer dead units, and sparser features; empirical illustrations in Figures 12–13 use p=0.5 but no numerical sparsity/dead-unit counts. Learning uses CD-1 and samples r per training case.

Section 9 (Marginalizing QX2): deterministic marginalization yields differentiable objectives. Linear regression closed form: E[||y-(R*X)w||^2] = ||y-pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Γw||^2; with ṽ=pw this is ||y-Xṽ||^2 + ((1-p)/p)||Γṽ||^2 — i.e. modified Y5F with coefficient (1-p)/p. For logistic/deep models closed-form marginalization is difficult; paper contains contradictory wording about cross-layer assumptions (claims both weaker assumptions and that those assumptions do not apply).

Section 10 (Multiplicative Gaussian noise): matches first/second moments of inverted Bernoulli by r_g ~ N(1,σ^2) with σ^2=(1-p)/p. Two representations (standard vs inverted) discussed; Gaussian has E[r]=1 so test-time scaling unnecessary. Table 10: H4Z errors P7V (Bernoulli) 1.08±0.04 vs D4K (Gaussian) 0.95±0.04; J3V 12.6±0.1 vs 12.5±0.1. Entropy claim: Gaussian maximum entropy for given moments; Bernoulli lower entropy.

Section 11 (Conclusion, current): restates QX2 trains sampled submodels; U2L fits this view; B8T shows empirical properties. Claims QX2 attains SOTA on A2F (Table 3: 2.47), K9D (Table 6 top-5: 16.4), W6R (Table 4: 37.20), H4Z (Table 2: 0.79). Other-domain improvements cited: Table 7 (23.4 vs 21.8), §6.3 table (31.05% vs 29.62%), Table 8 (440 vs 567). Training typically costs 2–3× standard; noisy updates and differing random submodels explained as causes. Noise marginalization recovers modified-Y5F; accelerating QX2 left as future work.

errors.claim: If a task’s optimal standard-net layer has n hidden units, a good QX2 layer should have at least n/p units. Removal reduces capacity: only pn units remain in expectation.
errors.evidence: "If a task’s optimal standard-net layer has n hidden units, a good QX2 layer should have at least n/p units." / "Removal reduces capacity: only pn units remain in expectation."
errors.explanation: These two sentences are arithmetically inconsistent: if you start with n/p units and retain each with probability p, the expected survivors are p*(n/p) = n, not p*n (pn). The text therefore contradicts itself about the expected number of surviving units.

steps.notes_before: Appendix A gives practical heuristics for QX2. A.1 recommends widening QX2 layers: "at least n/p units" when a standard-net layer has n units, but also states "only pn units remain in expectation" (internal arithmetic inconsistency). A.2: QX2 increases gradient noise; recommend much larger learning rates (typically 10–100× the optimal standard-net rate) and higher momentum (~0.95–0.99 vs common 0.9). A.3 (V9C): use max-norm bounds on incoming weight vectors; c in [3,4]. A.4 (Rate): retention p controls intensity; hidden-unit p typically 0.5–0.8, default ~0.5; real-valued inputs often p≈0.8; input retention generally closer to 1. Notes reiterate underfitting at low p (example p=0.1: 2.7% at fixed architecture vs 1.7% at fixed expected width). From earlier sections: B8T (Section 8) had parameter/label ambiguities and reported p=0.5 in figs; Section 9 marginalization gives closed-form linear-regression result equivalent to modified Y5F with regularizer coefficient (1-p)/p; Section 10: multiplicative Gaussian matching Bernoulli moments with σ^2=(1-p)/p and Gaussian has E[r]=1; Section 11 claims SOTA numbers on several datasets (Table refs) and training typically costs 2–3× standard due to noisy updates and varying submodels.

final_notes: Paper-wide: Dropout improves performance on MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet and can be applied to RBMs. Analytic: linear regression marginalization gives E=||y−pXw||^2 + p(1−p)||Γw||^2; multiplicative Gaussian noise matched via σ^2=(1−p)/p. Heuristics: scale network size ≈ n/p; use much larger LR (10–100×) and momentum 0.95–0.99; max-norm c≈3–4 (experiments vary: MNIST used c=2, SVHN used c=4); p_hidden ≈0.5–0.8, p_input ≈0.7–0.8. MNIST: reported dataset sizes ambiguous (claimed 60k/10k but also referenced training on 55k); architectures: 2/3/4 layers × {1024,2048} and tried 4096/8192; p_hidden=0.5, p_input=0.8; momentum=0.95; c=2. SVHN: ~600k train, 26k test, val=6k; RGB inputs zero-mean/unit-variance; best net: 3 conv layers (96,128,256; 5×5), pool 3×3 stride 2, then 2 FC layers of 2048 ReLU; dropout retention (input→conv→fc) = (0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5); c=4; momentum=0.95; reported best-on-validation model. Note: another experiment used the same architecture/dropout as SVHN but required smaller input-layer learning rates. CIFAR-10/100: 50k train/10k test; 5k val; per-channel global contrast normalization + ZCA whitening; tuned on val then combined with train for final runs. TIMIT: Kaldi preprocessing to log-filter banks; monophone forced alignment; windows of 21 frames; inputs mean-centered/unit variance; p_input=0.8, p_hidden=0.5; max-norm c=4 used; momentum=0.95; high LR=0.1 decayed as ε0(1+t/T)^{-1}; DBN pretraining with CD-1 (Gaussian RBM input variance fixed to 1); DBN finetuning with dropout used smaller LR ≈0.01 and adding max-norm during finetune did not help. Reuters: subset of 402,738 articles, vocab 2000, 50 single-label classes, split equally into train/test (~201k each); dropout gave modest improvements (dataset large so less overfitting). Alternative Splicing: 3665 exons, 1014 features, 4 tissue types → 4 softmax outputs each with 3 states (inc, exc, nc); code-quality metric is average over data of sum_{t,s} psi_{i,t,s} log(q_{t,s}(r_i)/p̄_s); trained 2-layer dropout net (1024 units each) with p_input=0.7, p_hidden=0.5, max-norm regularization and high decaying LRs; results averaged across same 5 folds as Xiong et al.

Paper: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (JMLR 15, 2014). Authors: Nitish Srivastava, Geoffrey Hinton, Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, Ruslan Salakhutdinov. Abstract/main claim: Dropout randomly drops units and their connections during training to prevent co-adaptation; training effectively samples from an exponential number of "thinned" networks. At test time, the effect of averaging these thinned networks is approximated by using a single unthinned network with scaled (smaller) weights. Dropout reportedly reduces overfitting and outperforms other regularization methods, producing major improvements and state-of-the-art results on benchmarks in vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology. Intro notes: deep nets are expressive and prone to overfitting; common regularizers include early stopping, L1/L2 penalties, and soft weight sharing. The paper states that with unlimited computation the best regularizer is averaging predictions over all parameter settings (sentence is cut off in this part). Figure 1 caption: left—standard net with 2 hidden layers; right—example thinned net after dropout where some units are dropped.

There are exponentially many thinned networks (paper elsewhere prints 2^n; an earlier printed '2n' looked like a typo). Total number of parameters remains O(n^2) or less due to sharing. Training: each update samples a new thinned network so any specific thinned net is trained rarely. Structure: Secs 2–9 and Appendix A (practical guide). New from current part: Motivation analogies — sexual reproduction: dropout viewed as preventing large co-adaptations, forcing each hidden unit to learn useful features that work with random subsets of partners, improving robustness; copying units to resist dropout is a poor solution (analogy to replica codes for noisy channels). Conspiracy analogy: many small conspiracies (small co-adaptations) more robust than one large co-adaptation, hence better generalization under non-stationarity. Related work: Dropout can be seen as regularization via adding noise to hidden units; this idea relates to Denoising Autoencoders (Vincent et al. 2008, 2010) which add noise to unit states.

steps.notes_before: Paper: Dropout trains by randomly dropping units (thinning) and sharing weights across exponentially many sub-networks. Training samples a new thinned net each presentation; backpropagate gradients through that thinned net. At test time use a single unthinned net with weights scaled by retention probabilities (W_test = p W^(l) per layer). Typical choices: drop ~50% hidden units (p_hidden ≈ 0.5), ~20% inputs (p_input ≈ 0.8); DAEs typically use 5% input noise but test-time scaling allows higher noise. Dropout can be applied to hidden layers and other neuron-based architectures (e.g., Boltzmann Machines, RBMs). Interpretation: stochastic regularization / model averaging; related to denoising autoencoders and marginalizing noise. Definition details: network with L hidden layers; y(0)=x; feed-forward recurrence given as z^{(l+1)} = W^{(l+1)} y^{(l)} + b^{(l+1)}, y^{(l+1)} = f(z^{(l+1)}). With dropout: sample r^{(l)} ~ Bernoulli(p) elementwise, form y_e^{(l)} = r^{(l)} * y^{(l)} and use y_e^{(l)} as input to next layer. Loss is minimized stochastically (expected loss); prior adversarial-drop work fixes max number dropped (no hidden-layer models).

Training: dropout nets trained by SGD on ‘‘thinned’’ nets — for each training case in a mini‑batch sample dropout mask, do forward/backprop on that thinned net; gradients averaged over mini‑batch; any case that omits a parameter contributes zero gradient for that parameter. Standard SGD tricks (momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 weight decay) help. Max‑norm regularization: constrain incoming weight vector w at each hidden unit to ||w||2 ≤ c by projecting back into the ball of radius c whenever it exceeds c (c is a tunable hyperparameter). Max‑norm often improves SGD even without dropout; combining dropout + max‑norm + large decaying LR + high momentum gives further gains (intuition: ball constraint prevents blowup so large LR can be used for exploration). Unsupervised pretraining: stacks of RBMs/autoencoders/DBMs can be used; pretraining stays the same, but when finetuning with dropout scale pretrained weights by 1/p so expected output under dropout matches pretraining output. If finetune LR is too large pretrained information can be lost; use smaller LR to retain gains. Experiments: datasets include MNIST, TIMIT, CIFAR‑10/100, SVHN, ImageNet, Reuters‑RCV1, and an Alternative Splicing RNA dataset; more details in Appendix B.

errors.claim: "For the Gaussian multiplicative noise, if we set σ 2 = (1 − p)/p, we end up multiplying hi by a random variable rg, where E[rg] = 1 and Var[rg] = (1 − p)/p."
errors.evidence: "For each layer, the value of σ in the Gaussian model was set to be 1−p     p using the p from the corresponding layer in the Bernoulli model."
errors.explanation: These two sentences are inconsistent about whether σ^2 equals (1−p)/p (first quote) or σ equals (1−p)/p (second quote). If σ^2 = (1−p)/p then σ = sqrt((1−p)/p), not (1−p)/p. The paper thus contradicts itself about which quantity is set to (1−p)/p.

steps.notes_before: Section 8 (RBMs): dropout yields much sparser activations and coarser features with few dead units (default p=0.5). Section 9 (Marginalizing dropout): for linear regression E_R ||y − (R X)w||^2 => ||y − p X w||^2 + p(1−p)||Γ w||^2, so absorbing p gives regularizer strength ∝ (1−p)/p. Logistic/deep nets: closed-form marginalization harder; Gaussian approximations (Wang & Manning) can be efficient. Reported classification results (Table): MNIST (2-layer, 1024 units) Bernoulli 1.08 ±0.04, Gaussian 0.95 ±0.04; CIFAR-10 (3 conv + 2 FC) Bernoulli 12.6 ±0.1, Gaussian 12.5 ±0.1. Section 10 (Multiplicative Gaussian Noise): propose multiplying activations by r0 ∼ N(1,σ^2) (special case N(1,1)); expectation preserved so no test-time scaling required. Equivalence: interpreting dropout as multiplying hi by rb ∈ {0,1/p} (E[rb]=1, Var=(1−p)/p); match moments by choosing Gaussian variance σ^2 = (1−p)/p. Paper claims Gaussian (higher entropy) may work slightly better; Table 10 uses MNIST p_hidden=0.5, p_input=0.8; CIFAR p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5) from input to top; results averaged over 10 seeds. Note: the paper inconsistently states σ^2 = (1−p)/p in one place and appears to set σ = (1−p)/p elsewhere (formatting garble), so it is unclear whether σ or σ^2 was intended.

errors.claim: "Smaller p requires big n which slows down the training and leads to underfitting."
errors.evidence: "Therefore, if an n-sized layer is optimal for a standard neural net on any given task, a good dropout net should have at least n/p units." (this part, Appendix A.1 Network Size)
errors.explanation: Appendix A.1 recommends increasing layer size to n/p when using dropout to preserve capacity; increasing capacity (larger n) should prevent underfitting, not cause it. Thus A.4's claim that 'big n ... leads to underfitting' contradicts A.1's guidance that larger n preserves capacity and avoids underfitting.

steps.notes_before: Final summary: dropout improves performance across many domains (SVHN, ImageNet, CIFAR-100, MNIST) and can be applied to RBMs. Drawbacks: training time typically 2–3× longer due to noisy updates; stochasticity helps prevent overfitting. Marginalization: for linear regression E_R||y−(R X)w||^2 = ||y−p X w||^2 + p(1−p)||Γ w||^2, giving a modified L2 regularizer with strength ∝ (1−p)/p; for complex models no simple closed form. Multiplicative Gaussian noise: multiply activations by r0∼N(1,σ^2); match Var to (1−p)/p so σ^2=(1−p)/p (paper inconsistently refers to σ vs σ^2 in places). Reported results: MNIST (2-layer,1024) Bernoulli 1.08±0.04 vs Gaussian 0.95±0.04; CIFAR-10 (3 conv+2 FC) Bernoulli 12.6±0.1 vs Gaussian 12.5±0.1.
