Paper: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al., JMLR 2014). Main idea: during training randomly drop units (Bernoulli retain prob p) to sample many "thinned" networks; at test time use a single unthinned network with outgoing weights scaled by p (W_test = p W) to approximate averaging. Key definitions: L layers, r^(l) Bernoulli masks, ~y^(l) after dropout. A net with n units corresponds to 2^n thinned nets; they share weights so parameter count stays O(n^2). Typical choices: p≈0.5 for hidden units (often close to optimal), input-unit p usually closer to 1. Scaling outgoing weights by p at test time ensures expected training-time output equals test-time output. Motivation: approximate an equally weighted geometric mean / Bayesian-like averaging of exponentially many models with much less computation. Dropout applicable beyond feed-forward nets (Dropout RBM introduced). Paper claims dropout + weight-scaling reduces overfitting and improves generalization across domains; experiments reported in Sections 6–8 (image results Tables 2–6, TIMIT Table 7, Reuters improvement 31.05%→29.62% in Sect.6.3, alternative-splicing bits in Table 8, Table 9 comparisons: Dropout+Max-norm 1.05% vs Max-norm 1.35% vs L2 1.62%). TIMIT learning-rate schedule earlier noted: ε0 (1 + t/T)^(-1). Paper structure: Sec 2 motivation, 3 related work, 4 model, 5 training, 6 experiments, 7 hyperparams/properties, 8 Dropout RBMs, 9 marginalizing dropout, Appendix A guidance.

Paper: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al., JMLR 2014). Core idea: during training randomly drop units (Bernoulli masks r^(l), retain prob p) to sample many thinned networks; at test time use the full network with outgoing weights scaled by p (weight-scaling) to approximate averaging. Typical p≈0.5 for hidden units; input p usually closer to 1. Scaling by p makes test-time output equal to the expected training-time output (approximate model averaging). Dropout applies beyond feed-forward nets (Dropout RBMs): Figures 12–13 show qualitative feature and sparsity comparisons but no numeric performance comparison is reported there. Experiments (Secs.6–8) report improved generalization across domains (image Tables 2–6, TIMIT Table 7, Tables 2–7 and 9 cited for cross-domain error reductions). Reuters (Sec.6.3) error improved from 31.05% to 29.62%. Table 9: Dropout+Max-norm 1.05% vs Max-norm 1.35% vs L2 1.62% (alternative-splicing results also in Table 8). TIMIT uses learning rate schedule ε0(1 + t/T)^(-1). Section 2 motivation uses analogies (sexual reproduction / mix-ability; conspiracies) to argue dropout reduces complex co-adaptations, forcing units to be robust and individually useful.

Paper: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al., JMLR 2014). Core idea: during training randomly drop units via Bernoulli masks r^(l) with retain prob p, sampling many thinned networks; at test time use full network with outgoing weights scaled by p (weight-scaling) to approximate averaging. Typical p ≈ 0.5 for hidden units; input p usually closer to 1. Dropout interpretable as adding noise to hidden-unit states; relates to Denoising Autoencoders (DAEs) which typically use ~5% input noise, but with weight-scaling dropout often uses much higher noise (e.g., drop 20% of inputs, 50% of hidden units). Dropout extends beyond unsupervised learning to supervised nets and other architectures (e.g., Dropout RBMs / Boltzmann Machines; Figures 12–13 show qualitative differences). In simple cases dropout noise can be marginalized analytically (Section 9.1 gives linear-regression derivations); related work on deterministic marginalization and "blankout" noise (van der Maaten et al., Wang & Manning, Chen et al.). Different adversarial-removal formulations studied by Globerson & Roweis (2006) and Dekel et al. (2010). Experiments (Secs. 6–8) report improved generalization across domains: Reuters (Sec.6.3) error improved from 31.05% to 29.62%; Table 9 reports Dropout+Max-norm 1.05% vs Max-norm 1.35% vs L2 1.62%; TIMIT used learning-rate schedule ε0(1 + t/T)^(-1). Section 2 gives motivational analogies (sexual reproduction/mix-ability, conspiracies).

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (Srivastava et al., JMLR 2014). Core idea: during training randomly drop units with independent Bernoulli masks r^{(l)} (retain prob p), sampling many thinned sub-networks; at test time use full network with outgoing weights scaled by p (weight-scaling). Typical p ≈ 0.5 for hidden units; input p usually closer to 1. Notation: L hidden layers (1..L); z^{(l)} = inputs into layer l, y^{(l)} = outputs (y^{(0)}=x), W^{(l)}, b^{(l)}. Standard forward: z_i^{(l+1)} = w_i^{(l+1)} y^{(l)} + b_i^{(l+1)}; y_i^{(l+1)} = f(z_i^{(l+1)}) (e.g., logistic f(x)=1/(1+e^{-x})). Dropout forward: r_j^{(l)} ~ Bernoulli(p) (each mask component independent, 1 with prob p), \tilde y^{(l)} = r^{(l)} * y^{(l)} (elementwise), then z_i^{(l+1)} = w_i^{(l+1)} \tilde y^{(l)} + b_i^{(l+1)}, y_i^{(l+1)} = f(z_i^{(l+1)}). Backpropagate loss derivatives through the sampled sub-network. Test-time: use full network without dropout and scale weights: W_test^{(l)} = p W^{(l)}. Section references: Sec.9.1 gives analytic marginalization in simple linear cases; experiments (Secs.6–8) report improved generalization (e.g., Reuters 31.05% → 29.62%; Table 9: Dropout+Max-norm 1.05% vs Max-norm 1.35% vs L2 1.62%); TIMIT used learning-rate schedule ε0(1+t/T)^{-1}. Figures illustrate standard vs dropout panels (bias +1, three inputs, masks in dropout).

errors.claim: "Pretrained weights should first be multiplied by 1/(1-p). This makes each unit’s expected output under dropout equal its output during pretraining."
errors.evidence: This part: "Pretrained weights should first be multiplied by 1/(1-p). This makes each unit’s expected output under dropout equal its output during pretraining."; Earlier notes/parts: "r^{(l)} ~ Bernoulli(p) (each mask component independent, 1 with prob p)" and "Test-time: use full network with outgoing weights scaled by p (weight-scaling). W_test^{(l)} = p W^{(l)}."
errors.explanation: With p defined as the probability a unit is retained, E[r_j]=p, so the expected input under dropout is p * (sum_j w_j y_j). To make this equal to the pretraining input (sum_j w_j y_j) one must scale weights by 1/p, not 1/(1-p). Multiplying by 1/(1-p) would yield expected input p/(1-p) times the pretraining input (only equal when p=1/2), so the paper's stated factor 1/(1-p) contradicts its earlier definition of p and the claimed goal.

Note: I previously recorded that 7.3's fixed-architecture run was 'without input dropout', but Section 7.4 (below) and Appendix B.1 state input p=0.8 — this is an internal inconsistency to track. 7.4: Varying MNIST training size (100,500,1k,5k,10k,50k) with architecture 784-1024-1024-2048-10, hidden p=0.5, input p=0.8; dropout gives no benefit at 100 and 500; gain grows then declines (a suggested 'sweet spot'). 7.5: Monte-Carlo averaging approximates weight scaling; about k≈50 samples match weight scaling; further sampling slightly improves but within one SD.

steps.notes_before: Section 7 (earlier): Dropout experiments on feed-forward nets. 7.1: 256-unit ReLU autoencoders on MNIST, hidden p=0.5 → similar reconstruction, more interpretable / less co-adaptation. 7.2: Dropout → sparser activations (mean ≈2.0 → ≈0.7) with strong zero mode. 7.3: Two p sweeps: (a) fixed arch 784-2048-2048-2048-10: underfitting at very low p, error decreases with p, flat 0.4≤p≤0.8, increases as p→1; (b) keep expected retained counts fixed → much smaller errors at low p; p≈0.6 best (0.5 close). Note flagged earlier: apparent inconsistency about input-dropout in 7.3 vs 7.4/Appendix B.1. 7.4: Vary training set size with arch 784-1024-1024-2048-10, hidden p=0.5, input p=0.8; dropout no benefit for 100/500 examples; gains peak then decline. 7.5: Monte-Carlo averaging approximates weight scaling; k≈50 matches. Section 8 (this part): Dropout RBM defined for v∈{0,1}^D, h∈{0,1}^F with joint P(h,v) ∝ exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v). Dropout mask r_j∼Bernoulli(p) forces h_j=0 when r_j=0. Conditionals given: P(h_j=1|r_j,v)=I(r_j=1) σ(b_j+Σ_i W_{ij}v_i), P(v_i=1|h)=σ(a_i+Σ_j W_{ij}h_j). Train by sampling r each mini-batch and applying CD-1. Experiments (MNIST, 256 hidden, p=0.5): dropout features appear coarser with fewer dead units; activation histograms show per-sample sparsity. Important internal inconsistency: bias notation a/b is inconsistent between joint and conditionals (labels swapped).

Section 7 (dropout on feed-forward nets): 7.1 256-unit ReLU autoencoders on MNIST, hidden p=0.5 → similar reconstruction, more interpretable / less co-adaptation. 7.2 Dropout → sparser activations (mean ≈2.0 → ≈0.7) with strong zero mode. 7.3 Two p-sweeps: (a) fixed arch 784-2048-2048-2048-10: underfitting at very low p, error decreases with p, flat for 0.4≤p≤0.8, error increases as p→1; (b) if expected retained counts fixed → much smaller errors at low p; best p≈0.6 (0.5 close). Note: flagged inconsistency about input-dropout between 7.3 and 7.4/Appendix B.1. 7.4 Vary training set size (784-1024-1024-2048-10), hidden p=0.5, input p=0.8; dropout gives no benefit for 100/500 examples; gains peak then decline. 7.5 Monte-Carlo averaging approximates weight scaling; k≈50 matches.

Section 8 (dropout RBM): RBM joint P(h,v) ∝ exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v). Dropout mask r_j∼Bernoulli(p) forces h_j=0 when r_j=0. Conditionals in text swap bias labels: P(h_j=1|r_j,v)=I(r_j=1) σ(b_j+Σ_i W_{ij}v_i), P(v_i=1|h)=σ(a_i+Σ_j W_{ij}h_j) — noted internal inconsistency that a/b are inconsistent between joint and conditionals. MNIST, 256 hidden, p=0.5: dropout features coarser, fewer dead units; per-sample sparsity in activations.

Section 9 (marginalizing dropout): deterministic averaged-dropout models (no random bits); gradients available. 9.1 Linear regression: E_R[||y-(R*X)w||^2] = ||y-pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Γ w||^2 with Γ=(diag(X^T X))^{1/2}. With ṽ = p w → ||y-Xṽ||^2 + ((1-p)/p)||Γ ṽ||^2 so regularization constant = (1-p)/p (increases as p decreases). 9.2 Logistic & deep nets: closed forms hard; Gaussian approximations for inputs/gradients (Wang & Manning 2013) yield efficient marginalized training that can beat Monte-Carlo dropout in time/generalization, but assumptions weaken with added layers so not directly applicable to deep networks.

Section 7 (dropout on feed-forward nets): 7.1 ReLU AEs (256 hidden, p=0.5) similar reconstructions, more interpretable; 7.2 dropout → sparser activations (mean ≈2.0 → ≈0.7) with strong zero mode; 7.3 two p-sweeps: (a) fixed 784-2048-2048-2048-10: underfitting at very low p, error decreases with p, flat for 0.4≤p≤0.8, error rises as p→1; (b) fixing expected retained counts reduces errors at low p; best p≈0.6; flagged input-dropout inconsistency between 7.3 and 7.4/Appendix B.1. 7.4 varying training set size (784-1024-1024-2048-10), hidden p=0.5, input p=0.8: dropout no benefit for 100/500 examples; gains peak then decline. 7.5 Monte-Carlo averaging approximates weight scaling; k≈50 matches. Section 8 (dropout RBM): RBM joint P(h,v) ∝ exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v); conditional formulas in text swap a/b labels (noted). Section 9 (marginalizing dropout): linear regression closed form gives regularizer (1-p)/p; logistic/deep nets use Gaussian approximations (Wang & Manning). Section 10 (multiplicative Gaussian noise): propose r' ~ N(1,σ^2) multiplying activations (equivalently add zero-mean noise with std = σ|h_i|); choose σ^2 = (1-p)/p to match first two moments of inverted Bernoulli multiplier r_b (1/p w.p. p else 0) so E[r]=1 and no test-time scaling needed. Table 10 (10 seeds): MNIST (2 hidden layers 1024): Bernoulli 1.08±0.04 vs Gaussian 0.95±0.04 (MNIST used hidden p=0.5, input p=0.8); CIFAR-10 (3 conv + 2 FC; input→top p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5)) Bernoulli 12.6±0.1 vs Gaussian 12.5±0.1. Claim: Gaussian (high-entropy) may be slightly better; both extremes work.

Section 7 (feed-forward/dropout): ReLU AEs (256 hidden, p=0.5) give similar, more interpretable reconstructions. Dropout yields much sparser activations (mean ≈2.0 → ≈0.7) with a strong zero-mode. Two p-sweeps: (a) fixed 784-2048-2048-2048-10 shows underfitting at very low p; error decreases with p, flat for 0.4≤p≤0.8, rises as p→1. (b) fixing expected retained counts reduces low-p errors; best p≈0.6. Note an input-dropout inconsistency between 7.3 and 7.4/Appendix B.1. Monte-Carlo averaging: k≈50 samples approximates weight-scaling test-time. Section 8 (RBM): joint P(h,v) defined; conditional formulas in text swap a/b labels; Dropout RBMs show different features and greater sparsity (Figs.12–13). Section 9 (marginalizing dropout): linear regression closed form → L2-like regularizer with factor (1-p)/p; deeper/logistic models use Gaussian approximations. Section 10 (multiplicative Gaussian): use r'~N(1,σ^2) with σ^2=(1-p)/p; Table 10: MNIST Bernoulli 1.08±0.04 vs Gaussian 0.95±0.04 (hidden p=0.5, input p=0.8); CIFAR-10 Bernoulli 12.6±0.1 vs Gaussian 12.5±0.1. Section 11 (conclusion): dropout reduces overfitting, claimed SOTA on SVHN/ImageNet/CIFAR-100/MNIST, extends to RBMs; training time typically 2–3×; marginalizing noise can yield modified L2 for linear regression. (Note: conclusion's Reuters citation '31.05% versus 29.62%' appears unlabeled/inconsistent.) Appendix A (practical heuristics): network-size heuristic n/p (use at least n/p hidden units if n is optimal without dropout). Learning rate: recommend 10–100× the standard-network optimum to counter gradient noise from dropout. Momentum: use ~0.95–0.99 (vs common 0.9). Max-norm regularization: bound incoming weight norm by c, typical c≈3–4. Dropout rates: hidden p typically 0.5–0.8; input p depends on input type (real-valued image patches/speech frames ≈0.8). Hidden p must be chosen jointly with hidden-unit count (smaller p → need larger n; very small p can cause underfitting).

steps.notes_before: Appendix B: GPU implementation using cudamat and cuda-convnet. B.1 MNIST: 60k train, 10k test; held out 10k for validation; hyperparams chosen so best val error at 1M updates, then retrained on full 60k for 1M updates. Figure 4 uses 2/3/4 hidden layers × {1024,2048} (6 nets); hidden p=0.5, input p=0.8; final momentum 0.95; max-norm c=2. Larger 2-layer nets (4096→1.01%, 8192→0.95%) improved; 3-layer nets slightly worse. B.2 SVHN: ~600k train, 26k test; 6k validation (400/class standard +200/class extra = 2/3 standard); RGB normalized to zero mean/unit variance; ZCA/contrast gave no noticeable improvement on SVHN. Architecture: 3 conv layers (96,128,256; 5×5), 3×3 pooling stride 2, two 2048-unit FCs, ReLU. Retention p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5); max-norm c=4; momentum 0.95; did not add val back for final training. B.3 CIFAR-10/100: 50k train, 10k test; 5k val; per-channel global contrast norm then ZCA whitening; architecture/dropout mirror SVHN except smaller input-layer LR. B.4 TIMIT: Kaldi log-filter banks, monophone forced alignment, 21-frame input window predicting central frame; inputs mean-centered/unit-variance. Note: earlier I flagged an unresolved input-dropout inconsistency between Section 7.3 and Appendix B.1 (Appendix B.1 claims input p=0.8 for MNIST; Section 7.3 describes input-dropout differently).

errors.claim: "Before QX2 finetuning, pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/(1-p). This matches each unit’s expected output under random removal to its pretraining output."
errors.evidence: Earlier part: "r_j^{(l)} ~ Bernoulli(p); \tilde y^{(l)} = r^{(l)} * y^{(l)}. At inference no units removed; test-time weights scaled by retention p: W_test^{(l)} = p W^{(l)}. Expected preactivation under training dropout equals test preactivation with scaled weights."
errors.explanation: If r ~ Bernoulli(p) (p = retention), the expected preactivation under dropout is p * (W y). To make the finetuning network match pretrained outputs one should set W_finetune = W_pre / p (multiply by 1/p). Multiplying by 1/(1-p) (the reciprocal of the drop probability) is inconsistent with the earlier definition and with the stated expectation; the correct factor should be 1/p.

errors.evidence: The paper first defines theta = {W, a, b} and the joint: P(h,v;theta) = (1/Z) exp( v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v ). Later it states the hidden conditional: P(h_j=1 | r_j, v) = 1(r_j=1) sigma( b_j + sum_i W_{ij} v_i ).
errors.explanation: Given the energy term a^T h + b^T v, the hidden-unit bias should be a_j, so the conditional should use a_j; the formula instead uses b_j, so the parameter names a and b are swapped/inconsistent.

errors.claim: P(v_i=1 | h) = sigma( a_i + sum_j W_{ij} h_j ) (i.e. the visible conditional uses a_i as the visible bias).
errors.evidence: The paper's joint energy is P(h,v;theta) proportional to exp( v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v ), which makes b the visible-bias vector. Yet it writes the visible conditional as P(v_i=1 | h) = sigma( a_i + sum_j W_{ij} h_j ).
errors.explanation: This uses a_i for the visible bias even though the energy term associates b with visible biases; again a and b are inconsistently used.

errors.claim: "The assumptions become successively weaker as layers are added. The results therefore do not apply directly to deep networks."
errors.evidence: "Under reasonable assumptions, logistic-unit input distributions and marginalized-model gradients are Gaussian, with efficiently computable means and variances. The assumptions become successively weaker as layers are added. The results therefore do not apply directly to deep networks."
errors.explanation: These two sentences contradict each other: if assumptions become successively weaker (i.e., less restrictive) as layers are added, one would expect the approximations to be more widely applicable, not less; yet the next sentence asserts the results do not apply to deep networks. The text thus contains an internal logical inconsistency (likely a misstatement about 'weaker').

errors.claim: "The modified-Y5F result is the §9.1 objective with coefficient ((1-p)/p);"

final_notes: QX2 trains random submodels; training noisier/slower (~2–3×). Key results: ILSVRC ensemble+QX2 test top-5 16.4%; single-net val top-5 18.2%; ILSVRC-2010 conv+QX2 17.0%. RBM-mixture (B8T, p=0.5) produced coarser filters; Gaussian multiplicative-noise slightly favored over Bernoulli. Paper notes two dropout-mask conventions; analytic marginalization inconsistency unresolved. Appendix heuristics: widen layers ≥ n/p; much larger LR (10–100×), momentum ≈0.95–0.99; max-norm c≈3–4; retention p hidden 0.5–0.8 (default 0.5), input ≈0.8. H4Z (MNIST-like): held-out val 10k; training endpoint 1M updates; arch sweep depths 2/3/4, widths 1024/2048; hidden p=0.5, input p=0.8; momentum 0.95; V9C c=2; very large 2-layer nets (>65M params) improved; some experiments combine val+train after hyperparam selection. A2F (conv): mixed-source val 6k; conv layers 96/128/256 (5×5) + 3×3 pooling; two FC 2048; p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5); V9C c=4; momentum 0.95. J3V/W6R: 50k train/10k test; val 5k; per-channel contrast-normalization + ZCA; arch & retention like A2F; input LRs smaller; after hyperparam selection val+train combined. N8Q (speech): 680 speakers ×10 sentences; log-filterbank windows; input p=0.8, hidden p=0.5; V9C c=4; momentum 0.95; high LR 0.1 decaying; G6W pretrain CD-1; best QX2 finetune LR ≈0.01; Table 7 phone error 19.7 for QX2-pretrained depths. M5X Reuters subset: 402,738 articles. Z7P (genetics): 3665 cassette exons, 1014 RNA features, 4 tissue types. New (this part): Z7P experiments average the same 5 folds as Xiong et al. (2011) (final settings-table row documents this). QX2 uses substantially more hidden units than the Bayesian comparison (settings table: “1000s” vs “a few tens”); trained QX2 net specified as two layers of 1024 units. Dropout: randomly remove units and their connections during training, effectively training many smaller networks that share parameters. At test time, use one complete network with reduced weights to approximate averaging the smaller networks' predictions. Claimed benefits: improves generalization over networks without dropout on every tested dataset; reports state-of-the-art results on several benchmarks. Experimental domains: images, speech, documents, gene-splicing prediction. Also examines learned features, sparsity, retention rates, effects of training-set size, Restricted Boltzmann Machines, noise marginalization, and Gaussian corruption. Training cost: typically takes 2–3× longer than training a standard network of the same architecture.

Dropout (QX2): randomly remove units and their connections during training; at test time use one unthinned network with outgoing weights multiplied by the retention probability (T6R) to approximate averaging the thinned-model predictions. The paper states this approximation corresponds to the geometric mean (equally weighted combination) of thinned-network predictions. Two corruption types: Bernoulli dropout (P7V) — binary multiplicative noise (Bernoulli variable =1 with prob p, 0 otherwise) — and Gaussian dropout (D4K) — Gaussian multiplicative noise. Marginalization = expectation over dropout noise to yield a deterministic objective/regularizer; Monte‑Carlo dropout/model averaging = stochastic sampling and averaging predictions from sampled thinned networks. Dropout RBM (B8T): described as a mixture of shared-weight RBMs using different hidden-unit subsets; U2L = RBM; pretraining (DBM/E5Q, DBN/G6W) then finetuning with backprop; mcRBM-G6W is a named pretrained variant. Regularizers: L1 (O3U), L2 (Y5F, Tikhonov), max-norm (V9C), KL-sparsity. Activations mentioned: logistic units, ReLU (F3N), maxout (L8J). Other glossary items to track: geometric mean vs. posterior-weighted averaging, blankout noise, ridge-regression connection (dropout expectation → ridge-like penalty matrix), convolutional-net components (filters, pooling variants), data augmentation, SVM/PCA baselines, terms like dead unit, mix-ability, replica code, and non-stationarity. These definitions and labels will be used in later parts for numerical and conceptual consistency checks.

Abstract summary: method called "QX2, or dropout"; it randomly removes units and their connections during training, inhibiting co-adaptation, sampling exponentially many thinned networks that share parameters. A single unthinned network with reduced weights approximates the averaged predictions of the thinned nets. Claims substantial reduction in overfitting and major improvements; supervised experiments in vision, speech recognition, document classification and computational biology reportedly attain state-of-the-art on many benchmarks. Evidence claimed in Tables 2–8 and an unnumbered text-classification table in §6.3; domain-specific comparisons listed in §6.

Paper: "Dropout (QX2)". Core idea: randomly remove units during training to train many shared-parameter thinned subnetworks (2^n possible thinned nets for n units) and approximate their combined predictions with one unthinned test-time network. Key terminology: QX2 = dropout; T6R = test-time weight scaling (use one unthinned net with scaled weights); X9M = Monte-Carlo model averaging (average sampled thinned nets at test); U2L/B8T = dropout extension to RBMs. Notation (carry-forward): n = unit count; expected retained width = p n; practical width heuristic = n/p; shared-parameter count O(n^2); L hidden layers with W^(l), b^(l), activations f; p = retention probability; test-time weights scaled by p (W_test = p W). Claims in this part: QX2 approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many models; a new thinned member is sampled and trained (rarely) per presentation of each training case; T6R is a cheap practical inference rule that gives significantly lower generalization error than other regularizers across varied problems; X9M is more expensive and needs around k≈50 samples (per §7.5 and App B.1) before matching T6R. Evidence pointer: Table 9 referenced for comparisons (rows quoted: Y5F=1.62, V9C=1.35, QX2+Y5F=1.25, QX2+V9C=1.05). Paper outline: §2 motivation, §3 prior work, §4 model, §5 training algorithm, §6 experiments, §7 effects and hyperparameter interactions, §8 RBM extension, §9 marginalization, Appendix A (practical guidance).

Paper: "Dropout (QX2)". Core idea: randomly remove units during training to train many shared-parameter thinned subnetworks (2^n possible thinned nets for n units) and approximate their combined predictions with one unthinned test-time network. Notation: n = unit count; p = retention probability; expected retained width = p n; practical width heuristic = n/p; shared-parameter count O(n^2); L hidden layers with W^(l), b^(l), activations f; test-time weights scaled by p (W_test = p W). Claims: QX2 approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many models; a new thinned member is sampled and trained (rarely unique) on each presentation of a training case; T6R (test-time weight scaling) is a cheap practical inference rule that gives significantly lower generalization error than other regularizers across varied problems; X9M (Monte-Carlo averaging) is more expensive and needs around k ≈ 50 samples (per §7.5 and App B.1) to match T6R. Evidence pointer: Table 9 comparisons (rows: Y5F=1.62, V9C=1.35, QX2+Y5F=1.25, QX2+V9C=1.05). New in §2: motivation via sexual-reproduction and conspiracy analogies — Livnat et al. (2010) "mix-ability" notion: selection favors genes that work well with random partners (robust, independently useful components). Analogy: QX2 forces hidden units to operate with randomly selected partners, discouraging complex co-adaptations and favoring robust features; replicating units is a poor remedy. Smaller cooperating subsets are argued to be more robust under non-stationarity than large co-adaptations. Outline pointers: §3 prior work, §4 model, §5 training algorithm, §6 experiments, §7 hyperparams, §8 RBM extension, §9 marginalization, Appendix A guidance.

Paper: "Dropout (QX2)". Core idea: randomly remove units during training to train many shared-parameter thinned subnetworks (2^n possible thinned nets for n units) and approximate their combined predictions with one unthinned test-time network. Notation/impl: n = unit count; p = retention probability; expected retained width = p n; practical width heuristic = n/p; shared-parameter count O(n^2); L hidden layers with weights W^(l), biases b^(l), activations f; test-time weights scaled by p (W_test = p W). Key claims: QX2 approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many models; a new thinned member is sampled and trained on each presentation; T6R (test-time weight scaling) is a cheap practical inference rule that often gives much lower generalization error than other regularizers; X9M (Monte-Carlo averaging) is more expensive and reportedly needs k ≈ 50 samples to match T6R (per §7.5 and App B.1). Empirical pointer: Table 9 example rows (Y5F=1.62, V9C=1.35, QX2+Y5F=1.25, QX2+V9C=1.05). Section 3 notes: DAEs (denoising autoencoders) corrupt inputs and reconstruct; QX2 extends corruption to hidden units and gives a model-averaging view; applies to supervised/unsupervised and other neuron-based architectures including Boltzmann Machines. T6R permits much higher noise than typical DAEs: table lists S2H/DAE typical best 5%, QX2 input-unit removal often optimal 20%, QX2 hidden-unit removal often optimal 50%. Related methods: Globerson & Roweis (2006) and Dekel et al. (2010) use adversarial removals (fixed max number) and have no hidden units. Marginalizing QX2 yields deterministic regularizers in simple cases; van der Maaten et al. (2013) call QX2 input noise "blankout noise" but limited to models without hidden layers; Chen et al. (2012) on marginalization for DAEs; Wang & Manning (2013) propose marginalization to accelerate QX2.

steps.notes_before: Paper: Dropout (QX2) — gate unit outputs during training, independently per unit with r_j^{(l)} ~ Bernoulli(p); tilde y^{(l)} = r^{(l)} * y^{(l)}. Both hidden and input (visible) units can be dropped. Validation can pick p; default often near optimal; input retention generally near complete retention. Forward equations: y^{(0)} = x; nominally z_i^{(l+1)} = w_i^{(l+1)} y^{(l)} + b_i^{(l+1)}, y_i^{(l+1)} = f(z_i^{(l+1)}). Example activation: logistic f(x)=1/(1+exp(-x)). Note: this part contains an indexing inconsistency — it first states l∈{1..L} then uses l∈{0..L-1} for the feed-forward formulas (treating y^{(0)} as input). Keep this in mind when later parts refer to layer indices.

errors.claim: P(h_j=1 | r_j, v) = 1(r_j=1) sigma(b_j + sum_i W_{ij} v_i) (i.e. the hidden conditional uses b_j as the hidden bias).
errors.evidence: The paper first defines theta = {W, a, b} and the joint: P(h,v;theta) = (1/Z) exp( v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v ). Later it states the hidden conditional: P(h_j=1 | r_j, v) = 1(r_j=1) sigma( b_j + sum_i W_{ij} v_i ).
errors.explanation: Given the energy term a^T h + b^T v, the hidden-unit bias should be a_j, so the conditional should use a_j; the formula instead uses b_j, so the parameter names a and b are swapped/inconsistent.

errors.claim: P(v_i=1 | h) = sigma( a_i + sum_j W_{ij} h_j ) (i.e. the visible conditional uses a_i as the visible bias).
errors.evidence: The paper's joint energy is P(h,v;theta) proportional to exp( v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v ), which makes b the visible-bias vector. Yet it writes the visible conditional as P(v_i=1 | h) = sigma( a_i + sum_j W_{ij} h_j ).
errors.explanation: This uses a_i for the visible bias even though the energy term associates b with visible biases; again a and b are inconsistently used.

errors.claim: "The assumptions become successively weaker as layers are added. The results therefore do not apply directly to deep networks."
errors.evidence: "Under reasonable assumptions, logistic-unit input distributions and marginalized-model gradients are Gaussian, with efficiently computable means and variances. The assumptions become successively weaker as layers are added. The results therefore do not apply directly to deep networks."
errors.explanation: These two sentences contradict each other: if assumptions become successively weaker (i.e., less restrictive) as layers are added, one would expect the approximations to be more widely applicable, not less; yet the next sentence asserts the results do not apply to deep networks. The text thus contains an internal logical inconsistency (likely a misstatement about 'weaker').

Marginalizing QX2: deterministic noise-marginalized models need no random bits and allow gradients of marginalized losses. Linear regression exact marginalization: E_R[||y-(R*X)w||^2] = ||y-p X w||^2 + p(1-p)||Γ w||^2, with Γ=(diag(X^T X))^{1/2}; with ̃w=pw this gives ||y-X̃w||^2 + ((1-p)/p)||Γ̃w||^2. Logistic regression: approximate marginalization (Wang & Manning 2013) can improve training time and generalization. grade.reason: Review item 3 (array index 2) identifies the incorrect 1/(1-p) scaling and explains the correct reciprocal is 1/p because expected contribution under Bernoulli(p) dropout is multiplied by p.

errors.claim: The paper says dropout approximates an 'equally weighted geometric mean' of many models' predictions, but later claims the test-time output equals the expected (training-time) output.
errors.evidence: This part states: 'We propose to do this by approximating an equally weighted geometric mean of the predictions of an exponential number of learned models that share parameters.' Later (Figure 2 caption) it states: 'The output at test time is same as the expected output at training time.'
errors.explanation: A geometric mean of predictions is not the same operation as the expectation (arithmetic mean) over predictions. The text asserts both without reconciling or explaining when they are equivalent, creating an internal inconsistency.

errors.claim: "A neural net with n units, can be seen as a collection of 2n possible thinned neural networks."
errors.evidence: "A neural net with n units, can be seen as a collection of 2n possible thinned neural networks." (this part)" and earlier note: "exponential number of 'thinned' networks."

Paper: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (JMLR 15, 2014). Authors: Nitish Srivastava, Geoffrey Hinton, Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, Ruslan Salakhutdinov. Abstract/main claim: Dropout randomly drops units and their connections during training to prevent co-adaptation; training effectively samples from an exponential number of "thinned" networks. At test time, the effect of averaging these thinned networks is approximated by using a single unthinned network with scaled (smaller) weights. Dropout reportedly reduces overfitting and outperforms other regularization methods, producing major improvements and state-of-the-art results on benchmarks in vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology. Intro notes: deep nets are expressive and prone to overfitting; common regularizers include early stopping, L1/L2 penalties, and soft weight sharing. The paper states that with unlimited computation the best regularizer is averaging predictions over all parameter settings (sentence is cut off in this part). Figure 1 caption: left—standard net with 2 hidden layers; right—example thinned net after dropout where some units are dropped.

steps.notes_before: Paper: Dropout (JMLR 2014). Dropout: randomly remove (drop) hidden and visible units during training to prevent co-adaptation; training samples from an exponential number of 'thinned' networks. Authors propose to approximate an equally weighted geometric mean of predictions of these many learned models (to approach Bayesian averaging) using shared parameters. Simple dropout: retain each unit with probability p (often p=0.5 for hidden units; input units usually have retention closer to 1); p can be chosen by validation. At test time use a single unthinned network with weights scaled by p (Figure 2 shows training: unit present with prob. p and weight w; test: unit always present and weight pw) and the caption asserts test output equals the expected training-time output. Key numbers/claims: exponential number of thinned models, p≈0.5 for hidden, input retention ≈1, test-time weight scaling by p.

steps.notes_before: Paper: Dropout (JMLR 2014). Dropout randomly removes hidden/visible units during training, sampling a 'thinned' network each presentation; weights are shared across thinned models. Paper states there are exponentially many thinned networks (2^n), though this part prints '2n' (likely a typo/inconsistency). Total number of parameters remains O(n^2) or less due to sharing. Training: each update samples a new thinned network; thus each specific thinned net is trained rarely. Test-time: use single unthinned network with outgoing weights scaled by retention probability p (if unit retained with prob p during training, multiply its outgoing weights by p at test time) so that test-time activations match expected training-time activations. Typical choices: p≈0.5 for hidden units; input-unit retention closer to 1; choose p by validation. Dropout not limited to feed-forward nets—paper introduces dropout RBM and compares to standard RBMs, claiming improvements in some respects. Paper: Dropout (JMLR 2014). Core idea: during training randomly remove (drop out) hidden/visible units, sampling a 'thinned' network each presentation; weights are shared across thinned models. There are exponentially many thinned networks (paper elsewhere prints 2^n; an earlier printed '2n' looked like a typo). Total number of parameters remains O(n^2) or less due to sharing. Training: each update samples a new thinned network so any specific thinned net is trained rarely. Test-time: use single unthinned network with outgoing weights scaled by the unit's retention probability p so test activations match expected training activations. Structure: Secs 2–9 and Appendix A (practical guide). New from current part: Motivation analogies — sexual reproduction: dropout viewed as preventing large co-adaptations, forcing each hidden unit to learn useful features that work with random subsets of partners, improving robustness; copying units to resist dropout is a poor solution (analogy to replica codes for noisy channels). Conspiracy analogy: many small conspiracies (small co-adaptations) more robust than one large co-adaptation, hence better generalization under non-stationarity. Related work: Dropout can be seen as regularization via adding noise to hidden units; this idea relates to Denoising Autoencoders (Vincent et al. 2008, 2010) which add noise to unit states.

steps.notes_before: Paper: Dropout trains by randomly dropping units (thinning) and sharing weights across exponentially many sub-networks. Training samples a new thinned net each presentation; backpropagate gradients through that thinned net. At test time use a single unthinned net with weights scaled by retention probabilities (W_test = p W^(l) per layer). Typical choices: drop ~50% hidden units (p_hidden ≈ 0.5), ~20% inputs (p_input ≈ 0.8); DAEs typically use 5% input noise but test-time scaling allows higher noise. Dropout can be applied to hidden layers and other neuron-based architectures (e.g., Boltzmann Machines, RBMs). Interpretation: stochastic regularization / model averaging; related to denoising autoencoders and marginalizing noise. Definition details: network with L hidden layers; y(0)=x; feed-forward recurrence given as z^{(l+1)} = W^{(l+1)} y^{(l)} + b^{(l+1)}, y^{(l+1)} = f(z^{(l+1)}). With dropout: sample r^{(l)} ~ Bernoulli(p) elementwise, form y_e^{(l)} = r^{(l)} * y^{(l)} and use y_e^{(l)} as input to next layer. Loss is minimized stochastically (expected loss); prior adversarial-drop work fixes max number dropped (no hidden-layer models).

Training: dropout nets trained by SGD on ‘‘thinned’’ nets — for each training case in a mini‑batch sample dropout mask, do forward/backprop on that thinned net; gradients averaged over mini‑batch; any case that omits a parameter contributes zero gradient for that parameter. Standard SGD tricks (momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 weight decay) help. Max‑norm regularization: constrain incoming weight vector w at each hidden unit to ||w||2 ≤ c by projecting back into the ball of radius c whenever it exceeds c (c is a tunable hyperparameter). Max‑norm often improves SGD even without dropout; combining dropout + max‑norm + large decaying LR + high momentum gives further gains (intuition: ball constraint prevents blowup so large LR can be used for exploration). Unsupervised pretraining: stacks of RBMs/autoencoders/DBMs can be used; pretraining stays the same, but when finetuning with dropout scale pretrained weights by 1/p so expected output under dropout matches pretraining output. If finetune LR is too large pretrained information can be lost; use smaller LR to retain gains. Experiments: datasets include MNIST, TIMIT, CIFAR‑10/100, SVHN, ImageNet, Reuters‑RCV1, and an Alternative Splicing RNA dataset; more details in Appendix B.

Section 8: Dropout RBMs. RBM: v∈{0,1}^D, h∈{0,1}^F, P(h,v;θ) ∝ exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v). Add r∈{0,1}^F with r_j ~ Bernoulli(p). Joint P(r,h,v)=P(r)P(h,v|r) where P(r)=∏ p^{r_j}(1-p)^{1-r_j}; P(h,v|r) ∝ exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v) ∏ g(h_j,r_j) with g enforcing h_j=0 if r_j=0. Conditioned on r, P(h|r,v) factorial with P(h_j=1|r_j,v)=1(r_j=1) σ(b_j + Σ_i W_ij v_i); P(v|h)=Π σ(a_i + Σ_j W_ij h_j). Learning: CD-1, sample r per training case. errors.explanation: These two statements conflict: having "very few dead units" implies fewer near-zero activations (less sparse), whereas claiming dropout RBMs "learn much sparser representations" implies more near-zero activations (more dead/inactive units). Both cannot be true as written about the same models without further clarification.

steps.notes_before: Fig.13: left histogram shows many units with activations away from zero; right shows many units close to zero and few with high activation. Text: dropout-RBM features appear coarser than standard RBM and "There seem to be very few dead units in the dropout RBM relative to the standard RBM." But 8.4 immediately states: "The histograms clearly indicate that the dropout RBMs learn much sparser representations than standard RBMs..." (internal contradiction about sparsity vs number of dead units). Earlier: Fig.12 compared 256-unit RBM features with/without dropout (p=0.5). Section 9 (Marginalizing Dropout): deterministic marginalized models (no random bits) can give gradients. Prior work cited (Globerson & Roweis; Chen et al.; Srivastava; Wang & Manning; van der Maaten; Wager). 9.1 Linear regression: dropout on inputs retained with prob p -> minimize E_R ||y - (R * X)w||^2 -> reduces to minimize ||y - p X w||^2 + p(1-p)||Γ w||^2 where Γ = (diag(X > X))^{1/2} (as written). Absorbing p: w_e = p w gives explicit dependence: stronger regularization as p decreases. 9.2: logistic/deep nets lack closed-form marginalization; approximate marginalization (Wang & Manning) assumes Gaussian inputs/gradients; approximations weaken with depth. Table: MNIST (2-layer 1024): Bernoulli 1.08±0.04, Gaussian 0.95±0.04; CIFAR-10 (3 conv+2 fc): Bernoulli 12.6±0.1, Gaussian 12.5±0.1.

Part 15 (Table 10 + Sec.10): Table 10 compares Bernoulli vs Gaussian multiplicative dropout. MNIST Bernoulli: p_hidden=0.5, p_input=0.8. CIFAR-10 Bernoulli p per-layer = (0.9, 0.75, 0.75, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5) from input to top. Gaussian dropout: r0 ~ N(1,σ^2); they set σ^2 = (1−p)/p (i.e. σ = sqrt((1−p)/p)) per layer to match mean and variance of Bernoulli case. Results (averaged over 10 seeds): MNIST error Bernoulli 1.08 ± 0.04, Gaussian 0.95 ± 0.04; CIFAR-10 Bernoulli 12.6 ± 0.1, Gaussian 12.5 ± 0.1. Key claims: Gaussian form retains E[activation], so no test-time scaling is required; Bernoulli can be seen as multiplying by rb ∈ {0,1/p} with E[rb]=1 and Var=(1−p)/p; matching σ^2 gives Gaussian the same mean/var but higher entropy; preliminary experiments suggest Gaussian (high-entropy) may work slightly better. Reminder of earlier sections: Sec.9 (marginalizing dropout) gave closed-form for linear regression: minimization reduces to ||y − pXw||^2 + p(1−p)||Γ w||^2 (Γ odd as printed); logistic / deep nets lack closed form, approximations assume Gaussian inputs/gradients and degrade with depth. Outstanding earlier internal note: RBM/feature-analysis statements were internally inconsistent (one place: "very few dead units in dropout RBM" vs Sec.8.4: "dropout RBMs learn much sparser representations"). Keep these numbers, formulas, and that unresolved RBM-sparsity contradiction for checking in later parts.

Summary of key points so far:
- Table10 / Sec.10 (Part15): Bernoulli vs Gaussian multiplicative dropout. MNIST: p_hidden=0.5, p_input=0.8. CIFAR-10 Bernoulli per-layer p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5). Gaussian dropout uses r0 ~ N(1,σ^2) with σ^2=(1−p)/p to match Bernoulli mean/variance. Results (10 seeds): MNIST error Bernoulli 1.08±0.04, Gaussian 0.95±0.04; CIFAR-10 Bernoulli 12.6±0.1, Gaussian 12.5±0.1. Claim: Gaussian retains E[activation], no test-time scaling; Bernoulli seen as rb∈{0,1/p} with E[rb]=1, Var=(1−p)/p; Gaussian has higher entropy and may perform slightly better.
- Marginalizing dropout: closed-form for linear regression gives a modified L2 regularizer; no closed form for deep nets (approximations assume Gaussian inputs/gradients and degrade with depth).
- RBMs: paper developed Dropout RBMs and reports they have desirable properties. Note unresolved internal inconsistency from earlier parts: one place said “very few dead units in dropout RBM” while Sec.8.4 said “dropout RBMs learn much sparser representations.” Keep this contradiction for checking.
- From current part (Appendix A): dropout increases training time (typical 2–3× longer). Marginalizing noise may give non-stochastic regularizers (linear case done).
- Practical heuristics: A.1 expected active units = p n; recommended layer size ≈ n/p if n was optimal for standard net. A.2 use much larger learning rates (≈10–100× standard-optimal) and higher momentum (≈0.95–0.99 vs usual 0.9) to offset noisy gradients. A.3 use max-norm regularization (incoming-weight norm ≤ c, typical c=3–4). A.4 typical p: hidden layers 0.5–0.8; real-valued input layers ≈0.8.
- Broad claims: dropout improves many tasks (SVHN, ImageNet, CIFAR-100, MNIST).

Appendix B: experimental details and data splits.
General: code at http://www.cs.toronto.edu/~nitish/dropout; GPU implementation using cudamat and cuda-convnet.
MNIST (60k train, 10k test): held out 10k for validation. Hyperparameters tuned so best validation error occurred after 1M weight updates; then validation merged with training and final training run for 1M updates. Architectures: all combinations of 2/3/4 layers × {1024,2048} units → 6 nets. Dropout: p_hidden=0.5, p_input=0.8. Momentum final=0.95. Max-norm constraint c=2. Also tried 2/3 layer nets with 4096/8192 units; 2-layer nets outperformed 3-layer ones at same dropout; increasing dropout helped but still didn’t beat 2-layer nets.
SVHN (~600k train including extras, ~26k test): validation set 6000 (400/class from standard, 200/class from extra). Inputs: RGB zero-mean, unit-variance. Best net: 3 conv layers (96,128,256 filters; 5×5 stride 1) each followed by 3×3 max-pool stride 2, then two FC layers of 2048 ReLU units. Dropout retain-probabilities p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5) from input→conv1→conv2→conv3→fc1→fc2. Max-norm c=4; momentum=0.95. Hyperparams tuned on validation; did NOT combine validation with training; reported test error for model with smallest validation error.
CIFAR-10/100: 50k train, 10k test; 5k validation. Followed MNIST procedure (tune on val then combine for final training). Preprocessing: per-channel global contrast normalization then ZCA whitening.
Keep unresolved earlier RBM inconsistency ("very few dead units" vs "much sparser representations").

errors.claim: "For a task whose optimal standard-net layer has n hidden units, a good QX2 layer should contain at least n/p units. Removing units reduces capacity: only pn units remain in expectation, their identities change at every sampling, and unrestricted co-adaptation is unavailable."
errors.evidence: "...a good QX2 layer should contain at least n/p units." and "...only pn units remain in expectation..."
errors.explanation: These two sentences contradict basic arithmetic: if you provision n/p units and each is retained with probability p, the expected number of active units is (n/p)*p = n, not p*n. The text therefore reports the wrong expectation.

Title: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting". Authors: Nitish Srivastava, Geoffrey Hinton, Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, Ruslan Salakhutdinov; Dept. of Computer Science, University of Toronto. Journal: JMLR 15 (2014). Header lists pages 1929–1958 while page map lists pages 1930–1955 (internal inconsistency noted). Abstract summary: introduces dropout (called "QX2: dropout") — a training procedure that temporarily removes randomly selected units and their connections, inhibiting excessive co-adaptation and effectively sampling exponentially many parameter-sharing thinned networks. At test time a single unthinned network with reduced weights approximates the averaged predictions of these thinned networks. Claims dropout substantially reduces overfitting versus other regularizers and yields major improvements, achieving state-of-the-art performance on many benchmarks in supervised vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology.

steps.notes_before: Title: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al., UToronto). Header/page-number inconsistency noted earlier. Dropout (QX2) randomly removes units/connections during training, producing exponentially many (2^n for n units) thinned networks; parameters are shared so total distinct parameters retained are O(n^2) or fewer. With unlimited computation, posterior-weighted averaging over parameters is ideal; the paper claims its method approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of these thinned models' predictions (introduction) — earlier abstract wording said it "approximates the averaged predictions", a potential arithmetic vs geometric-mean wording mismatch. Every presentation samples/trains a new thinned member; individual members are rarely trained thoroughly. Practical inference: T6R (weight scaling) uses one unthinned network at test time; X9M refers to Monte-Carlo model averaging (more expensive). Claims T6R gives much lower generalization error than other regularizers across tasks. Method extends to graphical models, e.g., Dropout RBM (B8T) from RBMs (U2L). Paper map: §2 motivation; §3 prior work; §4 formal model; §5 training algorithm; §6 experiments; §7 network/hyperparameter interactions; §8 Dropout RBMs; §9 marginalization; Appendix A practical guidance.

Title: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al.). Earlier: header/page-number inconsistency noted. Method overview: dropout (QX2) randomly removes units/connections during training, producing exponentially many (2^n) thinned networks; parameters are shared so total distinct parameters are O(n^2) or fewer. Training samples/train different thinned networks; individual thinned members rarely trained thoroughly. Test-time inference: T6R = weight-scaling using one unthinned network; X9M = Monte-Carlo model averaging (more expensive). Paper claims T6R yields much lower generalization error than other regularizers across tasks. Extensions: Dropout RBM (B8T). Paper map: §2 motivation; §3 prior work; §4 formal model; §5 training algorithm; §6 experiments; §7 interactions; §8 Dropout RBMs; §9 marginalization; Appendix A guidance. New from §2 (Motivation): authors use biological analogy—sexual vs asexual reproduction—and cite Livnat et al. (2010) arguing selection can favor gene "mix-ability" rather than individual-fitness optimization. Dropout is analogous: hidden units face randomly selected partners, which favors independently useful, robust features and reduces complex co-adaptations. Replicating units many times is deemed a poor robustness fix (analogy to replica codes and noisy channels). Conspiracy analogy: many small cooperating subsets are more robust under non-stationarity than a single large co-adapted set; complex co-adaptations may overfit training data and fail on novel test data.

Title: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al.). Method: dropout (QX2) randomly removes units/connections during training producing ~2^n thinned networks; parameters shared so distinct params O(n^2). Training: each SGD update samples a thinned network; individual thinned members rarely trained thoroughly. Test-time inference: T6R = weight-scaling using one unthinned network; X9M = Monte-Carlo model averaging (more expensive). Paper claims T6R gives much lower generalization error than other regularizers across tasks. Motivation (§2): biological analogy (mix-ability), reduces co-adaptations. Related work (§3): dropout interpretable as noise in hidden-unit states, extends denoising autoencoders (Vincent et al. 2008/2010) — effective hidden-layer corruption, model-averaging view, supervised/unsupervised use, applicable to Boltzmann Machines. Table: S2H (DAE) typical best noise ~5%; QX2 often optimal input-unit removal ~20%; QX2 often optimal hidden-unit removal ~50%. Adversarial-removal alternatives (Globerson & Roweis 2006; Dekel et al. 2010) consider worst-case removals under a budget and have no hidden units. Analytic marginalization can give deterministic regularizers in simple cases; van der Maaten et al. (2013) studied exponential-family input-noise (blankout) limited to models without hidden layers; Chen et al. (2012) studied marginalization for DAEs; Wang & Manning (2013) proposed marginalization to speed up dropout. Section map: §2 motivation; §3 prior work; §4 formal model; §5 training algorithm; §6 experiments; §7 interactions; §8 Dropout RBMs; §9 marginalization; Appendix A guidance.

Paper: Dropout regularization. Key idea: during training randomly delete (zero) units (hidden and/or visible) to sample many thinned subnetworks; parameters shared across subnetworks. Retention choices are independent Bernoulli variables with common probability p (can be chosen by validation). Typical defaults: hidden-unit retention p≈0.5 (i.e. ~50% removal); input-unit removal often ~20% (retention p≈0.8) — input retention usually nearer full. Training: each SGD update samples r^{(l)} (vector of independent Bernoulli(p)) and forms \tilde y^{(l)} = r^{(l)} * y^{(l)}; forward: z_i^{(l+1)} = w_i^{(l+1)} \tilde y^{(l)} + b_i^{(l+1)}, y_i^{(l+1)} = f(z_i^{(l+1)}). Backprop passes gradients through the sampled subnetwork. Notation: y^{(0)}=x; L hidden layers (indexed 1..L); feed-forward written for l=0..L-1 producing layer l+1. Activation f can be any (e.g. logistic). Test-time inference: no dropout; use one unthinned network with outgoing weights scaled by p: W_test^{(l)} = p W^{(l)} (equivalently unit outputs' expected training contribution equals test-time contribution with scaled weights). Figures illustrate training (stochastic gates r) vs testing (weights scaled by p). Other parts: training samples many subnetworks per SGD update; Monte-Carlo averaging at test-time is an alternative to weight-scaling but more expensive.

Part 5: QX2 (dropout) gives significant gains; combining it with high momentum, large decaying learning rates, and an incoming-weight constraint (V9C = max-norm) gives further improvement. V9C enforces ||w||_2 <= c with projection to the ball surface when exceeded; c is tuned by validation. Proposed optimization account claims large learning rates are safe inside the fixed-radius ball; QX2 provides noise exploration; learning rates decay to smaller steps. SGD differs from standard training only by per-case sampled thinned networks: each mini-batch case uses its own sampled network; gradients averaged across cases; a case not using a parameter contributes zero. Momentum, annealed (decaying) learning rates and other heuristics remain useful. Unsupervised pretraining is unchanged, but before QX2 finetuning pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p so each unit’s expected random-removal output matches its pretraining output. Smaller finetuning learning rates help preserve pretrained information. Pretraining (with unlabeled data) can improve over random init; applicable to stacked U2L, autoencoders, DBMs for finetuning.

errors.explanation: The joint definition uses a^T h + b^T v, so a_j is the hidden bias and b_i is the visible bias. The two conditional formulas reverse these: the hidden conditional uses b_j and the visible conditional uses a_i, which is inconsistent with the joint parameter labeling.

steps.notes_before: B8T: an RBM-style (U2L) model augmented with a binary retention mask r (each r_j ~ Bernoulli(p)), making B8T a mixture over retained hidden-subsets. Joint: P(h,v;θ) ∝ exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v). B8T: P(r) = ∏ p^{r_j}(1-p)^{1-r_j}; P(h,v|r) ∝ exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v) ∏ g(h_j,r_j) where g enforces h_j=0 if r_j=0. Visible/hidden conditionals are given, but there is an internal inconsistency: the joint uses a as hidden biases and b as visible biases, yet P(h_j=1|r,v) uses b_j and P(v_i=1|h) uses a_i (swapped). Learning: CD-1, sample r per training case in each mini-batch, train only retained units. Features: authors report B8T features "coarser than the sharply defined stroke-like U2L features" and "very few dead units relative to U2L" (Figure 12). Sparsity: without explicit sparsity regularizer, B8T yields much sparser representations than U2L; activation histograms (test mini-batch) show many activations near zero for p=0.5 (Figure 13). Previous results (earlier parts) on QX2, datasets, and numeric errors remain as recorded.

errors.claim: "QX2 linear regression is, in expectation, ridge regression with a particular penalty matrix: a dimension’s standard deviation scales its weight cost, squeezing more strongly the weights of highly variable dimensions."
errors.evidence: "\mathbf\Gamma = (\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X))^{1/2}."
errors.explanation: The text says a dimension's standard deviation scales the penalty, but the defined matrix Γ is the column-wise L2 norm (sqrt of the sum of squares) not the standard deviation (which would require mean-centering and normalization by N or √N). Thus the verbal description 'standard deviation' contradicts the explicit definition of Γ.

steps.notes_before: B8T: RBM-style (U2L) model with binary retention mask r_j ~ Bernoulli(p), producing a mixture over retained hidden-subsets. Joint given as P(h,v) ∝ exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v); earlier noted internal inconsistency: conditionals in text swap a and b. Learning via CD-1, sampling r per training case, train only retained units. Reported features: B8T coarser than U2L, few dead units; yields much sparser representations (many activations near zero at p=0.5), Figures 12–13. Part 9 (QX2 marginalization): deterministic noise-marginalized models need no random bits and admit gradients of marginalized losses. Linear regression: E_R ||y - (R*X)w||^2 = ||y - p X w||^2 + p(1-p) ||Γ w||^2 with Γ = (diag(X^T X))^{1/2}; equivalently with \tilde w = p w gives ||y - X \tilde w||^2 + ((1-p)/p) ||Γ \tilde w||^2. Note: paper's text calls Γ a 'standard deviation' scaling but Γ is column L2 norms (see error). Logistic/deep nets: approximate marginalization (Gaussian approximations for pre-activations/gradients) can be efficient; closed-form marginalized models are harder for deep networks.

Kept from earlier: B8T = RBM-style (U2L) with binary retention mask r_j ~ Bernoulli(p); joint written P(h,v) ∝ exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v) (text earlier swapped a and b); trained with CD-1 sampling r per case; B8T yields coarser features, few dead units, very sparse activations at p=0.5. QX2 (marginalization): deterministic noise-marginalized models need no random bits; linear regression identity E_R ||y-(R*X)w||^2 = ||y-p X w||^2 + p(1-p)||Γ w||^2 with Γ=(diag(X^T X))^{1/2}; equivalently with \tilde w = p w: ||y - X \tilde w||^2 + ((1-p)/p)||Γ \tilde w||^2. (Paper mislabels Γ as a 'standard deviation' scaling.) Logistic/deep nets: approximate marginalization via Gaussian approximations.

New (part 14): Multiplicative Gaussian dropout (D4K) vs Bernoulli dropout (P7V): preliminary Table 10 — H4Z (2 layers, 1024): P7V 1.08±0.04, D4K 0.95±0.04; J3V (3 conv + 2 FC): P7V 12.6±0.1, D4K 12.5±0.1. P7V p settings: H4Z hidden p=0.5, input p=0.8; J3V p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5). D4K per-layer σ = sqrt((1-p)/p) to match first/second moments; r'~N(1,σ^2) keeps E[activation] unchanged (no test-time scaling). Alternate representation: scale retained training activations by 1/p so Bernoulli multiplier r_b = 1/p w.p. p (else 0) has E[r_b]=1, Var[r_b]=(1-p)/p; choose Gaussian Var = (1-p)/p to match.

errors.claim: "For a task whose optimal standard-net layer has n hidden units, a good QX2 layer should contain at least n/p units. Removing units reduces capacity: only pn units remain in expectation, their identities change at every sampling, and unrestricted co-adaptation is unavailable."
errors.evidence: "...a good QX2 layer should contain at least n/p units." and "...only pn units remain in expectation..."
errors.explanation: These two sentences contradict basic arithmetic: if you provision n/p units and each is retained with probability p, the expected number of active units is (n/p)*p = n, not p*n. The text therefore reports the wrong expectation.

Dropout: reduces co-adaptation, gives sparser activations, helps many domains, increases training time ≈2–3×. MC model averaging: ~50 samples match weight-scaling approx on MNIST. Marginalizing linear dropout yields extra regularizer scaling (1-p)/p; approximations weaken with depth. Multiplicative Gaussian noise set σ^2=(1-p)/p to match Bernoulli; Gaussian sometimes slightly better (Table 10: MNIST Bernoulli 1.08±0.04 vs Gaussian 0.95±0.04; CIFAR-10 Bernoulli 12.6±0.1 vs Gaussian 12.5±0.1). MNIST (App. B.1): 60k train / 10k test; 10k held out val; hyperparams chosen to minimize val at 1M updates, then retrain on full 60k. Fig.4 architectures: 2/3/4 hidden layers × {1024,2048}; hidden p=0.5, input p=0.8; final momentum 0.95; weight constraint c=2 for those experiments. Larger 2-layer nets (4096,8192) improved results (Table 2: 1.01% and 0.95% with max-norm); 3-layer larger nets slightly worse. Paper summary: Introduces dropout — randomly removing units and their connections during training, which samples many smaller networks that share weights. At test time, a single full network with scaled weights approximates the ensemble of sampled networks. Reports improvements on image, speech, text, and alternative-splicing tasks. Compares dropout with other regularizers and Bayesian neural networks. Studies learned features, sparsity, dropout rates, network size, training-set size, and test-time averaging; finds Dropout Restricted Boltzmann Machines learn qualitatively different features and sparser representations. For linear regression, marginalizing dropout yields a modified ridge-regression objective. Preliminary experiments compare Bernoulli dropout to multiplicative Gaussian noise. Limitation noted: training time typically 2–3× longer than standard networks with the same architecture.

Paper introduces dropout: during training randomly remove units and their incoming/outgoing connections (Bernoulli dropout uses binary vars that equal 1 with probability p, the retention probability). At test time the ensemble is approximated by a single deterministic model via weight scaling (multiply a unit’s outgoing weights by p) or by marginalizing dropout noise (deterministic dropout model); Monte-Carlo dropout/model averaging samples thinned networks at test time. Gaussian (multiplicative) dropout multiplies activations by Gaussian noise; paper compares Bernoulli and Gaussian variants. For linear regression, marginalized dropout is equivalent in expectation to a modified ridge (Tikhonov) regression. Dropout-RBMs are RBMs augmented with binary retention variables; CD-1/Contrastive Divergence used for RBM training; partition function Z(θ) appears in RBM formulation. Code Quality (alternative-splicing task) is the negative KL-divergence metric (higher is better). Other key methods/terms: DBN/DBM pretraining, max-norm constraint (bound hidden-unit incoming weight norms), L1/L2 weight penalties, KL-sparsity regularizer, ReLU and maxout units, pooling (max, L2, L4) in image models, max-pooling after conv layers, permutation-invariant vs 2-D MNIST settings, Top-1/Top-5 ImageNet error definitions, PCA/ZCA whitening used in preprocessing, mix-ability measure for genes. Noted limitation: training time typically 2–3× longer than standard networks with same architecture.

Key methods: dropout — Bernoulli dropout uses binary retention vars (retain with prob p); at test time approximate ensemble by weight-scaling (multiply outgoing weights by p) or by marginalizing dropout noise (deterministic model); Monte-Carlo dropout averages samples of thinned networks at test time; Gaussian (multiplicative) dropout multiplies activations by Gaussian noise. For linear regression, marginalized dropout = modified ridge (Tikhonov). Dropout-RBMs include binary retention variables; trained with CD-1. Code Quality metric = negative KL-divergence (higher is better). Regularization/architecture details: DBN/DBM pretraining; max-norm constraint (bound hidden-unit incoming weight norms); L1/L2 penalties; KL-sparsity regularizer; ReLU and maxout units; pooling: max, L2, L4; max-pooling after conv layers; permutation-invariant vs 2-D MNIST distinction. Image tasks: Top-1/Top-5 ImageNet error metrics; PCA/ZCA whitening used in preprocessing. Datasets and features: MNIST; TIMIT (preprocessed to log-filter banks via Kaldi; monophone system used for forced alignment/speech-frame labels); CIFAR-10/100; SVHN (RGB pixels normalized; comparisons list Binary Features (WDCH), HOG, KMeans); ImageNet / ILSVRC (ILSVRC-2010, ILSVRC-2012; ILSVRC discussed in Sec. 6.1.4); Reuters-RCV1; Alternative Splicing dataset (RNA features; softmax targets inc/exc/nc; mix-ability measure). Image feature labels in comparisons: SIFT, LBP, GIST, CSIFT, FVs (Fisher Vectors), Color Statistics. Implementation/tools: GPU-based CUDA libraries (cudamat, cuda-convnet); code URL http://www.cs.toronto.edu/~nitish/dropout. Other: acknowledgments OGS/NSERC/Early Researcher Award; table codes/abbrev: NN, Avg, val/test, NA (SVM unit type/architecture in Table 2), '–' = unreported, K/M = thousands/millions, dim, bits = unit for Code Quality; reported training time typically ~2–3× longer than standard networks of same architecture.

Notation and key definitions: L (# hidden layers), l (layer index); i,j (unit/dim/data indices). x = network input (y^(0)). z^(l) = inputs to layer l; y^(l) = outputs; ~y^(l) = outputs after elementwise dropout mask. W^(l), w_i^(l), b^(l) = layer weights, unit incoming weights, biases. W_test^(l)=pW^(l) (test-time weight-scaling). f activation (example sigmoid 1/(1+exp(-x))); exp used in activations/probabilities. p = retention probability. r^(l) = Bernoulli mask vector for layer l; * = elementwise multiplication. n = # units (hidden units in a layer); 2^n possible thinned networks; O(n^2) shared parameter order; pn expected retained units. w general weight vector; ||w||_2 and max-norm bound c; squared norm notation ||·||^2. k = # MC samples for prediction averaging. RBM notation: v (visible), D (# visible), h (hidden), F (# hidden), binary spaces {0,1}^D/{0,1}^F, θ={W,a,b}, Z(θ) partition, r binary retention in Dropout RBM (and r as Gaussian noise in Sect.10), Z'(θ,r) conditional normalization, g(h_j,r_j) enforces h_j=0 if r_j=0, 1(·) indicator, P(·) probability, σ = RBM activation (and in Sect.10 Gaussian noise SD). Transpose, ∏, ∑ as usual. Regression: X∈R^{N×D}, y∈R^N, w∈R^D, R∈{0,1}^{N×D} with R_ij~Bernoulli(p). E, Var. Γ=(diag(X^T X))^{1/2} used in marginalized dropout penalty; ~w = p w. Multiplicative noise: h_i, r'~N(1,σ^2) with σ^2 matched to (1-p)/p; r_b rescaled Bernoulli =1/p w.p. p; r_g Gaussian mean 1 var (1-p)/p. Also listed N(1,1), N(0,1) as example Gaussians. Paper metadata: Title Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting. Authors: Nitish Srivastava, Geoffrey Hinton, Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, Ruslan Salakhutdinov (Univ. of Toronto). Editor: Yoshua Bengio. Journal: JMLR 15 (2014) 1929–1958.
Main idea: During training randomly remove units+connections (Bernoulli retention p) sampling exponential number of thinned networks; at test time use one unthinned network with scaled weights (W_test = p W) to approximate average predictions. Dropout claimed to reduce overfitting and prevent co-adaptation.
Claims/evidence (reported): improves across domains — image results in Tables 2–6; TIMIT rows in Table 7; Reuters: 31.05% (no dropout) -> 29.62% (with dropout) in Sect. 6.3; alternative-splicing rows 440 and 567 bits in Table 8; Table 9: dropout improves over other regularizers in all rows; Dropout+Max-norm = 1.05% vs Max-norm = 1.35% and L2 = 1.62%.
Key notation/definitions (from earlier): L layers; l index; x=y^(0); z^(l)=inputs; y^(l)=outputs; ~y^(l)=after dropout mask; W^(l), w_i^(l), b^(l); W_test^(l)=pW^(l); f activation (e.g. sigmoid); p retention prob; r^(l) Bernoulli mask; n units; k MC samples for averaging; max-norm c; regression and RBM notation summarized (X,y,w,R with R_ij~Bernoulli(p); RBM θ={W,a,b}, Z partition, etc.); multiplicative-noise and rescaled Bernoulli equivalents noted; TIMIT lr schedule ε0(1+t/T)^{-1}.

Paper: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al., JMLR 2014). Main idea: during training randomly drop units (Bernoulli retain prob p) to sample many "thinned" networks; at test time use a single unthinned network with outgoing weights scaled by p (W_test = p W) to approximate averaging. Key definitions: L layers, r^(l) Bernoulli masks, ~y^(l) after dropout. A net with n units corresponds to 2^n thinned nets; they share weights so parameter count stays O(n^2). Typical choices: p≈0.5 for hidden units (often close to optimal), input-unit p usually closer to 1. Scaling outgoing weights by p at test time ensures expected training-time output equals test-time output. Motivation: approximate an equally weighted geometric mean / Bayesian-like averaging of exponentially many models with much less computation. Dropout applicable beyond feed-forward nets (Dropout RBM introduced). Paper claims dropout + weight-scaling reduces overfitting and improves generalization across domains; experiments reported in Sections 6–8 (image results Tables 2–6, TIMIT Table 7, Reuters improvement 31.05%→29.62% in Sect.6.3, alternative-splicing bits in Table 8, Table 9 comparisons: Dropout+Max-norm 1.05% vs Max-norm 1.35% vs L2 1.62%). TIMIT learning-rate schedule earlier noted: ε0 (1 + t/T)^(-1). Paper structure: Sec 2 motivation, 3 related work, 4 model, 5 training, 6 experiments, 7 hyperparams/properties, 8 Dropout RBMs, 9 marginalizing dropout, Appendix A guidance.

Paper: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al., JMLR 2014). Core idea: during training randomly drop units (Bernoulli masks r^(l), retain prob p) to sample many thinned networks; at test time use the full network with outgoing weights scaled by p (weight-scaling) to approximate averaging. Typical p≈0.5 for hidden units; input p usually closer to 1. Scaling by p makes test-time output equal to the expected training-time output (approximate model averaging). Dropout applies beyond feed-forward nets (Dropout RBMs): Figures 12–13 show qualitative feature and sparsity comparisons but no numeric performance comparison is reported there. Experiments (Secs.6–8) report improved generalization across domains (image Tables 2–6, TIMIT Table 7, Tables 2–7 and 9 cited for cross-domain error reductions). Reuters (Sec.6.3) error improved from 31.05% to 29.62%. Table 9: Dropout+Max-norm 1.05% vs Max-norm 1.35% vs L2 1.62% (alternative-splicing results also in Table 8). TIMIT uses learning rate schedule ε0(1 + t/T)^(-1). Section 2 motivation uses analogies (sexual reproduction / mix-ability; conspiracies) to argue dropout reduces complex co-adaptations, forcing units to be robust and individually useful.

Paper: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al., JMLR 2014). Core idea: during training randomly drop units via Bernoulli masks r^(l) with retain prob p, sampling many thinned networks; at test time use full network with outgoing weights scaled by p (weight-scaling) to approximate averaging. Typical p ≈ 0.5 for hidden units; input p usually closer to 1. Dropout interpretable as adding noise to hidden-unit states; relates to Denoising Autoencoders (DAEs) which typically use ~5% input noise, but with weight-scaling dropout often uses much higher noise (e.g., drop 20% of inputs, 50% of hidden units). Dropout extends beyond unsupervised learning to supervised nets and other architectures (e.g., Dropout RBMs / Boltzmann Machines; Figures 12–13 show qualitative differences). In simple cases dropout noise can be marginalized analytically (Section 9.1 gives linear-regression derivations); related work on deterministic marginalization and "blankout" noise (van der Maaten et al., Wang & Manning, Chen et al.). Different adversarial-removal formulations studied by Globerson & Roweis (2006) and Dekel et al. (2010). Experiments (Secs. 6–8) report improved generalization across domains: Reuters (Sec.6.3) error improved from 31.05% to 29.62%; Table 9 reports Dropout+Max-norm 1.05% vs Max-norm 1.35% vs L2 1.62%; TIMIT used learning-rate schedule ε0(1 + t/T)^(-1). Section 2 gives motivational analogies (sexual reproduction/mix-ability, conspiracies).

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (Srivastava et al., JMLR 2014). Core idea: during training randomly drop units with independent Bernoulli masks r^{(l)} (retain prob p), sampling many thinned sub-networks; at test time use full network with outgoing weights scaled by p (weight-scaling). Typical p ≈ 0.5 for hidden units; input p usually closer to 1. Notation: L hidden layers (1..L); z^{(l)} = inputs into layer l, y^{(l)} = outputs (y^{(0)}=x), W^{(l)}, b^{(l)}. Standard forward: z_i^{(l+1)} = w_i^{(l+1)} y^{(l)} + b_i^{(l+1)}; y_i^{(l+1)} = f(z_i^{(l+1)}) (e.g., logistic f(x)=1/(1+e^{-x})). Dropout forward: r_j^{(l)} ~ Bernoulli(p) (each mask component independent, 1 with prob p), \tilde y^{(l)} = r^{(l)} * y^{(l)} (elementwise), then z_i^{(l+1)} = w_i^{(l+1)} \tilde y^{(l)} + b_i^{(l+1)}, y_i^{(l+1)} = f(z_i^{(l+1)}). Backpropagate loss derivatives through the sampled sub-network. Test-time: use full network without dropout and scale weights: W_test^{(l)} = p W^{(l)}. Section references: Sec.9.1 gives analytic marginalization in simple linear cases; experiments (Secs.6–8) report improved generalization (e.g., Reuters 31.05% → 29.62%; Table 9: Dropout+Max-norm 1.05% vs Max-norm 1.35% vs L2 1.62%); TIMIT used learning-rate schedule ε0(1+t/T)^{-1}. Figures illustrate standard vs dropout panels (bias +1, three inputs, masks in dropout).

Paper: Dropout (Srivastava et al., JMLR 2014). Core idea: during training randomly drop units with independent Bernoulli masks r^{(l)} (retain prob p), sampling many thinned sub-networks; at test time use full network with outgoing weights scaled by p (weight-scaling W_test = p W). Typical p ≈ 0.5 for hidden units; input p usually closer to 1. Training: use SGD (mini-batches); for each case sample a thinned network; forward/backprop only on that network. Gradients averaged across mini-batch; a case not using a parameter contributes zero gradient. Use momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 weight decay. Max-norm: constrain each unit’s incoming weight vector norm ||w||_2 ≤ c; if violated, project onto ball of radius c; c chosen by validation. Combining dropout with max-norm, large decaying learning rates and high momentum yields further gains. Reported MNIST figures (Table 9): Dropout + Max-norm 1.05%; Dropout + L2 1.25%; Max-norm (no dropout) 1.35%; L2 (no dropout) 1.62%. Unsupervised pretraining: can use RBMs, autoencoders, DBMs; pretraining uses unlabeled data and can help versus random init. When finetuning with dropout, pretrained weights should be multiplied by 1/p so each unit’s expected output under dropout equals its pretraining output. Authors observed pretrained information could be lost with large finetuning rates but preserved with smaller rates. Reported pretrained MNIST (Table 2): DBN rows 1.18% versus 0.92%; DBM rows 0.96% versus 0.79% (presented as dropout finetuning improving pretrained networks). Other notes: Reuters improved (31.05% → 29.62%); TIMIT used learning-rate schedule ε0(1+t/T)^{-1}.
