grade.reason: The second reported error points out the exact planted false claim about Goodfellow et al. saying maxout 'worsened' to 0.94% while the table shows 0.94% is actually an improvement over 0.95%, matching the planted-error description.

errors.claim: "\mathbf r^{(l)};r_j^{(l)}: Layer retention vector and its Bernoulli entries." (and similarly "\mathbf r;r_j: B8T hidden-unit retention vector and its entries.")
errors.evidence: "\(\mathbf r^{(l)};r_j^{(l)}\): Layer retention vector and its Bernoulli entries." and "\(r;r'\): Gaussian multipliers in the additive and multiplicative noise forms."
errors.explanation: The notation list uses the symbol r both for Bernoulli retention variables (discrete {0,1}) and elsewhere for Gaussian multipliers (continuous). The same symbol is given incompatible meanings in the paper's notation section, creating an internal inconsistency/ambiguity.

errors.claim: "L be the number of hidden layers. l\in\{1,...,L\} index those layers."
errors.evidence: "Let:\n- L be the number of hidden layers.\n- l\in\{1,\ldots,L\} index those layers." and later "For l\in\{0,\ldots,L-1\} and hidden unit i, ordinary feed-forward computation is ..."
errors.explanation: The part first defines the layer index l to range 1..L then immediately uses l ranging 0..L-1 (with y^{(0)} = x). These two ranges are inconsistent (off-by-one in the indexing convention).

The table lists dimensionality as 65536 but then parenthetically states "256 × 256 color". 256×256 = 65536 only for a single channel; for color (usually 3 channels) 256×256 color should be 196608. The numeric dimensionality and the parenthetical description contradict each other.

errors.claim: "L8J, or maxout, worsens results (Goodfellow et al., 2013)."
errors.evidence: Text: "L8J, or maxout, worsens results (Goodfellow et al., 2013)." Table 2 rows: "QX2 NN + V9C | F3N | 2 layers, 8192 units | 0.95" and "QX2 NN + V9C (Goodfellow et al., 2013) | L8J | 2 layers, (5 × 240) units | 0.94"
errors.explanation: The text claims maxout worsens results, but Table 2 shows the maxout result (0.94%) is slightly better than the immediately preceding ReLU+V9C result (0.95%), so the textual claim contradicts the table's numeric results.

errors.claim: "Prose comparison | Pre-QX2 error | 8-layer net | 20.5%"
errors.evidence: "Prose comparison | Pre-QX2 error | 8-layer net | 20.5%" (unnumbered prose table) versus Table 7 entry: "G6W-pretrained NN (8 layers) (Mohamed et al., 2010) | 20.7"
errors.explanation: The prose-comparison table gives a pre-QX2 baseline of 20.5% for the 8-layer network, while Table 7 lists 20.7% for the G6W-pretrained 8-layer baseline. These are two different values given for the same baseline.

errors.claim: "Table 2, 1.60 versus 1.35"
errors.evidence: "H4Z regularizer comparison (Table 9, test %): ... Y5F+O3U 1.60; ... V9C 1.35." (from earlier notes)
errors.explanation: This part attributes the 1.60 vs 1.35 numbers to Table 2, but those same numbers were previously recorded as appearing in Table 9, indicating an internal table-numbering or cross-reference inconsistency.

errors.claim: "QX2 improves the reported neural-net comparisons across the tested domains."
errors.evidence: "Table 8 (C4Y bits, higher better) — NN (early stop) 440; ... NN+QX2 567; Bayesian NN 623." and earlier note: "Claim: Bayesian nets beat QX2, QX2 beats other non-Bayesian methods."
errors.explanation: The paper's blanket claim that QX2 improves neural-net comparisons conflicts with its own Table 8 and earlier text: a Bayesian neural net (623) outperforms NN+QX2 (567), so QX2 does not improve over all reported neural-net methods.

errors.evidence: Earlier notes: "Earlier best on H4Z/MNIST noted 0.79% (pretrained+QX2) from Table 4."
errors.explanation: Table 4 is referenced elsewhere as containing a 0.79% result (H4Z/MNIST), yet here Table 4 is cited with entirely different numbers (15.60/43.48 etc.), implying inconsistent use or numbering of Table 4.

errors.claim: "Figure 10" horizontal ticks show dataset sizes 10^2,10^3,10^4,10^5 (i.e. 100, 1K, 10K, 100K).
errors.evidence: "Axis | Horizontal | Dataset size | 10^2,10^3,10^4,10^5" AND "Appendix B.1’s data-size row lists 100, 500, 1K, 5K, 10K and 50K; no exact curve errors are supplied."
errors.explanation: The figure ticks imply a maximum dataset size of 100,000 and a second-smallest tick of 1,000, but the text says Appendix B.1 uses 100, 500, 1K, 5K, 10K, 50K. The figure tickset and the appendix listing are inconsistent (50K vs 100K, presence of 500 and 5K in the appendix but not in the figure ticks).

errors.claim: P(h_j=1 | r_j, v) = 1(r_j=1) sigma(b_j + sum_i W_{ij} v_i) (equation in Section 8.1)
errors.evidence: Earlier in Section 8.1 the U2L energy is given as P(h,v;theta) ∝ exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v) (so a multiplies h and b multiplies v). The paper also states the visible conditional P(v_i=1 | h) = sigma(a_i + sum_j W_{ij} h_j).
errors.explanation: These lines imply a_j are hidden biases and b_i are visible biases, so the hidden-unit conditional should use a_j (not b_j). The paper has swapped a and b between the energy definition and the conditional expressions, an internal inconsistency in parameter naming.

errors.claim: Figure 13 caption/text: 'Without QX2: many activations away from zero. (b) QX2 with p=0.5: many activations near zero and very few high activations.' (Section 8.4)
errors.evidence: Section 8 introduces B8T as the dropout extension for RBMs and says 'This comparison tests whether the feature-quality effect of feed-forward QX2 transfers to B8T.' Immediately after, Figure 13 caption uses the label 'QX2' when describing the RBM activation histograms.
errors.explanation: The section is about B8T, but the figure caption/text refers to 'QX2' rather than 'B8T', creating a naming inconsistency (unclear whether the figures show B8T vs U2L or QX2 applied elsewhere).

errors.claim: The assumptions become successively weaker as layers are added. The results therefore do not apply directly to deep networks.
errors.evidence: Section 9.2: "Under reasonable assumptions, logistic-unit input distributions and marginalized-model gradients are Gaussian, with efficiently computable means and variances. The assumptions become successively weaker as layers are added. The results therefore do not apply directly to deep networks."
errors.explanation: This is internally inconsistent: if the assumptions become weaker as layers are added, they should be easier to satisfy for deeper networks, so one would expect the results to apply more directly rather than less. The two sentences contradict each other.

errors.claim: "The stated benchmark successes include ... Table 2’s H4Z error 0.79."
errors.evidence: "Table 10: H4Z (2-layer 1024): P7V 1.08±0.04 vs D4K 0.95±0.04" (earlier notes, Section 10)
errors.explanation: The conclusion cites H4Z test error 0.79 from Table 2 as evidence of state-of-the-art, but earlier experimental results for H4Z reported in the paper (Table 10 / Section 10) are 1.08±0.04 (P7V) and 0.95±0.04 (D4K). The paper therefore reports two different H4Z numbers without reconciling them.

errors.claim: "If a task’s optimal standard-net layer has \(n\) hidden units, a good QX2 layer should have at least \(n/p\) units. Removal reduces capacity: only \(pn\) units remain in expectation."
errors.evidence: "If a task’s optimal standard-net layer has \(n\) hidden units, a good QX2 layer should have at least \(n/p\) units. Removal reduces capacity: only \(pn\) units remain in expectation."
errors.explanation: These two sentences contradict each other: if you set the QX2 layer width to n/p, the expected number of survivors is p*(n/p)=n, not pn. Alternatively, starting from n units leads to pn survivors; the text mixes the two meanings of n.

final_notes:
Appendix B / experiment settings (key datasets):
- A2F (vision): mixed validation (2/3 standard: 400/class; 1/3 additional: 200/class → 6000 val); architecture = 3 conv layers (96,128,256 filters; 5×5 RF; stride1) each with 3×3 pooling (stride2), then 2 FC hidden layers of 2048 units; activations F3N. Retention vector (input through conv+FC): (0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5). V9C max-norm c=4 for conv+FC; momentum 0.95. Validation-tuned hyperparameters; final model chosen by smallest validation error.
- J3V/W6R (image collections): same A2F architecture + held-out validation; global contrast norm + ZCA whitening; 50k train / 10k test (J3V:10 classes, W6R:100); 5k validation from train; final optimization combines val+train.
- N8Q (speech): window 21 frames; input p=0.8, hidden p=0.5; V9C c=4; momentum 0.95; high lr 0.1 with decay ε0(1+t/T)^{-1}; G6W pretraining = U2L trained with CD-1; Gaussian-U2L input var fixed to 1; best finetune lr ≈0.01; adding V9C during finetune gave no improvement; Table 7 reports phone errors (19.7 for both QX2-pretrained depths).
- M5X (documents): 402,738 articles subset, 2000-word vocab, 50 classes; >200k training examples.
- Z7P (genetics): 3,665 exons, 1,014 RNA features, 4 tissues; model output = 4 softmaxes (one per tissue), each over 3 states {inc,exc,nc}; score C4Y = Σ_{i,t,s} p_{i,t}^s log(q_t^s(r_i)/bar p^s). QX2 hidden-unit scale = "1000s"; trained QX2 = 2 layers × 1024 units; hidden p=0.5, input p=0.7; V9C + high decaying lrs; results use 5-fold averaging as Xiong et al. (2011). Table 8 (Z7P comparison): QX2 = 567 bits, early-stopped neural net = 440 bits, Bayesian neural net = 623 bits.

steps.notes_before: (none yet: this is the first part)

Dropout: randomly remove units and their connections during training, effectively training many smaller networks that share parameters. At test time, use one complete network with reduced weights to approximate averaging the smaller networks' predictions. Claimed benefits: improves generalization over networks without dropout on every tested dataset; reports state-of-the-art results on several benchmarks. Experimental domains: images, speech, documents, gene-splicing prediction. Also examines learned features, sparsity, retention rates, effects of training-set size, Restricted Boltzmann Machines, noise marginalization, and Gaussian corruption. Training cost: typically takes 2–3× longer than training a standard network of the same architecture.

Dropout (QX2): randomly remove units and their connections during training; at test time use one unthinned network with outgoing weights multiplied by the retention probability (T6R) to approximate averaging the thinned-model predictions. The paper states this approximation corresponds to the geometric mean (equally weighted combination) of thinned-network predictions. Two corruption types: Bernoulli dropout (P7V) — binary multiplicative noise (Bernoulli variable =1 with prob p, 0 otherwise) — and Gaussian dropout (D4K) — Gaussian multiplicative noise. Marginalization = expectation over dropout noise to yield a deterministic objective/regularizer; Monte‑Carlo dropout/model averaging = stochastic sampling and averaging predictions from sampled thinned networks. Dropout RBM (B8T): described as a mixture of shared-weight RBMs using different hidden-unit subsets; U2L = RBM; pretraining (DBM/E5Q, DBN/G6W) then finetuning with backprop; mcRBM-G6W is a named pretrained variant. Regularizers: L1 (O3U), L2 (Y5F, Tikhonov), max-norm (V9C), KL-sparsity. Activations mentioned: logistic units, ReLU (F3N), maxout (L8J). Other glossary items to track: geometric mean vs. posterior-weighted averaging, blankout noise, ridge-regression connection (dropout expectation → ridge-like penalty matrix), convolutional-net components (filters, pooling variants), data augmentation, SVM/PCA baselines, terms like dead unit, mix-ability, replica code, and non-stationarity. These definitions and labels will be used in later parts for numerical and conceptual consistency checks.

Marginalization = expectation over dropout noise → deterministic objective/regularizer; Monte Carlo dropout/model averaging = sample thinned nets and average predictions. steps.notes_before: Notation added: n = unit count (2^n thinned nets); shared-parameter count O(n^2). L = # hidden layers; l = layer index. x input; z^{(l)} preactivations; y^{(l)} outputs; W^{(l)}, b^{(l)} weights/biases; f activation; exp used in activations/distributions. p = retention probability; W_test^{(l)} = p W^{(l)} (test-time scaled weights); w -> p w in Fig.2. +1 denotes bias-input. pn = expected retained width; n/p = practical width heuristic. k = # sampled networks for X9M. Regression: X (N×D), y, R (input-retention matrix R_{ij} Bernoulli), \tilde w = p w, penalty coeff (1-p)/p; Gamma = (diag(X^T X))^{1/2}. RBM notation: v,h, W,a,b, Z(θ), Z'(θ, r), g(h_j,r_j). Gaussian noise: N(0,1), N(1,1), N(1,σ^2); σ variance; r_b,r_g = rescaled Bernoulli/Gaussian multipliers. NOTE: the paper reuses the symbol r for Bernoulli retention vectors and also for Gaussian multipliers (ambiguous/conflicting), so watch for which meaning is intended in each section. Other persistent items from earlier parts: Bernoulli and Gaussian dropout/corruption types; Monte Carlo model averaging vs marginalization; datasets/metrics (MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR, ImageNet, TIMIT, C4Y scores, etc.).

Paper: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" by Nitish Srivastava, Geoffrey Hinton, Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, Ruslan Salakhutdinov (Univ. of Toronto). Notation/key definitions to carry forward: n = unit count (paper often considers 2^n thinned nets); expected retained width pn; practical width heuristic n/p; shared-parameter count O(n^2). Abstract summary: method called "QX2, or dropout"; it randomly removes units and their connections during training, inhibiting co-adaptation, sampling exponentially many thinned networks that share parameters. A single unthinned network with reduced weights approximates the averaged predictions of the thinned nets. Claims substantial reduction in overfitting and major improvements; supervised experiments in vision, speech recognition, document classification and computational biology reportedly attain state-of-the-art on many benchmarks. Evidence claimed in Tables 2–8 and an unnumbered text-classification table in §6.3; domain-specific comparisons listed in §6.

Paper: "Dropout (QX2)". Core idea: randomly remove units during training to train many shared-parameter thinned subnetworks (2^n possible thinned nets for n units) and approximate their combined predictions with one unthinned test-time network. Key terminology: QX2 = dropout; T6R = test-time weight scaling (use one unthinned net with scaled weights); X9M = Monte-Carlo model averaging (average sampled thinned nets at test); U2L/B8T = dropout extension to RBMs. Notation (carry-forward): n = unit count; expected retained width = p n; practical width heuristic = n/p; shared-parameter count O(n^2); L hidden layers with W^(l), b^(l), activations f; p = retention probability; test-time weights scaled by p (W_test = p W). Claims in this part: QX2 approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many models; a new thinned member is sampled and trained (rarely) per presentation of each training case; T6R is a cheap practical inference rule that gives significantly lower generalization error than other regularizers across varied problems; X9M is more expensive and needs around k≈50 samples (per §7.5 and App B.1) before matching T6R. Evidence pointer: Table 9 referenced for comparisons (rows quoted: Y5F=1.62, V9C=1.35, QX2+Y5F=1.25, QX2+V9C=1.05). Paper outline: §2 motivation, §3 prior work, §4 model, §5 training algorithm, §6 experiments, §7 effects and hyperparameter interactions, §8 RBM extension, §9 marginalization, Appendix A (practical guidance).

Paper: "Dropout (QX2)". Core idea: randomly remove units during training to train many shared-parameter thinned subnetworks (2^n possible thinned nets for n units) and approximate their combined predictions with one unthinned test-time network. Notation: n = unit count; p = retention probability; expected retained width = p n; practical width heuristic = n/p; shared-parameter count O(n^2); L hidden layers with W^(l), b^(l), activations f; test-time weights scaled by p (W_test = p W). Claims: QX2 approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many models; a new thinned member is sampled and trained (rarely unique) on each presentation of a training case; T6R (test-time weight scaling) is a cheap practical inference rule that gives significantly lower generalization error than other regularizers across varied problems; X9M (Monte-Carlo averaging) is more expensive and needs around k ≈ 50 samples (per §7.5 and App B.1) to match T6R. Evidence pointer: Table 9 comparisons (rows: Y5F=1.62, V9C=1.35, QX2+Y5F=1.25, QX2+V9C=1.05). New in §2: motivation via sexual-reproduction and conspiracy analogies — Livnat et al. (2010) "mix-ability" notion: selection favors genes that work well with random partners (robust, independently useful components). Analogy: QX2 forces hidden units to operate with randomly selected partners, discouraging complex co-adaptations and favoring robust features; replicating units is a poor remedy. Smaller cooperating subsets are argued to be more robust under non-stationarity than large co-adaptations. Outline pointers: §3 prior work, §4 model, §5 training algorithm, §6 experiments, §7 hyperparams, §8 RBM extension, §9 marginalization, Appendix A guidance.

Paper: "Dropout (QX2)". Core idea: randomly remove units during training to train many shared-parameter thinned subnetworks (2^n possible thinned nets for n units) and approximate their combined predictions with one unthinned test-time network. Notation/impl: n = unit count; p = retention probability; expected retained width = p n; practical width heuristic = n/p; shared-parameter count O(n^2); L hidden layers with weights W^(l), biases b^(l), activations f; test-time weights scaled by p (W_test = p W). Key claims: QX2 approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many models; a new thinned member is sampled and trained on each presentation; T6R (test-time weight scaling) is a cheap practical inference rule that often gives much lower generalization error than other regularizers; X9M (Monte-Carlo averaging) is more expensive and reportedly needs k ≈ 50 samples to match T6R (per §7.5 and App B.1). Empirical pointer: Table 9 example rows (Y5F=1.62, V9C=1.35, QX2+Y5F=1.25, QX2+V9C=1.05). Section 3 notes: DAEs (denoising autoencoders) corrupt inputs and reconstruct; QX2 extends corruption to hidden units and gives a model-averaging view; applies to supervised/unsupervised and other neuron-based architectures including Boltzmann Machines. T6R permits much higher noise than typical DAEs: table lists S2H/DAE typical best 5%, QX2 input-unit removal often optimal 20%, QX2 hidden-unit removal often optimal 50%. Related methods: Globerson & Roweis (2006) and Dekel et al. (2010) use adversarial removals (fixed max number) and have no hidden units. Marginalizing QX2 yields deterministic regularizers in simple cases; van der Maaten et al. (2013) call QX2 input noise "blankout noise" but limited to models without hidden layers; Chen et al. (2012) on marginalization for DAEs; Wang & Manning (2013) propose marginalization to accelerate QX2.

steps.notes_before: Paper: Dropout (QX2) — gate unit outputs during training, independently per unit with r_j^{(l)} ~ Bernoulli(p); tilde y^{(l)} = r^{(l)} * y^{(l)}. At inference no units removed; test-time weights scaled by retention p: W_test^{(l)} = p W^{(l)}. Expected preactivation under training dropout equals test preactivation with scaled weights. Both hidden and input (visible) units can be dropped. Validation can pick p; default often near optimal; input retention generally near complete retention. Forward equations: y^{(0)} = x; nominally z_i^{(l+1)} = w_i^{(l+1)} y^{(l)} + b_i^{(l+1)}, y_i^{(l+1)} = f(z_i^{(l+1)}). Example activation: logistic f(x)=1/(1+exp(-x)). Note: this part contains an indexing inconsistency — it first states l∈{1..L} then uses l∈{0..L-1} for the feed-forward formulas (treating y^{(0)} as input). Keep this in mind when later parts refer to layer indices.

Paper: QX2 = dropout (per-unit gate r_j^(l) ~ Bernoulli(p); ̃y^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l)). At test time do not drop units; scale weights by retention p (W_test = p W) so expected preactivation under dropout equals test preactivation. Both hidden and input units can be dropped (input retention usually near 1). Forward eqns use y^(0)=x; paper has an indexing inconsistency (uses l∈{1..L} then l∈{0..L-1}).

Sec.5 (Learning QX2 Nets): training = backprop through sampled subnetworks (one mask per case/minibatch case), gradients averaged across cases; a dropped parameter gets zero contribution. QX2 alone gives significant gains; combining QX2 with high momentum, large decaying learning rates and V9C (max-norm) gives further boost. V9C constrains each hidden unit's incoming weight vector via projection to ||w||_2 <= c (validation tunes c); projection returns w to the radius-c surface if exceeded. Proposed optimization story: fixed-radius weight ball allows huge LRs without explosion; QX2 noise explores; annealing settles.

Empirical notes cited: Table 9 rows: V9C=1.35, QX2+Y5F=1.25, QX2+V9C=1.05. Appendix A.2: practical LRs typically 10–100x optimal standard-net LR and momentum ~0.95–0.99. Pretraining: unchanged, but before QX2 finetuning multiply pretrained weights by 1/p so expected outputs under dropout match pretraining; use much smaller finetuning LR (Appendix B.4 reports ~0.01 best vs listed high LR 0.1). Table 2: G6W finetuning 1.18 -> 0.92 with QX2; E5Q 0.96 -> 0.79.

Paper: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (JMLR 15, 2014). Authors: Nitish Srivastava, Geoffrey Hinton, Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, Ruslan Salakhutdinov. Abstract/main claim: Dropout randomly drops units and their connections during training to prevent co-adaptation; training effectively samples from an exponential number of "thinned" networks. At test time, the effect of averaging these thinned networks is approximated by using a single unthinned network with scaled (smaller) weights. Dropout reportedly reduces overfitting and outperforms other regularization methods, producing major improvements and state-of-the-art results on benchmarks in vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology. Intro notes: deep nets are expressive and prone to overfitting; common regularizers include early stopping, L1/L2 penalties, and soft weight sharing. The paper states that with unlimited computation the best regularizer is averaging predictions over all parameter settings (sentence is cut off in this part). New from current part: Motivation analogies — sexual reproduction: dropout viewed as preventing large co-adaptations, forcing each hidden unit to learn useful features that work with random subsets of partners, improving robustness; copying units to resist dropout is a poor solution (analogy to replica codes for noisy channels). Conspiracy analogy: many small conspiracies (small co-adaptations) more robust than one large co-adaptation, hence better generalization under non-stationarity. Related work: Dropout can be seen as regularization via adding noise to hidden units; this idea relates to Denoising Autoencoders (Vincent et al. 2008, 2010) which add noise to unit states.

steps.notes_before: Paper: Dropout trains by randomly dropping units (thinning) and sharing weights across exponentially many sub-networks. Training samples a new thinned net each presentation; backpropagate gradients through that thinned net. At test time use a single unthinned net with weights scaled by retention probabilities (W_test = p W^(l) per layer). Typical choices: drop ~50% hidden units (p_hidden ≈ 0.5), ~20% inputs (p_input ≈ 0.8); DAEs typically use 5% input noise but test-time scaling allows higher noise. Dropout can be applied to hidden layers and other neuron-based architectures (e.g., Boltzmann Machines, RBMs). Interpretation: stochastic regularization / model averaging; related to denoising autoencoders and marginalizing noise. Definition details: network with L hidden layers; y(0)=x; feed-forward recurrence given as z^{(l+1)} = W^{(l+1)} y^{(l)} + b^{(l+1)}, y^{(l+1)} = f(z^{(l+1)}). With dropout: sample r^{(l)} ~ Bernoulli(p) elementwise, form y_e^{(l)} = r^{(l)} * y^{(l)} and use y_e^{(l)} as input to next layer. Loss is minimized stochastically (expected loss); prior adversarial-drop work fixes max number dropped (no hidden-layer models).

Training: dropout nets trained by SGD on ‘‘thinned’’ nets — for each training case in a mini‑batch sample dropout mask, do forward/backprop on that thinned net; gradients averaged over mini‑batch; any case that omits a parameter contributes zero gradient for that parameter. Standard SGD tricks (momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 weight decay) help. Max‑norm regularization: constrain incoming weight vector w at each hidden unit to ||w||2 ≤ c by projecting back into the ball of radius c whenever it exceeds c (c is a tunable hyperparameter). Max‑norm often improves SGD even without dropout; combining dropout + max‑norm + large decaying LR + high momentum gives further gains (intuition: ball constraint prevents blowup so large LR can be used for exploration). Unsupervised pretraining: stacks of RBMs/autoencoders/DBMs can be used; pretraining stays the same, but when finetuning with dropout scale pretrained weights by 1/p so expected output under dropout matches pretraining output. If finetune LR is too large pretrained information can be lost; use smaller LR to retain gains. Title: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting". Authors: Nitish Srivastava, Geoffrey Hinton, Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, Ruslan Salakhutdinov; Dept. of Computer Science, University of Toronto. Journal: JMLR 15 (2014). Header lists pages 1929–1958 while page map lists pages 1930–1955 (internal inconsistency noted). Abstract summary: introduces dropout (called "QX2: dropout") — a training procedure that temporarily removes randomly selected units and their connections, inhibiting excessive co-adaptation and effectively sampling exponentially many parameter-sharing thinned networks. At test time a single unthinned network with reduced weights approximates the averaged predictions of these thinned networks. Claims dropout substantially reduces overfitting versus other regularizers and yields major improvements, achieving state-of-the-art performance on many benchmarks in supervised vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology.

steps.notes_before: Title: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al., UToronto). Header/page-number inconsistency noted earlier. Dropout (QX2) randomly removes units/connections during training, producing exponentially many (2^n for n units) thinned networks; parameters are shared so total distinct parameters retained are O(n^2) or fewer. With unlimited computation, posterior-weighted averaging over parameters is ideal; the paper claims its method approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of these thinned models' predictions (introduction) — earlier abstract wording said it "approximates the averaged predictions", a potential arithmetic vs geometric-mean wording mismatch. Every presentation samples/trains a new thinned member; individual members are rarely trained thoroughly. Practical inference: T6R (weight scaling) uses one unthinned network at test time; X9M refers to Monte-Carlo model averaging (more expensive). Claims T6R gives much lower generalization error than other regularizers across tasks. Method extends to graphical models, e.g., Dropout RBM (B8T) from RBMs (U2L). Paper map: §2 motivation; §3 prior work; §4 formal model; §5 training algorithm; §6 experiments; §7 network/hyperparameter interactions; §8 Dropout RBMs; §9 marginalization; Appendix A practical guidance.

Title: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al.). Earlier: header/page-number inconsistency noted. Method overview: dropout (QX2) randomly removes units/connections during training, producing exponentially many (2^n) thinned networks; parameters are shared so total distinct parameters are O(n^2) or fewer. Training samples/train different thinned networks; individual thinned members rarely trained thoroughly. Test-time inference: T6R = weight-scaling using one unthinned network; X9M = Monte-Carlo model averaging (more expensive). Paper claims T6R yields much lower generalization error than other regularizers across tasks. Extensions: Dropout RBM (B8T). Paper map: §2 motivation; §3 prior work; §4 formal model; §5 training algorithm; §6 experiments; §7 interactions; §8 Dropout RBMs; §9 marginalization; Appendix A guidance. New from §2 (Motivation): authors use biological analogy—sexual vs asexual reproduction—and cite Livnat et al. (2010) arguing selection can favor gene "mix-ability" rather than individual-fitness optimization. Dropout is analogous: hidden units face randomly selected partners, which favors independently useful, robust features and reduces complex co-adaptations. Replicating units many times is deemed a poor robustness fix (analogy to replica codes and noisy channels). Conspiracy analogy: many small cooperating subsets are more robust under non-stationarity than a single large co-adapted set; complex co-adaptations may overfit training data and fail on novel test data.

Title: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al.). Method: dropout (QX2) randomly removes units/connections during training producing ~2^n thinned networks; parameters shared so distinct params O(n^2). Training: each SGD update samples a thinned network; individual thinned members rarely trained thoroughly. Test-time inference: T6R = weight-scaling using one unthinned network; X9M = Monte-Carlo model averaging (more expensive). Paper claims T6R gives much lower generalization error than other regularizers across tasks. Motivation (§2): biological analogy (mix-ability), reduces co-adaptations. Related work (§3): dropout interpretable as noise in hidden-unit states, extends denoising autoencoders (Vincent et al. 2008/2010) — effective hidden-layer corruption, model-averaging view, supervised/unsupervised use, applicable to Boltzmann Machines. Table: S2H (DAE) typical best noise ~5%; QX2 often optimal input-unit removal ~20%; QX2 often optimal hidden-unit removal ~50%. Adversarial-removal alternatives (Globerson & Roweis 2006; Dekel et al. 2010) consider worst-case removals under a budget and have no hidden units. Analytic marginalization can give deterministic regularizers in simple cases; van der Maaten et al. (2013) studied exponential-family input-noise (blankout) limited to models without hidden layers; Chen et al. (2012) studied marginalization for DAEs; Wang & Manning (2013) proposed marginalization to speed up dropout. Section map: §2 motivation; §3 prior work; §4 formal model; §5 training algorithm; §6 experiments; §7 interactions; §8 Dropout RBMs; §9 marginalization; Appendix A guidance.

Paper: Dropout regularization. Key idea: during training randomly delete (zero) units (hidden and/or visible) to sample many thinned subnetworks; parameters shared across subnetworks. Retention choices are independent Bernoulli variables with common probability p (can be chosen by validation). Typical defaults: hidden-unit retention p≈0.5 (i.e. ~50% removal); input-unit removal often ~20% (retention p≈0.8) — input retention usually nearer full. Training: each SGD update samples r^{(l)} (vector of independent Bernoulli(p)) and forms \tilde y^{(l)} = r^{(l)} * y^{(l)}; forward: z_i^{(l+1)} = w_i^{(l+1)} \tilde y^{(l)} + b_i^{(l+1)}, y_i^{(l+1)} = f(z_i^{(l+1)}). Backprop passes gradients through the sampled subnetwork. Notation: y^{(0)}=x; L hidden layers (indexed 1..L); feed-forward written for l=0..L-1 producing layer l+1. Activation f can be any (e.g. logistic). Test-time inference: no dropout; use one unthinned network with outgoing weights scaled by p: W_test^{(l)} = p W^{(l)} (equivalently unit outputs' expected training contribution equals test-time contribution with scaled weights). Figures illustrate training (stochastic gates r) vs testing (weights scaled by p). Other parts: training samples many subnetworks per SGD update; Monte-Carlo averaging at test-time is an alternative to weight-scaling but more expensive.

Part 5: QX2 (dropout) gives significant gains; combining it with high momentum, large decaying learning rates, and an incoming-weight constraint (V9C = max-norm) gives further improvement. V9C enforces ||w||_2 <= c with projection to the ball surface when exceeded; c is tuned by validation. Proposed optimization account claims large learning rates are safe inside the fixed-radius ball; QX2 provides noise exploration; learning rates decay to smaller steps. SGD differs from standard training only by per-case sampled thinned networks: each mini-batch case uses its own sampled network; gradients averaged across cases; a case not using a parameter contributes zero. Momentum, annealed (decaying) learning rates and other heuristics remain useful. Unsupervised pretraining is unchanged, but before QX2 finetuning pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p so each unit’s expected random-removal output matches its pretraining output. Smaller finetuning learning rates help preserve pretrained information. Pretraining (with unlabeled data) can improve over random init; applicable to stacked U2L, autoencoders, DBMs for finetuning.

Interpretation: an input-dimension-scaled ridge penalty; regularization strength (1-p)/p grows as p decreases. Logistic regression / deep nets: approximate marginalization can beat Monte-Carlo QX2 (Wang & Manning 2013); closed-form marginalization is hard but under assumptions inputs/gradients are approximately Gaussian with computable moments — these assumptions become less likely to hold as depth increases, so the Gaussian-approximation marginalization is not directly applicable to deep networks.

Marginalization (Part 9): linear regression identity E_R[||y-(R*X)w||^2]=||y-pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Γw||^2 with Γ=(diag(X^T X))^{1/2}; with 
̃w=pw gives ||y-X
̃w||^2 + ((1-p)/p)||Γ
̃w||^2 — i.e., input-dimension-scaled ridge, regularization ∝(1-p)/p.
Part 10 (this part): Multiplicative Gaussian noise (D4K) vs Bernoulli dropout (P7V): preliminary results — H4Z: P7V 1.08±0.04, D4K 0.95±0.04; J3V: P7V 12.6±0.1, D4K 12.5±0.1. Retention settings: H4Z hidden p=0.5, H4Z input p=0.8; J3V retention per layer p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5). D4K sets Gaussian std per layer σ = sqrt((1-p)/p) so r_g ~ N(1, (1-p)/p) matches scaled Bernoulli r_b (1/p w.p. p, else 0) which has E=1, Var=(1-p)/p. Gaussian multiplier has higher entropy; preliminary evidence slightly favors it. Equivalences noted: multiplying activations by r'~N(1,σ^2) ⇔ additive noise h_i→h_i+h_i r with r~N(0,σ^2); preserving expected activations removes test-time scaling.

Key empirical results: TIMIT/core: NN (6l)=23.4; QX2 NN (6l)=21.8. G6W-pre: (4l)=22.7, (6l)=22.4, (8l)=20.7; mcRBM-G6W-pre (5l)=20.5; best combos (G6W-pre+QX2) ≈ 19.7. M5X doc-class: baseline 31.05% → QX2 29.62%. Z7P (higher better): NN=440; Regression+PCA=463; SVM+PCA=487; NN+QX2=567; Bayesian NN=623 (paper earlier mis-stated Bayesian<QX2). H4Z regularizers: Y5F=1.62; Y5F+O3U=1.60; Y5F+KL=1.55; V9C=1.35; QX2+Y5F=1.25; QX2+V9C=1.05. QX2 yields localized edge/stroke features and a strong zero peak in activations; best retention p ≈ 0.6. Dataset-size effects: no QX2 gain at smallest sizes; X9M vs T6R cross-over k ≈ 50. B8T (dropout variant): per-case sampled retention vector r; P(h_j=1 | r_j, v)=1(r_j=1) σ(...); produces coarser features, fewer dead units, sparser representations without extra sparsity regularizer. Marginalization (linear regression): E_R[||y-(R X)w||^2] = ||y-pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Γw||^2, equivalently ||y - X ṽw||^2 + ((1-p)/p)||Γ ṽw||^2 — an input-dimension-scaled ridge, regularization ∝ (1-p)/p. D4K (multiplicative Gaussian) vs P7V (Bernoulli dropout) preliminary: H4Z P7V 1.08±0.04 vs D4K 0.95±0.04; J3V P7V 12.6±0.1 vs D4K 12.5±0.1. D4K sets σ = sqrt((1-p)/p) so r_g ~ N(1,(1-p)/p), matching scaled Bernoulli mean/var; Gaussian has higher entropy and is slightly favored in preliminaries. Conclusion: the large-model construction repeatedly samples/trains smaller submodels; U2L fits this construction and B8T shows desirable empirical properties. QX2 methods claim SOTA on A2F, K9D, W6R and H4Z and substantial gains over standard nets elsewhere. Training typically takes 2–3× as long as a standard net of the same architecture; noisy per-case parameter updates (different random subarchitecture each case, gradients not gradients of final inference architecture) are a major cause. Stochasticity likely reduces overfitting, yielding an overfitting–training-time trade-off (more training time permits stronger QX2 with less overfitting). Noise marginalization offers some benefits via an expectation-equivalent regularizer (linear regression → modified Y5F); equivalent regularizers for complex models are not obvious. Accelerating QX2 is future work.

Paper summary: Introduces dropout — randomly removing units and their connections during training, which samples many smaller networks that share weights. At test time, a single full network with scaled weights approximates the ensemble of sampled networks. Reports improvements on image, speech, text, and alternative-splicing tasks. Compares dropout with other regularizers and Bayesian neural networks. Studies learned features, sparsity, dropout rates, network size, training-set size, and test-time averaging; finds Dropout Restricted Boltzmann Machines learn qualitatively different features and sparser representations. For linear regression, marginalizing dropout yields a modified ridge-regression objective. Preliminary experiments compare Bernoulli dropout to multiplicative Gaussian noise. Limitation noted: training time typically 2–3× longer than standard networks with the same architecture.

Paper introduces dropout: during training randomly remove units and their incoming/outgoing connections (Bernoulli dropout uses binary vars that equal 1 with probability p, the retention probability). At test time the ensemble is approximated by a single deterministic model via weight scaling (multiply a unit’s outgoing weights by p) or by marginalizing dropout noise (deterministic dropout model); Monte-Carlo dropout/model averaging samples thinned networks at test time. Gaussian (multiplicative) dropout multiplies activations by Gaussian noise; paper compares Bernoulli and Gaussian variants. For linear regression, marginalized dropout is equivalent in expectation to a modified ridge (Tikhonov) regression. Dropout-RBMs are RBMs augmented with binary retention variables; CD-1/Contrastive Divergence used for RBM training; partition function Z(θ) appears in RBM formulation. Code Quality (alternative-splicing task) is the negative KL-divergence metric (higher is better). Other key methods/terms: DBN/DBM pretraining, max-norm constraint (bound hidden-unit incoming weight norms), L1/L2 weight penalties, KL-sparsity regularizer, ReLU and maxout units, pooling (max, L2, L4) in image models, max-pooling after conv layers, permutation-invariant vs 2-D MNIST settings, Top-1/Top-5 ImageNet error definitions, PCA/ZCA whitening used in preprocessing, mix-ability measure for genes. Noted limitation: training time typically 2–3× longer than standard networks with same architecture.

Paper: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al., JMLR 2014). Main idea: during training randomly drop units (Bernoulli retain prob p) to sample many "thinned" networks; at test time use a single unthinned network with outgoing weights scaled by p (W_test = p W) to approximate averaging. Key definitions: L layers, r^(l) Bernoulli masks, ~y^(l) after dropout. A net with n units corresponds to 2^n thinned nets; they share weights so parameter count stays O(n^2). Typical choices: p≈0.5 for hidden units (often close to optimal), input-unit p usually closer to 1. Scaling outgoing weights by p at test time ensures expected training-time output equals test-time output. Motivation: approximate an equally weighted geometric mean / Bayesian-like averaging of exponentially many models with much less computation. Dropout applicable beyond feed-forward nets (Dropout RBM introduced). Paper claims dropout + weight-scaling reduces overfitting and improves generalization across domains; experiments reported in Sections 6–8 (image results Tables 2–6, TIMIT Table 7, Reuters improvement 31.05%→29.62% in Sect.6.3, alternative-splicing bits in Table 8, Table 9 comparisons: Dropout+Max-norm 1.05% vs Max-norm 1.35% vs L2 1.62%). TIMIT learning-rate schedule earlier noted: ε0 (1 + t/T)^(-1). Paper structure: Sec 2 motivation, 3 related work, 4 model, 5 training, 6 experiments, 7 hyperparams/properties, 8 Dropout RBMs, 9 marginalizing dropout, Appendix A guidance.

Paper: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al., JMLR 2014). Core idea: during training randomly drop units (Bernoulli masks r^(l), retain prob p) to sample many thinned networks; at test time use the full network with outgoing weights scaled by p (weight-scaling) to approximate averaging. Typical p≈0.5 for hidden units; input p usually closer to 1. Scaling by p makes test-time output equal to the expected training-time output (approximate model averaging). Dropout applies beyond feed-forward nets (Dropout RBMs): Figures 12–13 show qualitative feature and sparsity comparisons but no numeric performance comparison is reported there. Experiments (Secs.6–8) report improved generalization across domains (image Tables 2–6, TIMIT Table 7, Tables 2–7 and 9 cited for cross-domain error reductions). Reuters (Sec.6.3) error improved from 31.05% to 29.62%. Table 9: Dropout+Max-norm 1.05% vs Max-norm 1.35% vs L2 1.62% (alternative-splicing results also in Table 8). TIMIT uses learning rate schedule ε0(1 + t/T)^(-1). Section 2 motivation uses analogies (sexual reproduction / mix-ability; conspiracies) to argue dropout reduces complex co-adaptations, forcing units to be robust and individually useful.

Paper: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al., JMLR 2014). Core idea: during training randomly drop units via Bernoulli masks r^(l) with retain prob p, sampling many thinned networks; at test time use full network with outgoing weights scaled by p (weight-scaling) to approximate averaging. Typical p ≈ 0.5 for hidden units; input p usually closer to 1. Dropout interpretable as adding noise to hidden-unit states; relates to Denoising Autoencoders (DAEs) which typically use ~5% input noise, but with weight-scaling dropout often uses much higher noise (e.g., drop 20% of inputs, 50% of hidden units). Dropout extends beyond unsupervised learning to supervised nets and other architectures (e.g., Dropout RBMs / Boltzmann Machines; Figures 12–13 show qualitative differences). In simple cases dropout noise can be marginalized analytically (Section 9.1 gives linear-regression derivations); related work on deterministic marginalization and "blankout" noise (van der Maaten et al., Wang & Manning, Chen et al.). Different adversarial-removal formulations studied by Globerson & Roweis (2006) and Dekel et al. (2010). Experiments (Secs. 6–8) report improved generalization across domains: Reuters (Sec.6.3) error improved from 31.05% to 29.62%; Table 9 reports Dropout+Max-norm 1.05% vs Max-norm 1.35% vs L2 1.62%; TIMIT used learning-rate schedule ε0(1 + t/T)^(-1). Section 2 gives motivational analogies (sexual reproduction/mix-ability, conspiracies).

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (Srivastava et al., JMLR 2014). Core idea: during training randomly drop units with independent Bernoulli masks r^{(l)} (retain prob p), sampling many thinned sub-networks; at test time use full network with outgoing weights scaled by p (weight-scaling). Typical p ≈ 0.5 for hidden units; input p usually closer to 1. Notation: L hidden layers (1..L); z^{(l)} = inputs into layer l, y^{(l)} = outputs (y^{(0)}=x), W^{(l)}, b^{(l)}. Standard forward: z_i^{(l+1)} = w_i^{(l+1)} y^{(l)} + b_i^{(l+1)}; y_i^{(l+1)} = f(z_i^{(l+1)}) (e.g., logistic f(x)=1/(1+e^{-x})). Dropout forward: r_j^{(l)} ~ Bernoulli(p) (each mask component independent, 1 with prob p), \tilde y^{(l)} = r^{(l)} * y^{(l)} (elementwise), then z_i^{(l+1)} = w_i^{(l+1)} \tilde y^{(l)} + b_i^{(l+1)}, y_i^{(l+1)} = f(z_i^{(l+1)}). Backpropagate loss derivatives through the sampled sub-network. Test-time: use full network without dropout and scale weights: W_test^{(l)} = p W^{(l)}. Section references: Sec.9.1 gives analytic marginalization in simple linear cases; experiments (Secs.6–8) report improved generalization (e.g., Reuters 31.05% → 29.62%; Table 9: Dropout+Max-norm 1.05% vs Max-norm 1.35% vs L2 1.62%); TIMIT used learning-rate schedule ε0(1+t/T)^{-1}. Figures illustrate standard vs dropout panels (bias +1, three inputs, masks in dropout).

Paper: Dropout (Srivastava et al., JMLR 2014). Core idea: during training randomly drop units with independent Bernoulli masks r^{(l)} (retain prob p), sampling many thinned sub-networks; at test time use full network with outgoing weights scaled by p (weight-scaling W_test = p W). Typical p ≈ 0.5 for hidden units; input p usually closer to 1. Training: use SGD (mini-batches); for each case sample a thinned network; forward/backprop only on that network. Gradients averaged across mini-batch; a case not using a parameter contributes zero gradient. Use momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 weight decay. Max-norm: constrain each unit’s incoming weight vector norm ||w||_2 ≤ c; if violated, project onto ball of radius c; c chosen by validation. Combining dropout with max-norm, large decaying learning rates and high momentum yields further gains. Reported MNIST figures (Table 9): Dropout + Max-norm 1.05%; Dropout + L2 1.25%; Max-norm (no dropout) 1.35%; L2 (no dropout) 1.62%. Unsupervised pretraining: can use RBMs, autoencoders, DBMs; pretraining uses unlabeled data and can help versus random init. When finetuning with dropout, pretrained weights should be multiplied by 1/p so each unit’s expected output under dropout equals its pretraining output. Authors observed pretrained information could be lost with large finetuning rates but preserved with smaller rates. Reported pretrained MNIST (Table 2): DBN rows 1.18% versus 0.92%; DBM rows 0.96% versus 0.79% (presented as dropout finetuning improving pretrained networks). Other notes: Reuters improved (31.05% → 29.62%); TIMIT used learning-rate schedule ε0(1+t/T)^{-1}.

errors.claim: The RBM joint distribution is defined as P(h,v;θ) = (1/Z(θ)) exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v), so a is the hidden-bias vector and b the visible-bias vector.
errors.evidence: Definition: "P(h,v;\theta) = \frac{1}{Z(\theta)} \exp\!\left(v^\top Wh+a^\top h+b^\top v\right)."  Later: "P(h_j=1\mid r_j,v) = \mathbf1(r_j=1) \sigma\!\left(b_j+\sum_i W_{ij}v_i\right)."  And: "P(v_i=1\mid h) = \sigma\!\left(a_i+\sum_j W_{ij}h_j\right)."
errors.explanation: The joint definition uses a^T h (a = hidden biases) and b^T v (b = visible biases), but the conditional formulas treat b_j as the hidden bias in P(h_j=1|...) and a_i as the visible bias in P(v_i=1|...), i.e. the roles of a and b are swapped, an internal naming inconsistency.

Appendix A (practical heuristics): A.1 sizing: because expected retained units = p n, if n units are optimal for a standard net use at least n/p units with dropout. A.2 optimization: dropout adds gradient noise; recommend learning rates 10–100× the standard-network optimum and momentum ~0.95–0.99 (vs common 0.9); high LR/momentum speed learning. A.3 max-norm: bound incoming weight vector norm by c to control growth; typical c in [3,4]. A.4 dropout rates: hidden p typically 0.5–0.8; input p ≈0.8 for images/speech; choose p together with n (smaller p ⇒ need larger n, slower training, risk underfitting if not compensated). Earlier results to keep for consistency checks: Section 7 autoencoder (784-256-784 ReLU) with dropout p=0.5 produced localized detectors; no-dropout showed co-adaptation; reconstruction errors similar; activations sparser with dropout (means ≈2.0 no-dropout vs ≈0.7 dropout); best p roughly 0.4–0.8; Monte Carlo ~50 samples approximates test-time weight scaling. Section 10 Gaussian multiplicative dropout: match moments with σ^2=(1-p)/p; Gaussian has E[r']=1 so no test-time scaling; Gaussian slightly outperformed Bernoulli on MNIST (Bernoulli 1.08±0.04% vs Gaussian 0.95±0.04%, p_hidden=0.5,p_input=0.8) and similar on CIFAR-10 (12.6±0.1% vs 12.5±0.1%). Section 11 conclusion: dropout reduces overfitting, applies broadly (including RBMs), but training typically takes ~2–3× longer due to noisy updates.

Appendix A heuristics: expected retained units = p n ⇒ use ~n/p units with dropout; LR should be 10–100× standard, momentum ≈0.95–0.99; use max-norm constraint c (typical [3,4]); hidden p typically 0.5–0.8, input p ≈0.8 for images/speech. Gaussian multiplicative dropout matching: σ^2=(1-p)/p; Gaussian needs no test-time scaling and slightly outperformed Bernoulli on MNIST/CIFAR-10. Training with dropout is noisier and typically takes ~2–3× longer.

B.1 MNIST: 60k train, 10k test; held out 10k train as validation. Hyperparameters chosen so best validation error occurs after 1M weight updates; then training+validation combined and trained 1M updates before test. Validation-tuned hyperparams; reported model = smallest validation error. J3V/W6R: 50k train / 10k test; J3V: 10 classes; W6R: 100 classes; validation uses 5k training images; preprocessing = per-channel global contrast normalization then ZCA whitening; arch and retention match A2F; input-layer LRs smaller. N8Q (speech): 680 speakers ×10 sentences; Kaldi log-filterbank features; forced-align; 21-frame window. Table settings: input p=0.8, hidden p=0.5, V9C all layers c=4, momentum 0.95, high LR=0.1, LR decay ε0(1+t/T)^{-1}. G6W pretraining: U2L with CD-1; Gaussian-U2L input variance fixed to 1. Best finetuning LR ≈0.01; adding V9C during G6W finetuning gave no improvement. M5X (Reuters subset): 402,738 articles, 2,000-word vocab, 50 classes; equal train/test splits (~201k each). Z7P (genetics): 3,665 cassette exons, 1,014 RNA features, 4 tissues. Outputs: 4 softmax distributions (per tissue) over 3 states {inc, exc, nc}. Score C4Y = Σ_i Σ_t Σ_s p_{i,t}^s log(q_t^s(r_i)/ȳ^s) with baseline ȳ^s averaged over i,t. QX2: scale = “1000s”, trained = 2 layers × 1024 units; retention input p=0.7, hidden p=0.5; V9C + decaying high LR; 5-fold averaging as in Xiong et al. Final reported Z7P (Table 8): QX2 = 567 bits, early-stopped NN = 440, Bayesian NN = 623.

Dropout: randomly remove units and their connections during training, effectively training many smaller networks that share parameters. At test time, use one complete network with reduced weights to approximate averaging the smaller networks' predictions. Claimed benefits: improves generalization over networks without dropout on every tested dataset; reports state-of-the-art results on several benchmarks. Experimental domains: images, speech, documents, gene-splicing prediction. Also examines learned features, sparsity, retention rates, effects of training-set size, Restricted Boltzmann Machines, noise marginalization, and Gaussian corruption. Training cost: typically takes 2–3× longer than training a standard network of the same architecture.

Dropout (QX2): randomly remove units and their connections during training; at test time use one unthinned network with outgoing weights multiplied by the retention probability (T6R) to approximate averaging the thinned-model predictions. The paper states this approximation corresponds to the geometric mean (equally weighted combination) of thinned-network predictions. Two corruption types: Bernoulli dropout (P7V) — binary multiplicative noise (Bernoulli variable =1 with prob p, 0 otherwise) — and Gaussian dropout (D4K) — Gaussian multiplicative noise. Marginalization = expectation over dropout noise to yield a deterministic objective/regularizer; Monte‑Carlo dropout/model averaging = stochastic sampling and averaging predictions from sampled thinned networks. Dropout RBM (B8T): described as a mixture of shared-weight RBMs using different hidden-unit subsets; U2L = RBM; pretraining (DBM/E5Q, DBN/G6W) then finetuning with backprop; mcRBM-G6W is a named pretrained variant. Regularizers: L1 (O3U), L2 (Y5F, Tikhonov), max-norm (V9C), KL-sparsity. Activations mentioned: logistic units, ReLU (F3N), maxout (L8J). Other glossary items to track: geometric mean vs. posterior-weighted averaging, blankout noise, ridge-regression connection (dropout expectation → ridge-like penalty matrix), convolutional-net components (filters, pooling variants), data augmentation, SVM/PCA baselines, terms like dead unit, mix-ability, replica code, and non-stationarity. These definitions and labels will be used in later parts for numerical and conceptual consistency checks.

Abstract summary: method called "QX2, or dropout"; it randomly removes units and their connections during training, inhibiting co-adaptation, sampling exponentially many thinned networks that share parameters. A single unthinned network with reduced weights approximates the averaged predictions of the thinned nets. Claims substantial reduction in overfitting and major improvements; supervised experiments in vision, speech recognition, document classification and computational biology reportedly attain state-of-the-art on many benchmarks. Evidence claimed in Tables 2–8 and an unnumbered text-classification table in §6.3; domain-specific comparisons listed in §6.

Paper: "Dropout (QX2)". Core idea: randomly remove units during training to train many shared-parameter thinned subnetworks (2^n possible thinned nets for n units) and approximate their combined predictions with one unthinned test-time network. Key terminology: QX2 = dropout; T6R = test-time weight scaling (use one unthinned net with scaled weights); X9M = Monte-Carlo model averaging (average sampled thinned nets at test); U2L/B8T = dropout extension to RBMs. Notation (carry-forward): n = unit count; expected retained width = p n; practical width heuristic = n/p; shared-parameter count O(n^2); L hidden layers with W^(l), b^(l), activations f; p = retention probability; test-time weights scaled by p (W_test = p W). Claims in this part: QX2 approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many models; a new thinned member is sampled and trained (rarely) per presentation of each training case; T6R is a cheap practical inference rule that gives significantly lower generalization error than other regularizers across varied problems; X9M is more expensive and needs around k≈50 samples (per §7.5 and App B.1) before matching T6R. Evidence pointer: Table 9 referenced for comparisons (rows quoted: Y5F=1.62, V9C=1.35, QX2+Y5F=1.25, QX2+V9C=1.05). Paper outline: §2 motivation, §3 prior work, §4 model, §5 training algorithm, §6 experiments, §7 effects and hyperparameter interactions, §8 RBM extension, §9 marginalization, Appendix A (practical guidance).

(2010) "mix-ability" notion: selection favors genes that work well with random partners (robust, independently useful components). Analogy: QX2 forces hidden units to operate with randomly selected partners, discouraging complex co-adaptations and favoring robust features; replicating units is a poor remedy. Smaller cooperating subsets are argued to be more robust under non-stationarity than large co-adaptations. steps.notes_before: Paper: Dropout (QX2) — gate unit outputs during training, independently per unit with r_j^{(l)} ~ Bernoulli(p); tilde y^{(l)} = r^{(l)} * y^{(l)}. At inference no units removed; test-time weights scaled by retention p: W_test^{(l)} = p W^{(l)}. Expected preactivation under training dropout equals test preactivation with scaled weights. Both hidden and input (visible) units can be dropped. Validation can pick p; default often near optimal; input retention generally near complete retention. Forward equations: y^{(0)} = x; nominally z_i^{(l+1)} = w_i^{(l+1)} y^{(l)} + b_i^{(l+1)}, y_i^{(l+1)} = f(z_i^{(l+1)}). Example activation: logistic f(x)=1/(1+exp(-x)). Note: this part contains an indexing inconsistency — it first states l∈{1..L} then uses l∈{0..L-1} for the feed-forward formulas (treating y^{(0)} as input). Keep this in mind when later parts refer to layer indices.

Paper: QX2 = dropout (per-unit gate r_j^(l) ~ Bernoulli(p); ̃y^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l)). At test time do not drop units; scale weights by retention p (W_test = p W) so expected preactivation under dropout equals test preactivation. Both hidden and input units can be dropped (input retention usually near 1). Forward eqns use y^(0)=x; paper has an indexing inconsistency (uses l∈{1..L} then l∈{0..L-1}).

Sec.5 (Learning QX2 Nets): training = backprop through sampled subnetworks (one mask per case/minibatch case), gradients averaged across cases; a dropped parameter gets zero contribution. QX2 alone gives significant gains; combining QX2 with high momentum, large decaying learning rates and V9C (max-norm) gives further boost. V9C constrains each hidden unit's incoming weight vector via projection to ||w||_2 <= c (validation tunes c); projection returns w to the radius-c surface if exceeded. Proposed optimization story: fixed-radius weight ball allows huge LRs without explosion; QX2 noise explores; annealing settles.

Empirical notes cited: Table 9 rows: V9C=1.35, QX2+Y5F=1.25, QX2+V9C=1.05. Appendix A.2: practical LRs typically 10–100x optimal standard-net LR and momentum ~0.95–0.99. Pretraining: unchanged, but before QX2 finetuning multiply pretrained weights by 1/p so expected outputs under dropout match pretraining; use much smaller finetuning LR (Appendix B.4 reports ~0.01 best vs listed high LR 0.1). MNIST: 60k train, 10k test; 10k val. Tuned so best val at 1M updates, then combined train+val and trained 1M updates. Archs: all combos of 2/3/4 layers × {1024,2048} units. Paper: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (JMLR 15, 2014). Authors: Nitish Srivastava, Geoffrey Hinton, Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, Ruslan Salakhutdinov. Abstract/main claim: Dropout randomly drops units and their connections during training to prevent co-adaptation; training effectively samples from an exponential number of "thinned" networks. At test time, the effect of averaging these thinned networks is approximated by using a single unthinned network with scaled (smaller) weights. Dropout reportedly reduces overfitting and outperforms other regularization methods, producing major improvements and state-of-the-art results on benchmarks in vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology. Intro notes: deep nets are expressive and prone to overfitting; common regularizers include early stopping, L1/L2 penalties, and soft weight sharing. The paper states that with unlimited computation the best regularizer is averaging predictions over all parameter settings (sentence is cut off in this part). Figure 1 caption: left—standard net with 2 hidden layers; right—example thinned net after dropout where some units are dropped.

New from current part: Motivation analogies — sexual reproduction: dropout viewed as preventing large co-adaptations, forcing each hidden unit to learn useful features that work with random subsets of partners, improving robustness; copying units to resist dropout is a poor solution (analogy to replica codes for noisy channels). Conspiracy analogy: many small conspiracies (small co-adaptations) more robust than one large co-adaptation, hence better generalization under non-stationarity. Related work: Dropout can be seen as regularization via adding noise to hidden units; this idea relates to Denoising Autoencoders (Vincent et al. 2008, 2010) which add noise to unit states.

steps.notes_before: Paper: Dropout trains by randomly dropping units (thinning) and sharing weights across exponentially many sub-networks. Training samples a new thinned net each presentation; backpropagate gradients through that thinned net. At test time use a single unthinned net with weights scaled by retention probabilities (W_test = p W^(l) per layer). Typical choices: drop ~50% hidden units (p_hidden ≈ 0.5), ~20% inputs (p_input ≈ 0.8); DAEs typically use 5% input noise but test-time scaling allows higher noise. Dropout can be applied to hidden layers and other neuron-based architectures (e.g., Boltzmann Machines, RBMs). Interpretation: stochastic regularization / model averaging; related to denoising autoencoders and marginalizing noise. Definition details: network with L hidden layers; y(0)=x; feed-forward recurrence given as z^{(l+1)} = W^{(l+1)} y^{(l)} + b^{(l+1)}, y^{(l+1)} = f(z^{(l+1)}). With dropout: sample r^{(l)} ~ Bernoulli(p) elementwise, form y_e^{(l)} = r^{(l)} * y^{(l)} and use y_e^{(l)} as input to next layer. Loss is minimized stochastically (expected loss); prior adversarial-drop work fixes max number dropped (no hidden-layer models).

Training: dropout nets trained by SGD on ‘‘thinned’’ nets — for each training case in a mini‑batch sample dropout mask, do forward/backprop on that thinned net; gradients averaged over mini‑batch; any case that omits a parameter contributes zero gradient for that parameter. Standard SGD tricks (momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 weight decay) help. Max‑norm regularization: constrain incoming weight vector w at each hidden unit to ||w||2 ≤ c by projecting back into the ball of radius c whenever it exceeds c (c is a tunable hyperparameter). Max‑norm often improves SGD even without dropout; combining dropout + max‑norm + large decaying LR + high momentum gives further gains (intuition: ball constraint prevents blowup so large LR can be used for exploration). Unsupervised pretraining: stacks of RBMs/autoencoders/DBMs can be used; pretraining stays the same, but when finetuning with dropout scale pretrained weights by 1/p so expected output under dropout matches pretraining output. If finetune LR is too large pretrained information can be lost; use smaller LR to retain gains. Experiments: datasets include MNIST, TIMIT, CIFAR‑10/100, SVHN, ImageNet, Reuters‑RCV1, and an Alternative Splicing RNA dataset; more details in Appendix B.

On MNIST, Monte-Carlo averaging reaches the approximate (weight-scaling) performance at about k≈50; for k>50 MC is slightly better but within one standard deviation—weight scaling is a fairly good approximation. Section 8: Dropout RBMs. Definitions: v∈{0,1}^D, h∈{0,1}^F, P(h,v;θ) ∝ exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v). Introduce r∈{0,1}^F with Pr(r_j=1)=p independent. Joint P(r,h,v)=P(r; p)P(h,v|r) where P(h,v|r) ∝ exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v)·∏_j g(h_j,r_j) with g enforcing h_j=0 when r_j=0. Thus conditioned on r the model is an RBM with a subset of h; overall a mixture of exponentially many RBMs with shared weights. Learning via CD-1 with a new r sampled per training case per minibatch. Fig.12: features from 256-hidden-unit RBMs (a) no dropout, (b) dropout p=0.5, ordered by L2 norm; section inspects whether dropout reduces co-adaptations in RBMs.

Section 8 (dropout RBMs): define dropout as masking r∈{0,1}^F (Pr(r_j=1)=p), yielding a mixture of RBMs; train with CD-1 sampling r per case per minibatch. Fig.12: features from 256-hidden-unit RBMs show dropout features coarser; few dead units in dropout RBM relative to standard RBM. 8.4: Figure 13 histograms show dropout RBMs produce much sparser hidden activations (many activations close to zero) versus standard RBM (many activations away from zero). Section 9 (marginalizing dropout): dropout can be marginalized to yield deterministic losses. 9.1: For linear regression, E_R ||y-(R*X)w||^2 = ||y-pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Γw||^2 with Γ = (diag(...) )^{1/2} (scales weight penalty by input std); absorbing p shows regularization grows as p decreases. 9.2: For logistic/deep nets closed-form marginalization hard; approximate Gaussian marginalization (Wang & Manning) can be efficient and may outperform MC in training time/generalization but assumptions weaken with depth. Section 9: dropout can be marginalized for linear regression yielding extra L2 term with strength growing as p decreases; Gaussian marginalization approximations possible for deep nets. Section 10 (this part): propose multiplicative Gaussian noise r0∼N(1,σ^2) (special case N(1,1) when p=0.5) as alternative to Bernoulli dropout; E[r0]=1 so no test-time scaling needed; to match Bernoulli mean/variance they set σ^2=(1−p)/p, so Gaussian and Bernoulli have same first two moments. Table 10 compares Bernoulli vs Gaussian (MNIST: Bernoulli p_hidden=0.5, p_input=0.8; CIFAR p-vector given); results averaged over 10 seeds and suggest Gaussian may be slightly better. Note: Table header contains a contradictory statement that σ was set to p (likely a typesetting/error) conflicting with σ^2=(1−p)/p in the text.

Conclusion & Appendix: Dropout shown to improve performance across domains; training typically takes ~2–3× longer due to noisy parameter updates. Marginalizing dropout noise yields a regularizer: for linear regression this is a modified L2; marginalization for complex models is harder. Appendix heuristics: network size — if n is optimal for standard net, use ≈ n/p hidden units with dropout; learning rate — use ~10–100× the LR optimal for standard nets; momentum — use ~0.95–0.99 (vs ~0.9 standard); use max-norm regularization to bound incoming weight-norm per unit (c≈3–4); dropout rates — hidden p typically 0.5–0.8, input (real-valued) p≈0.8. Earlier experimental notes to retain: Section 7 (MNIST autoencoder/regularization): dropout yields stroke/edge detectors; mean hidden activation ≈2.0 (no dropout) vs ≈0.7 (with dropout); p-variation: fixing expected active units improves small-p performance; best p≈0.6, default p=0.5 near-optimal; dataset-size sweep: dropout helps more as data grows; test-time averaging: Monte Carlo k≈50 matches weight-scaling approximation. Section 8 (RBMs): dropout RBMs produce coarser features and sparser hidden activations with few dead units. Section 9: marginalizing dropout for linear regression gives extra L2 term; Gaussian marginalization approximations possible for deep nets. Section 10: multiplicative Gaussian alternative r0~N(1,σ^2) with σ^2=(1−p)/p to match Bernoulli first two moments; Table comparing Bernoulli vs Gaussian averaged over 10 seeds; note earlier observed table-header contradiction claiming σ=p vs text σ^2=(1−p)/p.

Appendix B: experiment details. MNIST — 60,000 train, 10,000 test; 10,000 held out for validation. Tuned hyperparameters so best validation error occurred after 1M weight updates, then combined val+train and trained for 1M updates for final model. Architectures: all combinations of 2/3/4 layer nets with 1024 or 2048 units per layer (6 architectures). Dropout: p_hidden=0.5, p_input=0.8. Momentum=0.95. Max-norm constraint c=2 for MNIST experiments. Also tried very wide 2- and 3-layer nets (4096, 8192 units); 2-layer improved, 3-layer slightly worse; increasing dropout helped but not enough to beat 2-layer. SVHN — ~600k train, ~26k test; validation set 6000 (per-class: 400 from standard, 200 from extra). Inputs: RGB normalized to zero mean and unit variance (other preprocessing like contrast norm/ZCA did not help). Best arch: 3 conv layers (96,128,256 filters), 5x5 receptive fields stride 1; each conv followed by 3x3 max-pooling stride 2; then two FC hidden layers of 2048 units; ReLU units. Dropout retain-probs by layer (input->conv1->conv2->conv3->fc1->fc2) = (0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5). Max-norm c=4. Momentum=0.95. Tuned on validation and did not combine val with train for final SVHN model (reported test error from model with smallest val error). CIFAR-10/100 — 50k train, 10k test; used 5k for validation; preprocessing: per-channel global contrast normalization followed by ZCA whitening; followed MNIST procedure (tune on val then combine). Global earlier heuristics to keep: hidden size ≈ n/p, LR ≈10–100× standard, momentum ≈0.95–0.99, max-norm c≈3–4, hidden p typically 0.5–0.8, input p≈0.8. Also remember earlier noted inconsistency in Section 10: table header claimed σ=p while text gave σ^2=(1−p)/p.

errors.claim: "For a task whose optimal standard-net layer has \(n\) hidden units, a good QX2 layer should contain at least \(n/p\) units. Removing units reduces capacity: only \(pn\) units remain in expectation, their identities change at every sampling, and unrestricted co-adaptation is unavailable."
errors.evidence: "For a task whose optimal standard-net layer has \(n\) hidden units, a good QX2 layer should contain at least \(n/p\) units." and immediately after "Removing units reduces capacity: only \(pn\) units remain in expectation..." (both sentences appear in Appendix A.1 of this part).
errors.explanation: These two sentences conflict mathematically: if you set the layer size to n/p and each unit is retained with probability p, the expected number of retained units is p*(n/p)=n, not pn. Thus the claim 'only pn units remain in expectation' contradicts the immediately preceding recommendation.

final_notes:
Dropout (QX2) summary: improves generalization across domains (vision, speech, text, genomics); increases sparsity (mean activation ~2.0→~0.7); typical hidden p≈0.5, input p≈0.8 (some nets differ). Marginalization: linear-case closed form (ridge-like); multiplicative Gaussian approx matches Bernoulli variance σ^2=(1-p)/p. Experiments: earlier stated usually averaged over 10 seeds (but some datasets use different protocols; see Z7P below). Training 2–3× slower; use much larger LR (10–100× standard) and higher momentum (QX2 often 0.95–0.99). V9C max-norm bound typically 3–4. Appendix B specifics / reproduction code linked.

N8Q (speech): window=21 consecutive frames; input p=0.8, hidden p=0.5; V9C c=4; momentum=0.95; high LR=0.1 with decay ε0(1+t/T)^{-1}; G6W pretraining: U2L via CD-1, Gaussian-U2L input-unit variance fixed to 1; best QX2 finetune LR ≈0.01. Adding V9C during G6W finetuning gave no improvement; the smaller finetune LR mattered.

M5X: used subset 402,738 articles, 2000-word vocab, 50 disjoint categories; equal train/test splits → >200,000 train examples.

Z7P (genomics): 3,665 cassette exons, 1,014 RNA features, 4 tissue types (derived from 27 mouse tissues). Each input has four target softmaxes (one per tissue), each with states {inc, exc, nc}. Objective C4Y = Σ_i Σ_t Σ_s p_{i,t}^s log( q_t^s(r_i)/ ar p^s ). QX2 hidden-unit scale: 1000s; Bayesian nets: a few tens. Trained QX2: 2 layers × 1024 units; hidden p=0.5, input p=0.7; regularization/schedule: V9C with high decaying LRs; results averaged using same 5 folds as Xiong et al. (2011).

Title: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting". Authors: Nitish Srivastava, Geoffrey Hinton, Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, Ruslan Salakhutdinov; Dept. of Computer Science, University of Toronto. Journal: JMLR 15 (2014). Header lists pages 1929–1958 while page map lists pages 1930–1955 (internal inconsistency noted). Abstract summary: introduces dropout (called "QX2: dropout") — a training procedure that temporarily removes randomly selected units and their connections, inhibiting excessive co-adaptation and effectively sampling exponentially many parameter-sharing thinned networks. At test time a single unthinned network with reduced weights approximates the averaged predictions of these thinned networks. Claims dropout substantially reduces overfitting versus other regularizers and yields major improvements, achieving state-of-the-art performance on many benchmarks in supervised vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology.

steps.notes_before: Title: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al., UToronto). Header/page-number inconsistency noted earlier. Dropout (QX2) randomly removes units/connections during training, producing exponentially many (2^n for n units) thinned networks; parameters are shared so total distinct parameters retained are O(n^2) or fewer. With unlimited computation, posterior-weighted averaging over parameters is ideal; the paper claims its method approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of these thinned models' predictions (introduction) — earlier abstract wording said it "approximates the averaged predictions", a potential arithmetic vs geometric-mean wording mismatch. Every presentation samples/trains a new thinned member; individual members are rarely trained thoroughly. Practical inference: T6R (weight scaling) uses one unthinned network at test time; X9M refers to Monte-Carlo model averaging (more expensive). Claims T6R gives much lower generalization error than other regularizers across tasks. Method extends to graphical models, e.g., Dropout RBM (B8T) from RBMs (U2L). Paper map: §2 motivation; §3 prior work; §4 formal model; §5 training algorithm; §6 experiments; §7 network/hyperparameter interactions; §8 Dropout RBMs; §9 marginalization; Appendix A practical guidance.

Paper claims T6R yields much lower generalization error than other regularizers across tasks. Extensions: Dropout RBM (B8T). Paper map: §2 motivation; §3 prior work; §4 formal model; §5 training algorithm; §6 experiments; §7 interactions; §8 Dropout RBMs; §9 marginalization; Appendix A guidance. New from §2 (Motivation): authors use biological analogy—sexual vs asexual reproduction—and cite Livnat et al. (2010) arguing selection can favor gene "mix-ability" rather than individual-fitness optimization. Dropout is analogous: hidden units face randomly selected partners, which favors independently useful, robust features and reduces complex co-adaptations. Replicating units many times is deemed a poor robustness fix (analogy to replica codes and noisy channels). Conspiracy analogy: many small cooperating subsets are more robust under non-stationarity than a single large co-adapted set; complex co-adaptations may overfit training data and fail on novel test data.

Title: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al.). Method: dropout (QX2) randomly removes units/connections during training producing ~2^n thinned networks; parameters shared so distinct params O(n^2). Training: each SGD update samples a thinned network; individual thinned members rarely trained thoroughly. Test-time inference: T6R = weight-scaling using one unthinned network; X9M = Monte-Carlo model averaging (more expensive). Paper claims T6R gives much lower generalization error than other regularizers across tasks. Motivation (§2): biological analogy (mix-ability), reduces co-adaptations. Related work (§3): dropout interpretable as noise in hidden-unit states, extends denoising autoencoders (Vincent et al. 2008/2010) — effective hidden-layer corruption, model-averaging view, supervised/unsupervised use, applicable to Boltzmann Machines. Table: S2H (DAE) typical best noise ~5%; QX2 often optimal input-unit removal ~20%; QX2 often optimal hidden-unit removal ~50%. Adversarial-removal alternatives (Globerson & Roweis 2006; Dekel et al. 2010) consider worst-case removals under a budget and have no hidden units. Analytic marginalization can give deterministic regularizers in simple cases; van der Maaten et al. (2013) studied exponential-family input-noise (blankout) limited to models without hidden layers; Chen et al. (2012) studied marginalization for DAEs; Wang & Manning (2013) proposed marginalization to speed up dropout. Section map: §2 motivation; §3 prior work; §4 formal model; §5 training algorithm; §6 experiments; §7 interactions; §8 Dropout RBMs; §9 marginalization; Appendix A guidance.

Paper: Dropout regularization. Key idea: during training randomly delete (zero) units (hidden and/or visible) to sample many thinned subnetworks; parameters shared across subnetworks. Retention choices are independent Bernoulli variables with common probability p (can be chosen by validation). Typical defaults: hidden-unit retention p≈0.5 (i.e. ~50% removal); input-unit removal often ~20% (retention p≈0.8) — input retention usually nearer full. Training: each SGD update samples r^{(l)} (vector of independent Bernoulli(p)) and forms \tilde y^{(l)} = r^{(l)} * y^{(l)}; forward: z_i^{(l+1)} = w_i^{(l+1)} \tilde y^{(l)} + b_i^{(l+1)}, y_i^{(l+1)} = f(z_i^{(l+1)}). Backprop passes gradients through the sampled subnetwork. Notation: y^{(0)}=x; L hidden layers (indexed 1..L); feed-forward written for l=0..L-1 producing layer l+1. Activation f can be any (e.g. logistic). Test-time inference: no dropout; use one unthinned network with outgoing weights scaled by p: W_test^{(l)} = p W^{(l)} (equivalently unit outputs' expected training contribution equals test-time contribution with scaled weights). Figures illustrate training (stochastic gates r) vs testing (weights scaled by p). Other parts: training samples many subnetworks per SGD update; Monte-Carlo averaging at test-time is an alternative to weight-scaling but more expensive.

Part 5: QX2 (dropout) gives significant gains; combining it with high momentum, large decaying learning rates, and an incoming-weight constraint (V9C = max-norm) gives further improvement. V9C enforces ||w||_2 <= c with projection to the ball surface when exceeded; c is tuned by validation. Proposed optimization account claims large learning rates are safe inside the fixed-radius ball; QX2 provides noise exploration; learning rates decay to smaller steps. SGD differs from standard training only by per-case sampled thinned networks: each mini-batch case uses its own sampled network; gradients averaged across cases; a case not using a parameter contributes zero. Momentum, annealed (decaying) learning rates and other heuristics remain useful. Unsupervised pretraining is unchanged, but before QX2 finetuning pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p so each unit’s expected random-removal output matches its pretraining output. Smaller finetuning learning rates help preserve pretrained information. Pretraining (with unlabeled data) can improve over random init; applicable to stacked U2L, autoencoders, DBMs for finetuning.

(Note: an internal inconsistency was found in Part 12: bias names a and b are swapped between joint and conditional formulas.) Part 13 (Marginalizing QX2): Deterministic noise-marginalized models remove test-time randomness and admit gradients. For linear regression, marginalization yields minimize ||y - p X w||^2 + p(1-p)||Γ w||^2 with Γ = sqrt(diag(X^T X)); with \tilde w = p w this is ridge with penalty (1-p)/p ||Γ \tilde w||^2 (i.e., per-dimension penalty proportional to column norm/std). For logistic regression and deep nets, closed-form marginalization is hard; approximate marginalization treats inputs/gradients as Gaussian (weaker as depth increases) and can outperform Monte-Carlo QX2 in training time and generalization for logistic regression (Wang & Manning 2013).
