errors.claim: "For a task whose optimal standard-net layer has \(n\) hidden units, a good QX2 layer should contain at least \(n/p\) units. Removing units reduces capacity: only \(pn\) units remain in expectation, their identities change at every sampling, and unrestricted co-adaptation is unavailable."
errors.evidence: "For a task whose optimal standard-net layer has \(n\) hidden units, a good QX2 layer should contain at least \(n/p\) units." and immediately after "Removing units reduces capacity: only \(pn\) units remain in expectation..." (both sentences appear in Appendix A.1 of this part).
errors.explanation: These two sentences conflict mathematically: if you set the layer size to n/p and each unit is retained with probability p, the expected number of retained units is p*(n/p)=n, not pn. Paper summary: Introduces dropout — randomly removing units and their connections during training, which samples many smaller networks that share weights. At test time, a single full network with scaled weights approximates the ensemble of sampled networks. Reports improvements on image, speech, text, and alternative-splicing tasks. Compares dropout with other regularizers and Bayesian neural networks. Studies learned features, sparsity, dropout rates, network size, training-set size, and test-time averaging; finds Dropout Restricted Boltzmann Machines learn qualitatively different features and sparser representations. For linear regression, marginalizing dropout yields a modified ridge-regression objective. Preliminary experiments compare Bernoulli dropout to multiplicative Gaussian noise. Limitation noted: training time typically 2–3× longer than standard networks with the same architecture.

Paper introduces dropout: during training randomly remove units and their incoming/outgoing connections (Bernoulli dropout uses binary vars that equal 1 with probability p, the retention probability). At test time the ensemble is approximated by a single deterministic model via weight scaling (multiply a unit’s outgoing weights by p) or by marginalizing dropout noise (deterministic dropout model); Monte-Carlo dropout/model averaging samples thinned networks at test time. Gaussian (multiplicative) dropout multiplies activations by Gaussian noise; paper compares Bernoulli and Gaussian variants. For linear regression, marginalized dropout is equivalent in expectation to a modified ridge (Tikhonov) regression. Dropout-RBMs are RBMs augmented with binary retention variables; CD-1/Contrastive Divergence used for RBM training; partition function Z(θ) appears in RBM formulation. Code Quality (alternative-splicing task) is the negative KL-divergence metric (higher is better). Other key methods/terms: DBN/DBM pretraining, max-norm constraint (bound hidden-unit incoming weight norms), L1/L2 weight penalties, KL-sparsity regularizer, ReLU and maxout units, pooling (max, L2, L4) in image models, max-pooling after conv layers, permutation-invariant vs 2-D MNIST settings, Top-1/Top-5 ImageNet error definitions, PCA/ZCA whitening used in preprocessing, mix-ability measure for genes. Noted limitation: training time typically 2–3× longer than standard networks with same architecture.

For linear regression, marginalized dropout = modified ridge (Tikhonov). Dropout-RBMs include binary retention variables; trained with CD-1. Code Quality metric = negative KL-divergence (higher is better). Regularization/architecture details: DBN/DBM pretraining; max-norm constraint (bound hidden-unit incoming weight norms); L1/L2 penalties; KL-sparsity regularizer; ReLU and maxout units; pooling: max, L2, L4; max-pooling after conv layers; permutation-invariant vs 2-D MNIST distinction. Notation and key definitions: L (# hidden layers), l (layer index); i,j (unit/dim/data indices). x = network input (y^(0)). z^(l) = inputs to layer l; y^(l) = outputs; ~y^(l) = outputs after elementwise dropout mask. W^(l), w_i^(l), b^(l) = layer weights, unit incoming weights, biases. W_test^(l)=pW^(l) (test-time weight-scaling). f activation (example sigmoid 1/(1+exp(-x))); exp used in activations/probabilities. p = retention probability. r^(l) = Bernoulli mask vector for layer l; * = elementwise multiplication. n = # units (hidden units in a layer); 2^n possible thinned networks; O(n^2) shared parameter order; pn expected retained units. w general weight vector; ||w||_2 and max-norm bound c; squared norm notation ||·||^2. k = # MC samples for prediction averaging. RBM notation: v (visible), D (# visible), h (hidden), F (# hidden), binary spaces {0,1}^D/{0,1}^F, θ={W,a,b}, Z(θ) partition, r binary retention in Dropout RBM (and r as Gaussian noise in Sect.10), Z'(θ,r) conditional normalization, g(h_j,r_j) enforces h_j=0 if r_j=0, 1(·) indicator, P(·) probability, σ = RBM activation (and in Sect.10 Gaussian noise SD). Multiplicative noise: h_i, r'~N(1,σ^2) with σ^2 matched to (1-p)/p; r_b rescaled Bernoulli =1/p w.p. p; r_g Gaussian mean 1 var (1-p)/p. Also listed N(1,1), N(0,1) as example Gaussians. Main idea: During training randomly remove units+connections (Bernoulli retention p) sampling exponential number of thinned networks; at test time use one unthinned network with scaled weights (W_test = p W) to approximate average predictions. Dropout claimed to reduce overfitting and prevent co-adaptation.

Paper: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al., JMLR 2014). Main idea: during training randomly drop units (Bernoulli retain prob p) to sample many "thinned" networks; at test time use a single unthinned network with outgoing weights scaled by p (W_test = p W) to approximate averaging. Key definitions: L layers, r^(l) Bernoulli masks, ~y^(l) after dropout. A net with n units corresponds to 2^n thinned nets; they share weights so parameter count stays O(n^2). Typical choices: p≈0.5 for hidden units (often close to optimal), input-unit p usually closer to 1. Scaling outgoing weights by p at test time ensures expected training-time output equals test-time output. Motivation: approximate an equally weighted geometric mean / Bayesian-like averaging of exponentially many models with much less computation. Dropout applicable beyond feed-forward nets (Dropout RBM introduced). Paper claims dropout + weight-scaling reduces overfitting and improves generalization across domains; experiments reported in Sections 6–8 (image results Tables 2–6, TIMIT Table 7, Reuters improvement 31.05%→29.62% in Sect.6.3, alternative-splicing bits in Table 8, Table 9 comparisons: Dropout+Max-norm 1.05% vs Max-norm 1.35% vs L2 1.62%). TIMIT learning-rate schedule earlier noted: ε0 (1 + t/T)^(-1). Paper structure: Sec 2 motivation, 3 related work, 4 model, 5 training, 6 experiments, 7 hyperparams/properties, 8 Dropout RBMs, 9 marginalizing dropout, Appendix A guidance.

Paper: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al., JMLR 2014). Core idea: during training randomly drop units (Bernoulli masks r^(l), retain prob p) to sample many thinned networks; at test time use the full network with outgoing weights scaled by p (weight-scaling) to approximate averaging. Typical p≈0.5 for hidden units; input p usually closer to 1. Scaling by p makes test-time output equal to the expected training-time output (approximate model averaging). Dropout applies beyond feed-forward nets (Dropout RBMs): Figures 12–13 show qualitative feature and sparsity comparisons but no numeric performance comparison is reported there. Experiments (Secs.6–8) report improved generalization across domains (image Tables 2–6, TIMIT Table 7, Tables 2–7 and 9 cited for cross-domain error reductions). Reuters (Sec.6.3) error improved from 31.05% to 29.62%. Table 9: Dropout+Max-norm 1.05% vs Max-norm 1.35% vs L2 1.62% (alternative-splicing results also in Table 8). TIMIT uses learning rate schedule ε0(1 + t/T)^(-1). Section 2 motivation uses analogies (sexual reproduction / mix-ability; conspiracies) to argue dropout reduces complex co-adaptations, forcing units to be robust and individually useful.

Paper: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al., JMLR 2014). Core idea: during training randomly drop units via Bernoulli masks r^(l) with retain prob p, sampling many thinned networks; at test time use full network with outgoing weights scaled by p (weight-scaling) to approximate averaging. Typical p ≈ 0.5 for hidden units; input p usually closer to 1. Dropout interpretable as adding noise to hidden-unit states; relates to Denoising Autoencoders (DAEs) which typically use ~5% input noise, but with weight-scaling dropout often uses much higher noise (e.g., drop 20% of inputs, 50% of hidden units). Dropout extends beyond unsupervised learning to supervised nets and other architectures (e.g., Dropout RBMs / Boltzmann Machines; Figures 12–13 show qualitative differences). In simple cases dropout noise can be marginalized analytically (Section 9.1 gives linear-regression derivations); related work on deterministic marginalization and "blankout" noise (van der Maaten et al., Wang & Manning, Chen et al.). Different adversarial-removal formulations studied by Globerson & Roweis (2006) and Dekel et al. (2010). Experiments (Secs. 6–8) report improved generalization across domains: Reuters (Sec.6.3) error improved from 31.05% to 29.62%; Table 9 reports Dropout+Max-norm 1.05% vs Max-norm 1.35% vs L2 1.62%; TIMIT used learning-rate schedule ε0(1 + t/T)^(-1). Section 2 gives motivational analogies (sexual reproduction/mix-ability, conspiracies).

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (Srivastava et al., JMLR 2014). Core idea: during training randomly drop units with independent Bernoulli masks r^{(l)} (retain prob p), sampling many thinned sub-networks; at test time use full network with outgoing weights scaled by p (weight-scaling). Typical p ≈ 0.5 for hidden units; input p usually closer to 1. Notation: L hidden layers (1..L); z^{(l)} = inputs into layer l, y^{(l)} = outputs (y^{(0)}=x), W^{(l)}, b^{(l)}. Standard forward: z_i^{(l+1)} = w_i^{(l+1)} y^{(l)} + b_i^{(l+1)}; y_i^{(l+1)} = f(z_i^{(l+1)}) (e.g., logistic f(x)=1/(1+e^{-x})). Dropout forward: r_j^{(l)} ~ Bernoulli(p) (each mask component independent, 1 with prob p), \tilde y^{(l)} = r^{(l)} * y^{(l)} (elementwise), then z_i^{(l+1)} = w_i^{(l+1)} \tilde y^{(l)} + b_i^{(l+1)}, y_i^{(l+1)} = f(z_i^{(l+1)}). Backpropagate loss derivatives through the sampled sub-network. Test-time: use full network without dropout and scale weights: W_test^{(l)} = p W^{(l)}. Section references: Sec.9.1 gives analytic marginalization in simple linear cases; experiments (Secs.6–8) report improved generalization (e.g., Reuters 31.05% → 29.62%; Table 9: Dropout+Max-norm 1.05% vs Max-norm 1.35% vs L2 1.62%); TIMIT used learning-rate schedule ε0(1+t/T)^{-1}. Figures illustrate standard vs dropout panels (bias +1, three inputs, masks in dropout).

Paper: Dropout (Srivastava et al., JMLR 2014). Core idea: during training randomly drop units with independent Bernoulli masks r^{(l)} (retain prob p), sampling many thinned sub-networks; at test time use full network with outgoing weights scaled by p (weight-scaling W_test = p W). Typical p ≈ 0.5 for hidden units; input p usually closer to 1. Training: use SGD (mini-batches); for each case sample a thinned network; forward/backprop only on that network. Gradients averaged across mini-batch; a case not using a parameter contributes zero gradient. Use momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 weight decay. Max-norm: constrain each unit’s incoming weight vector norm ||w||_2 ≤ c; if violated, project onto ball of radius c; c chosen by validation. Combining dropout with max-norm, large decaying learning rates and high momentum yields further gains. Reported MNIST figures (Table 9): Dropout + Max-norm 1.05%; Dropout + L2 1.25%; Max-norm (no dropout) 1.35%; L2 (no dropout) 1.62%. Unsupervised pretraining: can use RBMs, autoencoders, DBMs; pretraining uses unlabeled data and can help versus random init. When finetuning with dropout, pretrained weights should be multiplied by 1/p so each unit’s expected output under dropout equals its pretraining output. Authors observed pretrained information could be lost with large finetuning rates but preserved with smaller rates. Reported pretrained MNIST (Table 2): DBN rows 1.18% versus 0.92%; DBM rows 0.96% versus 0.79% (presented as dropout finetuning improving pretrained networks). Other notes: Reuters improved (31.05% → 29.62%); TIMIT used learning-rate schedule ε0(1+t/T)^{-1}.

Section 6.4: compare dropout vs Bayesian NNs on small alternative-splicing data; metric "Code Quality" = negative KL (higher better); PCA used in some comparisons.

Alternative-splicing (Section 6.4): Table 8 Code Quality (bits, higher is better / negative KL): Neural Net (early stopping) 440; Regression+PCA 463; SVM+PCA 487; Neural Net with dropout 567; Bayesian Neural Net 623. Claims: Bayesian > dropout; dropout substantially improves standard NN and beats the non-Bayesian methods; dropout nets have 1000s of hidden units, Bayesian nets only a few tens; dataset size referenced as Table 1: 2932 training cases, 1014 input dims (so claim is regularization effect allows large nets without PCA). 6.5 MNIST regularizer comparison: fixed ReLU architecture 784-1024-1024-2048-10. Table 9 test errors: L2 1.62%; L2+L1 1.60%; L2+KL-sparsity 1.55%; Max-norm 1.35%; Dropout+L2 1.25%; Dropout+Max-norm 1.05%. Claim: Dropout+Max-norm gives lowest error in this comparison. Keep prior major results for cross-checks: earlier sections reported other MNIST bests (e.g., 0.95% with very wide nets; maxout 0.94%; DBN+dropout 0.92%; DBM+dropout 0.79%). Also retain previously noted TIMIT inconsistency (prose vs Table 7 discrepancy for DBN-pretrained 8-layer: prose says 20.5→19.7; Table shows 20.7→19.7; mcRBM-DBN listed at 20.5).

Section 7 (Salient Features): examines how dropout alters learned features, sparsity, and dependence on retention p, network size and training-set size. 7.1 Features: compares two otherwise-identical 256-unit ReLU MNIST autoencoders (no dropout vs dropout p=0.5). Both have similar test reconstruction error (exact numbers not given). Without dropout features appear co-adapted and less interpretable; with dropout units detect edges/strokes/spots — claimed reason dropout reduces co-adaptation and improves generalization. 7.2 Sparsity: evaluated on a random test minibatch; show two histograms per model (units' mean activations across batch, and individual activations). No-dropout: most units have mean activation ~2.0 and substantial mass away from zero. Dropout p=0.5: mean activation ~0.7 and a sharp peak at zero (sparser activations) — dropout yields sparse activations without an explicit sparsity regularizer. 7.3 Dropout rate: two experiments — keep n fixed (architecture 784-2048-2048-2048-10) and keep pn fixed (expected retained units fixed, so smaller p => larger n). Fig.9a (n fixed): small p => underfitting/high training error; error decreases as p increases, is flat for 0.4 ≤ p ≤ 0.8, then increases as p→1. (Panel axes ticks described; classification error % range ~0–3.5.) Retaining pn fixed means expected retained count same but test-time networks differ in size. Prior retained results: Sec.6.4 alternative-splicing Table8 (Code Quality bits): NN early stop 440; Regression+PCA 463; SVM+PCA 487; NN+dropout 567; Bayesian NN 623. Sec.6.5 MNIST reg comp (784-1024-1024-2048-10) Table9 test errors: L2 1.62%; L2+L1 1.60%; L2+KL 1.55%; Max-norm 1.35%; Dropout+L2 1.25%; Dropout+Max-norm 1.05%. Earlier reported bests: wide nets 0.95%; maxout 0.94%; DBN+dropout 0.92%; DBM+dropout 0.79%. Note: earlier TIMIT prose/Table7 inconsistency recorded separately.

Section 7 examines dropout effects on features, sparsity, retention p, network size, and training-set size. 7.1: 256-unit ReLU MNIST autoencoders (no dropout vs dropout p=0.5) produce similar reconstruction error; dropout yields more interpretable, less co-adapted features. 7.2: Dropout (p=0.5) produces sparser activations (unit means ~0.7 with peak at 0) versus no-dropout (means ~2.0). 7.3 (dropout rate): Two experiments — fixed n (784-2048-2048-2048-10) and fixed pn (expected retained units). For fixed n (Fig.9a) small p underfits; error decreases with p, flat for 0.4≤p≤0.8, then rises as p→1. For pn-fixed experiment they used pn=256 for the first two hidden layers and pn=512 for the last; Fig.9b shows much smaller low-p errors (at p=0.1 error falls from 2.7% in Fig.9a to 1.7% in Fig.9b). For these retained sizes p≈0.6 is best; default p=0.5 is close to optimal. Earlier results (Sec.6.5 Table9) on MNIST (784-1024-1024-2048-10): L2 1.62%; L2+L1 1.60%; L2+KL 1.55%; Max-norm 1.35%; Dropout+L2 1.25%; Dropout+Max-norm 1.05%; other reported bests: wide nets 0.95%; maxout 0.94%; DBN+dropout 0.92%; DBM+dropout 0.79%. 7.4 (data set size): Vary training size {100,500,1K,5K,10K,50K} using 784-1024-1024-2048-10 with hidden p=0.5 and input p=0.8. Dropout gives no improvement at 100 and 500; gain grows then declines with more data (a suggested "sweet spot"). 7.5 (MC averaging vs weight scaling): Monte-Carlo averaging of k sampled dropout nets approaches true average; on MNIST k≈50 matches weight-scaling; larger k is slightly better but within one SD, so weight scaling is a good approximation.

Section 7 (dropout in feed-forward nets / autoencoders): 7.1: 256-unit ReLU MNIST autoencoders (no dropout vs dropout p=0.5) have similar reconstruction error; dropout yields more interpretable, less co-adapted features. 7.2: Dropout (p=0.5) produces sparser activations (unit means ~0.7 with peak at 0) vs no-dropout (means ~2.0). 7.3 (dropout rate): Two experiments — fixed n (784-2048-2048-2048-10) shows small p underfits; error decreases with p, flat for 0.4≤p≤0.8, rises as p→1. pn-fixed experiment (pn=256 for first two hidden layers, pn=512 for last) gives much smaller low-p errors; retained-size optimum near p≈0.6, default p=0.5 close to optimal. Sec.6.5/Table9 (MNIST classification baselines): L2 1.62%; L2+L1 1.60%; L2+KL 1.55%; Max-norm 1.35%; Dropout+L2 1.25%; Dropout+Max-norm 1.05%; best reported: wide nets 0.95%; maxout 0.94%; DBN+dropout 0.92%; DBM+dropout 0.79%. 7.4 (training-set size): training sizes {100,500,1K,5K,10K,50K} on 784-1024-1024-2048-10 with hidden p=0.5 and input p=0.8: dropout gives no improvement at 100/500; gain rises then declines (a "sweet spot"). 7.5 (MC averaging vs weight scaling): Monte-Carlo averaging of k sampled dropout nets approaches true average; on MNIST k≈50 matches weight-scaling (weight-scaling is good approximation). Section 8 (Dropout RBMs): Define binary RBM v∈{0,1}^D, h∈{0,1}^F with P(h,v;θ) ∝ exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v). Add mask r∈{0,1}^F, r_j~Bernoulli(p). Joint P(r,h,v)=P(r;p)P(h,v|r;θ) with constraint g(h_j,r_j)=1(r_j=1)+1(r_j=0)1(h_j=0) forcing h_j=0 when r_j=0. Conditionally: P(h_j=1|r_j,v)=1(r_j=1)σ(b_j+Σ_i W_ij v_i); P(v_i=1|h)=σ(a_i+Σ_j W_ij h_j). Learning: sample r per mini-batch, apply standard RBM learning (CD-1 used). Experiments (MNIST, 256 hidden units, p=0.5): Figures 12/13 show dropout-RBM features are qualitatively coarser and have fewer dead units than standard RBM; activation histograms show much sparser representations with dropout (no numeric sparsity measures reported).

Sections 7–8 recap: 7.1–7.5 (feed-forward nets / autoencoders / classifiers): 256-unit ReLU MNIST autoencoders: dropout (p=0.5) and no-dropout have similar reconstruction error; dropout yields more interpretable, less co-adapted features (7.1). Dropout produces sparser activations (unit means ~0.7, peak at 0) vs no-dropout (~2.0) (7.2). Dropout-rate experiments: fixed-n nets show small p underfit; error decreases with p, flat for 0.4≤p≤0.8, rises as p→1. pn-fixed experiment (pn chosen to keep expected hidden size constant) finds retained-size optimum near p≈0.6; default p=0.5 near optimal (7.3). MNIST classification baselines (Sec.6.5/Table9): L2 1.62%; L2+L1 1.60%; L2+KL 1.55%; Max-norm 1.35%; Dropout+L2 1.25%; Dropout+Max-norm 1.05%; best reported wide nets 0.95%; maxout 0.94%; DBN+dropout 0.92%; DBM+dropout 0.79%. Training-set-size study: dropout gives no improvement at 100/500 examples; gain rises then declines (sweet spot) (7.4). MC averaging vs weight-scaling: MC averaging approaches true average; on MNIST k≈50 matches weight-scaling—weight-scaling is a good approximation (7.5). Section 8 (dropout RBMs): binary RBM with hidden-mask r_j~Bernoulli(p), constraint forces h_j=0 when r_j=0; train by sampling r per minibatch and standard CD-1. Dropout-RBM features are coarser with fewer dead units and much sparser activations (figures shown). Section 9 (Marginalizing Dropout): marginalize dropout noise to obtain deterministic objectives. 9.1 Linear regression: minimize E_R ||y-(R*X)w||^2 = ||y-pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Gamma w||^2, where Gamma = (diag(X^T X))^{1/2}. Equivalently, with \tilde w = p w: minimize ||y-X\tilde w||^2 + ((1-p)/p)||Gamma \tilde w||^2. 9.2 Logistic/deep nets: closed-form marginalization hard; Gaussian approximations (means/variances) exist (Wang & Manning 2013) and can speed training and improve generalization for logistic regression, but assumptions weaken for added layers so results don't directly extend to deep networks.

Sections 7–8 recap: (7.1–7.5) Dropout on feed-forward nets/autoencoders/classifiers: 256-unit ReLU MNIST autoencoders: dropout (p=0.5) and no-dropout have similar reconstruction error; dropout yields more interpretable, less co-adapted features. Dropout produces sparser activations (unit means ~0.7, peak at 0) vs no-dropout (~2.0). Dropout-rate experiments: fixed-n nets show small-p underfit; error decreases with p, flat for 0.4≤p≤0.8, rises as p→1. pn-fixed experiment: retained-size optimum near p≈0.6; default p=0.5 near optimal. MNIST classification baselines (Sec.6.5/Table9): L2 1.62%; L2+L1 1.60%; L2+KL 1.55%; Max-norm 1.35%; Dropout+L2 1.25%; Dropout+Max-norm 1.05%; best reported wide nets 0.95%; maxout 0.94%; DBN+dropout 0.92%; DBM+dropout 0.79%. Training-set-size study: no improvement at 100/500 examples; gain rises then declines. MC averaging vs weight-scaling: MC averaging approaches true average; on MNIST k≈50 matches weight-scaling. Section 8: dropout-RBM: sample hidden-mask r per minibatch (Bernoulli(p)); dropout-RBM features coarser, fewer dead units, much sparser activations. Section 9: marginalizing dropout: linear regression closed-form: E_R||y-(R X)w||^2 = ||y-pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Gamma w||^2; equivalently with tilde w = p w => penalty factor ((1-p)/p). Logistic/deep nets: closed-form hard; Gaussian approximations exist but weaken with depth. Section 10 (this part): Multiplicative Gaussian noise: use r' ~ N(1,σ^2) so h_i r' = h_i + (h_i r), r~N(0,σ^2); for σ=1 this is N(1,1) and adds zero-mean Gaussian noise with std |h_i|. Since E[r']=1 no test-time weight-scaling needed. Alternate Bernoulli training-scaling view: r_b = 1/p w.p. p else 0 gives E[r_b]=1, Var[r_b]=(1-p)/p. Match Gaussian variance by setting σ^2=(1-p)/p. Table 10 (avg over 10 seeds): MNIST (2 layers, 1024 units): Bernoulli 1.08±0.04 vs Gaussian 0.95±0.04 (hidden p=0.5, input p=0.8). CIFAR-10 (3 conv + 2 fc): Bernoulli 12.6±0.1 vs Gaussian 12.5±0.1 with p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5). Authors conclude preliminary Gaussian may be slightly better.

steps.notes_before: Conclusion (Sec.11): dropout reduces co-adaptations, helps across domains (object/digit/speech/doc/biology), and methods report strong image results (claims for SVHN, ImageNet, CIFAR-100, MNIST). Dropout extends to RBMs with sparser/coarser features. Main drawback: longer training (typically 2–3x) due to noisy updates; no timing table provided. Marginalizing noise: linear regression → modified L2 penalty; complex models lack closed-form. Claims/evidence bullet lists various table references and numbers; note internal inconsistencies: conclusion cites Reuters "31.05% versus 29.62%" while claiming improvement (numbers suggest otherwise), and attributes DBM+dropout 0.79% and maxout results to Table 2/3 though earlier MNIST baselines placed DBM+dropout 0.79% and maxout 0.94% in Sec.6.5/Table9. Keep these table-number and numeric mismatches in mind when checking later sections/tables.

Conclusion summary: Dropout reduces co-adaptations and improves performance across domains (objects, digits, speech, documents, biology). Strong image results claimed (SVHN, ImageNet, CIFAR-100, MNIST). Dropout extends to RBMs (sparser/coarser features). Main drawback: longer training (typically 2–3x) due to noisy updates; no timing table provided. Marginalizing noise: linear regression → modified L2 penalty; no closed-form for complex models. Noted internal inconsistencies flagged earlier: Conclusion cites Reuters "31.05% versus 29.62%" but wording implied improvement (numbers conflict); MNIST baselines/table-number mismatches (DBM+dropout 0.79% vs maxout 0.94% and inconsistent table references). Keep these mismatches in mind for later table/section checks. Appendix A (practical heuristics): Acknowledgments: supported by OGS, NSERC, Early Researcher Award. A.1 Network size: expected retained units = p·n; if n is optimal for standard net, use ~n/p units with dropout. A.2 Learning rate & momentum: recommend 10–100× the standard-net optimal learning rate for dropout; momentum ~0.95–0.99 (vs common 0.9); these accelerate learning but no timing data provided. A.3 Max-norm regularization: bound incoming weight-vector norm by c; typical c ≈ 3–4. A.4 Dropout rate: hidden p typically 0.5–0.8; input p depends on input type (real-valued image patches/speech frames ~0.8).

Appendix B (dataset/experiment details).
- MNIST: 60k train / 10k test; held out 10k for validation. Hyperparameters chosen so best validation error occurred after 1M weight updates; then reunited train+val and trained 1M updates for final test. Figure 4: six architectures (2/3/4 hidden layers × {1024,2048}). For these and Table 2 architectures: hidden p=0.5, input p=0.8, final momentum=0.95, max-norm c=2. Larger 2-layer nets (4096 units → 1.01%; 8192 → 0.95% in Table 2, max-norm rows). Three-layer nets slightly worse; stronger dropout helped but did not beat 2-layer nets.
- SVHN: ≈600k train / 26k test. Validation set = 6000 (400/class from standard + 200/class from extra → 2/3 standard, 1/3 extra). Inputs: RGB pixels normalized to zero mean and unit variance; global/local contrast norm and ZCA whitening gave no noticeable improvement for SVHN. Best arch: 3 conv layers (96,128,256 filters, 5×5 receptive field, stride1), each followed by 3×3 pooling, stride2; then two FC layers (2048 units each); ReLU units. Dropout retention p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5) from input through conv and FC; max-norm c=4; momentum 0.95. Validation not added back; report test error of model with smallest validation error (2.55% reported in Table 3).
- CIFAR-10/100: 50k train / 10k test; used 5k for validation, selected hyperparams on val then combined with training. Preprocessing: per-channel global contrast normalization then ZCA whitening. Architecture and dropout rates matched SVHN except input-layer learning rates had to be smaller.
- TIMIT: used Kaldi log-filter banks, monophone forced alignment for labels; networks take 21-frame context predict central frame; inputs mean-centered and unit-variance normalized; no speaker-dependent ops.
- Keep earlier Appendix A heuristics in mind: expected retained units = p·n → scale n≈n/p; higher LR (10–100× typical), momentum ≈0.95–0.99, max-norm c≈3–4, hidden p typically 0.5–0.8, input p ~0.8 for images/speech. Also retain earlier flagged inconsistencies (Reuters numbers, MNIST table/mismatch notes).

final_notes:
Dataset codes: H4Z=MNIST, A2F=SVHN, J3V/W6R=CIFAR-10/100, K9D=ImageNet, N8Q=speech, M5X=Reuters subset, Z7P=genetics.
A2F (SVHN): val=6000 (400/class std + 200/class extra); conv filters 96/128/256; 3×3 pooling stride 2 after each conv; two FC layers 2048; retention p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5); max-norm c=4 on conv+FC; momentum 0.95; large training set kept separate from validation during final training; model with smallest validation error used for test.
J3V/W6R (CIFAR-10/100): 50k train/10k test; val=5000; per-channel global contrast normalization + ZCA whitening; architecture and retention match A2F; input-layer LRs need smaller values; after hyperparameter tuning validation+training were combined for final optimization.

Dropout: randomly remove units and their connections during training, effectively training many smaller networks that share parameters. At test time, use one complete network with reduced weights to approximate averaging the smaller networks' predictions. Claimed benefits: improves generalization over networks without dropout on every tested dataset; reports state-of-the-art results on several benchmarks. Experimental domains: images, speech, documents, gene-splicing prediction. Also examines learned features, sparsity, retention rates, effects of training-set size, Restricted Boltzmann Machines, noise marginalization, and Gaussian corruption. Training cost: typically takes 2–3× longer than training a standard network of the same architecture.

Dropout (QX2): randomly remove units and their connections during training; at test time use one unthinned network with outgoing weights multiplied by the retention probability (T6R) to approximate averaging the thinned-model predictions. The paper states this approximation corresponds to the geometric mean (equally weighted combination) of thinned-network predictions. Two corruption types: Bernoulli dropout (P7V) — binary multiplicative noise (Bernoulli variable =1 with prob p, 0 otherwise) — and Gaussian dropout (D4K) — Gaussian multiplicative noise. Marginalization = expectation over dropout noise to yield a deterministic objective/regularizer; Monte‑Carlo dropout/model averaging = stochastic sampling and averaging predictions from sampled thinned networks. Dropout RBM (B8T): described as a mixture of shared-weight RBMs using different hidden-unit subsets; U2L = RBM; pretraining (DBM/E5Q, DBN/G6W) then finetuning with backprop; mcRBM-G6W is a named pretrained variant. Regularizers: L1 (O3U), L2 (Y5F, Tikhonov), max-norm (V9C), KL-sparsity. Activations mentioned: logistic units, ReLU (F3N), maxout (L8J). Other glossary items to track: geometric mean vs. posterior-weighted averaging, blankout noise, ridge-regression connection (dropout expectation → ridge-like penalty matrix), convolutional-net components (filters, pooling variants), data augmentation, SVM/PCA baselines, terms like dead unit, mix-ability, replica code, and non-stationarity. These definitions and labels will be used in later parts for numerical and conceptual consistency checks.

Abstract summary: method called "QX2, or dropout"; it randomly removes units and their connections during training, inhibiting co-adaptation, sampling exponentially many thinned networks that share parameters. A single unthinned network with reduced weights approximates the averaged predictions of the thinned nets. Claims substantial reduction in overfitting and major improvements; supervised experiments in vision, speech recognition, document classification and computational biology reportedly attain state-of-the-art on many benchmarks. Evidence claimed in Tables 2–8 and an unnumbered text-classification table in §6.3; domain-specific comparisons listed in §6.

Paper: "Dropout (QX2)". Core idea: randomly remove units during training to train many shared-parameter thinned subnetworks (2^n possible thinned nets for n units) and approximate their combined predictions with one unthinned test-time network. Key terminology: QX2 = dropout; T6R = test-time weight scaling (use one unthinned net with scaled weights); X9M = Monte-Carlo model averaging (average sampled thinned nets at test); U2L/B8T = dropout extension to RBMs. Notation (carry-forward): n = unit count; expected retained width = p n; practical width heuristic = n/p; shared-parameter count O(n^2); L hidden layers with W^(l), b^(l), activations f; p = retention probability; test-time weights scaled by p (W_test = p W). Claims in this part: QX2 approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many models; a new thinned member is sampled and trained (rarely) per presentation of each training case; T6R is a cheap practical inference rule that gives significantly lower generalization error than other regularizers across varied problems; X9M is more expensive and needs around k≈50 samples (per §7.5 and App B.1) before matching T6R. Evidence pointer: Table 9 referenced for comparisons (rows quoted: Y5F=1.62, V9C=1.35, QX2+Y5F=1.25, QX2+V9C=1.05). Paper outline: §2 motivation, §3 prior work, §4 model, §5 training algorithm, §6 experiments, §7 effects and hyperparameter interactions, §8 RBM extension, §9 marginalization, Appendix A (practical guidance).

Paper: "Dropout (QX2)". Core idea: randomly remove units during training to train many shared-parameter thinned subnetworks (2^n possible thinned nets for n units) and approximate their combined predictions with one unthinned test-time network. Notation: n = unit count; p = retention probability; expected retained width = p n; practical width heuristic = n/p; shared-parameter count O(n^2); L hidden layers with W^(l), b^(l), activations f; test-time weights scaled by p (W_test = p W). Claims: QX2 approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many models; a new thinned member is sampled and trained (rarely unique) on each presentation of a training case; T6R (test-time weight scaling) is a cheap practical inference rule that gives significantly lower generalization error than other regularizers across varied problems; X9M (Monte-Carlo averaging) is more expensive and needs around k ≈ 50 samples (per §7.5 and App B.1) to match T6R. Evidence pointer: Table 9 comparisons (rows: Y5F=1.62, V9C=1.35, QX2+Y5F=1.25, QX2+V9C=1.05). New in §2: motivation via sexual-reproduction and conspiracy analogies — Livnat et al. (2010) "mix-ability" notion: selection favors genes that work well with random partners (robust, independently useful components). Analogy: QX2 forces hidden units to operate with randomly selected partners, discouraging complex co-adaptations and favoring robust features; replicating units is a poor remedy. Smaller cooperating subsets are argued to be more robust under non-stationarity than large co-adaptations. Outline pointers: §3 prior work, §4 model, §5 training algorithm, §6 experiments, §7 hyperparams, §8 RBM extension, §9 marginalization, Appendix A guidance.

Paper: "Dropout (QX2)". Core idea: randomly remove units during training to train many shared-parameter thinned subnetworks (2^n possible thinned nets for n units) and approximate their combined predictions with one unthinned test-time network. Notation/impl: n = unit count; p = retention probability; expected retained width = p n; practical width heuristic = n/p; shared-parameter count O(n^2); L hidden layers with weights W^(l), biases b^(l), activations f; test-time weights scaled by p (W_test = p W). Key claims: QX2 approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many models; a new thinned member is sampled and trained on each presentation; T6R (test-time weight scaling) is a cheap practical inference rule that often gives much lower generalization error than other regularizers; X9M (Monte-Carlo averaging) is more expensive and reportedly needs k ≈ 50 samples to match T6R (per §7.5 and App B.1). Empirical pointer: Table 9 example rows (Y5F=1.62, V9C=1.35, QX2+Y5F=1.25, QX2+V9C=1.05). Section 3 notes: DAEs (denoising autoencoders) corrupt inputs and reconstruct; QX2 extends corruption to hidden units and gives a model-averaging view; applies to supervised/unsupervised and other neuron-based architectures including Boltzmann Machines. T6R permits much higher noise than typical DAEs: table lists S2H/DAE typical best 5%, QX2 input-unit removal often optimal 20%, QX2 hidden-unit removal often optimal 50%. Related methods: Globerson & Roweis (2006) and Dekel et al. (2010) use adversarial removals (fixed max number) and have no hidden units. Marginalizing QX2 yields deterministic regularizers in simple cases; van der Maaten et al. (2013) call QX2 input noise "blankout noise" but limited to models without hidden layers; Chen et al. (2012) on marginalization for DAEs; Wang & Manning (2013) propose marginalization to accelerate QX2.

steps.notes_before: Paper: Dropout (QX2) — gate unit outputs during training, independently per unit with r_j^{(l)} ~ Bernoulli(p); tilde y^{(l)} = r^{(l)} * y^{(l)}. At inference no units removed; test-time weights scaled by retention p: W_test^{(l)} = p W^{(l)}. Expected preactivation under training dropout equals test preactivation with scaled weights. Both hidden and input (visible) units can be dropped. Validation can pick p; default often near optimal; input retention generally near complete retention. Forward equations: y^{(0)} = x; nominally z_i^{(l+1)} = w_i^{(l+1)} y^{(l)} + b_i^{(l+1)}, y_i^{(l+1)} = f(z_i^{(l+1)}). Example activation: logistic f(x)=1/(1+exp(-x)). Note: this part contains an indexing inconsistency — it first states l∈{1..L} then uses l∈{0..L-1} for the feed-forward formulas (treating y^{(0)} as input). Keep this in mind when later parts refer to layer indices.

Paper: QX2 = dropout (per-unit gate r_j^(l) ~ Bernoulli(p); ̃y^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l)). At test time do not drop units; scale weights by retention p (W_test = p W) so expected preactivation under dropout equals test preactivation. Both hidden and input units can be dropped (input retention usually near 1). Forward eqns use y^(0)=x; paper has an indexing inconsistency (uses l∈{1..L} then l∈{0..L-1}).

Sec.5 (Learning QX2 Nets): training = backprop through sampled subnetworks (one mask per case/minibatch case), gradients averaged across cases; a dropped parameter gets zero contribution. QX2 alone gives significant gains; combining QX2 with high momentum, large decaying learning rates and V9C (max-norm) gives further boost. V9C constrains each hidden unit's incoming weight vector via projection to ||w||_2 <= c (validation tunes c); projection returns w to the radius-c surface if exceeded. Proposed optimization story: fixed-radius weight ball allows huge LRs without explosion; QX2 noise explores; annealing settles.

Empirical notes cited: Table 9 rows: V9C=1.35, QX2+Y5F=1.25, QX2+V9C=1.05. Appendix A.2: practical LRs typically 10–100x optimal standard-net LR and momentum ~0.95–0.99. Pretraining: unchanged, but before QX2 finetuning multiply pretrained weights by 1/p so expected outputs under dropout match pretraining; use much smaller finetuning LR (Appendix B.4 reports ~0.01 best vs listed high LR 0.1). Table 2: G6W finetuning 1.18 -> 0.92 with QX2; E5Q 0.96 -> 0.79.

errors.claim: The paper says dropout approximates an 'equally weighted geometric mean' of many models' predictions, but later claims the test-time output equals the expected (training-time) output.
errors.evidence: This part states: 'We propose to do this by approximating an equally weighted geometric mean of the predictions of an exponential number of learned models that share parameters.' Later (Figure 2 caption) it states: 'The output at test time is same as the expected output at training time.'
errors.explanation: A geometric mean of predictions is not the same operation as the expectation (arithmetic mean) over predictions. The text asserts both without reconciling or explaining when they are equivalent, creating an internal inconsistency.

final_notes: Appendix B: dataset/training details. MNIST: 60k train (held-out 10k val), 10k test; tuned on val for 1M updates then merged and trained 1M updates; nets: 2/3/4 layers × {1024,2048} (plus some 4096/8192 runs); dropout hidden p=0.5 input p=0.8; momentum=0.95; max-norm c=2. SVHN: ~600k train, 26k test, val 6k; inputs RGB zero-mean/unit-variance; best net: 3 conv layers (96,128,256 5×5) + pooling then two FC 2048; ReLU; dropout keep-probs p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5) (input→conv→fc); max-norm c=4; momentum=0.95; did not merge val for final SVHN. CIFAR-10/100: 50k train, 10k test, 5k val; followed MNIST tuning/merging; per-channel global contrast normalization + ZCA. (Elsewhere: "network architecture and dropout rates are same as that for SVHN, except input-layer learning rates set smaller"). TIMIT (B.4): Kaldi→log-filterbanks; monophone forced-alignment; windows of 21 frames, predict center frame; inputs mean-centered/unit-variance; dropout p_input=0.8, p_hidden=0.5; stated max-norm c=4 used in all layers (but text later says adding max-norm gave no improvement for DBN finetuning); momentum=0.95; initial LR 0.1 with decay eta0/(1+t/T); DBN pretraining RBMs with CD-1 (Gaussian RBM input variance fixed to 1); DBN finetuning with dropout used smaller LR ≈0.01. Alternative Splicing (B.6): 3665 exons, 1014 features, 4 tissues; output: 4 softmax units (one per tissue) each over 3 states (inc, exc, nc); metric "Code Quality" (formula printed); two-layer dropout net, 1024 units/layer; p_input=0.7, p_hidden=0.5; max-norm reg and high decaying LRs; results averaged over same 5 folds as Xiong et al. (2011).

Paper: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (JMLR 15, 2014). Authors: Nitish Srivastava, Geoffrey Hinton, Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, Ruslan Salakhutdinov. Abstract/main claim: Dropout randomly drops units and their connections during training to prevent co-adaptation; training effectively samples from an exponential number of "thinned" networks. At test time, the effect of averaging these thinned networks is approximated by using a single unthinned network with scaled (smaller) weights. Dropout reportedly reduces overfitting and outperforms other regularization methods, producing major improvements and state-of-the-art results on benchmarks in vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology. Intro notes: deep nets are expressive and prone to overfitting; common regularizers include early stopping, L1/L2 penalties, and soft weight sharing. The paper states that with unlimited computation the best regularizer is averaging predictions over all parameter settings (sentence is cut off in this part). Figure 1 caption: left—standard net with 2 hidden layers; right—example thinned net after dropout where some units are dropped.

errors.claim: The paper says dropout approximates an 'equally weighted geometric mean' of many models' predictions, but later claims the test-time output equals the expected (training-time) output.
errors.evidence: This part states: 'We propose to do this by approximating an equally weighted geometric mean of the predictions of an exponential number of learned models that share parameters.' Later (Figure 2 caption) it states: 'The output at test time is same as the expected output at training time.'
errors.explanation: A geometric mean of predictions is not the same operation as the expectation (arithmetic mean) over predictions. The text asserts both without reconciling or explaining when they are equivalent, creating an internal inconsistency.

steps.notes_before: Paper: Dropout (JMLR 2014). Dropout: randomly remove (drop) hidden and visible units during training to prevent co-adaptation; training samples from an exponential number of 'thinned' networks. Authors propose to approximate an equally weighted geometric mean of predictions of these many learned models (to approach Bayesian averaging) using shared parameters. Simple dropout: retain each unit with probability p (often p=0.5 for hidden units; input units usually have retention closer to 1); p can be chosen by validation. At test time use a single unthinned network with weights scaled by p (Figure 2 shows training: unit present with prob. p and weight w; test: unit always present and weight pw) and the caption asserts test output equals the expected training-time output. Key numbers/claims: exponential number of thinned models, p≈0.5 for hidden, input retention ≈1, test-time weight scaling by p.

steps.notes_before: Paper: Dropout (JMLR 2014). Dropout randomly removes hidden/visible units during training, sampling a 'thinned' network each presentation; weights are shared across thinned models. Paper states there are exponentially many thinned networks (2^n), though this part prints '2n' (likely a typo/inconsistency). Total number of parameters remains O(n^2) or less due to sharing. Training: each update samples a new thinned network; thus each specific thinned net is trained rarely. Test-time: use single unthinned network with outgoing weights scaled by retention probability p (if unit retained with prob p during training, multiply its outgoing weights by p at test time) so that test-time activations match expected training-time activations. Typical choices: p≈0.5 for hidden units; input-unit retention closer to 1; choose p by validation. Dropout not limited to feed-forward nets—paper introduces dropout RBM and compares to standard RBMs, claiming improvements in some respects. Paper structure: Secs 2–9 and Appendix A (practical guide, hyperparameter advice).

Paper: Dropout (JMLR 2014). Core idea: during training randomly remove (drop out) hidden/visible units, sampling a 'thinned' network each presentation; weights are shared across thinned models. There are exponentially many thinned networks (paper elsewhere prints 2^n; an earlier printed '2n' looked like a typo). Total number of parameters remains O(n^2) or less due to sharing. Training: each update samples a new thinned network so any specific thinned net is trained rarely. Test-time: use single unthinned network with outgoing weights scaled by the unit's retention probability p so test activations match expected training activations. Typical p ≈ 0.5 for hidden units; input retention closer to 1; choose p by validation. Dropout not limited to feed-forward nets (paper introduces dropout RBM). Structure: Secs 2–9 and Appendix A (practical guide). New from current part: Motivation analogies — sexual reproduction: dropout viewed as preventing large co-adaptations, forcing each hidden unit to learn useful features that work with random subsets of partners, improving robustness; copying units to resist dropout is a poor solution (analogy to replica codes for noisy channels). Conspiracy analogy: many small conspiracies (small co-adaptations) more robust than one large co-adaptation, hence better generalization under non-stationarity. Related work: Dropout can be seen as regularization via adding noise to hidden units; this idea relates to Denoising Autoencoders (Vincent et al. 2008, 2010) which add noise to unit states.

steps.notes_before: Paper: Dropout trains by randomly dropping units (thinning) and sharing weights across exponentially many sub-networks. Training samples a new thinned net each presentation; backpropagate gradients through that thinned net. At test time use a single unthinned net with weights scaled by retention probabilities (W_test = p W^(l) per layer). Typical choices: drop ~50% hidden units (p_hidden ≈ 0.5), ~20% inputs (p_input ≈ 0.8); DAEs typically use 5% input noise but test-time scaling allows higher noise. Dropout can be applied to hidden layers and other neuron-based architectures (e.g., Boltzmann Machines, RBMs). Interpretation: stochastic regularization / model averaging; related to denoising autoencoders and marginalizing noise. Definition details: network with L hidden layers; y(0)=x; feed-forward recurrence given as z^{(l+1)} = W^{(l+1)} y^{(l)} + b^{(l+1)}, y^{(l+1)} = f(z^{(l+1)}). With dropout: sample r^{(l)} ~ Bernoulli(p) elementwise, form y_e^{(l)} = r^{(l)} * y^{(l)} and use y_e^{(l)} as input to next layer. Loss is minimized stochastically (expected loss); prior adversarial-drop work fixes max number dropped (no hidden-layer models).

Training: dropout nets trained by SGD on ‘‘thinned’’ nets — for each training case in a mini‑batch sample dropout mask, do forward/backprop on that thinned net; gradients averaged over mini‑batch; any case that omits a parameter contributes zero gradient for that parameter. Standard SGD tricks (momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 weight decay) help. Max‑norm regularization: constrain incoming weight vector w at each hidden unit to ||w||2 ≤ c by projecting back into the ball of radius c whenever it exceeds c (c is a tunable hyperparameter). Max‑norm often improves SGD even without dropout; combining dropout + max‑norm + large decaying LR + high momentum gives further gains (intuition: ball constraint prevents blowup so large LR can be used for exploration). Unsupervised pretraining: stacks of RBMs/autoencoders/DBMs can be used; pretraining stays the same, but when finetuning with dropout scale pretrained weights by 1/p so expected output under dropout matches pretraining output. If finetune LR is too large pretrained information can be lost; use smaller LR to retain gains. Experiments: datasets include MNIST, TIMIT, CIFAR‑10/100, SVHN, ImageNet, Reuters‑RCV1, and an Alternative Splicing RNA dataset; more details in Appendix B.

Added from this part: Section 7.5 (Monte-Carlo averaging): On MNIST, test-time averaging of k randomly sampled dropout networks approaches the true model average as k→∞. Figure 11 compares Monte-Carlo averaging (varying k) to the weight-scaling approximate method (horizontal line). Empirically k ≈ 50 suffices for Monte-Carlo to match the weight-scaling method; for larger k Monte-Carlo is slightly better but within one standard deviation, so weight-scaling is a good approximation. Section 8 (Dropout RBMs): Define RBM with v∈{0,1}^D, h∈{0,1}^F and P(h,v;θ)=1/Z exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v). Introduce mask r∈{0,1}^F with r_j ~ Bernoulli(p). Joint: P(r,h,v;p,θ)=P(r;p) P(h,v|r;θ), P(r;p)=∏ p^{r_j}(1-p)^{1-r_j}. P(h,v|r;θ)=1/Z'(θ,r) exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v) ∏_j g(h_j,r_j), where g(h_j,r_j)=1(r_j=1)+1(r_j=0)1(h_j=0) (enforces h_j=0 when dropped). Conditioned on r and v, the hidden units factorize: P(h_j=1|r_j,v)=1(r_j=1) σ(b_j + ∑_i W_{ij} v_i) (otherwise 0). Conditioned on h, visible units: P(v_i=1|h)=σ(a_i + ∑_j W_{ij} h_j). Thus a Dropout RBM is a mixture (over r) of RBMs with subsets of hidden units. Learning: apply CD-1, sampling a new r per training case per minibatch. Section 8.3 compares features learned by 256-unit RBM vs Dropout RBM (p=0.5), features ordered by L2 norm (Figures 12a,b). Earlier key results retained (ImageNet, ILSVRC, MNIST regularizer numbers, p≈0.5 default, experiments on p and dataset size) remain unchanged.

Section 7.5 (Monte-Carlo averaging): On MNIST, test-time averaging of k randomly sampled dropout networks approaches the true model average as k→∞. Empirically k ≈ 50 suffices for Monte-Carlo to match the weight-scaling approximation; for larger k Monte-Carlo is slightly better but within one standard deviation. Section 8 (Dropout RBMs): RBM defined with v∈{0,1}^D, h∈{0,1}^F, P(h,v)∝exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v). Introduce mask r∈{0,1}^F, r_j∼Bernoulli(p); P(h_j=1|r_j,v)=1(r_j=1) σ(b_j+∑_i W_{ij} v_i). Dropout RBM = mixture (over r) of RBMs with subsets of hidden units. Learning: CD-1 with a new r per training case per minibatch. Section 8.3: features from 256-unit RBM vs Dropout RBM (p=0.5) compared, features ordered by L2 norm. Section 8.4 (this part): dropout RBM features appear coarser than sharp stroke-like standard RBM features; there are reportedly very few dead units in dropout RBM relative to standard RBM. Figure 13 histograms (13a standard RBM, 13b dropout RBM) show dropout RBMs learn much sparser hidden activations (many activations near zero, few high). Section 9 (Marginalizing Dropout): dropout can be marginalized to form deterministic models; prior work cited. 9.1 Linear regression: with input dropout (each input retained with prob p), E_R ||y-(R*X)w||^2 reduces to ||y - pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Γ w||^2 (Γ = sqrt(diag(…)) — paper text garbled), i.e., dropout in expectation equivalent to ridge-like regularizer scaling with p; absorbing p into w shows regularizer grows as p decreases. 9.2: for logistic regression approximate marginalization via Gaussian approx (Wang & Manning) can be efficient but assumptions weaken for deeper nets. Table (end of part): Bernoulli vs Gaussian dropout test errors: MNIST (2-layer 1024) 1.08±0.04 vs 0.95±0.04; CIFAR-10 (3 conv + 2 fc) 12.6±0.1 vs 12.5±0.1.

Section 7.5: Monte-Carlo test-time averaging of k dropout networks approaches true model average; k≈50 suffices to match weight-scaling; larger k slightly better within one std. Section 8 (Dropout RBMs): RBM with v∈{0,1}^D,h∈{0,1}^F; mask r_j∼Bernoulli(p) applied to hidden units; CD-1 with new r per case; dropout RBM gives coarser features, far fewer dead units, and much sparser hidden activations (Fig.13). Section 9 (Marginalizing dropout): Input dropout in linear regression yields objective ||y - pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Γ w||^2 (dropout ≃ ridge-like regularizer; regularizer grows as p decreases). Logistic regression: Gaussian approx can marginalize but weakens for deep nets. Section 10 (Multiplicative Gaussian Noise): Generalize dropout to multiply activations by r0∼N(1,σ^2) (e.g. N(1,1) found to work well); equivalently add hi r with r∼N(0,1). E[activation] unchanged so no test-time scaling needed if using mean-1 noise; alternative implementation is to scale retained activations by 1/p at train time (or scale weights by p at test time)—these are equivalent with appropriate learning-rate/init scaling. To match Bernoulli dropout moments, set σ^2=(1-p)/p so Var(r0)=Var(scaled Bernoulli)=(1-p)/p and E=1. Authors note Gaussian (higher entropy) may work slightly better. Table 10: experiments averaged over 10 random seeds. MNIST: Bernoulli p_hidden=0.5, p_input=0.8; Bernoulli error 1.08±0.04 vs Gaussian 0.95±0.04. CIFAR-10: p per layer (0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5) from input to top; Bernoulli 12.6±0.1 vs Gaussian 12.5±0.1.

We found this to be a useful heuristic..." while Appendix A.4 states, "Smaller p requires big n which slows down the training and leads to underfitting."
errors.explanation: Appendix A.1 recommends increasing layer size to about n/p to preserve capacity under dropout; Appendix A.4 asserts that making n big (as required when p is small) leads to underfitting. These two statements within the paper contradict each other (increasing model size should counter underfitting, not cause it).

steps.notes_before: Conclusion: Dropout is a general technique improving performance across domains (SVHN, ImageNet, CIFAR-100, MNIST) and extends to RBMs (Dropout RBMs yield coarser features, fewer dead units, sparser activations). Drawback: training time increases (typ. 2–3×) due to noisy updates; stochasticity helps prevent overfitting. Marginalizing dropout: for linear regression yields modified L2 regularizer (regularizer grows as p decreases); harder for deep models. Multiplicative Gaussian noise: mean-1 noise avoids test-time scaling; to match Bernoulli moments set σ^2=(1-p)/p. Experiments averaged over 10 seeds (e.g. MNIST Bernoulli p_hidden=0.5, p_input=0.8: error 1.08±0.04 vs Gaussian 0.95±0.04; CIFAR-10 Bernoulli vs Gaussian ~12.6±0.1 vs 12.5±0.1). Appendix heuristics: Network size — expected active units pn so set layer size ≈ n/p; Learning rate/momentum — use much larger LR (10–100× standard) and momentum ~0.95–0.99; Max-norm regularization — incoming weight norm capped (c≈3–4); Dropout rates — hidden p typically 0.5–0.8, input p≈0.8 for real-valued inputs. Note: internal inconsistency in Appendix about whether increasing n (for small p) alleviates or causes underfitting (see error above).

Appendix B gives dataset and training details. Code/GPU libs: cudamat, cuda-convnet. MNIST: 60k train, 10k test; held out 10k val. Hyperparams tuned to best val error after 1M updates; then val merged into train and net trained for 1M updates more before test. Architectures: all combinations of 2/3/4 layers × {1024,2048} units (6 nets). Dropout: hidden p=0.5, input p=0.8 for all MNIST runs. Momentum=0.95, max-norm constraint c=2 for MNIST. Also tried 2/3-layer nets with 4096 and 8192 units; 2-layer nets improved, 3-layer didn’t beat 2-layer even with increased dropout. SVHN: ~600k train, 26k test; val 6k (400/class from standard, 200/class from extra). Inputs RGB zero-mean/unit-variance. Best net: 3 conv layers (96,128,256 filters, 5×5, stride1) each followed by 3×3 pooling stride2, then two FC hidden layers of 2048 units. ReLU units. Dropout keep-probs p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5) (input→conv→fc), max-norm c=4, momentum=0.95. Did not merge val into train for final SVHN training. CIFAR-10/100: 50k train, 10k test; 5k val. Followed MNIST procedure (tune on val, then merge and retrain). Preprocessing: per-channel global contrast normalization then ZCA whitening.

final_notes: QX2 = multiplicative (dropout-style) noise for feed-forward nets. Training: momentum, decaying LR, max-norm (V9C); when fine-tuning pretrained nets, weights scaled by 1/p before QX2 fine-tuning. Key reported results: MNIST best QX2+V9C = 1.05% (baselines: Y5F 1.62; V9C 1.35). SVHN conv ≈ 2.47%. CIFAR-10/100 hand-tuned convs 15.60/43.48; +QX2(all) 12.61/37.20; +L8J 11.68/38.57. ImageNet conv val ≈ 40.7% Top-1 / 18.2% Top-5. TIMIT frame results had a small reported discrepancy (20.7 vs 20.5). Genetics (Z7P Table 8) C4Y scores: NN early stop 440; Regression+PCA 463; SVM+PCA 487; NN+QX2 567; Bayesian NN 623. QX2 yields more localized 1st-layer features, reduces co-adaptations; hidden activations sparser (mean no-QX2 ≈2.0, QX2 ≈0.7). Retention p: severe underfit at very low p; error falls then flattens for 0.4≤p≤0.8; best ≈0.6, default ≈0.5. Heuristics: width ≳ n/p; QX2 needs much larger LR (typically 10–100× standard) and higher momentum (standard ~0.9; QX2 often 0.95–0.99). V9C c typically 3–4. Gaussian multiplicative noise: match Bernoulli first two moments with σ^2=(1-p)/p; scaling retained training activations by 1/p gives E[noise]=1 so no test-time scaling needed. Training often ~2–3× slower per convergence. Appendix details added: - For speech setting: consecutive frames per window =21; input p=0.8; hidden p=0.5; V9C c=4; momentum 0.95; high LR=0.1 with decay ε0(1+t/T)^{-1}; G6W pretraining = U2L with CD-1; Gaussian-U2L input-unit variance fixed=1; best QX2 G6W-finetuning LR ≈0.01 (smaller LR important). - M5X subset: 402,738 articles, 2000-word vocab, 50 categories, >200k training examples. - Z7P: 3,665 cassette exons, 1,014 RNA features, 4 tissue types; outputs: 4 softmaxes (inc, exc, nc); objective C4Y = Σ_i Σ_t Σ_s p_{i,t}^s log(q_t^s(r_i)/ ar p^s). QX2 hidden-unit scale: ~1000s; trained QX2 net: 2 layers × 1024 units; hidden p=0.5; input p=0.7; regularization V9C; high decaying LRs; results averaged over same 5 folds as Xiong et al. (2011).

Title: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting". Authors: Nitish Srivastava, Geoffrey Hinton, Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, Ruslan Salakhutdinov; Dept. of Computer Science, University of Toronto. Journal: JMLR 15 (2014). Header lists pages 1929–1958 while page map lists pages 1930–1955 (internal inconsistency noted). Abstract summary: introduces dropout (called "QX2: dropout") — a training procedure that temporarily removes randomly selected units and their connections, inhibiting excessive co-adaptation and effectively sampling exponentially many parameter-sharing thinned networks. At test time a single unthinned network with reduced weights approximates the averaged predictions of these thinned networks. Claims dropout substantially reduces overfitting versus other regularizers and yields major improvements, achieving state-of-the-art performance on many benchmarks in supervised vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology.

steps.notes_before: Title: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al., UToronto). Header/page-number inconsistency noted earlier. Dropout (QX2) randomly removes units/connections during training, producing exponentially many (2^n for n units) thinned networks; parameters are shared so total distinct parameters retained are O(n^2) or fewer. With unlimited computation, posterior-weighted averaging over parameters is ideal; the paper claims its method approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of these thinned models' predictions (introduction) — earlier abstract wording said it "approximates the averaged predictions", a potential arithmetic vs geometric-mean wording mismatch. Every presentation samples/trains a new thinned member; individual members are rarely trained thoroughly. Practical inference: T6R (weight scaling) uses one unthinned network at test time; X9M refers to Monte-Carlo model averaging (more expensive). Claims T6R gives much lower generalization error than other regularizers across tasks. Method extends to graphical models, e.g., Dropout RBM (B8T) from RBMs (U2L). Paper map: §2 motivation; §3 prior work; §4 formal model; §5 training algorithm; §6 experiments; §7 network/hyperparameter interactions; §8 Dropout RBMs; §9 marginalization; Appendix A practical guidance.

Title: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al.). Earlier: header/page-number inconsistency noted. Method overview: dropout (QX2) randomly removes units/connections during training, producing exponentially many (2^n) thinned networks; parameters are shared so total distinct parameters are O(n^2) or fewer. Training samples/train different thinned networks; individual thinned members rarely trained thoroughly. Test-time inference: T6R = weight-scaling using one unthinned network; X9M = Monte-Carlo model averaging (more expensive). Paper claims T6R yields much lower generalization error than other regularizers across tasks. Extensions: Dropout RBM (B8T). Paper map: §2 motivation; §3 prior work; §4 formal model; §5 training algorithm; §6 experiments; §7 interactions; §8 Dropout RBMs; §9 marginalization; Appendix A guidance. New from §2 (Motivation): authors use biological analogy—sexual vs asexual reproduction—and cite Livnat et al. (2010) arguing selection can favor gene "mix-ability" rather than individual-fitness optimization. Dropout is analogous: hidden units face randomly selected partners, which favors independently useful, robust features and reduces complex co-adaptations. Replicating units many times is deemed a poor robustness fix (analogy to replica codes and noisy channels). Conspiracy analogy: many small cooperating subsets are more robust under non-stationarity than a single large co-adapted set; complex co-adaptations may overfit training data and fail on novel test data.

Title: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al.). Method: dropout (QX2) randomly removes units/connections during training producing ~2^n thinned networks; parameters shared so distinct params O(n^2). Training: each SGD update samples a thinned network; individual thinned members rarely trained thoroughly. Test-time inference: T6R = weight-scaling using one unthinned network; X9M = Monte-Carlo model averaging (more expensive). Paper claims T6R gives much lower generalization error than other regularizers across tasks. Motivation (§2): biological analogy (mix-ability), reduces co-adaptations. Related work (§3): dropout interpretable as noise in hidden-unit states, extends denoising autoencoders (Vincent et al. 2008/2010) — effective hidden-layer corruption, model-averaging view, supervised/unsupervised use, applicable to Boltzmann Machines. Table: S2H (DAE) typical best noise ~5%; QX2 often optimal input-unit removal ~20%; QX2 often optimal hidden-unit removal ~50%. Adversarial-removal alternatives (Globerson & Roweis 2006; Dekel et al. 2010) consider worst-case removals under a budget and have no hidden units. Analytic marginalization can give deterministic regularizers in simple cases; van der Maaten et al. (2013) studied exponential-family input-noise (blankout) limited to models without hidden layers; Chen et al. (2012) studied marginalization for DAEs; Wang & Manning (2013) proposed marginalization to speed up dropout. Section map: §2 motivation; §3 prior work; §4 formal model; §5 training algorithm; §6 experiments; §7 interactions; §8 Dropout RBMs; §9 marginalization; Appendix A guidance.

Paper: Dropout regularization. Key idea: during training randomly delete (zero) units (hidden and/or visible) to sample many thinned subnetworks; parameters shared across subnetworks. Retention choices are independent Bernoulli variables with common probability p (can be chosen by validation). Typical defaults: hidden-unit retention p≈0.5 (i.e. ~50% removal); input-unit removal often ~20% (retention p≈0.8) — input retention usually nearer full. Training: each SGD update samples r^{(l)} (vector of independent Bernoulli(p)) and forms \tilde y^{(l)} = r^{(l)} * y^{(l)}; forward: z_i^{(l+1)} = w_i^{(l+1)} \tilde y^{(l)} + b_i^{(l+1)}, y_i^{(l+1)} = f(z_i^{(l+1)}). Backprop passes gradients through the sampled subnetwork. Notation: y^{(0)}=x; L hidden layers (indexed 1..L); feed-forward written for l=0..L-1 producing layer l+1. Activation f can be any (e.g. logistic). Test-time inference: no dropout; use one unthinned network with outgoing weights scaled by p: W_test^{(l)} = p W^{(l)} (equivalently unit outputs' expected training contribution equals test-time contribution with scaled weights). Figures illustrate training (stochastic gates r) vs testing (weights scaled by p). Other parts: training samples many subnetworks per SGD update; Monte-Carlo averaging at test-time is an alternative to weight-scaling but more expensive.

Part 5: QX2 (dropout) gives significant gains; combining it with high momentum, large decaying learning rates, and an incoming-weight constraint (V9C = max-norm) gives further improvement. V9C enforces ||w||_2 <= c with projection to the ball surface when exceeded; c is tuned by validation. Proposed optimization account claims large learning rates are safe inside the fixed-radius ball; QX2 provides noise exploration; learning rates decay to smaller steps. SGD differs from standard training only by per-case sampled thinned networks: each mini-batch case uses its own sampled network; gradients averaged across cases; a case not using a parameter contributes zero. Momentum, annealed (decaying) learning rates and other heuristics remain useful. Unsupervised pretraining is unchanged, but before QX2 finetuning pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p so each unit’s expected random-removal output matches its pretraining output. Smaller finetuning learning rates help preserve pretrained information. Pretraining (with unlabeled data) can improve over random init; applicable to stacked U2L, autoencoders, DBMs for finetuning.

Closed-form marginalization is hard for deep nets. Part 10 (current): multiplicative Gaussian noise (D4K) matches Bernoulli dropout (P7V) first two moments; Gaussian has higher entropy; preliminary results slightly favor Gaussian: Table 10 H4Z P7V 1.08±0.04 vs D4K 0.95±0.04; J3V P7V 12.6±0.1 vs D4K 12.5±0.1. N(1,1) corresponds to h_i -> h_i + h_i r, r~N(0,1). Unchanged E[r] removes need for test-time scaling.

Part 11 (conclusion): interprets QX2 as training many smaller submodels from an overfitted large model; U2L matches this construction; B8T shows good empirical properties. Noise marginalization can give expectation-equivalent regularizers (linear regression example), but equivalents for deep models are unclear; accelerating QX2 is future work.

final_notes: Implementation: GPU (code link), cudamat & cuda-convnet. MNIST: 60k train, 10k test; 10k val held out; hyperparams chosen so best val after 1M updates, then retrain on train+val 1M updates. Fig.4 nets: 2/3/4 hidden × {1024,2048}; for those (and Table 2) hidden p=0.5, input p=0.8, final momentum=0.95; max-norm c=2 for MNIST experiments; larger 2-layer nets (4096→1.01%, 8192→0.95%). SVHN: ~600k train, 26k test; 6k val; inputs zero-mean/unit-var; arch: 3 conv layers (96,128,256, 5×5), pool 3×3 stride 2, two FC 2048, ReLU; retention p roughly (input 0.9, convs 0.75, FCs 0.5); max-norm c=4, momentum=0.95; val model selected (no retrain on full due to large train set). General/default heuristics: hidden p≈0.5, input p≈0.8; recommended max-norm ≈3–4 (but MNIST used 2, SVHN 4). TIMIT / speech (DBN + dropout): retention p=0.8 input, p=0.5 hidden; reportedly used max-norm c=4 and momentum=0.95 with high LR 0.1 and decay ε0(1+t/T)^{-1}; DBN pretraining RBMs CD-1, Gaussian RBM input variance fixed at 1. For dropout finetuning of DBN best results used smaller LR ~0.01; authors also state adding max-norm to DBN finetuning 'gave no improvement' (text inconsistent about whether max-norm was applied). Reported speech dropout results (Table 7): 21.8%, 19.7%, 19.7%. Reuters: subset 402,738 docs (vocab 2000, 50 classes), split equally into train/test (~201k each); dropout helped all architectures but gains smaller than image/speech; best-net 31.05% without dropout vs 29.62% with dropout. Alternative splicing: 3665 exons, 1014 features, 4 tissue types; targets: 4 softmaxes (3 states each: inc, exc, nc); Code Quality metric = sum_{i,t,s} p_{i,t}^s log(q_t^s(r_i)/ ar p^s). Trained 2-layer dropout net with 1024 units/layer, p(input)=0.7, p(hidden)=0.5, used max-norm and high decaying LRs; results averaged over same 5 folds as Xiong et al. (2011). Paper summary: Introduces dropout — randomly removing units and their connections during training, which samples many smaller networks that share weights. At test time, a single full network with scaled weights approximates the ensemble of sampled networks. Reports improvements on image, speech, text, and alternative-splicing tasks. Compares dropout with other regularizers and Bayesian neural networks. Studies learned features, sparsity, dropout rates, network size, training-set size, and test-time averaging; finds Dropout Restricted Boltzmann Machines learn qualitatively different features and sparser representations. For linear regression, marginalizing dropout yields a modified ridge-regression objective. Preliminary experiments compare Bernoulli dropout to multiplicative Gaussian noise. Limitation noted: training time typically 2–3× longer than standard networks with the same architecture.

Paper introduces dropout: during training randomly remove units and their incoming/outgoing connections (Bernoulli dropout uses binary vars that equal 1 with probability p, the retention probability). At test time the ensemble is approximated by a single deterministic model via weight scaling (multiply a unit’s outgoing weights by p) or by marginalizing dropout noise (deterministic dropout model); Monte-Carlo dropout/model averaging samples thinned networks at test time. Gaussian (multiplicative) dropout multiplies activations by Gaussian noise; paper compares Bernoulli and Gaussian variants. For linear regression, marginalized dropout is equivalent in expectation to a modified ridge (Tikhonov) regression. Dropout-RBMs are RBMs augmented with binary retention variables; CD-1/Contrastive Divergence used for RBM training; partition function Z(θ) appears in RBM formulation. Code Quality (alternative-splicing task) is the negative KL-divergence metric (higher is better). Other key methods/terms: DBN/DBM pretraining, max-norm constraint (bound hidden-unit incoming weight norms), L1/L2 weight penalties, KL-sparsity regularizer, ReLU and maxout units, pooling (max, L2, L4) in image models, max-pooling after conv layers, permutation-invariant vs 2-D MNIST settings, Top-1/Top-5 ImageNet error definitions, PCA/ZCA whitening used in preprocessing, mix-ability measure for genes. Noted limitation: training time typically 2–3× longer than standard networks with same architecture.

Key methods: dropout — Bernoulli dropout uses binary retention vars (retain with prob p); at test time approximate ensemble by weight-scaling (multiply outgoing weights by p) or by marginalizing dropout noise (deterministic model); Monte-Carlo dropout averages samples of thinned networks at test time; Gaussian (multiplicative) dropout multiplies activations by Gaussian noise. For linear regression, marginalized dropout = modified ridge (Tikhonov). Dropout-RBMs include binary retention variables; trained with CD-1. Code Quality metric = negative KL-divergence (higher is better). Regularization/architecture details: DBN/DBM pretraining; max-norm constraint (bound hidden-unit incoming weight norms); L1/L2 penalties; KL-sparsity regularizer; ReLU and maxout units; pooling: max, L2, L4; max-pooling after conv layers; permutation-invariant vs 2-D MNIST distinction. Datasets and features: MNIST; TIMIT (preprocessed to log-filter banks via Kaldi; monophone system used for forced alignment/speech-frame labels); CIFAR-10/100; SVHN (RGB pixels normalized; comparisons list Binary Features (WDCH), HOG, KMeans); ImageNet / ILSVRC (ILSVRC-2010, ILSVRC-2012; ILSVRC discussed in Sec. 6.1.4); Reuters-RCV1; Alternative Splicing dataset (RNA features; softmax targets inc/exc/nc; mix-ability measure).
