(Earlier: Sec 6.5 Table 9: Dropout+Max-norm best 1.05% test error; Sec 6.4 Table 8: Bayesian NN > Dropout NN > other non-Bayesian on small splicing dataset.) Section 8 (Dropout RBMs): defines binary RBM with dropout mask r in {0,1}^F (retain prob p). Joint P(r,h,v)=P(r;p)P(h,v|r;θ) with constraint g enforcing h_j=0 when r_j=0; conditional P(h_j=1|r_j,v)=1(r_j=1)·σ(b_j+Σ_i W_ij v_i). Learning: sample r each minibatch and train with standard RBM methods (CD-1 used). Experiments on MNIST, 256 hidden units, p=0.5: Figure 12 — dropout RBM features look coarser than stroke-like standard RBM and appear to have fewer dead units; Figure 13 — activation histograms show much sparser representations with dropout (no numeric sparsity measures reported).

Section 7 (Salient Features) key points: 7.1 One-layer autoencoders (256 ReLUs) on MNIST: dropout (p=0.5) yields more interpretable features (strokes/edges) vs. no dropout; test reconstruction errors similar. 7.2 Dropout induces sparser activations without explicit sparsity regularizer: mean activation per unit (test minibatch) drops ~2.0 -> ~0.7; activation histogram shows sharp peak at zero with dropout. 7.3 Retention p effects: (A) keep n fixed: small p underfits; classification error falls as p increases, flat for 0.4<=p<=0.8, then rises as p->1. (B) keep expected retained units pn fixed by increasing n as p decreases: low-p with larger n can give much smaller errors; p~0.6 best, default p=0.5 close. 7.4 Dataset size: dropout gives no gain for tiny sets (100,500); gain grows then declines as data increases (a "sweet spot"). 7.5 Monte-Carlo model averaging: sampling k networks approaches true average; ~50 samples matches weight-scaling approximation reasonably. (Earlier: Sec 6.5 Table 9: Dropout+Max-norm best 1.05% test error; Sec 6.4 Table 8: Bayesian NN > Dropout NN > other non-Bayesian on small splicing dataset.) Section 8 (Dropout RBMs): sample hidden-mask r per minibatch (p=0.5), train with CD-1; dropout RBM features coarser, sparser activations, fewer dead units. Section 9 (Marginalizing Dropout): marginalizing dropout yields deterministic objectives with computable gradients. 9.1 Linear regression: minimizing E_R ||y-(R*X)w||^2 reduces to ||y-pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Gamma w||^2 where Gamma = (diag(X^T X))^{1/2}; with tilde w = p w this is ||y-X tilde w||^2 + ((1-p)/p)||Gamma tilde w||^2, so regularization grows as p decreases. 9.2 Logistic/deep nets: closed-form marginalization hard; Wang & Manning (2013) give Gaussian-based approximations that speed training and can improve generalization for logistic regression, but assumptions weaken with added layers and don't directly extend to deep networks.

Section 7 (Salient Features): 7.1 One-layer autoencoders (256 ReLUs) on MNIST: dropout (p=0.5) yields more interpretable features (strokes/edges) vs. no dropout; test reconstruction errors similar. 7.2 Dropout induces sparser activations w/o explicit sparsity regularizer: mean activation per unit drops ~2.0 -> ~0.7; activation histogram shows sharp peak at zero with dropout. 7.3 Retention p effects: (A) keep n fixed: small p underfits; classification error falls as p increases, flat for 0.4<=p<=0.8, then rises as p->1. (B) keep expected retained units pn fixed by increasing n as p decreases: low-p with larger n can give much smaller errors; p~0.6 best, default p=0.5 close. 7.4 Dataset size: dropout gives no gain for tiny sets (100,500); gain grows then declines as data increases (a "sweet spot"). 7.5 Monte-Carlo model averaging: sampling k networks approaches true average; ~50 samples matches weight-scaling approximation reasonably. Section 8 (Dropout RBMs): sample hidden-mask r per minibatch (p=0.5), train CD-1; dropout RBM features coarser, sparser activations, fewer dead units. Section 9 (Marginalizing Dropout): marginalizing yields deterministic objectives; 9.1 Linear regression: marginalizing yields objective ||y-pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Gamma w||^2, equivalently ||y-X tilde w||^2 + ((1-p)/p)||Gamma tilde w||^2 so regularization grows as p decreases. 9.2 Logistic/deep nets: closed-form marginalization hard; Gaussian approximations exist but weaken with depth. Section 10 (Multiplicative Gaussian Noise): generalize dropout by multiplying activations by r'~N(1,σ^2); equivalently add zero-mean noise h_i r, r~N(0,1), with noise std equal to |h_i| when σ^2=1. Using training variant that scales retained activations by 1/p gives Bernoulli multiplier r_b with E[r_b]=1, Var[r_b]=(1-p)/p; match Gaussian by setting σ^2=(1-p)/p so E[r_g]=1, Var[r_g]=(1-p)/p. Expected activation unchanged for Gaussian so no test-time weight scaling needed. Authors claim Gaussian (higher entropy) may be slightly better than Bernoulli (lower entropy). Table 10 (10 seeds): MNIST (2×1024) Bernoulli 1.08±0.04 vs Gaussian 0.95±0.04 (hidden p=0.5, input p=0.8); CIFAR-10 (3 conv + 2 fc) Bernoulli 12.6±0.1 vs Gaussian 12.5±0.1 (p per layer = 0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5; σ set to sqrt((1-p)/p)). Results labeled preliminary.

Section 7: One-layer autoencoders (256 ReLUs) on MNIST — dropout (p=0.5) yields more interpretable features (strokes/edges) vs. no dropout; test reconstruction errors similar. Dropout induces sparser activations without explicit sparsity regularizer: mean activation per unit drops ~2.0 -> ~0.7; activation histogram shows sharp peak at zero. Retention p effects: (A) keeping n fixed: very small p underfits; classification error falls as p increases, flat for 0.4<=p<=0.8, then rises as p->1. (B) keeping expected retained units pn fixed by increasing n as p decreases: low-p with larger n can give much smaller errors; p~0.6 best, default p=0.5 close. Dataset size: no gain for tiny sets (100,500); gain grows then declines as data increases (a "sweet spot"). Monte Carlo model averaging: sampling k networks approaches true average; ~50 samples matches weight-scaling approximation reasonably. Section 8: Dropout RBMs (hidden-mask r per minibatch, p=0.5, CD-1) produce coarser features, sparser activations, fewer dead units. Section 9: Marginalizing dropout gives deterministic objectives; linear regression closed form: ||y - pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Γw||^2 (equivalently scaled form) so regularization grows as p decreases; logistic/deep nets lack closed form. Section 10: Multiplicative Gaussian noise r~N(1,σ^2) with σ^2=(1-p)/p matches Bernoulli variance; expected activation unchanged so no test-time scaling needed; preliminary results favor Gaussian slightly (MNIST 1.08±0.04 vs 0.95±0.04; CIFAR-10 12.6±0.1 vs 12.5±0.1). Section 11 (Conclusion): Dropout reduces overfitting by breaking co-adaptations; helps many domains (SVHN, ImageNet, CIFAR-100, MNIST) though Reuters is an exception (31.05% vs 29.62%); extends to RBMs; main drawback is longer training (typically 2–3×); marginalization/acceleration are future directions.

Dropout: randomly remove units and their connections during training, effectively training many smaller networks that share parameters. At test time, use one complete network with reduced weights to approximate averaging the smaller networks' predictions. Claimed benefits: improves generalization over networks without dropout on every tested dataset; reports state-of-the-art results on several benchmarks. Experimental domains: images, speech, documents, gene-splicing prediction. Also examines learned features, sparsity, retention rates, effects of training-set size, Restricted Boltzmann Machines, noise marginalization, and Gaussian corruption. Training cost: typically takes 2–3× longer than training a standard network of the same architecture.

Dropout (QX2): randomly remove units and their connections during training; at test time use one unthinned network with outgoing weights multiplied by the retention probability (T6R) to approximate averaging the thinned-model predictions. The paper states this approximation corresponds to the geometric mean (equally weighted combination) of thinned-network predictions. Two corruption types: Bernoulli dropout (P7V) — binary multiplicative noise (Bernoulli variable =1 with prob p, 0 otherwise) — and Gaussian dropout (D4K) — Gaussian multiplicative noise. Marginalization = expectation over dropout noise to yield a deterministic objective/regularizer; Monte‑Carlo dropout/model averaging = stochastic sampling and averaging predictions from sampled thinned networks. Dropout RBM (B8T): described as a mixture of shared-weight RBMs using different hidden-unit subsets; U2L = RBM; pretraining (DBM/E5Q, DBN/G6W) then finetuning with backprop; mcRBM-G6W is a named pretrained variant. Regularizers: L1 (O3U), L2 (Y5F, Tikhonov), max-norm (V9C), KL-sparsity. Activations mentioned: logistic units, ReLU (F3N), maxout (L8J). Other glossary items to track: geometric mean vs. posterior-weighted averaging, blankout noise, ridge-regression connection (dropout expectation → ridge-like penalty matrix), convolutional-net components (filters, pooling variants), data augmentation, SVM/PCA baselines, terms like dead unit, mix-ability, replica code, and non-stationarity. These definitions and labels will be used in later parts for numerical and conceptual consistency checks.

Abstract summary: method called "QX2, or dropout"; it randomly removes units and their connections during training, inhibiting co-adaptation, sampling exponentially many thinned networks that share parameters. A single unthinned network with reduced weights approximates the averaged predictions of the thinned nets. Claims substantial reduction in overfitting and major improvements; supervised experiments in vision, speech recognition, document classification and computational biology reportedly attain state-of-the-art on many benchmarks. Evidence claimed in Tables 2–8 and an unnumbered text-classification table in §6.3; domain-specific comparisons listed in §6.

Paper: "Dropout (QX2)". Core idea: randomly remove units during training to train many shared-parameter thinned subnetworks (2^n possible thinned nets for n units) and approximate their combined predictions with one unthinned test-time network. Key terminology: QX2 = dropout; T6R = test-time weight scaling (use one unthinned net with scaled weights); X9M = Monte-Carlo model averaging (average sampled thinned nets at test); U2L/B8T = dropout extension to RBMs. Notation (carry-forward): n = unit count; expected retained width = p n; practical width heuristic = n/p; shared-parameter count O(n^2); L hidden layers with W^(l), b^(l), activations f; p = retention probability; test-time weights scaled by p (W_test = p W). Claims in this part: QX2 approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many models; a new thinned member is sampled and trained (rarely) per presentation of each training case; T6R is a cheap practical inference rule that gives significantly lower generalization error than other regularizers across varied problems; X9M is more expensive and needs around k≈50 samples (per §7.5 and App B.1) before matching T6R. Evidence pointer: Table 9 referenced for comparisons (rows quoted: Y5F=1.62, V9C=1.35, QX2+Y5F=1.25, QX2+V9C=1.05). Paper outline: §2 motivation, §3 prior work, §4 model, §5 training algorithm, §6 experiments, §7 effects and hyperparameter interactions, §8 RBM extension, §9 marginalization, Appendix A (practical guidance).

Paper: "Dropout (QX2)". Core idea: randomly remove units during training to train many shared-parameter thinned subnetworks (2^n possible thinned nets for n units) and approximate their combined predictions with one unthinned test-time network. Notation: n = unit count; p = retention probability; expected retained width = p n; practical width heuristic = n/p; shared-parameter count O(n^2); L hidden layers with W^(l), b^(l), activations f; test-time weights scaled by p (W_test = p W). Claims: QX2 approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many models; a new thinned member is sampled and trained (rarely unique) on each presentation of a training case; T6R (test-time weight scaling) is a cheap practical inference rule that gives significantly lower generalization error than other regularizers across varied problems; X9M (Monte-Carlo averaging) is more expensive and needs around k ≈ 50 samples (per §7.5 and App B.1) to match T6R. Evidence pointer: Table 9 comparisons (rows: Y5F=1.62, V9C=1.35, QX2+Y5F=1.25, QX2+V9C=1.05). New in §2: motivation via sexual-reproduction and conspiracy analogies — Livnat et al. (2010) "mix-ability" notion: selection favors genes that work well with random partners (robust, independently useful components). Analogy: QX2 forces hidden units to operate with randomly selected partners, discouraging complex co-adaptations and favoring robust features; replicating units is a poor remedy. Smaller cooperating subsets are argued to be more robust under non-stationarity than large co-adaptations. Outline pointers: §3 prior work, §4 model, §5 training algorithm, §6 experiments, §7 hyperparams, §8 RBM extension, §9 marginalization, Appendix A guidance.

Paper: "Dropout (QX2)". Core idea: randomly remove units during training to train many shared-parameter thinned subnetworks (2^n possible thinned nets for n units) and approximate their combined predictions with one unthinned test-time network. Notation/impl: n = unit count; p = retention probability; expected retained width = p n; practical width heuristic = n/p; shared-parameter count O(n^2); L hidden layers with weights W^(l), biases b^(l), activations f; test-time weights scaled by p (W_test = p W). Key claims: QX2 approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many models; a new thinned member is sampled and trained on each presentation; T6R (test-time weight scaling) is a cheap practical inference rule that often gives much lower generalization error than other regularizers; X9M (Monte-Carlo averaging) is more expensive and reportedly needs k ≈ 50 samples to match T6R (per §7.5 and App B.1). Empirical pointer: Table 9 example rows (Y5F=1.62, V9C=1.35, QX2+Y5F=1.25, QX2+V9C=1.05). Section 3 notes: DAEs (denoising autoencoders) corrupt inputs and reconstruct; QX2 extends corruption to hidden units and gives a model-averaging view; applies to supervised/unsupervised and other neuron-based architectures including Boltzmann Machines. T6R permits much higher noise than typical DAEs: table lists S2H/DAE typical best 5%, QX2 input-unit removal often optimal 20%, QX2 hidden-unit removal often optimal 50%. Related methods: Globerson & Roweis (2006) and Dekel et al. (2010) use adversarial removals (fixed max number) and have no hidden units. Marginalizing QX2 yields deterministic regularizers in simple cases; van der Maaten et al. (2013) call QX2 input noise "blankout noise" but limited to models without hidden layers; Chen et al. (2012) on marginalization for DAEs; Wang & Manning (2013) propose marginalization to accelerate QX2.

steps.notes_before: Paper: Dropout (QX2) — gate unit outputs during training, independently per unit with r_j^{(l)} ~ Bernoulli(p); tilde y^{(l)} = r^{(l)} * y^{(l)}. At inference no units removed; test-time weights scaled by retention p: W_test^{(l)} = p W^{(l)}. Expected preactivation under training dropout equals test preactivation with scaled weights. Both hidden and input (visible) units can be dropped. Validation can pick p; default often near optimal; input retention generally near complete retention. Forward equations: y^{(0)} = x; nominally z_i^{(l+1)} = w_i^{(l+1)} y^{(l)} + b_i^{(l+1)}, y_i^{(l+1)} = f(z_i^{(l+1)}). Example activation: logistic f(x)=1/(1+exp(-x)). Note: this part contains an indexing inconsistency — it first states l∈{1..L} then uses l∈{0..L-1} for the feed-forward formulas (treating y^{(0)} as input). Keep this in mind when later parts refer to layer indices.

Paper: QX2 = dropout (per-unit gate r_j^(l) ~ Bernoulli(p); ̃y^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l)). At test time do not drop units; scale weights by retention p (W_test = p W) so expected preactivation under dropout equals test preactivation. Both hidden and input units can be dropped (input retention usually near 1). Forward eqns use y^(0)=x; paper has an indexing inconsistency (uses l∈{1..L} then l∈{0..L-1}).

Sec.5 (Learning QX2 Nets): training = backprop through sampled subnetworks (one mask per case/minibatch case), gradients averaged across cases; a dropped parameter gets zero contribution. QX2 alone gives significant gains; combining QX2 with high momentum, large decaying learning rates and V9C (max-norm) gives further boost. V9C constrains each hidden unit's incoming weight vector via projection to ||w||_2 <= c (validation tunes c); projection returns w to the radius-c surface if exceeded. Proposed optimization story: fixed-radius weight ball allows huge LRs without explosion; QX2 noise explores; annealing settles.

Empirical notes cited: Table 9 rows: V9C=1.35, QX2+Y5F=1.25, QX2+V9C=1.05. Appendix A.2: practical LRs typically 10–100x optimal standard-net LR and momentum ~0.95–0.99. Pretraining: unchanged, but before QX2 finetuning multiply pretrained weights by 1/p so expected outputs under dropout match pretraining; use much smaller finetuning LR (Appendix B.4 reports ~0.01 best vs listed high LR 0.1). Table 2: G6W finetuning 1.18 -> 0.92 with QX2; E5Q 0.96 -> 0.79.

Paper studies QX2 (dropout). Data sets: H4Z (MNIST) 60K train /10K test, dim 784; J3V/W6R (CIFAR-10/100) 60K/10K, dim 3072; A2F (SVHN) 600K/26K, dim 3072; K9D (ImageNet ILSVRC-2012) 1.2M/150K, dim 65536; N8Q (TIMIT) 1.1M frames/58K frames, 2520 dim; M5X (Reuters-RCV1) 200K/200K, 2000 dim; Z7P (Splicing) 2932/733, 1014 dim. Claim: QX2 improved generalization over nets without QX2 on every tested data set; applied to vision, speech, text, genetics. For vision, QX2 models reported state-of-the-art on all five vision collections. MNIST (permutation-invariant) results (Table 2): Standard NN (Simard et al.) logistic 2×800: 1.60%; SVM Gaussian: 1.40%; QX2 NN logistic 3×1024: 1.35%; QX2+ReLU (F3N) 3×1024: 1.25%; QX2+V9C (max-norm) F3N 3×1024: 1.06, 3×2048: 1.04; 2×4096: 1.01; 2×8192: 0.95; QX2+V9C maxout (Goodfellow et al.) 2 layers (5×240): 0.94. Pretraining baselines: G6W (DBN) finetuning 500-500-2000: 1.18 → G6W+QX2 finetuning: 0.92; E5Q finetuning: 0.96 → E5Q+QX2 finetuning: 0.79. Text notes: QX2 prevents overfitting of very large networks (no early stopping needed). When hyperparameters (including retention p) fixed across architectures, test-error trajectories form two separated clusters: with vs without QX2. Figure 4 tick ranges: updates 0..1,000,000; error axis 1.0..2.5%.

steps.notes_before: Sec 9 (Marginalizing dropout/QX2): marginalizing dropout produces deterministic objectives (no RNG) and enables gradients for the marginalized loss. 9.1 Linear regression: E_R[||y-(R*X)w||^2] = ||y - p X w||^2 + p(1-p) ||Γ w||^2, with Γ = (diag(X^T X))^{1/2}. With w̃ = p w this is ||y - X w̃||^2 + ((1-p)/p) ||Γ w̃||^2, so dropout yields a data-dependent quadratic penalty whose strength grows as p decreases. 9.2 Logistic regression & deep nets: Wang & Manning (2013) report approximate marginalization improves training time and generalization for logistic regression. Closed-form marginalization is harder for logistic units and for deep nets; the paper states Gaussian approximations for marginalized gradients under "reasonable assumptions," but it contains a contradictory sentence about how assumptions change with depth (flagged above).

Sec 9 (reminder): Marginalizing dropout yields deterministic objectives and gradients. Linear regression exact marginalization: E_R[||y-(R*X)w||^2] = ||y - p X w||^2 + p(1-p) ||Γ w||^2, with Γ=(diag(X^T X))^{1/2}. With w̃ = p w this is ||y - X w̃||^2 + ((1-p)/p) ||Γ w̃||^2 — penalty strength grows as p decreases. For logistic/deep nets closed-form marginalization harder; approximate Gaussian marginalization discussed (earlier part flagged a contradictory sentence about assumptions vs depth).  
Sec 10 (Multiplicative Gaussian Noise): compares Bernoulli (P7V) vs Gaussian (D4K) multiplicative noise. Claim: Gaussian as effective or slightly better. Table 10 (classification error %): H4Z (2 layers, 1024 units): P7V 1.08±0.04, D4K 0.95±0.04. J3V (3 conv + 2 FC): P7V 12.6±0.1, D4K 12.5±0.1. Settings: H4Z: p_hidden=0.5, p_input=0.8. J3V: p per layer = (0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5). D4K per-layer σ = sqrt((1-p)/p). Results averaged over 10 seeds. Notes on representations: for Bernoulli there are two equivalent scalings (scale test weights by p or scale training activations by 1/p); in the latter r_b is 1/p w.p. p else 0, so E[r_b]=1, Var[r_b]=(1-p)/p. Choosing r_g ~ N(1,σ^2) with σ^2=(1-p)/p matches moments: E[r_g]=1, Var[r_g]=(1-p)/p. For Gaussian multipliers expected activations unchanged so no test-time scaling needed. Paper also states Gaussian has maximal entropy for given moments while Bernoulli is low-entropy; preliminary evidence slightly favors the higher-entropy (Gaussian) case.

Sec 9: Marginalizing dropout can give deterministic objectives/gradients for some models. For linear regression: E_R[||y-(R*X)w||^2] = ||y - p X w||^2 + p(1-p) ||Γ w||^2 with Γ=(diag(X^T X))^{1/2}. With w̃ = p w this is ||y - X w̃||^2 + ((1-p)/p) ||Γ w̃||^2 — penalty coef = (1-p)/p (grows as p decreases). Closed-form marginalization for logistic/deep nets is harder; Gaussian approx discussed earlier (there was a flagged contradictory sentence about assumptions vs depth). Sec 10: Multiplicative Gaussian noise (r_g ~ N(1,σ^2)) can match Bernoulli-dropout moments if σ^2=(1-p)/p (so σ = sqrt((1-p)/p)). For Bernoulli scaled-training activations r_b = 1/p w.p. p else 0 => E[r_b]=1, Var[r_b]=(1-p)/p. Table 10 (classification errors, 10 seeds): H4Z: P7V 1.08±0.04, D4K 0.95±0.04 (H4Z p_hidden=0.5, p_input=0.8); J3V: P7V 12.6±0.1, D4K 12.5±0.1. Paper notes Gaussian (higher entropy) slightly favored. Part 22 (Conclusion): QX2 trains sampled submodels (U2L fits, B8T empirical properties). Claims QX2 SOTA on A2F, K9D, W6R, H4Z; cites Table3 A2F 2.47; Table6 K9D top-5 16.4; Table4 W6R 37.20; Table2 H4Z 0.79. M5X: standard nets better without QX2. Other-domain improvements cited: Table7 23.4 vs 21.8; §6.3 table 31.05% vs 29.62%; Table8 440 vs 567. B8T features/sparsity shown in Figs 12–13 with p=0.5. Training typically costs 2–3× standard; noisy parameter updates (each case trains a different random sub-architecture) blamed for extra time; stochasticity likely reduces overfitting — tradeoff between overfitting and training time. Noise marginalization can give an expectation-equivalent regularizer; for linear regression this yields the §9.1 penalty with coef (1-p)/p; equivalent regularizers for complex models not specified. Paper: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (JMLR 15, 2014). Authors: Nitish Srivastava, Geoffrey Hinton, Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, Ruslan Salakhutdinov. Abstract/main claim: Dropout randomly drops units and their connections during training to prevent co-adaptation; training effectively samples from an exponential number of "thinned" networks. At test time, the effect of averaging these thinned networks is approximated by using a single unthinned network with scaled (smaller) weights. Dropout reportedly reduces overfitting and outperforms other regularization methods, producing major improvements and state-of-the-art results on benchmarks in vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology. Intro notes: deep nets are expressive and prone to overfitting; common regularizers include early stopping, L1/L2 penalties, and soft weight sharing. The paper states that with unlimited computation the best regularizer is averaging predictions over all parameter settings (sentence is cut off in this part). Figure 1 caption: left—standard net with 2 hidden layers; right—example thinned net after dropout where some units are dropped.

steps.notes_before: Paper: Dropout (JMLR 2014). Dropout: randomly remove (drop) hidden and visible units during training to prevent co-adaptation; training samples from an exponential number of 'thinned' networks. Authors propose to approximate an equally weighted geometric mean of predictions of these many learned models (to approach Bayesian averaging) using shared parameters. Simple dropout: retain each unit with probability p (often p=0.5 for hidden units; input units usually have retention closer to 1); p can be chosen by validation. At test time use a single unthinned network with weights scaled by p (Figure 2 shows training: unit present with prob. p and weight w; test: unit always present and weight pw) and the caption asserts test output equals the expected training-time output. Key numbers/claims: exponential number of thinned models, p≈0.5 for hidden, input retention ≈1, test-time weight scaling by p.

Paper: Dropout (JMLR 2014). Core idea: during training randomly remove (drop out) hidden/visible units, sampling a 'thinned' network each presentation; weights are shared across thinned models. There are exponentially many thinned networks (paper elsewhere prints 2^n; an earlier printed '2n' looked like a typo). Total number of parameters remains O(n^2) or less due to sharing. Training: each update samples a new thinned network so any specific thinned net is trained rarely. Test-time: use single unthinned network with outgoing weights scaled by the unit's retention probability p so test activations match expected training activations. Typical p ≈ 0.5 for hidden units; input retention closer to 1; choose p by validation. Dropout not limited to feed-forward nets (paper introduces dropout RBM). Structure: Secs 2–9 and Appendix A (practical guide). New from current part: Motivation analogies — sexual reproduction: dropout viewed as preventing large co-adaptations, forcing each hidden unit to learn useful features that work with random subsets of partners, improving robustness; copying units to resist dropout is a poor solution (analogy to replica codes for noisy channels). Conspiracy analogy: many small conspiracies (small co-adaptations) more robust than one large co-adaptation, hence better generalization under non-stationarity. Related work: Dropout can be seen as regularization via adding noise to hidden units; this idea relates to Denoising Autoencoders (Vincent et al. 2008, 2010) which add noise to unit states.

steps.notes_before: Paper: Dropout trains by randomly dropping units (thinning) and sharing weights across exponentially many sub-networks. Training samples a new thinned net each presentation; backpropagate gradients through that thinned net. At test time use a single unthinned net with weights scaled by retention probabilities (W_test = p W^(l) per layer). Typical choices: drop ~50% hidden units (p_hidden ≈ 0.5), ~20% inputs (p_input ≈ 0.8); DAEs typically use 5% input noise but test-time scaling allows higher noise. Dropout can be applied to hidden layers and other neuron-based architectures (e.g., Boltzmann Machines, RBMs). Interpretation: stochastic regularization / model averaging; related to denoising autoencoders and marginalizing noise. Definition details: network with L hidden layers; y(0)=x; feed-forward recurrence given as z^{(l+1)} = W^{(l+1)} y^{(l)} + b^{(l+1)}, y^{(l+1)} = f(z^{(l+1)}). With dropout: sample r^{(l)} ~ Bernoulli(p) elementwise, form y_e^{(l)} = r^{(l)} * y^{(l)} and use y_e^{(l)} as input to next layer. Loss is minimized stochastically (expected loss); prior adversarial-drop work fixes max number dropped (no hidden-layer models).

Training: dropout nets trained by SGD on ‘‘thinned’’ nets — for each training case in a mini‑batch sample dropout mask, do forward/backprop on that thinned net; gradients averaged over mini‑batch; any case that omits a parameter contributes zero gradient for that parameter. Standard SGD tricks (momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 weight decay) help. Max‑norm regularization: constrain incoming weight vector w at each hidden unit to ||w||2 ≤ c by projecting back into the ball of radius c whenever it exceeds c (c is a tunable hyperparameter). Max‑norm often improves SGD even without dropout; combining dropout + max‑norm + large decaying LR + high momentum gives further gains (intuition: ball constraint prevents blowup so large LR can be used for exploration). Unsupervised pretraining: stacks of RBMs/autoencoders/DBMs can be used; pretraining stays the same, but when finetuning with dropout scale pretrained weights by 1/p so expected output under dropout matches pretraining output. If finetune LR is too large pretrained information can be lost; use smaller LR to retain gains. Experiments: datasets include MNIST, TIMIT, CIFAR‑10/100, SVHN, ImageNet, Reuters‑RCV1, and an Alternative Splicing RNA dataset; more details in Appendix B.

Section 9 (Marginalizing Dropout): considers deterministic models obtained by marginalizing dropout noise; these allow gradients and avoid Monte-Carlo noise; cites prior work. 9.1 Linear regression: with input dropout (retention p) and mask R, E_R ||y - (R * X)w||^2 reduces to ||y - p X w||^2 + p(1-p)||Γ w||^2, where paper writes Γ = (diag(X > X))^{1/2} (intended to be diag(X^T X)^{1/2}); this regularizer scales weight penalties by per-dimension data variability. Absorbing p into w shows regularization strength increases as p decreases. 9.2 Logistic/Deep nets: approximate marginalization via Gaussian approximations for unit inputs/gradients can be computed efficiently and reportedly outperforms Monte-Carlo dropout in training time and generalization; however, the text contains an internal contradiction about whether these assumptions remain valid as network depth increases. steps.notes_before: Conclusion and Appendix: Dropout improves many domains (SVHN, ImageNet, CIFAR-100, MNIST) and extends to RBMs (Dropout RBMs have desirable properties). Dropout increases training time (typical 2–3x) due to noisy updates; stochasticity reduces overfitting. Marginalizing dropout: linear regression yields a modified L2 regularizer; for deeper models deterministic approximations used. Table 10: MNIST p_hidden=0.5, p_input=0.8; CIFAR p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5) input→top; results averaged over 10 seeds. Appendix heuristics: Network size — to preserve capacity, if standard-net optimal is n, use ≈n/p units for dropout. Learning rate/momentum — recommend 10–100× the standard learning rate; momentum ~0.95–0.99. Use max-norm (incoming weight norm bound c≈3–4). Dropout rate — typical p_hidden 0.5–0.8, p_input ≈0.8. Note inconsistency: A.4 states "Smaller p requires big n which slows down the training and leads to underfitting," which conflicts with the earlier claim that high dropout reduces overfitting with more training and with A.1's rationale for increasing n to preserve capacity. Also retain earlier note that the paper gave inconsistent formulas for Gaussian-noise variance σ across sections (already flagged).

Earlier summary: Dropout reported to improve many domains (MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR, ImageNet) and RBMs; increases training time (~2–3×). Marginalizing dropout: linear regression → modified L2; deeper models use deterministic approximations. Heuristics: to preserve capacity scale hidden units ≈ n_standard / p; learning rates often much larger than usual (recommendation earlier 10–100×), momentum ≈ 0.95–0.99, use max-norm bound c ≈ 3–4, typical p_hidden 0.5–0.8 and p_input ≈ 0.8. Previously noted internal issues remain: A.4’s statement “Smaller p requires big n which slows down the training and leads to underfitting” conflicts with other claims about dropout/overfitting; inconsistent formulas for Gaussian-noise σ were also flagged.

New (Appendix B) experimental details: MNIST — 60k train/10k test, 10k held-out validation; tuned hyperparameters so best validation error occurred at 1M updates, then combined val+train and trained 1M updates for final model. Architectures: depths 2/3/4 × widths 1024 or 2048 (6 architectures). Dropout: p_hidden=0.5, p_input=0.8. Momentum=0.95, max-norm c=2 for MNIST. Also tried very wide nets (4096, 8192); 2-layer nets improved; 3-layer worse than 2-layer at same dropout.

SVHN — ~600k train/26k test; 6k validation (400/class from standard + 200/class from extra). Inputs normalized to zero mean/unit variance. Best arch: 3 conv layers (96,128,256 filters, 5×5), 3×3 pooling stride 2, then two FC layers of 2048 ReLUs. Dropout p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5) (input→conv→fc). Max-norm c=4, momentum=0.95; tuned on validation and did not recombine val+train.

CIFAR-10/100 — 50k train/10k test, 5k validation; tuned on val then combined with training; preprocessing: per-channel global contrast normalization then ZCA whitening.

final_notes: QX2 = dropout-style multiplicative noise: Bernoulli (P7V) and Gaussian (D4K, matched by moments). Gaussian noise σ = sqrt((1-p)/p). Marginalization for linear regression gives penalty coeff = (1-p)/p. Example p: H4Z hidden=0.5, input=0.8; J3V p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5). Table 10: H4Z (2-layer 1024) P7V 1.08±0.04, D4K 0.95±0.04; J3V P7V 12.6±0.1, D4K 12.5±0.1. Heuristics (App A): match layer n with ≥ n/p units; LR typically 10–100× standard; momentum often 0.95–0.99; V9C c≈3–4; hidden p typically 0.5–0.8; input p≈0.8. Appendix B experiments: H4Z — 10k val, 1M updates endpoint, depths 2–4, widths 1024/2048, hidden p=0.5 input p=0.8, momentum 0.95, V9C c=2 (noted inconsistent with heuristic), largest 2-layer >65M params. Title: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting". Authors: Nitish Srivastava, Geoffrey Hinton, Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, Ruslan Salakhutdinov; Dept. of Computer Science, University of Toronto. Journal: JMLR 15 (2014). Header lists pages 1929–1958 while page map lists pages 1930–1955 (internal inconsistency noted). Abstract summary: introduces dropout (called "QX2: dropout") — a training procedure that temporarily removes randomly selected units and their connections, inhibiting excessive co-adaptation and effectively sampling exponentially many parameter-sharing thinned networks. At test time a single unthinned network with reduced weights approximates the averaged predictions of these thinned networks. Claims dropout substantially reduces overfitting versus other regularizers and yields major improvements, achieving state-of-the-art performance on many benchmarks in supervised vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology.

steps.notes_before: Title: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al., UToronto). Header/page-number inconsistency noted earlier. Dropout (QX2) randomly removes units/connections during training, producing exponentially many (2^n for n units) thinned networks; parameters are shared so total distinct parameters retained are O(n^2) or fewer. With unlimited computation, posterior-weighted averaging over parameters is ideal; the paper claims its method approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of these thinned models' predictions (introduction) — earlier abstract wording said it "approximates the averaged predictions", a potential arithmetic vs geometric-mean wording mismatch. Every presentation samples/trains a new thinned member; individual members are rarely trained thoroughly. Practical inference: T6R (weight scaling) uses one unthinned network at test time; X9M refers to Monte-Carlo model averaging (more expensive). Claims T6R gives much lower generalization error than other regularizers across tasks. Method extends to graphical models, e.g., Dropout RBM (B8T) from RBMs (U2L). Paper map: §2 motivation; §3 prior work; §4 formal model; §5 training algorithm; §6 experiments; §7 network/hyperparameter interactions; §8 Dropout RBMs; §9 marginalization; Appendix A practical guidance.

Title: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al.). Earlier: header/page-number inconsistency noted. Method overview: dropout (QX2) randomly removes units/connections during training, producing exponentially many (2^n) thinned networks; parameters are shared so total distinct parameters are O(n^2) or fewer. Training samples/train different thinned networks; individual thinned members rarely trained thoroughly. Test-time inference: T6R = weight-scaling using one unthinned network; X9M = Monte-Carlo model averaging (more expensive). Paper claims T6R yields much lower generalization error than other regularizers across tasks. Extensions: Dropout RBM (B8T). Paper map: §2 motivation; §3 prior work; §4 formal model; §5 training algorithm; §6 experiments; §7 interactions; §8 Dropout RBMs; §9 marginalization; Appendix A guidance. New from §2 (Motivation): authors use biological analogy—sexual vs asexual reproduction—and cite Livnat et al. (2010) arguing selection can favor gene "mix-ability" rather than individual-fitness optimization. Dropout is analogous: hidden units face randomly selected partners, which favors independently useful, robust features and reduces complex co-adaptations. Replicating units many times is deemed a poor robustness fix (analogy to replica codes and noisy channels). Conspiracy analogy: many small cooperating subsets are more robust under non-stationarity than a single large co-adapted set; complex co-adaptations may overfit training data and fail on novel test data.

Title: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al.). Method: dropout (QX2) randomly removes units/connections during training producing ~2^n thinned networks; parameters shared so distinct params O(n^2). Training: each SGD update samples a thinned network; individual thinned members rarely trained thoroughly. Test-time inference: T6R = weight-scaling using one unthinned network; X9M = Monte-Carlo model averaging (more expensive). Paper claims T6R gives much lower generalization error than other regularizers across tasks. Motivation (§2): biological analogy (mix-ability), reduces co-adaptations. Related work (§3): dropout interpretable as noise in hidden-unit states, extends denoising autoencoders (Vincent et al. 2008/2010) — effective hidden-layer corruption, model-averaging view, supervised/unsupervised use, applicable to Boltzmann Machines. Table: S2H (DAE) typical best noise ~5%; QX2 often optimal input-unit removal ~20%; QX2 often optimal hidden-unit removal ~50%. Adversarial-removal alternatives (Globerson & Roweis 2006; Dekel et al. 2010) consider worst-case removals under a budget and have no hidden units. Analytic marginalization can give deterministic regularizers in simple cases; van der Maaten et al. (2013) studied exponential-family input-noise (blankout) limited to models without hidden layers; Chen et al. (2012) studied marginalization for DAEs; Wang & Manning (2013) proposed marginalization to speed up dropout. Section map: §2 motivation; §3 prior work; §4 formal model; §5 training algorithm; §6 experiments; §7 interactions; §8 Dropout RBMs; §9 marginalization; Appendix A guidance.

Paper: Dropout regularization. Key idea: during training randomly delete (zero) units (hidden and/or visible) to sample many thinned subnetworks; parameters shared across subnetworks. Retention choices are independent Bernoulli variables with common probability p (can be chosen by validation). Typical defaults: hidden-unit retention p≈0.5 (i.e. ~50% removal); input-unit removal often ~20% (retention p≈0.8) — input retention usually nearer full. Training: each SGD update samples r^{(l)} (vector of independent Bernoulli(p)) and forms \tilde y^{(l)} = r^{(l)} * y^{(l)}; forward: z_i^{(l+1)} = w_i^{(l+1)} \tilde y^{(l)} + b_i^{(l+1)}, y_i^{(l+1)} = f(z_i^{(l+1)}). Backprop passes gradients through the sampled subnetwork. Notation: y^{(0)}=x; L hidden layers (indexed 1..L); feed-forward written for l=0..L-1 producing layer l+1. Activation f can be any (e.g. logistic). Test-time inference: no dropout; use one unthinned network with outgoing weights scaled by p: W_test^{(l)} = p W^{(l)} (equivalently unit outputs' expected training contribution equals test-time contribution with scaled weights). Figures illustrate training (stochastic gates r) vs testing (weights scaled by p). Other parts: training samples many subnetworks per SGD update; Monte-Carlo averaging at test-time is an alternative to weight-scaling but more expensive.

Part 5: QX2 (dropout) gives significant gains; combining it with high momentum, large decaying learning rates, and an incoming-weight constraint (V9C = max-norm) gives further improvement. V9C enforces ||w||_2 <= c with projection to the ball surface when exceeded; c is tuned by validation. Proposed optimization account claims large learning rates are safe inside the fixed-radius ball; QX2 provides noise exploration; learning rates decay to smaller steps. SGD differs from standard training only by per-case sampled thinned networks: each mini-batch case uses its own sampled network; gradients averaged across cases; a case not using a parameter contributes zero. Momentum, annealed (decaying) learning rates and other heuristics remain useful. Unsupervised pretraining is unchanged, but before QX2 finetuning pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p so each unit’s expected random-removal output matches its pretraining output. Smaller finetuning learning rates help preserve pretrained information. Pretraining (with unlabeled data) can improve over random init; applicable to stacked U2L, autoencoders, DBMs for finetuning.

steps.notes_before: Part 8 (B8T): B8T = dropout-like mixture over U2L (binary RBM-like). Joint: P(h,v;θ) ∝ exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v). B8T adds r∈{0,1}^F with P(r)=∏ p^{r_j}(1-p)^{1-r_j} and P(h,v|r) ∝ exp(...) ∏ g(h_j,r_j) forcing h_j=0 when r_j=0. Conditional factorization: P(h|r,v)=∏ P(h_j|r_j,v), P(v|h)=∏ P(v_i|h). (Notation inconsistency found: the joint names hidden-bias vector a and visible-bias b, but the written conditionals use b_j in the hidden activation argument and a_i in the visible activation argument — swap of a/b must be resolved.) Learning: CD-1; sample r per case; train only retained hidden units. Empirical: B8T features described as coarser than U2L but with few dead units; B8T reportedly yields much sparser representations than U2L without extra sparsity regularizer. Figures: Fig.12 compares 256-hidden U2L vs B8T (p=0.5). Fig.13 shows activation histograms labeled 'without QX2' vs 'QX2 with p=0.5' (labeling ambiguous relative to B8T). Keep p≈0.5 convention from earlier sections (rate experiments). Previous key results (from earlier parts) retained: QX2 (dropout) improved many supervised tasks (SVHN, CIFAR, ImageNet, TIMIT etc.) and produced sparsity in feed-forward/autoencoder settings.

Part 8 (B8T): B8T = dropout-like mixture over U2L (binary RBM-like). Joint P(h,v) ∝ exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v). B8T introduces r∈{0,1}^F, R_j∼Bernoulli(p), and P(h,v|r) ∝ exp(...) ∏ g(h_j,r_j) forcing h_j=0 when r_j=0. Conditionals factorize: P(h|r,v)=∏ P(h_j|r_j,v), P(v|h)=∏ P(v_i|h). Notation error noted earlier: biases a and b appear swapped in the written conditionals. Learning: CD-1, sample r per case, train only retained hidden units. Empirical: B8T features described as coarser than U2L but with few dead units; yields much sparser representations than U2L without extra sparsity regularizer. Figures compare 256-hidden U2L vs B8T (p≈0.5). Earlier: QX2 (dropout) improved many supervised tasks and produced sparsity in feed-forward/autoencoder settings. Part 9 (Marginalizing QX2): Deterministic noise-marginalized models require no random bits and admit gradients of marginalized losses (contrast to Monte-Carlo QX2). Linear regression: with X∈R^{N×D}, y∈R^N, retaining inputs with prob p (elementwise R_ij∼Bernoulli(p)) gives marginalized objective E[||y - (R*X)w||^2] = ||y - p X w||^2 + p(1-p)||Γ w||^2, where Γ = (diag(X^T X))^{1/2} (diagonal matrix of per-feature l2 norms). Setting w˜ = p w yields ||y - X w˜||^2 + ((1-p)/p) ||Γ w˜||^2, i.e. a ridge-like penalty that scales each weight by the feature's std; penalty coefficient (1-p)/p is small near p→1 and larger when more removal (smaller p). Logistic regression and deep nets: closed-form marginalization is harder, but under reasonable Gaussian approximations for unit inputs and gradients marginalized quantities (means/variances) are efficiently computable; assumptions weaken with added layers making approximations applicable to arbitrary depth (refs: Wang & Manning 2013; Wager et al. 2013).

Part 8: B8T = dropout-like mixture over U2L (binary RBM-like). Joint P(h,v) ∝ exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v). B8T introduces r∈{0,1}^F, R_j∼Bernoulli(p), enforces h_j=0 when r_j=0; conditionals factorize. Learning by CD-1 sampling r per case; reported p≈0.5, features coarser than U2L but few dead units and much sparser representations without extra sparsity regularizer. Part 9: Marginalizing elementwise input dropout in linear regression yields E[||y-(R*X)w||^2] = ||y-p X w||^2 + p(1-p)||Γ w||^2, with Γ = (diag(X^T X))^{1/2}. Setting w˜=p w gives equivalent objective ||y-X w˜||^2 + ((1-p)/p)||Γ w˜||^2; penalty coefficient = (1-p)/p. Logistic/deep nets: closed-form marginalization harder but Gaussian approximations for unit inputs allow marginalizing means/vars. Part 14 (this part): Multiplicative Gaussian (D4K) vs Bernoulli (P7V) dropout—moment-matched (E=1, Var=(1-p)/p) but Gaussian has higher entropy and slightly better preliminary performance. Table 10 errors (%): H4Z (2-layer 1024) P7V 1.08±0.04, D4K 0.95±0.04; J3V (3 conv+2 FC) P7V 12.6±0.1, D4K 12.5±0.1. P7V p settings: H4Z hidden p=0.5, input p=0.8; J3V p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5). D4K per-layer σ = sqrt((1-p)/p). Multiplicative Gaussian: h_i→h_i r', r'~N(1,σ^2) (equivalently additive noise h_i + h_i r, r~N(0,σ^2)). Matching σ^2=(1-p)/p makes E[r]=1 and Var[r]=(1-p)/p, eliminating test-time scaling. Equivalence between test-time weight scaling by p and training-time activation scaling by 1/p holds up to rescaling of learning rates/initializations. Averaged over 10 seeds.

B8T = dropout-like binary-mask over U2L (RBM-like joint P(h,v) ∝ exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v)). B8T samples r∈{0,1}^F, R_j∼Bernoulli(p), enforces h_j=0 when r_j=0; conditionals factorize. Learning via CD-1 with r sampled per case; reported p≈0.5. B8T features coarser than U2L, few dead units, much sparser representations without extra sparsity regularizer. Marginalizing elementwise input dropout in linear regression: E[||y-(R*X)w||^2] = ||y-p X w||^2 + p(1-p)||Γ w||^2 with Γ = (diag(X^T X))^{1/2}; set w˜=p w to get ||y-X w˜||^2 + ((1-p)/p)||Γ w˜||^2, so penalty coefficient = (1-p)/p. Logistic/deep nets: closed-form marginalization harder; Gaussian approximations for unit inputs allow marginalizing means/vars. Multiplicative Gaussian (D4K) vs Bernoulli (P7V) dropout: moment-matched (E=1, Var=(1-p)/p), Gaussian has higher entropy and slightly better prelim. Table 10 (errors %): H4Z (2-layer 1024) P7V 1.08±0.04, D4K 0.95±0.04; J3V (3 conv+2 FC) P7V 12.6±0.1, D4K 12.5±0.1. P7V p settings: H4Z hidden p=0.5, input p=0.8; J3V p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5). D4K per-layer σ = sqrt((1-p)/p); multiplicative Gaussian: h_i→h_i r', r'~N(1,σ^2) (equiv. additive h_i+h_i r, r~N(0,σ^2)). Equivalence between test-time scaling and training-time activation scaling holds up to rescaling of LR/initialization. QX2 (dropout-style) methods claimed SOTA on A2F, K9D, W6R, H4Z and large improvements vs standard nets on other collections. Training typically takes 2–3× wall-clock of same-architecture standard network; noisy parameter updates (different random submodel per case; gradients not gradients of final inference net) likely reduce overfitting, producing an overfitting–training-time tradeoff. Noise marginalization gives some benefits via expectation-equivalent regularizer (linear-regression case above); general closed-form equivalents for complex models unclear. Accelerating QX2 left as future work.

QX2 = dropout-style multiplicative noise (Bernoulli P7V; Gaussian D4K matched by moments E=1, Var=(1-p)/p). Linear-regression marginalization: E[||y-(R*X)w||^2] = ||y-pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Γw||^2; with w˜=p w this is ||y-Xw˜||^2 + ((1-p)/p)||Γ w˜||^2, so penalty coeff = (1-p)/p. B8T used per-case Bernoulli r (p≈0.5); features coarser than U2L, sparse, few dead units. D4K σ = sqrt((1-p)/p) (multiplicative noise h_i→h_i r', r'~N(1,σ^2)). Reported Table 10 errors: H4Z (2-layer 1024) P7V 1.08±0.04, D4K 0.95±0.04; J3V (3 conv+2 FC) P7V 12.6±0.1, D4K 12.5±0.1. Appendix A heuristics: to match a standard layer of n units, use at least n/p units (expected active pn); QX2 LR typically 10–100× standard LR; standard momentum ~0.9, QX2 momentum often 0.95–0.99; use V9C to bound incoming weight-vector norms (c ~3–4); retention p for hidden units typically 0.5–0.8 (simple default 0.5), real-valued inputs typically p~0.8 and input-optimum generally closer to 1 than 0.5.

errors.evidence: Table 1 lists ImageNet dimensionality as "65536 (256 × 256 color)".

errors.claim: "This form essentially scales the cost on weight w_i by the standard deviation of data dimension i. Dimensions that vary more have their weights squeezed more."
errors.evidence: Definition: "\Gamma=\left(\operatorname{diag}(X^\top X)\right)^{1/2}." This is followed by the quoted claim about standard deviation.

Paper summary: Introduces dropout — randomly removing units and their connections during training, which samples many smaller networks that share weights. At test time, a single full network with scaled weights approximates the ensemble of sampled networks. Reports improvements on image, speech, text, and alternative-splicing tasks. Compares dropout with other regularizers and Bayesian neural networks. Studies learned features, sparsity, dropout rates, network size, training-set size, and test-time averaging; finds Dropout Restricted Boltzmann Machines learn qualitatively different features and sparser representations. For linear regression, marginalizing dropout yields a modified ridge-regression objective. Preliminary experiments compare Bernoulli dropout to multiplicative Gaussian noise. Limitation noted: training time typically 2–3× longer than standard networks with the same architecture.

Paper introduces dropout: during training randomly remove units and their incoming/outgoing connections (Bernoulli dropout uses binary vars that equal 1 with probability p, the retention probability). At test time the ensemble is approximated by a single deterministic model via weight scaling (multiply a unit’s outgoing weights by p) or by marginalizing dropout noise (deterministic dropout model); Monte-Carlo dropout/model averaging samples thinned networks at test time. Gaussian (multiplicative) dropout multiplies activations by Gaussian noise; paper compares Bernoulli and Gaussian variants. For linear regression, marginalized dropout is equivalent in expectation to a modified ridge (Tikhonov) regression. Dropout-RBMs are RBMs augmented with binary retention variables; CD-1/Contrastive Divergence used for RBM training; partition function Z(θ) appears in RBM formulation. Code Quality (alternative-splicing task) is the negative KL-divergence metric (higher is better). Other key methods/terms: DBN/DBM pretraining, max-norm constraint (bound hidden-unit incoming weight norms), L1/L2 weight penalties, KL-sparsity regularizer, ReLU and maxout units, pooling (max, L2, L4) in image models, max-pooling after conv layers, permutation-invariant vs 2-D MNIST settings, Top-1/Top-5 ImageNet error definitions, PCA/ZCA whitening used in preprocessing, mix-ability measure for genes. Noted limitation: training time typically 2–3× longer than standard networks with same architecture.

Paper: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al., JMLR 2014). Main idea: during training randomly drop units (Bernoulli retain prob p) to sample many "thinned" networks; at test time use a single unthinned network with outgoing weights scaled by p (W_test = p W) to approximate averaging. Key definitions: L layers, r^(l) Bernoulli masks, ~y^(l) after dropout. A net with n units corresponds to 2^n thinned nets; they share weights so parameter count stays O(n^2). Typical choices: p≈0.5 for hidden units (often close to optimal), input-unit p usually closer to 1. Scaling outgoing weights by p at test time ensures expected training-time output equals test-time output. Motivation: approximate an equally weighted geometric mean / Bayesian-like averaging of exponentially many models with much less computation. Dropout applicable beyond feed-forward nets (Dropout RBM introduced). Paper claims dropout + weight-scaling reduces overfitting and improves generalization across domains; experiments reported in Sections 6–8 (image results Tables 2–6, TIMIT Table 7, Reuters improvement 31.05%→29.62% in Sect.6.3, alternative-splicing bits in Table 8, Table 9 comparisons: Dropout+Max-norm 1.05% vs Max-norm 1.35% vs L2 1.62%). TIMIT learning-rate schedule earlier noted: ε0 (1 + t/T)^(-1). Paper structure: Sec 2 motivation, 3 related work, 4 model, 5 training, 6 experiments, 7 hyperparams/properties, 8 Dropout RBMs, 9 marginalizing dropout, Appendix A guidance.

Paper: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al., JMLR 2014). Core idea: during training randomly drop units (Bernoulli masks r^(l), retain prob p) to sample many thinned networks; at test time use the full network with outgoing weights scaled by p (weight-scaling) to approximate averaging. Typical p≈0.5 for hidden units; input p usually closer to 1. Scaling by p makes test-time output equal to the expected training-time output (approximate model averaging). Dropout applies beyond feed-forward nets (Dropout RBMs): Figures 12–13 show qualitative feature and sparsity comparisons but no numeric performance comparison is reported there. Experiments (Secs.6–8) report improved generalization across domains (image Tables 2–6, TIMIT Table 7, Tables 2–7 and 9 cited for cross-domain error reductions). Reuters (Sec.6.3) error improved from 31.05% to 29.62%. Table 9: Dropout+Max-norm 1.05% vs Max-norm 1.35% vs L2 1.62% (alternative-splicing results also in Table 8). TIMIT uses learning rate schedule ε0(1 + t/T)^(-1). Section 2 motivation uses analogies (sexual reproduction / mix-ability; conspiracies) to argue dropout reduces complex co-adaptations, forcing units to be robust and individually useful.

Paper: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al., JMLR 2014). Core idea: during training randomly drop units via Bernoulli masks r^(l) with retain prob p, sampling many thinned networks; at test time use full network with outgoing weights scaled by p (weight-scaling) to approximate averaging. Typical p ≈ 0.5 for hidden units; input p usually closer to 1. Dropout interpretable as adding noise to hidden-unit states; relates to Denoising Autoencoders (DAEs) which typically use ~5% input noise, but with weight-scaling dropout often uses much higher noise (e.g., drop 20% of inputs, 50% of hidden units). Dropout extends beyond unsupervised learning to supervised nets and other architectures (e.g., Dropout RBMs / Boltzmann Machines; Figures 12–13 show qualitative differences). In simple cases dropout noise can be marginalized analytically (Section 9.1 gives linear-regression derivations); related work on deterministic marginalization and "blankout" noise (van der Maaten et al., Wang & Manning, Chen et al.). Different adversarial-removal formulations studied by Globerson & Roweis (2006) and Dekel et al. (2010). Experiments (Secs. 6–8) report improved generalization across domains: Reuters (Sec.6.3) error improved from 31.05% to 29.62%; Table 9 reports Dropout+Max-norm 1.05% vs Max-norm 1.35% vs L2 1.62%; TIMIT used learning-rate schedule ε0(1 + t/T)^(-1). Section 2 gives motivational analogies (sexual reproduction/mix-ability, conspiracies).

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (Srivastava et al., JMLR 2014). Core idea: during training randomly drop units with independent Bernoulli masks r^{(l)} (retain prob p), sampling many thinned sub-networks; at test time use full network with outgoing weights scaled by p (weight-scaling). Typical p ≈ 0.5 for hidden units; input p usually closer to 1. Notation: L hidden layers (1..L); z^{(l)} = inputs into layer l, y^{(l)} = outputs (y^{(0)}=x), W^{(l)}, b^{(l)}. Standard forward: z_i^{(l+1)} = w_i^{(l+1)} y^{(l)} + b_i^{(l+1)}; y_i^{(l+1)} = f(z_i^{(l+1)}) (e.g., logistic f(x)=1/(1+e^{-x})). Dropout forward: r_j^{(l)} ~ Bernoulli(p) (each mask component independent, 1 with prob p), \tilde y^{(l)} = r^{(l)} * y^{(l)} (elementwise), then z_i^{(l+1)} = w_i^{(l+1)} \tilde y^{(l)} + b_i^{(l+1)}, y_i^{(l+1)} = f(z_i^{(l+1)}). Backpropagate loss derivatives through the sampled sub-network. Test-time: use full network without dropout and scale weights: W_test^{(l)} = p W^{(l)}. Section references: Sec.9.1 gives analytic marginalization in simple linear cases; experiments (Secs.6–8) report improved generalization (e.g., Reuters 31.05% → 29.62%; Table 9: Dropout+Max-norm 1.05% vs Max-norm 1.35% vs L2 1.62%); TIMIT used learning-rate schedule ε0(1+t/T)^{-1}. Figures illustrate standard vs dropout panels (bias +1, three inputs, masks in dropout).

Paper: Dropout (Srivastava et al., JMLR 2014). Core idea: during training randomly drop units with independent Bernoulli masks r^{(l)} (retain prob p), sampling many thinned sub-networks; at test time use full network with outgoing weights scaled by p (weight-scaling W_test = p W). Typical p ≈ 0.5 for hidden units; input p usually closer to 1. Training: use SGD (mini-batches); for each case sample a thinned network; forward/backprop only on that network. Gradients averaged across mini-batch; a case not using a parameter contributes zero gradient. Use momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 weight decay. Max-norm: constrain each unit’s incoming weight vector norm ||w||_2 ≤ c; if violated, project onto ball of radius c; c chosen by validation. Combining dropout with max-norm, large decaying learning rates and high momentum yields further gains. Reported MNIST figures (Table 9): Dropout + Max-norm 1.05%; Dropout + L2 1.25%; Max-norm (no dropout) 1.35%; L2 (no dropout) 1.62%. Unsupervised pretraining: can use RBMs, autoencoders, DBMs; pretraining uses unlabeled data and can help versus random init. When finetuning with dropout, pretrained weights should be multiplied by 1/p so each unit’s expected output under dropout equals its pretraining output. Authors observed pretrained information could be lost with large finetuning rates but preserved with smaller rates. Reported pretrained MNIST (Table 2): DBN rows 1.18% versus 0.92%; DBM rows 0.96% versus 0.79% (presented as dropout finetuning improving pretrained networks). Other notes: Reuters improved (31.05% → 29.62%); TIMIT used learning-rate schedule ε0(1+t/T)^{-1}.

errors.claim: "This form essentially scales the cost on weight w_i by the standard deviation of data dimension i. Dimensions that vary more have their weights squeezed more."
errors.evidence: Definition: "\Gamma=\left(\operatorname{diag}(X^\top X)\right)^{1/2}." This is followed by the quoted claim about standard deviation.
errors.explanation: Gamma as defined is the square root of the sum of squared entries per input dimension (i.e. sqrt(Σ_n x_{n,i}^2)), not the sample standard deviation (which would require centering and dividing by N). Thus calling it the 'standard deviation of data dimension i' is inconsistent with the given definition.

steps.notes_before: Section 7 summary: dropout (p=0.5) yields more interpretable features on MNIST autoencoders; induces sparser activations (mean/unit drop ~2.0->0.7; activation histogram peak at zero). Retention p effects: small p underfits if network size fixed; holding expected retained units pn fixed by increasing n as p decreases can improve classification (p~0.6 best; default p=0.5). Dataset-size experiments show a 'sweet spot' where dropout helps; Monte-Carlo model averaging: ~50 samples approximates weight-scaling. Sec 6.5: dropout+max-norm best 1.05% test error. Section 9 (Marginalizing Dropout): deterministic models by averaging out dropout noise; gradients obtainable. 9.1 Linear regression: minimize_E[||y-(R*X)w||^2] => objective ||y - p X w||^2 + p(1-p)||Γ w||^2 with Γ = (diag(X^T X))^{1/2}; rescaling "+\tilde w = p w" gives ridge form with regularization (1-p)/p. Note inconsistency in text: Γ as defined is sqrt(sum-of-squares per feature, but the paper also calls it the 'standard deviation' per dimension. 9.2 Logistic regression / deep nets: approximated via Gaussian approximations of unit inputs/gradients (Wang & Manning 2013 claim faster training and better generalization). Note internal contradiction: subsection header and Claims bullet say the result does NOT directly extend to deep networks, but a sentence in the body asserts the results "apply directly to networks of arbitrary depth."

steps.notes_before: Section 10: Introduces multiplicative Gaussian dropout: multiply activations by r' ~ N(1,σ^2) (equivalently additive noise h_i r, r~N(0,1)). For Bernoulli dropout under the alternative training scaling (scale retained activations by 1/p), r_b ∈ {0,1/p} has E[r_b]=1 and Var[r_b]=(1-p)/p. Match Gaussian variance σ^2=(1-p)/p so r_g has same mean and variance. For p=0.5 this gives N(1,1). Expected activation unchanged (mean 1) so no test-time weight scaling needed under that training convention. Table 10: MNIST (2 layers, 1024 units): Bernoulli 1.08±0.04% vs Gaussian 0.95±0.04% (used p_hidden=0.5, p_input=0.8; σ per layer = sqrt((1-p)/p)); CIFAR-10 (3 conv + 2 fc): Bernoulli 12.6±0.1% vs Gaussian 12.5±0.1% (p vector given from input upward). Results averaged over 10 seeds; authors call Gaussian advantage preliminary. Internal note: this 0.95% MNIST result conflicts with an earlier reported "best 1.05%" (dropout+max-norm) and the paper does not explain the relation or which result is the overall best. Key items to carry forward: σ^2=(1-p)/p matching, per-layer p settings and Table 10 numbers, and the claim that Gaussian (higher-entropy) and Bernoulli (lower-entropy) multipliers both work but Gaussian may be slightly better.

Section 11 (Conclusion): Dropout breaks co-adaptations, reduces overfitting, improves many domains (object/digit/speech/doc/biology). Appendix A (practical heuristics): A.1 sizing: because expected retained units = p n, if a standard network needs n units, use >= n/p units with dropout. A.2 optimization: recommend learning rates 10–100x the standard-network optimum; momentum ~0.95–0.99 (vs common 0.9); high LR/momentum said to significantly accelerate learning. A.3 max-norm: bound incoming weight norm by c; typical c in [3,4]. A.4 dropout rates: hidden p typically 0.5–0.8; input p ~0.8 for real-valued image/speech; smaller p requires larger n, slows training and can cause underfitting. Earlier important results/conflicts to track: Section 10 mapping Bernoulli ↔ multiplicative Gaussian with σ^2=(1-p)/p; experiments used p_hidden=0.5, p_input=0.8. Table 10 (MNIST, 2-layer, 1024) reported Bernoulli 1.08±0.04% vs Gaussian 0.95±0.04%. Conclusion/other sections reported multiple MNIST numbers without reconciliation (notably 1.05% and 0.79% in other tables/claims). Conclusion also listed state-of-the-art claims (SVHN, ImageNet, CIFAR-100, MNIST) and noted a drawback: training typically 2–3x longer. Note possible tension: Appendix A.2 claims high LR/momentum “significantly accelerate learning,” while Conclusion states dropout training is typically 2–3x longer — both may be true but should be checked for consistency with reported training times/epochs if presented later.

Appendix A heuristics: sizing: use >= n/p units with dropout; optimization: use learning rates 10–100x standard-network optimum, momentum ~0.95–0.99; max-norm incoming weight bound c, typical c in [3,4]; dropout rates: hidden p typically 0.5–0.8, input p ~0.8. Section 10 mapping Bernoulli ↔ multiplicative Gaussian: σ^2 = (1-p)/p. Experiments previously used p_hidden=0.5, p_input=0.8; noted MNIST/Gaussian/Bernoulli numbers (Table 10: MNIST 2-layer 1024 — Bernoulli 1.08±0.04% vs Gaussian 0.95±0.04%). Appendix B (this part) experimental details: MNIST: 60k train, 10k test; 10k held out for validation; hyperparameters chosen so best validation at 1M weight updates; then reunited data and trained 1M updates before testing. Architectures in Fig.4: combinations of 2/3/4 hidden layers × {1024,2048} units; for these and Table 2 architectures hidden p=0.5, input p=0.8, final momentum 0.95, max-norm c=2. Larger 2-layer nets: Table 2 max-norm rows: 4096 -> 1.01%, 8192 -> 0.95%; 3-layer ones slightly worse. SVHN: ~600k train, 26k test; 6k validation (400/class from standard, 200/class from extra; 2/3 standard,1/3 extra); inputs zero-mean/unit-variance; contrast norm and ZCA gave no benefit. Architecture: 3 conv layers (96,128,256 filters, 5x5, stride1), 3x3 pooling stride2, two FC 2048 units, ReLU. Retention p (input→conv→...→fc): (0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5). Max-norm c=4, momentum 0.95. Validation not added back. CIFAR-10/100: 50k train,10k test; 5k validation; preprocessing: global contrast norm per channel and ZCA whitening; architecture and dropout rates matched SVHN; input-layer learning rates smaller. TIMIT: Kaldi log-filter banks, monophone forced alignment; networks take 21 frames, predict central frame; inputs mean-centered and unit-variance.

final_notes: Appendix heuristics: widen QX2 layers ~n/p to preserve capacity; QX2 raises gradient noise → use LR ~10–100× standard-net and momentum ~0.95–0.99. V9C (max-norm) typical c≈3–4. Retention defaults: hidden ~0.5, input ~0.8; very low p can underfit (example p=0.1 gave 2.7% vs 1.7%). H4Z autoencoder: QX2 p=0.5 produced localized features; mean activity ~2.0 (no QX2) vs ~0.7 (QX2); optimal p≈0.6. H4Z sweep: 10k val, 1M updates, depths 2/3/4 widths 1024/2048; hidden p=0.5 input p=0.8 momentum 0.95 V9C c=2. Extra regs used widths 4096/8192; largest two-layer model >65M params. Note: Table 2 QX2+V9C F3N rows reported 1.01 (4096) and 0.95 (8192) but a later conclusion cites 0.79 (inconsistency flagged). Fixed-width/expected-width expts used pn=256 for first two hidden layers, pn=512 last. A2F convnet: mixed-source val 6000 (400/class standard, 200/class additional), convs 96/128/256 (5×5 rf), pool 3×3 stride 2, two FCs 2048, F3N activations, retention p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5), V9C c=4, momentum 0.95. Validation tuned hyperparams; large training set kept separate during final training; best-val model reported. J3V/W6R: 50k train,10k test; J3V 10 classes, W6R 100; val 5k; preprocessing: per-channel global contrast normalization and ZCA whitening; architecture & retention match A2F; input-layer needs smaller LR; after hyperparam selection, val+train combined for final training. N8Q speech: 680 speakers×10 sentences; Kaldi log-filter banks, monophone forced align; window 21 frames; input p=0.8 hidden p=0.5 V9C c=4 momentum 0.95; high LR 0.1 with decay ε0(1+t/T)^{-1}. G6W pretrain U2L CD-1 (Gaussian input var=1); best QX2 G6W-finetune LR ≈0.01; V9C during finetune gave no improvement; Table 7 reports phone errors (19.7 for both QX2-pretrained depths). M5X: Reuters subset 402,738 articles, 50 classes, 2k vocab, >200k training. Z7P genetics: 3665 exons, 1014 features, 4 tissues; 4 softmax outputs each with 3 states {inc,exc,nc}; C4Y score defined. QX2 hidden-unit scale: “1000s”; trained QX2 used two layers × 1024 units (matches settings table). Bayesian comparison used “a few tens” hidden units. Results averaged same 5 folds as Xiong et al. (2011). Table 8: QX2 = 567 bits, early-stopped NN = 440 bits, Bayesian NN = 623

Dropout: randomly remove units and their connections during training, effectively training many smaller networks that share parameters. At test time, use one complete network with reduced weights to approximate averaging the smaller networks' predictions. Claimed benefits: improves generalization over networks without dropout on every tested dataset; reports state-of-the-art results on several benchmarks. Experimental domains: images, speech, documents, gene-splicing prediction. Also examines learned features, sparsity, retention rates, effects of training-set size, Restricted Boltzmann Machines, noise marginalization, and Gaussian corruption. Training cost: typically takes 2–3× longer than training a standard network of the same architecture.

Dropout (QX2): randomly remove units and their connections during training; at test time use one unthinned network with outgoing weights multiplied by the retention probability (T6R) to approximate averaging the thinned-model predictions. The paper states this approximation corresponds to the geometric mean (equally weighted combination) of thinned-network predictions. Two corruption types: Bernoulli dropout (P7V) — binary multiplicative noise (Bernoulli variable =1 with prob p, 0 otherwise) — and Gaussian dropout (D4K) — Gaussian multiplicative noise. Marginalization = expectation over dropout noise to yield a deterministic objective/regularizer; Monte‑Carlo dropout/model averaging = stochastic sampling and averaging predictions from sampled thinned networks. Dropout RBM (B8T): described as a mixture of shared-weight RBMs using different hidden-unit subsets; U2L = RBM; pretraining (DBM/E5Q, DBN/G6W) then finetuning with backprop; mcRBM-G6W is a named pretrained variant. Regularizers: L1 (O3U), L2 (Y5F, Tikhonov), max-norm (V9C), KL-sparsity. Activations mentioned: logistic units, ReLU (F3N), maxout (L8J). Other glossary items to track: geometric mean vs. posterior-weighted averaging, blankout noise, ridge-regression connection (dropout expectation → ridge-like penalty matrix), convolutional-net components (filters, pooling variants), data augmentation, SVM/PCA baselines, terms like dead unit, mix-ability, replica code, and non-stationarity. These definitions and labels will be used in later parts for numerical and conceptual consistency checks.

Abstract summary: method called "QX2, or dropout"; it randomly removes units and their connections during training, inhibiting co-adaptation, sampling exponentially many thinned networks that share parameters. A single unthinned network with reduced weights approximates the averaged predictions of the thinned nets. Claims substantial reduction in overfitting and major improvements; supervised experiments in vision, speech recognition, document classification and computational biology reportedly attain state-of-the-art on many benchmarks. Evidence claimed in Tables 2–8 and an unnumbered text-classification table in §6.3; domain-specific comparisons listed in §6.

Paper: "Dropout (QX2)". Core idea: randomly remove units during training to train many shared-parameter thinned subnetworks (2^n possible thinned nets for n units) and approximate their combined predictions with one unthinned test-time network. Key terminology: QX2 = dropout; T6R = test-time weight scaling (use one unthinned net with scaled weights); X9M = Monte-Carlo model averaging (average sampled thinned nets at test); U2L/B8T = dropout extension to RBMs. Notation (carry-forward): n = unit count; expected retained width = p n; practical width heuristic = n/p; shared-parameter count O(n^2); L hidden layers with W^(l), b^(l), activations f; p = retention probability; test-time weights scaled by p (W_test = p W). Claims in this part: QX2 approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many models; a new thinned member is sampled and trained (rarely) per presentation of each training case; T6R is a cheap practical inference rule that gives significantly lower generalization error than other regularizers across varied problems; X9M is more expensive and needs around k≈50 samples (per §7.5 and App B.1) before matching T6R. Evidence pointer: Table 9 referenced for comparisons (rows quoted: Y5F=1.62, V9C=1.35, QX2+Y5F=1.25, QX2+V9C=1.05). Paper outline: §2 motivation, §3 prior work, §4 model, §5 training algorithm, §6 experiments, §7 effects and hyperparameter interactions, §8 RBM extension, §9 marginalization, Appendix A (practical guidance).

Paper: "Dropout (QX2)". Core idea: randomly remove units during training to train many shared-parameter thinned subnetworks (2^n possible thinned nets for n units) and approximate their combined predictions with one unthinned test-time network. Notation: n = unit count; p = retention probability; expected retained width = p n; practical width heuristic = n/p; shared-parameter count O(n^2); L hidden layers with W^(l), b^(l), activations f; test-time weights scaled by p (W_test = p W). Claims: QX2 approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many models; a new thinned member is sampled and trained (rarely unique) on each presentation of a training case; T6R (test-time weight scaling) is a cheap practical inference rule that gives significantly lower generalization error than other regularizers across varied problems; X9M (Monte-Carlo averaging) is more expensive and needs around k ≈ 50 samples (per §7.5 and App B.1) to match T6R. Evidence pointer: Table 9 comparisons (rows: Y5F=1.62, V9C=1.35, QX2+Y5F=1.25, QX2+V9C=1.05). New in §2: motivation via sexual-reproduction and conspiracy analogies — Livnat et al. (2010) "mix-ability" notion: selection favors genes that work well with random partners (robust, independently useful components). Analogy: QX2 forces hidden units to operate with randomly selected partners, discouraging complex co-adaptations and favoring robust features; replicating units is a poor remedy. Smaller cooperating subsets are argued to be more robust under non-stationarity than large co-adaptations. Outline pointers: §3 prior work, §4 model, §5 training algorithm, §6 experiments, §7 hyperparams, §8 RBM extension, §9 marginalization, Appendix A guidance.

Paper: "Dropout (QX2)". Core idea: randomly remove units during training to train many shared-parameter thinned subnetworks (2^n possible thinned nets for n units) and approximate their combined predictions with one unthinned test-time network. Notation/impl: n = unit count; p = retention probability; expected retained width = p n; practical width heuristic = n/p; shared-parameter count O(n^2); L hidden layers with weights W^(l), biases b^(l), activations f; test-time weights scaled by p (W_test = p W). Key claims: QX2 approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many models; a new thinned member is sampled and trained on each presentation; T6R (test-time weight scaling) is a cheap practical inference rule that often gives much lower generalization error than other regularizers; X9M (Monte-Carlo averaging) is more expensive and reportedly needs k ≈ 50 samples to match T6R (per §7.5 and App B.1). Empirical pointer: Table 9 example rows (Y5F=1.62, V9C=1.35, QX2+Y5F=1.25, QX2+V9C=1.05). Section 3 notes: DAEs (denoising autoencoders) corrupt inputs and reconstruct; QX2 extends corruption to hidden units and gives a model-averaging view; applies to supervised/unsupervised and other neuron-based architectures including Boltzmann Machines. T6R permits much higher noise than typical DAEs: table lists S2H/DAE typical best 5%, QX2 input-unit removal often optimal 20%, QX2 hidden-unit removal often optimal 50%. Related methods: Globerson & Roweis (2006) and Dekel et al. (2010) use adversarial removals (fixed max number) and have no hidden units. Marginalizing QX2 yields deterministic regularizers in simple cases; van der Maaten et al. (2013) call QX2 input noise "blankout noise" but limited to models without hidden layers; Chen et al. (2012) on marginalization for DAEs; Wang & Manning (2013) propose marginalization to accelerate QX2.

steps.notes_before: Paper: Dropout (QX2) — gate unit outputs during training, independently per unit with r_j^{(l)} ~ Bernoulli(p); tilde y^{(l)} = r^{(l)} * y^{(l)}. At inference no units removed; test-time weights scaled by retention p: W_test^{(l)} = p W^{(l)}. Expected preactivation under training dropout equals test preactivation with scaled weights. Both hidden and input (visible) units can be dropped. Validation can pick p; default often near optimal; input retention generally near complete retention. Forward equations: y^{(0)} = x; nominally z_i^{(l+1)} = w_i^{(l+1)} y^{(l)} + b_i^{(l+1)}, y_i^{(l+1)} = f(z_i^{(l+1)}). Example activation: logistic f(x)=1/(1+exp(-x)). Note: this part contains an indexing inconsistency — it first states l∈{1..L} then uses l∈{0..L-1} for the feed-forward formulas (treating y^{(0)} as input). Keep this in mind when later parts refer to layer indices.

Paper: QX2 = dropout (per-unit gate r_j^(l) ~ Bernoulli(p); ̃y^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l)). At test time do not drop units; scale weights by retention p (W_test = p W) so expected preactivation under dropout equals test preactivation. Both hidden and input units can be dropped (input retention usually near 1). Forward eqns use y^(0)=x; paper has an indexing inconsistency (uses l∈{1..L} then l∈{0..L-1}).

Sec.5 (Learning QX2 Nets): training = backprop through sampled subnetworks (one mask per case/minibatch case), gradients averaged across cases; a dropped parameter gets zero contribution. QX2 alone gives significant gains; combining QX2 with high momentum, large decaying learning rates and V9C (max-norm) gives further boost. V9C constrains each hidden unit's incoming weight vector via projection to ||w||_2 <= c (validation tunes c); projection returns w to the radius-c surface if exceeded. Proposed optimization story: fixed-radius weight ball allows huge LRs without explosion; QX2 noise explores; annealing settles.

Empirical notes cited: Table 9 rows: V9C=1.35, QX2+Y5F=1.25, QX2+V9C=1.05. Appendix A.2: practical LRs typically 10–100x optimal standard-net LR and momentum ~0.95–0.99. Pretraining: unchanged, but before QX2 finetuning multiply pretrained weights by 1/p so expected outputs under dropout match pretraining; use much smaller finetuning LR (Appendix B.4 reports ~0.01 best vs listed high LR 0.1). Paper: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (JMLR 15, 2014). Authors: Nitish Srivastava, Geoffrey Hinton, Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, Ruslan Salakhutdinov. Abstract/main claim: Dropout randomly drops units and their connections during training to prevent co-adaptation; training effectively samples from an exponential number of "thinned" networks. At test time, the effect of averaging these thinned networks is approximated by using a single unthinned network with scaled (smaller) weights. Dropout reportedly reduces overfitting and outperforms other regularization methods, producing major improvements and state-of-the-art results on benchmarks in vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology. Intro notes: deep nets are expressive and prone to overfitting; common regularizers include early stopping, L1/L2 penalties, and soft weight sharing. The paper states that with unlimited computation the best regularizer is averaging predictions over all parameter settings (sentence is cut off in this part). Figure 1 caption: left—standard net with 2 hidden layers; right—example thinned net after dropout where some units are dropped.
