steps.notes_before: Paper: Dropout (JMLR 2014). Dropout: randomly remove (drop) hidden and visible units during training to prevent co-adaptation; training samples from an exponential number of 'thinned' networks. Authors propose to approximate an equally weighted geometric mean of predictions of these many learned models (to approach Bayesian averaging) using shared parameters. Simple dropout: retain each unit with probability p (often p=0.5 for hidden units; input units usually have retention closer to 1); p can be chosen by validation. At test time use a single unthinned network with weights scaled by p (Figure 2 shows training: unit present with prob. p and weight w; test: unit always present and weight pw) and the caption asserts test output equals the expected training-time output. Key numbers/claims: exponential number of thinned models, p≈0.5 for hidden, input retention ≈1, test-time weight scaling by p.

Paper: Dropout (JMLR 2014). Core idea: during training randomly remove (drop out) hidden/visible units, sampling a 'thinned' network each presentation; weights are shared across thinned models. There are exponentially many thinned networks (paper elsewhere prints 2^n; an earlier printed '2n' looked like a typo). Total number of parameters remains O(n^2) or less due to sharing. Training: each update samples a new thinned network so any specific thinned net is trained rarely. Test-time: use single unthinned network with outgoing weights scaled by the unit's retention probability p so test activations match expected training activations. Typical p ≈ 0.5 for hidden units; input retention closer to 1; choose p by validation. Dropout not limited to feed-forward nets (paper introduces dropout RBM). Structure: Secs 2–9 and Appendix A (practical guide). New from current part: Motivation analogies — sexual reproduction: dropout viewed as preventing large co-adaptations, forcing each hidden unit to learn useful features that work with random subsets of partners, improving robustness; copying units to resist dropout is a poor solution (analogy to replica codes for noisy channels). Conspiracy analogy: many small conspiracies (small co-adaptations) more robust than one large co-adaptation, hence better generalization under non-stationarity. Related work: Dropout can be seen as regularization via adding noise to hidden units; this idea relates to Denoising Autoencoders (Vincent et al. 2008, 2010) which add noise to unit states.

steps.notes_before: Paper: Dropout trains by randomly dropping units (thinning) and sharing weights across exponentially many sub-networks. Training samples a new thinned net each presentation; backpropagate gradients through that thinned net. At test time use a single unthinned net with weights scaled by retention probabilities (W_test = p W^(l) per layer). Typical choices: drop ~50% hidden units (p_hidden ≈ 0.5), ~20% inputs (p_input ≈ 0.8); DAEs typically use 5% input noise but test-time scaling allows higher noise. Dropout can be applied to hidden layers and other neuron-based architectures (e.g., Boltzmann Machines, RBMs). Interpretation: stochastic regularization / model averaging; related to denoising autoencoders and marginalizing noise. Definition details: network with L hidden layers; y(0)=x; feed-forward recurrence given as z^{(l+1)} = W^{(l+1)} y^{(l)} + b^{(l+1)}, y^{(l+1)} = f(z^{(l+1)}). With dropout: sample r^{(l)} ~ Bernoulli(p) elementwise, form y_e^{(l)} = r^{(l)} * y^{(l)} and use y_e^{(l)} as input to next layer. Loss is minimized stochastically (expected loss); prior adversarial-drop work fixes max number dropped (no hidden-layer models).

Training: dropout nets trained by SGD on ‘‘thinned’’ nets — for each training case in a mini‑batch sample dropout mask, do forward/backprop on that thinned net; gradients averaged over mini‑batch; any case that omits a parameter contributes zero gradient for that parameter. Standard SGD tricks (momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 weight decay) help. Max‑norm regularization: constrain incoming weight vector w at each hidden unit to ||w||2 ≤ c by projecting back into the ball of radius c whenever it exceeds c (c is a tunable hyperparameter). Max‑norm often improves SGD even without dropout; combining dropout + max‑norm + large decaying LR + high momentum gives further gains (intuition: ball constraint prevents blowup so large LR can be used for exploration). Unsupervised pretraining: stacks of RBMs/autoencoders/DBMs can be used; pretraining stays the same, but when finetuning with dropout scale pretrained weights by 1/p so expected output under dropout matches pretraining output. If finetune LR is too large pretrained information can be lost; use smaller LR to retain gains. Experiments: datasets include MNIST, TIMIT, CIFAR‑10/100, SVHN, ImageNet, Reuters‑RCV1, and an Alternative Splicing RNA dataset; more details in Appendix B.

Authors note two equivalent dropout conventions: (a) retain units with prob p at training and scale weights by p at test time, or (b) scale retained activations by 1/p at training and leave weights unchanged at test time. Under (b) the Bernoulli multiplier rb = b/p (b∼Bern(p)) has E=1 and Var=(1−p)/p. Setting σ^2=(1−p)/p makes rg (Gaussian multiplier) match rb in mean and variance; authors claim rg has higher entropy than rb and report preliminary evidence (Table 10) that Gaussian (high-entropy) dropout can work slightly better. errors.claim: The conditional probabilities use b_j for the hidden bias and a_i for the visible bias.
errors.evidence:
The paper defines the joint U2L as P(h,v;θ) ∝ exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v) (so a is the hidden bias, b the visible bias), but then gives

P(h_j=1 | r_j, v) = 1(r_j=1) σ(b_j + Σ_i W_{ij} v_i)

and

P(v_i=1 | h) = σ(a_i + Σ_j W_{ij} h_j).
errors.explanation: The joint probability assigns a_j as the hidden-unit bias and b_i as the visible-unit bias (a^T h + b^T v), so the conditionals are inconsistent: they swap a and b (the hidden conditional should use a_j; the visible conditional should use b_i).

final_notes:
Appendix B: dataset/experiment details. H4Z: 10,000 validation; 1,000,000 update endpoint; arch depths {2,3,4}, widths {1024,2048}; input p=0.8, hidden p=0.5; final momentum 0.95; V9C c=2; largest two-layer model >65M params. Regularizer-comparison arch 784-1024-1024-2048-10. Data-size experiments: train sets 100,500,1k,5k,10k,50k. Fixed-width arch 784-2048-2048-2048-10.

A2F (SVHN): val=6000; conv layers (96,128,256), 5x5, pool 3x3 stride 2; two FC hidden layers 2048; activations F3N; retention p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5); V9C c=4; momentum 0.95; val-tuned hyperparams then final training.

J3V/W6R (CIFAR-10/100): 50k train, 10k test; 5k val from train; per-channel GCN + ZCA; arch/retention match A2F; smaller input-layer LR; follow H4Z retrain.

N8Q (TIMIT): 680 speakers ×10 sentences; log-filter-bank features; monophone alignments; predict central frame from windows; mean-centered unit-variance inputs; no speaker-dependent ops. TIMIT settings: window 21 frames; input p=0.8, hidden p=0.5; V9C c=4; momentum 0.95; high LR 0.1 with decay ε0(1+t/T)^{-1}; pretraining U2L (CD-1); Gaussian-U2L input-unit variance fixed to 1; best G6W finetune LR ≈0.01; paper also states adding V9C during G6W finetuning gave no improvement.

M5X: subset 402,738 articles; vocab 2000; 50 disjoint categories; equal train/test splits → ~201k training examples.

Z7P: 3665 cassette exons; 1014 RNA features; 4 tissue types (from 27 tissues); per-input four softmaxes (one per tissue) with states {inc,exc,nc}; loss C4Y = Σ_{i,t,s} p_{i,t}^s log(q_t^s(r_i)/ ar p^s) where  ar p^s averages p over i,t. QX2 scale: thousands; trained QX2 = 2 layers ×1024; hidden p=0.5, input p=0.7; regularization V9C; high decaying LR; results averaged over same 5 folds as Xiong et al. (2011).

Title: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting". Authors: Nitish Srivastava, Geoffrey Hinton, Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, Ruslan Salakhutdinov; Dept. of Computer Science, University of Toronto. Journal: JMLR 15 (2014). Header lists pages 1929–1958 while page map lists pages 1930–1955 (internal inconsistency noted). Abstract summary: introduces dropout (called "QX2: dropout") — a training procedure that temporarily removes randomly selected units and their connections, inhibiting excessive co-adaptation and effectively sampling exponentially many parameter-sharing thinned networks. At test time a single unthinned network with reduced weights approximates the averaged predictions of these thinned networks. Claims dropout substantially reduces overfitting versus other regularizers and yields major improvements, achieving state-of-the-art performance on many benchmarks in supervised vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology.

steps.notes_before: Title: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al., UToronto). Header/page-number inconsistency noted earlier. Dropout (QX2) randomly removes units/connections during training, producing exponentially many (2^n for n units) thinned networks; parameters are shared so total distinct parameters retained are O(n^2) or fewer. With unlimited computation, posterior-weighted averaging over parameters is ideal; the paper claims its method approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of these thinned models' predictions (introduction) — earlier abstract wording said it "approximates the averaged predictions", a potential arithmetic vs geometric-mean wording mismatch. Every presentation samples/trains a new thinned member; individual members are rarely trained thoroughly. Practical inference: T6R (weight scaling) uses one unthinned network at test time; X9M refers to Monte-Carlo model averaging (more expensive). Claims T6R gives much lower generalization error than other regularizers across tasks. Method extends to graphical models, e.g., Dropout RBM (B8T) from RBMs (U2L). Paper map: §2 motivation; §3 prior work; §4 formal model; §5 training algorithm; §6 experiments; §7 network/hyperparameter interactions; §8 Dropout RBMs; §9 marginalization; Appendix A practical guidance.

Title: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al.). Earlier: header/page-number inconsistency noted. Method overview: dropout (QX2) randomly removes units/connections during training, producing exponentially many (2^n) thinned networks; parameters are shared so total distinct parameters are O(n^2) or fewer. Training samples/train different thinned networks; individual thinned members rarely trained thoroughly. Test-time inference: T6R = weight-scaling using one unthinned network; X9M = Monte-Carlo model averaging (more expensive). Paper claims T6R yields much lower generalization error than other regularizers across tasks. Extensions: Dropout RBM (B8T). Paper map: §2 motivation; §3 prior work; §4 formal model; §5 training algorithm; §6 experiments; §7 interactions; §8 Dropout RBMs; §9 marginalization; Appendix A guidance. New from §2 (Motivation): authors use biological analogy—sexual vs asexual reproduction—and cite Livnat et al. (2010) arguing selection can favor gene "mix-ability" rather than individual-fitness optimization. Dropout is analogous: hidden units face randomly selected partners, which favors independently useful, robust features and reduces complex co-adaptations. Replicating units many times is deemed a poor robustness fix (analogy to replica codes and noisy channels). Conspiracy analogy: many small cooperating subsets are more robust under non-stationarity than a single large co-adapted set; complex co-adaptations may overfit training data and fail on novel test data.

Title: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al.). Method: dropout (QX2) randomly removes units/connections during training producing ~2^n thinned networks; parameters shared so distinct params O(n^2). Training: each SGD update samples a thinned network; individual thinned members rarely trained thoroughly. Test-time inference: T6R = weight-scaling using one unthinned network; X9M = Monte-Carlo model averaging (more expensive). Paper claims T6R gives much lower generalization error than other regularizers across tasks. Motivation (§2): biological analogy (mix-ability), reduces co-adaptations. Related work (§3): dropout interpretable as noise in hidden-unit states, extends denoising autoencoders (Vincent et al. 2008/2010) — effective hidden-layer corruption, model-averaging view, supervised/unsupervised use, applicable to Boltzmann Machines. Table: S2H (DAE) typical best noise ~5%; QX2 often optimal input-unit removal ~20%; QX2 often optimal hidden-unit removal ~50%. Adversarial-removal alternatives (Globerson & Roweis 2006; Dekel et al. 2010) consider worst-case removals under a budget and have no hidden units. Analytic marginalization can give deterministic regularizers in simple cases; van der Maaten et al. (2013) studied exponential-family input-noise (blankout) limited to models without hidden layers; Chen et al. (2012) studied marginalization for DAEs; Wang & Manning (2013) proposed marginalization to speed up dropout. Section map: §2 motivation; §3 prior work; §4 formal model; §5 training algorithm; §6 experiments; §7 interactions; §8 Dropout RBMs; §9 marginalization; Appendix A guidance.

Paper: Dropout regularization. Key idea: during training randomly delete (zero) units (hidden and/or visible) to sample many thinned subnetworks; parameters shared across subnetworks. Retention choices are independent Bernoulli variables with common probability p (can be chosen by validation). Typical defaults: hidden-unit retention p≈0.5 (i.e. ~50% removal); input-unit removal often ~20% (retention p≈0.8) — input retention usually nearer full. Training: each SGD update samples r^{(l)} (vector of independent Bernoulli(p)) and forms \tilde y^{(l)} = r^{(l)} * y^{(l)}; forward: z_i^{(l+1)} = w_i^{(l+1)} \tilde y^{(l)} + b_i^{(l+1)}, y_i^{(l+1)} = f(z_i^{(l+1)}). Backprop passes gradients through the sampled subnetwork. Notation: y^{(0)}=x; L hidden layers (indexed 1..L); feed-forward written for l=0..L-1 producing layer l+1. Activation f can be any (e.g. logistic). Test-time inference: no dropout; use one unthinned network with outgoing weights scaled by p: W_test^{(l)} = p W^{(l)} (equivalently unit outputs' expected training contribution equals test-time contribution with scaled weights). Figures illustrate training (stochastic gates r) vs testing (weights scaled by p). Other parts: training samples many subnetworks per SGD update; Monte-Carlo averaging at test-time is an alternative to weight-scaling but more expensive.

Part 5: QX2 (dropout) gives significant gains; combining it with high momentum, large decaying learning rates, and an incoming-weight constraint (V9C = max-norm) gives further improvement. V9C enforces ||w||_2 <= c with projection to the ball surface when exceeded; c is tuned by validation. Proposed optimization account claims large learning rates are safe inside the fixed-radius ball; QX2 provides noise exploration; learning rates decay to smaller steps. SGD differs from standard training only by per-case sampled thinned networks: each mini-batch case uses its own sampled network; gradients averaged across cases; a case not using a parameter contributes zero. Momentum, annealed (decaying) learning rates and other heuristics remain useful. Unsupervised pretraining is unchanged, but before QX2 finetuning pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p so each unit’s expected random-removal output matches its pretraining output. Smaller finetuning learning rates help preserve pretrained information. Pretraining (with unlabeled data) can improve over random init; applicable to stacked U2L, autoencoders, DBMs for finetuning.

errors.claim: The conditional probabilities use b_j for the hidden bias and a_i for the visible bias.
errors.evidence:
The paper defines the joint U2L as P(h,v;θ) ∝ exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v) (so a is the hidden bias, b the visible bias), but then gives

P(h_j=1 | r_j, v) = 1(r_j=1) σ(b_j + Σ_i W_{ij} v_i)

and

P(v_i=1 | h) = σ(a_i + Σ_j W_{ij} h_j).
errors.explanation: The joint probability assigns a_j as the hidden-unit bias and b_i as the visible-unit bias (a^T h + b^T v), so the conditionals are inconsistent: they swap a and b (the hidden conditional should use a_j; the visible conditional should use b_i).

Method/behavior highlights: QX2 yields localized detectors, reduces co-adaptation; activations mean ≈2.0 (no-QX2) vs ≈0.7 (QX2) with sharp zero peak. Paper summary: Introduces dropout — randomly removing units and their connections during training, which samples many smaller networks that share weights. At test time, a single full network with scaled weights approximates the ensemble of sampled networks. Reports improvements on image, speech, text, and alternative-splicing tasks. Compares dropout with other regularizers and Bayesian neural networks. Studies learned features, sparsity, dropout rates, network size, training-set size, and test-time averaging; finds Dropout Restricted Boltzmann Machines learn qualitatively different features and sparser representations. For linear regression, marginalizing dropout yields a modified ridge-regression objective. Preliminary experiments compare Bernoulli dropout to multiplicative Gaussian noise. Limitation noted: training time typically 2–3× longer than standard networks with the same architecture.

Paper introduces dropout: during training randomly remove units and their incoming/outgoing connections (Bernoulli dropout uses binary vars that equal 1 with probability p, the retention probability). At test time the ensemble is approximated by a single deterministic model via weight scaling (multiply a unit’s outgoing weights by p) or by marginalizing dropout noise (deterministic dropout model); Monte-Carlo dropout/model averaging samples thinned networks at test time. Gaussian (multiplicative) dropout multiplies activations by Gaussian noise; paper compares Bernoulli and Gaussian variants. For linear regression, marginalized dropout is equivalent in expectation to a modified ridge (Tikhonov) regression. Dropout-RBMs are RBMs augmented with binary retention variables; CD-1/Contrastive Divergence used for RBM training; partition function Z(θ) appears in RBM formulation. Code Quality (alternative-splicing task) is the negative KL-divergence metric (higher is better). Other key methods/terms: DBN/DBM pretraining, max-norm constraint (bound hidden-unit incoming weight norms), L1/L2 weight penalties, KL-sparsity regularizer, ReLU and maxout units, pooling (max, L2, L4) in image models, max-pooling after conv layers, permutation-invariant vs 2-D MNIST settings, Top-1/Top-5 ImageNet error definitions, PCA/ZCA whitening used in preprocessing, mix-ability measure for genes. Noted limitation: training time typically 2–3× longer than standard networks with same architecture.

For linear regression, marginalized dropout = modified ridge (Tikhonov). Dropout-RBMs include binary retention variables; trained with CD-1. Notation and key definitions: L (# hidden layers), l (layer index); i,j (unit/dim/data indices). x = network input (y^(0)). z^(l) = inputs to layer l; y^(l) = outputs; ~y^(l) = outputs after elementwise dropout mask. Main idea: During training randomly remove units+connections (Bernoulli retention p) sampling exponential number of thinned networks; at test time use one unthinned network with scaled weights (W_test = p W) to approximate average predictions. Dropout claimed to reduce overfitting and prevent co-adaptation.
Claims/evidence (reported): improves across domains — image results in Tables 2–6; TIMIT rows in Table 7; Reuters: 31.05% (no dropout) -> 29.62% (with dropout) in Sect. 6.3; alternative-splicing rows 440 and 567 bits in Table 8; Table 9: dropout improves over other regularizers in all rows; Dropout+Max-norm = 1.05% vs Max-norm = 1.35% and L2 = 1.62%.

Paper: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al., JMLR 2014). Main idea: during training randomly drop units (Bernoulli retain prob p) to sample many "thinned" networks; at test time use a single unthinned network with outgoing weights scaled by p (W_test = p W) to approximate averaging. Key definitions: L layers, r^(l) Bernoulli masks, ~y^(l) after dropout. A net with n units corresponds to 2^n thinned nets; they share weights so parameter count stays O(n^2). Typical choices: p≈0.5 for hidden units (often close to optimal), input-unit p usually closer to 1. Scaling outgoing weights by p at test time ensures expected training-time output equals test-time output. Motivation: approximate an equally weighted geometric mean / Bayesian-like averaging of exponentially many models with much less computation. Dropout applicable beyond feed-forward nets (Dropout RBM introduced). Paper claims dropout + weight-scaling reduces overfitting and improves generalization across domains; experiments reported in Sections 6–8 (image results Tables 2–6, TIMIT Table 7, Reuters improvement 31.05%→29.62% in Sect.6.3, alternative-splicing bits in Table 8, Table 9 comparisons: Dropout+Max-norm 1.05% vs Max-norm 1.35% vs L2 1.62%). TIMIT learning-rate schedule earlier noted: ε0 (1 + t/T)^(-1). Paper structure: Sec 2 motivation, 3 related work, 4 model, 5 training, 6 experiments, 7 hyperparams/properties, 8 Dropout RBMs, 9 marginalizing dropout, Appendix A guidance.

Paper: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al., JMLR 2014). Core idea: during training randomly drop units (Bernoulli masks r^(l), retain prob p) to sample many thinned networks; at test time use the full network with outgoing weights scaled by p (weight-scaling) to approximate averaging. Typical p≈0.5 for hidden units; input p usually closer to 1. Scaling by p makes test-time output equal to the expected training-time output (approximate model averaging). Dropout applies beyond feed-forward nets (Dropout RBMs): Figures 12–13 show qualitative feature and sparsity comparisons but no numeric performance comparison is reported there. Experiments (Secs.6–8) report improved generalization across domains (image Tables 2–6, TIMIT Table 7, Tables 2–7 and 9 cited for cross-domain error reductions). Reuters (Sec.6.3) error improved from 31.05% to 29.62%. Table 9: Dropout+Max-norm 1.05% vs Max-norm 1.35% vs L2 1.62% (alternative-splicing results also in Table 8). TIMIT uses learning rate schedule ε0(1 + t/T)^(-1). Section 2 motivation uses analogies (sexual reproduction / mix-ability; conspiracies) to argue dropout reduces complex co-adaptations, forcing units to be robust and individually useful.

Paper: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al., JMLR 2014). Core idea: during training randomly drop units via Bernoulli masks r^(l) with retain prob p, sampling many thinned networks; at test time use full network with outgoing weights scaled by p (weight-scaling) to approximate averaging. Typical p ≈ 0.5 for hidden units; input p usually closer to 1. Dropout interpretable as adding noise to hidden-unit states; relates to Denoising Autoencoders (DAEs) which typically use ~5% input noise, but with weight-scaling dropout often uses much higher noise (e.g., drop 20% of inputs, 50% of hidden units). Dropout extends beyond unsupervised learning to supervised nets and other architectures (e.g., Dropout RBMs / Boltzmann Machines; Figures 12–13 show qualitative differences). In simple cases dropout noise can be marginalized analytically (Section 9.1 gives linear-regression derivations); related work on deterministic marginalization and "blankout" noise (van der Maaten et al., Wang & Manning, Chen et al.). Different adversarial-removal formulations studied by Globerson & Roweis (2006) and Dekel et al. (2010). Experiments (Secs. 6–8) report improved generalization across domains: Reuters (Sec.6.3) error improved from 31.05% to 29.62%; Table 9 reports Dropout+Max-norm 1.05% vs Max-norm 1.35% vs L2 1.62%; TIMIT used learning-rate schedule ε0(1 + t/T)^(-1). Section 2 gives motivational analogies (sexual reproduction/mix-ability, conspiracies).

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (Srivastava et al., JMLR 2014). Core idea: during training randomly drop units with independent Bernoulli masks r^{(l)} (retain prob p), sampling many thinned sub-networks; at test time use full network with outgoing weights scaled by p (weight-scaling). Typical p ≈ 0.5 for hidden units; input p usually closer to 1. Notation: L hidden layers (1..L); z^{(l)} = inputs into layer l, y^{(l)} = outputs (y^{(0)}=x), W^{(l)}, b^{(l)}. Standard forward: z_i^{(l+1)} = w_i^{(l+1)} y^{(l)} + b_i^{(l+1)}; y_i^{(l+1)} = f(z_i^{(l+1)}) (e.g., logistic f(x)=1/(1+e^{-x})). Dropout forward: r_j^{(l)} ~ Bernoulli(p) (each mask component independent, 1 with prob p), \tilde y^{(l)} = r^{(l)} * y^{(l)} (elementwise), then z_i^{(l+1)} = w_i^{(l+1)} \tilde y^{(l)} + b_i^{(l+1)}, y_i^{(l+1)} = f(z_i^{(l+1)}). Backpropagate loss derivatives through the sampled sub-network. Test-time: use full network without dropout and scale weights: W_test^{(l)} = p W^{(l)}. Section references: Sec.9.1 gives analytic marginalization in simple linear cases; experiments (Secs.6–8) report improved generalization (e.g., Reuters 31.05% → 29.62%; Table 9: Dropout+Max-norm 1.05% vs Max-norm 1.35% vs L2 1.62%); TIMIT used learning-rate schedule ε0(1+t/T)^{-1}. Figures illustrate standard vs dropout panels (bias +1, three inputs, masks in dropout).

Paper: Dropout (Srivastava et al., JMLR 2014). Core idea: during training randomly drop units with independent Bernoulli masks r^{(l)} (retain prob p), sampling many thinned sub-networks; at test time use full network with outgoing weights scaled by p (weight-scaling W_test = p W). Typical p ≈ 0.5 for hidden units; input p usually closer to 1. Training: use SGD (mini-batches); for each case sample a thinned network; forward/backprop only on that network. Gradients averaged across mini-batch; a case not using a parameter contributes zero gradient. Use momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 weight decay. Max-norm: constrain each unit’s incoming weight vector norm ||w||_2 ≤ c; if violated, project onto ball of radius c; c chosen by validation. Combining dropout with max-norm, large decaying learning rates and high momentum yields further gains. Reported MNIST figures (Table 9): Dropout + Max-norm 1.05%; Dropout + L2 1.25%; Max-norm (no dropout) 1.35%; L2 (no dropout) 1.62%. Unsupervised pretraining: can use RBMs, autoencoders, DBMs; pretraining uses unlabeled data and can help versus random init. When finetuning with dropout, pretrained weights should be multiplied by 1/p so each unit’s expected output under dropout equals its pretraining output. Authors observed pretrained information could be lost with large finetuning rates but preserved with smaller rates. Reported pretrained MNIST (Table 2): DBN rows 1.18% versus 0.92%; DBM rows 0.96% versus 0.79% (presented as dropout finetuning improving pretrained networks). Other notes: Reuters improved (31.05% → 29.62%); TIMIT used learning-rate schedule ε0(1+t/T)^{-1}.

errors.claim: This form essentially scales the cost on weight w_i by the standard deviation of data dimension i.
errors.evidence: Definition: "\Gamma = (\operatorname{diag}(X^\top X))^{1/2}." Penalty: "p(1-p)\|\Gamma w\|^2."
errors.explanation: The displayed definition makes \Gamma the (square root of the) column-wise sum-of-squares (i.e. the L2 norm of each data column), so the penalty scales with \sqrt{\sum_n X_{ni}^2}, not the sample standard deviation (which would require dividing by sqrt(N) and typically centering). The text's wording "standard deviation" therefore contradicts the explicit formula unless an unstated normalization/centering is assumed.

Evaluation metric C4Y: sum_{i,t,s} p_{i,t}^s log( q_t^s(r_i) / \bar p^s ), with \bar p^s averaging p_{i,t}^s over i,t. QX2 hidden-unit scale: “1000s”; trained QX2 net used 2 layers × 1024 units. Dropout: hidden p=0.5, input p=0.7. Training: V9C with decaying high LR schedule. Results averaged over the same 5 folds as Xiong et al. (2011) (final settings-table row documents this). Settings table contrasts QX2 “1000s” units vs Bayesian “a few tens”. Table 8 (Z7P): Bayesian neural net = 623 bits, QX2 = 567 bits, early-stopped neural net = 440 bits.

Dropout: randomly remove units and their connections during training, effectively training many smaller networks that share parameters. At test time, use one complete network with reduced weights to approximate averaging the smaller networks' predictions. Claimed benefits: improves generalization over networks without dropout on every tested dataset; reports state-of-the-art results on several benchmarks. Experimental domains: images, speech, documents, gene-splicing prediction. Also examines learned features, sparsity, retention rates, effects of training-set size, Restricted Boltzmann Machines, noise marginalization, and Gaussian corruption. Training cost: typically takes 2–3× longer than training a standard network of the same architecture.

Dropout (QX2): randomly remove units and their connections during training; at test time use one unthinned network with outgoing weights multiplied by the retention probability (T6R) to approximate averaging the thinned-model predictions. The paper states this approximation corresponds to the geometric mean (equally weighted combination) of thinned-network predictions. Two corruption types: Bernoulli dropout (P7V) — binary multiplicative noise (Bernoulli variable =1 with prob p, 0 otherwise) — and Gaussian dropout (D4K) — Gaussian multiplicative noise. Marginalization = expectation over dropout noise to yield a deterministic objective/regularizer; Monte‑Carlo dropout/model averaging = stochastic sampling and averaging predictions from sampled thinned networks. Dropout RBM (B8T): described as a mixture of shared-weight RBMs using different hidden-unit subsets; U2L = RBM; pretraining (DBM/E5Q, DBN/G6W) then finetuning with backprop; mcRBM-G6W is a named pretrained variant. Regularizers: L1 (O3U), L2 (Y5F, Tikhonov), max-norm (V9C), KL-sparsity. Activations mentioned: logistic units, ReLU (F3N), maxout (L8J). Other glossary items to track: geometric mean vs. posterior-weighted averaging, blankout noise, ridge-regression connection (dropout expectation → ridge-like penalty matrix), convolutional-net components (filters, pooling variants), data augmentation, SVM/PCA baselines, terms like dead unit, mix-ability, replica code, and non-stationarity. These definitions and labels will be used in later parts for numerical and conceptual consistency checks.

Abstract summary: method called "QX2, or dropout"; it randomly removes units and their connections during training, inhibiting co-adaptation, sampling exponentially many thinned networks that share parameters. A single unthinned network with reduced weights approximates the averaged predictions of the thinned nets. Claims substantial reduction in overfitting and major improvements; supervised experiments in vision, speech recognition, document classification and computational biology reportedly attain state-of-the-art on many benchmarks. Evidence claimed in Tables 2–8 and an unnumbered text-classification table in §6.3; domain-specific comparisons listed in §6.

Paper: "Dropout (QX2)". Core idea: randomly remove units during training to train many shared-parameter thinned subnetworks (2^n possible thinned nets for n units) and approximate their combined predictions with one unthinned test-time network. Key terminology: QX2 = dropout; T6R = test-time weight scaling (use one unthinned net with scaled weights); X9M = Monte-Carlo model averaging (average sampled thinned nets at test); U2L/B8T = dropout extension to RBMs. Notation (carry-forward): n = unit count; expected retained width = p n; practical width heuristic = n/p; shared-parameter count O(n^2); L hidden layers with W^(l), b^(l), activations f; p = retention probability; test-time weights scaled by p (W_test = p W). Claims in this part: QX2 approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many models; a new thinned member is sampled and trained (rarely) per presentation of each training case; T6R is a cheap practical inference rule that gives significantly lower generalization error than other regularizers across varied problems; X9M is more expensive and needs around k≈50 samples (per §7.5 and App B.1) before matching T6R. Evidence pointer: Table 9 referenced for comparisons (rows quoted: Y5F=1.62, V9C=1.35, QX2+Y5F=1.25, QX2+V9C=1.05). Paper outline: §2 motivation, §3 prior work, §4 model, §5 training algorithm, §6 experiments, §7 effects and hyperparameter interactions, §8 RBM extension, §9 marginalization, Appendix A (practical guidance).

Paper: "Dropout (QX2)". Core idea: randomly remove units during training to train many shared-parameter thinned subnetworks (2^n possible thinned nets for n units) and approximate their combined predictions with one unthinned test-time network. Notation: n = unit count; p = retention probability; expected retained width = p n; practical width heuristic = n/p; shared-parameter count O(n^2); L hidden layers with W^(l), b^(l), activations f; test-time weights scaled by p (W_test = p W). Claims: QX2 approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many models; a new thinned member is sampled and trained (rarely unique) on each presentation of a training case; T6R (test-time weight scaling) is a cheap practical inference rule that gives significantly lower generalization error than other regularizers across varied problems; X9M (Monte-Carlo averaging) is more expensive and needs around k ≈ 50 samples (per §7.5 and App B.1) to match T6R. Evidence pointer: Table 9 comparisons (rows: Y5F=1.62, V9C=1.35, QX2+Y5F=1.25, QX2+V9C=1.05). New in §2: motivation via sexual-reproduction and conspiracy analogies — Livnat et al. (2010) "mix-ability" notion: selection favors genes that work well with random partners (robust, independently useful components). Analogy: QX2 forces hidden units to operate with randomly selected partners, discouraging complex co-adaptations and favoring robust features; replicating units is a poor remedy. Smaller cooperating subsets are argued to be more robust under non-stationarity than large co-adaptations. Outline pointers: §3 prior work, §4 model, §5 training algorithm, §6 experiments, §7 hyperparams, §8 RBM extension, §9 marginalization, Appendix A guidance.

Paper: "Dropout (QX2)". Core idea: randomly remove units during training to train many shared-parameter thinned subnetworks (2^n possible thinned nets for n units) and approximate their combined predictions with one unthinned test-time network. Notation/impl: n = unit count; p = retention probability; expected retained width = p n; practical width heuristic = n/p; shared-parameter count O(n^2); L hidden layers with weights W^(l), biases b^(l), activations f; test-time weights scaled by p (W_test = p W). Key claims: QX2 approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many models; a new thinned member is sampled and trained on each presentation; T6R (test-time weight scaling) is a cheap practical inference rule that often gives much lower generalization error than other regularizers; X9M (Monte-Carlo averaging) is more expensive and reportedly needs k ≈ 50 samples to match T6R (per §7.5 and App B.1). Empirical pointer: Table 9 example rows (Y5F=1.62, V9C=1.35, QX2+Y5F=1.25, QX2+V9C=1.05). Section 3 notes: DAEs (denoising autoencoders) corrupt inputs and reconstruct; QX2 extends corruption to hidden units and gives a model-averaging view; applies to supervised/unsupervised and other neuron-based architectures including Boltzmann Machines. T6R permits much higher noise than typical DAEs: table lists S2H/DAE typical best 5%, QX2 input-unit removal often optimal 20%, QX2 hidden-unit removal often optimal 50%. Related methods: Globerson & Roweis (2006) and Dekel et al. (2010) use adversarial removals (fixed max number) and have no hidden units. Marginalizing QX2 yields deterministic regularizers in simple cases; van der Maaten et al. (2013) call QX2 input noise "blankout noise" but limited to models without hidden layers; Chen et al. (2012) on marginalization for DAEs; Wang & Manning (2013) propose marginalization to accelerate QX2.

steps.notes_before: Paper: Dropout (QX2) — gate unit outputs during training, independently per unit with r_j^{(l)} ~ Bernoulli(p); tilde y^{(l)} = r^{(l)} * y^{(l)}. At inference no units removed; test-time weights scaled by retention p: W_test^{(l)} = p W^{(l)}. Expected preactivation under training dropout equals test preactivation with scaled weights. Both hidden and input (visible) units can be dropped. Validation can pick p; default often near optimal; input retention generally near complete retention. Forward equations: y^{(0)} = x; nominally z_i^{(l+1)} = w_i^{(l+1)} y^{(l)} + b_i^{(l+1)}, y_i^{(l+1)} = f(z_i^{(l+1)}). Example activation: logistic f(x)=1/(1+exp(-x)). Note: this part contains an indexing inconsistency — it first states l∈{1..L} then uses l∈{0..L-1} for the feed-forward formulas (treating y^{(0)} as input). Keep this in mind when later parts refer to layer indices.

Paper: QX2 = dropout (per-unit gate r_j^(l) ~ Bernoulli(p); ̃y^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l)). At test time do not drop units; scale weights by retention p (W_test = p W) so expected preactivation under dropout equals test preactivation. Both hidden and input units can be dropped (input retention usually near 1). Forward eqns use y^(0)=x; paper has an indexing inconsistency (uses l∈{1..L} then l∈{0..L-1}).

Sec.5 (Learning QX2 Nets): training = backprop through sampled subnetworks (one mask per case/minibatch case), gradients averaged across cases; a dropped parameter gets zero contribution. QX2 alone gives significant gains; combining QX2 with high momentum, large decaying learning rates and V9C (max-norm) gives further boost. V9C constrains each hidden unit's incoming weight vector via projection to ||w||_2 <= c (validation tunes c); projection returns w to the radius-c surface if exceeded. Proposed optimization story: fixed-radius weight ball allows huge LRs without explosion; QX2 noise explores; annealing settles.

Empirical notes cited: Table 9 rows: V9C=1.35, QX2+Y5F=1.25, QX2+V9C=1.05. Appendix A.2: practical LRs typically 10–100x optimal standard-net LR and momentum ~0.95–0.99. Pretraining: unchanged, but before QX2 finetuning multiply pretrained weights by 1/p so expected outputs under dropout match pretraining; use much smaller finetuning LR (Appendix B.4 reports ~0.01 best vs listed high LR 0.1). Table 2: G6W finetuning 1.18 -> 0.92 with QX2; E5Q 0.96 -> 0.79.

Paper studies QX2 (dropout). Data sets: H4Z (MNIST) 60K train /10K test, dim 784; J3V/W6R (CIFAR-10/100) 60K/10K, dim 3072; A2F (SVHN) 600K/26K, dim 3072; K9D (ImageNet ILSVRC-2012) 1.2M/150K, dim 65536; N8Q (TIMIT) 1.1M frames/58K frames, 2520 dim; M5X (Reuters-RCV1) 200K/200K, 2000 dim; Z7P (Splicing) 2932/733, 1014 dim. Claim: QX2 improved generalization over nets without QX2 on every tested data set; applied to vision, speech, text, genetics. For vision, QX2 models reported state-of-the-art on all five vision collections. MNIST (permutation-invariant) results (Table 2): Standard NN (Simard et al.) logistic 2×800: 1.60%; SVM Gaussian: 1.40%; QX2 NN logistic 3×1024: 1.35%; QX2+ReLU (F3N) 3×1024: 1.25%; QX2+V9C (max-norm) F3N 3×1024: 1.06, 3×2048: 1.04; 2×4096: 1.01; 2×8192: 0.95; QX2+V9C maxout (Goodfellow et al.) 2 layers (5×240): 0.94. Pretraining baselines: G6W (DBN) finetuning 500-500-2000: 1.18 → G6W+QX2 finetuning: 0.92; E5Q finetuning: 0.96 → E5Q+QX2 finetuning: 0.79. Text notes: QX2 prevents overfitting of very large networks (no early stopping needed). When hyperparameters (including retention p) fixed across architectures, test-error trajectories form two separated clusters: with vs without QX2. Figure 4 tick ranges: updates 0..1,000,000; error axis 1.0..2.5%.

New (Sec.9): Marginalizing QX2: deterministic marginalized objectives need no random bits and permit gradients (vs Monte-Carlo QX2). 9.1 Linear regression: E_R ||y-(R*X)w||^2 = ||y-pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Γ w||^2, with Γ=(diag(X^T X))^{1/2}. Rescaling w̃=pw yields ||y-X w̃||^2 + ((1-p)/p)||Γ w̃||^2; penalty→0 as p→1 and grows as p decreases. 9.2 Logistic/deep nets: Wang & Manning (2013) show approximate marginalization helps logistic regression (time/generalization). Closed-form marginalization is hard for logistic and deep nets; under assumptions input distributions/gradients can be approximated as Gaussian (means/variances computable), but assumptions weaken with more layers so direct application to deep networks is limited.

Earlier: QX2 dropout (p=0.5) on H4Z autoencoder (256 hidden) produced localized features; mean hidden activity ~2.0 (no QX2) vs ~0.7 (with QX2). Data-size sweep (100,500,1K,5K,10K,50K) showed no QX2 improvement at smallest sizes; QX2 gains rise then fall. B8T (dropout for RBMs) uses per-hidden retention r_j~Bernoulli(p); conditional P(h_j=1|r_j,v)=1(r_j=1)σ(b_j+Σ_i W_{ij}v_i); CD-1 samples r per case and updates only retained units; B8T features coarser than U2L and fewer dead units (256 hidden, p=0.5). Sec.9: marginalizing QX2 gives closed-form regularizer for linear regression: E_R||y-(R⊙X)w||^2 = ||y-pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Γw||^2 with Γ=(diag(X^T X))^{1/2}; rescale w̃=pw => penalty ((1-p)/p)·||Γw̃||^2. Logistic/deep nets: marginalization harder; Gaussian approximations sometimes used but weaken with depth. New (Sec.10): multiplicative Gaussian noise (D4K) compared to Bernoulli dropout (P7V). Table10 (classification error %): H4Z (2-layer, 1024 units): P7V 1.08±0.04 vs D4K 0.95±0.04; J3V (3 conv+2 FC): P7V 12.6±0.1 vs D4K 12.5±0.1. Settings: H4Z P7V hidden p=0.5, input p=0.8; J3V P7V p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5); D4K σ = sqrt((1-p)/p); results averaged over 10 seeds. Matching moments: use second representation (scale retained training activations by 1/p) so multipliers r_b take 1/p with prob p (E=1, Var=(1-p)/p); choose r_g~N(1,σ^2) with σ^2=(1-p)/p to match mean/var. Expected activations unchanged, so no test-time scaling needed. Paper reports preliminary slight advantage for high-entropy (Gaussian) multipliers.

steps.notes_before: QX2: trains sampled submodels from a large model to improve generalization; sampling increases training time (typically 2–3×). U2L fits this scheme; B8T (dropout-style for RBMs, p=0.5) shows coarser features than U2L and fewer dead units; Figures 12–13 illustrate B8T (no numeric score supplied there). H4Z autoencoder (256 hidden): QX2 dropout (p=0.5) produced localized features; mean hidden activity ≈2.0 (no QX2) vs ≈0.7 (with QX2). Data-size sweep (100,500,1K,5K,10K,50K): no QX2 improvement at smallest sizes; gains rise then fall. Sec.9 closed-form marginalization (linear regression): E_R||y-(R⊙X)w||^2 = ||y-pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Γw||^2 with Γ=(diag(X^T X))^{1/2}; with w̃=pw this gives penalty ((1-p)/p)||Γw̃||^2 ((1-p)/p coefficient noted). Logistic/deep nets: marginalization harder. Sec.10: multiplicative Gaussian D4K vs Bernoulli P7V; match moments by using scaled representation (scale retained activations by 1/p) so r_b has E=1 Var=(1-p)/p; choose r_g~N(1,σ^2) with σ^2=(1-p)/p => no test-time scaling needed. Table10 (classification %): H4Z P7V 1.08±0.04 vs D4K 0.95±0.04; J3V P7V 12.6±0.1 vs D4K 12.5±0.1. Conclusion asserts SOTA on A2F (Table3 2.47), K9D top-5 (Table6 16.4), W6R (Table4 37.20), and H4Z (Table2 0.79) and lists other-domain pairs (Table7 23.4 vs 21.8; §6.3 31.05% vs 29.62%; Table8 440 vs 567).

QX2 trains by sampling submodels from a large model (increases training time ~2–3×). Visual/feature results: B8T (dropout-style RBM, p=0.5) yields coarser features than U2L and fewer dead units (Figs.12–13). H4Z autoencoder (256 hidden): QX2 (p=0.5) produced localized features; mean hidden activity ≈2.0 (no QX2) vs ≈0.7 (with QX2). Data-size sweep (100, 500, 1k, 5k, 10k, 50k): no QX2 improvement at smallest sizes; gains rise then fall. Sec.9 (linear regression marginalization): E_R||y-(R⊙X)w||^2 = ||y-pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Γw||^2 with Γ=(diag(X^T X))^{1/2}; with w̃=pw this gives penalty ((1-p)/p)||Γw̃||^2. Logistic/deep nets: closed-form marginalization harder. Sec.10: using scaled representation (scale retained activations by 1/p) makes Bernoulli r_b have E=1 Var=(1-p)/p; choose multiplicative Gaussian r_g ~ N(1, σ^2) with σ^2=(1-p)/p to match moments (no test-time scaling). Table10 classification: H4Z P7V 1.08±0.04 vs D4K 0.95±0.04; J3V P7V 12.6±0.1 vs D4K 12.5±0.1. Conclusion claims SOTA numbers (Table2–Table8 references). Appendix A (practical heuristics): recommend QX2 layer width ≥ n/p if standard-net optimal is n (so expected survivors ≈n); removal reduces expected survivors to p·(original_units) if you don't compensate. QX2 increases gradient noise — use larger learning rates (typically 10–100× standard-optimal) and higher momentum (standard ~0.9; QX2 ~0.95–0.99). Use max-norm bounds V9C with c≈3–4. Retention p: hidden typical 0.5–0.8, real-valued inputs typically ~0.8, simple default 0.5; input-unit optimum closer to 1. Low-p can slow training and cause underfitting (Fig.9, §7.3 example: p=0.1 fixed-architecture error 2.7% vs fixed-expected-width 1.7%).

Appendix B supplies reproduction details and data prep; code at http://www.cs.toronto.edu/~nitish/dropout; GPU libs cudamat and cuda-convnet. Paper: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (JMLR 15, 2014). Authors: Nitish Srivastava, Geoffrey Hinton, Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, Ruslan Salakhutdinov. Abstract/main claim: Dropout randomly drops units and their connections during training to prevent co-adaptation; training effectively samples from an exponential number of "thinned" networks. At test time, the effect of averaging these thinned networks is approximated by using a single unthinned network with scaled (smaller) weights. Dropout reportedly reduces overfitting and outperforms other regularization methods, producing major improvements and state-of-the-art results on benchmarks in vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology. Intro notes: deep nets are expressive and prone to overfitting; common regularizers include early stopping, L1/L2 penalties, and soft weight sharing. The paper states that with unlimited computation the best regularizer is averaging predictions over all parameter settings (sentence is cut off in this part). New from current part: Motivation analogies — sexual reproduction: dropout viewed as preventing large co-adaptations, forcing each hidden unit to learn useful features that work with random subsets of partners, improving robustness; copying units to resist dropout is a poor solution (analogy to replica codes for noisy channels). Conspiracy analogy: many small conspiracies (small co-adaptations) more robust than one large co-adaptation, hence better generalization under non-stationarity. Related work: Dropout can be seen as regularization via adding noise to hidden units; this idea relates to Denoising Autoencoders (Vincent et al. 2008, 2010) which add noise to unit states.

steps.notes_before: Paper: Dropout trains by randomly dropping units (thinning) and sharing weights across exponentially many sub-networks. Training samples a new thinned net each presentation; backpropagate gradients through that thinned net. At test time use a single unthinned net with weights scaled by retention probabilities (W_test = p W^(l) per layer). Typical choices: drop ~50% hidden units (p_hidden ≈ 0.5), ~20% inputs (p_input ≈ 0.8); DAEs typically use 5% input noise but test-time scaling allows higher noise. Dropout can be applied to hidden layers and other neuron-based architectures (e.g., Boltzmann Machines, RBMs). Interpretation: stochastic regularization / model averaging; related to denoising autoencoders and marginalizing noise. Definition details: network with L hidden layers; y(0)=x; feed-forward recurrence given as z^{(l+1)} = W^{(l+1)} y^{(l)} + b^{(l+1)}, y^{(l+1)} = f(z^{(l+1)}). With dropout: sample r^{(l)} ~ Bernoulli(p) elementwise, form y_e^{(l)} = r^{(l)} * y^{(l)} and use y_e^{(l)} as input to next layer. Loss is minimized stochastically (expected loss); prior adversarial-drop work fixes max number dropped (no hidden-layer models).

Training: dropout nets trained by SGD on ‘‘thinned’’ nets — for each training case in a mini‑batch sample dropout mask, do forward/backprop on that thinned net; gradients averaged over mini‑batch; any case that omits a parameter contributes zero gradient for that parameter. Standard SGD tricks (momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 weight decay) help. Max‑norm regularization: constrain incoming weight vector w at each hidden unit to ||w||2 ≤ c by projecting back into the ball of radius c whenever it exceeds c (c is a tunable hyperparameter). Max‑norm often improves SGD even without dropout; combining dropout + max‑norm + large decaying LR + high momentum gives further gains (intuition: ball constraint prevents blowup so large LR can be used for exploration). Unsupervised pretraining: stacks of RBMs/autoencoders/DBMs can be used; pretraining stays the same, but when finetuning with dropout scale pretrained weights by 1/p so expected output under dropout matches pretraining output. If finetune LR is too large pretrained information can be lost; use smaller LR to retain gains. Experiments: datasets include MNIST, TIMIT, CIFAR‑10/100, SVHN, ImageNet, Reuters‑RCV1, and an Alternative Splicing RNA dataset; more details in Appendix B.

final_notes:
Section 8: Dropout = sampling retention vector r∈{0,1}^F. U2L = large-model construction sampling/training submodels; paper notes an internal inconsistency in U2L RBM parameterization (joint written P(h,v) ∝ exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v) but displayed conditionals swap a and b). B8T enforces h_j=0 when r_j=0 via g(h_j,r_j); trained with CD-1, r sampled per case. B8T yields coarser features and fewer dead units than U2L (Fig.12). QX2 methods (dropout variants) achieved SOTA on A2F, K9D, W6R, H4Z and improved standard nets elsewhere.

Section 9: Marginalizing dropout gives a deterministic differentiable loss; linear-regression identity E_R[||y-(R*X)w||^2] = ||y - p X w||^2 + p(1-p)||Γ w||^2 (and equivalently with w̃=pw).

Section 10: Multiplicative Gaussian noise (D4K) ≳ Bernoulli dropout (P7V); example H4Z P7V 1.08±0.04 vs D4K 0.95±0.04; J3V P7V 12.6±0.1 vs D4K 12.5±0.1. D4K per-layer σ^2=(1-p)/p; results averaged over 10 seeds. Conclusions: QX2 training 2–3× longer; noise reduces overfitting; marginalization helpful.

Appendix A heuristics: layer width ≥ n/p; QX2 LR often 10–100× standard-net optimal; momentum ≈0.95–0.99; V9C c≈3–4; retention p: hidden 0.5–0.8, inputs ~0.8 (default 0.5).

(2011).

Title: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting". Authors: Nitish Srivastava, Geoffrey Hinton, Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, Ruslan Salakhutdinov; Dept. of Computer Science, University of Toronto. Journal: JMLR 15 (2014). Header lists pages 1929–1958 while page map lists pages 1930–1955 (internal inconsistency noted). Abstract summary: introduces dropout (called "QX2: dropout") — a training procedure that temporarily removes randomly selected units and their connections, inhibiting excessive co-adaptation and effectively sampling exponentially many parameter-sharing thinned networks. At test time a single unthinned network with reduced weights approximates the averaged predictions of these thinned networks. Claims dropout substantially reduces overfitting versus other regularizers and yields major improvements, achieving state-of-the-art performance on many benchmarks in supervised vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology.

steps.notes_before: Title: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al., UToronto). Header/page-number inconsistency noted earlier. Dropout (QX2) randomly removes units/connections during training, producing exponentially many (2^n for n units) thinned networks; parameters are shared so total distinct parameters retained are O(n^2) or fewer. With unlimited computation, posterior-weighted averaging over parameters is ideal; the paper claims its method approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of these thinned models' predictions (introduction) — earlier abstract wording said it "approximates the averaged predictions", a potential arithmetic vs geometric-mean wording mismatch. Every presentation samples/trains a new thinned member; individual members are rarely trained thoroughly. Practical inference: T6R (weight scaling) uses one unthinned network at test time; X9M refers to Monte-Carlo model averaging (more expensive). Claims T6R gives much lower generalization error than other regularizers across tasks. Method extends to graphical models, e.g., Dropout RBM (B8T) from RBMs (U2L). Paper map: §2 motivation; §3 prior work; §4 formal model; §5 training algorithm; §6 experiments; §7 network/hyperparameter interactions; §8 Dropout RBMs; §9 marginalization; Appendix A practical guidance.

Title: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al.). Earlier: header/page-number inconsistency noted. Method overview: dropout (QX2) randomly removes units/connections during training, producing exponentially many (2^n) thinned networks; parameters are shared so total distinct parameters are O(n^2) or fewer. Training samples/train different thinned networks; individual thinned members rarely trained thoroughly. Test-time inference: T6R = weight-scaling using one unthinned network; X9M = Monte-Carlo model averaging (more expensive). Paper claims T6R yields much lower generalization error than other regularizers across tasks. Extensions: Dropout RBM (B8T). Paper map: §2 motivation; §3 prior work; §4 formal model; §5 training algorithm; §6 experiments; §7 interactions; §8 Dropout RBMs; §9 marginalization; Appendix A guidance. New from §2 (Motivation): authors use biological analogy—sexual vs asexual reproduction—and cite Livnat et al. (2010) arguing selection can favor gene "mix-ability" rather than individual-fitness optimization. Dropout is analogous: hidden units face randomly selected partners, which favors independently useful, robust features and reduces complex co-adaptations. Replicating units many times is deemed a poor robustness fix (analogy to replica codes and noisy channels). Conspiracy analogy: many small cooperating subsets are more robust under non-stationarity than a single large co-adapted set; complex co-adaptations may overfit training data and fail on novel test data.

Title: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al.). Method: dropout (QX2) randomly removes units/connections during training producing ~2^n thinned networks; parameters shared so distinct params O(n^2). Training: each SGD update samples a thinned network; individual thinned members rarely trained thoroughly. Test-time inference: T6R = weight-scaling using one unthinned network; X9M = Monte-Carlo model averaging (more expensive). Paper claims T6R gives much lower generalization error than other regularizers across tasks. Motivation (§2): biological analogy (mix-ability), reduces co-adaptations. Related work (§3): dropout interpretable as noise in hidden-unit states, extends denoising autoencoders (Vincent et al. 2008/2010) — effective hidden-layer corruption, model-averaging view, supervised/unsupervised use, applicable to Boltzmann Machines. Table: S2H (DAE) typical best noise ~5%; QX2 often optimal input-unit removal ~20%; QX2 often optimal hidden-unit removal ~50%. Adversarial-removal alternatives (Globerson & Roweis 2006; Dekel et al. 2010) consider worst-case removals under a budget and have no hidden units. Analytic marginalization can give deterministic regularizers in simple cases; van der Maaten et al. (2013) studied exponential-family input-noise (blankout) limited to models without hidden layers; Chen et al. (2012) studied marginalization for DAEs; Wang & Manning (2013) proposed marginalization to speed up dropout. Section map: §2 motivation; §3 prior work; §4 formal model; §5 training algorithm; §6 experiments; §7 interactions; §8 Dropout RBMs; §9 marginalization; Appendix A guidance.

Paper: Dropout regularization. Key idea: during training randomly delete (zero) units (hidden and/or visible) to sample many thinned subnetworks; parameters shared across subnetworks. Retention choices are independent Bernoulli variables with common probability p (can be chosen by validation). Typical defaults: hidden-unit retention p≈0.5 (i.e. ~50% removal); input-unit removal often ~20% (retention p≈0.8) — input retention usually nearer full. Training: each SGD update samples r^{(l)} (vector of independent Bernoulli(p)) and forms \tilde y^{(l)} = r^{(l)} * y^{(l)}; forward: z_i^{(l+1)} = w_i^{(l+1)} \tilde y^{(l)} + b_i^{(l+1)}, y_i^{(l+1)} = f(z_i^{(l+1)}). Backprop passes gradients through the sampled subnetwork. Notation: y^{(0)}=x; L hidden layers (indexed 1..L); feed-forward written for l=0..L-1 producing layer l+1. Activation f can be any (e.g. logistic). Test-time inference: no dropout; use one unthinned network with outgoing weights scaled by p: W_test^{(l)} = p W^{(l)} (equivalently unit outputs' expected training contribution equals test-time contribution with scaled weights). Figures illustrate training (stochastic gates r) vs testing (weights scaled by p). Other parts: training samples many subnetworks per SGD update; Monte-Carlo averaging at test-time is an alternative to weight-scaling but more expensive.

Part 5: QX2 (dropout) gives significant gains; combining it with high momentum, large decaying learning rates, and an incoming-weight constraint (V9C = max-norm) gives further improvement. V9C enforces ||w||_2 <= c with projection to the ball surface when exceeded; c is tuned by validation. Proposed optimization account claims large learning rates are safe inside the fixed-radius ball; QX2 provides noise exploration; learning rates decay to smaller steps. SGD differs from standard training only by per-case sampled thinned networks: each mini-batch case uses its own sampled network; gradients averaged across cases; a case not using a parameter contributes zero. Momentum, annealed (decaying) learning rates and other heuristics remain useful. Unsupervised pretraining is unchanged, but before QX2 finetuning pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p so each unit’s expected random-removal output matches its pretraining output. Smaller finetuning learning rates help preserve pretrained information. Pretraining (with unlabeled data) can improve over random init; applicable to stacked U2L, autoencoders, DBMs for finetuning.

errors.claim: In the U2L definition a is the hidden bias and b the visible bias, but the conditional formulas treat b as the hidden bias and a as the visible bias.
errors.evidence:
U2L definition: "P(h,v;\theta)=\frac{1}{Z(\theta)} \exp( v^\top W h + a^\top h + b^\top v )."
Conditional hidden probability: "P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\, \sigma\!(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i)."
Conditional visible probability: "P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma\!(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j)."
errors.explanation: The energy term a^T h + b^T v assigns a_j as hidden biases and b_i as visible biases, but the later conditional for hidden units uses b_j (not a_j) and the visible conditional uses a_i (not b_i), i.e. the roles of a and b are swapped, an internal inconsistency.

steps.notes_before: Section 8 defines B8T: dropout applied to U2L (a mixture over exponentially many shared-weight U2Ls) with retention vector r in {0,1}^F, P(r)=∏_j p^{r_j}(1-p)^{1-r_j}. U2L joint: P(h,v;θ) ∝ exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v) (so a = hidden biases, b = visible biases). B8T enforces h_j=0 when r_j=0 via factor g(h_j,r_j); conditionals given: P(h_j=1|r_j,v)=1(r_j=1) σ(b_j+Σ_i W_{ij} v_i) and P(v_i=1|h)=σ(a_i+Σ_j W_{ij} h_j) — note: this swaps a and b relative to the joint definition (inconsistency). Learning: apply CD-1, sample r per case and train only retained hidden units. Empirical claims: B8T features appear coarser than sharply defined stroke-like U2L features, with very few dead units relative to U2L (Fig.12). Without extra sparsity regularizer, B8T yields much sparser representations than U2L; Fig.13 shows activation histograms: "Without QX2: many activations away from zero" vs "QX2 p=0.5: many near zero and few high activations."

Section 8 (B8T): dropout applied to U2L as a mixture over shared-weight U2Ls. Retention vector r ∈ {0,1}^F with P(r)=∏_j p^{r_j}(1-p)^{1-r_j}. U2L joint given as P(h,v;θ) ∝ exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v) (so a labelled as hidden biases, b as visible), but the conditionals shown are P(h_j=1|r_j,v)=1(r_j=1) σ(b_j+Σ_i W_{ij} v_i) and P(v_i=1|h)=σ(a_i+Σ_j W_{ij} h_j) — this swaps a and b relative to the joint (noted inconsistency). B8T enforces h_j=0 when r_j=0 via g(h_j,r_j); learning via CD-1, sampling r per case and training only retained hidden units. Empirics: B8T features are coarser, very few dead units vs U2L (Fig.12); without extra sparsity B8T (QX2 p=0.5) produces much sparser activations (Fig.13) — histogram: no-QX2 many activations away from zero; QX2 many near zero and few high activations. Section 9 (this part): Marginalizing QX2 yields deterministic, gradientable losses (no Monte-Carlo randomness). For linear regression with input-mask R_{ij}∼Bernoulli(p), E_R[||y-(R*X)w||^2]=||y-pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Γ w||^2 where Γ=(diag(X^T X))^{1/2}. With ṽ=w̃=pw, equivalent form is ||y-X w̃||^2 + ((1-p)/p)||Γ w̃||^2. Thus dropout ↔ ridge with feature-wise penalty scaled by column std and global coeff (1-p)/p. 9.2: approximate marginalization helps logistic regression; closed-form marginalization is harder for logistic/deep nets, but Gaussian approximations for pre-activations/gradients can be used (assumptions weaken for deeper nets).

Section 8 (B8T): dropout applied to U2L as a mixture over shared-weight U2Ls. Retention vector r∈{0,1}^F with P(r)=∏_j p^{r_j}(1-p)^{1-r_j}. U2L joint written P(h,v;θ) ∝ exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v) but the conditionals shown swap a and b relative to that joint (noted inconsistency). B8T enforces h_j=0 when r_j=0 via g(h_j,r_j); trained with CD-1, sampling r per case. Empirics: B8T features coarser and far fewer dead units vs U2L (Fig.12). QX2 (dropout p=0.5) without extra sparsity yields much sparser activations when extra sparsity used; histograms differ (Fig.13). Section 9: marginalizing dropout gives deterministic, gradientable losses; linear regression with input-mask R yields E_R[||y-(R*X)w||^2]=||y-pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Γ w||^2, equivalent to ||y-X w̃||^2 + ((1-p)/p)||Γ w̃||^2 with w̃=pw — dropout ↔ ridge with feature-wise penalty scaled by column std and global coeff (1-p)/p. Section 10 (this part): Multiplicative Gaussian (D4K) performs as well or slightly better than Bernoulli dropout (P7V). Table 10: H4Z: P7V 1.08±0.04 vs D4K 0.95±0.04; J3V: P7V 12.6±0.1 vs D4K 12.5±0.1. Comparison settings: H4Z hidden p=0.5, input p=0.8; J3V p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5). D4K per-layer σ = sqrt((1-p)/p). Multiplying activations by r'∼N(1,σ^2) preserves E[h]; N(1,1) ↔ additive noise h_i r, r∼N(0,1) (std = |h_i|). Equivalence: scaling retained training activations by 1/p (so multiplier r_b = 1/p w.p. p, else 0) has E=1, Var=(1-p)/p; choose Gaussian σ^2=(1-p)/p to match mean and variance. Averaging over 10 random seeds.

Section 8 (U2L/B8T): dropout applied to hidden layer as sampling a retention vector r∈{0,1}^F (P(r)=∏ p^{r_j}(1-p)^{1-r_j}); U2L presented as large-model construction that repeatedly samples/trains smaller submodels. Paper showed an internal inconsistency in the U2L RBM parameterization: joint written P(h,v) ∝ exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v) but displayed conditionals swap a and b. B8T enforces h_j=0 when r_j=0 via g(h_j,r_j); trained with CD-1, sampling r per case. Empirics: B8T yields coarser features and fewer dead units than U2L (Fig.12). QX2 methods (dropout variants) produce state-of-the-art on datasets A2F, K9D, W6R, H4Z and improve standard nets on others. Section 9 (noise marginalization): marginalizing dropout gives deterministic, differentiable loss; for linear regression with input-mask R, E_R[||y-(R*X)w||^2] = ||y - p X w||^2 + p(1-p)||Γ w||^2 — equivalently with w̃=pw to ||y - X w̃||^2 + ((1-p)/p)||Γ w̃||^2 (dropout ↔ ridge-like feature-wise penalty). Section 10 (P7V vs D4K): multiplicative Gaussian noise D4K performs as well/slightly better than Bernoulli dropout P7V; Table 10 examples: H4Z P7V 1.08±0.04 vs D4K 0.95±0.04; J3V P7V 12.6±0.1 vs D4K 12.5±0.1. D4K per-layer σ^2 set to (1-p)/p to match mean=1 and var. Averaged results over 10 seeds. Section 8 (U2L/B8T): dropout = sampling retention vector r∈{0,1}^F with P(r)=∏ p^{r_j}(1-p)^{1-r_j}. U2L presented as large-model construction that repeatedly samples/trains smaller submodels. Paper previously showed an internal inconsistency in the U2L RBM parameterization: joint written P(h,v) ∝ exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v) but displayed conditionals swap a and b. B8T enforces h_j=0 when r_j=0 via g(h_j,r_j); trained with CD-1, sampling r per case. Empirics: B8T yields coarser features and fewer dead units than U2L (Fig.12). QX2 methods (dropout variants) produced state-of-the-art on datasets A2F, K9D, W6R, H4Z and improved standard nets on others. Section 9 (noise marginalization): marginalizing dropout gives deterministic differentiable loss; for linear regression with input-mask R, E_R[||y-(R*X)w||^2] = ||y - p X w||^2 + p(1-p)||Γ w||^2; with w̃=pw this is ||y - X w̃||^2 + ((1-p)/p)||Γ w̃||^2 (dropout ↔ feature-wise ridge-like penalty). Section 10 (P7V vs D4K): multiplicative Gaussian noise D4K performs as well/slightly better than Bernoulli dropout P7V (examples: H4Z P7V 1.08±0.04 vs D4K 0.95±0.04; J3V P7V 12.6±0.1 vs D4K 12.5±0.1). D4K per-layer σ^2 set to (1-p)/p to match mean=1 and variance. Results averaged over 10 seeds. Conclusion: training QX2 typically takes 2–3× longer than standard nets; noisy updates likely reduce overfitting; noise marginalization helps but equivalent regularizers for complex models unclear; accelerating QX2 left to future work. Appendix A (practical heuristics): choose QX2 layer width ≥ n/p (to keep expected retained units ≈ n); QX2 learning rate often 10–100× the optimal standard-net rate; momentum around 0.95–0.99 (standard 0.9); V9C (weight-norm bound) c≈3–4; retention p: hidden-unit range 0.5–0.8, real-valued inputs ~0.8, simple default 0.5, input-unit optimum closer to 1.

Section 8 (U2L / B8T): dropout = sampling retention vector r in {0,1}^F. QX2 methods (dropout variants) gave SOTA on A2F, K9D, W6R, H4Z and improved standard nets elsewhere. final_notes: Key methods and equivalences: dropout reduces co-adaptations/overfitting; test-time weight-scaling by p approximates model averaging (MC ~50 draws gives similar); Bernoulli dropout in linear regression yields an L2 term ∝ (1-p)/p; multiplicative Gaussian noise N(1,σ^2) matches Bernoulli with σ^2=(1-p)/p (so N(1,1) ↔ p=0.5). Appendix A heuristics: effective size ~n/p, learning rates ~10–100× usual, momentum ≈0.95–0.99, max-norm c≈3–4, typical p_hidden 0.5–0.8, p_input ≈0.8. MNIST (2-layer, 1024 per layer): Bernoulli 1.08±0.04% vs Gaussian 0.95±0.04% (hidden p=0.5, input p=0.8); larger 2-layer nets improved (4096→1.01%, 8192→0.95%); 3-layer slightly worse. Appendix B protocol: hold-out val sets used (e.g., MNIST 10k val), pick hyperparams by val at 1M updates then retrain on combined set. SVHN: ~600k train, best arch conv-conv-conv + 2 FC(2048), retention per layer (0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5), max-norm c=4, momentum 0.95, reported test 2.55% (model chosen by val). CIFAR-10/100: similar conv architecture; smaller input-layer LR; per-channel GCN then ZCA. TIMIT/DBN details (Appendix B.4): input p=0.8, hidden p=0.5, max-norm c=4, momentum 0.95, high LR 0.1 with decay ε0(1+t/T)^-1; RBMs CD-1 with Gaussian RBM input variance fixed at 1; DBN finetuning gave best results with smaller LR ≈0.01 and max-norm added no improvement; speech test errors (Table 7, dropout rows): 21.8%, 19.7%, 19.7%. Reuters (Appendix B.5): subset of 402,738 articles (vocab 2000, 50 classes) split equally → ≈201,369 train; dropout improved all tried architectures but gains smaller than image/speech; best-network: 31.05% (no dropout) vs 29.62% (dropout). Alternative splicing (B.6): 3665 cassette exons, 1014 features, 4 tissue types; targets are 4 softmaxes (each 3-way: inc/exc/nc); Code Quality = Σ_i Σ_t Σ_s p_{i,t}^s log(q_t^s(r_i)/ ar p^s); two-layer dropout net (1024 units/layer), p_hidden=0.5, p_input=0.7, max-norm and high decaying LR; results averaged over 5 folds.

Paper summary: Introduces dropout — randomly removing units and their connections during training, which samples many smaller networks that share weights. At test time, a single full network with scaled weights approximates the ensemble of sampled networks. Reports improvements on image, speech, text, and alternative-splicing tasks. Compares dropout with other regularizers and Bayesian neural networks. Studies learned features, sparsity, dropout rates, network size, training-set size, and test-time averaging; finds Dropout Restricted Boltzmann Machines learn qualitatively different features and sparser representations. For linear regression, marginalizing dropout yields a modified ridge-regression objective. Preliminary experiments compare Bernoulli dropout to multiplicative Gaussian noise. Limitation noted: training time typically 2–3× longer than standard networks with the same architecture.

Paper introduces dropout: during training randomly remove units and their incoming/outgoing connections (Bernoulli dropout uses binary vars that equal 1 with probability p, the retention probability). At test time the ensemble is approximated by a single deterministic model via weight scaling (multiply a unit’s outgoing weights by p) or by marginalizing dropout noise (deterministic dropout model); Monte-Carlo dropout/model averaging samples thinned networks at test time. Gaussian (multiplicative) dropout multiplies activations by Gaussian noise; paper compares Bernoulli and Gaussian variants. For linear regression, marginalized dropout is equivalent in expectation to a modified ridge (Tikhonov) regression. Dropout-RBMs are RBMs augmented with binary retention variables; CD-1/Contrastive Divergence used for RBM training; partition function Z(θ) appears in RBM formulation. Code Quality (alternative-splicing task) is the negative KL-divergence metric (higher is better). Other key methods/terms: DBN/DBM pretraining, max-norm constraint (bound hidden-unit incoming weight norms), L1/L2 weight penalties, KL-sparsity regularizer, ReLU and maxout units, pooling (max, L2, L4) in image models, max-pooling after conv layers, permutation-invariant vs 2-D MNIST settings, Top-1/Top-5 ImageNet error definitions, PCA/ZCA whitening used in preprocessing, mix-ability measure for genes. Noted limitation: training time typically 2–3× longer than standard networks with same architecture.

For linear regression, marginalized dropout = modified ridge (Tikhonov). Dropout-RBMs include binary retention variables; trained with CD-1. Code Quality metric = negative KL-divergence (higher is better). Regularization/architecture details: DBN/DBM pretraining; max-norm constraint (bound hidden-unit incoming weight norms); L1/L2 penalties; KL-sparsity regularizer; ReLU and maxout units; pooling: max, L2, L4; max-pooling after conv layers; permutation-invariant vs 2-D MNIST distinction. Notation and key definitions: L (# hidden layers), l (layer index); i,j (unit/dim/data indices). x = network input (y^(0)). z^(l) = inputs to layer l; y^(l) = outputs; ~y^(l) = outputs after elementwise dropout mask. W^(l), w_i^(l), b^(l) = layer weights, unit incoming weights, biases. W_test^(l)=pW^(l) (test-time weight-scaling). f activation (example sigmoid 1/(1+exp(-x))); exp used in activations/probabilities. p = retention probability. r^(l) = Bernoulli mask vector for layer l; * = elementwise multiplication. n = # units (hidden units in a layer); 2^n possible thinned networks; O(n^2) shared parameter order; pn expected retained units. w general weight vector; ||w||_2 and max-norm bound c; squared norm notation ||·||^2. k = # MC samples for prediction averaging. RBM notation: v (visible), D (# visible), h (hidden), F (# hidden), binary spaces {0,1}^D/{0,1}^F, θ={W,a,b}, Z(θ) partition, r binary retention in Dropout RBM (and r as Gaussian noise in Sect.10), Z'(θ,r) conditional normalization, g(h_j,r_j) enforces h_j=0 if r_j=0, 1(·) indicator, P(·) probability, σ = RBM activation (and in Sect.10 Gaussian noise SD). Transpose, ∏, ∑ as usual. Regression: X∈R^{N×D}, y∈R^N, w∈R^D, R∈{0,1}^{N×D} with R_ij~Bernoulli(p). E, Var. Γ=(diag(X^T X))^{1/2} used in marginalized dropout penalty; ~w = p w. Multiplicative noise: h_i, r'~N(1,σ^2) with σ^2 matched to (1-p)/p; r_b rescaled Bernoulli =1/p w.p. p; r_g Gaussian mean 1 var (1-p)/p. Also listed N(1,1), N(0,1) as example Gaussians.
