Paper metadata: Title Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting. Authors: Nitish Srivastava, Geoffrey Hinton, Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, Ruslan Salakhutdinov (Univ. of Toronto). Editor: Yoshua Bengio. Journal: JMLR 15 (2014) 1929–1958.
Main idea: During training randomly remove units+connections (Bernoulli retention p) sampling exponential number of thinned networks; at test time use one unthinned network with scaled weights (W_test = p W) to approximate average predictions. Dropout claimed to reduce overfitting and prevent co-adaptation.
Claims/evidence (reported): improves across domains — image results in Tables 2–6; TIMIT rows in Table 7; Reuters: 31.05% (no dropout) -> 29.62% (with dropout) in Sect. 6.3; alternative-splicing rows 440 and 567 bits in Table 8; Table 9: dropout improves over other regularizers in all rows; Dropout+Max-norm = 1.05% vs Max-norm = 1.35% and L2 = 1.62%.
Key notation/definitions (from earlier): L layers; l index; x=y^(0); z^(l)=inputs; y^(l)=outputs; ~y^(l)=after dropout mask; W^(l), w_i^(l), b^(l); W_test^(l)=pW^(l); f activation (e.g. sigmoid); p retention prob; r^(l) Bernoulli mask; n units; k MC samples for averaging; max-norm c; regression and RBM notation summarized (X,y,w,R with R_ij~Bernoulli(p); RBM θ={W,a,b}, Z partition, etc.); multiplicative-noise and rescaled Bernoulli equivalents noted; TIMIT lr schedule ε0(1+t/T)^{-1}.

Paper: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al., JMLR 2014). Main idea: during training randomly drop units (Bernoulli retain prob p) to sample many "thinned" networks; at test time use a single unthinned network with outgoing weights scaled by p (W_test = p W) to approximate averaging. Key definitions: L layers, r^(l) Bernoulli masks, ~y^(l) after dropout. A net with n units corresponds to 2^n thinned nets; they share weights so parameter count stays O(n^2). Typical choices: p≈0.5 for hidden units (often close to optimal), input-unit p usually closer to 1. Scaling outgoing weights by p at test time ensures expected training-time output equals test-time output. Motivation: approximate an equally weighted geometric mean / Bayesian-like averaging of exponentially many models with much less computation. Dropout applicable beyond feed-forward nets (Dropout RBM introduced). Paper claims dropout + weight-scaling reduces overfitting and improves generalization across domains; experiments reported in Sections 6–8 (image results Tables 2–6, TIMIT Table 7, Reuters improvement 31.05%→29.62% in Sect.6.3, alternative-splicing bits in Table 8, Table 9 comparisons: Dropout+Max-norm 1.05% vs Max-norm 1.35% vs L2 1.62%). TIMIT learning-rate schedule earlier noted: ε0 (1 + t/T)^(-1). Paper structure: Sec 2 motivation, 3 related work, 4 model, 5 training, 6 experiments, 7 hyperparams/properties, 8 Dropout RBMs, 9 marginalizing dropout, Appendix A guidance.

Paper: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al., JMLR 2014). Core idea: during training randomly drop units (Bernoulli masks r^(l), retain prob p) to sample many thinned networks; at test time use the full network with outgoing weights scaled by p (weight-scaling) to approximate averaging. Typical p≈0.5 for hidden units; input p usually closer to 1. Scaling by p makes test-time output equal to the expected training-time output (approximate model averaging). Dropout applies beyond feed-forward nets (Dropout RBMs): Figures 12–13 show qualitative feature and sparsity comparisons but no numeric performance comparison is reported there. Experiments (Secs.6–8) report improved generalization across domains (image Tables 2–6, TIMIT Table 7, Tables 2–7 and 9 cited for cross-domain error reductions). Reuters (Sec.6.3) error improved from 31.05% to 29.62%. Table 9: Dropout+Max-norm 1.05% vs Max-norm 1.35% vs L2 1.62% (alternative-splicing results also in Table 8). TIMIT uses learning rate schedule ε0(1 + t/T)^(-1). Section 2 motivation uses analogies (sexual reproduction / mix-ability; conspiracies) to argue dropout reduces complex co-adaptations, forcing units to be robust and individually useful.

Paper: "Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting" (Srivastava et al., JMLR 2014). Core idea: during training randomly drop units via Bernoulli masks r^(l) with retain prob p, sampling many thinned networks; at test time use full network with outgoing weights scaled by p (weight-scaling) to approximate averaging. Typical p ≈ 0.5 for hidden units; input p usually closer to 1. Dropout interpretable as adding noise to hidden-unit states; relates to Denoising Autoencoders (DAEs) which typically use ~5% input noise, but with weight-scaling dropout often uses much higher noise (e.g., drop 20% of inputs, 50% of hidden units). Dropout extends beyond unsupervised learning to supervised nets and other architectures (e.g., Dropout RBMs / Boltzmann Machines; Figures 12–13 show qualitative differences). In simple cases dropout noise can be marginalized analytically (Section 9.1 gives linear-regression derivations); related work on deterministic marginalization and "blankout" noise (van der Maaten et al., Wang & Manning, Chen et al.). Different adversarial-removal formulations studied by Globerson & Roweis (2006) and Dekel et al. (2010). Experiments (Secs. 6–8) report improved generalization across domains: Reuters (Sec.6.3) error improved from 31.05% to 29.62%; Table 9 reports Dropout+Max-norm 1.05% vs Max-norm 1.35% vs L2 1.62%; TIMIT used learning-rate schedule ε0(1 + t/T)^(-1). Section 2 gives motivational analogies (sexual reproduction/mix-ability, conspiracies).

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (Srivastava et al., JMLR 2014). Core idea: during training randomly drop units with independent Bernoulli masks r^{(l)} (retain prob p), sampling many thinned sub-networks; at test time use full network with outgoing weights scaled by p (weight-scaling). Typical p ≈ 0.5 for hidden units; input p usually closer to 1. Notation: L hidden layers (1..L); z^{(l)} = inputs into layer l, y^{(l)} = outputs (y^{(0)}=x), W^{(l)}, b^{(l)}. Standard forward: z_i^{(l+1)} = w_i^{(l+1)} y^{(l)} + b_i^{(l+1)}; y_i^{(l+1)} = f(z_i^{(l+1)}) (e.g., logistic f(x)=1/(1+e^{-x})). Dropout forward: r_j^{(l)} ~ Bernoulli(p) (each mask component independent, 1 with prob p), \tilde y^{(l)} = r^{(l)} * y^{(l)} (elementwise), then z_i^{(l+1)} = w_i^{(l+1)} \tilde y^{(l)} + b_i^{(l+1)}, y_i^{(l+1)} = f(z_i^{(l+1)}). Backpropagate loss derivatives through the sampled sub-network. Test-time: use full network without dropout and scale weights: W_test^{(l)} = p W^{(l)}. Section references: Sec.9.1 gives analytic marginalization in simple linear cases; experiments (Secs.6–8) report improved generalization (e.g., Reuters 31.05% → 29.62%; Table 9: Dropout+Max-norm 1.05% vs Max-norm 1.35% vs L2 1.62%); TIMIT used learning-rate schedule ε0(1+t/T)^{-1}. Figures illustrate standard vs dropout panels (bias +1, three inputs, masks in dropout).

Paper: Dropout (Srivastava et al., JMLR 2014). Core idea: during training randomly drop units with independent Bernoulli masks r^{(l)} (retain prob p), sampling many thinned sub-networks; at test time use full network with outgoing weights scaled by p (weight-scaling W_test = p W). Typical p ≈ 0.5 for hidden units; input p usually closer to 1. Training: use SGD (mini-batches); for each case sample a thinned network; forward/backprop only on that network. Gradients averaged across mini-batch; a case not using a parameter contributes zero gradient. Use momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 weight decay. Max-norm: constrain each unit’s incoming weight vector norm ||w||_2 ≤ c; if violated, project onto ball of radius c; c chosen by validation. Combining dropout with max-norm, large decaying learning rates and high momentum yields further gains. Reported MNIST figures (Table 9): Dropout + Max-norm 1.05%; Dropout + L2 1.25%; Max-norm (no dropout) 1.35%; L2 (no dropout) 1.62%. Unsupervised pretraining: can use RBMs, autoencoders, DBMs; pretraining uses unlabeled data and can help versus random init. When finetuning with dropout, pretrained weights should be multiplied by 1/p so each unit’s expected output under dropout equals its pretraining output. Authors observed pretrained information could be lost with large finetuning rates but preserved with smaller rates. Reported pretrained MNIST (Table 2): DBN rows 1.18% versus 0.92%; DBM rows 0.96% versus 0.79% (presented as dropout finetuning improving pretrained networks). Other notes: Reuters improved (31.05% → 29.62%); TIMIT used learning-rate schedule ε0(1+t/T)^{-1}.

MNIST regularizers (Section 6.5, one fixed ReLU architecture 784-1024-1024-2048-10): Test errors: L2 1.62%; L2+L1 (late) 1.60%; L2+KL-sparsity 1.55%; Max-norm 1.35%; Dropout+L2 1.25%; Dropout+Max-norm 1.05%. Claim: Dropout+Max-norm lowest in this comparison.

Carryforward key earlier results (for cross-checks): MNIST bests reported earlier—large dropout nets (2×8192) 0.95%; maxout 0.94%; DBN+dropout 0.92%; DBM 0.79%. SVHN conv net: baseline 3.95% → +dropout FC 3.02% → +dropout all 2.55%; maxout 2.47%. CIFAR-10/100: conv+maxpool 15.60/43.48; stochastic pooling 15.13/42.51; +dropout FC 14.32/41.26; +dropout all 12.61/37.20; maxout 11.68/38.57. ILSVRC-2010/2012 and TIMIT/Reuters results previously noted (including a TIMIT prose/table mismatch flagged earlier).

Section 7 investigates how dropout changes learned features, activation sparsity, and dependence on retention probability p.

7.1 Features: Compared two otherwise-identical MNIST one-hidden-layer autoencoders with 256 ReLU units: no dropout vs dropout p=0.5 (Figure 7). Both have similar test reconstruction error (exact numbers not given). Without dropout units appear co-adapted and less individually meaningful; with dropout units show localized edges/strokes/spots — supporting claim that dropout breaks co-adaptations.

7.2 Sparsity: Same 256-unit autoencoders evaluated on a test minibatch (Figure 8). No-dropout: histogram of units' mean activations centers near ~2.0 and activations show a large mode away from zero (many high activations). Dropout (p=0.5): units' mean activations drop to ~0.7 and the activation histogram has a sharp peak at zero. Conclusion: dropout yields sparser hidden activations without adding explicit sparsity regularizers.

7.3 Dropout rate: Two experimental regimes studied (Figure 9): (1) keep hidden-unit count n fixed (architecture 784-2048-2048-2048-10, no input dropout) and vary p; small p => few active units and high training error (underfitting); error decreases as p increases, is flat for 0.4<=p<=0.8, then increases as p->1. (2) keep pn fixed (expected retained units fixed) so smaller p uses larger networks; expected retained count same but different total network sizes.

Figures: Fig.7 (features), Fig.8 (sparsity histograms), Fig.9 (error vs p). No numerical contradictions with earlier notes were found in this part.

Section 7 summary and key numbers: 7.1 (Features) — One-hidden-layer MNIST autoencoders with 256 ReLU units compared: no-dropout vs dropout p=0.5 (Fig.7). Test reconstruction errors similar (numbers not given). Dropout units show more localized edge/stroke/spot features; no-dropout units appear co-adapted. 7.2 (Sparsity) — Same 256-unit autoencoder: no-dropout units have mean activations ~2.0 and many large activations; dropout (p=0.5) reduces mean activations to ~0.7 and yields a sharp peak at zero (sparser activations) (Fig.8). 7.3 (Dropout rate) — Two regimes: (A) fixed hidden-unit counts (architecture 784-2048-2048-2048-10, no input dropout): small p -> underfitting (few active units), error decreases as p increases, flat over 0.4<=p<=0.8, then rises as p->1 (Fig.9a). (B) keep expected retained units fixed (vary total n so pn constant): pn set to 256,256,512 for the three hidden layers; Fig.9b shows much smaller errors at low p than Fig.9a — at p=0.1 error falls from 2.7% (fixed-architecture) to 1.7% (fixed-pn). For these retained sizes p≈0.6 is best; default p=0.5 close to optimal. 7.4 (Data-set size) — Architecture 784-1024-1024-2048-10; hidden p=0.5, input p=0.8; training-set sizes: 100, 500, 1K, 5K, 10K, 50K. Dropout gives no improvement for 100 and 500; as data increases the benefit first grows then declines — a suggested “sweet spot” (Fig.10). 7.5 (Monte-Carlo vs weight scaling) — On MNIST, averaging k sampled dropout networks matches weight-scaling around k≈50; larger k is slightly better but within one standard deviation, so weight scaling is a good, cheap approximation (Fig.11).

Section 7 (earlier): Autoencoder experiments (MNIST), one-hidden-layer 256 ReLU units: dropout p=0.5 vs no-dropout. Dropout units show more localized edge/stroke/spot features; no-dropout units co-adapted. Dropout yields sparser activations: mean down ~2.0 -> ~0.7, sharp peak at zero. Dropout rate study: two regimes (fixed architecture vs fixed expected retained units pn); best p around 0.5–0.6; default p=0.5 near optimal. Data-size study: dropout benefit depends on training-set size (no benefit for 100/500), sweet spot as data increases. Monte-Carlo vs weight scaling: weight scaling approximates averaging k≈50 samples. Section 8 (current): Defines Dropout RBM: introduce mask r∈{0,1}^F with P(r)=∏ p^{r_j}(1-p)^{1-r_j}; joint P(r,h,v)=P(r)P(h,v|r) where P(h,v|r) = (1/Z'(r)) exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v) ∏_j g(h_j,r_j) and g enforces h_j=0 when r_j=0. Conditionals: P(h|r,v)=∏_j P(h_j|r_j,v) with P(h_j=1|r_j,v)=1_{r_j=1} σ(b_j+∑_i W_{ij}v_i). Visible conditional standard. Learning: sample r each minibatch, apply standard RBM learning (CD-1 used). Experiments (MNIST, 256 binary hidden units, p=0.5): Figure 12 shows dropout-RBM features appear coarser than standard RBM and have few dead units; Figure 13 shows activation histograms indicating dropout yields sparser hidden-unit activations (many units near zero) without extra sparsity regularizer. No numerical counts or sparsity metrics reported.

errors.explanation: The paper defines Γ as the square root of diag(X^T X), i.e. the L2 column norms (sqrt of sum of squared entries), not the standard deviation (which requires centering and normalization). Claiming Γ equals the standard deviation is inconsistent with the given definition unless the paper also assumes X is mean-centered and scaled (which it does not state).

steps.notes_before: Section 7 (earlier): Autoencoder (MNIST) with one hidden layer 256 ReLUs; dropout p=0.5 vs no-dropout: dropout yields more localized features, sparser activations (mean activation ~2.0 -> ~0.7 with a peak at zero); dropout-rate study: best p≈0.5–0.6; data-size study: dropout benefit depends on training-set size; Monte-Carlo vs weight scaling: weight scaling approximates averaging ~50 samples. Section 8: Dropout RBM: introduce mask r∈{0,1}^F with P(r)=∏ p^{r_j}(1-p)^{1-r_j}; P(h_j=1|r_j,v)=1_{r_j=1}σ(b_j+∑_i W_{ij}v_i); learn by sampling r each minibatch (CD-1 used); MNIST exp with 256 binary hidden units, p=0.5: dropout-RBM features coarser, few dead units; activations sparser (many near zero). Section 9 (current): Marginalizing dropout yields deterministic objectives. Linear regression: minimize E_R[||y-(R*X)w||^2] = ||y-pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Γ w||^2 with Γ=(diag(X^T X))^{1/2}; letting ṽw = p w gives ||y-Xṽw||^2 + ((1-p)/p)||Γ ṽw||^2, so regularization depends on p. Note: paper asserts Γ is the standard deviation per feature, but Γ as defined is the column L2 norm (no centering stated). Section 9.2: Logistic regression marginalization approximated via Gaussian approximations (Wang & Manning 2013) — faster and better than MC dropout for logistic regression, but assumptions weaken for deep networks so results don't directly extend.

Section 10: Multiplicative Gaussian Noise generalizes dropout by using multiplicative Gaussian r' ~ N(1,σ^2) (equivalently additive noise h_i r with r ~ N(0,σ^2)). With mean 1, expected activation is preserved so no test-time weight scaling is needed in this parameterization. The paper also uses an alternate Bernoulli parameterization r_b = 1/p with prob p else 0 (so E[r_b]=1, Var[r_b]=(1-p)/p). They match moments by setting σ^2 = (1-p)/p (σ = sqrt((1-p)/p)) per layer. N(1,1) corresponds to p=0.5. The paper notes Gaussian (highest differential entropy for fixed mean/var) may perform slightly better; Table 10 reports MNIST (2-layer 1024 units): Bernoulli 1.08±0.04% vs Gaussian 0.95±0.04% (p_hidden=0.5, p_input=0.8); CIFAR-10 (3 conv + 2 FC, p vector given including input) Bernoulli 12.6±0.1% vs Gaussian 12.5±0.1%. σ set from each layer’s Bernoulli p; results averaged over 10 seeds. Relevant earlier results: Section 9 linear-regression marginalization yielded a regularization factor ((1-p)/p) (consistent with σ^2 mapping); Section 7 found dropout best p≈0.5–0.6 and that weight-scaling at test approximates MC averaging (~50 samples).

Sec 7–11 key points: Dropout breaks co-adaptations and reduces overfitting; best hidden-unit keep prob p≈0.5–0.6. Test-time weight-scaling by p approximates averaging of submodels (MC averaging; ~50 samples gave similar results). Sec 9.1: marginalizing Bernoulli dropout in linear regression yields a modified L2 regularizer; analytical factor ∝(1-p)/p. Sec 10: multiplicative Gaussian noise parameterization r'~N(1,σ^2) (so E[activation] preserved; no test-time weight-scaling required in that parameterization). Match moments to Bernoulli by σ^2=(1-p)/p (σ = sqrt((1-p)/p)); N(1,1) corresponds to p=0.5. Table 10 (reported) MNIST (2-layer 1024): Bernoulli 1.08±0.04% vs Gaussian 0.95±0.04% (p_hidden=0.5, p_input=0.8); CIFAR-10 (3 conv + 2 FC): Bernoulli 12.6±0.1% vs Gaussian 12.5±0.1%. Results averaged over 10 seeds. Sec 11 (Conclusion): Dropout yields SOTA/strong results on SVHN, ImageNet, CIFAR-100, MNIST (paper cites specific table numbers); extends to RBMs (Dropout RBMs show different features and greater sparsity — Figs 12–13). Drawback: training typically 2–3× slower due to noisy updates and effectively training many random submodels; more training time trades off with overfitting. Marginalizing noise can help (linear case → modified L2); deriving equivalents for complex models is nontrivial; accelerating dropout is future work. Specific table callouts in conclusion: Reuters error improvement (31.05% → 29.62%), Table 2 DBM+dropout 0.79%, Table 3 maxout 2.47%, Table 4 CIFAR-100 37.20%, Tables 5–6 ImageNet rows.

steps.notes_before: (none yet: this is the first part)

Dropout: randomly remove units and their connections during training, effectively training many smaller networks that share parameters. At test time, use one complete network with reduced weights to approximate averaging the smaller networks' predictions. Claimed benefits: improves generalization over networks without dropout on every tested dataset; reports state-of-the-art results on several benchmarks. Experimental domains: images, speech, documents, gene-splicing prediction. Also examines learned features, sparsity, retention rates, effects of training-set size, Restricted Boltzmann Machines, noise marginalization, and Gaussian corruption. Training cost: typically takes 2–3× longer than training a standard network of the same architecture.

Dropout (QX2): randomly remove units and their connections during training; at test time use one unthinned network with outgoing weights multiplied by the retention probability (T6R) to approximate averaging the thinned-model predictions. The paper states this approximation corresponds to the geometric mean (equally weighted combination) of thinned-network predictions. Two corruption types: Bernoulli dropout (P7V) — binary multiplicative noise (Bernoulli variable =1 with prob p, 0 otherwise) — and Gaussian dropout (D4K) — Gaussian multiplicative noise. Marginalization = expectation over dropout noise to yield a deterministic objective/regularizer; Monte‑Carlo dropout/model averaging = stochastic sampling and averaging predictions from sampled thinned networks. Dropout RBM (B8T): described as a mixture of shared-weight RBMs using different hidden-unit subsets; U2L = RBM; pretraining (DBM/E5Q, DBN/G6W) then finetuning with backprop; mcRBM-G6W is a named pretrained variant. Regularizers: L1 (O3U), L2 (Y5F, Tikhonov), max-norm (V9C), KL-sparsity. Activations mentioned: logistic units, ReLU (F3N), maxout (L8J). Other glossary items to track: geometric mean vs. posterior-weighted averaging, blankout noise, ridge-regression connection (dropout expectation → ridge-like penalty matrix), convolutional-net components (filters, pooling variants), data augmentation, SVM/PCA baselines, terms like dead unit, mix-ability, replica code, and non-stationarity. These definitions and labels will be used in later parts for numerical and conceptual consistency checks.

Marginalization = expectation over dropout noise → deterministic objective/regularizer; Monte Carlo dropout/model averaging = sample thinned nets and average predictions. Regularizers: L1, L2 (Tikhonov), max-norm, KL-sparsity. Activations: logistic, ReLU, maxout. Abstract summary: method called "QX2, or dropout"; it randomly removes units and their connections during training, inhibiting co-adaptation, sampling exponentially many thinned networks that share parameters. A single unthinned network with reduced weights approximates the averaged predictions of the thinned nets. Claims substantial reduction in overfitting and major improvements; supervised experiments in vision, speech recognition, document classification and computational biology reportedly attain state-of-the-art on many benchmarks. Evidence claimed in Tables 2–8 and an unnumbered text-classification table in §6.3; domain-specific comparisons listed in §6.

Paper: "Dropout (QX2)". Core idea: randomly remove units during training to train many shared-parameter thinned subnetworks (2^n possible thinned nets for n units) and approximate their combined predictions with one unthinned test-time network. Key terminology: QX2 = dropout; T6R = test-time weight scaling (use one unthinned net with scaled weights); X9M = Monte-Carlo model averaging (average sampled thinned nets at test); U2L/B8T = dropout extension to RBMs. Notation (carry-forward): n = unit count; expected retained width = p n; practical width heuristic = n/p; shared-parameter count O(n^2); L hidden layers with W^(l), b^(l), activations f; p = retention probability; test-time weights scaled by p (W_test = p W). Claims in this part: QX2 approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many models; a new thinned member is sampled and trained (rarely) per presentation of each training case; T6R is a cheap practical inference rule that gives significantly lower generalization error than other regularizers across varied problems; X9M is more expensive and needs around k≈50 samples (per §7.5 and App B.1) before matching T6R. Evidence pointer: Table 9 referenced for comparisons (rows quoted: Y5F=1.62, V9C=1.35, QX2+Y5F=1.25, QX2+V9C=1.05). Paper outline: §2 motivation, §3 prior work, §4 model, §5 training algorithm, §6 experiments, §7 effects and hyperparameter interactions, §8 RBM extension, §9 marginalization, Appendix A (practical guidance).

Paper: "Dropout (QX2)". Core idea: randomly remove units during training to train many shared-parameter thinned subnetworks (2^n possible thinned nets for n units) and approximate their combined predictions with one unthinned test-time network. Notation: n = unit count; p = retention probability; expected retained width = p n; practical width heuristic = n/p; shared-parameter count O(n^2); L hidden layers with W^(l), b^(l), activations f; test-time weights scaled by p (W_test = p W). Claims: QX2 approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many models; a new thinned member is sampled and trained (rarely unique) on each presentation of a training case; T6R (test-time weight scaling) is a cheap practical inference rule that gives significantly lower generalization error than other regularizers across varied problems; X9M (Monte-Carlo averaging) is more expensive and needs around k ≈ 50 samples (per §7.5 and App B.1) to match T6R. Evidence pointer: Table 9 comparisons (rows: Y5F=1.62, V9C=1.35, QX2+Y5F=1.25, QX2+V9C=1.05). New in §2: motivation via sexual-reproduction and conspiracy analogies — Livnat et al. (2010) "mix-ability" notion: selection favors genes that work well with random partners (robust, independently useful components). Analogy: QX2 forces hidden units to operate with randomly selected partners, discouraging complex co-adaptations and favoring robust features; replicating units is a poor remedy. Smaller cooperating subsets are argued to be more robust under non-stationarity than large co-adaptations. Outline pointers: §3 prior work, §4 model, §5 training algorithm, §6 experiments, §7 hyperparams, §8 RBM extension, §9 marginalization, Appendix A guidance.

Paper: "Dropout (QX2)". Core idea: randomly remove units during training to train many shared-parameter thinned subnetworks (2^n possible thinned nets for n units) and approximate their combined predictions with one unthinned test-time network. Notation/impl: n = unit count; p = retention probability; expected retained width = p n; practical width heuristic = n/p; shared-parameter count O(n^2); L hidden layers with weights W^(l), biases b^(l), activations f; test-time weights scaled by p (W_test = p W). Key claims: QX2 approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many models; a new thinned member is sampled and trained on each presentation; T6R (test-time weight scaling) is a cheap practical inference rule that often gives much lower generalization error than other regularizers; X9M (Monte-Carlo averaging) is more expensive and reportedly needs k ≈ 50 samples to match T6R (per §7.5 and App B.1). Empirical pointer: Table 9 example rows (Y5F=1.62, V9C=1.35, QX2+Y5F=1.25, QX2+V9C=1.05). Section 3 notes: DAEs (denoising autoencoders) corrupt inputs and reconstruct; QX2 extends corruption to hidden units and gives a model-averaging view; applies to supervised/unsupervised and other neuron-based architectures including Boltzmann Machines. T6R permits much higher noise than typical DAEs: table lists S2H/DAE typical best 5%, QX2 input-unit removal often optimal 20%, QX2 hidden-unit removal often optimal 50%. Related methods: Globerson & Roweis (2006) and Dekel et al. (2010) use adversarial removals (fixed max number) and have no hidden units. Marginalizing QX2 yields deterministic regularizers in simple cases; van der Maaten et al. (2013) call QX2 input noise "blankout noise" but limited to models without hidden layers; Chen et al. (2012) on marginalization for DAEs; Wang & Manning (2013) propose marginalization to accelerate QX2.

steps.notes_before: Paper: Dropout (QX2) — gate unit outputs during training, independently per unit with r_j^{(l)} ~ Bernoulli(p); tilde y^{(l)} = r^{(l)} * y^{(l)}. At inference no units removed; test-time weights scaled by retention p: W_test^{(l)} = p W^{(l)}. Expected preactivation under training dropout equals test preactivation with scaled weights. Both hidden and input (visible) units can be dropped. Validation can pick p; default often near optimal; input retention generally near complete retention. Forward equations: y^{(0)} = x; nominally z_i^{(l+1)} = w_i^{(l+1)} y^{(l)} + b_i^{(l+1)}, y_i^{(l+1)} = f(z_i^{(l+1)}). Example activation: logistic f(x)=1/(1+exp(-x)). Note: this part contains an indexing inconsistency — it first states l∈{1..L} then uses l∈{0..L-1} for the feed-forward formulas (treating y^{(0)} as input). Keep this in mind when later parts refer to layer indices.

Paper: QX2 = dropout (per-unit gate r_j^(l) ~ Bernoulli(p); ̃y^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l)). At test time do not drop units; scale weights by retention p (W_test = p W) so expected preactivation under dropout equals test preactivation. Both hidden and input units can be dropped (input retention usually near 1). Forward eqns use y^(0)=x; paper has an indexing inconsistency (uses l∈{1..L} then l∈{0..L-1}).

Sec.5 (Learning QX2 Nets): training = backprop through sampled subnetworks (one mask per case/minibatch case), gradients averaged across cases; a dropped parameter gets zero contribution. QX2 alone gives significant gains; combining QX2 with high momentum, large decaying learning rates and V9C (max-norm) gives further boost. V9C constrains each hidden unit's incoming weight vector via projection to ||w||_2 <= c (validation tunes c); projection returns w to the radius-c surface if exceeded. Proposed optimization story: fixed-radius weight ball allows huge LRs without explosion; QX2 noise explores; annealing settles.

Empirical notes cited: Table 9 rows: V9C=1.35, QX2+Y5F=1.25, QX2+V9C=1.05. Appendix A.2: practical LRs typically 10–100x optimal standard-net LR and momentum ~0.95–0.99. Pretraining: unchanged, but before QX2 finetuning multiply pretrained weights by 1/p so expected outputs under dropout match pretraining; use much smaller finetuning LR (Appendix B.4 reports ~0.01 best vs listed high LR 0.1). Table 2: G6W finetuning 1.18 -> 0.92 with QX2; E5Q 0.96 -> 0.79.

Paper studies QX2 (dropout). Data sets: H4Z (MNIST) 60K train /10K test, dim 784; J3V/W6R (CIFAR-10/100) 60K/10K, dim 3072; A2F (SVHN) 600K/26K, dim 3072; K9D (ImageNet ILSVRC-2012) 1.2M/150K, dim 65536; N8Q (TIMIT) 1.1M frames/58K frames, 2520 dim; M5X (Reuters-RCV1) 200K/200K, 2000 dim; Z7P (Splicing) 2932/733, 1014 dim. Claim: QX2 improved generalization over nets without QX2 on every tested data set; applied to vision, speech, text, genetics. For vision, QX2 models reported state-of-the-art on all five vision collections. MNIST (permutation-invariant) results (Table 2): Standard NN (Simard et al.) logistic 2×800: 1.60%; SVM Gaussian: 1.40%; QX2 NN logistic 3×1024: 1.35%; QX2+ReLU (F3N) 3×1024: 1.25%; QX2+V9C (max-norm) F3N 3×1024: 1.06, 3×2048: 1.04; 2×4096: 1.01; 2×8192: 0.95; QX2+V9C maxout (Goodfellow et al.) 2 layers (5×240): 0.94. Pretraining baselines: G6W (DBN) finetuning 500-500-2000: 1.18 → G6W+QX2 finetuning: 0.92; E5Q finetuning: 0.96 → E5Q+QX2 finetuning: 0.79. Text notes: QX2 prevents overfitting of very large networks (no early stopping needed). When hyperparameters (including retention p) fixed across architectures, test-error trajectories form two separated clusters: with vs without QX2. Figure 4 tick ranges: updates 0..1,000,000; error axis 1.0..2.5%.

Paper studies QX2 (dropout) on multiple datasets (vision: H4Z/MNIST, J3V/CIFAR-10, W6R/CIFAR-100, A2F/SVHN, K9D/ImageNet; plus N8Q/TIMIT, M5X/RCV1, Z7P/Splicing). Core claim: QX2 improves generalization across all tested datasets and yields state-of-the-art on the vision collections. MNIST (Table 2, permutation-invariant): standard logistic 2×800 1.60%; SVM Gaussian 1.40%; QX2 logistic 3×1024 1.35%; QX2+ReLU (F3N) 3×1024 1.25%; QX2+max-norm (V9C) F3N 3×1024 1.06, 3×2048 1.04, 2×4096 1.01, 2×8192 0.95; QX2+maxout (Goodfellow) 2-layer (5×240) 0.94. Pretraining: DBN (G6W) finetune 1.18 → +QX2 0.92; E5Q finetune 0.96 → +QX2 0.79 (reported best permutation-invariant result). Claim: QX2 prevents overfitting of very large nets; with fixed hyperparameters the test-error trajectories form two clusters (with vs without QX2); Fig.4 shows trajectories over 0..1,000,000 updates (error axis ~1.0–2.5%), no numerical curves provided; large net reportedly does not require early stopping. A2F/SVHN (Table 3): non-conv baselines 36.7→9.4; conv variants: multi-stage avg 9.06, L2 5.36, L4+pad 4.90; Conv+max 3.95; +QX2 in FCs 3.02; stochastic pooling 2.80; +QX2 in all layers 2.55; L8J (Goodfellow) 2.47; human 2.0. Text notes the explanation that corrupting lower conv layers gives noisy inputs that regularize higher FC layers, but no independent test of that explanation. J3V/W6R (Table 4, no augmentation except input QX2): Conv+max 15.60/43.48; stochastic 15.13/42.51; Snoek 14.98/-; +QX2 FC 14.32/41.26; +QX2 all layers 12.61/37.20; L8J 11.68/38.57. Appendix A (practical heuristics): widen QX2 layers to ≳ n/p; learning rate typically 10–100× standard-net; momentum around 0.95–0.99 (vs standard 0.9); max-norm c ≈ 3–4; hidden retention typical 0.5–0.8, real-valued-input retention ≈0.8, appendix advises broad default p=0.5 (conflicts with Section 7 note of p≈0.6); underfitting at very low p illustrated (p=0.1 example: 2.7% fixed arch vs 1.7% fixed expected width). H4Z (MNIST): held-out validation = 10,000; weight-update endpoint (tuning & final combined-data) = 1,000,000 updates. Architecture sweep: depths {2,3,4}, uniform widths {1024,2048} (6 combos). Hidden-layer retention p=0.5; input retention p=0.8. Momentum=0.95; max-norm (V9C) c=2 (all layers). Additional reg-limit experiments: 2 & 3 layers, units 4096 & 8192; largest reported two-layer model >65M parameters. Regularizer-comparison & data-size-comparison arch: 784-1024-1024-2048-10. Data-size-comparison training sets: {100, 500, 1K, 5K, 10K, 50K}. Fixed-width rate-comparison arch: 784-2048-2048-2048-10 (no input corruption). Fixed-expected-width comparison: first two hidden layers pn=256, last pn=512. X9M: sample k thinned nets per test; k→∞ → true average; §7.5 reports ~k=50 to match T6R. A2F (SVHN): validation composition 400/class from standard (two-thirds) + 200/class from additional (one-third) → total 6000 validation samples. Preproc: RGB pixels normalized to zero mean/unit variance; ZCA/contrast norm gave no noticeable improvement. Architecture: 3 conv layers (filters 96,128,256), receptive field 5x5, stride=1; max-pooling after each conv (3x3 region, stride 2). Followed by 2 fully-connected hidden layers with 2048 units each. All hidden activations F3N. Retention (input through conv and FC) p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5) (interpretable as input, conv1, conv2, conv3, fc1, fc2). V9C bound c=4 (all weights). Momentum=0.95.

Resources: code http://www.cs.toronto.edu/~nitish/dropout; GPU libs cudamat, cuda-convnet.
H4Z (MNIST): held-out val=10,000; final weight-update endpoint (tuning & combined-data)=1,000,000 updates. Arch sweep depths {2,3,4} x widths {1024,2048}. Hidden retention p=0.5, input p=0.8. Momentum=0.95. V9C max-norm c=2 (H4Z). Reg-limit exps: 4096 & 8192 units; largest 2-layer >65M params. Regularizer-comparison/data-size arch: 784-1024-1024-2048-10. Data-size training sets {100,500,1k,5k,10k,50k}.
A2F (SVHN): val composition 6000 (400/class standard +200/class additional). Preproc: RGB mean/variance normalize; ZCA/contrast norm tried but gave no noticeable improvement. Arch: 3 conv layers (96,128,256 filters), RF=5x5 stride=1; max-pool after each (3x3 stride=2); then 2 FC layers 2048 units; activations F3N. Retention p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5). V9C c=4 (A2F). Momentum=0.95. Hyperparams tuned on val; A2F kept validation separate during final training; model with smallest val error used for reported test error.
J3V & W6R (images): use held-out val, contrast normalization and ZCA whitening with A2F architecture/retentions. Each: 50k train, 10k test (J3V:10 classes, W6R:100). Val used 5,000 training images. After tuning validation+training were recombined for final optimization (as in H4Z). Contrast-norm = subtract per-channel mean; then ZCA (center, rotate, scale, rotate back). Input-layer LRs need to be smaller.
N8Q (speech): 680 speakers, 8 dialects, 10 sentences each; features: Kaldi log-filter banks; 21-frame window. Table settings: input p=0.8, hidden p=0.5, V9C c=4, momentum=0.95, high LR=0.1, LR decay ε0(1+t/T)^{-1}; pretrain U2L with CD-1, Gaussian input-unit var=1; best finetune LR ~0.01. V9C during finetune gave no improvement. Table 7 reports phone errors (19.7 for both QX2 depths).
M5X (documents): Reuters subset 402,738 articles, 2000-word vocab, 50 classes, single-label. Equal train/test splits → >200,000 train examples.
Z7P (genetics): 3,665 cassette exons, 1,014 RNA features, 4 tissue types. Four softmax outputs (one per tissue), each with 3 states {inc,exc,nc}. C4Y score: Σ_i Σ_t Σ_s p_{i,t}^s log(q_t^s(r_i)/ p̄^s) with p̄^s average over i,t. QX2 scale ~1000s; trained QX2: 2 layers x 1024 units; input p=0.7, hidden p=0.5; V9C reg; 5-fold averaging as Xiong et al. (2011).
